The Frog-King, or Iron Henry

In the old days, when wishing still worked, there lived a king whose daughters were all beautiful — but the youngest was so beautiful that the sun itself, which has seen so much, was astonished every time it shone on her face. Close by the King's castle lay a great dark forest, and in the forest, under an old lime tree, there was a well. When the day was very hot the King's child would go out into the forest and sit down at the edge of the cool water; and when she was bored she would take a golden ball and throw it up in the air and catch it, and this ball was her favourite plaything.

Now one day it happened that the princess's golden ball did not fall into the little hand she was holding up for it, but past it onto the ground, and rolled straight into the water. The King's daughter followed it with her eyes, but it was gone, and the well was deep — so deep that you could not see the bottom. At that she began to cry, and cried louder and louder, and could not be comforted.

And while she was crying like this, somebody said to her, "What is the matter, princess? You are crying so hard that even a stone would feel sorry for you."

She looked round to see where the voice came from, and saw a frog poking its thick ugly head out of the water.

"Oh, it's you, is it, you old water-splasher?" she said. "I am crying for my golden ball, which has fallen into the well."

"Be quiet and stop crying," answered the frog. "I can help you. But what will you give me if I fetch your plaything up again?"

"Whatever you like, dear frog," she said. "My clothes, my pearls and jewels, even the golden crown I am wearing."

The frog answered, "I don't want your clothes, or your pearls and jewels, or your golden crown. But if you will love me and let me be your companion and playmate, and sit beside you at your little table, and eat off your little golden plate, and drink out of your little cup, and sleep in your little bed — if you will promise me that, I will go down and bring your golden ball up again."

"Oh yes," she said, "I promise you anything you like, if only you will bring me my ball back." But what she thought was: "What nonsense the silly frog talks! He lives in the water with the other frogs and croaks, and he can't be any sort of companion to a human being."

But the frog, once he had her promise, put his head under the water and sank down; and in a little while he came swimming up again with the ball in his mouth, and threw it out onto the grass. The King's daughter was delighted to see her pretty plaything again, and picked it up and ran off with it.

"Wait, wait!" called the frog. "Take me with you. I can't run the way you can." But what good did it do him to shout his croak, croak after her as loudly as he could? She did not listen. She ran home and soon forgot the poor frog, who had to go back down into his well.

The next day, when she had sat down at table with the King and all the court, and was eating off her little golden plate, something came creeping splish splash, splish splash up the marble staircase; and when it got to the top it knocked at the door and called, "Princess, youngest princess, open the door for me."

She ran to see who was outside; but when she opened the door, there sat the frog in front of it. She slammed the door shut in a great hurry, sat down at the table again, and was thoroughly frightened. The King could see plainly that her heart was thumping, and said, "My child, what are you so afraid of? Is there a giant outside who wants to carry you off?"

"Oh, no," she answered. "It isn't a giant, it's a disgusting frog."

"What does a frog want with you?"

"Oh, father dear, yesterday when I was in the forest sitting by the well, playing, my golden ball fell into the water. And because I cried so much, the frog fetched it out for me; and because he insisted on it, I promised he could be my companion — but I never thought he would be able to come up out of his water. And now he is outside and wants to come in to me."

Just then it knocked a second time, and called:

	"Princess, youngest princess,
	open the door for me!
	Have you forgotten what you promised
	yesterday, by the cool well water?
	Princess, youngest princess,
	open the door for me!"

Then the King said, "What you have promised, you must keep. Go and let him in."

She went and opened the door, and the frog hopped in and followed her, step by step, to her chair. There he sat and called, "Lift me up beside you." She hung back, until at last the King ordered her to do it. Once the frog was on the chair he wanted to be on the table, and once he was on the table he said, "Now push your little golden plate closer, so that we can eat together." She did it, but anybody could see she did not do it willingly. The frog thoroughly enjoyed his dinner, but almost every mouthful stuck in her throat.

At last he said, "I have eaten enough and I am full. Now I am tired — carry me up to your little room and get your little silk bed ready, and we will both lie down and go to sleep."

The King's daughter began to cry, because she was frightened of the cold frog that she did not even like to touch, and that was now to sleep in her pretty clean little bed. But the King grew angry and said, "The one who helped you when you were in trouble is not to be despised afterwards."

So she picked the frog up with two fingers, carried him upstairs and put him down in a corner. But when she was in bed he came creeping over to her and said, "I am tired. I want to sleep as much as you do. Lift me up, or I'll tell your father."

At that she lost her temper completely, picked him up and threw him with all her strength against the wall. "Now you'll be quiet, you horrible frog!"

But when he fell down he was no frog. He was a king's son with beautiful, kind eyes. And by her father's will he was now her dear companion and her husband. He told her how he had been put under a spell by a wicked witch, and how nobody in the world could have got him out of that well but her, and that tomorrow they would go together to his kingdom.

Then they went to sleep; and next morning, when the sun woke them, a carriage came driving up with eight white horses, with white ostrich feathers on their heads and harness of golden chains; and standing behind it was the young King's servant, Faithful Henry. Faithful Henry had been so unhappy when his master was turned into a frog that he had had three iron bands fastened round his heart to stop it bursting with grief.

The carriage was to take the young King home to his kingdom. Faithful Henry helped the two of them in and took his place behind again, and he was full of joy that his master was free.

When they had gone part of the way, the King's son heard a cracking behind him, as if something had broken. So he turned round and called, "Henry, the carriage is breaking!"

"No, master, it isn't the carriage. It is a band from around my heart, which was put there when I was in such pain, when you were a frog and shut up in that well."

Again, and once again, something cracked while they were on their way, and each time the King's son thought the carriage was breaking. But it was only the bands springing off the heart of faithful Henry, because his master was free and happy.

Cat and Mouse in Partnership

A certain cat got to know a mouse, and talked to her so much about the great love and friendship she felt for her that in the end the mouse agreed that they should live together and keep house.

"But we must lay in something for the winter, or we shall go hungry," said the cat. "And you, little mouse, can't go venturing everywhere — you'll get caught in a trap one of these days."

The good advice was taken, and they bought a pot of fat; but they did not know where to put it. At last, after a great deal of thought, the cat said, "I don't know anywhere it would be better stored than in the church, for nobody dares to take anything from there. We'll set it under the altar and not touch it until we really need it."

So the pot was put in a safe place. But it was not long before the cat began to have a great longing for it, and said to the mouse, "I want to tell you something, little mouse. My cousin has brought a little son into the world and has asked me to be godmother. He's white with brown spots, and I'm to hold him over the font at the christening. Let me go out today, and you look after the house on your own."

"Yes, yes," said the mouse, "off you go by all means; and if you get anything really good, think of me — I'd like a drop of the sweet red christening wine myself."

But none of it was true. The cat had no cousin and had not been asked to be anybody's godmother. She went straight to the church, crept to the pot of fat, and began to lick, and licked the top of the fat off. Then she took a stroll over the roofs of the town, looked out for opportunities, stretched herself in the sun, and licked her lips every time she thought of that pot of fat; and it was evening before she came home.

"Well, here you are again," said the mouse. "I'm sure you've had a lovely day."

"It all went off very well," said the cat.

"What name did they give the child?"

"Top-off," said the cat, quite coolly.

"Top-off!" cried the mouse. "What a very odd, uncommon name. Is it usual in your family?"

"What does it matter?" said the cat. "It's no worse than Crumb-stealer, which is what your godchildren are called."

Before long the cat was seized by another fit of longing. She said to the mouse, "You must do me a favour and manage the house alone for a day again. I have been asked to be godmother a second time, and since the child has a white ring round its neck, I can't refuse."

The good mouse agreed; but the cat slipped along behind the town walls to the church and ate half the pot of fat. "Nothing ever tastes as good as what you keep to yourself," she said, and was thoroughly satisfied with her day's work.

When she came home the mouse asked, "And what was this child christened?"

"Half-gone," answered the cat.

"Half-gone! What are you talking about? I never heard the name in my life. I'll wager anything it isn't in the calendar."

Soon the cat's mouth began to water for more licking. "Good things come in threes," she said. "I've been asked to stand godmother again. The child is completely black, only it has white paws; apart from that there isn't a single white hair on its whole body. That only happens once in a few years. You'll let me go, won't you?"

"Top-off! Half-gone!" said the mouse. "Such odd names — they set me thinking."

"That's because you sit at home," said the cat, "in your dark grey fur coat and your long tail, getting full of fancies. It comes of never going out in the daytime."

While the cat was away the mouse cleaned the house and put it in order. And the greedy cat emptied the pot of fat completely. "Once everything's eaten up, you get some peace," she said to herself; and, well filled and fat, she did not come home till night.

The mouse asked at once what name the third child had been given.

"It won't please you any better than the others," said the cat. "He's called All-gone."

"All-gone!" cried the mouse. "That's the most suspicious name of the lot. I've never seen it in print. All-gone — what can it mean?" And she shook her head, curled herself up, and went to sleep.

After that nobody invited the cat to be godmother any more. But when the winter came and there was nothing to be found outside, the mouse remembered their store and said, "Come along, cat, let's go to our pot of fat that we saved up. We shall enjoy that."

"Yes," said the cat, "you'll enjoy it about as much as you'd enjoy sticking that dainty tongue of yours out of the window."

They set off; and when they got there, the pot of fat was certainly still in its place — but it was empty.

"Oh!" said the mouse. "Now I see what has happened. Now it all comes out. Some friend you are! You ate the whole lot while you were standing godmother. First top off, then half gone, then —"

"Will you hold your tongue!" cried the cat. "One more word and I'll eat you too."

"All gone" was already on the poor mouse's lips. She had barely said it before the cat sprang, caught her, and swallowed her down.

And that is the way of the world.

Our Lady’s Child

At the edge of a great forest there lived a woodcutter and his wife, who had one child, a little girl three years old. They were so poor, though, that they no longer had their daily bread and did not know how to find food for her.

One morning the woodcutter went out to his work in the forest full of care; and while he was cutting wood, suddenly there stood in front of him a tall and beautiful woman with a crown of shining stars on her head, who said, "I am the Virgin Mary, the mother of the child Jesus. You are poor and in need. Bring me your child; I will take her with me and be her mother and care for her."

The woodcutter did as he was told, brought his child and gave her to the Virgin Mary, who took her up to heaven. There the child did well: she ate sugar cakes and drank sweet milk, her clothes were of gold, and the little angels played with her.

And when she was fourteen years old, the Virgin Mary called her one day and said, "Dear child, I am going on a long journey. Take the keys of the thirteen doors of heaven into your keeping. Twelve of them you may open, and see the glory inside; but the thirteenth, which this little key belongs to, is forbidden you. Take care not to open it, or you will bring misery on yourself."

The girl promised to obey; and when the Virgin Mary was gone she began to look through the dwellings of the kingdom of heaven. Every day she opened one of them, until she had been through all twelve. In each of them one of the Apostles sat in the middle of a great light, and she delighted in all the magnificence and splendour, and the little angels who always went with her delighted in it too.

Then only the forbidden door was left, and she felt a great longing to know what could be hidden behind it, and said to the angels, "I won't open it right up, and I won't go inside — I'll only unlock it so that we can see a little through the crack."

"Oh no," said the little angels, "that would be a sin. The Virgin Mary has forbidden it, and it could very easily be the ruin of you."

Then she said nothing more; but the longing in her heart was not quieted. It gnawed at her and tormented her and gave her no peace. And once, when the angels had all gone out, she thought, "Now I am quite alone, and I could peep in. If I do it, nobody will ever know."

She hunted out the key; and when she had it in her hand she put it in the lock, and when she had put it in, she turned it. Then the door sprang open, and there she saw the Trinity sitting in fire and splendour. She stood a while and looked at it all in amazement; then she touched the light with her finger, just a little, and her finger turned entirely to gold.

Immediately a great fear came over her. She slammed the door and ran away. And her terror would not leave her, whatever she did; her heart beat and beat and would not be still, and the gold stayed on her finger and would not come off, however much she rubbed it and washed it.

It was not long before the Virgin Mary came back from her journey. She called the girl to her and asked for the keys of heaven. When the girl handed her the bunch, the Virgin looked into her eyes and said, "Did you not open the thirteenth door as well?"

"No," she answered.

Then the Virgin laid her hand on the girl's heart and felt how it beat and beat, and saw perfectly well that she had disobeyed and had opened the door. So she said again, "Are you certain you did not do it?"

"Yes," said the girl, a second time.

Then the Virgin noticed the finger that had turned to gold from touching the fire of heaven, and saw plainly that the child had sinned, and said a third time, "Did you not do it?"

"No," said the girl, for the third time.

Then the Virgin Mary said, "You have not obeyed me, and on top of that you have lied. You are not fit to be in heaven any longer."

Then the girl fell into a deep sleep; and when she woke she was lying on the earth below, in the middle of a wilderness. She wanted to call out, but she could not make a sound. She jumped up and tried to run away, but whichever way she turned she was held back by thick hedges of thorns that she could not break through.

In the wilderness where she was shut in there stood an old hollow tree, and this had to be her home. She crept into it when night came, and slept there; and there she found shelter from storm and rain. But it was a miserable life, and she wept bitterly when she remembered how happy she had been in heaven and how the angels had played with her.

Roots and wild berries were all she had to eat, and she went as far as she could to look for them. In the autumn she gathered up the fallen nuts and leaves and carried them into her hollow. The nuts were her food in winter; and when the snow and ice came she crept in among the leaves like a poor little animal, so as not to freeze. Before long her clothes were all torn and fell off her, one piece after another. But as soon as the sun shone warm again she went out and sat in front of the tree, and her long hair covered her on every side like a cloak. And so she sat, year after year, and felt the pain and misery of the world.

One day, when the trees were freshly green again, the King of that country was hunting in the forest and chasing a deer; and as it had fled into the thicket that closed off this part of the forest, he got down from his horse, tore the bushes apart and cut himself a path with his sword. When at last he had forced his way through, he saw a wonderfully beautiful girl sitting under the tree, covered from head to foot in her own golden hair.

He stood still and looked at her, full of astonishment; then he spoke to her and said, "Who are you? Why are you sitting here in the wilderness?"

But she gave him no answer, because she could not open her mouth.

The King went on, "Will you come with me to my castle?"

At that she just nodded her head a little. The King took her up in his arms, carried her to his horse and rode home with her; and when he came to the royal castle he had her dressed in beautiful clothes and gave her everything in abundance. And although she could not speak, she was so beautiful and so charming that he began to love her with his whole heart, and it was not long before he married her.

When a year or so had gone by, the Queen brought a son into the world. And that night, as she lay in her bed alone, the Virgin Mary appeared to her and said, "If you will tell the truth and admit that you unlocked the forbidden door, I will open your mouth and give you back your speech. But if you go on in your sin and stubbornly deny it, I will take your new-born child away with me."

Then the Queen was allowed to answer; but she stayed hard, and said, "No, I did not open the forbidden door." And the Virgin Mary took the new-born child out of her arms and vanished with it.

Next morning, when the child was nowhere to be found, it was whispered among the people that the Queen was an eater of human flesh and had killed her own child. She heard it all and could say nothing against it; but the King would not believe it, because he loved her so much.

When a year had gone by the Queen bore another son, and in the night the Virgin Mary came to her again and said, "If you will admit that you opened the forbidden door, I will give you your child back and untie your tongue. But if you go on in your sin and deny it, I will take this new child too."

Then the Queen said again, "No, I did not open the forbidden door." And the Virgin took the child out of her arms and away with her to heaven.

Next morning, when this child had disappeared as well, the people said out loud that the Queen had devoured it, and the King's councillors demanded that she be brought to trial. But the King loved her so dearly that he would not believe it, and ordered the councillors, on pain of death, to say no more about it.

The following year the Queen gave birth to a beautiful little daughter; and for the third time the Virgin Mary appeared to her in the night and said, "Follow me."

She took the Queen by the hand and led her to heaven, and showed her there her two eldest children, who smiled at her and were playing with the ball of the world. When the Queen was gladdened by the sight, the Virgin Mary said, "Is your heart not softened yet? If you will own that you opened the forbidden door, I will give you back your two little sons."

But for the third time the Queen answered, "No, I did not open the forbidden door."

Then the Virgin let her sink down to earth again, and took her third child from her as well.

Next morning, when the loss was reported, all the people cried out, "The Queen is an eater of human flesh! She must be judged." And this time the King could not hold his councillors back. So a trial was held; and since she could not answer and could not defend herself, she was condemned to be burned alive.

The wood was piled up; and when she was tied fast to the stake and the fire began to burn around her, the hard ice of her pride melted, her heart was moved to repentance, and she thought, "If only I could confess before I die that I opened that door."

Then her voice came back to her, and she cried out loudly, "Yes, Mary, I did it!"

And at once rain fell from the sky and put out the flames, and a light broke out above her, and the Virgin Mary came down with the two little sons at her side and the new-born daughter in her arms. She spoke kindly to her and said, "Whoever repents of a sin and admits it is forgiven." Then she gave her the three children, untied her tongue, and granted her happiness for the whole of her life.

The Story of the Youth Who Went Forth to Learn What Fear Was

A certain father had two sons. The elder was sharp and sensible and could do anything, but the younger was slow and could neither learn nor understand a thing; and when people saw him they said, "There's a lad who'll give his father some trouble."

Whenever there was something to be done, it was always the elder who had to do it. But if his father sent him to fetch something late in the evening, or at night, and the way led past the churchyard or any other gloomy place, he would say, "Oh no, father, I'm not going there — it gives me the shudders." Because he was afraid.

Or in the evening, when stories were told by the fire that made your flesh creep, the listeners would sometimes say, "Oh, that gives me the shudders!" The younger boy sat in his corner and listened with the rest, and could not imagine what they meant. "They're always saying it gives them the shudders, it gives them the shudders. It doesn't give me the shudders," he thought. "That must be another one of these skills I know nothing about."

Now one day his father said to him, "Listen to me, you there in the corner. You're growing tall and strong, and it's time you learned something to earn your living by. Look how your brother works — you don't even earn your salt."

"Well, father," he answered, "I'm quite willing to learn something. In fact, if it could be managed, I'd like to learn how to shudder. I don't understand that at all yet."

The elder brother laughed when he heard it, and thought to himself, "Good God, what a blockhead my brother is. He'll never be any good as long as he lives. If you're going to be a sickle, you have to start bending early."

The father sighed and answered, "You'll soon enough learn what it is to shudder, but you won't earn your bread by it."

Soon afterwards the sexton came to the house on a visit, and the father poured out his troubles and told him how backward his younger son was in every way — he knew nothing and learned nothing. "Just think," he said, "when I asked him how he was going to earn his bread, he actually said he wanted to learn how to shudder."

"If that's all," said the sexton, "he can learn that with me. Send him over and I'll soon polish him up."

The father was glad to agree, because he thought, "It will lick the boy into shape a little." So the sexton took him into his house, and his job was to ring the bell.

After a day or two the sexton woke him at midnight and told him to get up and go to the church tower and ring the bell. "You'll soon find out what shuddering is," he thought; and he went up secretly ahead of him. And when the boy was at the top of the tower and turned round and was just reaching for the bell rope, he saw a white figure standing on the stairs opposite the sound hole.

"Who's there?" he called. But the figure gave no answer and did not move or stir.

"Answer me," called the boy, "or clear off. You've no business here at night."

But the sexton stood there without moving, so that the boy would take him for a ghost. The boy called a second time: "What do you want here? Speak up, if you're an honest man, or I'll throw you down the steps."

The sexton thought, "He can't really mean it," and made no sound and stood as if he were made of stone. So the boy called out to him a third time; and when that did no good either, he ran at him and pushed the ghost down the stairs, so that it fell ten steps and lay there in a corner.

Then he rang the bell, went home, got into bed without a word and fell asleep.

The sexton's wife waited a long time for her husband, but he did not come back. At last she grew uneasy, woke the boy, and asked, "Do you know where my husband is? He climbed up the tower before you did."

"No, I don't," said the boy. "But there was somebody standing by the sound hole on the other side of the steps, and as he wouldn't answer and wouldn't go away, I took him for a scoundrel and threw him down the stairs. Go and see whether it was him. I should be sorry if it was."

The woman ran off and found her husband lying in the corner, groaning, with a broken leg.

She carried him down, and then, screaming at the top of her voice, she rushed to the boy's father. "That boy of yours," she cried, "has caused a great misfortune! He threw my husband down the steps and broke his leg. Take the good-for-nothing out of our house."

The father was horrified. He ran over and scolded the boy. "What wicked tricks are these? The devil himself must have put it into your head."

"Father," he answered, "do listen to me. I am completely innocent. He was standing there in the night like a man who means some harm. I didn't know who it was, and I begged him three times to speak or go away."

"Ah," said the father, "you bring me nothing but misery. Get out of my sight. I don't want to see you again."

"Gladly, father — only wait till daylight. Then I'll go out and learn how to shudder, and at least I'll have one skill to keep me."

"Learn what you like," said the father. "It's all the same to me. Here are fifty thalers. Take them and go out into the wide world, and tell nobody where you come from or who your father is, because I've reason to be ashamed of you."

"Yes, father, just as you wish. If that's all you want of me, it's easy enough to remember."

So when the day dawned the boy put his fifty thalers in his pocket and set off along the highway, saying to himself over and over, "If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!"

Then a man came up who heard him talking to himself; and when they had walked a little further, to where they could see the gallows, the man said, "Look, there's the tree where seven men have married the ropemaker's daughter and are now learning to fly. Sit down underneath it and wait till night comes, and you'll soon learn how to shudder."

"If that's all it takes," said the boy, "it's easily done. And if I learn to shudder as fast as that, you shall have my fifty thalers. Just come back to me first thing in the morning."

So the boy went to the gallows, sat down underneath and waited for evening. And as he was cold he lit himself a fire; but at midnight the wind blew so sharply that even with his fire he could not get warm. And when the wind knocked the hanged men against one another so that they swung backwards and forwards, he thought, "Here am I shivering by the fire — how those poor fellows up there must be freezing."

And because he felt sorry for them, he set up the ladder, climbed up, untied them one after another and brought all seven down. Then he stirred the fire and blew it up and sat them round it to warm themselves. But they sat there without moving, and the fire caught their clothes.

So he said, "Careful, or I'll hang you up again." But the dead men did not hear, and stayed silent, and let their rags go on burning.

At that he grew angry and said, "If you won't take care, I can't help you — and I'm not going to be burnt along with you." And he hung them all up again, one by one. Then he sat down by his fire and fell asleep.

Next morning the man came for his fifty thalers and said, "Well, do you know what it is to shudder now?"

"No," he said. "How was I supposed to find out? Those fellows up there never opened their mouths, and they were so stupid they let the few old rags they had on their bodies get burnt."

Then the man saw he was not going to get the fifty thalers that day, and went off saying, "I never met anybody like that before."

The boy went on his way too, and began muttering to himself again, "Ah, if only I could shudder! Ah, if only I could shudder!"

A carter walking behind him heard it and asked, "Who are you?"

"I don't know."

"Where do you come from?"

"I don't know."

"Who is your father?"

"That I mustn't tell you."

"What is it you keep muttering through your teeth?"

"Ah," said the boy, "I do so wish I could shudder, and nobody can teach me how."

"Give up that foolish talk," said the carter. "Come along with me and I'll see about finding you a place."

So the boy went with the carter, and in the evening they came to an inn where they meant to spend the night. And at the door of the room the boy said again, quite loudly, "If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!"

The landlord heard him and laughed and said, "If that's what you want, there should be a good opportunity for you here."

"Oh, be quiet," said the landlady. "Too many inquisitive people have lost their lives already. It would be a pity and a shame if such fine eyes as those never saw daylight again."

But the boy said, "However hard it may be, I mean to learn it. That's what I came out for."

He gave the landlord no peace until the man told him that not far off there stood a haunted castle, where anybody could easily enough learn what shuddering was, if he would only keep watch in it for three nights. The King had promised that whoever dared to do it should have his daughter for a wife, and she was the most beautiful girl the sun ever shone on. There were great treasures in the castle too, guarded by evil spirits, and those treasures would then be set free and would make a poor man rich. Plenty of men had gone into the castle, but not one had ever come out again.

So next morning the boy went to the King and said that, if he were allowed, he would keep watch three nights in the haunted castle. The King looked him over, and as he liked the look of him, he said, "You may ask for three things to take into the castle with you, but they must be things that have no life in them."

He answered, "Then I ask for a fire, a wood-turner's lathe, and a cutting-board with the knife."

The King had these things carried into the castle for him during the day.

When night was drawing on, the boy went up, made himself a good bright fire in one of the rooms, set the cutting-board and knife beside it, and sat down by the lathe. "Ah, if only I could shudder," he said. "But I shan't learn it here either."

Towards midnight he was about to poke up his fire; and as he was blowing at it, something suddenly cried out from a corner, "Ow, miaow! How cold we are!"

"You fools," he called, "what are you howling about? If you're cold, come and sit by the fire and warm yourselves."

And when he had said it, two great black cats came with one tremendous leap and sat down on either side of him, staring at him savagely with their fiery eyes. After a while, when they had warmed themselves, they said, "Friend, shall we have a game of cards?"

"Why not?" he said. "But show me your paws first."

So they stretched out their claws.

"Well!" he said. "What long nails you have. Wait, I'll have to cut them for you first."

With that he took them by the throat, laid them on the cutting-board and screwed their feet down fast. "I've had a look at your fingers," he said, "and I've gone off the idea of card-playing." And he struck them dead and threw them out into the water.

But when he had got rid of those two and was about to sit down by his fire again, out of every hole and corner came black cats and black dogs with red-hot chains, more and more of them, until he could not move; and they howled horribly, and got on his fire and pulled it apart and tried to put it out.

He watched them quietly for a while; but at last, when they went too far, he took hold of his cutting-knife and cried, "Away with you, vermin!" and set about cutting them down. Some of them ran off, the rest he killed and threw out into the fish-pond.

When he came back he fanned the embers of his fire up again and warmed himself. And as he sat there his eyes would not stay open any longer, and he felt like sleeping. So he looked round and saw a great bed in the corner. "That's just the thing for me," he said, and got into it.

But just as he was going to shut his eyes, the bed began to move by itself and went all over the castle. "That's the way," he said. "Only go faster."

Then the bed rolled on as if six horses were harnessed to it, up and down, over thresholds and stairs — and then suddenly, hop, hop, it turned upside down and lay on top of him like a mountain. But he threw the quilts and pillows up in the air, climbed out and said, "Now anybody who likes can drive"; and he lay down by his fire and slept till daylight.

In the morning the King came; and when he saw him lying there on the floor, he thought the evil spirits had killed him and he was dead. So he said, "It's a pity, after all — he was a fine-looking man."

The boy heard it, sat up and said, "It hasn't come to that yet."

The King was astonished, but very glad, and asked how he had got on.

"Very well indeed," he said. "One night's over, and I'll get through the other two as well."

Then he went to the innkeeper, who opened his eyes very wide and said, "I never expected to see you alive again. Have you learnt to shudder yet?"

"No," he said. "It's all no use. If only somebody would tell me how."

The second night he went up into the old castle again, sat down by the fire and began his old song once more: "If only I could shudder."

When midnight came there was an uproar and a noise of tumbling about; faint at first, then louder and louder. Then it was quiet for a while, and at last, with a loud scream, half a man came down the chimney and fell in front of him.

"Hey!" he called. "There's another half belongs to this. This isn't enough."

Then the uproar began again, with roaring and howling, and the other half fell down too.

"Wait," he said, "I'll blow the fire up a bit for you first."

And when he had done that and looked round again, the two pieces had joined together and a frightful man was sitting in his place.

"That wasn't the bargain," said the boy. "That bench is mine."

The man tried to push him away, but the boy would not have it, shoved him off with all his strength and sat down in his own place again.

Then more men came falling down, one after another; they fetched nine dead men's leg-bones and two skulls, set them up and played skittles with them. The boy wanted to play too, and said, "Here — can I join in?"

"Yes, if you have any money."

"Money enough," he said, "but your balls aren't quite round."

So he took the skulls, put them in the lathe and turned them till they were round. "There — now they'll roll better," he said. "Hurrah! Now it's going nicely."

He played with them and lost some of his money; but when the clock struck twelve, everything vanished before his eyes. He lay down and quietly went to sleep.

Next morning the King came to ask after him. "How did you get on this time?"

"I've been playing skittles," he answered, "and I lost a couple of farthings."

"And you didn't shudder?"

"What, me?" he said. "I had a very good time. If only I knew what it was to shudder!"

The third night he sat down on his bench again and said, quite miserably, "If only I could shudder."

When it grew late, six tall men came in carrying a coffin. So he said, "Aha — that will be my little cousin, who died only a few days ago," and he beckoned with his finger and called, "Come along, little cousin, come along."

They set the coffin down on the ground and he went over and took the lid off; and there lay a dead man inside. He felt his face, and it was as cold as ice.

"Wait," he said, "I'll warm you a little." And he went to the fire, warmed his own hand and laid it on the dead man's face; but he stayed cold. So he lifted him out, sat down by the fire with him, laid him against his chest and rubbed his arms to get the blood moving again. When that did no good either, he thought, "When two people lie in bed together they keep each other warm"; and he carried him to the bed, covered him up and lay down beside him.

After a while the dead man grew warm too, and began to move.

Then the boy said, "There, little cousin — didn't I warm you?"

But the dead man got up and cried, "Now I am going to strangle you."

"What!" said he. "Is that how you thank me? Back into your coffin with you." And he picked him up, threw him in and shut the lid. Then the six men came and carried him away again.

"I can't manage to shudder," he said. "I shall never learn it here as long as I live."

Then a man came in who was taller than all the others and looked terrible. But he was old, and had a long white beard.

"You wretch," he cried, "you'll soon learn what it is to shudder, because you are going to die."

"Not so fast," said the boy. "If I'm to die, I'll have some say in it."

"I'll soon have hold of you," said the fiend.

"Gently, gently, don't talk so big. I'm as strong as you are — stronger, perhaps."

"We'll see about that," said the old man. "If you're stronger, I'll let you go. Come, we'll try."

Then he led him through dark passages to a smith's forge, took an axe and with one blow drove an anvil into the ground.

"I can do better than that," said the boy, and went to the other anvil. The old man stood close by to watch, with his white beard hanging down. Then the boy took hold of the axe, split the anvil at one blow, and wedged the old man's beard into the split.

"Now I have you," said the boy. "Now it's your turn to die."

And he took an iron bar and beat the old man until he groaned and begged him to stop, and promised him great riches. The boy pulled out the axe and let him go.

The old man led him back into the castle and showed him three chests full of gold in a cellar. "One share of this is for the poor," he said, "one for the King, and the third is yours."

Just then it struck twelve and the spirit vanished, leaving the boy in the dark. "I'll find my way out all the same," he said; and he felt about, found his way back to the room, and slept there by his fire.

Next morning the King came and said, "Now you must have learnt what shuddering is."

"No," he said. "What can it be? My dead cousin was here, and a bearded man came and showed me a great deal of money down below, but nobody told me what it is to shudder."

"Well," said the King, "you have set the castle free, and you shall marry my daughter."

"That's all very fine," he said, "but I still don't know what it is to shudder."

Then the gold was brought up and the wedding was celebrated; but however much the young king loved his wife, and however happy he was, he still kept saying, "If only I could shudder — if only I could shudder."

And at last she grew annoyed with it. Her waiting-maid said, "I'll find a cure for him. He shall soon learn what it is to shudder."

She went out to the stream that ran through the garden and had a whole bucketful of little fish brought to her. At night, when the young king was asleep, his wife was to pull the covers off him and empty the bucket of cold water and fish all over him, so that the little fish would go flapping about him.

And when it was done he woke up and cried, "Oh, what is making me shudder so? What is making me shudder so, dear wife? Ah — now I know what it is to shudder!"

The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids

Once upon a time there was an old goat who had seven little kids, and she loved them with all the love a mother has for her children.

One day she wanted to go into the forest and fetch some food, so she called all seven to her and said, "Dear children, I have to go into the forest. Be on your guard against the wolf. If he gets in, he will eat every one of you — skin, hair and all. The wretch often disguises himself, but you will know him at once by his rough voice and his black feet."

The kids said, "Dear mother, we will take good care of ourselves. You can go without worrying." So the old one bleated and set off with an easy mind.

It was not long before somebody knocked at the door and called, "Open the door, dear children. Your mother is here, and she has brought something back for each of you."

But the little kids knew from the rough voice that it was the wolf. "We won't open the door," they cried. "You are not our mother. She has a soft, gentle voice, and your voice is rough. You are the wolf."

So the wolf went off to a shopkeeper and bought himself a great lump of chalk, and ate it, and it made his voice soft. Then he came back, knocked at the door of the house and called, "Open the door, dear children. Your mother is here, and she has brought something back for each of you."

But the wolf had laid his black paws on the window sill, and the children saw them and cried, "We won't open the door. Our mother hasn't got black feet like yours. You are the wolf."

So the wolf ran to a baker and said, "I've hurt my feet — rub some dough over them for me." And when the baker had done it, he ran to the miller and said, "Sprinkle some white flour on my feet for me."

The miller thought to himself, "The wolf means to deceive somebody," and refused; but the wolf said, "If you won't do it, I'll eat you." So the miller was frightened, and whitened his paws for him. That is what people are like.

So now the wretch went to the door for the third time, knocked and said, "Open the door for me, children. Your dear little mother has come home, and she has brought something back from the forest for every one of you."

The little kids called out, "Show us your paws first, so that we can be sure you are our dear little mother." So he put his paws in at the window; and when the kids saw that they were white, they believed everything he said and opened the door.

And in walked the wolf.

They were terrified and tried to hide. One sprang under the table, the second into the bed, the third into the stove, the fourth into the kitchen, the fifth into the cupboard, the sixth under the washing-bowl, and the seventh into the clock-case. But the wolf found them all and did not stand on ceremony: one after another he swallowed them down. The only one he did not find was the youngest, in the clock-case.

When the wolf had eaten his fill he took himself off, lay down under a tree in the green meadow outside, and went to sleep.

Soon afterwards the old goat came home from the forest. Oh, what a sight met her there! The door stood wide open; the table, the chairs and the benches were thrown over, the washing-bowl lay in pieces, and the quilts and pillows had been dragged off the bed. She looked for her children, but they were nowhere to be found. She called them by name, one after another, and nobody answered. At last, when she came to the youngest, a small voice cried, "Dear mother, I am in the clock-case."

She got the kid out, and it told her how the wolf had come and eaten all the others. You can imagine how she wept over her poor children.

At last, in her grief, she went outside, and the youngest kid ran with her. When they came to the meadow, there lay the wolf under the tree, snoring so loudly that the branches shook. She looked him over from every side, and saw that something was moving and struggling inside his stuffed belly.

"Good heavens," she said, "can it be that my poor children, that he swallowed down for his supper, are still alive?"

So the kid had to run home and fetch scissors and a needle and thread; and the goat cut open the monster's stomach. She had hardly made one cut before a little kid stuck its head out; and as she cut further, all six sprang out one after another, and every one of them was still alive and had come to no harm at all, because in his greed the monster had swallowed them down whole.

What rejoicing there was! They hugged their dear mother and jumped about like a tailor at his wedding.

But their mother said, "Now go and find some big stones, and we'll fill the wicked beast's stomach with them while he is still asleep."

So the seven kids dragged the stones over as fast as they could and put as many into his stomach as would go in; and their mother sewed him up again in the greatest hurry, so that he noticed nothing and never so much as stirred.

When the wolf had finally had his sleep out, he got to his feet; and because the stones in his stomach made him very thirsty, he wanted to go to a well and drink. But when he began to walk and move about, the stones knocked against each other and rattled. And he cried:

	"What rumbles and tumbles
	about in my bones?
	I thought it was six kids,
	and it's nothing but stones."

And when he got to the well and leaned over the water and was just about to drink, the heavy stones pulled him in, and there was no help for it — he drowned miserably.

When the seven kids saw it they came running up, calling out, "The wolf is dead! The wolf is dead!" and danced for joy round the well with their mother.

Faithful John

Once upon a time there was an old king who was ill, and he thought to himself, "I am lying on what must be my deathbed."

Then he said, "Send Faithful John to me." Faithful John was his favourite servant, and he was called that because he had been true to him all his life long.

So when he came to the bedside, the King said to him, "My most faithful John, I feel my end coming, and I have no anxiety about anything except my son. He is still young and cannot always know how to manage himself. Unless you promise me to teach him everything he ought to know, and to be a foster-father to him, I cannot close my eyes in peace."

And Faithful John answered, "I will not desert him, and I will serve him faithfully, even if it costs me my life."

At that the old King said, "Now I can die in comfort and peace." And he went on: "After my death you shall show him the whole castle — all the rooms, the halls and the vaults, and all the treasure that lies in them. But the last room in the long gallery, where the portrait of the princess of the Golden Dwelling hangs, you must not show him. If he sees that picture he will fall violently in love with her and faint away, and he will go through great danger for her sake. You must keep him from it."

And when Faithful John had given the old King his promise on that too, the King said no more, but laid his head on the pillow and died.

When the old King had been carried to his grave, Faithful John told the young King everything he had promised his father on his deathbed, and said, "I will keep that promise, and I will be as faithful to you as I was to him, even if it costs me my life."

When the mourning was over, Faithful John said to him, "It is time you saw your inheritance. I will show you your father's palace."

So he took him everywhere, up and down, and showed him all the riches and the magnificent rooms — only there was one room he did not open, the one where the dangerous picture hung. But the picture was so placed that when the door was opened you looked straight at it, and it was so wonderfully painted that it seemed to breathe and live; and there was nothing lovelier or more beautiful in the whole world.

The young King noticed clearly that Faithful John always walked past this one door, and said, "Why do you never open that one for me?"

"There is something inside," he answered, "that would frighten you."

But the King said, "I have seen the whole palace, and I want to know what is in this room too" — and he went and tried to force the door open.

Then Faithful John held him back and said, "I promised your father before he died that you should not see what is in that room. It could bring the greatest misfortune on you and on me."

"Oh no," said the young King, "if I don't go in, it will be the ruin of me. I should have no peace day or night until I had seen it with my own eyes. I am not leaving this spot until you have unlocked the door."

Then Faithful John saw there was no help for it, and with a heavy heart and many sighs he hunted the key out of the great bunch. When he had opened the door he went in first, meaning to stand in front of the portrait and hide it so that the King should not see it. But what good was that? The King stood on tiptoe and looked over his shoulder.

And when he saw the portrait of the girl, so magnificent and shining with gold and precious stones, he fell to the ground in a faint.

Faithful John picked him up, carried him to his bed, and thought sorrowfully, "The misfortune has come. Lord God, what will be the end of it?" Then he gave him wine to strengthen him until he came round.

The first words the King said were, "Ah, that beautiful portrait! Whose is it?"

"That is the princess of the Golden Dwelling," answered Faithful John.

And the King went on, "My love for her is so great that if all the leaves on all the trees were tongues, they could not tell it. I will give my life to win her. You are my most faithful John — you must help me."

The faithful servant thought for a long time about how to go about it, because it was difficult even to get a sight of the King's daughter. At last he hit on a way, and said to the King, "Everything she has about her is of gold — tables, chairs, dishes, glasses, bowls, all her furniture. Among your treasures there are five tons of gold. Let the goldsmiths of the kingdom work them up into every kind of vessel and utensil, and into all sorts of birds and wild beasts and strange animals such as she would like; and we will go there with them and try our luck."

The King had all the goldsmiths brought to him, and they had to work night and day until at last the most splendid things were ready. When everything had been stowed aboard a ship, Faithful John put on a merchant's clothes, and the King had to do the same so as to be quite unrecognisable. Then they sailed across the sea, and sailed on until they came to the town where the princess of the Golden Dwelling lived.

Faithful John told the King to stay behind on the ship and wait for him. "Perhaps I shall bring the princess back with me," he said. "So see that everything is in order. Have the golden things set out and the whole ship decorated."

Then he gathered up all sorts of gold pieces in his apron, went ashore and walked straight to the royal palace.

When he came into the courtyard of the palace, a beautiful girl was standing by the well with two golden buckets in her hands, drawing water. And as she turned to carry the sparkling water away she saw the stranger and asked who he was.

"I am a merchant," he answered, and opened his apron and let her look inside.

"Oh, what beautiful golden things!" she cried, and put down her pails and looked at the golden wares one after another. Then she said, "The princess must see these. She takes such pleasure in golden things that she will buy everything you have."

She took him by the hand and led him upstairs, for she was the waiting-maid.

When the King's daughter saw the wares she was delighted and said, "They are so beautifully made that I will buy the whole lot from you."

But Faithful John said, "I am only the servant of a rich merchant. What I have here is nothing to what my master has in his ship. Those are the most beautiful and valuable things that were ever made in gold."

She wanted everything brought to her there, but he said, "There are so many of them it would take a great many days, and so many rooms would be needed to show them that your house is not big enough."

At that her curiosity and her longing were roused still more, until at last she said, "Take me to the ship. I will go there myself and see your master's treasures."

Faithful John was delighted, and led her to the ship. And when the King saw her, he saw that her beauty was even greater than the picture had shown, and he thought his heart would burst in two.

She came aboard and the King led her inside. But Faithful John stayed behind with the pilot and gave orders to cast off, calling, "Set every sail, and let her fly like a bird in the air."

Inside, the King showed her the golden vessels, every one of them, and the wild beasts and the strange animals too. Many hours went by while she was looking at everything, and in her delight she did not notice that the ship was sailing away. When she had looked at the last of them, she thanked the merchant and made to go home; but when she came to the side of the ship she saw that it was out on the deep sea, far from land, and hurrying on under full sail.

"Oh," she cried in alarm, "I am betrayed! I have been carried off and fallen into the hands of a merchant. I would rather die!"

But the King took her hand and said, "I am not a merchant. I am a king, and no lower born than you are. If I have carried you off by a trick, it is because I love you so very much. The first time I looked at your portrait I fell to the ground in a faint."

When the princess of the Golden Dwelling heard that she was comforted, and her heart turned to him, so that she willingly agreed to be his wife.

But it happened, as they were sailing on over the deep sea, that Faithful John, who was sitting in the bows making music, saw three ravens in the air, flying towards them. So he stopped playing and listened to what they were saying to one another, because he understood it perfectly well.

The first cried, "There he goes, carrying home the princess of the Golden Dwelling."

"Yes," said the second, "but he hasn't got her yet."

Said the third, "He has got her — she is sitting beside him in the ship."

Then the first began again: "What good will that do him? When they reach land, a chestnut horse will come bounding up to meet him, and the prince will want to mount it; and if he does, it will bolt with him and rise up into the air with him, and he will never see his bride again."

"But is there no escape?" said the second.

"Oh yes — if somebody else gets on it quickly and takes the pistol that will be in its holster and shoots the horse dead, the young King is saved. But who knows that? And whoever does know it and tells him will be turned to stone from his toes to his knees."

Then the second said, "I know more than that. Even if the horse is killed, the young King still won't keep his bride. When they go into the castle together there will be a wedding garment lying ready in a dish, and it will look as if it were woven of gold and silver; but it is nothing but sulphur and pitch, and if he puts it on it will burn him to the bone and the marrow."

"Is there no escape at all?" said the third.

"Oh yes," said the second. "If somebody with gloves on takes hold of the garment and throws it in the fire and burns it, the young King is saved. But what good is that? Whoever knows it and tells him will turn to stone from his knees to his heart."

Then the third said, "I know still more. Even if the wedding garment is burnt, the young King still won't have his bride. After the wedding, when the dancing begins and the young queen is dancing, she will suddenly turn pale and fall down as if she were dead; and unless somebody lifts her up and draws three drops of blood from her right breast and spits them out again, she will die. But anybody who knows that and says it out loud will turn to stone from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet."

When the ravens had talked it over they flew on; and Faithful John had understood every word. From that time he was quiet and sad, for if he kept what he had heard from his master, his master would come to grief; and if he told him, he must give his own life. At last, though, he said to himself, "I will save my master, even if it destroys me."

So when they came ashore, everything happened as the ravens had foretold, and a magnificent chestnut horse came bounding up.

"Good," said the King, "this shall carry me to my palace" — and he was about to mount it when Faithful John got in front of him, jumped up on it, pulled the pistol out of the holster and shot the horse.

Then the King's other attendants, who were not very fond of Faithful John anyway, cried, "What a shameful thing, to kill that beautiful animal that was to have carried the King to his palace!"

But the King said, "Hold your tongues and leave him alone. He is my most faithful John, and who knows what good may come of it?"

They went into the palace; and in the hall there stood a dish, and in it lay the wedding garment, looking for all the world as if it were made of gold and silver. The young King went towards it and was about to take hold of it, but Faithful John pushed him away, took it up with his gloves on, carried it quickly to the fire and burnt it.

The other attendants began muttering again and said, "Look at that — now he is even burning the King's wedding garment."

But the young King said, "Who knows what good he may have done? Leave him alone. He is my most faithful John."

And now the wedding was celebrated. The dancing began, and the bride joined in; and Faithful John kept watch and looked into her face — and suddenly she turned pale and fell to the ground as if she were dead.

He ran to her at once, lifted her up and carried her into a side room; then he laid her down, knelt, and sucked the three drops of blood from her right breast and spat them out. Immediately she breathed again and came to herself.

But the young King had seen it, and, not knowing why Faithful John had done it, he grew angry and cried, "Throw him into the dungeon."

Next morning Faithful John was condemned and led out to the gallows; and when he stood up there and was about to be executed, he said, "Everybody who has to die is allowed one last speech before the end. May I claim that right too?"

"Yes," answered the King, "it is granted you."

Then Faithful John said, "I have been condemned unjustly, and I have always been true to you." And he told how he had listened to the ravens talking out at sea, and how he had been forced to do all these things to save his master.

Then the King cried, "Oh, my most faithful John! Pardon, pardon — bring him down!"

But as Faithful John spoke his last word, he had already fallen down lifeless and turned to stone.

At that the King and the Queen were in great distress, and the King said, "Oh, how badly I have repaid such faithfulness!" And he had the stone figure taken up and set in his bedroom beside his bed. And every time he looked at it he wept and said, "Ah, if only I could bring you back to life, my most faithful John."

Some time passed, and the Queen bore twins, two sons who grew fast and were her delight. Once, when the Queen was at church and the two children were sitting playing beside their father, he looked at the stone figure again, full of grief, and sighed and said, "Ah, if only I could bring you back to life, my most faithful John."

Then the stone began to speak, and said, "You can bring me back to life, if you will give up for it what is dearest to you."

The King cried, "I will give everything I have in the world for you."

The stone went on, "If you will cut off the heads of your two children with your own hand, and sprinkle me with their blood, I shall come back to life."

The King was horrified when he heard that he must kill his own dearest children; but he thought of Faithful John's great faithfulness, and how he had died for him, and drew his sword and with his own hand cut off the children's heads. And when he had smeared the stone with their blood, life came back into it, and Faithful John stood before him again, safe and well.

He said to the King, "Your faithfulness shall not go unrewarded" — and he took the children's heads, set them on again and rubbed the wounds with their blood, and at once they were whole again and jumped about and went on playing as if nothing had happened.

Then the King was full of joy; and when he saw the Queen coming, he hid Faithful John and the two children in a great cupboard. When she came in he said to her, "Have you been praying in the church?"

"Yes," she answered, "but I have been thinking all the time of Faithful John, and what misfortune came to him through us."

Then he said, "Dear wife, we can give him his life back — but it will cost us our two little sons, whom we must sacrifice."

The Queen turned pale and her heart was full of horror, but she said, "We owe it to him, for his great faithfulness."

Then the King was glad that she thought as he had thought; and he went and opened the cupboard and brought out Faithful John and the children, and said, "God be praised, he is delivered, and we have our little sons again as well" — and he told her how it had all happened.

And they lived together in great happiness to the end of their days.

The Good Bargain

There was once a peasant who had driven his cow to the fair and sold her for seven thalers. On the way home he had to pass a pond, and from a long way off he could hear the frogs crying, "Aik, aik, aik, aik."

"Well," he said to himself, "they are talking without rhyme or reason. It's seven I got, not eight."

When he came to the water he called out to them, "Stupid creatures that you are! Don't you know any better? It's seven thalers, not eight."

But the frogs stuck to their "Aik, aik, aik, aik."

"Come on then, if you won't believe it, I can count it out for you." And he took his money out of his pocket and counted out the seven thalers, reckoning twenty-four groschen to the thaler.

But the frogs paid no attention to his reckoning and went on crying, "Aik, aik, aik, aik."

"What!" cried the peasant, thoroughly angry. "Since you're so determined to know better than I do, count it yourselves" — and he threw all the money into the water to them.

He stood still and waited for them to finish and give him his own back again; but the frogs held to their opinion and went on crying "Aik, aik, aik, aik," and what is more, they did not throw the money out again. He waited a long while, until evening came on and he had to go home. Then he swore at the frogs and called out, "You water-splashers, you thick-heads, you goggle-eyes! You have great mouths on you and can screech till a man's ears hurt, but you can't count seven thalers. Do you think I'm going to stand here till you've finished?"

And with that he went off; but the frogs went on crying "Aik, aik, aik, aik" after him, and he got home thoroughly angry.

After a while he bought another cow and killed it, and worked out that if he sold the meat well he might make as much as the two cows were worth, and have the hide into the bargain.

So when he got to the town with the meat, there was a great pack of dogs gathered in front of the gate, with a big greyhound at the head of them, which jumped at the meat, sniffed at it and barked, "Wow, wow, wow."

As there was no stopping him, the peasant said, "Yes, yes, I know perfectly well you're saying wow, wow, wow because you want some of the meat. But I'd come off badly if I gave it to you."

The dog answered nothing but "Wow, wow."

"Will you promise not to eat the lot, then? And will you stand surety for your companions?"

"Wow, wow, wow," said the dog.

"Well, if you insist on it, I'll leave it with you. I know you well enough, and I know who your master is. But I tell you this: I must have my money in three days, or it will go badly for you. You'll have to bring it out to me."

With that he unloaded the meat and turned back, and the dogs fell on it, barking loudly, "Wow, wow."

The countryman heard them from a distance and said to himself, "Listen to that — now they all want a share, but the big one is answerable to me for it."

When three days had gone by, the countryman thought, "Tonight my money will be in my pocket," and he was quite delighted. But nobody came to pay it.

"There's no trusting anybody nowadays," he said. And at last he lost patience and went into the town to the butcher and demanded his money.

The butcher thought it was a joke, but the peasant said, "Joking aside, I'll have my money. Didn't the big dog bring you a whole slaughtered cow three days ago?"

At that the butcher lost his temper, snatched up a broom handle and drove him out.

"Just wait," said the peasant. "There's still some justice in the world" — and he went to the royal palace and asked for an audience.

He was brought before the King, who was sitting there with his daughter, and was asked what wrong he had suffered.

"Alas," he said, "the frogs and the dogs have taken what was mine, and the butcher paid me for it with a stick" — and he told the whole story from beginning to end.

At that the King's daughter began to laugh out loud, and the King said, "I cannot give you justice in this, but you shall have my daughter for a wife instead. In her whole life she has never laughed as she has just laughed at you, and I promised her to the man who could make her laugh. You may thank God for your good fortune."

"Oh," said the peasant, "I don't want her. I have a wife already, and she is one too many for me. When I go home it is as bad as if there were a wife standing in every corner."

Then the King grew angry and said, "You are a boor."

"Ah, my lord King," said the peasant, "what can you expect from an ox but beef?"

"Wait," said the King. "You shall have another reward. Be off now, and come back in three days, and you shall have five hundred counted out in full."

As the peasant went out through the gate, the sentry said, "You made the King's daughter laugh, so you're bound to have got something good."

"Yes, that's what I think," said the peasant. "Five hundred are to be counted out to me."

"Listen," said the soldier, "give me some of it. What can you do with all that money?"

"Since it's you," said the peasant, "you shall have two hundred. Present yourself before the King in three days and have it paid to you."

A Jew who was standing by and had heard the conversation ran after the peasant, caught him by the coat and said, "Well, what a wonder! What a child of luck you are! I'll change it for you, I'll change it into small coin for you — what do you want with the big thalers?"

"Jew," said the countryman, "you can have three hundred more. Give it to me now in coin, and in three days from now the King will pay you for it."

The Jew was delighted with his profit and brought the sum in bad groschen, three of which were worth two good ones.

When the three days were up, the peasant went before the King as he had been told.

"Pull off his coat," said the King, "and he shall have his five hundred."

"Ah," said the peasant, "they don't belong to me any more. I made a present of two hundred of them to the sentry, and three hundred the Jew has changed for me, so by rights nothing at all belongs to me."

Meanwhile the soldier and the Jew came in and claimed what they had got from the peasant — and they received the blows, strictly counted out. The soldier bore it patiently and knew already how it tasted; but the Jew said sorrowfully, "Oh dear, oh dear, are these the heavy thalers?"

The King could not help laughing at the peasant, and as all his anger was gone he said, "Since you have already lost your reward before it came to you, I'll give you something in its place. Go into my treasure chamber and help yourself to as much money as you like."

The peasant did not need telling twice, and stuffed his big pockets with whatever would go in. Afterwards he went to an inn and counted out his money. The Jew had crept after him and heard him muttering to himself, "That rogue of a King has cheated me after all. Why couldn't he have given me the money himself, and then I'd have known what I had? How am I supposed to tell now whether what I happened to put in my pockets is right or not?"

"Good heavens," said the Jew to himself, "that man is speaking disrespectfully of our lord the King. I'll run and inform on him, and then I shall get a reward and he will be punished as well."

When the King heard what the peasant had said he flew into a rage and ordered the Jew to go and bring the offender to him.

The Jew ran to the peasant. "You're to go to my lord the King at once, in the very clothes you have on."

"I know better than that," said the peasant. "I shall have a new coat made first. Do you suppose a man with so much money in his pocket is going to turn up there in his ragged old coat?"

The Jew, seeing that the peasant would not stir without another coat, and afraid that if the King's anger cooled he would lose his own reward and the peasant his punishment, said, "Out of pure friendship, I'll lend you a coat for the short time. What won't a man do for love!"

The peasant was satisfied with that, put on the Jew's coat and went off with him.

The King reproached the countryman for the disrespectful words the Jew had informed him of.

"Ah," said the peasant, "what a Jew says is always false — no true word ever comes out of his mouth. That rascal there is capable of claiming that I have his coat on."

"What's this?" shrieked the Jew. "Is the coat not mine? Didn't I lend it to you out of pure friendship, so that you could appear before my lord the King?"

When the King heard that, he said, "The Jew has certainly deceived one or other of us — either me or the peasant" — and he ordered another sum to be counted out to him in hard thalers.

But the peasant went home in the good coat with the good money in his pocket, and said to himself, "This time I've hit it."

The Wonderful Musician

There was once a wonderful musician who was walking all alone through a forest, thinking of all kinds of things; and when he had nothing left to think about he said to himself, "Time is beginning to hang heavy here in the forest. I'll fetch myself a good companion."

So he took his fiddle off his back and played, and the sound rang through the trees. It was not long before a wolf came trotting through the thicket towards him.

"Ah, here's a wolf coming. I've no wish for him," said the musician.

But the wolf came nearer and said, "Ah, dear musician, how beautifully you play. I should like to learn that too."

"It's soon learnt," said the musician. "You have only to do everything I tell you."

"Oh, musician," said the wolf, "I'll obey you as a pupil obeys his master."

The musician told him to follow; and when they had gone part of the way together they came to an old oak tree that was hollow inside and split down the middle.

"Look," said the musician, "if you want to learn to fiddle, put your forepaws into this crack."

The wolf did as he was told; but the musician quickly picked up a stone and with one blow wedged his two paws in so fast that he had to stay there like a prisoner.

"Wait there till I come back," said the musician, and went on his way.

After a while he said to himself again, "Time is beginning to hang heavy here in the forest. I'll fetch myself another companion" — and he took his fiddle and played again. It was not long before a fox came creeping through the trees towards him.

"Ah, there's a fox coming," said the musician. "I've no wish for him."

The fox came up and said, "Oh, dear musician, how beautifully you play. I should like to learn that too."

"That's soon learnt," said the musician. "You have only to do everything I tell you."

"Oh, musician," said the fox, "I'll obey you as a pupil obeys his master."

"Follow me," said the musician. And when they had walked part of the way they came to a footpath with high bushes on both sides of it. There the musician stopped, bent a young hazel bush down to the ground from one side and put his foot on the top of it, and bent a young tree down from the other side as well.

"Now, little fox, if you want to learn something, give me your left front paw."

The fox obeyed, and the musician tied his paw to the left bough. "Little fox," he said, "now give me your right paw" — and he tied it to the right bough. And when he had made sure they were firm enough, he let go, and the bushes sprang up again and jerked the little fox up, so that he hung there struggling in the air.

"Wait there till I come back," said the musician, and went on his way.

Again he said to himself, "Time is beginning to hang heavy here in the forest. I'll fetch myself another companion" — so he took his fiddle, and the sound rang through the forest. And a little hare came springing towards him.

"Why, here's a hare coming," said the musician. "I don't want him."

"Ah, dear musician," said the hare, "how beautifully you fiddle. I should like to learn that too."

"That's soon learnt," said the musician. "You have only to do everything I tell you."

"Oh, musician," said the little hare, "I'll obey you as a pupil obeys his master."

They went part of the way together until they came to an open place in the forest where an aspen tree stood. The musician tied a long string round the little hare's neck and fastened the other end to the tree.

"Now look sharp, little hare — run twenty times round the tree," cried the musician; and the little hare obeyed. And when it had run round twenty times it had twisted the string twenty times round the trunk, and the little hare was caught; and it could pull and tug as much as it liked, it only cut the string into its tender neck.

"Wait there till I come back," said the musician, and went on.

Meanwhile the wolf had been pushing and pulling and biting at the stone, and had worked at it so long that he got his feet free and pulled them out of the crack again. Full of anger and rage he hurried after the musician, meaning to tear him to pieces.

When the fox saw him running, he began to wail and cried with all his might, "Brother wolf, come and help me — the musician has tricked me!"

The wolf pulled the little tree down, bit the cord in two and set the fox free, and the fox went along with him to take revenge on the musician. They found the tied-up hare and freed him as well, and then all three of them went looking for their enemy together.

The musician had been playing his fiddle again as he went on his way, and this time he had had better luck. The sound reached the ears of a poor woodcutter, who instantly, whether he wanted to or not, dropped his work and came with his hatchet under his arm to listen to the music.

"At last the right companion," said the musician, "for it was a human being I was looking for, and not wild beasts."

And he began to play, so beautifully and so delightfully that the poor man stood there as if he were bewitched, and his heart leapt for gladness. And as he stood there, up came the wolf, the fox and the hare; and he could see well enough that they meant harm. So he raised his glittering axe and put himself in front of the musician, as much as to say, "Whoever wants to touch him had better beware — he'll have me to deal with."

Then the beasts were frightened and ran back into the forest; and the musician played once more for the man, out of gratitude, and then went on his way.

The Twelve Brothers

Once upon a time there were a king and a queen who lived happily together and had twelve children — but they were all boys.

Then the King said to his wife, "If the thirteenth child you are about to bring into the world is a girl, the twelve boys must die, so that her fortune may be great and the kingdom fall to her alone."

He had twelve coffins made as well, already filled with wood shavings, and in each of them lay the little pillow for the dead; and he had them carried into a locked room, and gave the Queen the key of it and told her to speak of it to nobody.

But now the mother sat and grieved all day long, until the youngest son, who was always with her and whom she had named Benjamin, out of the Bible, said to her, "Dear mother, why are you so sad?"

"Dearest child," she answered, "I am not allowed to tell you."

But he gave her no peace until she went and unlocked the room and showed him the twelve coffins, ready and filled with shavings. Then she said, "My dearest Benjamin, your father had these coffins made for you and your eleven brothers; for if I bring a little girl into the world, you are all to be killed and buried in them."

And as she wept while she was saying it, her son comforted her and said, "Don't cry, dear mother. We will save ourselves and go away."

But she said, "Go out into the forest with your eleven brothers, and let one of you always sit in the highest tree that can be found and keep watch, looking towards the tower here at the castle. If I give birth to a little son, I will put up a white flag, and then you may risk coming home. But if I bear a daughter, I will hoist a red flag, and then fly away as fast as you can, and may the good God protect you. And every night I will get up and pray for you — in winter that you may have a fire to warm yourselves at, and in summer that you may not faint in the heat."

So when she had blessed her sons, they went out into the forest. They kept watch by turns, sitting in the highest oak and looking towards the tower. And when eleven days had gone by and it came to Benjamin's turn, he saw a flag being raised. But it was not the white one. It was the blood-red flag, which meant that they were all to die.

When the brothers heard it they were furious, and said, "Are we all to suffer death for the sake of a girl? We swear we will be revenged: wherever we find a girl, her red blood shall flow."

Then they went deeper into the forest; and in the middle of it, where it was darkest, they found a little enchanted hut standing empty.

"Here we will live," they said. "And you, Benjamin, who are the youngest and weakest, shall stay at home and keep house, and the rest of us will go out and get food."

So they went out into the forest and shot hares and wild deer, birds and pigeons, and whatever there was to eat, and brought it to Benjamin, who had to prepare it so that they could satisfy their hunger. They lived together in the little hut for ten years, and the time did not seem long to them.

The little daughter that their mother the Queen had borne was grown up by now. She was good-hearted and lovely to look at, and she had a golden star on her forehead.

Once, when it was the great washing day, she saw twelve men's shirts among the things, and asked her mother, "Whose are these twelve shirts? They are far too small for father."

Then the Queen answered with a heavy heart, "Dear child, they belong to your twelve brothers."

Said the girl, "Where are my twelve brothers? I have never even heard of them."
