"God knows where they are," she said. "They are wandering about the world somewhere."

Then she took the girl and opened the room for her and showed her the twelve coffins with the shavings and the pillows for the head. "These coffins," she said, "were meant for your brothers; but they went away in secret before you were born" — and she told her how it had all happened.

Then the girl said, "Dear mother, don't cry. I will go and find my brothers."

So she took the twelve shirts and set off, straight into the great forest. She walked all day, and in the evening she came to the enchanted hut. She went in and found a young boy there, who asked, "Where have you come from, and where are you going?" — and he was astonished that she was so beautiful, and wore royal clothes, and had a star on her forehead.

She answered, "I am a king's daughter, and I am looking for my twelve brothers, and I mean to walk as far as the sky is blue until I find them." And she showed him the twelve shirts that belonged to them.

Then Benjamin saw that she was his sister, and said, "I am Benjamin, your youngest brother."

She began to cry for joy, and Benjamin cried too, and they kissed and hugged each other with the greatest love. But afterwards he said, "Dear sister, there is still one difficulty. We agreed that every girl we met should die, because it was on account of a girl that we had to leave our kingdom."

Then she said, "I will die willingly, if by doing it I can set my twelve brothers free."

"No," he answered, "you shall not die. Sit down under this tub until our eleven brothers come, and I will soon come to terms with them."

She did so; and when night came the others got back from hunting and their dinner was ready. And as they sat at the table eating, they asked, "What's the news?"

Said Benjamin, "Don't you know anything?"

"No," they said.

He went on, "You have been in the forest and I have stayed at home, and yet I know more than you do."

"Tell us, then," they cried.

He answered, "But promise me that the first girl we meet shall not be killed."

"Yes," they all cried, "she shall be spared — only tell us."

Then he said, "Our sister is here" — and he lifted up the tub, and the King's daughter came out in her royal clothes with the golden star on her forehead, and she was beautiful and delicate and fair. Then they were all overjoyed, and fell on her neck and kissed her and loved her with all their hearts.

Now she stayed at home with Benjamin and helped him with the work. The eleven went out into the forest and caught game — deer and birds and wood pigeons — for food, and the little sister and Benjamin saw to getting it ready. She fetched the wood for the cooking and the herbs for the vegetables, and put the pans on the fire, so that dinner was always ready when the eleven came home. She kept the little house in order too, and put beautiful clean white covers on the little beds; and the brothers were always content and lived in great harmony with her.

One day the two at home had prepared a splendid meal; and when they were all together they sat down and ate and drank and were full of gladness.

Now there was a little garden belonging to the enchanted house, and in it stood twelve lily flowers. The sister wanted to give her brothers pleasure, so she picked the twelve flowers, meaning to give one to each of them at dinner. But at the very moment she picked the flowers, the twelve brothers were turned into twelve ravens and flew away over the forest, and the house and the garden vanished too.

And now the poor girl was alone in the wild forest; and when she looked round, there stood an old woman beside her, who said, "My child, what have you done? Why didn't you leave the twelve white flowers growing? Those were your brothers, and now they are turned into ravens for ever."

The girl said, weeping, "Is there no way of setting them free?"

"No," said the woman, "there is only one in the whole world, and it is so hard that you will not free them by it: you must be dumb for seven years, and must not speak or laugh; and if you speak a single word, even with only an hour of the seven years still to run, it is all in vain and your brothers will be killed by that one word."

Then the girl said in her heart, "I know for certain that I shall set my brothers free"; and she went and found a tall tree and settled herself in it and span, and neither spoke nor laughed.

Now it happened that a king was hunting in the forest, and he had a great greyhound which ran to the tree the girl was sitting in and sprang about it, whining and barking up at her. Then the King came by and saw the beautiful King's daughter with the golden star on her forehead, and he was so taken with her beauty that he called up to ask whether she would be his wife. She gave no answer, but nodded her head a little. So he climbed the tree himself, carried her down, set her on his horse and took her home.

The wedding was celebrated with great magnificence and rejoicing, but the bride neither spoke nor smiled.

When they had lived happily together for a few years, the King's mother, who was a wicked woman, began to speak against the young Queen, and said to the King, "This is some common beggar girl you have brought home with you. Who knows what ungodly tricks she gets up to in secret! Even if she is dumb and cannot speak, she might laugh once in a while; and people who never laugh have bad consciences."

At first the King would not believe it; but the old woman pressed it so long, and accused her of so many evil things, that at last the King let himself be persuaded, and sentenced her to death.

And now a great fire was lit in the courtyard where she was to be burned; and the King stood up at the window and watched with tears in his eyes, because he still loved her so much. And when she was tied fast to the stake, and the fire was licking at her clothes with its red tongue, the last instant of the seven years ran out.

Then a whirring was heard in the air, and twelve ravens came flying to the place and sank down; and when they touched the earth they were her twelve brothers, whom she had set free. They tore the fire apart, put out the flames, untied their dear sister and kissed and hugged her.

And now that she could open her mouth and speak, she told the King why she had been dumb and had never laughed. The King rejoiced when he heard that she was innocent, and they all lived together in great harmony until they died. The wicked stepmother was brought before the judge and put into a barrel filled with boiling oil and poisonous snakes, and died an evil death.

The Pack of Ragamuffins

The cock said one day to the hen, "It's the time of year when our nuts are ripe. Let's go up the hill together and eat our fill for once, before the squirrel carries them all off."

"Yes," said the hen, "come along, we'll have a good time together."

So off they went up the hill, and as it was a fine day they stayed there till evening. Now I do not know whether it was that they had eaten themselves too fat, or whether they had grown proud, but they would not go home on foot, and the cock had to build a little carriage out of nutshells.

When it was ready the little hen seated herself in it and said to the cock, "You can just harness yourself to it."

"I like that!" said the cock. "I'd sooner walk home than be harnessed to it. No, that wasn't the bargain. I don't mind being coachman and sitting on the box, but pull it myself I will not."

While they were arguing about it, a duck came quacking at them. "You thieving creatures, who told you to go to my nut hill? You'll suffer for it!" — and she ran at the cock with her beak open. But the cock was not idle either; he set on the duck boldly and in the end wounded her so with his spurs that she begged for mercy and let herself be harnessed to the carriage as a punishment, willingly enough.

So the little cock sat up on the box as coachman, and off they went at a gallop, with "Duck, go as fast as you can."

When they had driven part of the way they met two travellers on foot, a pin and a needle. "Stop, stop!" they cried; and they said it would soon be as dark as pitch and then they would not be able to go a step further, and the road was so dirty — couldn't they get into the carriage for a while? They had been at the tailor's alehouse by the gate and had sat too long over the beer. As they were thin people who did not take up much room, the cock let them both get in, but they had to promise not to tread on his feet or the hen's.

Late in the evening they came to an inn; and as they did not care to go on by night, and the duck was not steady on her feet either but kept lurching from side to side, they went in. The landlord at first made a great many objections — his house was full already, and besides, he did not think they could be very distinguished persons. But at last, as they made pleasant speeches and told him he could have the egg the little hen had laid on the way, and could keep the duck, which laid one every day, he said they might stay the night. And so they had themselves well waited on, and feasted and made a great noise.

Early in the morning, at daybreak, when everybody was asleep, the cock woke the hen, fetched the egg, pecked it open, and they ate it between them and threw the shell on the hearth. Then they went to the needle, which was still asleep, took it by the head and stuck it into the cushion of the landlord's chair, and put the pin in his towel; and then, without more ado, they flew away over the heath.

The duck, who liked sleeping in the open air and had stayed in the yard, heard them going, cheered up, found a stream and swam off down it, which was a much quicker way of travelling than being harnessed to a carriage.

The landlord did not get out of bed for another two hours. He washed himself and went to dry his face, and the pin went across it and drew a red streak from one ear to the other. Then he went into the kitchen to light a pipe; and when he came to the hearth the eggshell flew up into his eyes.

"Everything is going for my head this morning," he said, and sat down crossly in his grandfather's chair — and jumped straight up again crying, "Oh, misery!" — for the needle had pricked him worse than the pin had, and not in the head.

Now he was thoroughly angry, and suspected the guests who had come so late the night before; and when he went to look for them, they were gone. So he made a vow to take no more ragamuffins into his house: they eat a great deal, pay for nothing, and play spiteful tricks on you into the bargain, by way of thanks.

Little Brother and Little Sister

Little brother took his little sister by the hand and said, "Since our mother died we have had no happiness. Our stepmother beats us every day, and if we go near her she kicks us away with her foot. Our meals are the hard crusts of bread that are left over, and the little dog under the table is better off than we are, because she often throws it a good bit. Heaven help us — if our mother only knew! Come, we'll go out into the wide world together."

They walked the whole day over meadows and fields and stony places; and when it rained the little sister said, "Heaven and our hearts are weeping together." In the evening they came to a great forest, and they were so worn out with grief and hunger and the long walk that they crept into a hollow tree and fell asleep.

Next day, when they woke, the sun was already high and shining hot into the tree. Then the brother said, "Sister, I'm thirsty. If I knew of a little stream I'd go and have a drink. I think I can hear one running."

The brother got up and took his little sister by the hand, and they set off to find the stream.

But the wicked stepmother was a witch, and she had seen the two children go, and had crept after them in secret, the way witches creep, and had put a spell on every stream in the forest.

Now when they found a little stream leaping brightly over the stones, the brother was going to drink out of it; but the sister heard how it said as it ran, "Whoever drinks of me will be a tiger; whoever drinks of me will be a tiger."

So the sister cried, "Please, dear brother, don't drink, or you'll turn into a wild beast and tear me to pieces."

The brother did not drink, thirsty as he was, but said, "I'll wait for the next spring."

When they came to the next stream, the sister heard it say, "Whoever drinks of me will be a wolf; whoever drinks of me will be a wolf."

So the sister cried out, "Please, dear brother, don't drink, or you'll turn into a wolf and eat me."

The brother did not drink, but said, "I'll wait till we come to the next spring; but then I must drink, whatever you say, because my thirst is too great."

And when they came to the third stream, the sister heard it say as it ran, "Whoever drinks of me will be a roebuck; whoever drinks of me will be a roebuck."

The sister said, "Oh, I beg you, dear brother, don't drink, or you'll turn into a roebuck and run away from me."

But the brother had already knelt down by the stream and bent over and drunk some of the water; and as soon as the first drops touched his lips, there he lay, a young roebuck.

And now the sister wept over her poor enchanted brother, and the little roe wept too, and sat close beside her, full of sorrow. But at last the girl said, "Be quiet, dear little roe. I will never, never leave you."

Then she untied her golden garter and put it round the roebuck's neck, and she picked rushes and wove them into a soft cord. With this she led the little creature away, deeper and deeper into the forest.

And when they had gone a very long way they came at last to a little house; and the girl looked in, and as it was empty she thought, "We can stay here and live." Then she gathered leaves and moss to make a soft bed for the roe, and every morning she went out and gathered roots and berries and nuts for herself, and brought tender grass for the roe, who ate out of her hand and was contented and played about her. In the evening, when the sister was tired and had said her prayers, she laid her head on the roebuck's back — that was her pillow, and she slept soundly on it. And if only her brother had had his human shape, it would have been a delightful life.

For a while they were alone like this in the wilderness. But then it happened that the King of the country held a great hunt in the forest. The blasts of the horns, the barking of the dogs and the merry shouts of the huntsmen rang through the trees, and the roebuck heard it all and wanted more than anything to be there.

"Oh," he said to his sister, "let me go to the hunt, I can't bear it any longer" — and he begged so hard that at last she agreed.

"But," she said to him, "come back to me in the evening. I shall have to shut my door against the rough huntsmen; so knock and say, 'My little sister, let me in,' so that I know it is you. And if you don't say that, I shan't open the door."

Then the young roebuck sprang away, so happy and so merry in the open air.

The King and the huntsmen saw the beautiful creature and set off after him, but they could not catch him; and just when they thought they had him for certain, away he sprang through the bushes and was gone. When it was dark he ran to the cottage, knocked, and said, "My little sister, let me in." And the door was opened for him, and he jumped in and rested all night on his soft bed.

Next day the hunt began again, and when the roebuck heard the horns and the hallooing of the huntsmen he had no peace, and said, "Sister, let me out, I must go."

His sister opened the door for him and said, "But you must be back here in the evening and say your password."

When the King and his huntsmen saw the young roebuck with the golden collar again, they all gave chase; but he was too quick and nimble for them. It went on the whole day; but at last, towards evening, the huntsmen surrounded him, and one of them wounded him slightly in the foot, so that he limped and ran slowly. Then a huntsman crept after him to the cottage and heard him say, "My little sister, let me in," and saw the door open for him and shut again at once. The huntsman took note of it all, and went to the King and told him what he had seen and heard.

Then the King said, "Tomorrow we will hunt once more."

But the little sister was dreadfully frightened when she saw that her roe was hurt. She washed the blood off him, laid herbs on the wound, and said, "Go to your bed, dear roe, so that you get well again." But the wound was so slight that next morning the roebuck felt nothing of it any more; and when he heard the hunt outside again he said, "I can't bear it, I must be there. They shan't find it so easy to catch me."

The sister cried, and said, "This time they'll kill you, and here I shall be alone in the forest and forsaken by all the world. I won't let you out."

"Then you'll have me die of grief," said the roe. "When I hear those horns I feel as if I must jump out of my skin."

Then the sister could do nothing else, and opened the door for him with a heavy heart, and the roebuck bounded off into the forest, full of health and joy.

When the King saw him he said to his huntsmen, "Now chase him all day long, till nightfall; but take care that nobody does him any harm."

As soon as the sun had set, the King said to the huntsman, "Now come and show me the cottage in the wood." And when he was at the door he knocked and called, "Dear little sister, let me in."

The door opened and the King walked in, and there stood a girl more lovely than any he had ever seen. She was frightened when she saw that it was not her little roe but a man who came in, with a golden crown on his head. But the King looked at her kindly, held out his hand and said, "Will you come with me to my palace and be my dear wife?"

"Yes, gladly," said the girl, "but the little roe must come with me. I can't leave him."

The King said, "He shall stay with you as long as you live, and shall want for nothing."

Just then the roe came running in, and the sister tied him again with the rush cord, took it in her own hand and went away from the cottage with the King.

The King set the lovely girl on his horse and carried her to his palace, where the wedding was held with great splendour. She was Queen now, and they lived happily together for a long time; and the roebuck was cared for and cherished, and ran about in the palace garden.

But the wicked stepmother, who had driven the children out into the world, had been supposing all this time that the sister had been torn to pieces by the wild beasts in the wood, and that the brother had been shot for a roebuck by the huntsmen. So when she heard that they were so happy and so well off, envy and hatred rose in her heart and gave her no peace, and she thought of nothing but how to bring them to grief again.

Her own daughter, who was as ugly as night and had only one eye, grumbled at her and said, "A Queen! That ought to have been my luck."

"Just be quiet," said the old woman, and comforted her: "When the time comes, I shall be ready."

As time went on the Queen had a pretty little boy; and it happened that the King was out hunting. So the old witch took the shape of the chambermaid, went into the room where the Queen lay and said to her, "Come, your bath is ready. It will do you good and give you fresh strength. Be quick, before it gets cold."

Her daughter was close by too; and the two of them carried the weak Queen into the bathroom and put her in the bath, and then shut the door and ran away. But they had made up such a deadly heat in the bathroom that the beautiful young Queen was soon suffocated.

When that was done the old woman took her daughter, put a nightcap on her head and laid her in the bed in the Queen's place. She gave her the Queen's shape and the Queen's face as well; only she could not make good the missing eye. So that the King should not notice, she was to lie on the side where she had no eye.

In the evening, when he came home and heard that he had a son, he was heartily glad and was going to his dear wife's bed to see how she was. But the old woman called out quickly, "For your life, leave the curtains closed. The Queen must not see the light yet, and she must have rest." So the King went away, and never found out that a false Queen was lying in the bed.

But at midnight, when everybody was asleep, the nurse, who was sitting in the nursery by the cradle and was the only person awake, saw the door open and the true Queen come in. She took the child out of the cradle, laid it on her arm and fed it. Then she shook up its pillow, laid the child down again and covered it with the little quilt. And she did not forget the roebuck either, but went to the corner where he lay and stroked his back. Then she went out through the door again without a sound.

Next morning the nurse asked the guards whether anybody had come into the palace during the night, but they answered, "No, we saw nobody."

She came like this many nights and never spoke a word. The nurse always saw her, but did not dare tell anybody about it.

When some time had passed like this, the Queen began to speak in the night, and said:

	"How fares my child? How fares my roe?
	Twice more I come, then I must go."

The nurse did not answer; but when the Queen had gone she went to the King and told him everything.

The King said, "Ah, heavens, what can this be? Tomorrow night I will watch by the child myself."

In the evening he went into the nursery; and at midnight the Queen appeared again and said:

	"How fares my child? How fares my roe?
	Once more I come, then I must go."

And she nursed the child as she always did, before she disappeared. The King did not dare speak to her; but the next night he watched again. Then she said:

	"How fares my child? How fares my roe?
	This time I come, then I must go."

Then the King could not hold himself back. He sprang towards her and said, "You can be nobody but my dear wife."

She answered, "Yes, I am your dear wife" — and at that very moment her life came back to her, and by God's grace she was fresh and rosy and full of health again.

Then she told the King what a wicked thing the witch and her daughter had done to her. The King had them both brought before the judge, and sentence was passed on them. The daughter was taken out into the forest, where the wild beasts tore her to pieces; and the witch was thrown into the fire and miserably burnt. And the moment she was burnt, the roebuck changed his shape and had his human form again; so the sister and brother lived happily together all their lives.

Rapunzel

There were once a man and a woman who had long wished for a child in vain. At last the woman began to hope that God was going to grant her wish.

These people had a little window at the back of their house, and from it you could see a splendid garden, full of the most beautiful flowers and herbs. But it was surrounded by a high wall, and nobody dared go into it, because it belonged to an enchantress who had great powers and was feared by everybody in the world.

One day the woman was standing at this window looking down into the garden, when she saw a bed planted with the most beautiful rampion — rapunzel — and it looked so fresh and green that she longed for it and wanted more than anything to eat some. The longing grew stronger every day; and as she knew she could never have any, she pined away and looked pale and miserable.

Then her husband was alarmed, and asked, "What is the matter, dear wife?"

"Ah," she said, "if I can't get some of that rampion out of the garden behind our house, I shall die."

Her husband, who loved her, thought, "Rather than let your wife die, fetch her some of the rampion yourself, whatever it costs."

So in the dusk of the evening he climbed down over the wall into the enchantress's garden, hurriedly snatched a handful of rampion and took it to his wife. She made herself a salad of it at once and ate it with great relish. But she liked it so much — so very much — that the next day she longed for it three times as badly as before. If he was to have any peace, her husband would have to go down into the garden once more.

So in the gloom of the evening he let himself down again; but when he had climbed down the wall he was terrified, because there stood the enchantress in front of him.

"How dare you," she said, with a furious look, "climb into my garden and steal my rampion like a thief? You shall suffer for it."

"Ah," he answered, "let mercy take the place of justice. I only brought myself to do it out of necessity. My wife saw your rampion from the window, and she felt such a longing for it that she would have died if she hadn't got some to eat."

Then the enchantress let her anger cool, and said to him, "If it is as you say, I will let you take away as much rampion as you like — only on one condition: you must give me the child your wife is going to bring into the world. It shall be well treated, and I will care for it like a mother."

In his terror the man agreed to everything; and when the child was born, the enchantress appeared at once, gave the child the name Rapunzel, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew into the most beautiful child under the sun. When she was twelve years old, the enchantress shut her up in a tower that stood in a forest and had neither stairs nor door, but only a little window right at the top. When the enchantress wanted to go in, she stood underneath and called:

	"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
	let down your hair to me."

Rapunzel had magnificent long hair, as fine as spun gold; and when she heard the enchantress's voice she undid her braided tresses and wound them round one of the hooks of the window, and then the hair fell twenty ells down, and the enchantress climbed up by it.

After a year or two it happened that a king's son rode through the forest and passed the tower. And he heard a song so lovely that he stood still and listened. It was Rapunzel, who in her loneliness passed her time letting her sweet voice ring out. The King's son wanted to climb up to her and looked for the door of the tower, but there was none to be found. He rode home; but the singing had gone so deep into his heart that he went out into the forest every day to listen to it.

Once, when he was standing behind a tree like this, he saw an enchantress come to the tower, and heard her call:

	"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
	let down your hair to me."

Then Rapunzel let down the braids of her hair, and the enchantress climbed up to her.

"So that is the ladder people go up by," he said. "Then I'll try my luck too." And the next day, when it was beginning to get dark, he went to the tower and called:

	"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
	let down your hair to me."

At once the hair came down, and the King's son climbed up.

At first Rapunzel was terribly frightened when a man came in, such as her eyes had never seen before. But the King's son began to talk to her quite like a friend, and told her that his heart had been so stirred that it had given him no peace, and he had had to see her. Then Rapunzel lost her fear; and when he asked whether she would have him for a husband, and she saw that he was young and handsome, she thought, "He will love me better than old Mother Gothel does" — and she said yes, and laid her hand in his.

She said, "I will gladly go away with you, but I don't know how to get down. Bring a skein of silk with you every time you come, and I will weave a ladder out of it; and when it is ready I will climb down and you shall take me up on your horse."

They agreed that until then he should come to her every evening, because the old woman came by day.

The enchantress noticed nothing, until one day Rapunzel said to her, "Tell me, Mother Gothel, how is it that you are so much heavier for me to pull up than the young King's son? He is up here in a moment."

"You wicked child!" cried the enchantress. "What is this I hear you say? I thought I had cut you off from all the world, and you have deceived me!"

In her rage she seized Rapunzel's beautiful hair, wound it twice round her left hand, snatched up a pair of scissors in her right, and snip, snap, it was cut off, and the lovely braids lay on the ground. And she was so pitiless that she took poor Rapunzel out into a wilderness, where she had to live in great grief and misery.

But on the same day that she cast Rapunzel out, the enchantress fastened the braids she had cut off to the hook of the window; and in the evening, when the King's son came and called:

	"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
	let down your hair to me,"

she let the hair down. The King's son climbed up — and up there he did not find his dearest Rapunzel, but the enchantress, glaring at him with wicked, poisonous looks.

"Aha!" she cried mockingly. "You have come to fetch your darling; but the pretty bird is no longer sitting in the nest, singing. The cat has got her, and will scratch your eyes out as well. Rapunzel is lost to you. You will never see her again."

The King's son was beside himself with grief, and in his despair he leapt down from the tower. He escaped with his life, but the thorns he fell into put his eyes out. Then he wandered blind about the forest, ate nothing but roots and berries, and did nothing but grieve and weep for the loss of his dearest wife.

So he roamed about in misery for some years, and at last came to the wilderness where Rapunzel was living wretchedly with the twins she had given birth to, a boy and a girl. He heard a voice, and it seemed so familiar to him that he went towards it; and when he came near, Rapunzel knew him and fell on his neck and wept. Two of her tears fell on his eyes, and they grew clear again and he could see with them as he had before.

He took her home to his kingdom, where he was welcomed with joy, and they lived a long time afterwards, happy and content.

The Three Little Men in the Wood

There was once a man whose wife had died, and a woman whose husband had died; and the man had a daughter, and the woman had a daughter too. The girls knew each other and went out walking together, and afterwards came back to the woman's house.

Then she said to the man's daughter, "Listen: tell your father I should like to marry him, and then you shall wash in milk every morning and drink wine, while my own daughter washes in water and drinks water."

The girl went home and told her father what the woman had said. The man said, "What shall I do? Marriage is a joy, and it is also a torment."

At last, as he could not make up his mind, he pulled off his boot and said, "Take this boot — it has a hole in the sole. Go up to the loft with it, hang it on the big nail and pour water into it. If it holds the water, then I will take a wife again; and if it runs through, I won't."

The girl did as she was told; but the water drew the hole together and the boot filled up to the top. She told her father how it had turned out. Then he went up himself; and when he saw that she was right, he went to the widow and courted her, and the wedding was celebrated.

The next morning, when the two girls got up, there stood milk for the man's daughter to wash in and wine for her to drink; but for the woman's daughter there stood water to wash in and water to drink.

On the second morning there stood water for washing and water for drinking in front of the man's daughter just as in front of the woman's daughter.

And on the third morning there stood water for washing and water for drinking in front of the man's daughter, and milk for washing and wine for drinking in front of the woman's daughter; and so it went on.

The woman turned bitterly unkind to her stepdaughter, and did her best to treat her worse every day. She was envious as well, because her stepdaughter was beautiful and lovable and her own daughter ugly and disagreeable.

Once, in winter, when everything was frozen as hard as stone and hill and valley lay under snow, the woman made a frock out of paper, called her stepdaughter and said, "Here, put this dress on and go out into the wood and fetch me a little basketful of strawberries. I have a fancy for some."

"Good heavens," said the girl, "strawberries don't grow in winter. The ground is frozen, and the snow has covered everything besides. And why must I go in this paper frock? It's so cold outside that your very breath freezes. The wind will blow straight through it and the thorns will tear it off my body."

"Are you contradicting me again?" said the stepmother. "See that you go, and don't show your face here until you have the basketful of strawberries." Then she gave her a little piece of hard bread and said, "That will do you for the day" — and thought to herself, "You will die of cold and hunger out there and I shall never set eyes on you again."

So the girl did as she was told, put on the paper frock and went out with the basket. Far and wide there was nothing but snow, and not a green blade to be seen.

When she came into the wood she saw a little house with three dwarfs peeping out of it. She wished them good day and knocked modestly at the door. They called, "Come in" — and she went into the room and sat down on the bench by the stove and began to warm herself and eat her breakfast.

The little men said, "Give us some of it too."

"Gladly," she said, and broke her bit of bread in two and gave them half.

They asked, "What are you doing here in the forest in winter, in that thin dress?"

"Ah," she answered, "I have to find a basketful of strawberries, and I'm not to go home until I can take them with me."

When she had eaten her bread they gave her a broom and said, "Sweep the snow away at the back door with this."

But when she was outside, the three little men said to one another, "What shall we give her, since she is so good and has shared her bread with us?"

The first said, "My gift is that she shall grow more beautiful every day."

The second said, "My gift is that gold pieces shall fall out of her mouth every time she speaks."

The third said, "My gift is that a king shall come and take her for his wife."

Meanwhile the girl did as the little men had told her, swept the snow away behind the little house with the broom — and what should she find but real ripe strawberries, coming up dark red out of the snow! In her delight she quickly gathered her basket full, thanked the little men, shook hands with each of them, and ran home to bring her stepmother what she had wanted so badly.

When she went in and said good evening, a piece of gold fell out of her mouth at once. Then she told what had happened to her in the wood; but with every word she spoke gold pieces fell out of her mouth, until before long the whole room was covered with them.

"Just look at her showing off," cried the stepsister, "throwing gold about like that!" — but secretly she was envious, and wanted to go into the forest to look for strawberries too.

Her mother said, "No, my dear little daughter, it is too cold, you might freeze to death." But her daughter gave her no peace, so at last she gave in, made her a magnificent fur dress, which she had to put on, and gave her bread and butter and cake to take with her.

The girl went into the forest and straight up to the little house. The three little men peeped out again, but she did not greet them, and without so much as looking at them or speaking to them she blundered into the room, sat down by the stove and began to eat her bread and butter and cake.

"Give us some of it," cried the little men.

But she answered, "There isn't enough for me, so how am I supposed to give it away to other people?"

When she had finished eating they said, "There's a broom for you — sweep it all clean for us outside by the back door."

"Pooh, sweep for yourselves," she answered. "I'm not your servant."

And when she saw that they were not going to give her anything, she went out of the door.

Then the little men said to one another, "What shall we give her, since she is so ill-natured and has a wicked envious heart that will never let her do anybody a good turn?"

The first said, "I grant that she shall grow uglier every day."

The second said, "I grant that at every word she says a toad shall jump out of her mouth."

The third said, "I grant that she shall die a miserable death."

The girl looked for strawberries outside; but as she found none, she went home in a temper. And when she opened her mouth to tell her mother what had happened to her in the wood, at every word a toad jumped out of it, so that everybody was seized with disgust at her.

Then the stepmother was angrier than ever, and thought of nothing but how to do the man's daughter every possible injury — while the girl's beauty grew greater by the day.

At last she took a cauldron, set it on the fire and boiled yarn in it. When it was boiled she flung it over the poor girl's shoulder and gave her an axe, so that she could go out on the frozen river, cut a hole in the ice and rinse the yarn.

She did as she was told, went out and cut a hole in the ice; and while she was in the middle of her cutting, a splendid carriage came driving up with the King in it. The carriage stopped, and the King asked, "My child, who are you, and what are you doing here?"

"I am a poor girl, and I am rinsing yarn."

Then the King felt pity for her; and when he saw how very beautiful she was, he said, "Will you come away with me?"

"Ah yes, with all my heart," she answered — for she was glad to get away from her stepmother and stepsister.

So she got into the carriage and drove away with the King; and when they came to his palace the wedding was celebrated with great splendour, exactly as the little men had granted.

When a year had gone by, the young Queen bore a son; and as the stepmother had heard of her great good fortune, she came to the palace with her daughter and pretended she wanted to pay a visit. But once, when the King had gone out and there was nobody else there, the wicked woman seized the Queen by the head and her daughter seized her by the feet, and they lifted her out of bed and threw her out of the window into the stream that flowed past. Then the ugly daughter lay down in the bed, and the old woman covered her up over her head.

When the King came home and wanted to speak to his wife, the old woman cried, "Hush, hush, not now — she is in a heavy sweat, you must let her rest today."

The King suspected nothing, and did not come back until the next morning; and as he talked with his wife and she answered him, at every word a toad leapt out, where before a piece of gold had always fallen. So he asked what that could be; but the old woman said it came of the heavy sweating and would soon pass off.

But in the night the kitchen boy saw a duck come swimming up the gutter, and it said:

	"King, what are you doing now?
	Are you sleeping, or awake?"

And when he gave no answer, it said:

	"And my guests — what do they do?"

The kitchen boy said:

	"They are sleeping soundly too."

Then it asked again:

	"And my baby — what does she?"

He answered:

	"Sleeping in her cradle, she."

Then she went upstairs in the Queen's own shape, fed the baby, shook up its little bed, covered it over, and then swam away down the gutter again as a duck.

She came like that for two nights; and on the third she said to the kitchen boy, "Go and tell the King to take his sword and swing it three times over me on the threshold."

So the kitchen boy ran and told the King, who came with his sword and swung it three times over the spirit; and at the third time his wife stood before him, strong and living and healthy, just as she had been before.

At that the King was full of joy; but he kept the Queen hidden in a room until the Sunday, when the baby was to be christened. And when it had been christened, he said, "What does a person deserve who drags somebody out of bed and throws them in the water?"

"The wretch deserves nothing better," said the old woman, "than to be put in a barrel stuck full of nails and rolled downhill into the water."

"Then," said the King, "you have passed sentence on yourself."

And he ordered such a barrel to be brought, and the old woman put into it with her daughter; and then the lid was hammered on and the barrel was rolled downhill until it went into the river.

The Three Spinners

There was once a girl who was idle and would not spin; and whatever her mother said to her, she could not bring her to it. At last the mother was so overcome with anger and impatience one day that she beat her, and the girl began to cry loudly.

Now at that very moment the Queen drove past; and when she heard the crying she stopped her carriage, went into the house and asked the mother why she was beating her daughter so that the cries could be heard out on the road.

The woman was ashamed to tell anybody how lazy her daughter was, and said, "I can't get her to stop spinning. She insists on spinning for ever and ever, and I am poor and can't get hold of the flax."

Then the Queen answered, "There is nothing I like better to hear than spinning, and I am never happier than when the wheels are humming. Let me take your daughter with me to the palace. I have flax enough, and she shall spin there as much as she likes."

The mother was heartily glad of it, and the Queen took the girl away with her.

When they came to the palace she led her up to three rooms which were filled from floor to ceiling with the finest flax. "Now spin me this flax," she said, "and when you have done it you shall have my eldest son for a husband. I don't mind that you are poor — your tireless industry is dowry enough."

The girl was secretly terrified, because she could not have spun that flax — no, not if she had lived to be three hundred years old and sat at it every day from morning till night. So when she was alone she began to cry, and sat like that for three days without moving a finger.

On the third day the Queen came; and when she saw that nothing had been spun yet, she was surprised. But the girl excused herself by saying that she had not been able to start because she was so upset at leaving her mother's house. The Queen was satisfied with that, but said as she was going, "Tomorrow you must begin work."

When the girl was alone again she did not know what to do, and in her distress she went to the window. And there she saw three women coming towards her: the first had a broad flat foot; the second had such a great underlip that it hung down over her chin; and the third had a broad thumb.

They stopped in front of the window, looked up and asked the girl what was the matter with her. She told them her trouble, and then they offered her their help and said, "If you will invite us to the wedding, and not be ashamed of us, and call us your aunts, and seat us at your table, we will spin the flax up for you, and in a very short time too."

"With all my heart," she said. "Only come in and start the work at once."

So she let the three strange women in and cleared a space in the first room, where they sat down and began their spinning. One drew out the thread and trod the wheel, the second wetted the thread, the third twisted it and struck the table with her finger; and every time she struck it, a skein of thread fell to the floor, spun in the finest way possible.

The girl kept the three spinners hidden from the Queen, and every time she came showed her the great quantity of spun thread, until the Queen could not praise her enough. When the first room was empty they went to the second, and at last to the third, and that was soon cleared as well.

Then the three women took their leave and said to the girl, "Don't forget what you promised us. It will make your fortune."

When the girl showed the Queen the empty rooms and the great heap of yarn, she gave orders for the wedding; and the bridegroom was delighted that he was to have such a clever, hard-working wife, and praised her mightily.

"I have three aunts," said the girl, "and as they have been very good to me, I shouldn't like to forget them now that I have such good fortune. Let me invite them to the wedding, and let them sit with us at table."

The Queen and the bridegroom said, "Why should we not allow that?"

So when the feast began, the three women came in, dressed very strangely, and the bride said, "Welcome, dear aunts."

"Ah," said the bridegroom, "how do you come to have such hideous friends?"

And he went over to the one with the broad flat foot and said, "How did you come by such a broad foot?"

"By treading," she answered, "by treading."

Then the bridegroom went to the second and said, "How did you come by that hanging lip?"

"By licking," she answered, "by licking."

Then he asked the third, "How did you come by that broad thumb?"

"By twisting thread," she answered, "by twisting thread."

At that the King's son was alarmed, and said, "Neither now nor ever shall my beautiful bride touch a spinning wheel."

And so she was rid of the hateful flax-spinning.

Hansel and Gretel

At the edge of a great forest there lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children. The boy was called Hansel and the girl Gretel. He had little enough to eat at the best of times; and once, when a great famine came over the land, he could no longer even get their daily bread.

Lying in bed at night thinking about it, tossing and turning with worry, he groaned and said to his wife, "What is to become of us? How are we to feed our poor children when we have nothing even for ourselves?"

"I'll tell you what, husband," said the woman. "Early tomorrow morning we'll take the children out into the forest, to the thickest part of it. We'll light them a fire and give them each one more piece of bread, and then we'll go off to our work and leave them there. They won't find the way home again, and we shall be rid of them."

"No, wife," said the man, "I won't do it. How could I bear to leave my children alone in the forest? The wild animals would soon come and tear them to pieces."

"You fool," she said. "Then all four of us will starve, and you may as well start planing the boards for our coffins." And she gave him no peace until he agreed.

"But I do feel very sorry for the poor children, all the same," said the man.

The two children had not been able to sleep for hunger either, and had heard what their stepmother said to their father. Gretel wept bitter tears and said to Hansel, "Now it's all over with us."

"Be quiet, Gretel," said Hansel. "Don't upset yourself. I'll soon find a way to help us."

And when the old people had fallen asleep he got up, put on his little coat, opened the door downstairs and crept outside. The moon was shining brightly, and the white pebbles lying in front of the house glittered like real silver coins. Hansel bent down and put as many of them into his coat pocket as would go in.

Then he went back and said to Gretel, "Don't worry, dear little sister, and sleep in peace. God won't forsake us" — and he lay down in his bed again.

When day broke, before the sun had risen, the woman came and woke the two children. "Get up, you lazybones. We're going into the forest to fetch wood." She gave each of them a little piece of bread and said, "There's something for your dinner, but don't eat it before then, because you'll get nothing else."

Gretel put the bread under her apron, because Hansel had the stones in his pocket. Then they all set out together on the way to the forest.

When they had walked a little way, Hansel stopped and looked back at the house, and did it again and again.

His father said, "Hansel, what are you looking at back there, and why are you falling behind? Pay attention and don't forget how to use your legs."

"Ah, father," said Hansel, "I'm looking at my little white cat, sitting up on the roof and wanting to say goodbye to me."

The wife said, "Fool, that isn't your cat, that's the morning sun shining on the chimney."

But Hansel had not been looking at the cat at all. He had been dropping one of the white pebbles out of his pocket onto the road, over and over.

When they had come to the middle of the forest, the father said, "Now, children, gather some wood, and I'll light a fire so that you don't get cold."

Hansel and Gretel gathered brushwood into a pile as high as a little hill. The brushwood was lit; and when the flames were burning high, the woman said, "Now, children, lie down by the fire and rest. We're going into the forest to cut wood. When we've finished, we'll come back and fetch you."

Hansel and Gretel sat by the fire; and when noon came they each ate their little piece of bread. And as they could hear the strokes of an axe, they thought their father was nearby. But it was not an axe: it was a branch he had tied to a dead tree, which the wind was knocking backwards and forwards.

And as they had been sitting so long, their eyes closed with tiredness and they fell fast asleep. When at last they woke, it was already black night. Gretel began to cry and said, "How are we ever to get out of the forest now?"

But Hansel comforted her: "Just wait a little, until the moon has risen, and then we'll soon find the way."

And when the full moon had risen, Hansel took his little sister by the hand and followed the pebbles, which shone like newly minted silver and showed them the way.

They walked the whole night long, and at daybreak came back to their father's house. They knocked at the door; and when the woman opened it and saw that it was Hansel and Gretel, she said, "You wicked children, why did you sleep so long in the forest? We thought you were never coming back at all."

But their father was overjoyed, because it had cut him to the heart to leave them behind on their own.

Not long afterwards there was famine everywhere again, and the children heard their mother saying to their father in the night, "Everything is eaten up again. We have half a loaf left, and after that it's the end. The children must go. We'll take them further into the wood, so that they can't find their way out again. There's no other way of saving ourselves."

The man's heart was heavy, and he thought, "It would be better to share the last mouthful with your children." But the woman would not listen to anything he said; she scolded him and reproached him. Whoever says A must say B as well; and as he had given in the first time, he had to give in the second time too.

But the children were still awake and had heard the conversation. When the old people were asleep, Hansel got up again and wanted to go out and pick up pebbles as he had done before; but the woman had locked the door and he could not get out. All the same, he comforted his little sister and said, "Don't cry, Gretel. Go to sleep quietly. The good God will help us."

Early in the morning the woman came and got the children out of their beds. They were given their bit of bread, but it was even smaller than last time. On the way into the forest Hansel crumbled his in his pocket, and kept stopping to throw a crumb on the ground.

"Hansel, why do you keep stopping and looking round?" said his father. "Get along."

"I'm looking back at my little pigeon, sitting on the roof and wanting to say goodbye to me," answered Hansel.

"Simpleton," said the woman, "that isn't your pigeon, that's the morning sun shining on the chimney."

But little by little, Hansel dropped all his crumbs on the path.

The woman led the children still deeper into the forest, where they had never been in their lives before. Again a great fire was made, and the mother said, "Just sit there, children, and if you're tired you can sleep a little. We're going into the forest to cut wood, and this evening when we've finished we'll come and fetch you."

When it was noon Gretel shared her piece of bread with Hansel, who had scattered his along the way. Then they fell asleep; and the evening came and went, and nobody came for the poor children.

They did not wake until it was black night; and Hansel comforted his little sister and said, "Just wait, Gretel, until the moon rises, and then we shall see the breadcrumbs I scattered. They'll show us the way home."

When the moon came up they set off; but they found no crumbs, because the many thousands of birds that fly about the woods and the fields had picked them all up.

Hansel said to Gretel, "We'll soon find the way" — but they did not find it. They walked the whole night and the next day too, from morning till evening, and still they did not get out of the forest; and they were terribly hungry, because they had nothing to eat but a few berries growing on the ground. And when they were so tired that their legs would not carry them any further, they lay down under a tree and fell asleep.

It was now the third morning since they had left their father's house. They began walking again, but they only went deeper into the forest; and if help did not come soon they must die of hunger and exhaustion.

At midday they saw a beautiful snow-white bird sitting on a branch, singing so sweetly that they stood still and listened. And when it had finished its song it spread its wings and flew on ahead of them, and they followed it until they came to a little house, and it settled on the roof. And when they came right up to the little house, they saw that it was built of bread and roofed with cake, and the windows were of clear sugar.

"We'll set to work on that," said Hansel, "and have a proper meal. I'll eat a bit of the roof, and you can eat some of the window, Gretel — that will taste sweet."

Hansel reached up and broke off a bit of the roof to try how it tasted, and Gretel leaned against the window and nibbled at the panes. Then a soft voice called from inside:

	"Nibble, nibble, little mouse,
	who is nibbling at my house?"

The children answered:

	"The wind, the wind,
	the heavenly child" —

and went on eating without troubling themselves. Hansel, who found the roof very good indeed, tore down a great piece of it; and Gretel pushed a whole round pane out of the window, sat down and enjoyed herself with it.

Then suddenly the door opened, and a very, very old woman came creeping out, leaning on a crutch. Hansel and Gretel were so terrified that they dropped what they were holding.

But the old woman nodded her head and said, "Oh, you dear children, who brought you here? Do come in and stay with me. No harm shall come to you."

She took them both by the hand and led them into her little house. Then good food was set in front of them — milk and pancakes with sugar, apples and nuts. Afterwards two pretty little beds were made up with clean white linen, and Hansel and Gretel lay down in them and thought they were in heaven.

But the old woman had only pretended to be kind. In truth she was a wicked witch who lay in wait for children, and had built the little house of bread on purpose to lure them there. When a child came into her power she killed it, cooked it and ate it, and that was a feast day for her.

Witches have red eyes and cannot see far, but they have a keen sense of smell like animals, and know when a human being is coming near. When Hansel and Gretel came into her neighbourhood she laughed spitefully and said with a sneer, "I have them. They shan't escape me again."

Early in the morning, before the children were awake, she was up already; and when she saw the two of them sleeping and looking so pretty, with their plump red cheeks, she muttered to herself, "That will be a dainty mouthful."

Then she seized Hansel with her withered hand, carried him out to a little stable and shut him in behind a barred door. He could scream as much as he liked; it was no use.

Then she went to Gretel, shook her till she woke, and cried, "Get up, lazy thing, fetch water and cook something good for your brother. He's out in the stable, and he's to be fattened. When he's fat, I shall eat him."

Gretel began to weep bitterly, but it was all in vain; she had to do what the wicked witch told her.

And now the best food was cooked for poor Hansel, and Gretel got nothing but crab shells. Every morning the old woman crept out to the little stable and cried, "Hansel, stick out your finger, so that I can feel whether you'll soon be fat."

But Hansel used to stick out a little bone; and the old woman, whose eyes were dim, could not see it and thought it was Hansel's finger, and was astonished that he would not fatten.

When four weeks had gone by and Hansel was still thin, impatience got the better of her and she would not wait any longer. "Hey, Gretel," she called to the girl, "look sharp and fetch water. Fat or thin, tomorrow I'm going to kill Hansel and cook him."

Oh, how the poor little sister grieved as she carried the water, and how the tears ran down her cheeks! "Dear God, help us," she cried. "If only the wild beasts in the forest had eaten us, at least we should have died together."

"Just keep your noise to yourself," said the old woman. "None of it will help you."

Early in the morning Gretel had to go out and hang up the cauldron of water and light the fire. "We'll bake first," said the old woman. "I've heated the oven already and kneaded the dough." And she pushed poor Gretel out to the oven, with the flames already darting out of it.

"Creep in," said the witch, "and see whether it's properly heated, so that we can put the bread in."

And once Gretel was inside, she meant to shut the oven and let her bake in it, and then eat her too. But Gretel saw what she had in mind, and said, "I don't know how to do it. How do you get in?"

"Silly goose," said the old woman, "the opening is big enough — look, I could get in myself." And she hobbled up and stuck her head into the oven.

Then Gretel gave her a shove that drove her right inside, and slammed the iron door and shot the bolt. Oh, how horribly she began to howl! But Gretel ran away, and the godless witch was miserably burnt to death.

Gretel ran like lightning to Hansel, opened his little stable and cried, "Hansel, we're saved! The old witch is dead."

Then Hansel sprang out like a bird from a cage when the door is opened for it. How they rejoiced, and hugged each other, and danced about and kissed each other! And as they had nothing to fear from her any more, they went into the witch's house; and in every corner there stood chests full of pearls and jewels.

"These are much better than pebbles," said Hansel, and stuffed his pockets with as much as would go in; and Gretel said, "I'll take something home too," and filled her pinafore full.

"But now we'll go," said Hansel, "so that we get out of this witch's forest."

When they had walked for two hours they came to a great stretch of water. "We can't get across," said Hansel. "I can't see any stepping-plank or any bridge."

"And there's no boat either," answered Gretel. "But there's a white duck swimming there. If I ask her, she'll help us over." And she called:

	"Little duck, little duck, do you see
	Hansel and Gretel, waiting here?
	There's never a plank or a bridge in sight —
	carry us over on your back so white."

The duck came to them, and Hansel sat down on her back and told his sister to sit beside him.

"No," said Gretel, "that will be too heavy for the little duck. She shall take us across one after the other."

The good little duck did so; and when they were safely across and had walked a short way, the forest began to seem more and more familiar to them, and at last they saw their father's house in the distance. Then they began to run, and rushed into the parlour and threw themselves into their father's arms.

The man had not known one happy hour since he left the children in the forest; and the woman was dead.

Gretel shook out her pinafore until the pearls and precious stones went bouncing about the room, and Hansel threw one handful after another out of his pocket to join them. And so all their troubles were over, and they lived together in perfect happiness.

My tale is done; there runs a mouse; whoever catches it may make himself a great big fur cap out of it.

The Three Snake-Leaves

Once upon a time there was a poor man who could no longer support his only son.

So the son said, "Dear father, things are going so badly with us that I am a burden to you. I would rather go away and see how I can earn my own bread."

His father gave him his blessing and took leave of him with great sorrow.

At that time the King of a mighty empire was at war, and the young man took service with him and went out to fight. And when he came in front of the enemy there was a battle and great danger, and it rained shot until his comrades fell on every side; and when their commander was killed as well, the rest were about to run — but the young man stepped forward, spoke boldly to them, and cried, "We will not let our country be ruined!"

Then the others followed him, and he pressed on and defeated the enemy. And when the King heard that he owed the victory to him alone, he raised him above all the rest, gave him great treasures, and made him the first man in the kingdom.

The King had a daughter who was very beautiful, but very strange as well. She had made a vow to take no man for her lord and husband unless he promised to let himself be buried alive with her if she died first. "If he loves me with his whole heart," she said, "what use will life be to him afterwards?" And she would do the same on her side: if he died first, she would go down into the grave with him.

This strange oath had frightened off every suitor so far; but the young man became so enchanted by her beauty that he cared for nothing, and asked her father for her.

"But do you know what you must promise?" said the King.

"I must be buried with her," he answered, "if I outlive her. But my love is so great that I don't mind the danger."

So the King consented, and the wedding was celebrated with great splendour.

They lived happily and contentedly together for a while; and then it happened that the young Queen fell gravely ill, and no doctor could save her. And as she lay there dead, the young King remembered what he had been obliged to promise, and was horrified at having to lie down alive in the grave; but there was no escape. The King had set sentries at all the gates, and there was no avoiding his fate.

When the day came for the body to be buried, he was taken down into the royal vault with it, and then the door was shut and bolted.

Near the coffin stood a table with four candles on it, four loaves of bread and four bottles of wine; and when these ran out he would have to die of hunger. So he sat there full of pain and grief, ate only a little piece of bread each day and drank only a mouthful of wine, and all the same saw death coming nearer every day.

And while he sat staring in front of him, he saw a snake creep out of a corner of the vault and go towards the dead body. Thinking it had come to gnaw at her, he drew his sword and said, "As long as I am alive you shall not touch her," and cut the snake into three pieces.

After a while a second snake crept out of the hole; but when it saw the other lying dead and cut in pieces, it went back, and soon came again with three green leaves in its mouth. Then it took the three pieces of the snake, laid them together as they ought to go, and put one of the leaves on each wound. Immediately the severed parts joined together, the snake stirred and came alive again, and the two of them hurried away together, leaving the leaves lying on the ground.

Then it came into the mind of the unhappy man, who had been watching all this, to wonder whether the wonderful power of the leaves, which had brought the snake back to life, might not do the same for a human being. So he picked up the leaves and laid one of them on his dead wife's mouth and the other two on her eyes.

And hardly had he done it before the blood stirred in her veins, rose into her pale face and gave it colour again. Then she drew breath, opened her eyes and said, "Ah, God, where am I?"

"You are with me, dear wife," he answered; and he told her how it had all happened and how he had brought her back to life. Then he gave her some wine and bread; and when she had got her strength back he helped her up, and they went to the door and knocked and called so loudly that the sentries heard them and told the King.

The King came down himself and opened the door, and there he found them both strong and well, and rejoiced with them that all the sorrow was over.

But the young King took the three snake-leaves with him and gave them to a servant, saying, "Keep them for me carefully and carry them about with you always. Who knows what trouble they may yet get us out of?"

A change had come over his wife, though. After she had been brought back to life, it was as if all love for her husband had gone out of her heart. Some time later, when he wanted to make a voyage across the sea to visit his old father, and they had gone aboard a ship, she forgot the great love and faithfulness he had shown her, and which had rescued her from death, and took a wicked fancy to the captain.

And once, when the young King lay asleep, she called the captain in and took the sleeping man by the head, and the captain took him by the feet, and so they threw him down into the sea.

When the shameful thing was done, she said, "Now let us go home and say that he died on the way. I will praise you so highly to my father that he will marry me to you and make you heir to his crown."

But the faithful servant, who had seen everything they did without being seen himself, unfastened a little boat from the ship, got into it and rowed after his master, and let the traitors go on their way. He fished up the dead body, and with the help of the three snake-leaves he carried about with him, laid on the eyes and the mouth, he happily brought the young King back to life.

Then the two of them rowed with all their strength, day and night, and their little boat flew so fast that they reached the old King before the others did. He was astonished to see them come alone, and asked what had happened.

When he learned how wicked his daughter had been, he said, "I cannot believe she has behaved so badly; but the truth will soon come out" — and he told them both to go into a hidden room and keep out of everybody's sight.

Soon afterwards the great ship came sailing in, and the godless woman appeared before her father with a troubled face.

He said, "Why do you come back alone? Where is your husband?"

"Ah, dear father," she said, "I come home in great grief. On the voyage my husband suddenly fell ill and died, and if the good captain had not helped me it would have gone badly with me. He was there when he died and can tell you everything."

The King said, "I will bring the dead man back to life" — and he opened the room and told the two of them to come out.

When the woman saw her husband she was thunderstruck, and fell on her knees and begged for mercy.

The King said, "There is no mercy. He was ready to die with you and brought you back to life; and you murdered him in his sleep, and shall have the reward you deserve."

Then she was put with her accomplice into a ship that had been bored full of holes and sent out to sea, where they soon went down among the waves.

The White Snake

A long time ago there lived a king who was famous throughout the land for his wisdom. Nothing was hidden from him, and it seemed as though news of the most secret things was carried to him through the air.

But he had a strange custom. Every day after dinner, when the table had been cleared and nobody else was there, a trusted servant had to bring him one more dish. It was covered, though, and even the servant did not know what was in it; nor did anybody else, because the King never took the cover off to eat from it until he was quite alone.

This went on for a long time; and then one day the servant who took the dish away was overcome with such curiosity that he could not help carrying it into his own room. When he had carefully locked the door he lifted the cover, and saw a white snake lying on the dish. And at the sight of it he could not deny himself a taste, so he cut off a little piece and put it in his mouth.

No sooner had it touched his tongue than he heard a strange whispering of little voices outside his window. He went and listened, and found it was the sparrows chattering together, telling one another all sorts of things they had seen in the fields and woods. Eating the snake had given him the power of understanding the language of animals.

Now it happened that on that very day the Queen lost her most beautiful ring, and the suspicion of having stolen it fell on this trusted servant, who was allowed to go everywhere. The King had the man brought before him and threatened him angrily that unless he could name the thief by the next day, he would be counted guilty himself and executed. He declared his innocence in vain; he was sent away with no better answer.

In his trouble and fear he went down into the courtyard and tried to think how to help himself out of it. Now some ducks were sitting quietly together by a brook, resting; and while they smoothed their feathers with their bills they were having a confidential conversation. The servant stood by and listened.

They were telling one another about all the places they had waddled about in that morning and what good food they had found; and one said in a pitiful voice, "Something lies heavy on my stomach. I was eating in such a hurry that I swallowed a ring that was lying under the Queen's window."

The servant seized her by the neck at once, carried her into the kitchen and said to the cook, "Here's a fine duck — kill her, will you?"

"Yes," said the cook, weighing her in his hand. "She has spared no trouble fattening herself, and has been waiting to be roasted long enough."

So he cut off her head; and as she was being made ready for the spit, the Queen's ring was found inside her.

Now the servant could easily prove his innocence; and the King, to make up for the wrong, told him to ask a favour, and promised him the best position at court that he could wish for. The servant refused everything, and only asked for a horse and some money for travelling, as he had a mind to see the world and go about a little.

When his request had been granted he set out; and one day he came to a pond, where he saw three fish caught in the reeds and gasping for water. Now, although fish are said to be dumb, he heard them lamenting that they must die so miserably; and as he had a kind heart he got off his horse and put the three prisoners back into the water. They wriggled with delight, put out their heads and called to him, "We will remember you and repay you for saving us."

He rode on; and after a while it seemed to him that he heard a voice in the sand at his feet. He listened, and heard an ant-king complaining, "Why can't people keep their clumsy beasts off us? That stupid horse is treading my people down without mercy with his heavy hooves."

So he turned aside onto a side path, and the ant-king called after him, "We will remember you — one good turn deserves another."

The path led him into a wood, and there he saw two old ravens standing by their nest, throwing their young ones out. "Out with you, you idle good-for-nothings," they were crying. "We can't find food for you any longer. You're big enough to provide for yourselves."

But the poor young ravens lay on the ground flapping their wings and crying, "Oh, what helpless creatures we are! We're to shift for ourselves, and we can't even fly. What can we do but lie here and starve?"

So the good young man got down, killed his horse with his sword and gave it to them for food. Then they came hopping up, satisfied their hunger, and cried, "We will remember you — one good turn deserves another."

And now he had to use his own legs; and when he had walked a long way he came to a great city. There was a crowd and a great noise in the streets, and a man came riding up crying aloud, "The King's daughter wants a husband. But whoever asks for her hand must perform a hard task, and if he fails he forfeits his life."

Many had tried already, and all in vain; but when the young man saw the King's daughter he was so overcome by her great beauty that he forgot all the danger, went before the King and declared himself a suitor.

So he was led out to the sea, and a gold ring was thrown into it before his eyes; and the King ordered him to fetch this ring up from the bottom of the sea, and added, "If you come up again without it, you will be thrown back in, again and again, until you die among the waves."

All the people were sorry for the handsome young man; and then they went away and left him alone by the sea.

He stood on the shore wondering what to do, when suddenly he saw three fish come swimming towards him — and they were the very fish whose lives he had saved. The one in the middle held a mussel in its mouth, and laid it on the shore at his feet; and when he had picked it up and opened it, there lay the gold ring in the shell.

Full of joy he took it to the King, expecting him to grant the promised reward. But when the proud princess saw that he was not her equal in birth, she looked down on him and demanded that he perform another task first. She went down into the garden and scattered ten sackfuls of millet seed on the grass with her own hands, and then said, "Tomorrow morning before sunrise these must be picked up again, and not a single grain missing."

The young man sat down in the garden and tried to think how the task might be done; but he could think of nothing, and there he sat, sorrowfully waiting for daybreak, when he would be led out to die.

But as soon as the first rays of the sun shone into the garden, he saw all ten sacks standing side by side, quite full, and not a single grain missing. The ant-king had come in the night with many thousands of ants, and the grateful creatures had industriously picked up every grain of millet and gathered it into the sacks.

Presently the King's daughter came down into the garden herself, and was amazed to see that the young man had done what she set him. But she still could not conquer her proud heart, and said, "Although he has performed both tasks, he shall not be my husband until he brings me an apple from the Tree of Life."

The young man did not know where the Tree of Life stood, but he set out, and would have gone on for ever as long as his legs would carry him, though he had no hope of finding it. After he had wandered through three kingdoms, he came one evening to a wood and lay down under a tree to sleep.

But he heard a rustling in the branches, and a golden apple fell into his hand. At the same moment three ravens flew down to him, perched on his knee and said, "We are the three young ravens you saved from starving. When we had grown big and heard that you were looking for the Golden Apple, we flew over the sea to the end of the world, where the Tree of Life stands, and have brought you the apple."

Full of joy the young man set out for home, and took the Golden Apple to the King's beautiful daughter, who now had no excuses left. They cut the Apple of Life in two and ate it together; and then her heart filled with love for him, and they lived in undisturbed happiness to a great age.

The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean

In a village there lived a poor old woman who had collected a dish of beans and wanted to cook them. So she made a fire on her hearth, and to make it burn up quicker she lit it with a handful of straw.

When she was tipping the beans into the pan, one dropped without her noticing and lay on the floor beside a straw; and soon afterwards a burning coal jumped down out of the fire to join them.

Then the straw began, and said, "Dear friends, where have you come from?"

The coal answered, "I was lucky enough to leap out of the fire; and if I hadn't got out by main force I should certainly have died — I'd have been burnt to ashes."

The bean said, "I got away with a whole skin too. But if the old woman had got me into the pan, I'd have been made into broth without any mercy, like my companions."

"And would a better fate have come to me?" said the straw. "The old woman has destroyed all my brothers in fire and smoke. She grabbed sixty of them at once and took their lives. I slipped through her fingers by good luck."

"But what shall we do now?" said the coal.

"I think," said the bean, "that as we have all so luckily escaped death, we should stick together like good companions; and in case some fresh misfortune comes on us here, we should go away together and travel to a foreign country."

The other two liked the idea, and they set off together. Soon, though, they came to a little brook; and as there was no bridge and no plank across it, they did not know how they were to get over.

The straw hit on a good idea and said, "I'll lay myself straight across, and then you can walk over me as if I were a bridge."

So the straw stretched itself from one bank to the other; and the coal, who was of a hasty disposition, tripped quite boldly onto the newly built bridge. But when she got to the middle and heard the water rushing underneath, she took fright after all and stood still and dared not go any further. And the straw began to burn, broke in two and fell into the stream. The coal slipped after her, hissed as she hit the water, and breathed her last.

The bean, who had prudently stayed behind on the bank, could not help laughing at all this; and she could not stop, and laughed so heartily that she burst.

And that would have been the end of her too, if by good luck a tailor had not been travelling in search of work and sat down to rest by the brook. As he had a kind heart he took out his needle and thread and sewed her together again. The bean thanked him very prettily; but as the tailor had used black thread, all beans have had a black seam ever since.

The Fisherman and His Wife

Once upon a time there was a fisherman who lived with his wife in a miserable hovel close by the sea, and every day he went out fishing.

And once, as he sat with his rod looking into the clear water, his line went down, far down below; and when he pulled it up again he brought out a great flounder. And the flounder said to him, "Listen, fisherman, I beg you, let me live. I am no flounder really, but an enchanted prince. What good will it do you to kill me? I shouldn't be good to eat. Put me back in the water and let me go."

"Come," said the fisherman, "there's no need for so many words about it. A fish that can talk I would certainly let go anyway." And with that he put him back into the clear water, and the flounder went down to the bottom, leaving a long streak of blood behind him.

Then the fisherman got up and went home to his wife in the hovel.

"Husband," said the woman, "haven't you caught anything today?"

"No," said the man. "I did catch a flounder, who said he was an enchanted prince, so I let him go again."

"Didn't you wish for anything first?" said the woman.

"No," said the man. "What should I wish for?"

"Ah," said the woman, "it's hard having to live always in this dirty hovel. You might have wished for a little cottage for us. Go back and call him. Tell him we want a little cottage. He's sure to give us that."

"Ah," said the man, "why should I go there again?"

"Why," said the woman, "you caught him and you let him go again — he's sure to do it. Go at once."

The man still did not much want to go, but he did not want to cross his wife either, and he went to the sea.

When he got there the sea was all green and yellow and no longer smooth. So he stood still and said:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
