	wills not as I'd have her will."

Then the flounder came swimming up and said, "Well, what does she want, then?"

"Ah," said the man, "I did catch you, and my wife says I really ought to have wished for something. She doesn't want to live in a wretched hovel any longer. She would like a cottage."

"Go home, then," said the flounder. "She has it already."

When the man got home his wife was not in the hovel any more; in its place there stood a little cottage, and she was sitting on a bench in front of the door. She took him by the hand and said, "Just come inside. Look — now isn't this a great deal better?"

So they went in; and there was a little porch and a pretty little parlour and bedroom, a kitchen and a pantry, with the best of furniture and fitted out with beautiful things of tin and brass, everything anybody could want. And behind the cottage there was a little yard with hens and ducks, and a little garden with flowers and fruit.

"Look," said the wife, "isn't that nice?"

"Yes," said the husband, "and so we must always think it. Now we shall live quite contented."

"We'll think about that," said the wife.

With that they had something to eat and went to bed.

Everything went well for a week or a fortnight, and then the woman said, "Listen, husband, this cottage is much too small for us, and the garden and the yard are little. The flounder might just as well have given us a bigger house. I should like to live in a great stone castle. Go to the flounder and tell him to give us a castle."

"Ah, wife," said the man, "the cottage is quite good enough. Why should we live in a castle?"

"What!" said the woman. "Just go there — the flounder can always do it."

"No, wife," said the man, "the flounder has only just given us the cottage. I don't like to go back so soon; it might make him angry."

"Go," said the woman. "He can do it easily enough and will be glad to. Just you go to him."

The man's heart grew heavy and he did not want to go. He said to himself, "It isn't right" — and yet he went.

And when he came to the sea, the water was quite purple and dark blue and grey and thick, and no longer green and yellow; but it was still calm. And he stood there and said:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
	wills not as I'd have her will."

"Well, what does she want, then?" said the flounder.

"Alas," said the man, half frightened, "she wants to live in a great stone castle."

"Go to her, then. She is standing in front of the door," said the flounder.

So the man went off, meaning to go home; but when he got there he found a great stone palace, and his wife was standing at the top of the steps just going in. She took him by the hand and said, "Come inside."

So he went in with her; and in the castle there was a great hall paved with marble, and a crowd of servants who flung the doors wide open. The walls were all bright with beautiful hangings, and in the rooms were chairs and tables of pure gold, and crystal chandeliers hung from the ceilings; and all the rooms and bedrooms had carpets, and food and wine of the very best stood on all the tables, so that they nearly broke under it. Behind the house there was a great courtyard too, with stables for horses and cows and the very best of carriages; and there was a magnificent great garden with the most beautiful flowers and fruit trees, and a park a good half mile long with stags and deer and hares in it, and everything anybody could wish for.

"Come," said the woman, "isn't that beautiful?"

"Yes indeed," said the man. "Now let it be at that. We'll live in this beautiful castle and be content."

"We'll consider it," said the woman, "and sleep on it." And with that they went to bed.

Next morning the wife woke first. It was just daybreak, and from her bed she could see the beautiful country lying in front of her. Her husband was still stretching himself, so she poked him in the side with her elbow and said, "Get up, husband, and look out of the window. Couldn't we be King over all that land? Go to the flounder. We will be King."

"Ah, wife," said the man, "why should we be King? I don't want to be King."

"Well," said the wife, "if you won't be King, I will. Go to the flounder, because I mean to be King."

"Ah, wife," said the man, "why do you want to be King? I don't like to say that to him."

"Why not?" said the woman. "Go to him this instant. I must be King."

So the man went, and was thoroughly unhappy that his wife wanted to be King. "It isn't right, it isn't right," he thought. He did not want to go; but he went.

And when he came to the sea, it was quite dark grey, and the water heaved up from below and smelt foul. So he stood by it and said:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
	wills not as I'd have her will."

"Well, what does she want, then?" said the flounder.

"Alas," said the man, "she wants to be King."

"Go to her. She is King already."

So the man went; and when he came to the palace, the castle had grown much bigger, with a great tower and magnificent ornaments; and a sentry was standing in front of the door, and there were crowds of soldiers with kettledrums and trumpets. And when he went inside, everything was of real marble and gold, with velvet covers and great golden tassels. Then the doors of the hall were opened, and there was the whole court in its splendour; and his wife was sitting on a high throne of gold and diamonds with a great gold crown on her head and a sceptre of pure gold and jewels in her hand, and on either side of her stood her maids of honour in a row, each one a head shorter than the last.

Then he went and stood in front of her and said, "Ah, wife, so now you are King."

"Yes," said the woman, "now I am King."

So he stood and looked at her; and when he had looked at her a while he said, "And now that you are King, let everything else be. Now we shall wish for nothing more."

"No, husband," said the woman, quite restlessly, "the time hangs very heavy on me. I can't bear it any longer. Go to the flounder. I am King, but I must be Emperor too."

"Alas, wife, why do you want to be Emperor?"

"Husband," she said, "go to the flounder. I will be Emperor."

"Alas, wife," said the man, "he can't make you Emperor. I can't say such a thing to the fish. There is only one Emperor in the land. The flounder can't make you an Emperor — I promise you he can't."

"What!" said the woman. "I am King, and you are nothing but my husband. Will you go this minute? Go at once! If he can make a King he can make an Emperor. I will be Emperor. Go this instant."

So he had to go. But as he went he was troubled in his mind, and thought to himself, "This will not end well. It will not end well. Emperor is too shameless. The flounder will get tired of it in the end."

With that he came to the sea; and the sea was quite black and thick and began to boil up from below, so that it threw up bubbles, and such a sharp wind blew over it that it curdled; and the man was afraid. So he stood by it and said:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
	wills not as I'd have her will."

"Well, what does she want, then?" said the flounder.

"Alas, flounder," he said, "my wife wants to be Emperor."

"Go to her," said the flounder. "She is Emperor already."

So the man went; and when he got there the whole palace was of polished marble with alabaster figures and golden ornaments, and soldiers were marching up and down in front of the door blowing trumpets and beating cymbals and drums; and inside the house barons and counts and dukes were going about as servants. Then they opened the doors to him, and they were of pure gold.

And when he came in, there sat his wife on a throne made out of one solid piece of gold, and it was fully two miles high; and she wore a great golden crown three yards high, set with diamonds and rubies, and in one hand she held the sceptre and in the other the imperial orb. And on both sides of her stood the yeomen of the guard in two rows, each one smaller than the man before him, from the biggest giant, who was two miles high, down to the very smallest dwarf, no bigger than my little finger. And in front of them stood a great many princes and dukes.

Then the man went and stood among them and said, "Wife, are you Emperor now?"

"Yes," she said, "now I am Emperor."

So he stood and looked at her properly; and when he had looked at her a while he said, "Ah, wife, be content now that you are Emperor."

"Husband," she said, "why are you standing there? Now I am Emperor, but I will be Pope too. Go to the flounder."

"Alas, wife," said the man, "what will you not wish for next? You can't be Pope. There is only one in all Christendom. He can't make you Pope."

"Husband," she said, "I will be Pope. Go this moment. I must be Pope this very day."

"No, wife," said the man, "I don't like to say that to him. It won't do. It is too much. The flounder can't make you Pope."

"Husband," she said, "what nonsense! If he can make an Emperor he can make a Pope. Go to him directly. I am Emperor and you are nothing but my husband. Will you go at once?"

Then he was frightened, and went; but he felt quite faint, and shivered and shook, and his knees and his legs trembled under him. And a high wind was blowing over the land, and the clouds raced, and towards evening everything grew dark, and the leaves fell from the trees, and the water rose and roared as if it were boiling and beat upon the shore. And far off he saw ships firing their guns in their distress, pitching and tossing on the waves. And still there was a small patch of blue in the middle of the sky, though all round it was as red as a heavy storm.

So, full of despair, he went and stood there in great fear and said:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
	wills not as I'd have her will."

"Well, what does she want, then?" said the flounder.

"Alas," said the man, "she wants to be Pope."

"Go to her, then," said the flounder. "She is Pope already."

So he went; and when he got there he saw what seemed to be a great church surrounded by palaces. He pushed his way through the crowd. Inside, everything was lit up with thousands and thousands of candles, and his wife was dressed in gold and sitting on a far higher throne, with three great golden crowns on her head; and round about her was all the splendour of the Church, and on both sides of her stood a row of candles, the biggest as tall as the very tallest tower and the smallest no bigger than a kitchen candle; and all the emperors and kings were on their knees before her, kissing her shoe.

"Wife," said the man, looking at her carefully, "are you Pope now?"

"Yes," she said, "I am Pope."

So he stood and looked at her, and it was just as if he were looking into the bright sun. And when he had stood looking at her a little while, he said, "Ah, wife, if you are Pope, do let well alone."

But she sat as stiff as a post and did not move or give any sign of life.

Then he said, "Wife, now that you are Pope, be satisfied. There is nothing greater you can become now."

"I'll consider that," said the woman.

And with that they both went to bed; but she was not satisfied, and her greed would not let her sleep, because she was thinking all the time what there was left for her to be.

The man slept well and soundly, for he had run about a great deal that day; but the woman could not get to sleep at all, and flung herself from one side to the other the whole night through, thinking always what more there was left for her to be, and unable to think of anything.

At last the sun began to rise; and when the woman saw the red of the dawn she sat up in bed and looked at it. And when she saw the sun rising through the window she said, "Can't I make the sun and the moon rise too?"

"Husband," she said, poking him in the ribs with her elbows, "wake up. Go to the flounder. I want to be like God."

The man was still half asleep, but he was so horrified that he fell out of bed. He thought he must have misheard, and rubbed his eyes and said, "Alas, wife, what are you saying?"

"Husband," she said, "if I can't make the sun and the moon rise, and have to sit and watch the sun and the moon rising, I can't bear it. I shall never know another happy hour unless I can make them rise myself."

And she looked at him so terribly that a shudder ran through him, and said, "Go at once. I want to be like God."

"Alas, wife," said the man, falling on his knees in front of her, "the flounder can't do that. He can make an emperor and a pope. I beg you, stay as you are and be Pope."

Then she flew into a rage, and her hair went flying wildly about her head, and she cried, "I won't put up with it, I won't stand it any longer. Will you go?"

Then he pulled on his trousers and ran off like a madman. But outside a great storm was raging and blowing so hard that he could scarcely keep his feet. Houses and trees were toppling over, the mountains shook, rocks rolled into the sea, the sky was pitch black, and it thundered and lightened, and the sea came in with black waves as high as church towers and mountains, every one of them crested with white foam.

Then he cried out, and could not hear his own words:

	"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
	come, I beg you, here to me;
	for my wife, good Ilsabil,
	wills not as I'd have her will."

"Well, what does she want, then?" said the flounder.

"Alas," he said, "she wants to be like God."

"Go to her. You will find her back in the dirty hovel."

And there they are living to this very day.

The Valiant Little Tailor

One summer morning a little tailor was sitting on his table by the window, in good spirits and sewing with all his might. Along the street came a peasant woman crying, "Good jam, cheap! Good jam, cheap!"

That rang pleasantly in the tailor's ears. He put his delicate head out of the window and called, "Up here, my good woman — here's where you'll get rid of your goods."

The woman came up the three steps to the tailor with her heavy basket, and he made her unpack every one of the pots for him. He inspected them all, lifted them up, put his nose to them, and at last said, "The jam seems good to me. Weigh me out four ounces, my good woman — and if it comes to a quarter of a pound, that's no matter."

The woman, who had been hoping for a good sale, gave him what he asked for, but went off thoroughly annoyed and grumbling.

"Now, God bless this jam to my use," cried the little tailor, "and give me health and strength." And he fetched the bread out of the cupboard, cut himself a slice right across the loaf and spread the jam on it. "That won't taste bitter," he said, "but I'll just finish the jacket before I take a bite."

He laid the bread beside him, sewed away, and in his happiness made his stitches bigger and bigger.

Meanwhile the smell of the sweet jam went up the wall, where the flies were sitting in great numbers, and they were drawn to it and came down on it in swarms.

"Hey! Who invited you?" said the little tailor, and drove the uninvited guests away. But the flies, who understood no German, would not be driven off and came back in ever greater companies.

At last the little tailor lost all patience, got a scrap of cloth from the hole under his work table and, saying, "Wait, and I'll give it to you," struck at them without mercy. When he took the cloth away and counted, there lay no fewer than seven of them in front of him, dead, with their legs stretched out.

"Are you that sort of fellow?" he said, and could not help admiring his own bravery. "The whole town shall hear of this!"

And the little tailor hurriedly cut himself a belt, stitched it, and embroidered on it in big letters, "Seven at one stroke!"

"The town!" he went on. "The whole world shall hear of it!" And his heart wagged for joy like a lamb's tail.

The tailor put on the belt and resolved to go out into the world, because he thought his workshop was too small for such valour. Before he went, he hunted about the house to see whether there was anything he could take with him; but he found nothing except an old cheese, and that he put in his pocket. In front of the door he noticed a bird that had caught itself in a bush. That had to go into his pocket along with the cheese.

Then he took to the road boldly; and as he was light and nimble he felt no weariness. The road led him up a mountain; and when he had reached the highest point of it, there sat a powerful giant, looking about him quite comfortably.

The little tailor went up to him bravely and spoke to him: "Good day, friend. So there you sit, looking out over the wide world. I'm just on my way there myself, to try my luck. Have you any mind to come with me?"

The giant looked at the tailor contemptuously and said, "You ragamuffin! You miserable little creature!"

"Oh, indeed?" answered the little tailor, and unbuttoned his coat and showed the giant his belt. "There you may read what sort of a man I am."

The giant read, "Seven at one stroke," and supposed they had been men the tailor had killed, and began to feel a little respect for the tiny fellow. All the same, he thought he would test him first. He took a stone in his hand and squeezed it until water dripped out of it.

"Do the same," said the giant, "if you have the strength."

"Is that all?" said the tailor. "That's child's play where I come from." And he put his hand in his pocket, took out the soft cheese and squeezed it until the liquid ran out of it. "There," he said, "that was a bit better, wasn't it?"

The giant did not know what to say, and could not believe it of the little man. Then he picked up a stone and threw it so high that the eye could hardly follow it. "Now then, you mite of a man, do the same."

"Well thrown," said the tailor, "but after all, the stone came down to earth again. I'll throw you one that will never come back at all."

And he put his hand in his pocket, took out the bird and threw it into the air. The bird, delighted with its freedom, rose and flew away and did not come back.

"How do you like that shot, friend?" asked the tailor.

"You can throw, certainly," said the giant, "but now we'll see whether you can carry anything properly."

He took the little tailor to a mighty oak tree that lay felled on the ground and said, "If you're strong enough, help me carry this tree out of the forest."

"Gladly," said the little man. "You take the trunk on your shoulders, and I'll lift the branches and twigs — they're the heaviest part, after all."

The giant took the trunk on his shoulder, but the tailor sat himself down on a branch; and the giant, who could not look round, had to carry away the whole tree and the little tailor into the bargain. And the tailor behind was quite merry and happy, and whistled the song "Three tailors rode out at the gate," as if carrying the tree were child's play.

When the giant had dragged the heavy load part of the way he could go no further, and cried, "Look here, I shall have to drop the tree."

The tailor jumped nimbly down, took hold of the tree with both arms as if he had been carrying it all along, and said to the giant, "Such a big fellow as you, and you can't even carry a tree!"

They went on together; and as they were passing a cherry tree, the giant took hold of the top of it, where the ripest fruit was hanging, bent it down, put it into the tailor's hand and told him to eat. But the little tailor was far too weak to hold the tree; and when the giant let go, it sprang back and the tailor was whipped up into the air with it.

When he had come down again unhurt, the giant said, "What's this? Haven't you strength enough to hold a weak little branch?"

"There's no lack of strength," said the little tailor. "Do you suppose that would be anything to a man who struck down seven at one blow? I jumped over the tree because the huntsmen are shooting down there in the thicket. Jump it yourself, if you can."

The giant tried, but could not get over the tree and stuck fast in the branches; so the tailor kept the upper hand there too.

The giant said, "If you're such a valiant fellow, come with me to our cave and spend the night with us."

The little tailor was willing and went along. When they came into the cave, other giants were sitting there by the fire, each with a roasted sheep in his hand, eating it. The little tailor looked round and thought, "There's a good deal more room here than in my workshop."

The giant showed him a bed and told him to lie down in it and sleep. But the bed was too big for the little tailor; he did not lie down in it, but crept into a corner.

When it was midnight, and the giant thought the little tailor was sound asleep, he got up, took a great iron bar and cut the bed through with one blow, thinking he had finished off the grasshopper for good.

At the first light of dawn the giants went off into the forest, having quite forgotten the little tailor — when all at once he came walking up to them, perfectly cheerful and bold. The giants were terrified, and afraid that he would strike them all dead, and ran away in a great hurry.

The little tailor went on, always following his own sharp nose. After he had walked a long time he came to the courtyard of a royal palace; and as he was tired, he lay down on the grass and fell asleep.

While he lay there, people came and looked him over on all sides, and read on his belt, "Seven at one stroke."

"Ah," they said, "what is a great warrior doing here in the middle of peacetime? He must be a mighty lord."

They went and told the King about him, and gave it as their opinion that if war were to break out this would be a weighty and useful man, who ought on no account to be let go. The advice pleased the King, and he sent one of his courtiers to the little tailor to offer him a commission when he woke.

The messenger stood by the sleeper, waited until he stretched himself and opened his eyes, and then put the offer to him.

"That is the very reason I came here," said the tailor. "I am ready to enter the King's service."

So he was received with honour and given quarters of his own.

But the soldiers were set against the little tailor and wished him a thousand miles away. "What is to come of this?" they said among themselves. "If we quarrel with him and he lays about him, seven of us will fall at every blow. Not one of us can stand against him."

So they came to a decision, went in a body to the King and asked to be discharged. "We are not prepared," they said, "to stay with a man who kills seven at one stroke."

The King was sorry to lose all his faithful servants for the sake of one man, and wished he had never set eyes on the tailor, and would gladly have been rid of him again. But he did not dare dismiss him, for fear he should strike him and all his people dead and set himself on the royal throne.

He thought about it a long time, and at last hit on a plan. He sent to the little tailor to say that, as he was such a great warrior, he had one request to make of him. In a forest of his kingdom there lived two giants who did great damage with their robbing and murdering, their ravaging and burning, and nobody could go near them without risking his life. If the tailor conquered and killed these two giants, the King would give him his only daughter for a wife and half the kingdom for a dowry; and a hundred horsemen should go with him to help.

"That would be a fine thing for a man like me," thought the little tailor. "A man isn't offered a beautiful princess and half a kingdom every day of his life."

"Oh, yes," he answered, "I'll soon settle the giants, and I don't need a hundred horsemen to do it. A man who can kill seven at one blow needn't be afraid of two."

The little tailor set off, and the hundred horsemen followed him. When he came to the edge of the forest he said to his followers, "Just wait here — I'll soon finish off the giants by myself."

Then he sprang into the forest and looked about him, right and left. After a while he caught sight of the two giants. They lay asleep under a tree, snoring so that the branches swayed up and down.

The little tailor, not being idle, gathered two pocketfuls of stones and climbed up into the tree with them. When he was half way up he slipped along a branch until he was sitting just above the sleepers, and then let one stone after another drop onto the chest of one of the giants.

For a long time the giant felt nothing; but at last he woke, shoved his companion and said, "Why are you hitting me?"

"You must be dreaming," said the other. "I'm not hitting you."

They lay down to sleep again; and then the tailor dropped a stone onto the second one.

"What's the meaning of this?" cried the second. "Why are you pelting me?"

"I am not pelting you," growled the first.

They argued about it for a while; but as they were tired they let it drop, and their eyes closed again.

Then the little tailor began his game once more, picked out the biggest stone and threw it with all his strength onto the chest of the first giant.

"This is too much!" he cried, and sprang up like a madman and shoved his companion against the tree until it shook. The other paid him back in the same coin, and they got into such a rage that they tore up trees and belaboured each other with them so long that at last they both fell dead on the ground at the same moment.

Then the little tailor jumped down. "It's a lucky thing," he said, "that they didn't tear up the tree I was sitting in, or I'd have had to jump to another like a squirrel. But we tailors are nimble."

He drew his sword and gave each of them a couple of thrusts in the chest, and then went out to the horsemen and said, "The work is done. I've given them both their finishing stroke — but it was hard work. In their extremity they tore up trees and defended themselves with them; but none of that is any use when a man like me comes along, who can kill seven at one blow."

"Aren't you wounded?" asked the horsemen.

"Not at all," answered the tailor. "They haven't bent a hair of my head."

The horsemen would not believe him and rode into the forest; and there they found the giants swimming in their blood, with the torn-up trees lying all round about.

The little tailor demanded the promised reward from the King; but the King had repented of his promise and was thinking again how he could get rid of the hero.

"Before you have my daughter and half my kingdom," he said to him, "you must perform one more heroic deed. In the forest there roams a unicorn that does a great deal of harm, and you must catch it first."

"I'm even less afraid of one unicorn than of two giants. Seven at one blow — that's my line of business."

He took a rope and an axe with him, went out into the forest, and again told those who were sent with him to wait outside. He did not have to look long. The unicorn soon came at him, and rushed straight for him as if it meant to spit him on its horn without further ceremony.

"Steady, steady," he said. "It can't be done as fast as that." And he stood still and waited until the animal was quite close, and then sprang nimbly behind the tree.

The unicorn ran at the tree with all its might and drove its horn so fast into the trunk that it had not the strength to pull it out again, and so it was caught.

"Now I've got the bird," said the tailor; and he came out from behind the tree, put the rope round its neck, then chopped the horn out of the trunk with his axe; and when everything was ready he led the beast away and brought it to the King.

Even so the King would not give him the promised reward, and made a third demand. Before the wedding the tailor was to catch him a wild boar that was doing great damage in the forest, and the huntsmen should help him.

"Willingly," said the tailor. "That's child's play."

He did not take the huntsmen into the forest with him, and they were well pleased about it, because the wild boar had received them several times in a way that gave them no wish to lie in wait for him again.

When the boar caught sight of the tailor it ran at him with foaming mouth and gnashing tusks and was about to throw him to the ground; but the nimble hero sprang into a chapel that stood nearby, and up to the window in a moment, and out again at a single bound. The boar ran in after him; but the tailor ran round outside and shut the door behind it, and so the raging beast, which was far too heavy and clumsy to leap out of the window, was caught.

The little tailor called the huntsmen over, so that they could see the prisoner with their own eyes; and the hero went to the King, who now, whether he liked it or not, had to keep his promise, and gave him his daughter and half his kingdom. If he had known that it was no warrior hero but a little tailor standing in front of him, it would have gone to his heart even more than it did.

So the wedding was held with great magnificence and small joy, and out of a tailor a king was made.

Some time afterwards the young Queen heard her husband saying in his sleep at night, "Boy, make me that doublet and patch those trousers, or I'll rap the yardstick over your ears." Then she found out what sort of family the young lord had been born into; and next morning she complained to her father and begged him to help her get rid of a husband who was nothing but a tailor.

The King comforted her and said, "Leave your bedroom door open tonight. My servants shall stand outside; and when he has fallen asleep they shall go in, tie him up, and put him aboard a ship that will carry him away into the wide world."

The woman was satisfied with this. But the King's armour-bearer, who had heard it all, was friendly with the young lord and told him the whole plot.

"I'll put a stop to that," said the little tailor.

That night he went to bed with his wife at the usual time; and when she thought he had fallen asleep she got up, opened the door, and lay down again. The little tailor, who was only pretending to sleep, began to call out in a clear voice, "Boy, make me that doublet and patch me those trousers, or I'll rap the yardstick over your ears! I struck seven at one blow, I killed two giants, I led away a unicorn and I caught a wild boar — and am I to be afraid of the men standing outside my room?"

When those men heard the tailor talking like that, a great terror came over them and they ran as if the wild huntsman were behind them, and not one of them would venture anything further against him.

So the little tailor was a king, and remained one to the end of his life.

Cinderella

The wife of a rich man fell ill; and when she felt her end coming near she called her only daughter to her bedside and said, "Dear child, be good and pious, and then the good God will always protect you, and I will look down on you from heaven and be near you."

With that she closed her eyes and died. Every day the girl went out to her mother's grave and wept, and she stayed pious and good. When winter came the snow spread a white sheet over the grave; and when the spring sun had drawn it off again, the man had taken another wife.

The woman had brought two daughters into the house with her, who were beautiful and fair of face but vile and black-hearted. Now a bad time began for the poor stepchild.

"Is the stupid goose to sit in the parlour with us?" they said. "Whoever wants to eat bread must earn it. Out with the kitchen maid."

They took away her pretty clothes, put an old grey smock on her and gave her wooden shoes. "Just look at the proud princess, all dressed up," they cried, and laughed, and led her into the kitchen.

There she had to do heavy work from morning till night: get up before daybreak, carry water, light the fires, cook and wash. And on top of that the sisters did her every injury they could think of — they mocked her, and tipped her peas and lentils into the ashes so that she had to sit and pick them out again. In the evening, when she had worked until she was worn out, she had no bed to go to but had to sleep by the hearth in the ashes. And because that made her always look dusty and dirty, they called her Cinderella.

It happened once that the father was going to the fair, and he asked his two stepdaughters what he should bring back for them.

"Beautiful dresses," said one.

"Pearls and jewels," said the second.

"And you, Cinderella," he said, "what will you have?"

"Father, break off for me the first branch that knocks against your hat on the way home."

So he bought beautiful dresses and pearls and jewels for his two stepdaughters; and on the way home, as he was riding through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and knocked his hat off. So he broke off the branch and took it with him.

When he got home he gave his stepdaughters what they had asked for, and he gave Cinderella the branch from the hazel bush. Cinderella thanked him, went to her mother's grave and planted the branch on it, and wept so much that her tears fell on it and watered it. And it grew and became a fine tree. Three times a day Cinderella went and sat under it and wept and prayed; and a little white bird always came to the tree, and if Cinderella wished for anything, the bird threw down to her what she had wished for.

Now it happened that the King proclaimed a festival, to last three days, to which all the beautiful young girls in the country were invited, so that his son might choose a bride. When the two stepsisters heard that they were to appear among them, they were delighted, and called Cinderella and said, "Comb our hair for us, brush our shoes and fasten our buckles. We are going to the festival at the King's palace."

Cinderella did as she was told, but she wept, because she too would have liked to go to the dance; and she begged her stepmother to let her.

"You, Cinderella!" she said. "You're dusty and dirty, and you want to go to the festival? You have no clothes and no shoes, and you want to dance?"

But as Cinderella kept on asking, the stepmother said at last, "I have tipped a dish of lentils into the ashes for you. If you have picked them out again in two hours, you shall go with us."

The girl went out through the back door into the garden and called, "You tame pigeons, you turtle doves, and all you birds under the sky, come and help me to pick —

	the good ones into the pot,
	the bad ones into your crop."

Then two white pigeons came in at the kitchen window, and after them the turtle doves; and at last all the birds under the sky came whirring and crowding in and settled among the ashes. And the pigeons nodded their heads and began, pick, pick, pick, pick; and the rest began too, pick, pick, pick, pick, and gathered all the good grains into the dish. Hardly an hour had gone by before they had finished and all flew out again.

Then the girl took the dish to her stepmother, glad at heart, believing that now she would be allowed to go to the festival. But the stepmother said, "No, Cinderella. You have no clothes and you can't dance. You would only be laughed at."

And as Cinderella wept at this, the stepmother said, "If you can pick two dishes of lentils out of the ashes for me in one hour, you shall come with us" — and thought to herself, "She certainly can't do that."

When the stepmother had tipped the two dishes of lentils into the ashes, the girl went out through the back door into the garden and called, "You tame pigeons, you turtle doves, and all you birds under the sky, come and help me to pick —

	the good ones into the pot,
	the bad ones into your crop."

Then two white pigeons came in at the kitchen window, and after them the turtle doves; and at last all the birds under the sky came whirring and crowding in and settled among the ashes. And the doves nodded their heads and began, pick, pick, pick, pick; and the others began too, pick, pick, pick, pick, and gathered all the good seeds into the dishes. And before half an hour was over they had finished and all flew out again.

Then the girl carried the dishes to her stepmother, delighted, believing that now she might go to the festival. But the stepmother said, "None of this will help you. You are not coming with us, because you have no clothes and you can't dance. We should be ashamed of you."

And with that she turned her back on Cinderella and hurried off with her two proud daughters.

Now that nobody was at home, Cinderella went to her mother's grave under the hazel tree and called:

	"Shiver and quiver, little tree,
	throw gold and silver down on me."

Then the bird threw down a dress of gold and silver, and slippers embroidered with silk and silver. She put the dress on as fast as she could and went to the festival. Her stepsisters and her stepmother did not know her, and thought she must be some foreign princess, she looked so beautiful in the golden dress. They never once thought of Cinderella, and supposed she was sitting at home in the dirt picking lentils out of the ashes.

The prince came to meet her, took her by the hand and danced with her. He would dance with no other girl and never let go of her hand; and if anybody else came to ask her, he said, "This is my partner."

She danced until it was evening, and then she wanted to go home. But the King's son said, "I'll come with you and see you home" — because he wanted to see whose daughter the beautiful girl was. She got away from him, though, and sprang into the pigeon house.

The King's son waited until her father came, and then told him that the strange girl had jumped into the pigeon house. The old man thought, "Can it be Cinderella?" — and they had to bring him an axe and a pick so that he could chop the pigeon house to pieces; but there was nobody inside. And when they came home, Cinderella was lying in her dirty clothes among the ashes, with a dim little oil lamp burning on the mantelpiece; for Cinderella had jumped down quickly at the back of the pigeon house and run to the little hazel tree, and there she had taken off her beautiful clothes and laid them on the grave, and the bird had taken them away again, and then she had set herself down in the kitchen among the ashes in her grey gown.

Next day, when the festival began again and her parents and her stepsisters had gone, Cinderella went to the hazel tree and said:

	"Shiver and quiver, little tree,
	throw gold and silver down on me."

Then the bird threw down a dress far more beautiful than the day before. And when Cinderella appeared at the festival in this dress, everybody was astonished at her beauty. The King's son had been waiting until she came, and took her hand at once and danced with nobody but her. When others came and asked her, he said, "She is my partner."

When evening came she wanted to leave, and the King's son followed her, meaning to see which house she went into. But she sprang away from him and into the garden behind the house. In it stood a beautiful tall tree hung with the most magnificent pears. She climbed up among the branches as nimbly as a squirrel, and the King's son did not know where she had gone.

He waited until her father came and said to him, "The strange girl has escaped me, and I think she has climbed the pear tree."

The father thought, "Can it be Cinderella?" — and had an axe brought and cut the tree down; but there was nobody in it. And when they came into the kitchen, Cinderella was lying among the ashes as usual, for she had jumped down on the other side of the tree, taken the beautiful dress back to the bird on the little hazel tree, and put on her grey gown.

On the third day, when her parents and sisters had gone, Cinderella went once more to her mother's grave and said to the little tree:

	"Shiver and quiver, little tree,
	throw gold and silver down on me."

And now the bird threw down a dress more splendid and magnificent than any she had had yet, and the slippers were of gold. And when she came to the festival in that dress, nobody could find words for their astonishment. The King's son danced with her alone; and if anybody asked her to dance, he said, "She is my partner."

When evening came Cinderella wanted to leave, and the King's son was eager to go with her; but she got away from him so quickly that he could not follow. The King's son had used a trick, though: he had had the whole staircase smeared with pitch, and as she ran down, the girl's left slipper stuck fast in it. The King's son picked it up, and it was small and dainty and all of gold.

Next morning he went with it to the father and said, "Nobody shall be my wife but the one whose foot this golden slipper fits."

Then the two sisters were glad, because they had pretty feet. The eldest went into her room with the shoe to try it on, and her mother stood by. But she could not get her big toe in, and the shoe was too small for her. So her mother handed her a knife and said, "Cut the toe off. When you are Queen you won't need to go on foot any more."

The girl cut off her toe, forced her foot into the shoe, swallowed the pain and went out to the King's son. He took her up on his horse as his bride and rode away with her. But they had to pass the grave; and there on the hazel tree sat the two pigeons, crying:

	"Turn and peep, turn and peep,
	there's blood inside the shoe.
	The shoe is far too small for her;
	the true bride waits for you."

Then he looked at her foot and saw the blood streaming from it. He turned his horse round and took the false bride home again and said she was not the right one, and that the other sister must put the shoe on.

So she went into her room and got her toes safely into the shoe, but her heel was too big. Her mother handed her a knife and said, "Cut a piece off your heel. When you are Queen you won't need to go on foot any more."

The girl cut a piece off her heel, forced her foot into the shoe, swallowed the pain and went out to the King's son. He took her up on his horse as his bride and rode away with her; but as they passed the hazel tree the two little pigeons sat on it and cried:

	"Turn and peep, turn and peep,
	there's blood inside the shoe.
	The shoe is far too small for her;
	the true bride waits for you."

He looked down at her foot and saw the blood running out of the shoe and staining her white stocking red. Then he turned his horse and took the false bride home again.

"This isn't the right one either," he said. "Have you no other daughter?"

"No," said the man. "There's only a stunted little kitchen drudge my late wife left behind — but she can't possibly be the bride."

The King's son said he was to send her up to him; but the mother answered, "Oh no, she is much too dirty, she can't let herself be seen."

He absolutely insisted, though, and Cinderella had to be called. First she washed her hands and face clean, and then she came and bowed before the King's son, who handed her the golden shoe. She sat down on a stool, drew her foot out of the heavy wooden shoe and put it into the slipper — and it fitted like a glove.

And when she stood up and the King's son looked at her face, he knew her for the beautiful girl who had danced with him, and cried, "This is the true bride!"

The stepmother and the two sisters were horrified and turned pale with rage; but he took Cinderella up on his horse and rode away with her. As they passed the hazel tree the two white doves cried:

	"Turn and peep, turn and peep,
	no blood is in the shoe.
	The shoe is not too small for her;
	the true bride rides with you."

And when they had said it, the two came flying down and settled on Cinderella's shoulders, one on the right and the other on the left, and stayed sitting there.

When the wedding with the King's son was to be celebrated, the two false sisters came and wanted to get into Cinderella's good graces and share her good fortune. As the betrothed couple went to church, the elder was on the right and the younger on the left, and the pigeons pecked out one eye from each of them. Afterwards, as they came back, the elder was on the left and the younger on the right, and then the pigeons pecked out the other eye from each. And so, for their wickedness and their lying, they were punished with blindness as long as they lived.

The Riddle

There was once a King's son who was seized with a longing to travel about the world, and he took nobody with him but one faithful servant.

One day he came to a great forest; and when darkness came on he could find no shelter and did not know where to spend the night. Then he saw a girl going towards a little house; and when he came nearer he saw that she was young and beautiful. He spoke to her and said, "Dear child, can my servant and I find shelter for the night in that little house?"

"Oh yes," said the girl in a sad voice, "you certainly can, but I don't advise you to risk it. Don't go in."

"Why not?" asked the King's son.

The girl sighed and said, "My stepmother practises wicked arts. She means no good to strangers."

Then he saw plainly that he had come to a witch's house. But as it was dark and he could go no further, and he was not afraid either, he went in.

The old woman was sitting in an armchair by the fire, and looked at the stranger with her red eyes. "Good evening," she growled, and pretended to be quite friendly. "Sit down and rest yourselves." And she blew up the fire, on which she was cooking something in a little pot.

The daughter warned the two of them to be careful and to eat nothing and drink nothing, because the old woman brewed evil drinks. They slept quietly until early morning.

When they were making ready to leave, and the King's son was already on his horse, the old woman said, "Wait a moment, I'll fetch you a parting drink." And while she went to get it, the King's son rode off; so that the servant, who had stayed to buckle his saddle tight, was the only one there when the wicked witch came with the drink.

"Take that to your master," she said. But at that moment the glass broke and the poison spurted over the horse, and it was so strong that the animal dropped down dead on the spot.

The servant ran after his master and told him what had happened; but he did not want to leave his saddle behind, and ran back to fetch it. When he came to the dead horse, though, a raven was already sitting on it, eating.

"Who knows whether we shall find anything better today?" said the servant. So he killed the raven and took it with him.

And now they journeyed on into the forest all day long, but could not get out of it. By nightfall they came to an inn and went in. The servant gave the raven to the innkeeper to get ready for supper.

But they had stumbled on a den of murderers; and in the dark twelve of them came in, meaning to kill the strangers and rob them. Before they set about the work they sat down to supper, and the innkeeper and the witch sat down with them, and together they ate a dish of soup with the flesh of the raven cut up in it.

They had hardly swallowed a couple of mouthfuls, though, before they all fell down dead; for the raven had passed on to them the poison from the horseflesh.

There was nobody left in the house but the innkeeper's daughter, who was honest and had taken no part in their godless doings. She opened all the doors to the stranger and showed him the heaped-up treasures. But the King's son said she might keep the lot; he would have none of it; and he rode on with his servant.

After they had travelled about for a long time, they came to a town where there was a beautiful but proud princess, who had had it proclaimed that whoever could set her a riddle she could not solve should be her husband; but if she solved it, his head must be cut off. She had three days to guess it in; but she was so clever that she always found the answer to any riddle she was given before the time was up. Nine suitors had died in this way already, when the King's son arrived and, blinded by her great beauty, was willing to stake his life on it.

So he went to her and set her his riddle. "What is this?" he said. "One killed none, and yet killed twelve."

She did not know what it could be. She thought and thought, and could not find it out. She opened her riddle books, and it was not in them. In short, her wisdom was at an end.

As she could not help herself, she ordered her maid to creep into the gentleman's bedroom and listen to his dreams, thinking that perhaps he would talk in his sleep and give the riddle away. But the clever servant had put himself in the bed instead of his master; and when the maid came in he tore off the cloak she had wrapped herself in and chased her out with a stick.

The second night the King's daughter sent her lady-in-waiting, to see whether she would do better at listening; but the servant took her cloak away too and chased her out with a stick.

Now the master thought himself safe for the third night, and lay down in his own bed. And then the princess herself came, wrapped in a misty-grey cloak, and sat down beside him. And when she thought he was asleep and dreaming, she spoke to him and hoped he would answer in his sleep, as many people do. But he was awake, and understood and heard everything perfectly well.

Then she asked, "One killed none — what is that?"

He answered, "A raven, which ate of a dead and poisoned horse and died of it."

She asked further, "And yet killed twelve — what is that?"

He answered, "That means twelve murderers, who ate the raven and died of it."

When she knew the answer to the riddle she tried to steal away; but he held her cloak so fast that she had to leave it behind her.

Next morning the King's daughter announced that she had guessed the riddle, and sent for the twelve judges and explained it in front of them. But the young man asked for a hearing and said, "She crept into my room in the night and questioned me; otherwise she could never have found it out."

The judges said, "Bring us proof of that."

Then the servant brought in the three cloaks; and when the judges saw the misty-grey one that the King's daughter usually wore, they said, "Let that cloak be embroidered with gold and silver, and then it shall be your wedding cloak."

The Mouse, the Bird, and the Sausage

Once upon a time a mouse, a bird and a sausage went into partnership, kept house together, lived well and happily with one another, and increased their property wonderfully. The bird's work was to fly into the forest every day and bring back wood. The mouse had to carry water, light the fire and lay the table; but the sausage had to do the cooking.

Whoever is too well off is always longing for something new. So one day the bird met another bird on the way, and told it what excellent circumstances it was in, and boasted about them. But the other bird called it a poor simpleton for doing all the hard work, and said the two at home had an easy time of it. For when the mouse had made her fire and carried her water, she went into her little room to rest until they called her to lay the table; and the sausage stayed by the pot, saw that the food was cooking nicely, and when it was nearly dinner time rolled itself once or twice through the broth or the vegetables, and then they were buttered and salted and ready. And when the bird came home and put down his load, they sat down to dinner; and after they had eaten, they slept their fill till next morning. It was a splendid life.

Next day the bird, put up to it by the other one, would go into the wood no more. He said he had been their servant long enough and had been made a fool of by them, and that they must change round for once and try arranging it some other way. And although the mouse and the sausage begged him most earnestly, the bird would have his way and said it must be tried. They drew lots about it; and the lot fell so that the sausage was to carry wood, the mouse became cook, and the bird was to fetch water.

And what happened? The little sausage set off towards the wood; the little bird lit the fire; and the mouse stayed by the pot and waited alone for the little sausage to come home and bring wood for the next day.

But the little sausage stayed away so long on the road that the two of them were afraid something was wrong, and the bird flew out a little way into the air to meet it. Not far off, though, he met a dog on the road who had fallen on the poor sausage as fair game, seized it and swallowed it down. The bird accused the dog of barefaced robbery, but it was no use talking, because the dog said he had found forged papers on the sausage, and its life was forfeit to him on that account.

The bird sadly took up the wood, flew home and told what he had seen and heard. They were very much upset, but agreed to do their best and stay together. So the bird laid the cloth, and the mouse got the food ready and meant to dress it; and she wanted to get into the pot the way the sausage used to, and roll and creep about among the vegetables to mix them. But before she was well into the middle of them she was stopped, and lost her skin and her hair and her life in the attempt.

When the bird came to carry the dinner up, there was no cook there. In his distress the bird threw the wood about here and there, called and searched, but no cook was to be found. And through his carelessness the wood caught fire and the place burst into flames; and the bird hurried off to fetch water, and then the bucket slipped out of his claws into the well, and he fell in after it and could not get out again, but had to drown there.

Mother Holle

There was once a widow who had two daughters, one of them pretty and hard-working, the other ugly and idle. But she was much fonder of the ugly, idle one, because she was her own daughter; and the other, who was a stepdaughter, had to do all the work and be the household drudge.

Every day the poor girl had to sit by a well beside the road and spin, and spin until her fingers bled.

Now one day it happened that the shuttle was marked with her blood, so she dipped it into the well to wash the mark off; but it slipped out of her hand and fell to the bottom. She began to cry, and ran to her stepmother and told her what had happened. But the stepmother scolded her sharply, and was so merciless as to say, "Since you let the shuttle fall in, you can fetch it out again."

So the girl went back to the well and did not know what to do; and in the misery of her heart she jumped into the well to get the shuttle. She lost her senses; and when she came round again she was in a lovely meadow, with the sun shining and many thousands of flowers growing.

She walked on across this meadow and at last came to a baker's oven full of bread; and the bread cried out, "Oh, take me out, take me out, or I shall burn! I've been baking a long time." So she went up to it and took all the loaves out, one after another, with the bread shovel.

After that she went on, and came to a tree covered with apples, which called out to her, "Oh, shake me, shake me! We apples are all ripe." So she shook the tree until the apples fell like rain, and went on shaking until they were all down; and when she had gathered them into a heap, she went on her way.

At last she came to a little house, out of which an old woman was peeping. But she had such big teeth that the girl was frightened and was about to run away.

The old woman called out to her, though: "What are you afraid of, dear child? Stay with me. If you do all the housework properly, you shall be the better for it. Only you must take care to make my bed well and shake it thoroughly, until the feathers fly — because then it snows on the earth. I am Mother Holle."

As the old woman spoke to her so kindly, the girl took heart and agreed to enter her service. She saw to everything to her mistress's satisfaction, and always shook the bed so hard that the feathers flew about like snowflakes. And so she had a pleasant life with her: never an angry word, and boiled or roast meat every day.

She stayed some time with Mother Holle, and then she grew sad. At first she did not know what was the matter with her, but at last she found that it was homesickness. Although she was many thousand times better off here than at home, still she longed to be there.

At last she said to the old woman, "I am homesick; and however well off I am down here, I can't stay any longer. I must go up again to my own people."

Mother Holle said, "I am pleased that you long for home again; and as you have served me so faithfully, I will take you up myself."

With that she took her by the hand and led her to a great door. The door was opened; and just as the girl was standing under the doorway, a heavy shower of golden rain fell, and all the gold stuck to her, so that she was covered with it from head to foot.

"That is for you, because you have been so hard-working," said Mother Holle; and at the same time she gave her back the shuttle she had let fall into the well.

Then the door closed, and the girl found herself up above on the earth, not far from her mother's house. And as she came into the yard, the cock was standing by the well and crowed:

	"Cock-a-doodle-doo!
	Your golden girl's come back to you!"

So she went in to her mother; and as she arrived covered with gold like that, she was made welcome by both her mother and her sister.

The girl told everything that had happened to her; and as soon as the mother heard how she had come by so much wealth, she was very eager to get the same good luck for her ugly, lazy daughter. She had to sit by the well and spin; and so that her shuttle should be stained with blood, she stuck her hand into a thorn bush and pricked her finger. Then she threw the shuttle into the well and jumped in after it.

Like her sister, she came to the beautiful meadow and walked along the very same path. When she got to the oven, the bread cried out again, "Oh, take me out, take me out, or I shall burn! I've been baking a long time."

But the lazy thing answered, "As if I wanted to get myself dirty!" — and on she went.

Soon she came to the apple tree, which cried, "Oh, shake me, shake me! We apples are all ripe."

But she answered, "I like that! One of you might fall on my head" — and went on.

When she came to Mother Holle's house she was not afraid, because she had already heard about the big teeth, and she hired herself out to her at once.

The first day she made herself work hard and did what Mother Holle told her, because she was thinking about all the gold she would give her. But on the second day she began to be lazy, and on the third day lazier still, and then she would not get up in the morning at all. She did not make Mother Holle's bed properly either, and did not shake it so as to make the feathers fly.

Mother Holle was soon tired of this and gave her notice to leave. The lazy girl was quite willing to go, and thought that now the golden rain would come. Mother Holle led her to the great door too; but as she was standing under it, instead of the gold a great kettleful of pitch was emptied over her.

"That is the reward for your service," said Mother Holle, and shut the door.

So the lazy girl went home, but she was covered all over with pitch; and the cock by the well, as soon as he saw her, crowed:

	"Cock-a-doodle-doo!
	Your pitchy girl's come back to you!"

And the pitch stuck fast to her and could not be got off as long as she lived.

The Seven Ravens

There was once a man who had seven sons, and still no daughter, however much he wished for one. At last his wife gave him hope of another child; and when it came into the world it was a girl. There was great joy; but the child was sickly and small and had to be baptized privately because it was so weak.

The father sent one of the boys in a hurry to the spring to fetch water for the baptism. The other six went with him; and as each of them wanted to be the first to fill it, the jug fell into the well. There they stood and did not know what to do, and not one of them dared go home.

As they still did not come back, the father grew impatient and said, "They have certainly forgotten about it for some game, the wicked boys." He grew afraid that the girl would have to die unbaptized, and in his anger he cried, "I wish the boys were all turned into ravens."

Hardly was the word spoken before he heard a whirring of wings over his head in the air, looked up, and saw seven coal-black ravens flying away.

The parents could not take the curse back; and however sad they were at the loss of their seven sons, they comforted themselves to some extent with their dear little daughter, who soon grew strong and became more beautiful every day.

For a long time she did not know that she had had brothers, because her parents were careful not to mention them in front of her. But one day she happened to overhear some people saying about her that the girl was certainly beautiful, but that in truth she was to blame for the misfortune that had come on her seven brothers.

Then she was very much troubled, and went to her father and mother and asked whether it was true that she had had brothers, and what had become of them. Her parents did not dare keep the secret any longer, but said that what had happened to her brothers was the will of Heaven, and that her birth had only been the innocent cause of it.

But the girl took it to heart, day after day, and thought she must set her brothers free. She had no rest and no peace until she set out in secret and went off into the wide world to find her brothers and free them, whatever it cost. She took nothing with her but a little ring belonging to her parents, as a keepsake; a loaf of bread against hunger; a little jug of water against thirst; and a little stool in case she grew tired.

And now she went on and on, far, far away to the very end of the world. Then she came to the sun; but it was too hot and terrible, and it devoured little children. She ran away in a hurry and ran to the moon; but the moon was far too cold, and dreadful and spiteful as well, and when it saw the child it said, "I smell, I smell the flesh of a human being."

So she ran quickly away and came to the stars, who were kind and good to her, and each of them was sitting on its own little stool. And the morning star got up and gave her a chicken's leg bone and said, "Without this bone you cannot open the glass mountain, and it is in the glass mountain that your brothers are."

The girl took the bone, wrapped it up carefully in a cloth, and went on until she came to the glass mountain. The door was shut, and she meant to take out the bone; but when she undid the cloth it was empty, and she had lost the good star's present.

What was she to do now? She wanted to rescue her brothers, and had no key to the glass mountain. So the good sister took a knife, cut off one of her little fingers, put it in the door and managed to open it.

When she had gone inside, a little dwarf came to meet her and said, "My child, what are you looking for?"

"I am looking for my brothers, the seven ravens," she answered.

The dwarf said, "The lord ravens are not at home; but if you will wait here until they come, step inside."

Then the little dwarf carried in the ravens' dinner on seven little plates and in seven little glasses; and the little sister ate a morsel from each plate and took a sip from each glass; and into the last glass she dropped the ring she had brought with her.

Suddenly she heard a whirring of wings and a rushing through the air, and the little dwarf said, "Now the lord ravens are flying home."

Then they came, and wanted to eat and drink, and looked for their little plates and glasses. And one after another they said, "Who has been eating off my plate? Who has been drinking out of my glass? It was a human mouth."

And when the seventh came to the bottom of his glass, the ring rolled against his mouth. He looked at it and saw that it was a ring belonging to his father and mother, and said, "God grant that our sister may be here, and then we shall be free."

When the girl, who was standing behind the door and listening, heard that wish, she came out; and at once all the ravens got their human shape back again. And they hugged and kissed one another, and went joyfully home.

Little Red-Cap

Once upon a time there was a dear little girl who was loved by everybody who set eyes on her, but most of all by her grandmother, who would have given her anything in the world. Once she gave her a little cap of red velvet, which suited her so well that she would never wear anything else; and so she was always called Little Red-Cap.

One day her mother said to her, "Come, Little Red-Cap, here is a piece of cake and a bottle of wine. Take them to your grandmother — she is ill and weak and they will do her good. Set off before it gets hot; and when you're on your way, walk nicely and quietly and don't run off the path, or you may fall and break the bottle, and then your grandmother will get nothing. And when you go into her room, don't forget to say good morning, and don't go peeping into every corner first."

"I'll take great care," said Little Red-Cap to her mother, and shook hands on it.

The grandmother lived out in the wood, half a league from the village; and just as Little Red-Cap came into the wood, a wolf met her. Red-Cap did not know what a wicked creature he was, and was not at all afraid of him.

"Good day, Little Red-Cap," he said.

"Thank you kindly, wolf."

"Where are you off to so early, Little Red-Cap?"

"To my grandmother's."

"What have you got there under your apron?"

"Cake and wine. Yesterday was baking day, so my poor sick grandmother is to have something good to make her stronger."

"Where does your grandmother live, Little Red-Cap?"

"A good quarter of a league further on in the wood. Her house stands under the three big oak trees, with the nut trees just below. You must know it," said Little Red-Cap.

The wolf thought to himself, "What a tender young creature — what a nice plump mouthful. She'll be better eating than the old woman. I must go about it craftily, so as to catch them both."

So he walked along beside Little Red-Cap for a while, and then said, "Look, Little Red-Cap, at the pretty flowers all about here. Why don't you look round you? And I don't believe you hear how sweetly the little birds are singing. You walk along as solemnly as if you were going to school, and out here in the wood everything else is merry."

Little Red-Cap looked up; and when she saw the sunbeams dancing here and there among the trees, and pretty flowers growing everywhere, she thought, "Suppose I take grandmother a fresh bunch of flowers — that would please her too. It's so early in the day that I shall still get there in good time." And so she ran off the path into the wood to look for flowers. And whenever she had picked one, she thought she saw a prettier one further off and ran after it, and so got deeper and deeper into the wood.

Meanwhile the wolf ran straight to the grandmother's house and knocked at the door.

"Who's there?"

"Little Red-Cap," answered the wolf. "I've brought cake and wine. Open the door."

"Lift the latch," called the grandmother. "I'm too weak to get up."

The wolf lifted the latch, the door flew open, and without a word he went straight to the grandmother's bed and ate her up. Then he put on her clothes and her cap, lay down in the bed and drew the curtains.

Little Red-Cap, meanwhile, had been running about picking flowers; and when she had gathered so many that she could carry no more, she remembered her grandmother and set off on the way to her.

She was surprised to find the cottage door standing open; and when she came into the room she had such a strange feeling that she said to herself, "Oh dear, how uneasy I feel today — and other times I like being at grandmother's so much."

She called out, "Good morning," but got no answer. So she went to the bed and drew back the curtains. There lay her grandmother with her cap pulled far down over her face, and looking very strange.

"Oh, grandmother, what big ears you have!"

"The better to hear you with, my child."

"But, grandmother, what big eyes you have!"

"The better to see you with, my dear."

"But, grandmother, what big hands you have!"

"The better to hug you with."

"Oh, but grandmother, what a terrible big mouth you have!"

"The better to eat you with!"

And hardly had the wolf said it before he was out of bed at one bound and had swallowed up Red-Cap.

When the wolf had satisfied his appetite he lay down in the bed again, fell asleep and began to snore very loudly. The huntsman was just passing the house and thought, "How the old woman is snoring! I'd better see whether she wants anything."

So he went into the room; and when he came to the bed he saw the wolf lying in it. "Do I find you here, you old sinner?" he said. "I've been looking for you a long time."

Then, just as he was going to fire at him, it occurred to him that the wolf might have eaten the grandmother and that she might still be saved. So he did not fire, but took a pair of scissors and began to cut open the sleeping wolf's stomach. When he had made two snips he saw the little red cap shining; and when he had made two more, the little girl sprang out, crying, "Oh, how frightened I was! How dark it was inside the wolf!" And after that the old grandmother came out alive too, though she could scarcely breathe.

Then Red-Cap quickly fetched some great stones, and they filled the wolf's body with them; and when he woke up he tried to run away, but the stones were so heavy that he collapsed at once and fell down dead.

Then all three of them were delighted. The huntsman skinned the wolf and went home with the skin; the grandmother ate the cake and drank the wine Red-Cap had brought, and revived; but Red-Cap thought to herself, "As long as I live I will never leave the path and run off into the wood by myself again, when my mother has told me not to."

It is also told that once, when Red-Cap was taking cakes to the old grandmother again, another wolf spoke to her and tried to tempt her off the path. But Red-Cap was on her guard and went straight on her way, and told her grandmother that she had met the wolf, and that he had said good morning to her, but with such a wicked look in his eyes that if they had not been on the public road she was certain he would have eaten her up.

"Well," said the grandmother, "we'll shut the door, so that he can't get in."

Soon afterwards the wolf knocked and called, "Open the door, grandmother, I'm Little Red-Cap and I've brought you some cakes."

But they said nothing and did not open the door. So the grey-beard prowled round the house two or three times and at last jumped up onto the roof, meaning to wait until Red-Cap went home in the evening and then creep after her and eat her in the dark.

But the grandmother saw what he had in mind. In front of the house there was a great stone trough, so she said to the child, "Take the pail, Red-Cap. I boiled some sausages yesterday — carry the water I boiled them in out to the trough."

Red-Cap carried it until the great trough was quite full. Then the smell of the sausages reached the wolf, and he sniffed and peered down, and at last stretched his neck so far out that he could not keep his footing and began to slide, and slid off the roof straight into the great trough and was drowned.

And Red-Cap went home in high spirits, and nobody ever did her any harm.

The Bremen Town-Musicians

A certain man had a donkey which had carried sacks of corn to the mill tirelessly for many a long year; but his strength was failing and he was growing less and less fit for work. So his master began to consider how he could save the cost of feeding him. But the donkey, seeing that there was no good wind blowing, ran away and set out on the road to Bremen. "There," he thought, "I can surely be a town musician."

When he had walked a little way he found a hound lying in the road, panting like somebody who has run himself out.

"What are you panting like that for, you big fellow?" asked the donkey.

"Ah," said the hound, "because I'm old and getting weaker every day and can't hunt any more, my master wanted to kill me, so I ran for it. But how am I to earn my bread now?"

"I'll tell you what," said the donkey. "I'm going to Bremen to be a town musician there. Come with me and take a job as a musician too. I'll play the lute and you shall beat the kettledrum."

The hound agreed, and on they went.

Before long they came to a cat sitting by the road with a face like three rainy days.

"Now then, old whiskers, what's gone wrong with you?" asked the donkey.

"Who can be cheerful when his neck's in danger?" said the cat. "Because I'm getting old now, and my teeth are worn to stumps, and I'd rather sit by the fire and purr than go chasing about after mice, my mistress wanted to drown me. So I ran away. But good advice is scarce. Where am I to go?"

"Come to Bremen with us. You know all about night music — you can be a town musician."

The cat thought well of the idea and went with them.

After this the three runaways came to a farmyard, where the cock was sitting on the gate crowing with all his might.

"That crow of yours goes right through a man," said the donkey. "What's the matter?"

"I've been foretelling fine weather," said the cock, "because it's the day when Our Lady washes the Christ-child's little shirts and wants to dry them. But guests are coming for Sunday, so the mistress has no pity and has told the cook she means to eat me in the soup tomorrow, and this evening I'm to have my head cut off. So I'm crowing at full pitch while I still can."

"Ah, red-comb," said the donkey, "you'd do better to come away with us. We're going to Bremen. You can find something better than death anywhere. You have a good voice, and if we make music together it's bound to be something worth hearing."

The cock liked the plan, and all four went on together.

They could not reach the city of Bremen in one day, though; and in the evening they came to a forest where they meant to spend the night. The donkey and the hound lay down under a big tree, and the cat and the cock settled themselves in the branches — but the cock flew right to the top, where he was safest.

Before he went to sleep he looked round on all four sides, and thought he saw a little spark burning in the distance. So he called down to his companions that there must be a house not far off, because he could see a light.

The donkey said, "In that case we'd better get up and go on, because the lodgings here are bad." And the hound thought a few bones with some meat on them would do him no harm either.

So they made their way towards the light; and soon they saw it shining brighter and growing bigger, until they came to a well-lit robbers' house.

The donkey, as the tallest, went to the window and looked in.

"What do you see, old grey horse?" asked the cock.

"What do I see?" said the donkey. "A table covered with good things to eat and drink, and robbers sitting round it enjoying themselves."

"That would be the sort of thing for us," said the cock.

"Yes indeed. Ah, how I wish we were there," said the donkey.

Then the animals put their heads together to work out how they could drive the robbers away, and at last they hit on a plan. The donkey was to put his forefeet up on the window ledge, the hound was to jump on the donkey's back, the cat was to climb up on the dog, and last of all the cock was to fly up and perch on the cat's head.

When that was done, at a given signal, they began to perform their music together: the donkey brayed, the hound barked, the cat mewed and the cock crowed. Then they burst in through the window into the room, so that the glass went clattering.

At this horrible din the robbers sprang up, thinking it could be nothing but a ghost coming in, and fled in great terror out into the forest.

Then the four companions sat down at the table, well satisfied with what was left, and ate as if they were going to fast for a month.

As soon as the four minstrels had finished, they put out the light and each looked for a sleeping place to suit his own nature. The donkey lay down on some straw in the yard, the hound behind the door, the cat on the hearth near the warm ashes, and the cock perched on a roof beam; and as they were tired from their long walk, they soon fell asleep.

When it was past midnight, and the robbers saw from a distance that the light was no longer burning in their house and everything seemed quiet, the captain said, "We shouldn't have let ourselves be frightened out of our wits" — and ordered one of them to go and examine the house.

The messenger found everything still, and went into the kitchen to light a candle; and, taking the cat's glittering fiery eyes for live coals, he held a match to them to light it. But the cat did not see the joke and flew at his face, spitting and scratching.

He was dreadfully frightened and ran for the back door; but the dog, who was lying there, sprang up and bit him in the leg. And as he ran across the yard past the straw heap, the donkey gave him a smart kick with his hind foot. And the cock, who had been woken by the noise and was thoroughly lively by now, called down from the beam, "Cock-a-doodle-doo!"

Then the robber ran back to his captain as fast as he could and said, "Ah, there's a horrible witch sitting in the house, who spat at me and scratched my face with her long claws; and by the door there's a man with a knife, who stabbed me in the leg; and out in the yard there's a black monster lying, who hit me with a wooden club; and up on the roof sits the judge, who called out, 'Bring the rascal here to me!' So I got away as best I could."

After that the robbers never dared go into the house again; but it suited the four Bremen musicians so well that they never cared to leave it.

And the mouth of the man who last told this story is still warm.

The Singing Bone

In a certain country there was once great grief on account of a wild boar which laid waste the farmers' fields, killed the cattle, and ripped people's bodies open with its tusks. The King promised a large reward to anybody who would rid the land of this plague; but the beast was so big and so strong that nobody dared go near the forest it lived in. At last the King announced that whoever captured or killed the wild boar should have his only daughter for a wife.

Now there lived in that country two brothers, the sons of a poor man, who declared themselves willing to undertake the dangerous business: the elder, who was crafty and cunning, out of pride; the younger, who was innocent and simple, out of kindness of heart.

The King said, "So that you may be the surer of finding the beast, you must go into the forest from opposite sides." So the elder went in on the west side and the younger on the east.

When the younger had gone a little way, a little man came up to him. He had a black spear in his hand, and he said, "I give you this spear because your heart is pure and good. With this you can attack the wild boar boldly, and it will do you no harm."

He thanked the little man, shouldered the spear and went on without fear.

Before long he saw the beast, which rushed at him; but he held the spear out towards it, and in its blind fury it ran so hard against the point that its heart was split in two. Then he took the monster on his back and set off home with it to the King.

As he came out on the other side of the wood, there stood a house at the edge of it where people were making merry with wine and dancing. His elder brother had gone in there; and, thinking that the boar was not going to run away from him after all, he meant to drink until he felt brave.
