But when he saw his young brother coming out of the wood loaded with his prize, his envious, evil heart gave him no peace.

He called out to him, "Come in, dear brother, rest and refresh yourself with a cup of wine."

The young man, suspecting nothing, went in and told him about the good little man who had given him the spear he had killed the boar with.

The elder brother kept him there until the evening, and then they went away together. And when they came in the darkness to a bridge over a brook, the elder brother let the other go first; and when he was half way across he struck him such a blow from behind that he fell down dead.

He buried him under the bridge, took the boar and carried it to the King, pretending that he had killed it; and so he got the King's daughter in marriage. And when his younger brother did not come back he said, "The boar must have killed him" — and everybody believed it.

But as nothing stays hidden from God, this black deed too was to come to light.

Years afterwards a shepherd was driving his flock across the bridge, and saw a snow-white little bone lying in the sand below. He thought it would make a good mouthpiece, so he climbed down and picked it up and cut a mouthpiece for his horn out of it. But when he blew through it for the first time, to his great astonishment the bone began, of its own accord, to sing:

	"Ah, friend, you're blowing on my bone.
	Long have I lain here by the water.
	My brother killed me for the boar,
	and took for his wife the King's own daughter."

"What a wonderful horn," said the shepherd. "It sings by itself. I must take it to my lord the King."

And when he came with it to the King, the horn began to sing its little song again. The King understood it all, and had the ground below the bridge dug up, and the whole skeleton of the murdered man came to light. The wicked brother could not deny the deed, and was sewn up in a sack and drowned; but the bones of the murdered man were laid to rest in a beautiful tomb in the churchyard.

The Devil With the Three Golden Hairs

There was once a poor woman who gave birth to a little son; and as he came into the world with a caul on his head, it was foretold that in his fourteenth year he would have the King's daughter for his wife.

It happened that soon afterwards the King came into the village, and nobody knew that he was the King; and when he asked the people what news there was, they answered, "A child has just been born with a caul on. Whatever anybody born like that undertakes turns out well. And it is prophesied too that in his fourteenth year he will have the King's daughter for his wife."

The King, who had a bad heart and was angry about the prophecy, went to the parents and, seeming perfectly friendly, said, "You poor people, let me have your child and I will take care of it."

At first they refused; but when the stranger offered them a great deal of gold for it, and they thought, "It's a luck-child, and everything is bound to turn out well for it," they agreed at last and gave him the child.

The King put it in a box and rode away with it until he came to a deep stretch of water; and then he threw the box in and thought, "I have rid my daughter of a suitor she never asked for."

But the box did not sink. It floated like a boat, and not a drop of water got into it. And it floated to within two miles of the King's capital city, where there was a mill, and came to a stop at the mill dam.

A miller's boy who happened by good luck to be standing there noticed it and pulled it out with a hook, thinking he had found a great treasure. But when he opened it, there lay a pretty boy inside, quite fresh and lively. He took him to the miller and his wife; and as they had no children they were glad, and said, "God has given him to us." They took great care of the foundling, and he grew up good in every way.

It happened once, in a storm, that the King went into the mill, and asked the mill folk whether the tall lad was their son.

"No," they said, "he's a foundling. Fourteen years ago he came floating down to the mill dam in a box, and the mill boy pulled him out of the water."

Then the King knew that it was none other than the luck-child he had thrown into the water, and he said, "My good people, could the lad not take a letter to the Queen for me? I'll give him two gold pieces as a reward."

"Just as the King commands," they answered, and told the boy to make himself ready.

Then the King wrote a letter to the Queen, in which he said, "As soon as the boy arrives with this letter, let him be killed and buried; and let it all be done before I come home."

The boy set out with this letter; but he lost his way, and in the evening came to a great forest. In the darkness he saw a small light, and went towards it and came to a cottage. When he went in, an old woman was sitting by the fire all alone. She started when she saw the boy, and said, "Where do you come from, and where are you going?"

"I come from the mill," he answered, "and I want to go to the Queen, to take her a letter. But I've lost my way in the forest, and I should like to stay here overnight."

"You poor boy," said the woman, "you have come into a den of thieves, and when they get home they will kill you."

"Let them come," said the boy. "I'm not afraid. But I'm so tired that I can't go any further." And he stretched himself out on a bench and fell asleep.

Soon afterwards the robbers came, and asked angrily what strange boy that was lying there.

"Ah," said the old woman, "it's an innocent child who has lost himself in the forest, and I let him in out of pity. He has a letter to take to the Queen."

The robbers opened the letter and read it, and in it was written that the boy was to be put to death as soon as he arrived. Then the hard-hearted robbers felt pity, and their leader tore the letter up and wrote another, saying that as soon as the boy came he was to be married at once to the King's daughter. Then they let him lie quietly on the bench until the next morning; and when he woke they gave him the letter and showed him the right road.

And the Queen, when she had received the letter and read it, did as it said. She had a splendid wedding feast prepared, and the King's daughter was married to the luck-child; and as the young man was handsome and pleasant, she lived with him in joy and contentment.

After some time the King came back to his palace and saw that the prophecy had been fulfilled and the luck-child married to his daughter.

"How has this come about?" he said. "I gave quite different orders in my letter."

So the Queen gave him the letter and said he could see for himself what was written in it. The King read the letter and saw perfectly well that it had been changed for another. He asked the young man what had become of the letter entrusted to him, and why he had brought a different one instead.

"I know nothing about it," he answered. "It must have been changed in the night, when I was asleep in the forest."

The King said in a rage, "You shan't have things quite so much your own way. Whoever marries my daughter must fetch me three golden hairs from the Devil's head, out of hell. Bring me what I want, and you shall keep my daughter." In this way the King hoped to be rid of him for good.

But the luck-child answered, "I'll fetch the golden hairs. I'm not afraid of the Devil." And with that he took his leave of them and began his journey.

The road led him to a large town, where the watchman at the gate asked him what his trade was and what he knew.

"I know everything," answered the luck-child.

"Then you can do us a favour," said the watchman, "if you'll tell us why our market fountain, which once ran with wine, has gone dry and doesn't even give water any more."

"You shall know that," he answered. "Only wait till I come back."

Then he went further and came to another town, and there too the gatekeeper asked him what his trade was and what he knew.

"I know everything," he answered.

"Then you can do us a favour and tell us why a tree in our town that once bore golden apples doesn't so much as put out leaves now."

"You shall know that," he answered. "Only wait till I come back."

Then he went on and came to a wide river which he had to cross. The ferryman asked him what his trade was and what he knew.

"I know everything," he answered.

"Then you can do me a favour," said the ferryman, "and tell me why I have to row backwards and forwards for ever and am never set free."

"You shall know that," he answered. "Only wait till I come back."

When he had crossed the water he found the entrance to hell. Inside it was black and sooty, and the Devil was not at home, but his grandmother was sitting in a great armchair.

"What do you want?" she said to him — but she did not look so very wicked.

"I should like three golden hairs from the Devil's head," he answered, "or I can't keep my wife."

"That's a great deal to ask," she said. "If the Devil comes home and finds you here, it will cost you your life. But as I'm sorry for you, I'll see whether I can't help you."

She turned him into an ant and said, "Creep into the folds of my dress; you'll be safe there."

"Yes," he answered, "so far so good. But there are three other things I want to know: why a fountain that once ran with wine has gone dry and doesn't even give water; why a tree that once bore golden apples doesn't so much as put out leaves; and why a ferryman must go backwards and forwards for ever and is never set free."

"Those are difficult questions," she answered. "But just keep quiet and still, and pay attention to what the Devil says when I pull the three golden hairs out."

As the evening came on, the Devil came home. He had hardly got in before he noticed that the air was not pure. "I smell human flesh," he said. "Something's not right here." And he pried into every corner and searched, but could find nothing.

His grandmother scolded him. "It's just been swept," she said, "and everything put in order, and now you're turning it all upside down again. You've always got human flesh in your nose. Sit down and eat your supper."

When he had eaten and drunk he was tired, and laid his head in his grandmother's lap, and before long he was fast asleep, snoring and breathing heavily. Then the old woman took hold of a golden hair, pulled it out and laid it down beside her.

"Ow!" cried the Devil. "What are you doing?"

"I had a bad dream," said the grandmother, "so I caught hold of your hair."

"What did you dream, then?" said the Devil.

"I dreamed that a fountain in a market place, which once ran with wine, had dried up, and not even water would come out of it. What's the cause of that?"

"Oho, if they only knew," answered the Devil. "There's a toad sitting under a stone in the well. If they killed it, the wine would flow again."

He went to sleep again and snored until the windows shook. Then she pulled the second hair out.

"Hey! What are you doing?" cried the Devil angrily.

"Don't take it badly," she said. "I did it in my sleep."

"What have you dreamed this time?"

"I dreamed that in a certain kingdom there stood an apple tree which had once borne golden apples, and now wouldn't even bear leaves. What do you suppose was the reason?"

"Oh, if they only knew," answered the Devil. "There's a mouse gnawing at the root. If they killed it they'd have golden apples again; but if it gnaws much longer the tree will wither away altogether. Now leave me alone with your dreams. If you disturb me in my sleep again you'll get a box on the ear."

The grandmother spoke gently to him until he fell asleep again and snored. Then she took hold of the third golden hair and pulled it out. The Devil jumped up, roared out and would have handled her roughly if she had not quieted him once more and said, "Who can help bad dreams?"

"What was the dream, then?" he asked, and was quite curious.

"I dreamed about a ferryman who complained that he has to ferry from one bank to the other for ever and is never released. What's the cause of that?"

"Ah, the fool," answered the Devil. "When somebody comes along and wants to cross, he must put the oar in his hand, and then the other man will have to do the ferrying and he'll be free."

As the grandmother had now pulled out the three golden hairs and had her three questions answered, she left the old serpent alone, and he slept until daybreak.

When the Devil had gone out again, the old woman took the ant out of the folds of her dress and gave the luck-child his human shape back. "There are the three golden hairs for you," she said. "And I suppose you heard what the Devil said to your three questions?"

"Yes," he answered, "I heard, and I'll take care to remember."

"Then you have what you wanted," she said, "and you can go your way."

He thanked the old woman for helping him in his need, and left hell well pleased that everything had turned out so happily.

When he came to the ferryman, he was expected to give the promised answer. "Ferry me across first," said the luck-child, "and then I'll tell you how you can be set free." And when he reached the other bank he gave him the Devil's advice: "Next time somebody comes who wants to be ferried over, just put the oar in his hand."

He went on and came to the town where the barren tree stood, and there too the watchman wanted his answer. So he told him what he had heard from the Devil: "Kill the mouse that is gnawing at its root, and it will bear golden apples again." The watchman thanked him, and gave him two donkeys loaded with gold as a reward, which followed him.

At last he came to the town whose well was dry. He told the watchman what the Devil had said: "There is a toad in the well under a stone. You must find it and kill it, and the well will give wine in plenty again." The watchman thanked him, and gave him two donkeys loaded with gold as well.

And at last the luck-child got home to his wife, who was heartily glad to see him again and to hear how well everything had gone with him. He took the King what he had asked for, the Devil's three golden hairs; and when the King saw the four donkeys loaded with gold he was quite content, and said, "Now all the conditions are met and you can keep my daughter. But tell me, dear son-in-law, where did all that gold come from? This is tremendous wealth."

"I was rowed across a river," he answered, "and got it there. It lies on the shore there instead of sand."

"Can I fetch some of it too?" said the King, and was quite eager about it.

"As much as you like," he answered. "There's a ferryman on the river. Let him ferry you over, and you can fill your sacks on the other side."

The greedy King set out in all haste; and when he came to the river he beckoned to the ferryman to put him across. The ferryman came and told him to get in; and when they reached the other bank he put the oar in his hand and sprang out.

And from that time on the King had to do the ferrying, as a punishment for his sins.

Is he ferrying still? If he is, it is because nobody has taken the oar from him.

The Louse and the Flea

A louse and a flea kept house together and were brewing beer in an eggshell. Then the little louse fell in and scalded herself. At that the little flea began to scream loudly.

Then the little room door said, "Little flea, why are you screaming?"

"Because the louse has scalded herself."

Then the little door began to creak. At that a little broom in the corner said, "Why are you creaking, little door?"

"Haven't I reason to creak?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping."

So the little broom began to sweep furiously. Then a little cart came past and said, "Why are you sweeping, little broom?"

"Haven't I reason to sweep?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping,
	the little door is creaking."

So the little cart said, "Then I will run" — and began to run wildly. Then the ash heap it ran past said, "Why are you running like that, little cart?"

"Haven't I reason to run?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping,
	the little door is creaking,
	the little broom is sweeping."

The ash heap said, "Then I will burn furiously" — and began to burn with clear flames. A little tree stood near the ash heap and said, "Ash heap, why are you burning?"

"Haven't I reason to burn?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping,
	the little door is creaking,
	the little broom is sweeping,
	the little cart is running."

The little tree said, "Then I will shake myself" — and began to shake herself so hard that all her leaves fell off. A girl who came up with her water pitcher saw it and said, "Little tree, why are you shaking yourself?"

"Haven't I reason to shake myself?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping,
	the little door is creaking,
	the little broom is sweeping,
	the little cart is running,
	the little ash heap is burning."

At that the girl said, "Then I will break my little water pitcher" — and she broke her little water pitcher. Then the little spring the water ran from said, "Girl, why are you breaking your water jug?"

"Haven't I reason to break my water jug?

	The little louse has scalded herself,
	the little flea is weeping,
	the little door is creaking,
	the little broom is sweeping,
	the little cart is running,
	the little ash heap is burning,
	the little tree is shaking itself."

"Oho," said the spring, "then I will begin to flow" — and it began to flow violently. And everything was drowned in the water: the girl, the little tree, the little ash heap, the little cart, the broom, the little door, the little flea and the little louse, all together.

The Girl Without Hands

A certain miller had little by little fallen into poverty, and had nothing left but his mill and a big apple tree behind it.

Once, when he had gone into the forest to fetch wood, an old man he had never seen before came up to him and said, "Why do you plague yourself with cutting wood? I will make you rich, if you will promise me what is standing behind your mill."

"What can that be but my apple tree?" thought the miller; and he said yes, and gave the stranger a promise in writing.

But the stranger laughed mockingly and said, "When three years have gone by I shall come and carry away what is mine" — and then he went off.

When the miller got home his wife came to meet him and said, "Tell me, miller, where has this sudden wealth in our house come from? All at once every box and chest is full. Nobody brought anything in, and I don't know how it happened."

He answered, "It comes from a stranger who met me in the forest and promised me great treasure. In return I promised him what stands behind the mill. We can very well let him have the big apple tree for it."

"Oh, husband," said his wife in terror, "that must have been the Devil. He didn't mean the apple tree — he meant our daughter, who was standing behind the mill sweeping the yard."

The miller's daughter was a beautiful, pious girl, and she lived through the three years in the fear of God and without sin. So when the time was up, and the day came when the Evil One was to fetch her, she washed herself clean and drew a circle round herself with chalk.

The Devil appeared very early, but he could not come near her. He said angrily to the miller, "Take all the water away from her, so that she can't wash herself any more; otherwise I have no power over her."

The miller was afraid, and did it. Next morning the Devil came again, but she had wept on her hands and they were perfectly clean. Again he could not get near her, and he said furiously to the miller, "Cut her hands off, or I can't get the better of her."

The miller was horrified and answered, "How could I cut off my own child's hands?"

Then the Evil One threatened him and said, "If you don't do it, you are mine and I shall take you yourself."

The father took fright and promised to obey. So he went to the girl and said, "My child, if I don't cut off both your hands the Devil will carry me off, and in my terror I promised to do it. Help me in my need, and forgive me the harm I do you."

She answered, "Dear father, do what you like with me. I am your child."

And with that she laid down both her hands and let them be cut off.

The Devil came for the third time; but she had wept so long and so much on the stumps that they too were perfectly clean. So he had to give in, and had lost all right over her.

The miller said to her, "Through you I have come into such great wealth that I will keep you in the greatest comfort as long as you live."

But she answered, "I cannot stay here. I will go out into the world; compassionate people will give me as much as I need."

So she had her maimed arms bound behind her back, and at sunrise she set out and walked the whole day until night fell.

Then she came to a royal garden, and by the shimmer of the moon she saw that trees covered with beautiful fruit grew in it. But she could not get in, because there was a moat of water all round it. And as she had walked the whole day and not eaten a mouthful, and hunger tormented her, she thought, "Ah, if only I were inside, so that I could eat some of the fruit! Otherwise I shall die of hunger."

Then she knelt down and called on God the Lord, and prayed. And suddenly an angel came to her, who made a dam in the water so that the moat went dry and she could walk through it.

So she went into the garden, and the angel went with her. She saw a tree covered with beautiful pears, but they had all been counted. She went up to it and, to still her hunger, ate one of them with her mouth off the tree, but no more.

The gardener was watching; but as the angel was standing there he was afraid, and thought the girl was a spirit, and said nothing, and did not dare to call out or to speak to the spirit. When she had eaten the pear she was satisfied, and went and hid herself among the bushes.

The King, whose garden it was, came down to it next morning, and counted, and saw that one of the pears was missing, and asked the gardener what had become of it, since it was not lying under the tree but was simply gone.

The gardener answered, "Last night a spirit came in, with no hands, and ate one of the pears off with its mouth."

The King said, "How did the spirit get across the water, and where did it go after it had eaten the pear?"

The gardener answered, "Somebody in a snow-white garment came from heaven and dammed the water and held it back, so that the spirit could walk through the moat. And as it must have been an angel, I was afraid, and asked no questions and did not call out. When the spirit had eaten the pear, it went back again."

The King said, "If it is as you say, I will watch with you tonight."

When it grew dark the King came into the garden and brought a priest with him, who was to speak to the spirit. All three sat down under the tree and watched.

At midnight the girl came creeping out of the thicket, went to the tree and again ate one pear off it with her mouth; and beside her stood the angel in white.

Then the priest came out to them and said, "Do you come from heaven or from earth? Are you a spirit or a human being?"

She answered, "I am no spirit, but an unhappy mortal deserted by everybody but God."

The King said, "If you are forsaken by all the world, I will not forsake you."

He took her home with him to his royal palace; and as she was so beautiful and so good he loved her with all his heart, and had silver hands made for her, and married her.

After a year the King had to go to war, so he entrusted his young Queen to his mother's care and said, "If she is brought to bed, take care of her, nurse her well, and let me know of it at once by letter."

Then she gave birth to a fine boy. So the old mother hurried to write and tell him the joyful news. But the messenger rested by a brook on the way, and as he was tired out by the great distance, he fell asleep. And the Devil came, who was always looking for a way to injure the good Queen, and changed the letter for another, in which it was written that the Queen had brought a monster into the world.

When the King read the letter he was shocked and very much distressed, but he wrote back that they were to take great care of the Queen and nurse her well until he came home. The messenger went back with the letter, but rested in the same place and again fell asleep. And the Devil came once more and put a different letter in his pocket, in which it was written that they were to put the Queen and her child to death.

The old mother was horrified when she got the letter and could not believe it. She wrote to the King again, but got no other answer, because each time the Devil substituted a false letter; and in the last letter it was written as well that she was to keep the Queen's tongue and eyes as proof that she had obeyed.

But the old mother wept to think of such innocent blood being shed, and had a hind brought in the night and cut out its tongue and eyes and kept them.

Then she said to the Queen, "I cannot have you killed as the King commands; but you cannot stay here any longer. Go out into the wide world with your child, and never come back here again."

The poor woman tied her child on her back and went away with her eyes full of tears. She came into a great wild forest, and there she fell on her knees and prayed to God; and the angel of the Lord appeared to her and led her to a little house with a sign on it that said, "Here all dwell free."

A snow-white girl came out of the little house and said, "Welcome, my lady Queen" — and led her inside. Then they untied the little boy from her back and held him to her breast to feed, and laid him in a beautifully made little bed.

Then the poor woman said, "How did you know that I was a queen?"

The white girl answered, "I am an angel sent by God to watch over you and your child."

The Queen stayed seven years in the little house and was well looked after; and by God's grace, because of her piety, the hands that had been cut off grew again.

At last the King came home from the war, and his first wish was to see his wife and the child. Then his aged mother began to weep and said, "You wicked man, why did you write to me that I was to take those two innocent lives?" And she showed him the two letters the Evil One had forged, and went on, "I did as you told me" — and she showed him the tokens, the tongue and the eyes.

Then the King began to weep for his poor wife and his little son so much more bitterly than she was weeping, that the old mother took pity on him and said, "Be comforted — she is still alive. I secretly had a hind killed and took the tokens from it; but I tied the child on your wife's back and told her to go out into the wide world, and made her promise never to come back here, because you were so angry with her."

Then the King said, "I will go as far as the sky is blue, and I will neither eat nor drink until I have found my dear wife and my child again — if they have not been killed or died of hunger in the meantime."

So the King travelled about for seven long years and looked for her in every cleft of the rocks and every cave, and did not find her, and thought she must have died of want. During the whole of that time he neither ate nor drank, but God kept him alive.

At length he came into a great forest and found in it the little house with the sign, "Here all dwell free." Out came the white girl, took him by the hand, led him in and said, "Welcome, my lord King" — and asked him where he came from.

He answered, "I have been travelling about for nearly seven years now, looking for my wife and her child, and I cannot find them."

The angel offered him food and drink, but he would take nothing and only wanted to rest a little. So he lay down to sleep, and put a handkerchief over his face.

Then the angel went into the room where the Queen was sitting with her son, whom she usually called Sorrowful, and said to her, "Go out with your child. Your husband has come."

So she went to the place where he was lying, and the handkerchief fell off his face. Then she said, "Sorrowful, pick up your father's handkerchief and cover his face again."

The child picked it up and put it over his face again. The King heard it in his sleep, and enjoyed letting the handkerchief fall once more. But the child grew impatient and said, "Dear mother, how can I cover my father's face when I have no father in this world? I have learned to say the prayer 'Our Father, which art in Heaven'; you told me my father was in Heaven and was the good God — and how can I know a wild man like this? He isn't my father."

When the King heard that, he got up and asked who they were.

Then she said, "I am your wife, and this is your son, Sorrowful."

And he saw her living hands and said, "My wife had silver hands."

She answered, "The good God has made my own hands grow again" — and the angel went into the inner room and brought out the silver hands and showed them to him.

Then he knew for certain that it was his dear wife and his dear child, and he kissed them and was glad, and said, "A heavy stone has fallen from my heart."

Then the angel of God gave them one meal with her; and after that they went home to the King's aged mother. There were great rejoicings everywhere, and the King and Queen were married again and lived contentedly to their happy end.

Clever Hans

Hans's mother said, "Where are you off to, Hans?"

Hans answered, "To Gretel."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"Oh, I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What have you brought that's good?"

"I've brought nothing. I want to be given something."

Gretel gives Hans a needle. Hans says, "Goodbye, Gretel."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans takes the needle, sticks it into a hay cart and follows the cart home.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took nothing. Had something given me."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"Gave me a needle."

"Where is the needle, Hans?"

"Stuck it in the hay cart."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have stuck the needle in your sleeve."

"Never mind, I'll do better next time."

"Where are you off to, Hans?"

"To Gretel, mother."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"Oh, I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What have you brought that's good?"

"I've brought nothing. I want to be given something."

Gretel gives Hans a knife. "Goodbye, Gretel."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans takes the knife, sticks it in his sleeve and goes home.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took her nothing. She gave me something."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"Gave me a knife."

"Where is the knife, Hans?"

"Stuck in my sleeve."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have put the knife in your pocket."

"Never mind, I'll do better next time."

"Where are you off to, Hans?"

"To Gretel, mother."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"Oh, I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?"

"I've brought nothing. I want something given me."

Gretel gives Hans a young goat. "Goodbye, Gretel."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans takes the goat, ties its legs and puts it in his pocket. By the time he gets home it has smothered.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took nothing. She gave me something."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"She gave me a goat."

"Where is the goat, Hans?"

"Put it in my pocket."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have put a rope round the goat's neck."

"Never mind, I'll do better next time."

"Where are you off to, Hans?"

"To Gretel, mother."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"Oh, I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?"

"I've brought nothing. I want something given me."

Gretel gives Hans a piece of bacon. "Goodbye, Gretel."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans takes the bacon, ties it to a rope and drags it along behind him. The dogs come and eat the bacon. When he gets home he has the rope in his hand and there is nothing on the end of it.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took her nothing. She gave me something."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"Gave me a bit of bacon."

"Where is the bacon, Hans?"

"Tied it to a rope, brought it home, dogs took it."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have carried the bacon on your head."

"Never mind, I'll do better next time."

"Where are you off to, Hans?"

"To Gretel, mother."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?"

"I've brought nothing, but I'd like something given me."

Gretel gives Hans a calf. "Goodbye, Gretel."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans takes the calf, puts it on his head, and the calf kicks him in the face.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took nothing, but had something given me."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"A calf."

"Where have you got the calf, Hans?"

"Set it on my head and it kicked my face."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have led the calf and put it in the stall."

"Never mind, I'll do better next time."

"Where are you off to, Hans?"

"To Gretel, mother."

"Behave yourself, Hans."

"I'll behave. Goodbye, mother."

"Goodbye, Hans."

Hans comes to Gretel. "Good day, Gretel."

"Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?"

"I've brought nothing, but I'd like something given me."

Gretel says to Hans, "I'll come with you myself."

Hans takes Gretel, ties her to a rope, leads her to the manger and ties her up fast. Then Hans goes to his mother.

"Good evening, mother."

"Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?"

"With Gretel."

"What did you take her?"

"Took her nothing."

"What did Gretel give you?"

"She gave me nothing. She came with me."

"Where have you left Gretel?"

"Led her by the rope, tied her to the manger and scattered some grass for her."

"That was badly done, Hans. You should have cast friendly eyes on her."

"Never mind, I'll do better."

Hans went into the stable, cut out all the calves' and the sheep's eyes and threw them in Gretel's face. Then Gretel got angry, tore herself loose and ran away — and became the bride of Hans.

The Three Languages

There once lived an aged count in Switzerland who had an only son; but the son was stupid and could learn nothing.

So the father said, "Listen to me, my son. I can get nothing into your head, try as I may. You must go away from here. I will put you in the care of a famous master, who shall see what he can do with you."

The young man was sent to a strange town and stayed a whole year with the master. At the end of that time he came home again, and his father asked, "Now, my son, what have you learned?"

"Father, I have learned what the dogs say when they bark."

"Lord have mercy on us!" cried the father. "Is that all you have learned? I will send you to another town, to another master."

The young man was taken there and stayed a year with this master too. When he came back his father asked again, "My son, what have you learned?"

He answered, "Father, I have learned what the birds say."

Then the father flew into a rage and said, "Oh, you lost creature, you have spent all that precious time and learned nothing! Aren't you ashamed to come before my eyes? I will send you to a third master; but if you learn nothing this time either, I will be your father no longer."

The young man stayed a whole year with the third master as well; and when he came home again and his father asked, "My son, what have you learned?" — he answered, "Dear father, this year I have learned what the frogs croak."

Then the father fell into the most furious rage, sprang up, called his people in and said, "This man is no son of mine. I drive him out, and I order you to take him into the forest and kill him."

They took him out; but when it came to killing him, they could not do it for pity, and let him go; and they cut the eyes and tongue out of a deer to carry to the old man as proof.

The young man wandered on, and after a while came to a fortress where he begged for a night's lodging.

"Yes," said the lord of the castle, "if you will spend the night down there in the old tower, go and do it; but I warn you, it is at the risk of your life, because it is full of wild dogs that bark and howl without stopping, and at certain hours a man has to be given to them, and they devour him at once."

The whole district was in grief and dismay because of them, and yet nobody could do anything about it.

The young man, though, was not afraid, and said, "Just let me go down to the barking dogs, and give me something to throw to them. They will do me no harm."

As he insisted on it himself, they gave him some food for the wild animals and led him down to the tower. When he went inside the dogs did not bark at him, but wagged their tails round him quite amicably, ate what he set in front of them, and did not hurt a hair of his head.

Next morning, to everybody's astonishment, he came out again safe and unharmed, and said to the lord of the castle, "The dogs have told me, in their own language, why they live there and bring trouble on the country. They are under a spell, and are made to guard a great treasure that lies below in the tower, and they can have no rest until it is taken away; and I have learned from their talk how that is to be done."

Then everybody who heard it rejoiced, and the lord of the castle said he would adopt him as a son if he brought it off. He went down again; and as he knew what he had to do, he did it thoroughly, and brought out a chest full of gold. From then on the howling of the wild dogs was heard no more; they had disappeared, and the country was free of the trouble.

After some time he took it into his head to travel to Rome. On the way he passed a marsh where a number of frogs were sitting and croaking. He listened to them; and when he understood what they were saying, he grew very thoughtful and sad.

At last he arrived in Rome, where the Pope had just died and there was great difficulty about whom they should appoint as his successor. At last they agreed that the man should be chosen as pope who was marked out by some divine and miraculous sign. And just as that had been decided, the young count came into the church, and suddenly two snow-white doves flew onto his shoulders and stayed sitting there.

The churchmen recognised the sign from above and asked him on the spot whether he would be pope. He was undecided and did not know whether he was worthy of it; but the doves advised him to do it, and at last he said yes.

So he was anointed and consecrated; and so what he had heard from the frogs on his way, which had affected him so much, was fulfilled: that he was to be his Holiness the Pope.

Then he had to sing a mass, and did not know one word of it; but the two doves sat on his shoulders the whole time and said it all in his ear.

Clever Elsie

There was once a man who had a daughter called Clever Elsie. And when she had grown up her father said, "We must get her married."

"Yes," said her mother, "if only somebody would come who would have her."

At last a man came from a distance and courted her, whose name was Hans; but he made it a condition that Clever Elsie should really be wise.

"Oh," said her father, "she's sharp enough."

And her mother said, "Oh, she can see the wind coming up the street and hear the flies coughing."

"Well," said Hans, "if she isn't really wise, I won't have her."

When they were sitting at dinner and had eaten, the mother said, "Elsie, go down to the cellar and fetch some beer."

So Clever Elsie took the jug down from the wall and went into the cellar, tapping the lid briskly as she went, so that the time should not seem long. When she was down there she fetched herself a chair and set it in front of the barrel, so that she need not stoop and would not hurt her back or do herself any unexpected injury. Then she put the can in front of her and turned the tap; and while the beer was running she would not let her eyes be idle either, but looked up at the wall; and after a good deal of peering here and there she saw a pickaxe directly above her, which the masons had left behind by accident.

Then Clever Elsie began to weep, and said, "If I get Hans, and we have a child, and he grows big, and we send him down into the cellar here to draw beer, then the pickaxe will fall on his head and kill him."

And she sat and wept and shrieked with all the strength in her body over the misfortune that lay ahead of her.

Upstairs they were waiting for their drink, and still Clever Elsie did not come. So the mother said to the servant girl, "Just go down into the cellar and see where Elsie is."

The girl went, and found her sitting in front of the barrel screaming loudly. "Elsie, what are you weeping for?" she asked.

"Ah," she answered, "haven't I reason to weep? If I get Hans, and we have a child, and he grows big, and has to draw beer down here, the pickaxe may fall on his head and kill him."

Then the girl said, "What a clever Elsie we have!" — and sat down beside her and began to weep loudly over the misfortune herself.

After a while, as the servant girl did not come back either, and they were thirsty for their beer upstairs, the man said to the boy, "Just go down into the cellar and see where Elsie and the girl have got to."

The boy went down, and there sat Clever Elsie and the girl weeping together. So he asked, "What are you weeping for?"

"Ah," said Elsie, "haven't I reason to weep? If I get Hans, and we have a child, and he grows big, and has to draw beer down here, the pickaxe will fall on his head and kill him."

Then the boy said, "What a clever Elsie we have!" — and sat down beside her and began to howl loudly as well.

Upstairs they waited for the boy; and as he did not come back either, the man said to his wife, "Just go down into the cellar and see where Elsie is."

The woman went down and found all three of them in the middle of their lamentations, and asked what the cause was. And Elsie told her too that her future child was to be killed by the pickaxe, when it grew big and had to draw beer and the pickaxe fell down.

Then the mother said, "What a clever Elsie we have!" — and sat down and wept with them.

The man upstairs waited a little while; but as his wife did not come back and his thirst grew greater and greater, he said, "I shall have to go down into the cellar myself and see where Elsie is."

But when he got into the cellar and they were all sitting there crying, and he heard the reason — that Elsie's child was the cause of it, and that Elsie might perhaps bring one into the world some day, and that it might be killed by the pickaxe if it happened to be sitting underneath it drawing beer at the very moment when it fell — he cried, "Oh, what a clever Elsie!" — and sat down and wept with them too.

The bridegroom sat upstairs alone for a long time; and then, as nobody came back, he thought, "They must be waiting for me downstairs. I'd better go and see what they're up to."

When he got down there, all five of them were sitting screaming and lamenting most pitifully, each of them outdoing the last.

"What misfortune has happened, then?" he asked.

"Ah, dear Hans," said Elsie, "if we marry each other and have a child, and he grows big, and we perhaps send him down here to draw something to drink, then that pickaxe that's been left up there might dash his brains out if it fell down. So haven't we reason to weep?"

"Come," said Hans, "more understanding than that isn't needed in my household. As you are such a clever Elsie, I'll have you" — and he took her by the hand and led her upstairs and married her.

When Hans had had her for some time, he said, "Wife, I'm going out to work and earn some money for us. Go into the field and cut the corn, so that we can have some bread."

"Yes, dear Hans, I'll do that."

After Hans had gone away she cooked herself some good broth and took it out to the field with her. When she got to the field she said to herself, "What shall I do — shall I cut first, or shall I eat first? Oh, I'll eat first."

So she emptied her bowl of broth; and when she was thoroughly full, she said again, "What shall I do — shall I cut first, or shall I sleep first? I'll sleep first." And she lay down among the corn and fell asleep.

Hans had been at home a long time, but Elsie did not come. So he said, "What a clever Elsie I have! She's so hard-working that she doesn't even come home to eat."

But as she still stayed away, and it was getting to be evening, Hans went out to see how much she had cut. Nothing was cut at all, and she was lying among the corn asleep.

Then Hans hurried home and fetched a fowler's net with little bells on it, and hung it round her, and still she went on sleeping. Then he ran home, shut the house door, sat down in his chair and got on with his work.

At last, when it was quite dark, Clever Elsie woke up; and when she got to her feet there was a jingling all round her, and the bells rang at every step she took. Then she was alarmed, and grew uncertain whether she really was Clever Elsie or not, and said, "Is it me, or isn't it me?"

But she did not know what answer to give to that, and stood there a while in doubt. At last she thought, "I'll go home and ask whether it's me or not. They'll be sure to know."

She ran to the door of her own house, but it was shut. So she knocked at the window and called, "Hans, is Elsie inside?"

"Yes," answered Hans, "she is inside."

At that she was terrified, and said, "Ah, heavens — then it isn't me!" — and went to another door. But when the people heard the jingling of the bells they would not open it, and she could get in nowhere.

Then she ran out of the village, and nobody has seen her since.

The Tailor in Heaven

One very fine day it came about that the good God wished to take his pleasure in the heavenly garden, and took all the apostles and saints with him, so that nobody was left in heaven but Saint Peter. The Lord had ordered him to let nobody in while he was away, so Peter stood by the door and kept watch.

Before long somebody knocked. Peter asked who was there and what he wanted.

"I am a poor, honest tailor, praying to be let in," said a smooth voice.

"Honest indeed," said Peter, "like the thief on the gallows! You've been light-fingered and snipped bits off people's cloth. You won't get into heaven. The Lord has forbidden me to let anybody in while he's out."

"Come, do be merciful," cried the tailor. "Little scraps that fall off the table of their own accord aren't stolen and aren't worth talking about. Look, I'm lame, and I've got blisters on my feet from walking here — I can't possibly turn back again. Just let me in, and I'll do all the rough work. I'll carry the children and wash their clothes, and wash and scrub the benches they've been playing on, and patch all their torn clothes."

Saint Peter let himself be moved by pity, and opened the door of heaven just wide enough for the lame tailor to slip his lean body through. He had to sit down in a corner behind the door and stay there quietly and peaceably, so that the Lord, when he came back, should not notice him and be angry.

The tailor obeyed. But once, when Saint Peter had gone outside the door, he got up and, full of curiosity, went poking round into every corner of heaven and inspecting how everything was arranged.

At last he came to a place where a great many beautiful and delightful chairs were standing, and in the middle of them a seat all of gold, set with shining jewels, much higher than the other chairs, with a footstool of gold in front of it. It was in fact the seat the Lord sat on when he was at home, and from which he could see everything that happened on earth.

The tailor stood still and looked at the seat for a long time, because it pleased him better than anything else. At last he could not master his curiosity any longer, and climbed up and sat down in the chair.

Then he saw everything that was happening on earth; and he noticed an ugly old woman standing washing by a stream, secretly laying two veils aside for herself. The sight of it made the tailor so angry that he took hold of the golden footstool and threw it down through heaven to earth at the old thief.

But as he could not get the stool back again, he slipped quietly out of the chair, sat down in his own place behind the door, and behaved as if he had never moved from the spot.

When the Lord and master came back with his heavenly companions, he did not see the tailor behind the door; but when he sat down on his chair, the footstool was missing. He asked Saint Peter what had become of the stool, but Peter did not know. Then he asked whether he had let anybody in.

"I know of nobody who has been here," answered Peter, "except a lame tailor, who is still sitting behind the door."

Then the Lord had the tailor brought before him, and asked whether he had taken the stool away, and where he had put it.

"Oh Lord," answered the tailor cheerfully, "I threw it down to earth in my anger, at an old woman I saw stealing two veils at the washing."

"Oh, you rogue," said the Lord. "If I were to judge the way you judge, how do you suppose you would have got off so long? I should have had no chairs left, nor benches, nor seats — no, nor so much as an oven-fork — but should have thrown everything down at the sinners. From now on you can stay in heaven no longer, but must go outside the door again. Then go where you like. Nobody hands out punishment here but I alone, the Lord."

So Peter had to take the tailor out of heaven again; and as his shoes were torn and his feet covered with blisters, he took a stick in his hand and went off to Wait-a-Bit, where the good soldiers sit and make merry.

The Wishing-Table, the Gold-Ass, and the Cudgel in the Sack

Once upon a time there was a tailor who had three sons and only one goat. But as the goat kept the whole of them with her milk, she had to have good food and be taken out to pasture every day. So the sons did this, each in his turn.

Once the eldest took her to the churchyard, where the finest herbs were to be found, and let her eat and run about there. At night, when it was time to go home, he asked, "Goat, have you had enough?"

The goat answered:

	"I have eaten so much,
	not a leaf more I'll touch — meh! meh!"

"Come home, then," said the young man, and took hold of the cord round her neck, led her into the stable and tied her up securely.

"Well," said the old tailor, "has the goat had as much food as she ought?"

"Oh," said his son, "she has eaten so much, not a leaf more she'll touch."

But the father wanted to satisfy himself, and went down to the stable, stroked the dear animal and asked, "Goat, are you satisfied?"

The goat answered:

	"How should I be satisfied?
	Among the graves I leapt about,
	and found no leaf, so went without — meh! meh!"

"What's this I hear?" cried the tailor; and he ran upstairs and said to the young man, "You liar! You said the goat had had enough, and you let her go hungry!" And in his anger he took the yardstick down from the wall and drove him out with blows.

Next day it was the second son's turn. He looked out a place by the garden fence where nothing but good herbs grew, and the goat cleared them all off. At night, when he wanted to go home, he asked, "Goat, are you satisfied?"

The goat answered:

	"I have eaten so much,
	not a leaf more I'll touch — meh! meh!"

"Come home, then," said the young man, and led her home and tied her up in the stable.

"Well," said the old tailor, "has the goat had as much food as she ought?"

"Oh," said his son, "she has eaten so much, not a leaf more she'll touch."

The tailor would not rely on that, but went down to the stable and said, "Goat, have you had enough?"

The goat answered:

	"How should I be satisfied?
	Among the graves I leapt about,
	and found no leaf, so went without — meh! meh!"

"The godless wretch!" cried the tailor. "To let such a good creature go hungry!" And he ran up and drove the young man out of doors with the yardstick.

Now it was the third son's turn. He wanted to do the thing properly, and sought out some bushes with the finest leaves and let the goat eat them all. In the evening, when he wanted to go home, he asked, "Goat, have you had enough?"

The goat answered:

	"I have eaten so much,
	not a leaf more I'll touch — meh! meh!"

"Come home, then," said the young man, and led her into the stable and tied her up.

"Well," said the old tailor, "has the goat had a proper amount of food?"

"She has eaten so much, not a leaf more she'll touch."

The tailor did not trust that either, but went down and asked, "Goat, have you had enough?"

The wicked beast answered:

	"How should I be satisfied?
	Among the graves I leapt about,
	and found no leaf, so went without — meh! meh!"

"Oh, the brood of liars!" cried the tailor. "Each as wicked and as careless of his duty as the last! You shall make a fool of me no longer." And, quite beside himself with rage, he ran upstairs and belaboured the poor young fellow so hard with the yardstick that he leapt out of the house.

Now the old tailor was alone with his goat. Next morning he went down into the stable, made much of the goat and said, "Come, my dear little creature, I'll take you out to feed myself."

He took her by the rope and led her to green hedges, and among yarrow and whatever else goats like to eat. "There, for once you can eat to your heart's content," he said to her, and let her browse till evening. Then he asked, "Goat, are you satisfied?"

She answered:

	"I have eaten so much,
	not a leaf more I'll touch — meh! meh!"

"Come home, then," said the tailor, and led her into the stable and tied her fast. As he was going away he turned round again and said, "Well, are you satisfied for once?"

But the goat behaved no better to him, and cried:

	"How should I be satisfied?
	Among the graves I leapt about,
	and found no leaf, so went without — meh! meh!"

When the tailor heard that he was appalled, and saw clearly that he had driven his three sons away for nothing.

"Wait, you ungrateful creature," he cried. "It isn't enough to drive you out — I'll mark you so that you'll never dare show your face among honest tailors again."

In great haste he ran upstairs, fetched his razor, lathered the goat's head and shaved her as bare as the palm of his hand. And as the yardstick would have been too good for her, he fetched the horsewhip and gave her such cuts with it that she ran off in a great hurry.

Left all alone in his house like this, the tailor fell into great grief and would gladly have had his sons back again; but nobody knew where they had gone.

The eldest had apprenticed himself to a joiner, and learned hard and tirelessly; and when the time came for him to go travelling, his master gave him a little table which was nothing much to look at and was made of common wood, but which had one good quality. If anybody set it down and said, "Little table, spread yourself," the good little table was at once covered with a clean little cloth, and there was a plate on it and a knife and fork beside it, and dishes of boiled and roast meat, as many as there was room for, and a great glass of red wine shining so that it made the heart glad.

The young journeyman thought, "With this you have enough for your whole life" — and went about the world in high spirits, and never troubled himself whether an inn was good or bad or whether there was anything to be had in it. When it suited him he did not go into an inn at all, but out on the plain, or in a wood, or in a meadow, or wherever he fancied, he took the little table off his back, set it down in front of him and said, "Spread yourself" — and everything his heart desired appeared.

At length he took it into his head to go back to his father, whose anger would have cooled by now and who would gladly take him in with his wishing-table.

It happened that on the way home he came one evening to an inn that was full of guests. They made him welcome and invited him to sit and eat with them, since otherwise he would have trouble getting anything.

"No," said the joiner, "I won't take the few bites out of your mouths. You shall be my guests instead."

They laughed and thought he was joking with them; but he set his wooden table down in the middle of the room and said, "Little table, spread yourself."

Instantly it was covered with food, so good that the landlord could never have got hold of it, and the smell of it went up pleasantly into the guests' nostrils.

"Fall to, dear friends," said the joiner. And when the guests saw that he meant it, they did not need asking twice, but drew up, pulled out their knives and set to work valiantly. And what surprised them most was that when a dish became empty, a full one at once took its place of its own accord.

The innkeeper stood in a corner and watched it all. He had no idea what to say, but thought, "You could find a use for a cook like that in your kitchen."

The joiner and his companions made merry until late into the night; at length they lay down to sleep, and the young journeyman went to bed too, and stood his magic table against the wall.

But the landlord's thoughts gave him no rest. It occurred to him that there was a little old table in his lumber room that looked just like the journeyman's, and he brought it out very softly and exchanged it for the wishing-table.

Next morning the joiner paid for his bed, took up his table without a thought that he had got a false one, and went on his way. At midday he reached his father, who received him with great joy.

"Well, my dear son, what have you learned?" he said.

"Father, I have become a joiner."

"A good trade," said the old man. "But what have you brought back from your apprenticeship?"

"Father, the best thing I've brought back is this little table."

The tailor looked it over on all sides and said, "You didn't make a masterpiece when you made that. It's a bad old table."

"But it's a table that spreads itself," said his son. "When I set it down and tell it to spread itself, the most beautiful dishes appear on it, and wine too, that gladdens the heart. Just invite all our relations and friends — they shall refresh themselves and enjoy themselves for once, because the table will give them everything they want."

When the company was assembled, he put his table in the middle of the room and said, "Little table, spread yourself." But the little table did not stir, and stayed as bare as any other table that does not understand language.

Then the poor journeyman saw that his table had been changed, and was ashamed at having to stand there like a liar. The relations laughed at him and had to go home without having eaten or drunk anything. The father brought out his patches again and went back to his tailoring, and the son went to work for a master in the trade.

The second son had gone to a miller and apprenticed himself to him. When his years were up, the master said, "As you have behaved so well, I'll give you a donkey of a peculiar kind. He won't pull a cart and he won't carry a sack."

"What use is he, then?" asked the young journeyman.

"He drops gold out of his mouth," said the miller. "If you stand him on a cloth and say 'Bricklebrit,' the good animal will drop gold pieces for you."

"That's a fine thing," said the journeyman; and he thanked his master and went out into the world. Whenever he needed gold he had only to say "Bricklebrit" to his donkey, and it rained gold pieces, and he had nothing to do but pick them up off the ground. Wherever he went, only the best was good enough for him, and the dearer the better, because his purse was always full.

When he had seen something of the world he thought, "You must go and find your father. If you turn up with the gold-donkey he'll forget his anger and take you in gladly."

It happened that he came to the very same inn where his brother's table had been exchanged. He was leading his donkey by the bridle, and the landlord was about to take the animal from him and tie it up; but the young journeyman said, "Don't trouble yourself, I'll take my grey horse into the stable and tie him up myself, because I have to know where he is."

That struck the landlord as odd, and he thought a man who had to look after his own donkey could not have much to spend. But when the stranger put his hand in his pocket, brought out two gold pieces and told him to get him something good, the landlord's eyes opened wide, and he ran and hunted out the best he could find.

After dinner the guest asked what he owed. The landlord saw no reason not to double the reckoning, and said the journeyman must give him two more gold pieces. He felt in his pocket, but his gold had just run out.

"Wait a moment, landlord," he said, "I'll go and fetch some money" — and he took the tablecloth with him.

The landlord could not imagine what that could mean; and being curious, he stole after him; and as the guest bolted the stable door, he peeped through a knot hole in the wood. The stranger spread the cloth out under the animal and cried, "Bricklebrit" — and immediately the beast began to let gold pieces fall, so that it fairly rained money on the ground.

"Well, upon my word," said the landlord, "ducats are quickly minted there. A purse like that is not to be sneezed at."

The guest paid his bill and went to bed; but in the night the landlord crept down into the stable, led away the master of the mint and tied up another donkey in his place.

Early next morning the journeyman travelled off with his donkey, thinking he had his gold-donkey. At midday he reached his father, who was delighted to see him again and took him in gladly.

"What have you made of yourself, my son?" asked the old man.

"A miller, dear father."

"What have you brought back from your travels?"

"Nothing but a donkey."

"There are donkeys enough here," said his father. "I'd rather have had a good goat."

"Yes," said his son, "but this is no ordinary donkey — it's a gold-donkey. When I say 'Bricklebrit,' the good beast opens its mouth and drops out a whole sheetful of gold pieces. Just call all our relations here, and I'll make them rich."

"That suits me," said the tailor, "because then I shan't have to torment myself with the needle any longer" — and he ran out himself and called the relations together.

As soon as they were assembled, the miller told them to make room, spread out his cloth and led the donkey into the room. "Now watch," he said, and cried, "Bricklebrit."

But no gold pieces fell, and it was plain that the animal knew nothing of the art — for not every donkey reaches such perfection.

Then the poor miller pulled a long face, saw that he had been cheated, and begged his relations' pardon; and they went home as poor as they had come. There was no help for it: the old man had to take to his needle once more, and the young man hired himself out to a miller.

The third brother had apprenticed himself to a turner; and as that is skilled work, he was the longest in learning it. His brothers, though, wrote and told him how badly things had gone with them, and how the innkeeper had cheated them of their beautiful magic gifts on the last evening before they got home.

When the turner had served his time and had to set out on his travels, his master, because he had behaved so well, gave him a sack and said, "There's a cudgel inside it."

"I can carry the sack," he said, "and it may be useful to me. But why should the cudgel be in it? It only makes it heavy."

"I'll tell you why," said his master. "If anybody does you an injury, you have only to say, 'Cudgel, out of the sack!' and the cudgel will leap out among them and dance such a dance on their backs that they won't be able to stir or move for a week; and it won't leave off until you say, 'Cudgel, into the sack!'"

The journeyman thanked him and put the sack on his back; and whenever anybody came too near him and meant to attack him, he said, "Cudgel, out of the sack!" — and instantly the cudgel sprang out and dusted one coat or jacket after another on their backs, and never stopped until it had beaten it off them; and it was done so quickly that before anybody knew it, it was already his turn.

In the evening the young turner reached the inn where his brothers had been cheated. He laid his sack on the table in front of him and began to talk about all the wonderful things he had seen in the world.

"Yes," he said, "people can easily enough come across a table that spreads itself, or a gold-donkey, or things of that kind — excellent things, and I don't despise them in the least. But they're nothing compared with the treasure I've won for myself and carry about with me in that sack there."

The innkeeper pricked up his ears. "What in the world can that be?" he thought. "The sack must be filled with nothing but jewels. I ought to get hold of those cheap too — all good things come in threes."

When it was time for sleep, the guest stretched himself out on the bench and put his sack under him for a pillow. When the innkeeper thought his guest was sound asleep, he went to him and pushed and pulled very gently and carefully at the sack, to see whether he could possibly draw it out and lay another in its place.

But the turner had been waiting for this a long while; and just as the innkeeper was about to give a hearty tug, he cried, "Cudgel, out of the sack!"

Instantly the little cudgel came out and fell on the innkeeper and gave him a sound thrashing. The landlord cried for mercy; but the louder he cried, the harder the cudgel beat time on his back, until at last he fell to the floor exhausted.

Then the turner said, "If you don't give back the table that spreads itself and the gold-donkey, the dance shall begin again."

"Oh no," cried the landlord, quite humbly, "I'll gladly hand everything over — only make that accursed goblin creep back into the sack."

Then the journeyman said, "I'll let mercy take the place of justice — but beware of getting into mischief again." And he cried, "Cudgel, into the sack!" and let him have some peace.

Next morning the turner went home to his father with the wishing-table and the gold-donkey. The tailor rejoiced when he saw him once more, and asked him too what he had learned in foreign parts.

"Dear father," he said, "I have become a turner."

"A skilled trade," said his father. "What have you brought back from your travels?"

"A precious thing, dear father," said his son. "A cudgel in a sack."

"What!" cried his father. "A cudgel! That was worth the trouble, I must say. You can cut yourself one off any tree."

"But not one like this, dear father. If I say, 'Cudgel, out of the sack!' the cudgel springs out and leads anybody who means me harm a weary dance, and never stops until he is lying on the ground praying for fair weather. Look — with this cudgel I've got back the wishing-table and the gold-donkey that the thieving innkeeper took from my brothers. Now send for them both, and invite all our kinsfolk. I'll give them food and drink and fill their pockets with gold into the bargain."

The old tailor did not quite believe it, but all the same he got the relations together. Then the turner spread a cloth in the room and led in the gold-donkey, and said to his brother, "Now, dear brother, speak to him."

The miller said, "Bricklebrit" — and instantly the gold pieces came down on the cloth like a thunder shower, and the donkey did not stop until every one of them had as much as he could carry. (I can see by your face that you would have liked to be there too.)

Then the turner brought out the little table and said, "Now, dear brother, speak to it."

And hardly had the joiner said, "Little table, spread yourself," before it was laid and amply covered with the most exquisite dishes.

Then there was such a meal as the good tailor had never known in his house; and the whole party of relations stayed together far into the night, and were all merry and glad. The tailor locked needle and thread and yardstick and pressing iron away in a cupboard, and lived with his three sons in joy and splendour.

(And what became of the goat, whose fault it was that the tailor drove out his three sons? I'll tell you. She was ashamed of having a bald head, and ran to a fox's hole and crept into it. When the fox came home, two great eyes shone at him out of the darkness, and he was terrified and ran away.

A bear met him; and as the fox looked thoroughly upset, he said, "What's the matter with you, brother fox? Why are you looking like that?"

"Ah," said Redskin, "there's a fierce beast in my den, and it glared at me with its fiery eyes."

"We'll soon drive him out," said the bear, and went with him to the den and looked in. But when he saw the fiery eyes, fear took hold of him too; he would have nothing to do with the raging beast, and took to his heels.

A bee met him; and as she saw he was ill at ease, she said, "Bear, you're really pulling a very sorry face. What's become of all your good cheer?"

"It's all very well for you to talk," said the bear. "There's a raging beast with staring eyes in Redskin's house, and we can't drive it out."

The bee said, "Bear, I'm sorry for you. I'm a poor weak creature that you wouldn't turn your head to look at; but all the same, I think I can help you."

She flew into the fox's den, settled on the goat's smoothly shaven head and stung her so violently that she sprang up crying "Meh, meh!" and ran off into the world like a mad thing; and to this hour nobody knows where she has got to.)

Thumbling

There was once a poor peasant who sat by the hearth in the evening poking the fire, while his wife sat and span. And he said, "How sad it is that we have no children. It's so quiet here with us, and in other houses it's noisy and lively."

"Yes," said his wife, and sighed. "Even if we had only one, and it were quite small — no bigger than a thumb — I should be quite satisfied, and we would still love it with all our hearts."

Now it happened that the woman fell ill; and after seven months she gave birth to a child that was perfect in every limb, but no longer than a thumb.

Then they said, "It is just as we wished, and it shall be our dear child" — and because of its size they called it Thumbling. They did not let it go short of food; but the child did not grow any taller, and stayed just as it had been at first. All the same, it looked out of its eyes with good sense, and soon showed itself to be a clever and nimble creature, for everything it did turned out well.

One day the peasant was getting ready to go into the forest to cut wood, and said, as if to himself, "How I wish there were somebody to bring the cart out to me."

"Oh, father," cried Thumbling, "I'll bring the cart, you can rely on that. It shall be in the forest at the proper time."

The man laughed and said, "How can that be done? You're far too small to lead the horse by the reins."

"That doesn't matter, father. If mother will only harness it, I'll sit in the horse's ear and call out to him which way to go."

"Well," said the man, "we'll try it for once."

When the time came, the mother harnessed the horse and set Thumbling in its ear; and then the little creature called out, "Gee up! Gee up!"

And the horse went along quite properly, as if his master were driving him, and the cart went the right way into the forest.

It so happened that just as he was turning a corner, and the little one was crying "Gee up!", two strangers came towards him.

"Upon my word," said one of them, "what's this? There's a cart coming, and a driver calling to the horse, and no driver to be seen!"

"That can't be right," said the other. "We'll follow the cart and see where it stops."

But the cart went right on into the forest, exactly to the place where the wood had been cut. When Thumbling saw his father he called to him, "You see, father, here I am with the cart. Now take me down."

The father got hold of the horse with his left hand and with his right took his little son out of its ear. Thumbling sat down quite happily on a straw; but when the two strangers saw him they did not know what to say for astonishment.

Then one of them took the other aside and said, "Listen, that little fellow would make our fortune if we showed him for money in a big town. Let's buy him."

They went to the peasant and said, "Sell us the little man. He'll be well treated with us."

"No," said the father, "he's the apple of my eye, and all the money in the world can't buy him from me."

But Thumbling, hearing the bargaining, had climbed up the folds of his father's coat, settled on his shoulder and whispered in his ear, "Father, do let me go. I'll soon be back again."

So his father parted with him to the two men for a handsome sum of money.

"Where will you sit?" they asked him.

"Oh, just set me on the brim of your hat, and then I can walk up and down and look at the country, and still not fall off."

They did as he wanted; and when Thumbling had said goodbye to his father, they went off with him. They walked until it was dusk, and then the little fellow said, "Do put me down, I want to get down."

The man took off his hat and put the little fellow on the ground at the side of the road; and he leapt and crept about a little among the clods, and then suddenly slipped into a mouse hole that he had been looking out for.

"Good evening, gentlemen — go home without me," he called to them, and laughed at them. They ran up and poked their sticks into the mouse hole, but it was all wasted labour. Thumbling crept still further in; and as it soon grew quite dark, they had to go home with their annoyance and their empty purses.

When Thumbling saw that they had gone, he crept back out of the underground passage. "It's so dangerous walking on the ground in the dark," he said. "How easily a man breaks his neck or his leg!"

Luckily he knocked against an empty snail shell. "Thank God," he said, "I can spend the night safely in there" — and got inside.

Not long afterwards, when he was just going to sleep, he heard two men walk past, and one of them was saying, "How can we manage to get hold of the rich parson's silver and gold?"

"I could tell you that," cried Thumbling, interrupting them.

"What was that?" said one of the thieves in fright. "I heard somebody speaking."

They stood still and listened, and Thumbling spoke again and said, "Take me with you and I'll help you."

"But where are you?"

"Just look on the ground and see where my voice is coming from," he answered.

At last the thieves found him and picked him up. "You little imp, how are you going to help us?" they said.

"A great deal," he said. "I'll creep into the parson's room between the iron bars and hand out to you whatever you want."

"Come along, then," they said, "and we'll see what you can do."

When they came to the parson's house, Thumbling crept into the room — and immediately shouted at the top of his voice, "Do you want everything that's in here?"

The thieves were alarmed and said, "Do speak softly, so as not to wake anybody."

But Thumbling behaved as if he had not understood, and shouted again, "What do you want? Do you want everything that's in here?"

The cook, who slept in the next room, heard it, sat up in bed and listened. The thieves, though, had run some distance away in their fright; but at last they took courage and thought, "The little rascal is making fun of us." They came back and whispered to him, "Come now, be serious, and hand something out to us."

Then Thumbling shouted again as loudly as he could, "I really will give you everything — just put your hands in."

The maid, who was listening, heard that quite distinctly, jumped out of bed and rushed to the door. The thieves took flight and ran as if the Wild Huntsman were behind them; but as the maid could not see anything, she went to fetch a light. And when she came back with it, Thumbling slipped off unnoticed to the granary; and the maid, after searching every corner and finding nothing, went back to bed and thought that after all she must have been dreaming with her eyes and ears open.

Thumbling had climbed up among the hay and found a beautiful place to sleep in. There he meant to rest until daylight and then go home to his parents. But he had other things to go through first. Truly, there is a great deal of trouble and misery in this world.

When day broke, the maid got up to feed the cows. Her first errand was to the barn, where she took up an armful of hay — and precisely the armful that poor Thumbling was lying asleep in. He was sleeping so soundly, though, that he knew nothing about it, and did not wake until he was in the mouth of the cow, who had picked him up with the hay.

"Good heavens," he cried, "how have I got into the fulling mill?" — but he soon found out where he was. Then he had to be careful not to get between the teeth and be crushed; but all the same he had to slide down into the stomach with the hay.

"They've forgotten the windows in this little room," he said, "and no sun shines in, and nobody brings a candle either."

He thought very poorly of his quarters; and the worst of it was that more and more hay kept coming in at the door and the space got smaller and smaller. At last, in his distress, he cried as loudly as he could, "Bring me no more fodder! Bring me no more fodder!"

The maid was just milking the cow; and when she heard somebody speaking and could see nobody, and recognised the same voice she had heard in the night, she was so terrified that she slipped off her stool and spilt the milk. She ran in a great hurry to her master and said, "Oh heavens, parson, the cow has been talking!"

"You're out of your mind," said the parson; but he went to the cowshed himself to see what was there. And hardly had he set foot inside before Thumbling cried again, "Bring me no more fodder! Bring me no more fodder!"

Then the parson himself was alarmed, and thought an evil spirit had got into the cow, and ordered her to be killed. She was killed; but the stomach, with Thumbling inside it, was thrown on the dunghill.

Thumbling had great difficulty working his way through it; but he got far enough to make himself a little room — and then, just as he was about to put his head out, a new misfortune happened. A hungry wolf came running up and swallowed the whole stomach at a gulp.

Thumbling did not lose heart. "Perhaps," he thought, "the wolf will listen to what I have to say" — and he called out to him from inside, "Dear wolf, I know where there's a magnificent feast for you."

"Where's it to be had?" said the wolf.

"In such and such a house. You must creep in through the kitchen drain, and you'll find cakes and bacon and sausages, as much as you can eat" — and he described his father's house exactly.

The wolf did not need telling twice. He squeezed in at night through the drain and ate his fill in the larder. When he had eaten enough he wanted to get out again; but he had grown so fat that he could not get out the same way.

Thumbling had counted on that, and now began to make a violent noise in the wolf's body, and raged and screamed as loudly as he could.
