"Will you be quiet?" said the wolf. "You'll wake the people up."

"What of it?" said the little fellow. "You've eaten your fill, and now I'll enjoy myself too" — and began to scream again with all his strength.

At last his father and mother were woken by it, and ran to the room and looked in through the crack of the door. When they saw that there was a wolf inside, they ran off, and the husband fetched his axe and the wife her scythe.

"Stay behind me," said the man as they came into the room. "When I've given him a blow, if he isn't killed by it, you must cut at him and hack his body open."

Then Thumbling heard his parents' voices and cried, "Dear father, I'm here — I'm inside the wolf!"

His father said, full of joy, "Thank God, we've found our dear child again!" — and told his wife to put down her scythe, in case Thumbling should be hurt with it. Then he raised his arm and struck the wolf such a blow on the head that he fell down dead; and then they got knives and scissors and cut his body open and drew the little fellow out.

"Ah," said his father, "what sorrow we've been through for your sake."

"Yes, father, I've been about the world a good deal. Thank heaven I'm breathing fresh air again."

"And where have you been?"

"Ah, father, I've been in a mouse hole, in a cow's stomach and in a wolf's. Now I'll stay with you."

"And we won't sell you again, not for all the riches in the world," said his parents, and hugged and kissed their dear Thumbling. They gave him food and drink and had new clothes made for him, because his own had been spoiled on his travels.

The Wedding of Mrs. Fox

First Story

There was once an old fox with nine tails, who believed his wife was not faithful to him and wanted to test her. He stretched himself out under the bench, did not move a limb, and behaved as if he were stone dead.

Mrs. Fox went up to her room and shut herself in; and her maid, Miss Cat, sat by the fire and did the cooking. When it became known that the old fox was dead, suitors began to present themselves.

The maid heard somebody standing at the house door, knocking. She went and opened it, and it was a young fox, who said:

	"What may you be about, Miss Cat?
	Are you asleep, or wide awake?"

She answered:

	"I'm not asleep, I'm wide awake.
	Would you like to know what I make?
	I'm boiling warm beer with butter so nice —
	will the gentleman come in and drink some likewise?"

"No, thank you, miss," said the fox. "What is Mrs. Fox doing?"

The maid answered:

	"She sits all alone
	and makes her moan,
	and weeps her little eyes quite red,
	because old Mr. Fox is dead."

"Do just tell her, miss, that a young fox is here who would like to court her."

"Certainly, young sir."

	The cat goes up the stairs, trip, trap;
	she knocks upon the door, tap, tap.
	"Mistress Fox, are you inside?"
	"Oh yes, my little cat," she cried.
	"A suitor's standing at the door."
	"Tell me what he's like, my dear."

"But has he nine beautiful tails, like the late Mr. Fox?"

"Oh no," said the cat, "he has only one."

"Then I won't have him."

Miss Cat went downstairs and sent the suitor away. Soon afterwards there was another knock, and there was another fox at the door who wanted to court Mrs. Fox. He had two tails, but he fared no better than the first. After that still more came, each with one tail more than the last; but they were all turned away, until at last one came who had nine tails, like old Mr. Fox.

When the widow heard that, she said joyfully to the cat:

	"Now open the gates and the doors all wide,
	and carry old Mr. Fox outside."

But just as the wedding was about to be celebrated, old Mr. Fox stirred under the bench and cudgelled the whole rabble, and drove them and Mrs. Fox out of the house.

Second Story

When old Mr. Fox was dead, the wolf came courting and knocked at the door; and the cat, who was Mrs. Fox's servant, opened it for him. The wolf greeted her and said:

	"Good day to you, Mrs. Cat of Kehrewit.
	How is it that all alone you sit?
	And what good thing are you making?"

The cat answered:

	"In milk I'm breaking bread so sweet —
	will the gentleman come in and eat?"

"No, thank you, Mrs. Cat," said the wolf. "Is Mrs. Fox not at home?"

The cat said:

	"She sits upstairs in her room,
	bewailing her sorrowful doom,
	bewailing her trouble so sore,
	for old Mr. Fox is no more."

The wolf answered:

	"If she's in want of a husband now,
	then will it please her to step below?"
	The cat runs quickly up the stair
	and lets her tail fly here and there,
	until she comes to the parlour door
	and with her five gold rings she knocks:
	"Are you within, good Mistress Fox?
	If you're in want of a husband now,
	then will it please you to step below?"

Mrs. Fox asked, "Has the gentleman got red stockings on, and has he a pointed muzzle?"

"No," said the cat.

"Then he won't do for me."

When the wolf had gone, there came a dog, a stag, a hare, a bear, a lion, and all the beasts of the forest, one after another. But every one of them lacked one of the good points that old Mr. Fox had had, and the cat had to keep sending the suitors away.

At length a young fox came. Then Mrs. Fox said, "Has the gentleman got red stockings on, and has he a little pointed muzzle?"

"Yes," said the cat, "he has."

"Then let him come upstairs," said Mrs. Fox — and ordered the servant to get the wedding feast ready.

	"Sweep me the room as clean as you can,
	up with the window, fling out my old man!
	For many a fine fat mouse he brought,
	yet of his wife he never thought,
	but ate up every one he caught."

Then the wedding was celebrated with young Mr. Fox, and there was a great deal of rejoicing and dancing; and if they haven't left off, they are dancing still.

The Elves

First Story

A shoemaker, through no fault of his own, had grown so poor that at last he had nothing left but the leather for one pair of shoes. So in the evening he cut out the shoes that he meant to start on next morning; and as he had a good conscience, he lay down quietly in his bed, commended himself to God, and fell asleep.

In the morning, after he had said his prayers and was just going to sit down to work, the two shoes stood on his table, quite finished. He was astounded and did not know what to say about it. He took the shoes in his hands to look at them more closely, and they were so neatly made that there was not one bad stitch in them, as if they had been meant for a masterpiece.

Soon afterwards a buyer came in; and as the shoes pleased him so well, he paid more for them than was usual, and with the money the shoemaker could buy leather for two pairs of shoes. He cut them out in the evening and next morning was about to set to work with fresh heart; but there was no need, because when he got up they were made already. And there were buyers for those too, who gave him money enough to buy leather for four pairs.

The next morning he found the four pairs made as well; and so it went on continually. Whatever he cut out in the evening was finished by morning, so that he soon had a decent living again, and at last became a wealthy man.

Now it happened one evening not long before Christmas, when the man had been cutting out, that he said to his wife before going to bed, "What would you say to sitting up tonight to see who it is that gives us this helping hand?"

His wife liked the idea, and lit a candle; and then they hid in a corner of the room behind some clothes that were hanging there, and watched.

At midnight two pretty little naked men came in, sat down at the shoemaker's table, took all the work that had been cut out and began to stitch and sew and hammer so skilfully and so quickly with their little fingers that the shoemaker could not take his eyes off them for astonishment. They did not stop until everything was done and standing finished on the table; and then they ran quickly away.

Next morning the wife said, "The little men have made us rich, and we really must show that we're grateful. They run about like that with nothing on, and they must be cold. I'll tell you what I'll do: I'll make them little shirts and coats and waistcoats and trousers, and knit them both a pair of stockings; and you make them two little pairs of shoes."

The man said, "I'll be very glad to." And one night, when everything was ready, they laid their presents out together on the table instead of the cut-out work, and then hid themselves to see how the little men would behave.

At midnight they came bounding in and were going to set to work at once; but when they found no leather cut out, but only the pretty little clothes, they were astonished at first and then showed the greatest delight. They dressed themselves with enormous speed, putting the pretty clothes on and singing:

	"Now we're boys so fine to see,
	why should we longer cobblers be?"

Then they danced and skipped and leapt over the chairs and benches. At last they danced out of the door. From that time on they never came again; but as long as the shoemaker lived all went well with him, and everything he undertook prospered.

Second Story

There was once a poor servant girl who was hard-working and clean, and swept the house every day and emptied her sweepings on the great heap in front of the door.

One morning, when she was just going back to her work, she found a letter on the heap; and as she could not read, she put her broom in the corner and took the letter to her master and mistress. And it was an invitation from the elves, who asked the girl to hold a child for them at its christening.

The girl did not know what to do; but at last, after a good deal of persuading, and as they told her it was not right to refuse an invitation of that kind, she agreed.

Then three elves came and led her to a hollow mountain where the little folk lived. Everything there was small, but more elegant and beautiful than can be described. The baby's mother lay in a bed of black ebony decorated with pearls, the covers were embroidered with gold, the cradle was of ivory and the bath of gold.

The girl stood godmother, and then wanted to go home again; but the little elves urgently begged her to stay three days with them. So she stayed, and passed the time in pleasure and gaiety, and the little folk did everything they could to make her happy.

At last she set out for home. First they filled her pockets quite full of money, and after that they led her out of the mountain again.

When she got home she wanted to get on with her work, and took the broom, which was still standing in the corner, and began to sweep. Then some strangers came out of the house and asked her who she was and what business she had there. And she had not, as she thought, been three days with the little men in the mountain, but seven years — and in the meantime her old master and mistress had died.

Third Story

A certain mother's child had been carried off out of its cradle by the elves, and a changeling with a huge head and staring eyes, which would do nothing but eat and drink, had been laid in its place.

In her trouble she went to her neighbour and asked her advice. The neighbour said she should carry the changeling into the kitchen, set it down on the hearth, light a fire and boil some water in two eggshells; that would make the changeling laugh, and if he laughed it would be all over with him.

The woman did everything her neighbour told her. And when she put the eggshells of water on the fire, the imp said, "I am as old now as the Wester forest, and I've never yet seen anybody boil anything in an eggshell" — and began to laugh about it.

And while he was laughing, a host of little elves suddenly came in, who brought the right child, set it down on the hearth and took the changeling away with them.

The Robber Bridegroom

There was once a miller who had a beautiful daughter; and when she was grown up he wanted to see her provided for and well married. He thought, "If a decent suitor comes and asks for her, I'll give her to him."

Not long afterwards a suitor came who seemed to be very rich; and as the miller could find no fault with him, he promised him his daughter.

The girl, though, did not like him as much as a girl ought to like the man she is engaged to, and had no confidence in him. Whenever she saw him, or thought about him, she felt a secret horror.

Once he said to her, "You're my betrothed, and yet you've never once come to visit me."

The girl answered, "I don't know where your house is."

Then the bridegroom said, "My house is out there in the dark forest."

She tried to excuse herself and said she would not be able to find the way there.

The bridegroom said, "Next Sunday you must come out to me. I've invited the guests already, and I'll scatter ashes so that you can find your way through the forest."

When Sunday came and the girl had to set out, she grew very uneasy, though she did not herself know exactly why; and to mark her way she filled both her pockets with peas and lentils.

Ashes had been scattered at the entrance to the forest, and she followed them; but at every step she threw a couple of peas on the ground. She walked almost the whole day, until she reached the middle of the forest, where it was darkest; and there stood a house standing all by itself, which she did not like, because it looked so dark and dismal. She went inside, but there was nobody there, and the most complete stillness reigned.

Suddenly a voice cried:

	"Turn back, turn back, young maiden dear —
	it's a murderer's house you enter here."

The girl looked up and saw that the voice came from a bird hanging in a cage on the wall. And again it cried:

	"Turn back, turn back, young maiden dear —
	it's a murderer's house you enter here."

The girl went on further, from one room to another, and walked through the whole house; but it was completely empty and not a living soul was to be found. At last she came to the cellar, and there sat an extremely old woman whose head shook all the time.

"Can you tell me," said the girl, "whether my betrothed lives here?"

"Alas, poor child," said the old woman, "where have you come to? You're in a murderers' den. You think you're a bride soon to be married, but the wedding you'll keep is with death. Look — they've made me put that great kettle of water on, and when they have you in their power they'll cut you to pieces without mercy, and cook you and eat you, because they are eaters of human flesh. Unless I take pity on you and save you, you are lost."

With that the old woman led her behind a great barrel where she could not be seen. "Be as still as a mouse," she said. "Don't make a sound or move, or it will be all over with you. Tonight, when the robbers are asleep, we'll escape. I've been waiting a long time for a chance."

Hardly was it done before the godless crew came home. They dragged another young girl in with them. They were drunk, and paid no attention to her screams and her weeping. They gave her wine to drink, three glasses full, one glass of white wine, one of red and one of yellow — and with that her heart burst in two.

Then they tore off her fine clothes, laid her on a table, cut her beautiful body in pieces and scattered salt over them. The poor bride behind the barrel trembled and shook, because she saw perfectly well what fate the robbers had in mind for her.

One of them noticed a gold ring on the murdered girl's little finger; and as it would not come off at once, he took an axe and chopped the finger off. But it sprang up into the air, over the barrel, and fell straight into the bride's bosom. The robber took a candle and went to look for it, but could not find it.

Then another of them said, "Have you looked behind the big barrel?"

But the old woman called out, "Come and get something to eat, and leave off looking till morning — the finger won't run away from you."

Then the robbers said, "The old woman is right," and gave up their search and sat down to eat; and the old woman poured a sleeping draught into their wine, so that before long they lay down in the cellar and slept and snored.

When the bride heard that, she came out from behind the barrel; and she had to step over the sleepers, because they were lying in rows on the floor, and she was in terror of waking one of them. But God helped her, and she got safely over. The old woman went up with her, opened the doors, and they hurried out of the murderers' den as fast as they could go.

The wind had blown the scattered ashes away, but the peas and lentils had sprouted and come up, and showed them the way in the moonlight. They walked the whole night, until in the morning they reached the mill; and then the girl told her father everything, exactly as it had happened.

When the day came for the wedding to be celebrated, the bridegroom appeared, and the miller had invited all his relations and friends. As they sat at table, each of them was asked to tell something. The bride sat still and said nothing.

Then the bridegroom said to her, "Come, my darling, do you know nothing? Tell us something, like the rest."

She answered, "Then I'll tell you a dream. I was walking alone through a wood, and at last I came to a house where there wasn't a living soul; but there was a bird in a cage on the wall, which cried:

	'Turn back, turn back, young maiden dear —
	it's a murderer's house you enter here.'

And it cried it once more. My darling, I only dreamed this.

"Then I went through all the rooms, and they were all empty, and there was something so horrible about them. At last I went down into the cellar, and there sat a very, very old woman whose head shook. I asked her, 'Does my bridegroom live in this house?' She answered, 'Alas, poor child, you've come into a murderers' den. Your bridegroom does live here, but he'll hack you to pieces and kill you, and then he'll cook you and eat you.' My darling, I only dreamed this.

"But the old woman hid me behind a great barrel; and hardly was I hidden before the robbers came home, dragging a girl with them, and gave her three kinds of wine to drink, white, red and yellow, and her heart broke in two with it. My darling, I only dreamed this.

"Then they pulled off her pretty clothes and hacked her lovely body to pieces on a table and sprinkled salt on them. My darling, I only dreamed this.

"And one of the robbers saw that there was still a ring on her little finger; and as it was hard to pull off, he took an axe and chopped it off — but the finger sprang up into the air and over the great barrel and fell into my bosom. And here is the finger, with the ring!"

And with these words she drew it out and showed it to the company.

The robber, who had turned as pale as ashes during the story, jumped up and tried to escape; but the guests held him fast and handed him over to justice. And he and his whole gang were executed for their infamous deeds.

Herr Korbes

There were once a cock and a hen who wanted to go on a journey together. So the cock built a beautiful carriage with four red wheels, and harnessed four mice to it. The hen got in with the cock, and away they drove.

Not long afterwards they met a cat, who said, "Where are you going?"

The cock answered, "We're going to Herr Korbes's house."

"Take me with you," said the cat.

The cock answered, "Very gladly. Get up behind, or you'll fall off in front. And take great care not to dirty my little red wheels.

	And you, little wheels, roll on,
	and you, little mice, pipe out,
	as we go on our way
	to the house of Herr Korbes."

After that came a millstone, then an egg, then a duck, then a pin, and last of all a needle, and they all sat down in the carriage and drove along with them.

But when they reached Herr Korbes's house, Herr Korbes was not at home. The mice pulled the carriage into the barn; the hen flew up onto a perch with the cock; the cat sat down by the hearth; the duck settled on the well-pole; the egg rolled itself up in the towel; the pin stuck itself into the chair cushion; the needle jumped onto the bed into the middle of the pillow; and the millstone laid itself over the door.

Then Herr Korbes came home, went to the hearth and was about to light the fire, when the cat threw a quantity of ashes in his face. He ran into the kitchen in a great hurry to wash it off, and the duck splashed water in his face. He went to dry it with the towel, and the egg rolled against him and broke and gummed up his eyes. He wanted to rest and sat down in the chair, and the pin pricked him. He lost his temper and flung himself down on his bed; but as soon as he laid his head on the pillow, the needle pricked him, so that he screamed out loud and was just going to run off into the wide world in his fury — but when he came to the house door, the millstone leapt down and struck him dead.

Herr Korbes must have been a very wicked man.

The Godfather

A poor man had so many children that he had already asked everybody in the world to be godfather; and when yet another child was born there was nobody left he could invite. He did not know what to do; and in his perplexity he lay down and fell asleep.

Then he dreamed that he was to go outside the gate and ask the first person who met him to be godfather. When he woke he decided to obey his dream, and went outside the gate and asked the first person who came up to him to be godfather.

The stranger gave him a little glass of water and said, "This is a wonderful water. With it you can heal the sick — only you must see where Death is standing. If he is standing at the patient's head, give the patient some of the water and he will be healed; but if Death is standing at his feet, all your trouble will be wasted, because the sick man must die."

From that time on the man could always say whether a patient could be saved or not, and became famous for his skill and earned a great deal of money. Once he was called in to the King's child; and when he came in he saw Death standing at the child's head, and cured it with the water. And he did the same a second time. But the third time Death was standing at its feet, and then he knew the child must die.

One day the man thought he would visit his child's godfather and tell him how he had got on with the water. But when he went into the house, what a strange establishment it was!

On the first flight of stairs the broom and the shovel were quarrelling and knocking each other about violently. He asked them, "Where does the godfather live?"

The broom answered, "One flight of stairs higher up."

When he came to the second flight he saw a heap of dead fingers lying there. He asked, "Where does the godfather live?"

One of the fingers answered, "One flight higher."

On the third flight lay a heap of dead heads, which again sent him up to the flight beyond. On the fourth flight he saw fish on the fire, frizzling in the pans and baking themselves. They too said, "One flight higher."

And when he had climbed the fifth, he came to the door of a room and peeped through the keyhole — and there he saw the godfather, with a pair of long horns on his head.

When he opened the door and went in, the godfather got into bed in a great hurry and covered himself up.

Then the man said, "Sir godfather, what a strange household you have! When I came to your first flight of stairs, the shovel and the broom were quarrelling and beating each other violently."

"How stupid you are," said the godfather. "That was the boy and the maid talking to each other."

"But on the second flight I saw dead fingers lying."

"Oh, how silly you are. Those were some roots of scorzonera."

"On the third flight lay a heap of dead men's heads."

"Foolish man, those were cabbages."

"On the fourth flight I saw fish in a pan, hissing and baking themselves." And when he had said that, the fish came in and served themselves up.

"And when I got to the fifth flight, I peeped through the keyhole of a door — and there, godfather, I saw you, and you had long, long horns."

"Oh, that's a lie!"

The man took fright and ran out; and if he had not, who knows what the godfather would have done to him.

Frau Trude

There was once a little girl who was obstinate and inquisitive; and when her parents told her to do anything she would not obey them — so how could things go well with her?

One day she said to her parents, "I've heard so much about Frau Trude that I mean to go and see her one day. People say everything about her looks so strange, and that there are such odd things in her house, that I've grown quite curious."

Her parents absolutely forbade it, and said, "Frau Trude is a bad woman who does wicked things; and if you go to her, you are no child of ours."

But the girl would not be turned aside by her parents' prohibition, and went to Frau Trude all the same.

And when she got there, Frau Trude said, "Why are you so pale?"

"Ah," she said, and her whole body trembled, "I've been so frightened by what I saw."

"What did you see?"

"I saw a black man on your steps."

"That was a charcoal burner."

"Then I saw a green man."

"That was a huntsman."

"After that I saw a blood-red man."

"That was a butcher."

"Ah, Frau Trude, I was terrified. I looked in through the window and I saw, not you, but — as I truly believe — the Devil himself, with a head of fire."

"Oho," she said, "then you've seen the witch in her proper dress. I've been waiting for you and wanting you a long time already. You shall give me some light."

Then she turned the girl into a block of wood and threw it on the fire. And when it was blazing well she sat down close to it and warmed herself at it, and said, "That gives a bright light for once."

Godfather Death

A poor man had twelve children, and had to work night and day to give them even bread. So when the thirteenth came into the world he did not know what to do in his trouble, but ran out onto the great highway and resolved to ask the first person he met to be godfather.

The first to meet him was the good God, who already knew what was in his heart, and said to him, "Poor man, I am sorry for you. I will hold your child at its christening, and take care of it and make it happy on earth."

The man said, "Who are you?"

"I am God."

"Then I don't want you for a godfather," said the man. "You give to the rich and leave the poor to go hungry."

So the man spoke, because he did not know how wisely God shares out riches and poverty. So he turned away from the Lord and went on further.

Then the Devil came to him and said, "What are you looking for? If you'll have me as godfather for your child, I'll give him gold in plenty and all the joys of the world besides."

The man asked, "Who are you?"

"I am the Devil."

"Then I don't want you for a godfather," said the man. "You deceive people and lead them astray."

He went on; and then Death came striding up to him on his withered legs and said, "Take me as godfather."

The man asked, "Who are you?"

"I am Death, and I make all men equal."

Then the man said, "You're the right one. You take the rich as well as the poor, without distinction. You shall be godfather."

Death answered, "I will make your child rich and famous, because whoever has me for a friend can lack for nothing."

The man said, "Next Sunday is the christening. Be there at the right time."

Death appeared as he had promised, and stood godfather in the usual way.

When the boy had grown up, his godfather appeared one day and told him to come with him. He led him out into a forest and showed him a herb growing there, and said, "Now you shall have your godfather's present. I make you a famous physician. When you are called to a patient, I shall always appear to you. If I stand at the sick man's head, you may say with confidence that you will make him well again, and if you give him some of this herb he will recover. But if I stand at the patient's feet, he is mine, and you must say that all remedies are useless and that no physician in the world could save him. But beware of using the herb against my will, or it may go badly with you."

It was not long before the young man was the most famous physician in the whole world. "He has only to look at a patient and he knows his condition at once, and whether he will recover or must die," people said of him; and they came to him from far and wide, and sent for him whenever anybody was ill, and gave him so much money that he soon became a rich man.

Now it happened that the King fell ill, and the physician was summoned and was to say whether recovery was possible. But when he came to the bed, Death was standing at the sick man's feet, and no herb grew that could save him.

"If I could only cheat Death for once," thought the physician. "He's sure to take it badly if I do; but as I'm his godson he'll shut one eye. I'll risk it."

So he took up the sick man and laid him the other way round, so that now Death was standing at his head. Then he gave the King some of the herb, and he recovered and grew healthy again.

But Death came to the physician, looking very black and angry, and shook his finger at him and said, "You've got the better of me. This time I'll pardon it, as you are my godson; but if you venture it again it will cost you your neck, because I'll take you away with me myself."

Soon afterwards the King's daughter fell gravely ill. She was his only child, and he wept day and night until he began to lose his sight; and he made it known that whoever rescued her from death should be her husband and inherit the crown.

When the physician came to the sick girl's bed he saw Death at her feet. He ought to have remembered his godfather's warning; but he was so infatuated by the King's daughter's great beauty and by the happiness of becoming her husband that he threw all thought to the winds. He did not see that Death was casting angry looks at him, that he was raising his hand in the air and threatening him with his withered fist. He lifted the sick girl up and put her head where her feet had been. Then he gave her some of the herb, and instantly the colour came back to her cheeks and life stirred in her again.

When Death saw that he had been cheated of his property a second time, he walked up to the physician with long strides and said, "It's all over with you, and now the lot falls on you" — and seized him so firmly with his ice-cold hand that he could not resist, and led him into a cave under the earth.

There he saw how thousands and thousands of candles were burning in countless rows, some large, some half-sized, some small. Every moment some of them went out and others flared up again, so that the flames seemed to leap here and there in perpetual change.

"Look," said Death. "These are the lights of men's lives. The big ones belong to children, the half-sized ones to married people in their prime, the little ones to old people. But children and young folk often have only a tiny candle too."

"Show me the light of my life," said the physician; and he thought it would still be very tall.

Death pointed to a little stub that was just threatening to go out, and said, "There it is."

"Ah, dear godfather," said the horrified physician, "light me a new one — do it for love of me, so that I may enjoy my life, and be King, and the husband of the King's beautiful daughter."

"I cannot," answered Death. "One must go out before a new one is lit."

"Then set the old one on top of a new one, so that it will go on burning at once when the old one has come to an end," begged the physician.

Death behaved as if he were going to grant his wish, and took hold of a tall new candle; but as he wanted his revenge, he made a mistake in fixing it on purpose, and the little stub fell down and went out. And immediately the physician fell to the ground, and now he was in Death's hands himself.

Thumbling as Journeyman

A certain tailor had a son who happened to be small — no bigger than a thumb — and so he was always called Thumbling. He had some courage in him, though, and said to his father, "Father, I must and will go out into the world."

"That's right, my son," said the old man; and he took a long darning needle and made a knob of sealing wax on it at the candle. "And there's a sword for you to take with you on the way."

Then the little tailor wanted to have one more meal at home, and hopped into the kitchen to see what his lady mother had cooked for the last time. It had just been dished up, and the dish was standing on the hearth.

"Mother," he said, "what is there to eat today?"

"See for yourself," said his mother.

So Thumbling jumped onto the hearth and peeped into the dish; but he stretched his neck in too far, and the steam from the food caught hold of him and carried him up the chimney. He rode about in the air on the steam for a while, until at length he sank down to the ground again.

So now the little tailor was out in the wide world; and he travelled about and took work with a master in his trade, but the food was not good enough for him.

"Mistress," said Thumbling, "if you don't give us better food, I'll go away, and early tomorrow morning I'll write on your front door in chalk: Too many potatoes, too little meat. Farewell, Mr. Potato-King."

"What would you have, then, grasshopper?" said the mistress, and grew angry and snatched up a dishcloth and was going to hit him. But my little tailor crept nimbly under a thimble, peeped out from under it and put his tongue out at the mistress. She picked up the thimble and tried to get hold of him, but little Thumbling hopped into the dishcloth; and while the mistress was shaking it out and looking for him, he got into a crack in the table.

"Ho, ho, my lady mistress," he cried, sticking his head out; and when she started hitting at him he leapt down into the drawer. At last, though, she caught him and drove him out of the house.

The little tailor journeyed on and came to a great forest, and there he fell in with a band of robbers who had a plan to steal the King's treasure. When they saw the little tailor they thought, "A little fellow like that can creep through a keyhole and be a picklock for us."

"Hey there," one of them cried, "you giant Goliath, will you come to the treasure chamber with us? You can slip yourself inside and throw the money out."

Thumbling thought about it for a while, and at length he said yes, and went with them to the treasure chamber. There he looked at the doors, top and bottom, to see whether there was any crack in them; and it was not long before he spied one that was wide enough to let him in.

He was about to get in at once, but one of the two sentries standing in front of the door noticed him and said to the other, "What an ugly spider that is, crawling there. I'll kill it."

"Leave the poor creature alone," said the other. "It's done you no harm."

So Thumbling got safely through the crack into the treasure chamber, opened the window under which the robbers were standing, and threw out one thaler after another to them.

When the little tailor was in the full swing of the work, he heard the King coming to inspect his treasure chamber, and crept hastily into a hiding place. The King noticed that a number of solid thalers were missing, but could not imagine who could have stolen them, since the locks and bolts were in good order and everything seemed well guarded. So he went away again and said to the sentries, "Keep watch — somebody is after the money."

So when Thumbling started work again, they heard the money moving and a sound of clink, clink, clink. They ran in quickly to catch the thief; but the little tailor, who heard them coming, was quicker still, and leapt into a corner and covered himself with a thaler so that nothing could be seen of him — and at the same time he mocked the sentries and called, "Here I am!"

The sentries ran over; but by the time they got there he had already hopped into another corner under a thaler, and was calling, "Ho, ho, here I am!" The watchmen sprang over there in a hurry, but Thumbling had long since got into a third corner and was calling, "Ho, ho, here I am!"

And so he made fools of them and chased them round and round the treasure chamber until they were worn out and went away. Then he threw all the thalers out, one by one, sending the last one out with all his strength, and then hopped nimbly onto it and flew down with it through the window.

The robbers paid him great compliments. "You're a valiant hero," they said. "Will you be our captain?"

Thumbling declined, though, and said he wanted to see the world first. They divided up the booty, but the little tailor asked only for a farthing, because he could not carry more.

Then he buckled on his sword again, said goodbye to the robbers and took to the road. First he went to work for some masters, but he had no liking for that; and at last he hired himself out as a manservant at an inn.

The maids could not endure him, though, because he saw everything they did in secret without their seeing him, and told the master and mistress what they had taken off the plates and carried out of the cellar for themselves.

"Wait," they said, "and we'll pay you out" — and arranged between them to play him a trick.

Soon afterwards, when one of the maids was mowing in the garden and saw Thumbling jumping about and creeping up and down the plants, she mowed him up quickly along with the grass, tied it all in a great cloth and secretly threw it to the cows. Now among them there was a great black one, who swallowed him down without hurting him.

Down there, though, he liked it very ill, because it was quite dark and there was no candle burning. When the cow was being milked he called out:

	"Strip, strap, strull,
	will the pail soon be full?"

But the noise of the milking stopped anybody understanding him.

After this the master of the house came into the cowshed and said, "That cow shall be killed tomorrow."

Then Thumbling was so alarmed that he cried out in a clear voice, "Let me out first — I'm shut up inside her!"

The master heard that quite well, but did not know where the voice was coming from. "Where are you?" he asked.

"In the black one," answered Thumbling; but the master did not understand what that meant, and went out.

Next morning the cow was killed. Luckily Thumbling did not take a single blow in the cutting up and chopping; he got in among the sausage meat. And when the butcher came in and started his work, he cried out with all his might, "Don't chop too deep, don't chop too deep, I'm in among it!"

Nobody heard it, because of the noise of the chopping knife. Now poor Thumbling was in trouble; but trouble sharpens the wits, and he sprang about so nimbly between the blows that none of them touched him and he escaped with a whole skin.

But still he could not get away; there was nothing for it but to let himself be stuffed into a black pudding along with the bits of bacon. His quarters there were rather cramped; and besides that he was hung up in the chimney to be smoked, and there the time hung terribly heavy on his hands.

At length, in the winter, he was taken down again, because the black pudding was to be set before a guest. When the landlady was cutting it into slices he took care not to stretch his head out too far, in case a bit of it should be cut off; and at last he saw his chance, cleared a passage for himself and jumped out.

The little tailor would not stay any longer, though, in a house where he had fared so badly, and set out on his travels again at once. But his liberty did not last long. Out in the open country he met a fox, who snapped him up without thinking.

"Hey there, Mr. Fox," cried the little tailor, "it's me sticking in your throat. Set me free again."

"You're right," said the fox. "You're next to nothing to me. But if you'll promise me the fowls in your father's yard, I'll let you go."

"With all my heart," said Thumbling. "You shall have all the cocks and hens, I promise you."

So the fox let him go, and even carried him home himself. And when his father saw his dear son again, he willingly gave the fox all the fowls he had.

"And here I bring you a handsome bit of money too," said Thumbling, and gave his father the farthing he had earned on his travels.

"But why did the fox get the poor chickens to eat?"

"Oh, you goose — surely your father would love his child far more than the fowls in the yard."

Fitcher’s Bird

There was once a wizard who used to take the form of a poor man and go to houses and beg, and catch pretty girls. Nobody knew where he carried them, because they were never seen again.

One day he appeared at the door of a man who had three pretty daughters. He looked like a poor, weak beggar and carried a basket on his back, as though he meant to collect gifts of charity in it. He begged for a little food; and when the eldest daughter came out and was just handing him a piece of bread, he only touched her — and she was forced to jump into his basket.

Then he hurried away with long strides and carried her off into a dark forest, to his house that stood in the middle of it.

Everything in the house was magnificent. He gave her whatever she could possibly want and said, "My darling, you will certainly be happy with me, because you have everything your heart can wish for."

This lasted a few days, and then he said, "I have to go on a journey and leave you alone for a short time. Here are the keys of the house. You may go everywhere and look at everything, except into one room, which this little key opens; and that I forbid you on pain of death."

He also gave her an egg, and said, "Take good care of this egg for me and carry it about with you all the time, because great misfortune would come of losing it."

She took the keys and the egg and promised to obey him in everything. When he had gone she went all round the house from bottom to top and examined everything. The rooms shone with silver and gold, and she thought she had never seen such splendour.

At length she came to the forbidden door. She meant to pass it by, but curiosity gave her no peace. She looked at the key; it looked just like any other. She put it in the keyhole and turned it a little, and the door sprang open.

But what did she see when she went in? A great bloody basin stood in the middle of the room, and in it lay human beings, dead and hacked to pieces; and close by stood a block of wood with a gleaming axe lying on it.

She was so terrified that the egg she was holding fell into the basin. She got it out and washed the blood off, but it was no use — it appeared again in a moment. She washed and scrubbed, but she could not get it off.

It was not long before the man came back from his journey, and the first things he asked for were the key and the egg. She gave them to him, but she trembled as she did it; and he saw at once by the red spots that she had been in the bloody chamber.

"Since you went into that room against my will," he said, "you shall go back into it against your own. Your life is over."

He threw her down, dragged her there by the hair, cut her head off on the block and hacked her to pieces so that her blood ran on the floor. Then he threw her into the basin with the rest.

"Now I'll fetch myself the second," said the wizard; and he went to the house again in the shape of a poor man and begged. Then the second daughter brought him a piece of bread; and he caught her like the first, simply by touching her, and carried her off.

She fared no better than her sister. She let her curiosity get the better of her, opened the door of the bloody chamber, looked in, and had to pay for it with her life when the wizard came back.

Then he went and fetched the third sister; but she was clever and crafty. When he had given her the keys and the egg and had gone, she first put the egg away with great care, and then explored the house, and last of all went into the forbidden room.

Oh, what she saw there! Both her sisters lay in the basin, cruelly murdered and cut to pieces. But she began to gather their limbs together and put them in order — head, body, arms and legs. And when nothing more was missing, the limbs began to move and join themselves together, and both the girls opened their eyes and were alive again. Then they rejoiced and kissed and hugged one another.

When the man came home he demanded the keys and the egg at once; and as he could see no trace of blood on it, he said, "You have stood the test. You shall be my bride."

Now he had no power over her any more, and had to do whatever she wished.

"Very well," she said, "but first you shall take a basketful of gold to my father and mother, and carry it yourself on your back. Meanwhile I'll get ready for the wedding."

Then she ran to her sisters, whom she had hidden in a little room, and said, "The moment has come when I can save you. The wretch shall carry you home himself. But as soon as you're at home, send help to me."

She put them both in a basket and covered them right over with gold, so that nothing of them could be seen; and then she called the wizard in and said, "Now carry the basket away. But I shall be looking out of my little window and watching, to see whether you stop on the road to stand still or to rest."

The wizard lifted the basket onto his back and set off with it; but it weighed him down so heavily that the sweat ran off his face. So he sat down and wanted to rest a while; but immediately one of the girls in the basket cried, "I'm looking out of my little window and I can see you resting. Will you get on at once?"

He thought it was his bride calling to him, and got to his feet again. Once more he was going to sit down, and instantly she cried, "I'm looking out of my little window and I can see you resting. Will you get on this minute?"

And whenever he stood still she cried it, and then he had to go on; until at last, groaning and out of breath, he brought the basket with the gold and the two girls into their parents' house.

At home, meanwhile, the bride was preparing the wedding feast and sending out invitations to the wizard's friends. Then she took a skull with grinning teeth, put some ornaments on it and a wreath of flowers, carried it up to the attic window and set it looking out.

When everything was ready, she got into a barrel of honey, and then cut the feather bed open and rolled herself in it until she looked like some wonderful bird and nobody could have recognised her.

Then she went out of the house; and on the way she met some of the wedding guests, who asked:

	"Oh, Fitcher's bird, how come you here?"
	"I come from Fitcher's house, quite near."
	"And what may the young bride be doing?"
	"From cellar to attic she's swept all clean,
	and now from the window she's peeping, I ween."

At last she met the bridegroom, who was coming slowly back. He asked her, like the others:

	"Oh, Fitcher's bird, how come you here?"
	"I come from Fitcher's house, quite near."
	"And what may the young bride be doing?"
	"From cellar to attic she's swept all clean,
	and now from the window she's peeping, I ween."

The bridegroom looked up, saw the decked-out skull, thought it was his bride and nodded to her, greeting her kindly.

But when he and his guests had all gone into the house, the bride's brothers and kinsmen arrived, who had been sent to rescue her. They locked all the doors of the house so that nobody could escape, and set fire to it; and the wizard and all his crew had to burn.

The Juniper-Tree

It is a long time ago now, quite two thousand years, since there was a rich man who had a beautiful and pious wife, and they loved each other dearly. They had no children, though, however much they wished for them; and the woman prayed for them day and night, and still they had none.

Now in front of their house there was a courtyard, and in it stood a juniper tree; and one day in winter the woman was standing under it paring an apple, and while she was paring it she cut her finger, and the blood fell on the snow.

"Ah," said the woman, and sighed heavily, and looked at the blood in front of her, and was very unhappy, "if only I had a child as red as blood and as white as snow!"

And as she said it she grew quite happy in her mind, and felt just as if it were going to happen. Then she went into the house.

And a month went by, and the snow was gone; and two months, and everything was green; and three months, and all the flowers came up out of the earth; and four months, and all the trees in the wood grew thicker and the green branches were closely twined together, and the birds sang until the wood rang, and the blossom fell from the trees. And the fifth month passed, and she stood under the juniper tree, which smelt so sweet that her heart leapt, and she fell on her knees and was beside herself with joy. And when the sixth month was over the fruit was large and fine, and then she grew quite still. And in the seventh month she snatched at the juniper berries and ate them greedily, and then she grew sick and sorrowful. And the eighth month went by, and she called her husband to her, and wept, and said, "If I die, bury me under the juniper tree."

Then she was quite comforted and happy until the next month was over; and then she had a child as white as snow and as red as blood; and when she saw it she was so delighted that she died.

So her husband buried her under the juniper tree, and began to weep bitterly. After a time he grew easier, and though he still wept he could bear it; and after a while longer he took another wife.

By this second wife he had a daughter; but the first wife's child was a little son, and he was as red as blood and as white as snow. When the woman looked at her daughter she loved her very much; but then she looked at the little boy, and it seemed to cut her to the heart, because the thought came into her mind that he would always stand in her way; and she was for ever thinking how she could get the whole fortune for her daughter. And the Evil One filled her mind with this until she was quite furious with the little boy, and slapped him here and cuffed him there, so that the unhappy child lived in constant terror; for when he came out of school there was nowhere he could have any peace.

One day the woman had gone upstairs to her room, and her little daughter went up too, and said, "Mother, give me an apple."

"Yes, my child," said the woman, and gave her a fine apple out of the chest — but the chest had a great heavy lid with a great sharp iron lock.

"Mother," said the little daughter, "isn't brother to have one too?"

That made the woman angry; but she said, "Yes, when he comes out of school."

And when she saw from the window that he was coming, it was just as if the Devil got into her, and she snatched the apple away from her daughter again and said, "You shan't have one before your brother."

Then she threw the apple into the chest and shut it.

Then the little boy came in at the door; and the Devil made her say to him kindly, "My son, would you like an apple?" — and she looked at him wickedly.

"Mother," said the little boy, "how dreadful you look! Yes, give me an apple."

Then it seemed to her that she was forced to say to him, "Come with me" — and she opened the lid of the chest and said, "Take out an apple for yourself." And while the little boy was stooping inside, the Devil prompted her, and crash! she slammed the lid down, and his head flew off and fell among the red apples.

Then she was overwhelmed with terror, and thought, "If only I could make them think it wasn't me!" So she went up to her room to her chest of drawers and took a white handkerchief out of the top drawer, and set the head on the neck again and tied the handkerchief so that nothing could be seen; and she sat him on a chair in front of the door and put the apple in his hand.

After this Marlinchen came into the kitchen to her mother, who was standing by the fire with a pan of hot water in front of her, stirring it round and round.

"Mother," said Marlinchen, "brother is sitting at the door and he looks quite white and has an apple in his hand. I asked him to give me the apple, but he didn't answer me, and I was quite frightened."

"Go back to him," said her mother, "and if he won't answer you, box his ears."

So Marlinchen went to him and said, "Brother, give me the apple." But he said nothing; so she boxed his ears — and his head fell off.

Marlinchen was terrified and began crying and screaming, and ran to her mother and said, "Oh, mother, I've knocked my brother's head off!" — and she wept and wept and could not be comforted.

"Marlinchen," said her mother, "what have you done? But be quiet and let nobody know about it. It can't be helped now. We'll make him into black puddings."

Then the mother took the little boy and chopped him in pieces and put him in the pan and made him into black puddings; and Marlinchen stood by weeping and weeping, and all her tears fell into the pan, so that there was no need of any salt.

Then the father came home and sat down to dinner and said, "But where is my son?"

And the mother served up a great dish of black puddings; and Marlinchen wept and could not stop.

Then the father said again, "But where is my son?"

"Ah," said the mother, "he's gone off across the country to his mother's great-uncle. He'll stay there a while."

"And what has he gone to do there? He didn't even say goodbye to me."

"Oh, he wanted to go, and asked me whether he might stay six weeks. He's well looked after there."

"Ah," said the man, "I feel so unhappy, in case something isn't right. He ought to have said goodbye to me."

With that he began to eat, and said, "Marlinchen, why are you crying? Your brother will certainly come back."

And then he said, "Ah, wife, how delicious this food is. Give me some more." And the more he ate, the more he wanted, and he said, "Give me some more. You shan't have any of it. It seems to me as if it were all mine."

And he ate and ate and threw all the bones under the table, until he had finished the whole lot.

But Marlinchen went to her chest of drawers and took her best silk handkerchief out of the bottom drawer, and got all the bones from under the table and tied them up in her silk handkerchief and carried them outside the door, weeping tears of blood.

Then the juniper tree began to stir itself, and the branches parted and moved together again, just as if somebody were rejoicing and clapping his hands. At the same time a mist seemed to rise from the tree, and in the middle of the mist it burned like a fire; and out of the fire flew a beautiful bird, singing magnificently, and he flew high up into the air. And when he was gone, the juniper tree was just as it had been before, and the handkerchief with the bones was no longer there.

But Marlinchen was as gay and happy as if her brother were still alive; and she went merrily into the house and sat down to dinner and ate.

But the bird flew away and settled on a goldsmith's house, and began to sing:

	"My mother, she killed me;
	my father, he ate me;
	my sister, little Marlinchen,
	gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

The goldsmith was sitting in his workshop making a gold chain when he heard the bird singing on his roof, and the song seemed very beautiful to him. He stood up, and as he crossed the threshold he lost one of his slippers. But he went right on up the middle of the street with one shoe on and one sock; he had his apron on, and in one hand he had the gold chain and in the other his pincers, and the sun was shining brightly on the street.

Then he went right up and stood still and said to the bird, "Bird, how beautifully you sing! Sing me that piece again."

"No," said the bird, "I won't sing it twice for nothing. Give me the golden chain, and then I'll sing it again for you."

"There," said the goldsmith, "there's the golden chain for you. Now sing me that song again."

Then the bird came and took the golden chain in his right claw, and went and sat in front of the goldsmith and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;
	my father, he ate me;
	my sister, little Marlinchen,
	gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

Then the bird flew away to a shoemaker's, and settled on his roof and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;
	my father, he ate me;
	my sister, little Marlinchen,
	gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

The shoemaker heard it and ran out of doors in his shirtsleeves and looked up at his roof, and had to hold his hand in front of his eyes to keep the sun from blinding him.

"Bird," he said, "how beautifully you sing!" Then he called in at his door, "Wife, just come outside — there's a bird here. Look at that bird. He really can sing well."

Then he called his daughter and his children and his apprentices, boys and girls, and they all came up the street and looked at the bird and saw how beautiful he was, and what fine red and green feathers he had, and how his neck was like real gold, and how the eyes in his head shone like stars.

"Bird," said the shoemaker, "now sing me that song again."

"No," said the bird, "I don't sing twice for nothing. You must give me something."

"Wife," said the man, "go up to the garret. On the top shelf there's a pair of red shoes; bring them down."

So his wife went and fetched the shoes.

"There, bird," said the man, "now sing me that piece again."

Then the bird came and took the shoes in his left claw and flew back up onto the roof and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;
	my father, he ate me;
	my sister, little Marlinchen,
	gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

And when he had sung it all through he flew away. In his right claw he had the chain and in his left the shoes; and he flew far away to a mill, and the mill went klipp klapp, klipp klapp, klipp klapp. And in the mill sat twenty of the miller's men hewing a stone, and cutting, hick hack, hick hack, hick hack; and the mill went klipp klapp, klipp klapp, klipp klapp.

Then the bird went and sat in a lime tree that stood in front of the mill, and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;"

Then one of them stopped working.

	"my father, he ate me;"

Then two more stopped working and listened.

	"my sister, little Marlinchen,"

Then four more stopped.

	"gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief"

Now only eight were hewing.

	"and laid them under"

Now only five.

	"the juniper tree."

And now only one.

	"Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

Then the last one stopped too, and heard the last words.

"Bird," he said, "how beautifully you sing! Let me hear it too. Sing it once more for me."

"No," said the bird, "I won't sing twice for nothing. Give me the millstone, and then I'll sing it again."

"Yes," he said, "if it belonged to me alone, you should have it."

"Yes," said the others, "if he sings again he shall have it."

Then the bird came down, and the twenty millers set to with a beam and raised the stone up. And the bird stuck his neck through the hole and put the stone on like a collar, and flew back to the tree and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;
	my father, he ate me;
	my sister, little Marlinchen,
	gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

And when he had finished singing he spread his wings; and in his right claw he had the chain, and in his left the shoes, and round his neck the millstone; and he flew far away to his father's house.

In the room sat the father, the mother and Marlinchen at dinner; and the father said, "How light-hearted I feel, how happy I am!"

"No," said the mother, "I feel so uneasy, just as if a heavy storm were coming."

Marlinchen, though, sat weeping and weeping.

Then the bird came flying up; and as it settled on the roof, the father said, "Ah, I feel so truly happy, and the sun is shining so beautifully outside. I feel just as if I were going to see an old friend again."

"No," said the woman, "I feel so anxious. My teeth are chattering and I seem to have fire in my veins." And she tore her bodice open.

But Marlinchen sat in a corner crying, and held her plate in front of her eyes and cried until it was quite wet.

Then the bird settled in the juniper tree and sang:

	"My mother, she killed me;"

Then the mother stopped her ears and shut her eyes and would not see or hear; but there was a roaring in her ears like the most violent storm, and her eyes burned and flashed like lightning.

	"my father, he ate me;"

"Ah, mother," says the man, "that's a beautiful bird. He sings so splendidly, and the sun is so warm, and there's a smell just like cinnamon."

	"my sister, little Marlinchen,"

Then Marlinchen laid her head on her knees and wept without stopping; but the man said, "I'm going out. I must see the bird close to."

"Oh, don't go," said the woman. "I feel as if the whole house were shaking and on fire."

But the man went out and looked at the bird.

	"gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief
	and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

At that the bird let the golden chain fall, and it fell exactly round the man's neck, so exactly that it fitted beautifully. Then he went in and said, "Just look what a fine bird that is, and what a handsome gold chain he's given me, and how pretty he is!"

But the woman was terrified and fell down on the floor of the room, and her cap fell off her head.

Then the bird sang once more:

	"My mother, she killed me;"

"I wish I were a thousand feet under the earth, so as not to hear it!"

	"my father, he ate me;"

Then the woman fell down again as if she were dead.

	"my sister, little Marlinchen,"

"Ah," said Marlinchen, "I'll go out too and see whether the bird will give me anything" — and she went out.

	"gathered up all my bones,
	tied them in a silken handkerchief"

Then he threw the shoes down to her.

	"and laid them under the juniper tree.
	Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!"

Then she was light-hearted and full of joy, and put on the new red shoes and danced and skipped into the house.

"Ah," she said, "I was so sad when I went out, and now I'm so light-hearted. That's a splendid bird — he's given me a pair of red shoes!"

"Well," said the woman, and sprang to her feet, and her hair stood up like flames of fire, "I feel as if the world were coming to an end. I'll go out too and see whether my heart feels lighter."

And as she went out at the door — crash! — the bird threw the millstone down on her head, and she was crushed to pieces by it.

The father and Marlinchen heard what had happened and went out; and smoke and flames and fire were rising from the place. And when that was over, there stood the little brother; and he took his father and Marlinchen by the hand, and all three were full of joy, and they went into the house and sat down to dinner and ate.

Old Sultan

A farmer once had a faithful dog called Sultan, who had grown old and lost all his teeth, so that he could no longer hold onto anything.

One day the farmer was standing with his wife in front of the house door and said, "Tomorrow I mean to shoot Old Sultan. He's no use any more."

His wife, who felt sorry for the faithful creature, answered, "He's served us so long and been so faithful that we might well keep him."

"Eh, what?" said the man. "You're not very sharp. He hasn't a tooth left in his head, and not a thief is afraid of him. Now he can go. If he's served us, he's had good feeding for it."

The poor dog, who was lying stretched out in the sun not far off, had heard everything, and was sorry that tomorrow was to be his last day. He had a good friend, the wolf; and in the evening he crept out into the forest to him and complained of the fate that was waiting for him.

"Listen, old friend," said the wolf, "be of good cheer. I'll help you out of your trouble. I've thought of something. Tomorrow morning early your master is going haymaking with his wife, and they'll take their little child with them, because nobody will be left behind in the house. While they're working they always lay the child down under the hedge in the shade. You lie down there too, just as if you meant to guard it. Then I'll come out of the wood and carry the child off. You must rush after me as fast as you can, as if you were going to take it back from me. I'll let it fall, and you'll bring it back to its parents; and they'll think you saved it, and they'll be far too grateful to do you any harm. On the contrary, you'll be in high favour, and they'll never let you want for anything again."

The dog liked the plan, and it was carried out exactly as arranged. The father screamed when he saw the wolf running across the field with his child; but when Old Sultan brought it back, then he was full of joy, and stroked him and said, "Not a hair of yours shall be harmed. You shall eat my bread free as long as you live."

And to his wife he said, "Go home at once and make Old Sultan some bread and milk that he won't have to bite; and bring the pillow out of my bed — I'll give him that to lie on."

From then on Old Sultan was as well off as he could wish to be.

Soon afterwards the wolf came to visit him, and was pleased that everything had gone so well. "But, old friend," he said, "you'll just wink an eye, won't you, if I get a chance to carry off one of your master's fat sheep?"

"Don't count on that," said the dog. "I shall stay true to my master. I can't agree to that."

The wolf, who did not think this could be meant seriously, came creeping about in the night and was going to take the sheep. But the farmer, who had been told the wolf's plan by faithful Sultan, caught him and dressed his hide soundly with the flail. The wolf had to make off; but he called out to the dog, "Just wait, you scoundrel, you'll pay for this."

Next morning the wolf sent the boar to challenge the dog to come out into the forest and settle the matter. Old Sultan could find nobody to stand by him but a cat with only three legs; and as they went out together the poor cat limped along, and at the same time stuck her tail up in the air with the pain.

The wolf and his friend were already at the appointed place; but when they saw their enemy coming they thought he was bringing a sabre with him, because they took the cat's outstretched tail for one. And whenever the poor creature hopped on her three legs, they could only think each time that she was picking up a stone to throw at them.

So they were both frightened. The wild boar crept into the undergrowth and the wolf jumped up a tree.

When the dog and the cat came up they wondered that there was nobody to be seen. The wild boar, though, had not been able to hide himself completely, and one of his ears was still showing. While the cat was looking carefully about, the boar moved his ear; and the cat, thinking it was a mouse moving there, jumped on it and bit it hard. The boar made a fearful noise and ran off, crying out, "The guilty one is up in the tree!"

The dog and the cat looked up and saw the wolf, who was ashamed of having shown himself so timid, and made friends with the dog.

The Six Swans

Once upon a time a certain King was hunting in a great forest, and he chased a wild beast so eagerly that none of his attendants could keep up with him. When evening came on he stopped and looked round him, and then he saw that he had lost his way. He looked for a way out and could not find one.

Then he caught sight of an old woman, whose head nodded all the time, coming towards him; but she was a witch.

"Good woman," he said to her, "can you show me the way out of the forest?"

"Oh yes, my lord King," she answered, "I certainly can — but on one condition; and if you don't keep it, you'll never get out of the forest and will starve to death in it."

"What sort of condition is it?" asked the King.

"I have a daughter," said the old woman, "who is as beautiful as anybody in the world, and well deserves to be your consort. If you'll make her your Queen, I'll show you the way out of the forest."

In the anguish of his heart the King consented, and the old woman led him to her little hut, where her daughter was sitting by the fire. She received the King as if she had been expecting him; and he saw that she was very beautiful, but all the same she did not please him, and he could not look at her without a secret horror.

After he had taken the girl up on his horse, the old woman showed him the way, and the King reached his royal palace again, where the wedding was celebrated.

The King had been married once before, and by his first wife he had seven children, six boys and a girl, whom he loved better than anything in the world. And as he now feared that their stepmother might not treat them well, or might even do them some harm, he took them to a lonely castle that stood in the middle of a forest. It lay so hidden, and the way was so hard to find, that he would not have found it himself if a wise woman had not given him a ball of yarn with wonderful properties: when he threw it down in front of him, it unwound itself and showed him his path.

But the King went off to his dear children so often that the Queen noticed his absences. She was curious, and wanted to know what he did when he was out alone in the forest. She gave a great deal of money to his servants, and they betrayed the secret to her and told her about the ball, which alone could show the way.

And now she had no rest until she had found out where the King kept the ball of yarn. Then she made little shirts of white silk; and as she had learned the art of witchcraft from her mother, she sewed a charm into them.

And once, when the King had ridden out hunting, she took the little shirts and went into the forest, and the ball showed her the way. The children, seeing from a distance that somebody was coming, thought it was their dear father coming to them, and ran to meet him full of joy. Then she threw one of the little shirts over each of them; and no sooner had the shirts touched their bodies than they were turned into swans and flew away over the forest.

The Queen went home quite delighted, thinking she had got rid of her stepchildren; but the girl had not run out with her brothers, and the Queen knew nothing about her.

Next day the King came to visit his children, but he found nobody there but the little girl.

"Where are your brothers?" asked the King.

"Alas, dear father," she answered, "they have gone away and left me alone" — and she told him how she had seen from her little window how her brothers had flown away over the forest as swans; and she showed him the feathers they had dropped in the courtyard, which she had picked up.

The King grieved, but he did not think the Queen had done this wicked thing; and as he was afraid the girl would be stolen away from him too, he wanted to take her home with him. But she was afraid of her stepmother, and begged the King to let her stay just one more night in the forest castle.

The poor girl thought, "I can't stay here any longer. I'll go and look for my brothers." And when night came she ran away and went straight into the forest.

She walked the whole night long, and the next day too, without stopping, until she could go no further for weariness. Then she saw a hut in the forest and went into it, and found a room with six little beds; but she did not dare get into one of them, and crept under one instead and lay down on the hard ground, meaning to spend the night there.

Just before sunset, though, she heard a rustling, and saw six swans come flying in at the window. They settled on the ground and blew at one another and blew all their feathers off, and their swan skins came off like shirts. Then the girl looked at them and recognised her brothers, and was glad, and crept out from under the bed.

The brothers were no less delighted to see their little sister, but their joy did not last long.

"You can't stay here," they told her. "This is a robbers' den. If they come home and find you, they'll kill you."

"But can't you protect me?" asked the little sister.

"No," they said. "Only for a quarter of an hour each evening can we lay our swan skins aside and have our human shape; after that we're turned into swans again."

The little sister wept and said, "Can't you be set free?"

"Alas, no," they said. "The conditions are too hard. For six years you may neither speak nor laugh, and in that time you must sew six little shirts of starwort for us. And if a single word falls from your lips, all your work will be lost."

And when the brothers had said this, the quarter of an hour was over, and they flew out of the window again as swans.

But the girl firmly resolved to set her brothers free, even if it cost her her life. She left the hut, went into the middle of the forest, settled herself in a tree and passed the night there.

Next morning she went out and gathered starwort and began to sew. She could not speak to anybody, and she had no inclination to laugh; she sat there and looked at nothing but her work.

When she had already spent a long time there, it happened that the King of the country was hunting in the forest, and his huntsmen came to the tree the girl was sitting in. They called up to her and said, "Who are you?" But she gave no answer.

"Come down to us," they said. "We won't do you any harm."

She only shook her head. And when they pressed her further with questions, she threw her golden necklace down to them, thinking to satisfy them with that. But they did not stop; and then she threw her belt down to them; and as that was no use either, her garters; and by degrees everything she had on that she could do without, until she had nothing left but her shift.

The huntsmen would not be turned aside by any of it, but climbed the tree and fetched the girl down and led her before the King.

The King asked, "Who are you? What are you doing in that tree?" But she did not answer. He put the question in every language he knew, but she stayed as mute as a fish.

As she was so beautiful, the King's heart was touched, and he was seized with a great love for her. He put his cloak round her, took her up on his horse in front of him and carried her to his castle. Then he had her dressed in rich clothes, and she shone in her beauty like bright daylight; but not a word could be got out of her.

He seated her at his side at table, and her modest bearing and her courtesy pleased him so much that he said, "She is the one I want to marry, and no other woman in the world." And after a few days he married her.

But the King had a wicked mother who was displeased with this marriage and spoke ill of the young Queen. "Who knows where this creature who can't speak comes from?" she said. "She isn't worthy of a king."

After a year had gone by, when the Queen brought her first child into the world, the old woman took it away from her and smeared her mouth with blood as she slept. Then she went to the King and accused the Queen of being an eater of human flesh. The King would not believe it, and would not let anybody do her any harm. But she went on sewing at the shirts all the time, and cared for nothing else.

The next time, when she bore another beautiful boy, the false stepmother used the same treachery; but the King could not bring himself to believe her words. He said, "She is too pious and good to do anything of that kind. If she weren't dumb and could defend herself, her innocence would come to light."

But when the old woman stole the newborn child away the third time and accused the Queen, who did not speak one word in her own defence, the King could do nothing else but hand her over to justice; and she was sentenced to be burned to death.

When the day came for the sentence to be carried out, it was the last day of the six years in which she was not to speak or laugh, and she had delivered her dear brothers from the power of the enchantment. The six shirts were ready; only the left sleeve of the sixth was missing.

So when she was led to the stake she laid the shirts over her arm; and when she was standing up there and the fire was just about to be lit, she looked round — and six swans came flying through the air towards her. Then she saw that her deliverance was near, and her heart leapt for joy.

The swans swept towards her and sank down so that she could throw the shirts over them; and as the shirts touched them, their swan skins fell away, and her brothers stood in front of her in their own bodily shape, strong and handsome. Only the youngest was missing his left arm, and had a swan's wing on his shoulder instead of it.

They hugged and kissed one another, and the Queen went to the King, who was deeply moved; and she began to speak and said, "Dearest husband, now I may speak and tell you that I am innocent and falsely accused." And she told him of the old woman's treachery, and how she had taken away her three children and hidden them.

Then, to the King's great joy, they were brought there; and as a punishment the wicked stepmother was bound to the stake and burnt to ashes. But the King and the Queen and her six brothers lived many years in happiness and peace.

Briar-Rose

A long time ago there were a King and Queen who said every day, "Ah, if only we had a child!" — and they never had one.

But it happened that once, when the Queen was bathing, a frog crept out of the water onto the land and said to her, "Your wish shall be granted. Before a year has gone by you shall have a daughter."

What the frog had said came true, and the Queen had a little girl who was so pretty that the King could not contain himself for joy, and gave orders for a great feast. He invited not only his kinsfolk and friends and acquaintances, but the Wise Women too, so that they might be kind and well disposed towards the child. There were thirteen of them in his kingdom; but as he only had twelve golden plates for them to eat off, one of them had to be left at home.

The feast was held with all possible splendour; and when it came to an end, the Wise Women bestowed their magic gifts on the baby: one gave virtue, another beauty, a third riches, and so on with everything in the world that anybody could wish for.

When eleven of them had made their promises, suddenly the thirteenth came in. She wanted to revenge herself for not having been invited; and without a greeting, or so much as looking at anybody, she cried in a loud voice, "In her fifteenth year the King's daughter shall prick herself with a spindle and fall down dead." And without another word she turned round and left the room.

They were all appalled; but the twelfth, whose good wish was still unspoken, came forward; and as she could not undo the evil sentence, but only soften it, she said, "It shall not be death, but a deep sleep of a hundred years, that the princess falls into."

The King, wanting to keep his dear child from the misfortune, gave orders that every spindle in the whole kingdom should be burnt. Meanwhile the gifts of the Wise Women were fulfilled to the full in the young girl; for she was so beautiful, modest, good-natured and wise that everybody who saw her could not help loving her.

It happened that on the very day she turned fifteen the King and Queen were not at home, and the girl was left in the palace all alone. So she went round into all sorts of places, and looked into the rooms and bedchambers just as she liked, and at last came to an old tower.
