She climbed the narrow winding staircase and came to a little door. There was a rusty key in the lock, and when she turned it the door sprang open — and there in a little room sat an old woman with a spindle, busily spinning her flax.

"Good day, old dame," said the King's daughter. "What are you doing there?"

"I am spinning," said the old woman, and nodded her head.

"What sort of thing is that, that rattles round so merrily?" said the girl; and she took the spindle and wanted to spin too.

But hardly had she touched the spindle before the magic decree was fulfilled, and she pricked her finger with it.

And at the very moment she felt the prick, she fell down on the bed that stood there and lay in a deep sleep. And that sleep spread over the whole palace. The King and Queen, who had just come home and had come into the great hall, began to fall asleep, and the whole court with them. The horses fell asleep in the stable, the dogs in the yard, the pigeons on the roof, the flies on the wall. Even the fire that was flaming on the hearth grew quiet and slept; the roasting meat left off sizzling; and the cook, who was just about to pull the kitchen boy's hair because he had forgotten something, let him go and fell asleep. And the wind dropped, and on the trees in front of the castle not one leaf stirred again.

But round about the castle a hedge of thorns began to grow, which got higher every year, and at last grew right up round the castle and all over it, so that there was nothing of it to be seen, not even the flag on the roof.

But the story of the beautiful sleeping Briar-Rose — for so the princess was called — went about the country, so that from time to time kings' sons came and tried to get through the thorn hedge into the castle. They found it impossible, though, because the thorns held fast together as if they had hands, and the young men were caught in them and could not get loose again, and died a miserable death.

After long, long years another King's son came to that country, and heard an old man talking about the thorn hedge, and how there was said to be a castle behind it in which a wonderfully beautiful princess named Briar-Rose had been asleep for a hundred years, and the King and Queen and the whole court were asleep as well. He had heard, too, from his grandfather, that a great many kings' sons had already come and tried to get through the thorn hedge, and had stuck fast in it and died a pitiful death.

Then the young man said, "I'm not afraid. I'm going to see the beautiful Briar-Rose." However much the good old man tried to dissuade him, he would not listen to a word of it.

But by now the hundred years had just passed, and the day had come when Briar-Rose was to wake again. When the King's son came near the thorn hedge, it was nothing but great and beautiful flowers, which parted of their own accord and let him pass unhurt, and then closed behind him like a hedge again.

In the castle yard he saw the horses and the spotted hounds lying asleep; on the roof sat the pigeons with their heads under their wings. And when he went into the house, the flies were asleep on the wall, the cook in the kitchen was still holding out his hand to grab the boy, and the maid was sitting by the black hen she had been going to pluck.

He went further, and in the great hall he saw the whole court lying asleep, and up by the throne lay the King and Queen.

Then he went further still, and everything was so quiet that he could hear his own breathing; and at last he came to the tower and opened the door into the little room where Briar-Rose was sleeping. There she lay, so beautiful that he could not take his eyes off her; and he bent down and gave her a kiss.

And as soon as he kissed her, Briar-Rose opened her eyes and woke, and looked at him quite sweetly.

Then they went downstairs together; and the King woke, and the Queen, and the whole court, and they all looked at one another in great astonishment. And the horses in the yard got up and shook themselves; the hounds jumped up and wagged their tails; the pigeons on the roof pulled their heads out from under their wings, looked round and flew off into the open country; the flies on the wall began to crawl again; the fire in the kitchen flared up and flickered and cooked the food; the joint began to turn and sizzle again; and the cook gave the boy such a box on the ear that he yelled, and the maid finished plucking the fowl for the spit.

And then the marriage of the King's son and Briar-Rose was celebrated with all splendour, and they lived contented to the end of their days.

Fundevogel (Bird-foundling)

There was once a forester who went into the forest to hunt; and as he came into it he heard a sound of screaming, as if a little child were there. He followed the sound, and at last came to a tall tree, and at the top of it a little child was sitting; for the mother had fallen asleep under the tree with the child, and a bird of prey had seen it in her arms and flown down and snatched it away and set it in the tall tree.

The forester climbed up and brought the child down, and thought to himself, "You'll take him home with you and bring him up with your Lina." So he took it home, and the two children grew up together. The one he had found in a tree was called Fundevogel, because a bird had carried it away. Fundevogel and Lina loved each other so dearly that when they could not see each other they were miserable.

Now the forester had an old cook, who one evening took two pails and began fetching water, and did not go out to the spring once only but many times over.

Lina saw it and said, "Listen, old Sanna, why are you fetching so much water?"

"If you'll never tell anybody, I'll tell you why."

So Lina said, no, she would never tell anybody; and then the cook said, "Early tomorrow morning, when the forester is out hunting, I'll heat the water; and when it's boiling in the kettle I'll throw Fundevogel in and boil him in it."

Early next morning the forester got up and went out hunting, and when he had gone the children were still in bed.

Then Lina said to Fundevogel, "If you'll never leave me, I'll never leave you either."

Fundevogel said, "Neither now nor ever will I leave you."

Then Lina said, "Then I'll tell you. Last night old Sanna carried so many buckets of water into the house that I asked her why she was doing it, and she said that if I'd promise not to tell anybody she'd tell me; and I said I'd be sure not to tell; and she said that early this morning, when father was out hunting, she'd fill the kettle with water and throw you in and boil you. But we'll get up quickly and dress and go away together."

So the two children got up, dressed quickly and went away.

When the water in the kettle was boiling, the cook went into the bedroom to fetch Fundevogel and throw him in. But when she came in and went to the beds, both the children were gone. Then she was terribly alarmed, and said to herself, "What shall I say when the forester comes home and sees the children gone? They must be followed at once and brought back."

So the cook sent three servants after them, who were to run and overtake the children.

The children, though, were sitting outside the forest; and when they saw the three servants running in the distance, Lina said to Fundevogel, "Never leave me, and I'll never leave you."

Fundevogel said, "Neither now nor ever."

Then Lina said, "You become a rose bush, and I'll be the rose on it."

When the three servants came to the forest there was nothing there but a rose bush with one rose on it, and the children were nowhere to be seen.

So they said, "There's nothing to be done here" — and went home and told the cook they had seen nothing in the forest but a little rose bush with one rose on it.

Then the old cook scolded them and said, "You simpletons, you should have cut the rose bush in two and broken off the rose and brought it home with you. Go and do it at once."

So they had to go out and look a second time. But the children saw them coming a long way off.

Then Lina said, "Fundevogel, never leave me, and I'll never leave you."

Fundevogel said, "Neither now nor ever."

Lina said, "Then you become a church, and I'll be the chandelier in it."

So when the three servants came, there was nothing there but a church with a chandelier in it. So they said to one another, "What can we do here? Let's go home."

When they got home the cook asked whether they had found them; and they said no, they had found nothing but a church with a chandelier in it.

And the cook scolded them and said, "You fools! Why didn't you pull the church to pieces and bring the chandelier home with you?"

And now the old cook got on her own legs and went with the three servants in pursuit of the children.

But the children saw from a long way off that the three servants were coming, with the cook waddling after them.

Then Lina said, "Fundevogel, never leave me, and I'll never leave you."

Then Fundevogel said, "Neither now nor ever."

Lina said, "Be a fishpond, and I'll be the duck on it."

The cook came up to them; and when she saw the pond she lay down beside it and was going to drink it dry. But the duck swam up quickly, seized her head in its beak and pulled her into the water; and there the old witch had to drown.

Then the children went home together and were heartily glad; and if they are not dead, they are living still.

King Thrushbeard

A King had a daughter who was beautiful beyond all measure, but so proud and haughty with it that no suitor was good enough for her. She sent them away one after another, and made fun of them into the bargain.

Once the King held a great feast and invited to it, from far and near, all the young men who might marry her. They were drawn up in a row according to their rank and standing: first the kings, then the grand dukes, then the princes, the earls, the barons and the gentry. Then the King's daughter was led along the ranks; but she had some objection to make to every one of them.

One was too fat: "The wine barrel," she said. Another was too tall: "Long and thin has little in." The third was too short: "Short and thick is never quick." The fourth was too pale: "As pale as death." The fifth too red: "A fighting cock." The sixth was not straight enough: "A green log dried behind the stove."

So she had something to say against every one of them; but she made herself especially merry over a good king who stood quite high up in the row, and whose chin had grown a little crooked.

"Well!" she cried, laughing, "he has a chin like a thrush's beak!" And from that time he was called King Thrushbeard.

But the old King, when he saw that his daughter did nothing but mock people and despised all the suitors who had gathered there, was very angry, and swore that she should have for her husband the very first beggar who came to his door.

A few days afterwards a fiddler came and sang under the windows, trying to earn a small alms. When the King heard him he said, "Let him come up."

So the fiddler came in, in his dirty ragged clothes, and sang in front of the King and his daughter; and when he had finished he asked for some small gift.

The King said, "Your song has pleased me so well that I'll give you my daughter there for a wife."

The King's daughter shuddered; but the King said, "I have sworn an oath to give you to the very first beggar man, and I mean to keep it."

Everything she could say was useless. The priest was fetched, and she had to let herself be married to the fiddler on the spot.

When that was done the King said, "Now it isn't proper for you, a beggar woman, to stay any longer in my palace. You can just go off with your husband."

The beggar man led her out by the hand, and she had to walk away on foot with him.

When they came to a great forest she asked, "Who does that beautiful forest belong to?"

"It belongs to King Thrushbeard. If you had taken him, it would have been yours."

"Ah, unhappy girl that I am — if only I had taken King Thrushbeard!"

Afterwards they came to a meadow, and she asked again, "Who does this beautiful green meadow belong to?"

"It belongs to King Thrushbeard. If you had taken him, it would have been yours."

"Ah, unhappy girl that I am — if only I had taken King Thrushbeard!"

Then they came to a large town, and she asked again, "Who does this fine large town belong to?"

"It belongs to King Thrushbeard. If you had taken him, it would have been yours."

"Ah, unhappy girl that I am — if only I had taken King Thrushbeard!"

"It doesn't please me," said the fiddler, "to hear you always wishing for another husband. Am I not good enough for you?"

At last they came to a very small hut, and she said, "Oh, goodness, what a tiny house! Who does this miserable little hovel belong to?"

The fiddler answered, "That is my house and yours, where we shall live together."

She had to stoop to get in at the low door.

"Where are the servants?" said the King's daughter.

"What servants?" answered the beggar man. "You must do for yourself whatever you want done. Just make a fire at once and put water on to cook my supper. I'm quite worn out."

But the King's daughter knew nothing about lighting fires or cooking, and the beggar man had to lend a hand himself to get anything decently done. When they had finished their scanty meal they went to bed; but he made her get up very early in the morning to look after the house.

For a few days they lived like this as well as they could, and came to the end of all their provisions. Then the man said, "Wife, we can't go on eating and drinking here and earning nothing. You shall weave baskets."

He went out, cut some willows and brought them home. Then she began to weave; but the tough willows cut her delicate hands.

"I see that won't do," said the man. "You'd better spin — perhaps you can manage that better."

She sat down and tried to spin; but the hard thread soon cut her soft fingers so that the blood ran down.

"There," said the man, "you're fit for no sort of work. I've made a bad bargain in you. Now I'll try setting up in pots and earthenware. You must sit in the marketplace and sell the ware."

"Alas," she thought, "if any of the people from my father's kingdom come to the market and see me sitting there selling, how they'll mock me!" But it was no use; she had to give in unless she wanted to starve.

The first time it went well, because people were glad to buy the woman's wares since she was good-looking, and paid her what she asked; and many of them even gave her the money and left the pots with her as well.

So they lived on what she had earned as long as it lasted; and then her husband bought a great stock of new crockery. She sat down with it at a corner of the marketplace and set it out round her, ready for sale.

But suddenly a drunken cavalryman came galloping along and rode right in among the pots, so that they were all broken into a thousand pieces. She began to cry, and did not know what to do for fear.

"Oh, what will become of me?" she cried. "What will my husband say to this?"

She ran home and told him of the disaster.

"Who ever heard of sitting at the corner of a marketplace with crockery?" said the man. "Stop crying. I can see perfectly well that you can't do any ordinary work. So I've been to our King's palace and asked whether they can't find a place for a kitchen maid, and they've promised to take you. That way you'll get your food for nothing."

So now the King's daughter was a kitchen maid, and had to be at the cook's beck and call and do the dirtiest work. In both her pockets she fastened a little jar, in which she carried home her share of the leavings; and that was what they lived on.

It happened that the wedding of the King's eldest son was to be celebrated; so the poor woman went up and stood by the door of the hall to watch. And when all the candles were lit, and the people came in, each more splendid than the last, and everything was full of pomp and splendour, she thought of her lot with a heavy heart, and cursed the pride and haughtiness that had humbled her and brought her to such poverty.

The smell of the delicious dishes being carried in and out reached her, and now and then the servants threw her a few scraps of them; and these she put into her jars to take home.

All at once the King's son came in, dressed in velvet and silk, with gold chains round his neck. And when he saw the beautiful woman standing by the door, he took her by the hand and would have danced with her. But she refused and shrank back in terror, because she saw that it was King Thrushbeard, the suitor she had driven away with her scorn.

Her struggling was no use; he drew her into the hall. But the string her pockets were hung by broke, the pots fell down, the soup ran out and the scraps were scattered all over the floor. And when the people saw it, there was general laughter and mockery; and she was so ashamed that she would rather have been a thousand fathoms under the ground.

She sprang to the door and would have run away, but a man caught her on the stairs and brought her back; and when she looked at him it was King Thrushbeard again.

He said to her kindly, "Don't be afraid. I and the fiddler who has been living with you in that wretched hovel are one and the same. For love of you I disguised myself like that; and I was the cavalryman too, who rode through your crockery. All this was done to humble your proud spirit, and to punish you for the insolence with which you mocked me."

Then she wept bitterly and said, "I have done a great wrong, and I am not worthy to be your wife."

But he said, "Be comforted — the bad days are over. Now we'll celebrate our wedding."

Then the maids of honour came and dressed her in the most splendid clothes; and her father came with his whole court and wished her happiness in her marriage with King Thrushbeard; and now the rejoicing began in earnest.

I wish you and I had been there too.

Little Snow-White

Once upon a time, in the middle of winter, when the snowflakes were falling like feathers from the sky, a queen sat sewing at a window with a frame of black ebony. And while she was sewing and looking out at the snow, she pricked her finger with the needle, and three drops of blood fell on the snow. And the red looked so beautiful on the white snow that she thought to herself, "If only I had a child as white as snow, as red as blood, and as black as the wood of this window frame."

Soon after that she had a little daughter, who was as white as snow and as red as blood, and her hair was as black as ebony; and so she was called Little Snow-White. And when the child was born, the Queen died.

After a year had gone by, the King took another wife. She was a beautiful woman, but proud and haughty, and she could not bear that anybody should be more beautiful than she was. She had a wonderful mirror; and when she stood in front of it and looked at herself and said:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

the mirror answered:

	"You, my Queen, are the fairest of all."

Then she was satisfied, because she knew the mirror spoke the truth.

But Snow-White was growing up, and growing more and more beautiful; and when she was seven years old she was as beautiful as the day, and more beautiful than the Queen herself. And once, when the Queen asked her mirror:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

it answered:

	"You are the fairest here, it's true,
	but Snow-White is fairer far than you."

Then the Queen was appalled, and turned yellow and green with envy. From that hour, whenever she looked at Snow-White her heart heaved in her breast, she hated the girl so much.

And envy and pride grew higher and higher in her heart like a weed, so that she had no peace day or night. She called a huntsman and said, "Take the child away into the forest. I will not have her in my sight any longer. Kill her, and bring me back her heart as proof."

The huntsman obeyed and took her away; but when he had drawn his knife and was about to pierce Snow-White's innocent heart, she began to cry and said, "Ah, dear huntsman, spare my life! I'll run away into the wild forest and never come home again."

And because she was so beautiful, the huntsman took pity on her and said, "Run away, then, you poor child."

"The wild beasts will soon have eaten you," he thought; and yet it was as though a stone had been rolled off his heart, now that he did not have to kill her. And as a young boar came running by just then, he killed it and cut out its heart and took it to the Queen as proof that the child was dead. The cook had to salt it, and the wicked Queen ate it, and thought she had eaten Snow-White's heart.

But now the poor child was all alone in the great forest, and so terrified that she stared at every leaf on every tree and did not know what to do. Then she began to run, and ran over sharp stones and through thorns; and the wild beasts ran past her but did her no harm.

She ran as long as her feet would carry her, until it was nearly evening; and then she saw a little cottage and went in to rest.

Everything in the cottage was small, but neater and cleaner than words can tell. There was a table with a white cloth on it and seven little plates, and on each plate a little spoon; and there were seven little knives and forks and seven little mugs. Against the wall stood seven little beds side by side, covered with snow-white bedspreads.

Little Snow-White was so hungry and thirsty that she ate a little of the vegetables and bread from each plate and drank a drop of wine out of each mug, because she did not want to take everything from one alone. Then, as she was so tired, she lay down on one of the little beds; but none of them suited her — one was too long, another too short — until at last she found that the seventh was just right; and there she stayed, said her prayers and went to sleep.

When it was quite dark the owners of the cottage came home. They were seven dwarfs who dug and delved in the mountains for ore. They lit their seven candles; and as the cottage was light now, they saw that somebody had been there, because not everything was in the order they had left it in.

The first said, "Who has been sitting on my chair?"

The second, "Who has been eating off my plate?"

The third, "Who has been taking some of my bread?"

The fourth, "Who has been eating my vegetables?"

The fifth, "Who has been using my fork?"

The sixth, "Who has been cutting with my knife?"

The seventh, "Who has been drinking out of my mug?"

Then the first looked round and saw that there was a little hollow in his bed, and he said, "Who has been getting into my bed?"

The others came running up and each of them called out, "Somebody has been lying in my bed too."

But when the seventh looked at his bed he saw Little Snow-White lying asleep in it. And he called the others, who came running, and they cried out in astonishment and brought their seven little candles and let the light fall on Little Snow-White.

"Oh, heavens! Oh, heavens!" they cried. "What a lovely child!" And they were so delighted that they did not wake her, but let her sleep on in the bed. And the seventh dwarf slept with his companions, an hour with each, and so got through the night.

When it was morning Little Snow-White woke, and was frightened when she saw the seven dwarfs. But they were friendly, and asked her what her name was.

"My name is Snow-White," she answered.

"How did you come to our house?" said the dwarfs.

Then she told them that her stepmother had wanted to have her killed, but that the huntsman had spared her life, and that she had run the whole day until at last she had found their house.

The dwarfs said, "If you will keep house for us — cook, make the beds, wash, sew and knit, and keep everything neat and clean — you can stay with us, and you shall want for nothing."

"Yes," said Snow-White, "with all my heart." And she stayed with them.

She kept the house in order for them. In the mornings they went off to the mountains to look for copper and gold, and in the evenings they came back, and then their supper had to be ready. The girl was alone all day, so the good dwarfs warned her and said, "Beware of your stepmother. She'll soon know you're here. Be sure you let nobody in."

But the Queen, believing that she had eaten Snow-White's heart, could not help thinking that she was the first and most beautiful of all again; and she went to her mirror and said:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

and the mirror answered:

	"My Queen, you are the fairest I can see,
	but over the hills, where the seven dwarfs dwell,
	Snow-White is still alive and well,
	and none is so fair as she."

Then she was astounded, because she knew that the mirror never spoke falsely, and she knew that the huntsman had betrayed her and that Little Snow-White was still alive.

And so she thought and thought again how she might kill her; because as long as she was not the fairest in the whole land, envy gave her no rest. And when she had at last thought of something, she painted her face and dressed herself as an old pedlar woman, and nobody could have recognised her.

In this disguise she went over the seven mountains to the seven dwarfs, and knocked at the door and called, "Pretty things to sell, very cheap, very cheap!"

Little Snow-White looked out of the window and called, "Good day, my good woman. What have you to sell?"

"Good things, pretty things," she answered. "Laces of every colour" — and she pulled one out that was woven of bright-coloured silk.

"I can let this worthy old woman in," thought Snow-White; and she unbolted the door and bought the pretty laces.

"Child," said the old woman, "what a sight you look. Come, let me lace you up properly for once."

Snow-White suspected nothing, and stood in front of her and let herself be laced with the new laces. But the old woman laced so fast and so tight that Snow-White lost her breath and fell down as if dead.

"Now I am the most beautiful," said the Queen to herself, and ran away.

Not long afterwards, in the evening, the seven dwarfs came home; and how shocked they were when they saw their dear Little Snow-White lying on the floor, not stirring or moving, and seeming to be dead. They lifted her up; and as they saw that she had been laced too tightly, they cut the laces. Then she began to breathe a little, and after a while came back to life.

When the dwarfs heard what had happened, they said, "That old pedlar woman was nobody but the wicked Queen. Take care, and let nobody in when we're not with you."

But the wicked woman, when she got home, went in front of her mirror and asked:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

and it answered as it had before:

	"My Queen, you are the fairest I can see,
	but over the hills, where the seven dwarfs dwell,
	Snow-White is still alive and well,
	and none is so fair as she."

When she heard that, all the blood rushed to her heart with fright, because she saw plainly that Little Snow-White was alive again.

"But now," she said, "I'll think of something that will be the end of you." And by the witchcraft she understood she made a poisoned comb. Then she disguised herself and took the shape of a different old woman.

So she went over the seven mountains to the seven dwarfs, knocked at the door and called, "Good things to sell, cheap, cheap!"

Little Snow-White looked out and said, "Go away. I can't let anybody in."

"I suppose you're allowed to look," said the old woman, and pulled out the poisoned comb and held it up.

It pleased the girl so much that she let herself be tempted and opened the door. When they had struck their bargain, the old woman said, "Now let me comb your hair properly for once."

Poor Little Snow-White suspected nothing and let the old woman do as she liked; but hardly had she put the comb in her hair before the poison in it took effect, and the girl fell down senseless.

"You paragon of beauty," said the wicked woman, "you're finished now" — and went away.

But by good luck it was nearly evening, and the seven dwarfs came home. When they saw Snow-White lying on the ground as if dead, they suspected the stepmother at once, and looked, and found the poisoned comb. Hardly had they taken it out before Snow-White came to herself and told them what had happened. Then they warned her once more to be on her guard and to open the door to nobody.

At home the Queen went in front of her mirror and said:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

and it answered as it had before:

	"My Queen, you are the fairest I can see,
	but over the hills, where the seven dwarfs dwell,
	Snow-White is still alive and well,
	and none is so fair as she."

When she heard the mirror speak like that, she trembled and shook with rage. "Snow-White shall die," she cried, "even if it costs me my own life."

Then she went into a secret, lonely room where nobody ever came, and there she made a very poisonous apple. On the outside it looked beautiful — white with a red cheek — so that anybody who saw it longed for it; but whoever ate a piece of it must die.

When the apple was ready she painted her face and dressed herself up as a countrywoman, and went over the seven mountains to the seven dwarfs. She knocked at the door.

Snow-White put her head out of the window and said, "I can't let anybody in. The seven dwarfs have forbidden it."

"It's all the same to me," said the woman. "I shall soon get rid of my apples. Here — I'll give you one."

"No," said Snow-White, "I daren't take anything."

"Are you afraid of poison?" said the old woman. "Look — I'll cut the apple in two. You eat the red cheek and I'll eat the white."

But the apple had been so cunningly made that only the red cheek was poisoned. Snow-White longed for the beautiful apple; and when she saw the woman eating part of it she could hold out no longer, and put out her hand and took the poisoned half. But hardly had she a bit of it in her mouth before she fell down dead.

Then the Queen looked at her with a dreadful look and laughed aloud and said, "White as snow, red as blood, black as ebony! This time the dwarfs can't wake you."

And when she asked her mirror at home:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

it answered at last:

	"My Queen, in this land you are the fairest of all."

Then her envious heart had rest — so far as an envious heart can have rest.

When the dwarfs came home in the evening they found Snow-White lying on the ground. She was not breathing, and she was dead. They lifted her up and looked to see whether they could find anything poisonous; they unlaced her, combed her hair, washed her with water and with wine; but it was all no use. The poor child was dead, and stayed dead.

They laid her on a bier, and all seven of them sat round it and wept for her, and wept three whole days.

Then they were going to bury her; but she still looked as if she were living, and still had her pretty red cheeks. They said, "We can't put her into the dark ground" — and they had a transparent coffin of glass made, so that she could be seen from every side, and laid her in it and wrote her name on it in golden letters, and that she was a king's daughter. Then they set the coffin out on the mountain, and one of them always stayed by it and kept watch. And the birds came too and wept for Snow-White: first an owl, then a raven, and last a dove.

And now Snow-White lay a long, long time in the coffin, and she did not change, but looked as if she were asleep; for she was still as white as snow, as red as blood, and her hair as black as ebony.

But it happened that a king's son came into the forest and went to the dwarfs' house to spend the night. He saw the coffin on the mountain, and beautiful Snow-White inside it, and read what was written on it in golden letters.

Then he said to the dwarfs, "Let me have the coffin. I'll give you whatever you want for it."

But the dwarfs answered, "We wouldn't part with it for all the gold in the world."

Then he said, "Then give it to me, because I can't live without seeing Snow-White. I will honour her and prize her as my dearest possession."

As he spoke like that, the good dwarfs took pity on him and gave him the coffin.

And now the King's son had it carried away on his servants' shoulders. And it happened that they stumbled over a tree stump; and with the jolt the poisoned piece of apple that Snow-White had bitten off came out of her throat. And before long she opened her eyes, lifted the lid of the coffin, sat up and was alive again.

"Oh, heavens, where am I?" she cried.

The King's son, full of joy, said, "You are with me" — and told her what had happened, and said, "I love you more than anything in the world. Come with me to my father's palace, and be my wife."

And Snow-White was willing, and went with him; and their wedding was held with great show and splendour.

But Snow-White's wicked stepmother was invited to the feast as well. When she had dressed herself in beautiful clothes she went in front of her mirror and said:

	"Mirror, mirror on the wall,
	who is the fairest of them all?"

and the mirror answered:

	"My Queen, of all here the fairest are you,
	but the young Queen is fairer by far, that's true."

Then the wicked woman uttered a curse, and was so wretched, so utterly wretched, that she did not know what to do. At first she would not go to the wedding at all; but she had no peace, and had to go and see the young Queen. And when she went in she recognised Snow-White, and stood still with rage and terror and could not stir.

But iron slippers had already been put on the fire; and they were brought in with tongs and set in front of her. Then she was made to put on the red-hot shoes and to dance until she dropped down dead.

The Knapsack, the Hat, and the Horn

There were once three brothers who had fallen deeper and deeper into poverty, until at last things were so bad that they had to go hungry and had nothing to eat or drink.

So they said, "We can't go on like this. We'd better go out into the world and seek our fortune."

So they set out, and had already walked along many a long road and over many a blade of grass, and had not yet met with any luck.

One day they came into a great forest, and in the middle of it was a hill; and when they came nearer they saw that the hill was all silver.

Then the eldest said, "Now I have found the good luck I wanted, and I want nothing more." He took as much of the silver as he could possibly carry, and then turned back and went home.

But the other two said, "We want more from good luck than mere silver" — and did not touch it, but went on.

After they had walked another two days without stopping, they came to a hill that was all gold. The second brother stopped and thought about it and could not decide.

"What shall I do?" he said. "Shall I take enough of this gold to keep me for the rest of my life, or shall I go on?"

At length he made up his mind, and putting as much into his pockets as would go in, said goodbye to his brother and went home.

But the third said, "Silver and gold don't move me. I won't give up my chance of fortune. Perhaps something better still will be given me."

He journeyed on; and when he had walked for three days he got into a forest that was even bigger than the last one, and that seemed never to come to an end; and as he found nothing to eat or drink, he was nearly exhausted.

Then he climbed a tall tree to see whether from up there he could make out the end of the forest; but as far as his eye could reach he saw nothing but treetops. So he began to climb down again; but hunger tormented him, and he thought, "If only I could eat my fill just once more!"

When he got down he saw with astonishment a table under the tree, richly spread with food, and the steam of it rising up to meet him.

"This time," he said, "my wish has been granted at just the right moment." And without asking who had brought the food or who had cooked it, he went up to the table and ate with enjoyment until his hunger was satisfied.

When he had finished he thought, "It would be a pity, after all, if this pretty little tablecloth were to be spoilt out here in the forest" — and he folded it up tidily and put it in his pocket.

Then he went on; and in the evening, when he began to feel hungry again, he wanted to test his little cloth, and spread it out and said, "I want you to be covered with good cheer again." And hardly had the wish crossed his lips before there stood on the table as many dishes of the most exquisite food as there was room for.

"Now I see what kitchen my cooking is done in," he said. "You shall be dearer to me than the mountains of silver and gold." For he saw plainly that it was a wishing-cloth.

But the cloth was still not enough to make him want to settle down quietly at home; he would rather wander about the world and go on after his fortune.

One night, in a lonely wood, he met a dusty black charcoal burner, who was burning charcoal there and had some potatoes by the fire that he was going to make a meal of.

"Good evening, blackbird," said the young man. "How do you get on in your solitude?"

"One day is like another," said the charcoal burner, "and every night potatoes. Have you a mind for some? Will you be my guest?"

"Many thanks," said the traveller, "but I won't rob you of your supper. You weren't expecting a visitor. If you'll put up with what I have, though, you're invited."

"And who's to prepare it for you?" said the charcoal burner. "I can see you have nothing with you, and there isn't a soul within two hours' walk who could give you anything."

"And yet there shall be a meal," said the young man, "and a better one than you've ever tasted."

With that he took his cloth out of his knapsack, spread it on the ground and said, "Little cloth, cover yourself" — and instantly boiled meat and roast meat stood there, as hot as if it had just come out of the kitchen.

The charcoal burner stared, but did not need much pressing; he fell to, and thrust bigger and bigger mouthfuls into his black mouth. When they had eaten everything, the charcoal burner smiled contentedly and said:

"Listen — that tablecloth of yours has my approval. It would be a fine thing for me here in this forest, where nobody ever cooks me anything good. I'll propose an exchange. Over there in the corner hangs a soldier's knapsack. It's certainly old and shabby, but there are wonderful powers hidden in it; and as I don't use it any more, I'll give it to you for the tablecloth."

"I must know first what these wonderful powers are," said the young man.

"That I'll tell you," said the charcoal burner. "Every time you tap it with your hand, a corporal comes with six men armed from head to foot, and they do whatever you command them."

"As far as I'm concerned," said the young man, "if nothing else can be done, we'll exchange." And he gave the charcoal burner the cloth, took the knapsack off its hook, put it on and said goodbye.

When he had walked a while he wanted to test the magic powers of his knapsack, and tapped it. Immediately the seven soldiers stepped up to him, and the corporal said, "What does my lord and master wish for?"

"March as fast as you can to the charcoal burner and demand my wishing-cloth back."

They turned to the left, and it was not long before they brought him what he wanted, having taken it from the charcoal burner without asking many questions.

The young man dismissed them and went on, and hoped fortune would shine on him more brightly still.

At sunset he came to another charcoal burner, who was getting his supper ready by the fire. "If you'll eat some potatoes with salt and no dripping, come and sit down with me," said the sooty fellow.

"No," he answered, "this time you shall be my guest" — and he spread out his cloth, which was instantly covered with the most beautiful dishes.

They ate and drank together and enjoyed themselves heartily. When the meal was over, the charcoal burner said, "Up there on that shelf lies a little old worn-out hat with strange properties. When anybody puts it on and turns it round on his head, the cannons go off as if twelve of them were fired together, and they shoot everything down so that nobody can stand against them. The hat is no use to me, and I'll gladly give it for your tablecloth."

"That suits me very well," he answered; and he took the hat and put it on and left his tablecloth behind him.

Hardly had he walked away, though, before he tapped his knapsack, and his soldiers had to fetch the cloth back again.

"One thing comes on top of another," he thought, "and I feel as if my luck hadn't come to an end yet."

Nor had his thoughts deceived him. After he had walked a whole day more, he came to a third charcoal burner, who invited him, like the others, to potatoes without dripping. But he let this one dine with him from his wishing-cloth too; and the charcoal burner liked it so much that at last he offered him a horn for it, which had quite different properties from the hat. When anybody blew it, all walls and fortifications fell down, and all towns and villages became ruins.

He gave the charcoal burner the cloth for it, sure enough — and afterwards sent his soldiers to demand it back again, so that in the end he had knapsack, hat and horn, all three.

"Now," he said, "I'm a made man; and it's time I went home and saw how my brothers are getting on."

When he reached home, his brothers had built themselves a handsome house with their silver and gold and were living in clover. He went to see them; but as he came in a ragged coat, with his shabby hat on his head and his old knapsack on his back, they would not acknowledge him as their brother.

They mocked him and said, "You give out that you're our brother, who despised silver and gold and wanted something better still for himself. He'll come in his carriage in full splendour like a mighty king, not like a beggar" — and they drove him out of doors.

Then he flew into a rage and tapped his knapsack until a hundred and fifty men stood in front of him, armed from head to foot. He ordered them to surround his brothers' house, and two of them to take hazel sticks with them and beat the two insolent men until they knew who he was.

A violent disturbance broke out; people came running and wanted to help the two in their trouble, but against the soldiers they could do nothing.

News of it reached the King at last, who was very angry and ordered a captain to march out with his troop and drive this disturber of the peace out of the town. But the man with the knapsack soon got a larger body of men together, who beat back the captain and his men, so that they had to retreat with bloody noses.

The King said, "This vagabond isn't brought to order yet" — and next day sent a still larger force against him; but they could do even less. The young man set still more men against them; and to have done with it sooner, he turned his hat twice round on his head, and the heavy guns began to play, and the King's men were beaten and put to flight.

"And now," he said, "I won't make peace until the King gives me his daughter for a wife and I govern the whole kingdom in his name."

He had this announced to the King; and the King said to his daughter, "Necessity is a hard nut to crack. What is there left for me but to do what he wants? If I want peace, and to keep the crown on my head, I must give you away."

So the wedding was celebrated; but the King's daughter was vexed that her husband should be a common man who wore a shabby hat and carried an old knapsack. She badly wanted to be rid of him, and thought day and night how she might manage it.

Then she thought to herself, "Is it possible that his wonderful powers lie in that knapsack?" And she dissembled and made much of him; and when his heart was softened she said, "If you would only put that ugly knapsack aside — it disfigures you so that I can't help being ashamed of you."

"Dear child," he said, "this knapsack is my greatest treasure. As long as I have it there's no power on earth I'm afraid of." And he told her what wonderful virtue it had.

Then she threw herself into his arms as if she were going to kiss him, and deftly slipped the knapsack off his shoulders and ran away with it. As soon as she was alone she tapped it and ordered the soldiers to seize their former master and take him out of the royal palace. They obeyed; and the false wife sent still more men after him to drive him right out of the country.

And then he would have been ruined, if he had not had the little hat. But his hands were hardly free before he turned it twice. Immediately the cannon began to thunder and struck everything down; and the King's daughter herself had to come and beg for mercy. And as she pleaded in such moving terms and promised to do better, he let himself be persuaded and granted her peace.

She behaved in a friendly way to him and acted as if she loved him dearly; and after some time she managed to fool him so far that he confided to her that even if somebody got the knapsack into his power, they could do nothing against him as long as the old hat was still his.

When she knew the secret she waited until he was asleep, and then took the hat away from him and had it thrown out into the street.

But the horn was still left to him; and in great anger he blew it with all his strength. Instantly all the walls, fortifications, towns and villages toppled down and crushed the King and his daughter to death. And if he had not put the horn down, and had blown just a little longer, everything would have been in ruins and not one stone left standing on another.

After that nobody opposed him any longer, and he made himself King of the whole country.

Rumpelstiltskin

Once there was a miller who was poor, but who had a beautiful daughter. Now it happened that he had to go and speak to the King; and in order to make himself seem important he said to him, "I have a daughter who can spin straw into gold."

The King said to the miller, "That is an art that pleases me well. If your daughter is as clever as you say, bring her to my palace tomorrow and I'll see what she can do."

And when the girl was brought to him, he took her into a room that was quite full of straw, gave her a spinning wheel and a reel, and said, "Now set to work; and if by early tomorrow morning you haven't spun this straw into gold during the night, you must die." Then he locked the room himself and left her in it alone.

So there sat the poor miller's daughter, and for the life of her she could not think what to do. She had no idea how straw could be spun into gold, and she grew more and more miserable, until at last she began to cry.

But all at once the door opened, and in came a little man, and said, "Good evening, Mistress Miller. Why are you crying so?"

"Alas," said the girl, "I have to spin straw into gold, and I don't know how to do it."

"What will you give me," said the little man, "if I do it for you?"

"My necklace," said the girl.

The little man took the necklace, sat down in front of the wheel, and whirr, whirr, whirr — three turns, and the reel was full. Then he put another one on, and whirr, whirr, whirr — three times round, and the second was full too. And so it went on until the morning, when all the straw was spun and all the reels were full of gold.

At daybreak the King was there already; and when he saw the gold he was astonished and delighted, but his heart only grew greedier. He had the miller's daughter taken into another room full of straw, much larger than the first, and ordered her to spin that too in one night, if she valued her life.

The girl did not know what to do, and was crying, when the door opened again and the little man appeared and said, "What will you give me if I spin that straw into gold for you?"

"The ring on my finger," said the girl.

The little man took the ring, began to turn the wheel again, and by morning had spun all the straw into glittering gold.

The King was overjoyed at the sight, but still he had not gold enough; and he had the miller's daughter taken into a still larger room full of straw, and said, "You must spin this too in the course of this night; and if you succeed, you shall be my wife."

"Even if she is a miller's daughter," he thought, "I couldn't find a richer wife in the whole world."

When the girl was alone the little man came for the third time and said, "What will you give me if I spin the straw for you this time as well?"

"I have nothing left that I could give," said the girl.

"Then promise me your first child, if you become Queen."

"Who knows whether that will ever happen?" thought the miller's daughter; and, not knowing what else to do in her difficulty, she promised the little man what he asked; and for that he once more spun the straw into gold.

And when the King came in the morning and found everything as he had wished, he married her, and the pretty miller's daughter became a Queen.

A year later she had a beautiful child, and never gave the little man a thought. But suddenly he came into her room and said, "Now give me what you promised."

The Queen was horror-struck, and offered the little man all the riches of the kingdom if he would leave her the child. But the little man said, "No. Something living is dearer to me than all the treasures in the world."

Then the Queen began to weep and lament, so that the little man took pity on her. "I'll give you three days," he said. "If in that time you find out my name, you shall keep your child."

So the Queen lay awake the whole night thinking of all the names she had ever heard, and she sent a messenger about the country to enquire far and wide for any other names there might be.

When the little man came the next day, she began with Caspar, Melchior, Balthazar, and said all the names she knew, one after another; but to every one of them the little man said, "That is not my name."

On the second day she had enquiries made in the neighbourhood about the names of the people there, and repeated the most uncommon and curious ones to the little man. "Perhaps your name is Shortribs, or Sheepshanks, or Laceleg?" But he always answered, "That is not my name."

On the third day the messenger came back and said, "I haven't been able to find a single new name; but as I came to a high mountain at the end of the forest, where the fox and the hare say good night to each other, I saw a little house; and in front of the house a fire was burning; and round the fire a quite ridiculous little man was jumping, hopping on one leg and shouting:

	'Today I bake, tomorrow I brew,
	and then the young Queen's child I'll claim.
	How glad I am that nobody knew
	that Rumpelstiltskin is my name!'"

You can imagine how glad the Queen was when she heard that name.

And when soon afterwards the little man came in and asked, "Now, Mistress Queen, what is my name?" — at first she said, "Is your name Conrad?"

"No."

"Is your name Harry?"

"No."

"Perhaps your name is Rumpelstiltskin?"

"The devil told you that! The devil told you that!" cried the little man; and in his rage he drove his right foot so deep into the earth that his whole leg went in; and then in his fury he pulled at his left leg so hard with both hands that he tore himself in two.

Sweetheart Roland

There was once a woman who was a real witch, and she had two daughters: one ugly and wicked, and this one she loved because she was her own daughter; and one beautiful and good, and this one she hated, because she was her stepdaughter.

The stepdaughter once had a pretty apron, which the other took such a fancy to that she grew envious, and told her mother she must and would have that apron.

"Be quiet, my child," said the old woman, "and you shall have it. Your stepsister has long deserved to die. Tonight, when she's asleep, I'll come and cut her head off. Only be careful to lie on the far side of the bed, and push her well to the front."

It would have been all over with the poor girl if she had not happened to be standing in a corner just then and heard the whole thing. All day long she did not dare go out of doors; and when bedtime came, the witch's daughter got into bed first so as to lie on the far side. But when she was asleep, the other pushed her gently to the front and took the place at the back for herself, close against the wall.

In the night the old woman came creeping in. She had an axe in her right hand, and felt with her left to see whether anybody was lying at the outside; and then she gripped the axe in both hands and cut her own child's head off.

When she had gone away, the girl got up and went to her sweetheart, who was called Roland, and knocked at his door. When he came out she said to him, "Listen, dearest Roland, we must run for it at once. My stepmother meant to kill me, and she has struck down her own child. When daylight comes and she sees what she has done, we shall be lost."

"But," said Roland, "I advise you to take her magic wand away first, or we can't escape if she comes after us."

The girl fetched the magic wand; and she took the dead girl's head and let three drops of blood fall on the floor: one in front of the bed, one in the kitchen and one on the stairs. Then she hurried away with her sweetheart.

When the old witch got up next morning she called her daughter and was going to give her the apron; but she did not come.

Then the witch cried, "Where are you?"

"Here on the stairs — I'm sweeping," answered the first drop of blood.

The old woman went out, but saw nobody on the stairs, and called again, "Where are you?"

"Here in the kitchen — I'm warming myself," called the second drop of blood.

She went into the kitchen and found nobody. So she called again, "Where are you?"

"Ah, here in bed — I'm asleep," called the third drop of blood.

She went into the room, to the bed. And what did she see there? Her own child, whose head she had cut off, lying in her own blood.

The witch flew into a fury, sprang to the window; and as she could see a long way out into the world, she caught sight of her stepdaughter hurrying off with her sweetheart Roland.

"That won't help you," she cried. "Even if you've got a long way off, you still shan't escape me."

She put on her seven-league boots, which covered an hour's walk at every stride, and it was not long before she overtook them. But the girl, when she saw the old woman striding towards her, changed her sweetheart Roland with the magic wand into a lake, and herself into a duck swimming in the middle of it.

The witch stood on the bank and threw breadcrumbs in and took every possible pains to lure the duck over; but the duck would not be lured, and the old woman had to go home at night as she had come.

At that the girl and her sweetheart Roland took their own shapes again, and they walked on the whole night until daybreak. Then the girl changed herself into a beautiful flower standing in the middle of a briar hedge, and her sweetheart Roland into a fiddler.

It was not long before the witch came striding up to them, and said to the musician, "Dear musician, may I pick that beautiful flower for myself?"

"Oh, yes," he answered. "I'll play to you while you do it."

And as she was hurriedly creeping into the hedge and was just about to pick the flower — for she knew perfectly well who the flower was — he began to play; and whether she wanted to or not, she had to dance, because it was a magic dance. The faster he played, the more violent leaps she had to make; and the thorns tore the clothes off her body and pricked her and wounded her till she bled. And as he did not stop, she had to dance until she lay dead on the ground.

When they were free of her, Roland said, "Now I'll go to my father and arrange the wedding."

"Then in the meantime I'll stay here and wait for you," said the girl. "And so that nobody recognises me, I'll change myself into a red stone boundary marker."

So Roland went away, and the girl stood like a red boundary stone in the field and waited for her beloved.

But when Roland got home he fell into the snares of another woman, who so prevailed on him that he forgot the girl. The poor girl stayed there a long time; but at last, as he did not come back at all, she grew sad and changed herself into a flower, and thought, "Somebody is bound to come this way and trample me down."

It happened, though, that a shepherd was pasturing his sheep in the field and saw the flower; and as it was so pretty he picked it and took it home with him and put it away in his chest.

From that time on, strange things happened in the shepherd's house. When he got up in the morning, all the work was already done: the room was swept, the table and the benches cleaned, the fire lit on the hearth and the water fetched. And at noon, when he came home, the table was laid and a good dinner served. He could not imagine how it came about, because he never saw another human being in his house and nobody could have hidden in it.

He was pleased enough with such good service; but at last he was so uneasy that he went to a wise woman and asked her advice.

The wise woman said, "There is some enchantment behind it. Listen very early one morning to hear whether anything is moving in the room; and if you see anything — whatever it may be — throw a white cloth over it, and then the magic will be stopped."

The shepherd did as she told him; and next morning, just as day was breaking, he saw the chest open and the flower come out. He sprang towards it quickly and threw a white cloth over it. Instantly the transformation came to an end, and a beautiful girl stood in front of him, who admitted to him that she had been the flower and had been keeping house for him all this time.

She told him her story; and as she pleased him, he asked her whether she would marry him. But she answered no, because she wanted to stay faithful to her sweetheart Roland, even though he had deserted her. All the same she promised not to go away, but to go on keeping house for the shepherd.

And now the time drew near for Roland's wedding to be celebrated; and, by an old custom of that country, it was announced that all the girls were to be present at it and sing in honour of the bridal pair. When the faithful girl heard of it she grew so sad that she thought her heart would break, and she would not go; but the other girls came and fetched her.

When it came to her turn to sing, she kept stepping back, until at last she was the only one left, and then she could not refuse. But when she began her song, and it reached Roland's ears, he sprang up and cried, "I know that voice! That is the true bride, and I'll have no other!"

Everything he had forgotten, everything that had gone out of his mind, had all at once come home to his heart again.

So the faithful girl held her wedding with her sweetheart Roland; and grief came to an end and joy began.

The Golden Bird

In the old days there was a king who had behind his palace a beautiful pleasure garden, and in it a tree that bore golden apples. When the apples were getting ripe they were counted; but on the very next morning one was missing. This was reported to the King, and he ordered a watch to be kept under the tree every night.

The King had three sons, and he sent the eldest into the garden as soon as night came on; but at midnight he could not keep himself from falling asleep, and next morning another apple was gone.

The following night the second son had to keep watch, and it went no better with him: as soon as twelve had struck he fell asleep, and in the morning an apple was gone.

Now it came to the third son's turn to watch. He was quite ready to do it, but the King had not much faith in him, and thought he would be of even less use than his brothers; but at last he let him go.

The young man lay down under the tree, but kept awake and did not let sleep get the better of him. When it struck twelve, something rustled through the air, and in the moonlight he saw a bird coming whose feathers were all shining with gold. The bird settled in the tree and had just plucked off an apple when the young man shot an arrow at it. The bird flew off, but the arrow had struck its plumage, and one of its golden feathers fell down.

The young man picked it up, and next morning took it to the King and told him what he had seen in the night. The King called his council together, and every one of them declared that a feather like this was worth more than the whole kingdom.

"If the feather is so precious," said the King, "one alone will not do for me. I must and will have the whole bird."

The eldest son set out. He trusted to his cleverness and thought he would easily find the Golden Bird. When he had gone some distance he saw a fox sitting at the edge of a wood, so he cocked his gun and took aim at him.

The fox cried, "Don't shoot me, and in return I'll give you some good advice. You are on your way to the Golden Bird; and this evening you'll come to a village where there are two inns opposite one another. One of them is brightly lit and everything goes on merrily inside; but don't go into that one. Go into the other, even though it looks a poor place."

"How can a silly animal give sensible advice?" thought the King's son, and pulled the trigger. But he missed the fox, who stretched out his tail and ran quickly into the wood.

So he went on his way, and by evening came to the village with the two inns. In one of them there was singing and dancing; the other looked poor and miserable.

"I should be a fool indeed," he thought, "if I went into the shabby tavern and passed by the good one." So he went into the cheerful one, and lived there in riot and revelry, and forgot the bird and his father and all good advice.

When some time had passed, and month after month went by and the eldest son did not come home, the second set out, meaning to find the Golden Bird. The fox met him as he had met the eldest, and gave him the good advice that he paid no attention to. He came to the two inns; and his brother was standing at the window of the one the music came from and called out to him. He could not resist, but went in and lived for nothing but pleasure.

Again some time passed, and then the King's youngest son wanted to set out and try his luck; but his father would not allow it.

"It's no use," he said. "He'll find the Golden Bird even less than his brothers did; and if some mishap befell him he wouldn't know how to help himself. He's a little wanting at the best of times."

But at last, as he got no peace, he let him go.

Again the fox was sitting outside the wood, and begged for his life and offered his good advice. The young man was good-natured, and said, "Don't worry, little fox, I won't do you any harm."

"You shan't be sorry for it," said the fox. "And so that you get along faster, climb up behind on my tail."

And hardly had he seated himself before the fox began to run, and away he went over stock and stone until his hair whistled in the wind.

When they came to the village the young man got off. He followed the good advice, and without looking round turned into the little inn, where he spent the night quietly.

The next morning, as soon as he got out into open country, there sat the fox already, and said, "I'll tell you what else you have to do. Go straight on, and at last you'll come to a castle, with a whole regiment of soldiers lying in front of it; but don't trouble yourself about them, because they'll all be asleep and snoring. Go straight through the middle of them into the castle, and go through all the rooms, until at last you come to a chamber where a golden bird is hanging in a wooden cage. Close by there stands an empty gold cage for show; but beware of taking the bird out of the common cage and putting it into the fine one, or it may go badly with you."

With these words the fox stretched out his tail again, and the King's son sat on it, and away he went over stock and stone until his hair whistled in the wind.

When he came to the castle he found everything as the fox had said. The King's son went into the chamber where the Golden Bird was shut in a wooden cage, with a golden one standing close by; and the three golden apples were lying about the room.

"But," he thought, "it would be absurd to leave the beautiful bird in the common ugly cage" — so he opened the door, took hold of it and put it into the golden cage.

But at that same moment the bird let out a shrill cry. The soldiers woke, rushed in and carried him off to prison. Next morning he was brought before a court of justice; and as he confessed everything, he was sentenced to death.

The King said, though, that he would grant him his life on one condition: if he brought him the Golden Horse, which ran faster than the wind. And in that case he should have the Golden Bird as well, over and above, as a reward.

The King's son set off, but he sighed and was full of sorrow, for how was he to find the Golden Horse? And then all at once he saw his old friend the fox sitting by the road.

"You see," said the fox, "this has happened because you didn't listen to me. Still, take heart. I'll help you and tell you how to get to the Golden Horse. You must go straight on, and you'll come to a castle where the horse is standing in the stable. The grooms will be lying in front of the stable, but they'll be asleep and snoring, and you can quietly lead the Golden Horse out. But one thing you must be careful of: put the common saddle of wood and leather on him, and not the golden one hanging close by, or it will go badly with you."

Then the fox stretched out his tail, the King's son sat on it, and away he went over stock and stone until his hair whistled in the wind.

Everything happened just as the fox had said. The prince came to the stable where the Golden Horse was standing; but just as he was going to put the common saddle on him he thought, "It will be a shame to such a beautiful animal if I don't give him the good saddle that belongs to him by right."

But hardly had the golden saddle touched the horse before he began to neigh loudly. The grooms woke, seized the young man and threw him into prison. Next morning he was sentenced to death by the court; but the King promised to grant him his life, and the Golden Horse as well, if he could bring back the beautiful princess from the Golden Castle.

With a heavy heart the young man set out; but luckily for him he soon found the trusty fox.

"I ought to leave you to your bad luck," said the fox, "but I'm sorry for you, and I'll help you out of your trouble once more. This road takes you straight to the Golden Castle; you'll reach it by evening. And at night, when everything is quiet, the beautiful princess goes to the bath-house to bathe. When she goes in, run up to her and give her a kiss, and then she'll follow you and you can take her away with you. Only don't let her go and say goodbye to her parents first, or it will go badly with you."

Then the fox stretched out his tail, the King's son sat on it, and away the fox went over stock and stone until his hair whistled in the wind.

When he reached the Golden Castle it was just as the fox had said. He waited until midnight, when everything lay in deep sleep and the beautiful princess was going to the bath-house. Then he sprang out and gave her a kiss.

She said she would gladly go with him, but she begged him piteously, with tears, to let her say goodbye to her parents first. At first he stood out against her pleading; but when she wept more and more and fell at his feet, he gave in at last.

But no sooner had the girl reached her father's bedside than he and everybody else in the castle woke, and the young man was seized and put into prison.

Next morning the King said to him, "Your life is forfeit; and you can only find mercy if you take away the hill that stands in front of my windows and stops me seeing beyond it. And you must get it all done within eight days. If you do that, you shall have my daughter as your reward."

The King's son began, and dug and shovelled without stopping; but when after seven days he saw how little he had done, and how all his work was as good as nothing, he fell into great sorrow and gave up all hope.

But on the evening of the seventh day the fox appeared and said, "You don't deserve that I should take any trouble over you. But just go away and lie down to sleep, and I'll do the work for you."

Next morning, when he woke and looked out of the window, the hill was gone. The young man ran to the King, full of joy, and told him the task was done; and whether he liked it or not, the King had to keep his word and give him his daughter.

So the two of them set out together, and it was not long before the trusty fox came up with them.

"You've certainly got the best of it," he said, "but the Golden Horse belongs to the maiden of the Golden Castle as well."

"How am I to get it?" asked the young man.

"I'll tell you," said the fox. "First take the beautiful girl to the King who sent you to the Golden Castle. There'll be unheard-of rejoicing; they'll gladly give you the Golden Horse and bring it out to you. Mount it as quickly as you can, and offer your hand to everybody in farewell — last of all to the beautiful girl. And as soon as you have taken her hand, swing her up onto the horse and gallop away; and nobody will be able to bring you back, because the horse runs faster than the wind."

It was all carried out successfully, and the King's son carried off the beautiful princess on the Golden Horse.

The fox did not stay behind, and said to the young man, "Now I'll help you get the Golden Bird. When you come near the castle where the Golden Bird is, let the girl get down, and I'll take care of her. Then ride into the castle yard with the Golden Horse. There'll be great rejoicing at the sight of it, and they'll bring the Golden Bird out to you. As soon as you have the cage in your hand, gallop back to us and take the girl up again."

When the plan had succeeded, and the King's son was about to ride home with his treasures, the fox said, "Now you shall reward me for my help."

"What do you want for it?" asked the young man.

"When you get into that wood over there, shoot me dead and chop off my head and my feet."

"That would be fine gratitude," said the King's son. "I couldn't possibly do that for you."

The fox said, "If you won't do it, I must leave you. But before I go I'll give you a piece of good advice. Be careful about two things. Buy no gallows-flesh, and don't sit on the edge of any well." And then he ran off into the wood.

The young man thought, "That's a strange animal, with strange whims. Who is ever going to buy gallows-flesh? And as for a desire to sit on the edge of a well, that has never come over me yet."

He rode on with the beautiful girl, and his road took him again through the village where his two brothers had stayed. There was a great stir and noise there; and when he asked what was going on, he was told that two men were to be hanged. As he came nearer to the place he saw that they were his brothers, who had been playing all kinds of wicked tricks and had squandered everything they had.

He asked whether they could not be set free.

"If you'll pay for them," the people said. "But why should you waste your money on wicked men and buy them their freedom?"

He did not think twice about it, but paid for them; and when they had been set free they all went on their way together.

They came to the wood where the fox had first met them; and as it was cool and pleasant in it, the two brothers said, "Let's rest a little by this well, and eat and drink."

He agreed; and while they were talking he forgot himself and sat down on the edge of the well, thinking no harm. But the two brothers threw him backwards into it, and took the girl, the horse and the bird, and went home to their father.

"Here we bring you not only the Golden Bird," they said. "We've won the Golden Horse as well, and the maiden from the Golden Castle."

Then there was great joy — but the horse would not eat, the bird would not sing, and the girl sat and wept.

But the youngest brother was not dead. By good fortune the well was dry, and he fell on soft moss without being hurt; but he could not get out again. Even in this extremity the faithful fox did not desert him: he came and leapt down to him and scolded him for forgetting his advice.

"But I can't leave it at that," he said. "I'll help you up into the daylight again." He told him to take hold of his tail and keep tight hold of it; and then he pulled him up.

"You're not out of all danger yet," said the fox. "Your brothers weren't certain you were dead, and they've surrounded the wood with watchers who are to kill you if you show yourself."

But there was a poor man sitting by the road, and the young man changed clothes with him, and in this way got to the King's palace.

Nobody knew him; but the bird began to sing, the horse began to eat, and the beautiful girl left off weeping.

The King, astonished, asked, "What does this mean?"

Then the girl said, "I don't know; but I have been so sorrowful, and now I'm so happy. I feel as if my true bridegroom had come." And she told him everything that had happened, although the other brothers had threatened her with death if she betrayed anything.

The King ordered everybody in his castle to be brought before him; and among them came the young man in his ragged clothes. But the girl knew him at once and fell on his neck. The wicked brothers were seized and put to death; but he was married to the beautiful girl and declared the King's heir.

But how did it go with the poor fox? Long afterwards the King's son was walking in the wood once again, when the fox met him and said, "You have everything now that you could wish for; but there's never an end to my misery, and it's in your power to set me free." And again he begged him, with tears, to shoot him dead and chop off his head and his feet.

So he did it; and hardly was it done before the fox was changed into a man, and was none other than the brother of the beautiful princess, freed at last from the spell that had been laid on him.

And now nothing more was wanting to their happiness as long as they lived.

The Dog and the Sparrow

A sheepdog had a bad master — one who let him go hungry. As he could stay with him no longer, he went sadly away.

On the road he met a sparrow, who said, "Brother dog, why are you so sad?"

The dog answered, "I'm hungry, and I have nothing to eat."

Then the sparrow said, "Dear brother, come into the town with me and I'll satisfy your hunger."

So they went into the town together; and when they came in front of a butcher's shop the sparrow said to the dog, "Wait there and I'll peck a bit of meat down for you." And he settled on the stall, looked about him to see that nobody was watching, and pecked and pulled and tore so long at a piece lying on the edge that it slipped down. Then the dog grabbed it, ran into a corner and ate it.

The sparrow said, "Now come with me to another shop, and I'll get you one more piece, so that you have enough."

When the dog had eaten the second piece as well, the sparrow asked, "Brother dog, have you had enough now?"

"Yes, I've had enough meat," he answered, "but I've had no bread yet."

Said the sparrow, "You shall have that too. Come with me."

Then he took him to a baker's shop and pecked at a couple of little rolls until they rolled down; and as the dog wanted still more, he led him to another stall and got him bread again. When that was eaten, the sparrow said, "Brother dog, have you had enough now?"

"Yes," he said. "Now let's walk a while outside the town."

So they both went out onto the highway. But it was warm weather; and when they had gone a little way the dog said, "I'm tired, and I'd like to sleep."

"Well, sleep, then," said the sparrow, "and in the meantime I'll perch on a branch."

So the dog lay down on the road and fell fast asleep.

While he lay sleeping there, a carter came driving by with a cart and three horses, loaded with two barrels of wine. The sparrow saw that he was not going to turn aside but was keeping to the wheel rut the dog was lying in, so he cried, "Carter, don't do it, or I'll make you poor."

But the carter growled to himself, "You won't make me poor" — and cracked his whip and drove the cart over the dog, and the wheels killed him.

Then the sparrow cried, "You've run over my brother dog and killed him. It shall cost you your cart and horses."

"Cart and horses indeed!" said the carter. "What harm can you do me?" — and drove on.

Then the sparrow crept under the cover of the cart and pecked so long at one of the bungholes that he got the bung out; and all the wine ran out without the driver noticing. But once, when he happened to look behind him, he saw the cart dripping, and looked at the barrels and saw that one of them was empty.

"Unlucky man that I am," he cried.

"Not unlucky enough yet," said the sparrow, and flew onto the head of one of the horses and pecked its eyes out.

When the driver saw that, he pulled out his axe and tried to hit the sparrow; but the sparrow flew up into the air, and he hit his horse on the head, and it fell down dead.

"Oh, what an unlucky man I am," he cried.

"Not unlucky enough yet," said the sparrow. And when the driver drove on with the two horses, the sparrow crept under the cover again and pecked the bung out of the second cask, so that all that wine was spilt too.

When the driver realised it, he cried again, "Oh, what an unlucky man I am!"

But the sparrow answered, "Not unlucky enough yet" — and settled on the second horse's head and pecked its eyes out. The driver ran up and raised his axe to strike; but the sparrow flew into the air, and the blow struck the horse, which fell.

"Oh, what an unlucky man I am!"

"Not unlucky enough yet," said the sparrow, and settled on the third horse's head and pecked out its eyes. The driver, in his rage, struck at the sparrow without looking, and missed him and killed his third horse as well.

"Oh, what an unlucky man I am," he cried.

"Not unlucky enough yet," answered the sparrow. "Now I'll make you unlucky at home" — and flew away.

The driver had to leave the wagon standing, and went home full of anger and vexation.

"Ah," he said to his wife, "what misfortunes I've had! My wine has run out, and all three horses are dead."

"Alas, husband," she answered, "what a spiteful bird has got into the house! It has gathered together every bird there is in the world, and they've got at our corn up there and are eating it."

He went upstairs, and there were thousands and thousands of birds sitting in the loft, and they had eaten all the corn, and the sparrow was sitting in the middle of them.

Then the driver cried, "Oh, what an unlucky man I am!"

"Not unlucky enough yet," answered the sparrow. "Carter, it shall cost you your life as well" — and flew out.

So now the carter had lost all his property. He went downstairs into the room, sat down behind the stove and was in a furious, bitter temper.

But the sparrow sat outside in front of the window and cried, "Carter, it shall cost you your life."

Then the carter snatched up the axe and threw it at the sparrow; but it only broke the window and did not hit the bird.

The sparrow now hopped inside, perched on the stove and cried, "Carter, it shall cost you your life."
