The man, quite mad and blind with rage, smashed the stove in two; and as the sparrow flew from one place to another, so it went with all his household furniture — mirror, benches, table, and at last the walls of his house — and still he could not hit the bird.

At length, though, he caught it in his hand.

Then his wife said, "Shall I kill it?"

"No," he cried, "that would be too merciful. It shall die much more cruelly" — and he took it and swallowed it whole.

But the sparrow began to flutter about inside him, and fluttered up again into the man's mouth; and then it stuck its head out and cried, "Carter, it shall still cost you your life."

The driver handed the axe to his wife and said, "Wife, kill the bird in my mouth for me."

The woman struck, and missed her blow, and hit the carter right on the head, so that he fell down dead.

But the sparrow flew up and away.

Frederick and Catherine

There was once a man called Frederick and a woman called Catherine, who had married each other and were living together as a young married couple.

One day Frederick said, "I'm going out to plough now, Catherine. When I come back there must be some roast meat on the table for my hunger and a fresh drink for my thirst."

"Off you go, Frederick," said Kate. "Off you go, I'll have it all ready for you."

So when dinner time drew near she got a sausage down out of the chimney, put it in the frying pan with some butter and set it on the fire. The sausage began to fry and hiss; Catherine stood beside it holding the handle of the pan, and had her own thoughts while she did it.

Then it occurred to her, "While the sausage is cooking you could go down to the cellar and draw the beer." So she set the frying pan safely on the fire, took a can and went down into the cellar to draw the beer.

The beer ran into the can and Kate watched it; and then she thought, "Oh dear! The dog upstairs isn't shut up — it might get the sausage out of the pan. Well thought of."

And in a trice she was up the cellar steps again; but the dog already had the sausage in his mouth and was dragging it away along the ground.

But Catherine, who was not idle, set off after him and chased him a long way into the field. The dog, though, was faster than Catherine and did not let the sausage travel easily, but went skipping over the furrows with it.

"What's gone is gone," said Kate, and turned round; and as she had run herself weary, she walked back quietly and comfortably and cooled herself down.

All this time the beer was still running out of the cask, because Kate had not turned the tap off. And when the can was full and there was nowhere else for it to go, it ran out over the cellar floor and did not stop until the whole cask was empty.

As soon as Kate was on the steps she saw the disaster. "Good gracious!" she cried. "What shall I do now to stop Frederick finding out?"

She thought for a while, and at last remembered that up in the garret there was still a sack of the finest wheat flour from the last fair; she would fetch that down and scatter it over the beer.

"Yes," she said, "whoever saves a thing when he ought has it afterwards when he needs it." And she climbed up to the garret and carried the sack down and threw it straight down onto the can of beer, which she knocked over, so that Frederick's drink was swimming in the cellar too.

"It's all right," said Kate. "Where the one is, the other ought to be as well." And she scattered the flour all over the cellar.

When it was done she was heartily delighted with her work, and said, "How clean and wholesome it does look down here!"

At midday Frederick came home. "Now, wife, what have you got ready for me?"

"Ah, Freddy," she answered, "I was frying a sausage for you; but while I was drawing the beer to go with it, the dog took it out of the pan; and while I was running after the dog, all the beer ran out; and while I was drying up the beer with the flour, I knocked the can over as well. But don't fret — the cellar is quite dry again."

Said Frederick, "Kate, Kate, you shouldn't have done that! To let the sausage be carried off, and the beer run out of the cask, and throw away all our flour into the bargain!"

"Really, Frederick, I didn't know. You should have told me."

The man thought, "If my wife is like this, I shall have to look after things more."

Now he had got together a good number of thalers, which he changed into gold; and he said to Catherine, "Look, these are counters for playing games. I'll put them in a pot and bury them in the stable under the cow's manger. But mind you keep away from them, or it will be the worse for you."

"Oh, no, Frederick," she said, "I certainly won't go near them."

And when Frederick had gone, some pedlars came into the village with cheap earthenware bowls and pots, and asked the young woman whether there was nothing she wanted to bargain for.

"Oh, my dear people," said Catherine, "I've no money and can't buy anything. But if you have any use for yellow counters, I'll buy from you."

"Yellow counters? Why not? But let's have a look at them."

"Then go into the stable and dig under the cow's manger, and you'll find the yellow counters. I'm not allowed to go there."

The rogues went off, dug, and found pure gold. Then they took hold of it and ran away, and left their pots and bowls behind in the house.

Catherine thought she had better make use of her new things; and as she had no shortage in the kitchen without them, she knocked the bottom out of every pot and set them all as ornaments on the fence that ran round the house.

When Frederick came and saw the new decorations, he said, "Catherine, what have you been up to?"

"I bought them, Frederick, with the counters that were under the cow's manger. I didn't go there myself — the pedlars had to dig them out for themselves."

"Ah, wife," said Frederick, "what have you done? Those weren't counters, they were pure gold, and all we had in the world. You shouldn't have done that."

"Really, Frederick," she said, "I didn't know. You should have warned me."

Catherine stood a while and thought to herself; then she said, "Listen, Frederick, we'll soon get the gold back. We'll run after the thieves."

"Come on then," said Frederick, "we'll try it. But bring some butter and cheese with you so that we have something to eat on the way."

"Yes, Frederick, I'll bring them."

They set out; and as Frederick was the better walker, Catherine followed behind. "It's to my advantage," she thought. "When we turn back I'll be a little way ahead."

Then she came to a hill with deep ruts on both sides of the road. "There, you can see," said Catherine, "how they've torn and skinned and galled the poor earth. It'll never be whole again as long as it lives." And out of the compassion of her heart she took her butter and smeared the ruts to right and left, so that they should not be so hurt by the wheels.

And as she was bending down in her charity like this, one of the cheeses rolled out of her pocket and away down the hill.

Said Catherine, "I've made my way up here once; I'm not going down again. Somebody else can run and fetch it back." So she took another cheese and rolled it down after it.

But the cheeses did not come back; so she let a third one run down, thinking, "Perhaps they're waiting for company and don't like to walk alone."

And as all three stayed away, she said, "I don't know what that can mean. Perhaps the third one didn't find the way and has gone wrong. I'll just send a fourth to call them."

But the fourth did no better than the third. Then Catherine got angry, and threw down the fifth and the sixth as well, and those were her last.

She stood for some time watching for them to come; but when they still did not come, she said, "Oh, you're fine ones to send to fetch death! You stay away a good long time. Do you think I'm going to wait any longer for you? I'm going on my way — you can run after me. You've got younger legs than I have."

Catherine went on and found Frederick, who had stopped and was waiting for her, because he wanted something to eat.

"Now let's have what you brought with you," he said.

She gave him the dry bread.

"Where are the butter and the cheeses?" asked her husband.

"Ah, Freddy," said Catherine, "I smeared the cart ruts with the butter, and the cheeses will be along soon. One of them ran away from me, so I sent the others after it to call it back."

Said Frederick, "You shouldn't have done that, Catherine — smearing the butter on the road and letting the cheeses run away down the hill!"

"Really, Frederick, you should have told me."

Then they ate the dry bread together, and Frederick said, "Catherine, did you make the house secure when you came away?"

"No, Frederick — you should have told me to before."

"Then go back home and make the house secure before we go any further, and bring something else to eat with you. I'll wait here for you."

Catherine went back and thought, "Frederick wants something more to eat. He doesn't like butter and cheese, so I'll take a handkerchief full of dried pears and a jug of vinegar for him to drink."

Then she bolted the top half of the door fast, but lifted the bottom half off its hinges and took it on her back, believing that when she had got the door safe, the house must be well taken care of.

Catherine took her time on the way, and thought, "Frederick will get all the longer rest."

When she reached him at last she said, "Here's the house door for you, Frederick, and now you can look after the house yourself."

"Oh, heavens," he said, "what a wise wife I have! She takes the bottom half of the door off its hinges so that anything at all can walk in, and bolts the top half. It's too late to go home again now; but since you've brought the door here, you can just carry it further."

"I'll carry the door, Frederick, but the dried pears and the vinegar jug will be too heavy for me. I'll hang them on the door — it can carry them."

And now they went into the forest and looked for the rogues, but did not find them. At length, as it grew dark, they climbed into a tree and decided to spend the night there.

But hardly had they settled at the top of it before the very rascals came along who carry off what does not want to go and find things before they are lost. They sat down under the very tree Frederick and Catherine were sitting in, lit a fire and were about to share out their booty.

Frederick got down on the other side and collected some stones. Then he climbed up again with them, meaning to throw them at the thieves and kill them. But the stones did not hit them, and the rogues said, "It'll soon be morning — the wind is shaking the fir cones down."

Catherine still had the door on her back; and as it pressed so heavily on her, she thought it was the fault of the dried pears, and said, "Frederick, I must throw the pears down."

"No, Catherine, not now," he said. "They might give us away."

"Oh, but Frederick, I must. They weigh me down far too much."

"Do it, then, and be hanged!"

So the dried pears came rolling down through the branches, and the rascals below said, "The leaves are falling."

A short time afterwards, as the door was still heavy, Catherine said, "Ah, Frederick, I must pour the vinegar out."

"No, Catherine, you mustn't. It might give us away."

"Ah, but Frederick, I must. It weighs me down far too much."

"Then do it and be hanged!"

So she emptied the vinegar out, and it sprinkled all over the robbers. They said among themselves, "The dew is falling already."

At length Catherine thought, "Can it really be the door that weighs me down so?" — and said, "Frederick, I must throw the door down."

"No, not now, Catherine. It might give us away."

"Oh, but Frederick, I must. It weighs me down far too much."

"Oh no, Catherine, do hold onto it."

"Ah, Frederick, I'm letting it fall!"

"Let it go, then, in the devil's name."

Then it fell down with a tremendous crash, and the rascals below cried, "The devil is coming down the tree!" — and they ran away and left everything behind them.

Early next morning, when the two of them came down, they found all their gold again and carried it home.

When they were home once more, Frederick said, "And now, Catherine, you must be industrious and do some work."

"Yes, Frederick, I'll do that at once. I'll go into the field and cut the corn."

When Catherine got to the field she said to herself, "Shall I eat before I cut, or shall I sleep before I cut? Oh, I'll eat first."

So Catherine ate, and the eating made her sleepy; and she began to cut, and half in a dream cut all her clothes to pieces — her apron, her gown and her shift.

When Catherine woke up after a long sleep, she was standing there half naked, and said to herself, "Is it me, or isn't it me? Alas, it isn't me."

Meanwhile night came on, and Catherine ran into the village, knocked at her husband's window and called, "Frederick!"

"What's the matter?"

"I should very much like to know whether Catherine is in."

"Yes, yes," said Frederick, "she must be in and asleep."

Said she, "Well then, I'm certainly at home already" — and ran away.

Outside, Catherine met some vagabonds who were going out to steal. So she went up to them and said, "I'll help you steal."

The rascals thought she knew the lie of the land, and were willing. Catherine went along in front of the houses and called out, "Good people, have you got anything? We want to steal."

The thieves thought to themselves, "That's a fine way of going about it" — and wished themselves rid of Catherine again. So they said to her, "Outside the village the parson has some turnips in his field. Go there and pull up some turnips for us."

Catherine went to the field and began pulling them up, but was so lazy that she did not gather them together.

Then a man came by and saw her, and stood still, and thought it was the devil rooting about among the turnips like that. He ran off into the village to the parson and said, "Reverend sir, the devil is in your turnip field, rooting up turnips."

"Ah, heavens," said the parson, "I have a lame foot. I can't go out and drive him away."

Said the man, "Then I'll carry you on my back" — and carried him out on his back.

And when they came to the field, Catherine stood up to her full height.

"Ah, the devil!" cried the parson; and they both hurried away; and in his great fright the parson could run better on his lame foot than the man who had carried him could on his sound one.

The Two Brothers

There were once two brothers, one rich and the other poor. The rich one was a goldsmith and evil-hearted; the poor one kept himself by making brooms, and was good and honourable.

The poor one had two children, twin brothers, as like each other as two drops of water. The two boys went back and forth to the rich house and often got some of the scraps to eat.

It happened once, when the poor man was going into the forest to fetch brushwood, that he saw a bird that was all of gold and more beautiful than any he had ever come across. He picked up a small stone and threw it at the bird and was lucky enough to hit it; but only one golden feather fell down, and the bird flew away.

The man took the feather and carried it to his brother, who looked at it and said, "It's pure gold" — and gave him a great deal of money for it.

Next day the man climbed into a birch tree and was about to cut off a couple of branches when the same bird flew out; and when the man searched, he found a nest with an egg lying in it, and the egg was of gold. He took the egg home and carried it to his brother, who again said, "It's pure gold" — and gave him what it was worth.

At last the goldsmith said, "I should very much like to have the bird itself."

The poor man went into the forest for the third time, and again saw the golden bird sitting in the tree; so he took a stone and brought it down and carried it to his brother, who gave him a great heap of gold for it.

"Now I can get along," he thought, and went home contented.

The goldsmith was crafty and cunning, and knew perfectly well what kind of bird it was. He called his wife and said, "Roast me that golden bird, and take care that none of it is lost. I have a fancy to eat it all myself."

For the bird was no common one, but of such a wondrous kind that whoever ate its heart and liver found a piece of gold under his pillow every morning.

The woman made the bird ready, put it on the spit and let it roast. Now it happened that while it was at the fire, and the woman had to leave the kitchen for some other work, the two children of the poor broom-maker ran in, stood by the spit and turned it round once or twice. And just at that moment two little bits of the bird fell down into the dripping pan, and one of the boys said, "We'll eat these two little bits. I'm so hungry, and nobody will ever miss them."

So the two of them ate the pieces. But the woman came into the kitchen and saw that they were eating something, and said, "What have you been eating?"

"Two little scraps that fell out of the bird," they answered.

"That must have been the heart and the liver," said the woman, thoroughly frightened; and so that her husband should not miss them and be angry, she quickly killed a young cockerel, took out its heart and liver and put them with the golden bird.

When it was ready she carried it to the goldsmith, who ate it all by himself and left nothing. But next morning, when he felt under his pillow and expected to bring out a piece of gold, there were no more gold pieces there than there had always been.

The two children had no idea what a piece of good fortune had fallen to them. Next morning when they got up, something fell rattling to the floor; and when they picked it up there were two gold pieces. They took them to their father, who was astonished and said, "How can that have happened?"

And when they found two more the next morning, and so on every day, he went to his brother and told him the strange story.

The goldsmith knew at once how it had come about, and that the children had eaten the heart and liver of the golden bird; and to revenge himself, and because he was envious and hard-hearted, he said to their father, "Your children are in league with the Evil One. Don't take the gold, and don't let them stay in your house any longer, because he has them in his power and may ruin you as well."

The father feared the Evil One; and painful as it was to him, he led the twins out into the forest and left them there with a sad heart.

And now the two children ran about the forest looking for the way home again, but could not find it, and only lost themselves more and more.

At length they met a huntsman, who asked, "Whose children are you?"

"We're the poor broom-maker's boys," they answered; and they told him that their father would not keep them in the house any longer, because a piece of gold lay under their pillows every morning.

"Come," said the huntsman, "there's nothing so very bad in that, so long as you stay honest and don't get idle."

And as the good man liked the children and had none of his own, he took them home with him and said, "I'll be your father and bring you up till you're grown."

They learned huntsmanship from him; and the gold piece that each of them found when he woke was put away for them, in case they should need it in the future.

When they were grown up, their foster-father took them into the forest with him one day and said, "Today you shall make your trial shot, so that I can release you from your apprenticeship and make you huntsmen."

They went with him and lay in wait a long time, but no game appeared. Then the huntsman looked up and saw a flight of wild geese flying in the shape of a triangle, and said to one of them, "Shoot me down one from each corner."

He did it, and so made his trial shot. Soon afterwards another flight came by in the shape of a figure two, and the huntsman told the other to bring down one from each corner too; and his trial shot was just as successful.

"Now," said their foster-father, "I pronounce you out of your apprenticeship. You are skilled huntsmen."

At this the two brothers went off together into the forest and took counsel with one another and made a plan. And in the evening, when they had sat down to supper, they said to their foster-father, "We won't touch food or take one mouthful until you have granted us a request."

Said he, "And what is your request?"

They answered, "We've finished learning now, and we must prove ourselves in the world. Let us go away and travel."

Then the old man said joyfully, "You talk like brave huntsmen. What you ask has been my own wish. Go — everything will go well with you."

And with that they ate and drank joyfully together.

When the appointed day came, their foster-father gave each of them a good gun and a dog, and let each take as many of his saved-up gold pieces as he liked. Then he went part of the way with them; and as he took his leave he gave them a bright knife and said, "If you ever separate, stick this knife into a tree at the place where you part; and when one of you comes back he'll be able to see how his absent brother is faring, because the side of the knife turned in the direction he took will rust if he dies, and will stay bright as long as he's alive."

The two brothers went on further, and came to a forest so large that they could not get out of it in a day. So they spent the night in it and ate what they had in their hunting bags; and they walked all the second day as well, and still did not get out.

As they had nothing to eat, one of them said, "We must shoot something for ourselves or we shall go hungry" — and loaded his gun and looked about him. And when an old hare came running towards them, he raised his gun to his shoulder; but the hare cried:

	"Dear huntsman, do but let me live,
	and two young ones to you I'll give"

— and sprang instantly into the thicket and brought two young ones. But the little creatures played so merrily, and were so pretty, that the huntsmen could not find it in their hearts to kill them. So they kept them with them, and the little hares followed on foot.

Soon after this a fox crept past. They were just going to shoot it, but the fox cried:

	"Dear huntsman, do but let me live,
	and two young ones to you I'll give."

He too brought two little foxes; and the huntsmen did not like to kill them either, but gave them to the hares for company, and they followed on behind.

It was not long before a wolf came striding out of the thicket. The huntsmen made ready to shoot him, but the wolf cried:

	"Dear huntsman, do but let me live,
	and two young ones to you I'll give."

The huntsmen put the two wolves with the other animals, and they followed on behind.

Then a bear came, who wanted to trot about a little longer, and cried:

	"Dear huntsman, do but let me live,
	and two young ones to you I'll give."

The two young bears were added to the rest, and there were eight of them already.

And at length who should come but a lion, tossing his mane. But the huntsmen did not let themselves be frightened, and took aim at him too; and the lion said as well:

	"Dear huntsman, do but let me live,
	and two young ones to you I'll give."

And he brought them his young ones; and now the huntsmen had two lions, two bears, two wolves, two foxes and two hares, who followed them and served them.

Meanwhile their hunger was not satisfied by any of this, so they said to the foxes, "Listen, you cunning fellows, get us something to eat. You're crafty and deep."

They answered, "Not far from here there's a village where we've already fetched many a fowl. We'll show you the way."

So they went into the village, bought themselves something to eat, had food given to their beasts, and then travelled on. The foxes knew their way very well about the district and where the poultry yards were, and were able to guide the huntsmen.

Now they travelled about for a while, but could find no positions where they could stay together; so they said, "There's nothing else for it — we must part."

They divided the animals, so that each of them had a lion, a bear, a wolf, a fox and a hare; then they took leave of one another, promised to love each other like brothers until they died, and stuck the knife their foster-father had given them into a tree; after which one went east and the other went west.

The younger one came with his beasts to a town that was all hung with black crape. He went into an inn and asked the landlord whether he could put his animals up.

The innkeeper gave him a stable with a hole in the wall; and the hare crept out and fetched himself a cabbage head, and the fox fetched himself a hen, and when he had eaten that, got the cock as well. But the wolf, the bear and the lion could not get out, because they were too big. So the innkeeper had them taken to a place where a cow was lying on the grass just then, and let them eat their fill.

And when the huntsman had seen to his animals, he asked the innkeeper why the town was all hung with black crape.

Said the landlord, "Because our King's only daughter is to die tomorrow."

The huntsman asked whether she was sick to death.

"No," said the landlord, "she's strong and healthy; and all the same she must die."

"How is that?" asked the huntsman.

"There's a high hill outside the town where a dragon lives, and every year he must have a pure virgin, or he lays the whole country waste. And now all the girls have been given to him already and there's nobody left but the King's daughter; and there's no mercy for her — she must be handed over to him, and that is to be done tomorrow."

Said the huntsman, "Why isn't the dragon killed?"

"Ah," said the landlord, "so many knights have tried it, and it has cost every one of them his life. The King has promised that whoever conquers the dragon shall have his daughter for a wife, and shall govern the kingdom after his own death."

The huntsman said nothing more to that; but next morning he took his animals and went up the dragon's hill with them.

At the top of it stood a little church, and on the altar were three full cups, with the inscription: "Whoever empties these cups will become the strongest man on earth, and will be able to wield the sword that is buried in front of the threshold."

The huntsman did not drink, but went out and looked for the sword in the ground; and he could not shift it from its place. So he went in and emptied the cups; and now he was strong enough to take the sword up, and his hand could wield it quite easily.

When the hour came for the girl to be given up to the dragon, the King, the marshal and the courtiers went with her. From a long way off she saw the huntsman on the dragon's hill and thought it was the dragon standing there waiting for her, and did not want to go up to him; but at last, because otherwise the whole town would have been destroyed, she was forced to make that miserable journey.

The King and the courtiers went home full of grief; but the King's marshal was to stay and watch it all from a distance.

When the King's daughter got to the top of the hill it was not the dragon standing there but the young huntsman, who comforted her and said he would save her, and led her into the church and locked her in.

It was not long before the seven-headed dragon came there with a loud roaring. When he caught sight of the huntsman he was astonished and said, "What business have you here on this hill?"

The huntsman answered, "I want to fight you."

Said the dragon, "Many knights have left their lives here; I shall soon have made an end of you too" — and he breathed fire out of seven jaws. The fire was meant to set the dry grass alight and the huntsman was meant to be suffocated in the heat and the smoke; but the animals came running up and trampled the fire out.

Then the dragon rushed at the huntsman; but he swung his sword until it sang through the air, and struck off three of his heads.

At that the dragon grew truly furious, and rose up into the air and spat flames of fire down over the huntsman, and was about to plunge down on him; but the huntsman drew his sword once more and cut off three more heads.

The monster grew faint and sank down; and yet it still just managed to rush at the huntsman, and he with his last strength struck its tail off; and as he could fight no longer he called up his animals, who tore it to pieces.

When the struggle was over the huntsman unlocked the church and found the King's daughter lying on the floor, for she had lost her senses with fear and terror during the fight. He carried her out; and when she came to herself and opened her eyes, he showed her the dragon all cut to pieces and told her that she was delivered.

She rejoiced and said, "Now you will be my dearest husband, for my father promised me to whoever killed the dragon."

And with that she took off her necklace of coral and divided it among the animals to reward them, and the lion had the golden clasp. But her handkerchief, with her name on it, she gave to the huntsman, who went and cut the tongues out of the dragon's seven heads, wrapped them in the handkerchief and put them carefully away.

That done, he was so faint and weary with the fire and the fighting that he said to the girl, "We're both worn out; let's sleep a while." She said yes, and they lay down on the ground; and the huntsman said to the lion, "You must keep watch, so that nobody surprises us in our sleep." Then they both fell asleep. The lion lay down beside them to watch, but he too was so tired from the fight that he called the bear and said, "Lie down near me, I must sleep a little. If anything comes, wake me." So the bear lay down beside him; but he was tired as well, and called the wolf and said, "Lie down by me, I must sleep a little; if anything comes, wake me." So the wolf lay down by him; but he was tired too, and called the fox and said, "Lie down by me, I must sleep a little. If anything comes, wake me." So the fox lay down beside him; but he was weary as well, and called the hare and said, "Lie down near me, I must sleep a little, and if anything should come, wake me." So the hare sat down by him; but the poor hare was tired too, and had nobody he could call to keep watch, and fell asleep. And now the King's daughter, the huntsman, the lion, the bear, the wolf, the fox and the hare were all sleeping a sound sleep.

The marshal, who was supposed to be watching from a distance, took courage when he did not see the dragon flying away with the girl; and finding that the whole hill had gone quiet, he climbed it. There lay the dragon, hacked and hewn to pieces on the ground; and not far off were the King's daughter and a huntsman with his animals, all of them sunk in a sound sleep. And as he was wicked and godless, he took his sword, cut off the huntsman's head, seized the girl in his arms and carried her down the hill.

Then she woke and was terrified; but the marshal said, "You're in my hands. You'll say that it was I who killed the dragon."

"I can't do that," she answered. "It was a huntsman with his animals who did it."

Then he drew his sword and threatened to kill her if she did not obey him, and forced her until she promised.

Then he took her to the King, who did not know how to contain himself for joy when he looked on his dear child alive again, whom he had believed to be torn to pieces by the monster. The marshal said to him, "I killed the dragon and delivered the girl and the whole kingdom as well; and so I claim her as my wife, as was promised."

The King said to his daughter, "Is what he says true?"

"Ah, yes," she answered, "it must indeed be true. But I won't consent to have the wedding celebrated until a year and a day have gone by" — for she thought that in that time she would hear something of her dear huntsman.

The animals, meanwhile, were still lying asleep beside their dead master on the dragon's hill. Then a great bumblebee came and settled on the hare's nose; but the hare wiped it off with his paw and went on sleeping. The bumblebee came a second time, and again the hare rubbed it off and slept on. Then it came a third time and stung his nose so that he woke up.

As soon as the hare was awake he roused the fox, and the fox the wolf, and the wolf the bear, and the bear the lion. And when the lion woke and saw that the girl was gone and his master was dead, he began to roar frightfully and cried, "Who has done that? Bear, why didn't you wake me?"

The bear asked the wolf, "Why didn't you wake me?" and the wolf the fox, "Why didn't you wake me?" and the fox the hare, "Why didn't you wake me?"

The poor hare alone did not know what answer to make, and the blame rested with him. They were just going to fall on him, but he begged them and said, "Don't kill me. I'll bring our master back to life. I know a mountain where a root grows that cures anyone of every illness and every wound, if it's put in his mouth. But the mountain lies two hundred hours' journey from here."

The lion said, "In four-and-twenty hours you must have run there and come back, and have brought the root with you."

So the hare sprang away, and in four-and-twenty hours he was back and had brought the root. The lion put the huntsman's head on again, and the hare laid the root in his mouth; and at once everything joined together again, and his heart beat, and life came back.

Then the huntsman woke and was dismayed at not seeing the girl, and thought, "She must have gone away while I was asleep, to be rid of me."

The lion in his great hurry had put his master's head on back to front, but the huntsman did not notice it, because of his gloomy thoughts about the King's daughter. It was only at noon, when he was going to eat something, that he saw his head was turned backwards, and could not understand it, and asked the animals what had happened to him in his sleep. Then the lion told him that they had all fallen asleep from weariness too, and on waking had found him dead with his head cut off; that the hare had fetched the life-giving root, and that he himself, in his haste, had taken hold of the head the wrong way round — but that he would put his mistake right. Then he tore the huntsman's head off again, turned it round, and the hare healed it with the root.

The huntsman, though, was sad at heart, and travelled about the world making his animals dance in front of people. And it came about that exactly at the end of a year he came back to the same town where he had delivered the King's daughter from the dragon; and this time the town was gaily hung with red cloth.

So he said to the innkeeper, "What does this mean? Last year the town was all hung with black crape. What is the red cloth for today?"

The host answered, "Last year our King's daughter was to have been handed over to the dragon; but the marshal fought it and killed it, and so tomorrow their wedding is to be celebrated. That's why the town was hung with black crape then for mourning, and is covered with red cloth today for joy."

Next day, when the wedding was to take place, the huntsman said to the innkeeper at midday, "Do you believe, sir host, that I shall eat bread from the King's own table here with you today?"

"No," said the host. "I'd bet a hundred pieces of gold that that won't come true."

The huntsman took the wager, and set against it a purse with just the same number of gold pieces in it. Then he called the hare and said, "Go, my dear runner, and fetch me some of the bread the King is eating."

Now the little hare was the lowest of the animals and could not pass the order on to any of the others, but had to get on his legs himself. "Oh dear," he thought, "if I go bounding through the streets alone like this, the butchers' dogs will all be after me."

It happened as he expected: the dogs came after him and wanted to make holes in his good skin. But he sprang away as you never saw a hare run, and sheltered in a sentry box without the soldier being aware of it. The dogs came and wanted to have him out; but the soldier did not understand a joke, and hit them with the butt end of his gun till they ran away yelping and howling.

As soon as the hare saw that the way was clear he ran into the palace and straight to the King's daughter, sat down under her chair and scratched at her foot.

"Will you get away?" she said, thinking it was her dog.

The hare scratched her foot a second time, and again she said, "Will you get away?" thinking it was her dog. But the hare would not be turned from his purpose, and scratched her a third time. Then she looked down and knew the hare by his collar. She took him on her lap, carried him into her room and said, "Dear Hare, what is it you want?"

He answered, "My master, who killed the dragon, is here, and has sent me to ask for a loaf of bread like the one the King eats."

Then she was full of joy, and had the baker summoned and ordered him to bring a loaf such as the King ate.

The little hare said, "But the baker must carry it there for me as well, so that the butchers' dogs do me no harm."

So the baker carried it for him as far as the door of the inn, and then the hare got up on his hind legs, took the loaf in his front paws and carried it to his master.

"There, sir host," said the huntsman, "the hundred pieces of gold are mine."

The host was astonished; but the huntsman went on, "Yes, sir host, I have the bread. Now I'll have some of the King's roast meat as well."

The host said, "I should like to see that," but he would make no more wagers.

The huntsman called the fox and said, "My little fox, go and fetch me some roast meat, such as the King eats."

The red fox knew the back ways better, and went by holes and corners without a single dog seeing him, seated himself under the King's daughter's chair and scratched her foot. Then she looked down and recognised the fox by his collar, took him into her room with her and said, "Dear Fox, what is it you want?"

He answered, "My master, who killed the dragon, is here, and has sent me. I'm to ask for some roast meat such as the King is eating."

So she sent for the cook, who had to prepare a roast joint just like the King's and carry it for the fox as far as the door. Then the fox took the dish, waved away with his tail the flies that had settled on the meat, and carried it to his master.

"There, sir host," said the huntsman, "we have bread and meat. Now I'll have the proper vegetables with it too, such as the King eats." So he called the wolf and said, "Dear Wolf, go there and fetch me vegetables such as the King eats."

The wolf went straight to the palace, since he feared nobody; and when he got to the King's daughter's room he gave the back of her dress a twitch, so that she was obliged to look round. She recognised him by his collar, took him into her room with her and said, "Dear Wolf, what is it you want?"

He answered, "My master, who killed the dragon, is here. I'm to ask for some vegetables, such as the King eats."

So she sent for the cook, who had to get ready a dish of vegetables such as the King ate, and carry it for the wolf as far as the door; and then the wolf took the dish from him and carried it to his master.

"There, sir host," said the huntsman, "now I have bread and meat and vegetables. But I'll have some pastry too, like the King's." He called the bear and said, "Dear Bear, you're fond of licking anything sweet. Go and bring me some confectionery, such as the King eats."

So the bear trotted off to the palace, and everybody got out of his way; but when he came to the guard, they levelled their muskets and would not let him into the royal palace. He got up on his hind legs, though, and gave them a few boxes on the ears, right and left, with his paws, so that the whole watch broke up; and then he went straight to the King's daughter, placed himself behind her and growled a little. She looked round, knew the bear, and told him to come into her room with her, and said, "Dear Bear, what is it you want?"

He answered, "My master, who killed the dragon, is here, and I'm to ask for some confectionery, such as the King eats."

So she summoned her confectioner, who had to bake confectionery such as the King ate and carry it to the door for the bear. Then the bear first licked up the sweets that had rolled off, and then he stood upright, took the dish and carried it to his master.

"There, sir host," said the huntsman, "now I have bread, meat, vegetables and confectionery. But I'll drink wine as well, and wine such as the King drinks." He called his lion to him and said, "Dear Lion, you like a drink yourself till you're tipsy. Go and fetch me some wine, such as the King drinks."

Then the lion strode down the streets, and the people fled from him; and when he came to the watch they tried to bar the way against him, but he only roared once and they all ran away. Then the lion went to the royal apartments and knocked on the door with his tail. The King's daughter came out and was nearly frightened of the lion; but she knew him by the golden clasp of her necklace, and told him to come with her into her room, and said, "Dear Lion, what will you have?"

He answered, "My master, who killed the dragon, is here, and I'm to ask for some wine such as the King drinks."

So she had the cup-bearer called, who was to give the lion wine like the King's.

The lion said, "I'll go with him and see that I get the right wine."

So he went down with the cup-bearer; and when they were below, the cup-bearer was going to draw him some of the ordinary wine that the King's servants drank. But the lion said, "Stop. I'll taste the wine first" — and he drew half a measure and swallowed it at one draught. "No," he said, "that isn't right."

The cup-bearer looked at him sideways, but went on and was about to give him some out of another barrel, which was the King's marshal's. The lion said, "Stop, let me taste the wine first" — and drew half a measure and drank it. "That's better, but still not right," he said.

Then the cup-bearer grew angry and said, "How can a stupid animal like you understand wine?" But the lion gave him a blow behind the ears that knocked him down by no means gently; and when he had got up again he took the lion, without a word, into a little cellar apart, where the King's own wine lay, that nobody else ever drank. The lion first drew half a measure and tried the wine, and then he said, "That may possibly be the right sort" — and told the cup-bearer to fill six bottles of it.

And now they went upstairs again; but when the lion came out of the cellar into the open air he reeled this way and that, and was rather drunk, and the cup-bearer had to carry the wine as far as the door for him. Then the lion took the handle of the basket in his mouth and brought it to his master.

The huntsman said, "There, sir host, here I have bread, meat, vegetables, confectionery and wine such as the King has; and now I'll dine with my animals." And he sat down and ate and drank, and gave the hare, the fox, the wolf, the bear and the lion food and drink too, and was in good spirits, for he could see that the King's daughter still loved him.

And when he had finished his dinner he said, "Sir host, now I've eaten and drunk as the King eats and drinks, and now I'll go to the King's court and marry the King's daughter."

Said the host, "How can that be, when she already has a betrothed husband, and when the wedding is to be celebrated today?"

Then the huntsman drew out the handkerchief the King's daughter had given him on the dragon's hill, in which the monster's seven tongues were folded, and said, "What I have in my hand will help me to do it."

The innkeeper looked at the handkerchief and said, "Whatever else I believe, I don't believe that; and I'm willing to stake my house and yard on it."

The huntsman, though, took a bag with a thousand gold pieces in it, put it on the table and said, "I stake that on it."

Now at the royal table the King said to his daughter, "What did all those wild animals want, that have been coming to you and going in and out of my palace?"

She answered, "I'm not allowed to tell you; but send for the master of these animals and have him brought here, and you'll do well."

The King sent a servant to the inn to invite the stranger, and the servant arrived just as the huntsman had laid his wager with the innkeeper.

"There, sir host," said the huntsman, "now the King sends his servant and invites me; but I don't go in this fashion." And he said to the servant, "I request the Lord King to send me royal clothing, and a carriage with six horses, and servants to attend me."

When the King heard the answer he said to his daughter, "What shall I do?"

She said, "Have him fetched as he wishes to be fetched, and you'll do well."

So the King sent royal apparel, a carriage with six horses, and servants to wait on him. When the huntsman saw them coming he said, "There, sir host, now I'm fetched just as I wanted to be" — and he put on the royal garments, took the handkerchief with the dragon's tongues with him, and drove off to the King.

When the King saw him coming he said to his daughter, "How shall I receive him?"

She answered, "Go to meet him, and you'll do well."

So the King went to meet him and led him in, and his animals followed. The King gave him a seat beside himself and his daughter; and the marshal, as bridegroom, sat on the other side, but did not know the huntsman any more.

And now at that very moment the dragon's seven heads were carried in to be shown, and the King said, "These seven heads were cut off the dragon by the marshal; and so today I give him my daughter for a wife."

At that the huntsman stood up, opened the seven mouths, and said, "Where are the dragon's seven tongues?"

Then the marshal was terrified, and grew pale, and did not know what answer to make; and at last in his distress he said, "Dragons have no tongues."

The huntsman said, "Liars ought to have none. But the dragon's tongues are the victor's proof." And he unfolded the handkerchief, and there all seven of them lay inside it. And he put each tongue into the mouth it belonged to, and every one fitted exactly.

Then he took the handkerchief with the princess's name embroidered on it, showed it to her, and asked whom she had given it to; and she answered, "To the man who killed the dragon."

And then he called his animals and took the collar off each of them, and the golden clasp from the lion, and showed them to her, and asked whom they belonged to. She answered, "The necklace and the golden clasp were mine, and I divided them among the animals that helped to conquer the dragon."

Then the huntsman said, "When I was resting after the fight, and was asleep with weariness, the marshal came and cut off my head. Then he carried the King's daughter away and gave out that it was he who had killed the dragon. That he lied, I prove with the tongues, the handkerchief and the necklace."

And then he told how his animals had healed him with a wonderful root, and how he had travelled about with them for a year, and had come there again at last and learned the marshal's treachery from the innkeeper's story.

Then the King asked his daughter, "Is it true that this man killed the dragon?"

And she answered, "Yes, it's true. Now I can reveal the marshal's wicked deed, since it has come out without my breaking my word — for he wrung a promise of silence out of me. And that was why I made the condition that the marriage should not be celebrated for a year and a day."

Then the King ordered twelve councillors to be summoned to pass judgement on the marshal, and they sentenced him to be torn to pieces by four bulls. So the marshal was executed; but the King gave his daughter to the huntsman and named him viceroy over the whole kingdom.

The wedding was celebrated with great joy, and the young King sent for his father and his foster-father and loaded them with treasures. He did not forget the innkeeper either, but sent for him and said, "There, sir host — I've married the King's daughter, and your house and yard are mine."

The host said, "Yes, by rights that's so."

But the young King said, "It shall go by mercy instead," and told him he should keep his house and yard, and gave him the thousand gold pieces as well.

And now the young King and Queen were thoroughly happy and lived in gladness together. He often went out hunting, because it was a delight to him, and the faithful animals had to go with him. In the neighbourhood, though, there was a forest that was said to be haunted, and that whoever once went into it did not easily get out again. But the young King had a great longing to hunt in it, and gave the old King no peace until he was allowed to.

So he rode out with a great following; and when he came to the forest he saw a snow-white hart, and said to his people, "Wait here until I come back. I want to chase that beautiful creature." And he rode into the forest after it, with nobody following him but his animals.

His attendants halted and waited until evening, but he did not come back; so they rode home and told the young Queen that the young King had followed a white hart into the enchanted forest and had not returned. Then she was in the greatest anxiety about him.

He, meanwhile, had gone riding on and on after the beautiful creature, and had never been able to overtake it. Whenever he thought he was near enough to take aim, he saw it bound away into the far distance; and at last it vanished altogether. And now he realised how deep into the forest he had come, and blew his horn; but no answer came back, for his attendants could not hear it. And as night was falling too, he saw he could not get home that day; so he dismounted, lit himself a fire by a tree, and made up his mind to spend the night there.

While he was sitting by the fire, with his animals lying down beside him, he thought he heard a human voice. He looked round but could see nothing. Soon afterwards he heard a groan again, as if from above him; and then he looked up and saw an old woman sitting in the tree, wailing without a stop, "Oh, oh, oh, how cold I am!"

Said he, "Come down and warm yourself, if you're cold."

But she said, "No, your animals will bite me."

He answered, "They'll do you no harm, old mother. Do come down."

She was a witch, however, and said, "I'll throw a wand down out of the tree; and if you strike them on the back with it, they'll do me no harm."

So she threw him down a little wand, and he struck them with it; and instantly they lay still and were turned to stone. And when the witch was safe from the animals, she jumped down and touched him with a wand as well, and changed him to stone. Then she laughed, and dragged him and the animals into a vault where a great many more such stones were already lying.

But as the young King did not come back at all, the Queen's anguish and worry grew greater and greater.

And it happened that at this very time the other brother, who had turned east when they separated, came into that kingdom. He had looked for a position and found none, and had gone travelling about here and there, making his animals dance. Then it came into his head that he would just go and look at the knife they had driven into the tree trunk when they parted, so as to learn how his brother was faring. When he got there, his brother's side of the knife was half rusty and half bright.

Then he was alarmed and thought, "Some great misfortune must have come to my brother; but perhaps I can still save him, since half the knife is still bright."

So he and his animals travelled westwards; and when he came in at the town gate the guard came to meet him and asked whether he should announce him to his consort the young Queen, who had been in the greatest distress for a couple of days about his staying away, and was afraid he had been killed in the enchanted forest. The sentries had no other idea than that he was the young King himself, for he looked so like him and had wild animals running behind him.

Then he saw that they were speaking of his brother, and thought, "It will be better if I let them take me for him. Then I can rescue him more easily." So he let the guard escort him into the castle, and was received with the greatest joy.

The young Queen truly believed he was her husband, and asked him why he had stayed away so long.

He answered, "I lost myself in a forest and couldn't find my way out any sooner."

At night he was taken to the royal bed, but he laid a two-edged sword between himself and the young Queen. She did not know what that could mean, but did not dare to ask.

He stayed in the palace a couple of days, and in that time he found out everything there was to know about the enchanted forest; and at last he said, "I must hunt there once more."

The King and the young Queen tried to talk him out of it, but he held out against them and went off with a still larger following.

When he had got into the forest it went with him as it had with his brother. He saw a white hart and said to his people, "Stay here and wait until I come back. I want to chase that lovely creature." And then he rode into the forest, and his animals ran after him.

But he could not overtake the hart, and got so deep into the forest that he had to spend the night there. And when he had lit a fire he heard somebody wailing above him, "Oh, oh, oh, how cold I am!"

Then he looked up, and there was the very same witch sitting in the tree.

Said he, "If you're cold, come down, little old mother, and warm yourself."

She answered, "No, your animals will bite me."

But he said, "They won't hurt you."

Then she cried, "I'll throw a wand down to you, and if you strike them with it they'll do me no harm."

When the huntsman heard that, he had no faith in the old woman, and said, "I won't strike my animals. Come down, or I'll fetch you."

Then she cried, "What do you want? You shan't touch me."

But he answered, "If you don't come, I'll shoot you."

Said she, "Shoot away — I'm not afraid of your bullets."

So he took aim and fired at her; but the witch was proof against all leaden bullets, and laughed and shrieked and cried, "You shan't hit me!"

The huntsman knew what to do. He tore three silver buttons off his coat and loaded his gun with them, for against those her arts were useless; and when he fired she fell down at once with a scream.

Then he set his foot on her and said, "Old witch, if you don't tell me this instant where my brother is, I'll take hold of you with both hands and throw you into the fire."

She was in a great fright, and begged for mercy, and said, "He and his animals are lying in a vault, turned to stone."

Then he made her go there with him, and threatened her, and said, "Old sea-cat, now you shall bring my brother and all the human beings lying here back to life, or you go into the fire."

She took a wand and touched the stones; and then his brother came to life again with his animals, and many others as well — merchants, craftsmen and shepherds — who got up and thanked him for their deliverance and went off to their homes.

And when the twin brothers saw each other again they kissed each other and rejoiced with all their hearts. Then they seized the witch and bound her and laid her on the fire; and when she was burnt, the forest opened of its own accord and grew light and clear, and the King's palace could be seen about three hours' walk away.

After that the two brothers went home together, and on the way told each other their histories. And when the younger said that he was ruler of the whole country in the King's place, the other remarked, "I noticed that very well. When I came to the town and was taken for you, all royal honours were paid to me; the young Queen looked on me as her husband, and I had to eat at her side and sleep in your bed."

When the other heard that, he grew so jealous and angry that he drew his sword and struck off his brother's head. But when he saw him lying there dead, and saw his red blood flowing, he repented terribly. "My brother delivered me," he cried, "and I've killed him for it!" — and he wept aloud over him.

Then his hare came and offered to go and fetch some of the root of life, and bounded away and brought it while there was still time; and the dead man was brought back to life and knew nothing about the wound.

After this they journeyed on, and the younger said, "You look like me, you have royal clothes on as I do, and the animals follow you as they do me. We'll go in by opposite gates and come before the old King from the two sides at the same moment."

So they separated; and at the same moment the watchmen came from the one gate and from the other, and announced that the young King had come back from the chase with his animals.

The King said, "That's not possible. The gates are a good mile apart."

But meanwhile the two brothers were coming into the palace courtyard from opposite sides, and both climbed the steps.

Then the King said to his daughter, "Say which is your husband. They look exactly alike; I can't tell."

Then she was in great distress and could not tell. But at last she remembered the necklace she had given to the animals; and she looked, and found her little golden clasp on the lion, and cried out in her delight, "The one this lion follows is my true husband!"

Then the young King laughed and said, "Yes, he's the right one" — and they sat down to table together, and ate and drank and were merry.

That night, when the young King went to bed, his wife said, "Why have you laid a two-edged sword in our bed every night lately? I thought you had a mind to kill me."

Then he knew how faithful his brother had been.

The Little Peasant

There was once a village where nobody lived but really rich farmers, and just one poor one, whom they called the little peasant. He did not own so much as a cow, still less the money to buy one; and he and his wife did so long to have one.

One day he said to her, "Listen, I've had a good idea. There's our friend the carpenter — he shall make us a wooden calf and paint it brown, so that it looks like any other; and in time it will surely grow big and be a cow."

The woman liked the idea too; and their friend the carpenter cut and planed the calf and painted it as it ought to be, and made it with its head hanging down, as if it were eating.

Next morning, when the cows were being driven out, the little peasant called the cowherd and said, "Look, I've a little calf here; but it's still small and has to be carried."

"All right," said the cowherd — and he took it in his arms and carried it to the pasture and set it down in the grass. The little calf went on standing there like one that was eating, and the cowherd said, "It will soon be running about on its own. Just look how it eats already!"

In the evening, when he was going to drive the herd home again, he said to the calf, "If you can stand there and eat your fill, you can go on your own four legs as well. I don't care to be dragging you home again in my arms."

But the little peasant stood at his door waiting for his little calf; and when the cowherd drove the cows through the village and the calf was missing, he asked where it was.

The cowherd answered, "It's still standing out there eating. It wouldn't stop and come along with us."

But the little peasant said, "Oh no — I must have my beast back again."

So they went back to the meadow together; but somebody had stolen the calf and it was gone.

The cowherd said, "It must have run away."

The peasant, though, said, "Don't tell me that" — and brought the cowherd before the mayor, who condemned him for his carelessness to give the peasant a cow for the calf that had run away.

And now the little peasant and his wife had the cow they had wished for so long, and they were heartily glad. But they had no fodder for it and could give it nothing to eat, so it soon had to be slaughtered. They salted the meat, and the peasant went to town meaning to sell the hide there, so that he could buy a new calf with the money.

On the way he passed a mill, and there sat a raven with broken wings; and out of pity he picked it up and wrapped it in the hide. But the weather turned so bad, and there was such a storm of wind and rain, that he could go no further; so he turned back to the mill and asked for shelter.

The miller's wife was alone in the house, and said to the peasant, "Lie down there on the straw" — and gave him a slice of bread with cheese on it.

The peasant ate it and lay down with his hide beside him, and the woman thought, "He's tired and has gone to sleep."

Meanwhile the parson arrived. The miller's wife made him welcome and said, "My husband's out, so we'll have a feast."

The peasant listened; and when he heard about feasting he was vexed that he had had to make do with a slice of bread and cheese. Then the woman brought out four different things: roast meat, salad, cakes and wine.

Just as they were about to sit down and eat there was a knocking outside.

"Oh, heavens!" said the woman. "It's my husband!"

She quickly hid the roast meat inside the tiled stove, the wine under the pillow, the salad on the bed, the cakes under it, and the parson in the cupboard in the passage. Then she opened the door to her husband and said, "Thank heaven you're back! There's such a storm, it looks as if the world were coming to an end."

The miller saw the peasant lying on the straw and asked, "What's that fellow doing there?"

"Ah," said his wife, "the poor man came in the wind and rain and begged for shelter, so I gave him a bit of bread and cheese and showed him where the straw was."

The man said, "I've no objection. But be quick and get me something to eat."

The woman said, "But I've nothing except bread and cheese."

"I'm content with anything," her husband answered. "As far as I'm concerned, bread and cheese will do." And he looked at the peasant and said, "Come and eat some more with me."

The peasant did not need to be asked twice, but got up and ate.

After this the miller noticed the hide lying on the ground with the raven in it, and asked, "What have you got there?"

The peasant answered, "There's a soothsayer inside it."

"Can he foretell anything for me?" said the miller.

"Why not?" answered the peasant. "But he only says four things, and the fifth he keeps to himself."

The miller was curious and said, "Let him foretell something for once."

So the peasant pinched the raven's head, and it croaked and made a noise like krr, krr.

The miller said, "What did he say?"

The peasant answered, "In the first place, he says there's some wine hidden under the pillow."

"Bless me!" cried the miller, and went and found the wine. "Now go on."

The peasant made the raven croak again, and said, "In the second place, he says there's roast meat in the tiled stove."

"Upon my word!" cried the miller, and went there and found the roast meat.

The peasant made the raven prophesy still more, and said, "Thirdly, he says there's salad on the bed."

"That would be a fine thing!" cried the miller, and went and found the salad.

At last the peasant pinched the raven once more till it croaked, and said, "Fourthly, he says there are cakes under the bed."

"That would be a fine thing!" cried the miller, and looked there and found the cakes.

And now the two of them sat down at the table together; but the miller's wife was frightened to death, and went to bed and took all the keys with her.

The miller would very much have liked to know the fifth thing; but the little peasant said, "First we'll eat up the four quickly, for the fifth is something bad."

So they ate; and after that they bargained over how much the miller was to give for the fifth prophecy, until they settled on three hundred thalers.

Then the peasant pinched the raven's head once more till it croaked loudly.

The miller asked, "What did he say?"

The peasant replied, "He says the Devil is hiding out there in the cupboard in the passage."

The miller said, "The Devil must go out" — and opened the house door. Then the woman was forced to hand over the keys, and the peasant unlocked the cupboard. The parson ran out as fast as he could, and the miller said, "It was true. I saw the black rascal with my own eyes."

The peasant, though, made off at daybreak next morning with the three hundred thalers.

At home the little peasant gradually began to spread himself. He built a beautiful house, and the other farmers said, "The little peasant has certainly been where the golden snow falls, and people carry the gold home by the shovelful."

Then the little peasant was brought before the mayor and told to say where his wealth came from. He answered, "I sold my cow's hide in the town for three hundred thalers."

When the farmers heard that, they wanted a share of this great profit too, and ran home, killed all their cows and stripped off the hides, so as to sell them in town to the best advantage.

The mayor, however, said, "But my servant must go first."

When she came to the merchant in the town he gave her no more than two thalers for a hide; and when the others came he did not give them even that much, and said, "What am I to do with all these hides?"

Then the farmers were furious that the little peasant should have taken them in like that, and wanted revenge, and accused him of this trickery before the mayor. The innocent little peasant was sentenced to death by common consent, and was to be rolled into the water in a barrel pierced full of holes.

He was led out, and a priest was fetched to say a mass for his soul. The rest all had to withdraw to a distance; and when the peasant looked at the priest he recognised the man who had been with the miller's wife.

He said to him, "I set you free from the cupboard — set me free from the barrel."

At that very moment who should come by with a flock of sheep but the shepherd, who the peasant knew had long been wanting to be mayor. So he cried out with all his might, "No, I won't do it! If the whole world insists on it, I won't do it!"

The shepherd heard him, came up and asked, "What are you about? What is it you won't do?"

The peasant said, "They want to make me mayor if I'll only get into the barrel; but I won't do it."

The shepherd said, "If that's all that's needed to be mayor, I'd get into the barrel this minute."

The peasant said, "If you'll get in, you'll be mayor."

The shepherd was willing, and got in, and the peasant shut the lid down on him; then he took the shepherd's flock for himself and drove it away.

The parson went over to the crowd and announced that the mass had been said. Then they came and rolled the barrel towards the water. When it began to roll, the shepherd called out, "I'm quite willing to be mayor!"

They supposed it was nobody but the peasant saying it, and answered, "That's what we intend. But first you shall have a look round down below there" — and they rolled the barrel into the water.

After that the farmers went home; and as they were coming into the village the little peasant came quietly in too, driving a flock of sheep and looking perfectly content.

Then the farmers were astonished, and said, "Peasant, where have you come from? Have you come out of the water?"

"Yes, indeed," replied the peasant. "I sank down deep, deep, until at last I got to the bottom; and I pushed the bottom out of the barrel and crept out, and there were beautiful meadows with any number of lambs feeding on them, and I brought this flock away with me."

Said the farmers, "Are there any more there?"

"Oh, yes," said he, "more than I knew what to do with."

Then the farmers made up their minds to fetch some sheep for themselves, a flock apiece; but the mayor said, "I come first."

So they went to the water together. And just then there were some of the small fleecy clouds in the blue sky that people call little lambs, and they were reflected in the water; whereupon the farmers cried, "We can see the sheep down there already!"

The mayor pressed forward and said, "I'll go down first and look round, and if it all looks promising I'll call you."

So he jumped in — splash went the water — and he made a sound as if he were calling them, and the whole crowd plunged in after him as one man.

Then the entire village was dead, and the little peasant, as sole heir, became a rich man.

The Queen Bee

Two king's sons once went out in search of adventures and fell into a wild, disorderly way of living, so that they never came home again. The youngest, who was called Simpleton, set out to look for his brothers; but when he did at last find them, they mocked him for supposing that he, with his simplicity, could make his way in the world, when the two of them could not manage it and were so much cleverer.

The three of them travelled on together and came to an ant hill. The two elder ones wanted to knock it down, to see the little ants scurrying about in their terror and carrying off their eggs; but Simpleton said, "Leave the creatures in peace. I won't let you disturb them."

Then they went on and came to a lake with a great many ducks swimming on it. The two brothers wanted to catch a couple and roast them, but Simpleton would not have it, and said, "Leave the creatures in peace. I won't let you kill them."

At last they came to a bees' nest with so much honey in it that it was running down the trunk of the tree. The two wanted to light a fire under the tree and smoke the bees to death so as to take the honey; but Simpleton stopped them again and said, "Leave the creatures in peace. I won't let you burn them."

At length the three brothers arrived at a castle where stone horses were standing in the stables and not a single human being was to be seen. They went through all the halls, until right at the end they came to a door with three locks in it. In the middle of the door, though, there was a little pane through which they could see into the room; and there they saw a little grey man sitting at a table. They called to him once, and twice, but he did not hear; and at the third call he got up, opened the locks and came out.

He said nothing, but led them to a handsomely laid table; and when they had eaten and drunk he took each of them to a bedroom.

Next morning the little grey man came to the eldest, beckoned to him and led him to a stone table on which three tasks were carved, by the doing of which the castle could be delivered.

The first was that the princess's pearls, a thousand of them, lay in the forest under the moss and must be picked up; and if a single pearl were missing at sunset, whoever had been looking for them would be turned to stone.

The eldest went there and searched the whole day; but when it came to an end he had found only a hundred, and what was written on the table came to pass, and he was changed into stone.

Next day the second brother undertook the adventure; but it went not much better with him than with the eldest. He did not find more than two hundred pearls, and was changed to stone.

At last it was Simpleton's turn as well, and he searched in the moss. But the pearls were so hard to find and he got on so slowly that he sat down on a stone and wept. And while he was sitting there, the King of the ants, whose life he had once saved, came with five thousand ants; and before long the little creatures had all the pearls collected and laid in a heap.

The second task, though, was to fetch the key of the King's daughter's bedchamber out of the lake. When Simpleton came to the lake, the ducks he had saved swam up to him, dived down and brought the key up out of the water.

But the third task was the hardest of all: the youngest and dearest of the King's three sleeping daughters had to be picked out from among them. They looked exactly alike, and there was nothing to tell them apart except that they had each eaten a different sweet thing before falling asleep — the eldest a lump of sugar, the second a little syrup, and the youngest a spoonful of honey.

Then the Queen of the bees, which Simpleton had saved from the fire, came and tasted the lips of all three; and at last she stayed sitting on the mouth that had eaten honey, and so the King's son knew the right princess.

Then the enchantment was at an end. Everything was released from its sleep, and all those who had been turned to stone got their own shapes back again. Simpleton married the youngest and sweetest princess, and became King after her father's death; and his two brothers got the other two sisters.

The Three Feathers

There was once a King who had three sons. Two of them were clever and quick-witted; but the third did not say much, and was simple, and was called the Simpleton.

When the King had grown old and weak and was thinking about his end, he did not know which of his sons should inherit the kingdom after him. So he said to them, "Go out into the world, and whichever of you brings me the most beautiful carpet shall be King after my death."

And so that there should be no quarrelling among them, he took them outside his castle, blew three feathers into the air, and said, "You shall go where they fly."

One feather flew east and one flew west; but the third flew straight up and did not fly far, and soon dropped to the ground.

And now one brother went to the right and the other to the left, and they mocked Simpleton, who had to stay where the third feather had fallen.

He sat down and was sad; and then all at once he saw that there was a trapdoor close by the feather. He lifted it, found some steps and went down them, and then came to another door and knocked at it, and heard somebody inside calling:

	"Little green maiden, hopping so free,
	hop to the door and see who it may be."

The door opened, and he saw a great fat toad sitting there with a crowd of little toads around her.

The fat toad asked what he wanted. He answered, "I should like to have the prettiest and finest carpet in the world."

Then she called one of the young ones and said:

	"Little green maiden, hop away quick,
	the great box yonder is what I pick."

The young toad brought the box, and the fat toad opened it and gave Simpleton a carpet out of it, so beautiful and so finely made that up on the earth above nobody could have woven the like of it. So he thanked her and climbed up again.

The other two had thought their youngest brother so stupid that they were sure he would find and bring nothing at all.

"Why should we give ourselves any trouble to search?" they said — and they got a couple of coarse handkerchiefs from the first shepherds' wives they met, and carried them home to the King.

At the same moment Simpleton came back too, and brought his beautiful carpet; and when the King saw it he was astonished and said, "If justice is done, the kingdom belongs to the youngest."

But the other two gave their father no peace, and said it was impossible that Simpleton, who had no sense in anything, should be King, and begged him to make a new bargain with them.

So the father said, "Whoever brings me the most beautiful ring shall inherit the kingdom" — and he led the three brothers out and blew three feathers into the air for them to follow.

The two eldest ones' feathers went east and west again, and Simpleton's flew straight up and dropped down beside the door into the earth. So he went down again to the fat toad and told her that he wanted the most beautiful ring in the world. She at once ordered her great box to be brought, and gave him a ring out of it that sparkled with jewels, and was so beautiful that no goldsmith on earth could have made it.

The two eldest laughed at Simpleton for going to look for a golden ring. They gave themselves no trouble at all, but knocked the nails out of an old cartwheel-ring and took that to the King. But when Simpleton produced his golden ring, his father said again, "The kingdom belongs to him."

The two eldest did not stop tormenting the King until he made a third condition, and declared that whoever brought home the most beautiful woman should have the kingdom. He blew the three feathers into the air again, and they flew as they had before.

Then Simpleton went straight down to the fat toad and said, "I'm to take home the most beautiful woman!"

"Oho," answered the toad, "the most beautiful woman! She isn't to hand at the moment, but you shall have her all the same."

She gave him a hollowed-out yellow turnip with six mice harnessed to it. Then Simpleton said quite miserably, "What am I to do with that?"

The toad answered, "Just put one of my little toads inside it."

So he took one at random out of the ring of them and set her in the yellow carriage; and hardly was she seated in it before she turned into a wonderfully beautiful girl, and the turnip into a carriage, and the six mice into horses. So he kissed her and drove off at a good pace and brought her to the King.

His brothers came along afterwards. They had given themselves no trouble at all to look for beautiful girls, but had brought the first peasant women they happened to meet.

When the King saw them he said, "After my death the kingdom belongs to my youngest son."

But the two eldest deafened the King's ears again with their outcry — "We can't consent to Simpleton's being King" — and demanded that the one whose wife could jump through a ring hanging in the middle of the hall should have the preference. They thought, "The peasant women can do that easily, they're strong enough; but the delicate girl will jump herself to death."

The old King agreed to this as well. So the two peasant women jumped, and jumped through the ring, but were so heavy that they fell and broke their coarse arms and legs. And then the pretty girl Simpleton had brought with him sprang, and sprang through as lightly as a deer, and all opposition had to come to an end.

So he was given the crown, and has ruled wisely for a long time now.

The Golden Goose

There was a man who had three sons, the youngest of whom was called Simpleton, and was despised and mocked and put down at every turn.

It happened that the eldest wanted to go into the forest to cut wood; and before he went, his mother gave him a beautiful sweet cake and a bottle of wine, so that he should not go hungry or thirsty.

When he came into the forest, a little grey-haired old man met him and wished him good day, and said, "Do give me a piece of the cake in your pocket, and let me have a drink of your wine. I'm so hungry and thirsty."

But the prudent young man answered, "If I give you my cake and my wine, I shall have none for myself. Be off with you." And he left the little man standing there and went on.

But when he began to cut down a tree, it was not long before he made a false stroke and the axe cut into his arm, so that he had to go home and have it bound up. And that was the little grey man's doing.

After this the second son went into the forest, and his mother gave him a cake and a bottle of wine, as she had the eldest. The little old grey man met him too, and asked him for a piece of the cake and a drink of the wine. But the second son said, just as sensibly, "Whatever I give you is taken away from me. Be off!" And he left the little man standing there and went on.

His punishment was not slow in coming either: he had struck the tree only a few times when he struck his own leg, and had to be carried home.

Then Simpleton said, "Father, do let me go and cut wood."

His father answered, "Your brothers have hurt themselves at it. Leave it alone — you know nothing about it."

But Simpleton begged so long that at last he said, "Off you go, then. Hurting yourself will teach you sense."

His mother gave him a cake made with water and baked in the ashes, and a bottle of sour beer to go with it.
