When he came to the forest, the little old grey man met him as well, and greeted him and said, "Give me a piece of your cake and a drink out of your bottle. I'm so hungry and thirsty."

Simpleton answered, "I've nothing but a cinder-cake and sour beer. If that suits you, we'll sit down and eat."

So they sat down; and when Simpleton pulled out his cinder-cake, it was a fine sweet cake, and the sour beer had turned into good wine. So they ate and drank; and afterwards the little man said, "Since you have a good heart and are willing to share what you have, I'll give you good luck. There's an old tree standing over there — cut it down, and you'll find something among the roots." And with that the little man took his leave.

Simpleton went and cut down the tree; and when it fell there was a goose sitting among the roots, with feathers of pure gold. He picked her up and took her with him to an inn, where he meant to stay the night.

Now the innkeeper had three daughters, who saw the goose and were curious to know what sort of wonderful bird it might be, and would have liked one of its golden feathers.

The eldest thought, "I shall soon find a chance to pull out a feather"; and as soon as Simpleton had gone out, she took hold of the goose by the wing — and her finger and hand stuck fast to it.

The second came soon afterwards, thinking of nothing but how she might get a feather for herself; but she had hardly touched her sister before she was held fast too.

At last the third came with the same idea, and the others screamed out, "Keep away! For goodness' sake keep away!" But she could not see why she should keep away. "The others are there," she thought. "I may as well be there too" — and she ran to them; but the moment she touched her sister she stuck fast to her. So they had to spend the night with the goose.

Next morning Simpleton took the goose under his arm and set out, without troubling himself about the three girls hanging on behind. They had to keep running after him, now left, now right, wherever he happened to want to go.

Out in the middle of the fields the parson met them; and when he saw the procession he said, "For shame, you good-for-nothing girls! Why are you running across the fields after this young man? Is that proper?" And at the same time he took hold of the youngest by the hand to pull her away — but as soon as he touched her he stuck fast as well, and had to run along behind.

Before long the sexton came by and saw his master the parson running along behind three girls. He was astonished at this and called out, "Hi there, your reverence, where are you off to in such a hurry? Don't forget we've a christening today!" And he ran after him and took him by the sleeve, and was held fast to it.

While the five of them were trotting along one behind the other, two labourers came in from the fields with their hoes. The parson called out to them and begged them to set him and the sexton free; but they had hardly touched the sexton before they were held fast too, and now there were seven of them running along behind Simpleton and the goose.

Soon afterwards he came to a city where a king reigned who had a daughter so solemn that nobody could make her laugh. So he had put out a proclamation that whoever could make her laugh should marry her.

When Simpleton heard this he went with his goose and all its train before the King's daughter; and as soon as she saw the seven people running along, on and on, one behind the other, she began to laugh out loud, and as if she would never stop. At that Simpleton asked to have her for his wife, and the wedding was celebrated. After the King's death Simpleton inherited the kingdom, and lived contentedly with his wife for a long time.

Allerleirauh

There was once a King who had a wife with golden hair, and she was so beautiful that her equal was not to be found on earth. It came about that she fell ill; and as she felt that she must soon die, she called the King and said, "If you wish to marry again after my death, take nobody who isn't quite as beautiful as I am, and who hasn't golden hair just like mine. You must promise me that." And after the King had promised her, she closed her eyes and died.

For a long time the King could not be comforted, and had no thought of taking another wife. At length his councillors said, "There's no help for it — the King must marry again, so that we may have a Queen." And now messengers were sent far and wide to look for a bride who was the late Queen's equal in beauty. But in the whole world none was to be found; and even if one had been found, there would still have been nobody with such golden hair. So the messengers came home no wiser than they went.

Now the King had a daughter who was just as beautiful as her dead mother, and had the same golden hair. When she was grown up, the King looked at her one day and saw that in every respect she was the image of his late wife, and all at once he felt a violent love for her. Then he said to his councillors, "I'll marry my daughter, for she is the very likeness of my late wife; and apart from her I can find no bride who resembles her."

When the councillors heard that they were appalled, and said, "God has forbidden a father to marry his daughter. No good can come of such a crime, and the kingdom will be dragged down in the ruin."

The daughter was still more appalled when she learned of her father's decision, but she hoped to turn him from his plan. So she said to him, "Before I do what you wish, I must have three dresses: one as golden as the sun, one as silvery as the moon, and one as bright as the stars. And besides that I want a cloak made of a thousand different kinds of fur and hide sewn together, and every kind of animal in your kingdom must give a piece of its skin for it." But she thought, "Getting that will be quite impossible, and so I shall turn my father away from his wicked intentions."

The King, however, did not give up. The cleverest girls in his kingdom had to weave the three dresses — one as golden as the sun, one as silvery as the moon, and one as bright as the stars; and his huntsmen had to catch one of every kind of animal in the whole kingdom and take a piece of its skin, and out of these a cloak of a thousand kinds of fur was made. At last, when everything was ready, the King had the cloak brought and spread out in front of her, and said, "The wedding shall be tomorrow."

So when the King's daughter saw that there was no hope left of turning her father's heart, she made up her mind to run away from him. In the night, while everybody was asleep, she got up and took three things out of her treasures: a golden ring, a golden spinning wheel and a golden reel. The three dresses of the sun, the moon and the stars she packed into a nutshell; then she put on her cloak of all kinds of fur and blackened her face and hands with soot. Then she commended herself to God and went away, and walked the whole night until she came to a great forest. And as she was tired she climbed into a hollow tree and fell asleep.

The sun rose and she slept on, and she was still sleeping when it was broad day. Now it happened that the King to whom this forest belonged was hunting in it. When his dogs came to the tree they sniffed and ran round it barking.

The King said to his huntsmen, "Just see what sort of wild beast has hidden itself in there."

The huntsmen did as he ordered; and when they came back they said, "There's a wonderful beast lying in the hollow tree. We've never seen anything like it. Its coat is fur of a thousand different kinds — but it's lying there asleep."

Said the King, "See if you can catch it alive; then tie it to the carriage and we'll take it with us."

When the huntsmen laid hold of the girl she woke in terror and cried out to them, "I'm a poor child, deserted by father and mother. Have pity on me and take me with you."

Then they said, "Allerleirauh — All-Kinds-of-Fur — you'll do to work in the kitchen. Come along with us, you can sweep up the ashes."

So they put her in the carriage and took her home to the royal palace. There they showed her a cupboard under the stairs where no daylight came, and said, "Hairy animal, you can live and sleep in there." Then she was sent into the kitchen, and there she carried wood and water, swept the hearth, plucked the fowls, picked over the vegetables, raked out the ashes, and did all the dirty work.

Allerleirauh lived there a long time in great wretchedness. Ah, lovely princess, what is to become of you now!

It happened one day, though, that a feast was held in the palace, and she said to the cook, "May I go upstairs for a while and watch? I'll stand outside the door."

The cook answered, "Yes, go along; but you must be back here in half an hour to sweep the hearth."

So she took her oil lamp and went into her den, took off her fur dress and washed the soot off her face and hands, so that her full beauty came to light again. And she opened the nut and took out her dress that shone like the sun; and when she had put it on she went up to the feast, and everybody made way for her, because nobody knew her, and they took her for nothing less than a king's daughter. The King came to meet her and gave her his hand and danced with her, and thought in his heart, "My eyes have never seen anyone so beautiful." When the dance was over she curtsied; and when the King looked round again she had vanished, and nobody knew where. The guards standing outside the palace were called and questioned, but not one of them had seen her.

She had run into her little den, though, and quickly taken off her dress and made her face and hands black again and put on her fur cloak, and was Allerleirauh once more. And now, when she went into the kitchen and was about to get to work and sweep up the ashes, the cook said, "Leave that until morning, and make the King his soup. I want to go up for a while too and take a look. But don't let any hairs fall into it, or you shall have nothing to eat in future."

So the cook went off, and Allerleirauh made the King's soup, and made it bread soup and as good as she knew how; and when it was ready she fetched her golden ring from her little den and put it in the bowl the soup was served in.

When the dancing was over the King had his soup brought and ate it, and liked it so much that it seemed to him he had never tasted better. But when he came to the bottom of the bowl he saw a golden ring lying there, and could not imagine how it had got in. So he ordered the cook to come before him.

The cook was terrified when he heard the order, and said to Allerleirauh, "You've certainly let a hair fall into the soup; and if you have, you'll be beaten for it."

When he came before the King, the King asked who had made the soup.

The cook replied, "I made it."

But the King said, "That's not true. It was far better than usual, and cooked differently."

He answered, "I must admit that I didn't make it. It was made by the hairy animal."

The King said, "Go and tell it to come up here."

When Allerleirauh came, the King said, "Who are you?"

"I'm a poor girl who has no father or mother any more."

He asked further, "What use are you in my palace?"

She answered, "I'm good for nothing but to have boots thrown at my head."

He went on, "Where did you get the ring that was in the soup?"

She answered, "I know nothing about any ring."

So the King could learn nothing, and had to send her away again.

After a while there was another feast, and then, as before, Allerleirauh begged the cook for leave to go and watch. He answered, "Yes, but come back in half an hour and make the King the bread soup he likes so much."

Then she ran into her den, washed herself quickly, and took out of the nut the dress that was as silvery as the moon, and put it on. Then she went up, and was like a princess; and the King stepped forward to meet her and was delighted to see her again, and as the dance was just beginning they danced it together. But when it ended she disappeared again so quickly that the King could not see where she went.

She sprang into her den, though, and made herself a hairy animal once more, and went into the kitchen to make the bread soup. When the cook had gone upstairs, she fetched the little golden spinning wheel and put it in the bowl, so that the soup covered it.

Then it was carried to the King, who ate it and liked it as much as before, and had the cook brought in; and this time too he was forced to admit that Allerleirauh had made the soup. Allerleirauh came before the King again; but she answered that she was good for nothing but to have boots thrown at her head, and that she knew nothing at all about the little golden spinning wheel.

When the King held a feast for the third time, it all happened as it had before. The cook said, "Upon my word, rough-skin, you're a witch. You're always putting something in the soup that makes it so good that the King likes it better than mine." But she begged so hard that he let her go up at the appointed time.

And now she put on the dress that shone like the stars, and went into the hall in it. Again the King danced with the beautiful girl, and thought that she had never yet been so lovely. And while she was dancing he contrived, without her noticing it, to slip a golden ring onto her finger; and he had given orders that the dance should last a very long time. When it ended he wanted to hold her fast by the hands, but she tore herself free and sprang away through the crowd so quickly that she vanished from his sight.

She ran as fast as she could into her den under the stairs; but as she had been too long, and had stayed more than half an hour, she could not get her pretty dress off, and only threw the fur cloak over it; and in her haste she did not make herself quite black, but left one finger white. Then Allerleirauh ran into the kitchen and cooked the King's bread soup; and as the cook was away, she put her golden reel into it.

When the King found the reel at the bottom, he had Allerleirauh summoned; and then he caught sight of the white finger, and saw the ring he had put on it during the dance. Then he took her by the hand and held her fast; and when she tried to get free and run away, her fur cloak fell open a little and the star dress shone out. The King seized the cloak and tore it off. Then her golden hair came shining out, and she stood there in her full splendour and could hide herself no longer. And when she had washed the soot and ashes off her face, she was more beautiful than anyone who had ever been seen on earth.

But the King said, "You are my dear bride, and we shall never part from each other again."

And with that the marriage was celebrated, and they lived happily until their deaths.

The Hare’s Bride

There was once a woman and her daughter who had a pretty garden with cabbages in it; and a little hare got in and ate up all the cabbages during the winter.

Then says the mother to the daughter, "Go into the garden and chase that hare away."

The girl says to the little hare, "Shoo, shoo, hare, you're still eating up all our cabbages."

Says the hare, "Come along, my girl, and sit yourself down on my little hare's tail, and come with me to my little hare's hut."

The girl won't do it.

Next day the hare comes again and eats the cabbages; so the mother says to the daughter, "Go into the garden and drive that hare away."

The girl says to the hare, "Shoo, shoo, little hare, you're still eating all the cabbages."

The little hare says, "My girl, sit yourself down on my little hare's tail and come with me to my little hare's hut."

The girl refuses.

The third day the hare comes again and eats the cabbages. At that the mother says to the daughter, "Go into the garden and chase that hare off."

Says the girl, "Shoo, shoo, little hare, you're still eating all our cabbages."

Says the little hare, "Come along, my girl, sit yourself down on my little hare's tail and come with me to my little hare's hut."

The girl sits down on the little hare's tail, and then the hare carries her far away to his little hut, and says, "Now cook green cabbage and millet, and I'll go and invite the wedding guests."

Then all the wedding guests came together. (Who were the wedding guests? I can tell you that, just as another told it to me.) They were all hares; and the crow was there as parson to marry the bride and bridegroom, and the fox as clerk, and the altar was under the rainbow.

The girl, though, was sad, because she was all alone.

The little hare comes and says, "Open the doors, open the doors, the wedding guests are merry."

The bride says nothing, but weeps. The little hare goes away.

The little hare comes back and says, "Take off the lid, take off the lid, the wedding guests are hungry."

The bride again says nothing, and weeps. The little hare goes away.

The little hare comes back and says, "Take off the lid, take off the lid, the wedding guests are waiting."

Then the bride says nothing, and the hare goes away; but she dresses a straw doll in her clothes and gives her a spoon to stir with, and sets her by the pan of millet, and goes back to her mother.

The little hare comes once more and says, "Take off the lid, take off the lid" — and gets up and hits the doll on the head, so that her cap falls off.

Then the little hare sees that it is not his bride, and goes away, and is sorrowful.

The Twelve Huntsmen

There was once a King's son who was betrothed to a girl he loved very much. And once when he was sitting beside her, very happy, news came that his father lay sick to death and wanted to see him once more before the end.

So he said to his beloved, "I must go now and leave you. I give you this ring to remember me by. When I am King I'll come back and fetch you."

So he rode away; and when he reached his father, the old man was dangerously ill and near his death. He said to him, "Dear son, I wanted to see you once more before my end. Promise me to marry as I wish" — and he named a certain King's daughter who was to be his wife.

The son was in such distress that he did not think what he was doing, and said, "Yes, dear father, your will shall be done." And with that the King closed his eyes and died.

So when the son had been proclaimed King and the time of mourning was over, he was obliged to keep the promise he had given his father, and had the King's daughter asked for in marriage, and she was promised to him.

His first betrothed heard of it, and grieved so much over his faithlessness that she nearly died. Then her father said to her, "Dearest child, why are you so sad? You shall have whatever you want."

She thought for a moment and said, "Dear father, I want eleven girls exactly like me in face and figure and height."

The father said, "If it's possible, your wish shall be granted." And he had a search made through his whole kingdom until eleven young girls were found who were the exact likeness of his daughter in face and figure and height.

When they came to the King's daughter, she had twelve suits of huntsmen's clothes made, all alike; and the eleven girls had to put on the huntsmen's clothes, and she herself put on the twelfth suit. Then she took leave of her father and rode away with them, and rode to the court of the man she had been betrothed to and loved so dearly.

There she asked whether he needed any huntsmen, and whether he would take all of them into his service. The King looked at her and did not know her; but as they were such handsome fellows he said yes, he would gladly take them. And now they were the King's twelve huntsmen.

But the King had a lion that was a marvellous creature, for it knew everything hidden and secret. One evening it happened that the lion said to the King, "You think you have twelve huntsmen?"

"Yes," said the King, "they are twelve huntsmen."

The lion went on, "You're mistaken. They are twelve girls."

The King said, "That can't be true. How will you prove it to me?"

"Oh, just have some peas scattered in your antechamber," answered the lion, "and then you'll soon see. Men have a firm tread, and when they walk over peas not one of them stirs; but girls trip and skip and drag their feet, and the peas roll about."

The King was well pleased with the advice, and had the peas scattered.

But there was a servant of the King's who was fond of the huntsmen; and when he heard that they were to be put to this test he went to them and told them everything, and said, "The lion wants to make the King believe you're girls."

Then the King's daughter thanked him, and said to her girls, "Put some strength into it, and tread firmly on the peas."

So next morning, when the King had the twelve huntsmen called before him and they came into the antechamber where the peas were lying, they trod so firmly on them, and walked so strongly and surely, that not one pea rolled or stirred. Then they went out again, and the King said to the lion, "You've lied to me. They walk just like men."

The lion said, "They found out that they were going to be tested, and put on some strength. Just have twelve spinning wheels brought into the antechamber one day, and they'll go up to them and be pleased with them — and that's what no man would do."

The King liked this advice, and had the spinning wheels set out in the antechamber.

But the servant, who was well disposed to the huntsmen, went and told them the plan. Then, when they were alone, the King's daughter said to her eleven girls, "Keep a hold on yourselves, and don't look round at the spinning wheels."

And next morning, when the King had his twelve huntsmen summoned, they went through the antechamber and never once looked at the spinning wheels.

Then the King said to the lion again, "You've deceived me. They're men — they didn't look at the spinning wheels."

The lion replied, "They found out that they were going to be tested, and held themselves in."

But the King would not believe the lion any more.

The twelve huntsmen always went with the King to the chase, and his liking for them kept growing. Now it happened once, when they were out hunting, that news came that the King's betrothed was on her way. When the true bride heard it, it hurt her so much that her heart was nearly broken, and she fell fainting to the ground.

The King thought something had happened to his dear huntsman, and ran to him and tried to help him, and pulled off his glove. Then he saw the ring he had given his first bride; and when he looked in her face he knew her. Then his heart was so touched that he kissed her; and when she opened her eyes he said, "You are mine and I am yours, and nobody in the world can alter that."

He sent a messenger to the other bride and begged her to go back to her own kingdom, since he had a wife already, and a man who has just found an old dish has no need of a new one.

And with that the wedding was celebrated, and the lion was taken back into favour — because after all it had told the truth.

The Thief and his Master

Hans wanted to have his son taught a trade, so he went into the church and prayed to our Lord God to tell him which would do the boy most good. Then the clerk got behind the altar and said, "Thieving, thieving."

So Hans goes back to his son and tells him he is to learn thieving, and that the Lord God has said so. And he goes off with his son to look for a man who understands thieving.

They walk a long while and come into a great forest, where there stands a little house with an old woman in it. Hans says, "Do you know of a man who understands thieving?"

"You can learn that here well enough," says the woman. "My son is a master of it."

So he speaks with the son and asks whether he really knows thieving well.

The master thief says, "I'll teach him properly. Come back when a year is out; and then, if you recognise your son, I'll take no payment at all for teaching him; but if you don't know him, you must give me two hundred thalers."

The father goes home again, and the son learns witchcraft and thieving thoroughly.

When the year is out, the father is full of worry about how he is to manage to recognise his son. And as he is going about in his trouble, he meets a little dwarf, who says, "Man, what's the matter with you, that you're always in such distress?"

"Oh," says Hans, "a year ago I placed my son with a master thief, who told me to come back when the year was out; and that if I then didn't know my son when I saw him, I was to pay two hundred thalers, but if I did know him I was to pay nothing. And now I'm afraid I shan't know him, and I can't think where I'm to get the money."

Then the dwarf tells him to take a little basket of bread with him and stand under the chimney. "There on the crossbeam is a basket with a little bird peeping out of it, and that is your son."

Hans goes there and throws down a little basket full of black bread in front of the basket with the bird in it; and the little bird comes out and looks up.

"Hullo, my son, are you there?" says the father; and the son is delighted to see his father.

But the master thief says, "The devil must have prompted you — how else could you have known your son?"

"Father, let's go," said the boy.

Then father and son set out for home. On the way a carriage comes driving by, and the son says to his father, "I'll change myself into a big greyhound, and then you can make a lot of money out of me."

Then the gentleman calls out of the carriage, "My man, will you sell your dog?"

"Yes," says the father.

"How much do you want for him?"

"Thirty thalers."

"Well, man, that's a great deal; but as he's such a very fine dog I'll have him."

The gentleman takes him into the carriage; but when they have driven a little way, the dog springs out of the carriage window and goes back to his father, and is a greyhound no longer.

They go home together. Next day there is a fair in the next town, so the young man says to his father, "Now I'll change myself into a beautiful horse, and you can sell me. But when you've sold me, you must take off my bridle, or I can't become a man again."

So the father goes to the fair with the horse; and the master thief comes and buys the horse for a hundred thalers. But the father forgets, and does not take the bridle off.

So the man goes home with the horse and puts it in the stable. When the maid crosses the threshold, the horse says, "Take off my bridle, take off my bridle."

Then the maid stands still and says, "What — can you talk?" And she goes and takes the bridle off; and the horse turns into a sparrow and flies out at the door, and the wizard turns into a sparrow too and flies after him.

Then they come together and cast lots; but the master loses, and takes to the water and is a fish. Then the young man becomes a fish as well, and they cast lots again, and the master loses. So the master changes himself into a cock, and the young man becomes a fox and bites the master's head off; and he died, and has stayed dead to this day.

Jorinda and Joringel

There was once an old castle in the middle of a large, thick forest, and in it an old woman who was a witch lived all alone. By day she changed herself into a cat or a screech owl, but in the evening she took her proper human shape again. She could lure wild animals and birds to her, and then she killed them and boiled and roasted them.

If anyone came within a hundred paces of the castle he was forced to stand still and could not move from the spot until she gave him leave. But whenever an innocent girl came inside this circle, she changed her into a bird and shut her up in a wickerwork cage and carried the cage into a room in the castle. She had about seven thousand cages of rare birds in that castle.

Now there was once a girl called Jorinda, who was lovelier than all other girls. She and a handsome young man named Joringel had promised to marry each other. They were still in their days of betrothal, and their greatest happiness was to be together.

One day, so that they could talk quietly, they went for a walk in the forest. "Take care," said Joringel, "not to go too near the castle."

It was a beautiful evening; the sun shone brightly between the tree trunks into the dark green of the forest, and the turtle doves sang mournfully on the young boughs of the birches.

Jorinda wept now and then; she sat down in the sunshine and was sorrowful. Joringel was sorrowful too. They were as sad as if they were about to die. Then they looked about them and were quite at a loss, for they did not know which way they should go to get home. The sun was still half above the mountain and half set.

Joringel looked through the bushes and saw the old walls of the castle close at hand. He was horror-struck and filled with a deadly fear. Jorinda was singing:

	"My little bird, with the necklace red,
	sings sorrow, sorrow, sorrow;
	he sings that the dove must soon be dead,
	sings sorrow, sor — jug, jug, jug."

Joringel looked for Jorinda. She had been changed into a nightingale, and sang, "jug, jug, jug." A screech owl with glowing eyes flew three times round about her, and three times cried, "to-whoo, to-whoo, to-whoo!"

Joringel could not move. He stood there like a stone, and could not weep or speak or move hand or foot.

The sun had set now. The owl flew into the thicket, and directly afterwards a crooked old woman came out of it, yellow and lean, with great red eyes and a hooked nose whose tip reached her chin. She muttered to herself, caught the nightingale and carried it away in her hand.

Joringel could neither speak nor stir from the spot; the nightingale was gone. At last the woman came back and said in a hollow voice, "Greetings, Zachiel. When the moon shines on the cage, Zachiel, let him loose at once."

Then Joringel was free. He fell on his knees before the woman and begged her to give him back his Jorinda; but she said he should never have her again, and went away. He called, he wept, he lamented, but all in vain. "Ah, what is to become of me?"

Joringel went away and came at last to a strange village, where he kept sheep for a long time. He often walked round and round the castle, but never too close to it.

At last he dreamed one night that he found a blood-red flower with a beautiful large pearl in the middle of it; that he picked the flower and went with it to the castle, and that everything he touched with the flower was freed from enchantment. He dreamed too that by means of it he got his Jorinda back.

In the morning when he woke, he began to search over hill and dale to see whether he could find such a flower. He searched until the ninth day, and then, early in the morning, he found the blood-red flower. In the middle of it there was a great dewdrop, as big as the finest pearl.

Day and night he travelled with this flower to the castle. When he came within a hundred paces of it he was not held fast, but walked on to the door. Joringel was full of joy. He touched the door with the flower and it sprang open. He walked in across the courtyard and listened for the sound of the birds. At last he heard it. He went on and found the room it came from, and there the witch was, feeding the birds in the seven thousand cages.

When she saw Joringel she was angry — very angry — and scolded and spat poison and gall at him; but she could not come within two paces of him. He took no notice of her, but went and looked over the cages of birds. But there were many hundreds of nightingales in them. How was he to find his Jorinda again?

Just then he saw the old woman quietly taking away a cage with a bird in it, and going towards the door.

In a flash he sprang after her, touched the cage with the flower, and the old woman too. Now she could bewitch nobody any more; and Jorinda was standing there with her arms round his neck, and she was as beautiful as ever.

The Three Sons of Fortune

A father once called his three sons before him and gave the first a cock, the second a scythe and the third a cat.

"I'm an old man now," he said. "My death is near, and I wanted to make some provision for you before my end. Money I have none, and what I'm giving you now seems worth very little; but it all depends on your making sensible use of it. Only find a country where such things are still unknown, and your fortune is made."

After the father's death the eldest went off with his cock; but wherever he came the cock was known already. In the towns he could see one from a long way off, sitting on the steeples and turning round with the wind; and in the villages he heard more than one of them crowing. Nobody would show the least wonder at the creature, so it did not look as if he would make his fortune by it.

At last, though, it happened that he came to an island where the people knew nothing about cocks, and did not even understand how to divide up their time. They knew well enough when it was morning or evening; but at night, if they did not sleep through it, not one of them could tell the time.

"Look," said he, "what a proud creature this is! It has a ruby-red crown on its head and wears spurs like a knight; it calls you three times in the night, at fixed hours; and when it calls the last time the sun soon rises. But if it crows in broad daylight, take notice, for there'll certainly be a change in the weather."

The people were delighted. For a whole night they did not sleep, and listened with great pleasure as the cock proclaimed the time loudly and clearly at two, four and six o'clock. They asked whether the creature was for sale, and how much he wanted for it.

"About as much gold as a donkey can carry," he answered.

"A ridiculously small price for such a precious creature!" they all cried, and gladly gave him what he had asked.

When he came home with his wealth his brothers were astonished; and the second said, "Well, I'll go out and see whether I can't get rid of my scythe as profitably."

But it did not look as if he could, for he met labourers everywhere, and they had scythes on their shoulders as well as he.

At last, though, he happened on an island where the people knew nothing about scythes. When the corn was ripe there they took cannon out into the fields and shot it down. Now that was a rather uncertain business: many shot right over it, and others hit the ears instead of the stalks and shot them clean away, so that a great deal was lost; and on top of it all it made a terrible noise. So the man set to work and mowed the corn down so quietly and quickly that the people gaped with astonishment. They agreed to give him whatever he asked for the scythe, and he was given a horse loaded with as much gold as it could carry.

And now the third brother wanted to take his cat to the right man. It went with him just as it had with the others: as long as he stayed on the mainland there was nothing to be done. Every place had cats, and there were so many of them that newborn kittens were generally drowned in the ponds.

At last he sailed over to an island, and it luckily happened that no cats had ever been seen there, and that the mice had got the upper hand so completely that they danced on the tables and benches whether the master of the house was at home or not. The people complained bitterly of the plague. The King himself, in his palace, did not know how to protect himself from them; mice squeaked in every corner and gnawed whatever they could get their teeth into.

But now the cat began her hunting, and soon cleared a couple of rooms; and the people begged the King to buy the wonderful animal for the country. The King gladly gave what was asked, which was a mule loaded with gold; and the third brother came home with the greatest treasure of all.

The cat, meanwhile, was making merry with the mice in the royal palace, and killed so many that they could not be counted. At last she grew hot with the work and thirsty, so she stood still, lifted up her head and cried, "Mew! Mew!"

When they heard this strange cry, the King and all his people were frightened, and in their terror ran out of the palace all together. Then the King took counsel about what was best to be done; and at last it was decided to send a herald to the cat and demand that she leave the palace, and to warn her that if she did not, she must expect force to be used against her. The councillors said, "We'd rather be plagued with the mice — we're used to that misfortune — than give up our lives to a monster like this."

So a young nobleman was sent to ask the cat whether she would quit the castle peaceably. But the cat, whose thirst had grown greater still, only answered, "Mew! Mew!"

The young man understood her to say, "Most certainly not! Most certainly not!" — and took this answer back to the King.

"Then," said the councillors, "she shall yield to force."

Cannon were brought up, and the palace was soon in flames. When the fire reached the room where the cat was sitting, she sprang safely out of the window; but the besiegers did not leave off until the whole palace had been shot to the ground.

How Six Men Got on in the World

There was once a man who was master of all kinds of skills. He served in the war and behaved well and bravely; but when the war was over he got his discharge and three farthings for his expenses on the road.

"Wait a bit," said he. "I shan't be content with this. If I can only meet the right people, the King will yet have to give me the whole treasure of the country."

Then he went into the forest full of anger, and saw a man standing there who had pulled up six trees as if they were stalks of corn. He said to him, "Will you be my servant and come along with me?"

"Yes," he answered, "but first I'll take this little bundle of sticks home to my mother." And he took one of the trees and wound it round the other five, lifted the bundle onto his back and carried it away. Then he came back and went off with his master, who said, "The two of us ought to be able to get through the world very well."

When they had walked a little way they found a huntsman kneeling down with his gun at his shoulder, about to fire.

The master said to him, "Huntsman, what are you going to shoot?"

He answered, "Two miles from here there's a fly sitting on the branch of an oak tree, and I want to shoot its left eye out."

"Oh, come with me," said the man. "If the three of us are together we certainly ought to get on in the world."

The huntsman was willing and went along with him; and they came to seven windmills whose sails were turning round at great speed, although no wind was blowing on the right hand or the left and not a leaf was stirring.

Then the man said, "I don't know what is driving those windmills — there isn't a breath of air." And he went on with his servants; and when they had walked two miles they saw a man sitting in a tree, holding one nostril shut and blowing out of the other.

"Good gracious, what are you doing up there?"

He answered, "Two miles away there are seven windmills. Look — I'm blowing to keep them turning."

"Oh, come with me," said the man. "If the four of us are together we'll carry the whole world before us."

So the blower came down and went with him; and after a while they saw a man standing on one leg, who had taken the other one off and laid it down beside him.

The master said, "You've made yourself very comfortable for a rest."

"I'm a runner," he replied, "and to stop myself running much too fast I've taken one of my legs off; for if I run with both, I go quicker than any bird can fly."

"Oh, come with me. If the five of us are together we'll carry the whole world before us."

So he went along with them; and it was not long before they met a man wearing a cap, but wearing it right over one ear.

The master said to him, "Gently, gently — don't stick your cap over one ear like that. You look like a perfect fool."

"I mustn't wear it any other way," said he, "for if I set my hat straight, a terrible frost comes on, and all the birds in the air freeze and drop dead to the ground."

"Oh, come with me," said the master. "If the six of us are together we can carry the whole world before us."

Now the six came to a town where the King had proclaimed that whoever ran a race against his daughter and won should be her husband — but whoever lost should lose his head.

Then the man presented himself and said, "I'll do it; but I'll let my servant run for me."

The King replied, "Then his life must be staked as well, so that his head and yours are both set on the victory."

When that was settled and agreed, the man buckled the other leg onto the runner and said to him, "Now be quick, and help us to win."

It was arranged that whoever was first to bring back water from a far-off well should be the winner. The runner was given a pitcher, and the King's daughter one too, and they set off at the same moment. But in an instant, when the King's daughter had gone only a very little way, the people watching could see no more of the runner; it was just as if the wind had whistled past.

In a short time he reached the well, filled his pitcher with water and turned back. Halfway home, though, he was overcome with tiredness, and set his pitcher down and lay down himself and fell asleep. He had made a pillow of a horse's skull that was lying on the ground, so that he should lie uncomfortably and soon wake up again.

Meanwhile the King's daughter, who could also run very well — quite as well as any ordinary person can — had reached the well, and was hurrying back with her pitcher full of water; and when she saw the runner lying there asleep she was glad and said, "My enemy is delivered into my hands" — and she emptied his pitcher and ran on.

And now all would have been lost, if by good luck the huntsman had not been standing at the top of the castle and seen the whole thing with his sharp eyes.

"The King's daughter shan't get the better of us all the same," said he. And he loaded his gun and shot so cleverly that he shot the horse's skull out from under the runner's head without hurting him.

Then the runner woke and jumped up, and saw that his pitcher was empty and that the King's daughter was already far ahead. But he did not lose heart. He ran back to the well with his pitcher, drew water again, and was home ten minutes before the King's daughter.

"There," said he. "I hadn't stirred myself till now. What went before didn't deserve to be called running."

But it galled the King, and still more his daughter, that she should be carried off by a common discharged soldier like that; and they took counsel together about how to be rid of him and his companions.

Then the King said to her, "I've thought of a way. Don't be afraid — they shan't come back."

And he said to them, "You shall make merry together now, and eat and drink." And he led them into a room that had an iron floor; the doors were iron too, and the windows were guarded with iron bars. In the room stood a table covered with delicious food, and the King said to them, "Go in and enjoy yourselves."

And when they were inside, he ordered the doors to be shut and bolted. Then he sent for the cook and told him to light a fire under the room until the iron was red hot. The cook did it, and the six sitting at the table began to feel quite warm, and thought the heat came from the food. But as it grew still greater, and they wanted to get out and found the doors and windows bolted, they realised that the King must mean them harm and was trying to suffocate them.

"He shan't manage it, though," said the one with the cap. "I'll bring on a frost that will make the fire ashamed of itself and creep away."

Then he put his cap on straight, and immediately there came such a frost that all the heat vanished, and the food on the dishes began to freeze.

When an hour or two had gone by, and the King believed that they had died in the heat, he had the doors opened so as to see for himself. But when the doors were opened, all six were standing there alive and well, and said that they would very much like to get out and warm themselves, since the very food was frozen fast to the dishes with the cold.

Then the King went down to the cook in a fury, and scolded him, and asked why he had not done as he was told. But the cook replied, "There's heat enough there. Look for yourself."

Then the King saw that a fierce fire was burning under the iron room, and understood that there was no getting the better of the six that way.

The King thought again about how to be rid of his unwelcome guests, and had their leader brought to him, and said, "If you'll take gold and give up my daughter, you shall have as much as you like."

"Oh yes, Lord King," he answered. "Give me as much as my servant can carry, and I won't ask for your daughter."

The King was satisfied with that, and the other went on, "I'll come and fetch it in a fortnight."

Then he called together all the tailors in the whole kingdom, and they had to sit for a fortnight and sew a sack. And when it was ready, the strong one who could pull up trees had to take it on his back and go with it to the King.

Then the King said, "Who can that powerful fellow be, carrying a bundle of linen on his back as big as a house?" And he took fright and said, "What a lot of gold he'll be able to carry away!"

Then he ordered a ton of gold to be brought; it took sixteen of his strongest men to carry it, but the strong one snatched it up in one hand, put it in his sack and said, "Why don't you bring more at the same time? That hardly covers the bottom."

So little by little the King had all his treasure brought there, and the strong one shoved it into the sack, and even then the sack was not half full with it.

"Bring more," he cried. "These few crumbs don't fill it."

Then seven thousand cartloads of gold had to be gathered from the whole kingdom, and the strong one thrust them into his sack, oxen and all.

"I won't look them over any longer," said he. "I'll just take what comes, so long as the sack gets full."

When all that was inside there was still room for a great deal more; so he said, "I'll just make an end of the business. People do sometimes tie up a sack even when it isn't full."

So he took it on his back and went off with his comrades.

When the King saw one single man carrying away the entire wealth of the country, he flew into a rage, and ordered his horsemen to mount and go after the six and take the sack away from the strong one.

Two regiments soon overtook the six and called out, "You're prisoners! Put down that sack of gold, or you'll all be cut to pieces."

"What's that you say?" cried the blower. "That we're prisoners? Sooner than that, the lot of you shall go dancing about in the air." And he closed one nostril and blew on the two regiments with the other. Then they were scattered away from one another and carried up into the blue sky over all the mountains, one here and another there.

One sergeant cried for mercy; he had nine wounds and was a brave fellow who did not deserve rough treatment. The blower left off for a moment, so that he came down without harm; and then the blower said to him, "Now go home to your King and tell him he had better send some more horsemen — I'll blow every one of them into the air."

When the King was told this he said, "Let the rascals go. They have the better of it."

Then the six carried the riches home, divided them among themselves, and lived contented until their deaths.

The Wolf and the Man

Once upon a time the fox was talking to the wolf about the strength of man: how no animal could stand against him, and how all of them had to use cunning to keep themselves safe from him.

Then the wolf answered, "If I only had the chance of seeing a man just once, I'd go for him all the same."

"I can help you to that," said the fox. "Come to me early tomorrow morning and I'll show you one."

The wolf turned up in good time, and the fox took him out to the road the huntsmen used every day.

First an old discharged soldier came along. "Is that a man?" asked the wolf.

"No," answered the fox. "That was one."

Afterwards a little boy came by, going to school. "Is that a man?"

"No. That's going to be one."

At length a hunter came along, with his double-barrelled gun on his back and a short sword at his side.

Said the fox to the wolf, "Look, there comes a man. You must go for him — but I'll be off to my hole."

Then the wolf rushed at the man. When the huntsman saw him he said, "What a pity I haven't loaded with a bullet" — and took aim and fired his small shot into his face.

The wolf pulled a very sour face, but would not let himself be frightened, and went at him again; whereupon the huntsman gave him the second barrel. The wolf swallowed down the pain and rushed at the huntsman; but he drew out his bright blade and gave him a few cuts with it, right and left, so that he ran back to the fox howling and bleeding all over.

"Well, brother wolf," said the fox, "how did you get on with man?"

"Ah," replied the wolf, "I never imagined the strength of man was anything like that. First he took a stick off his shoulder and blew into it, and something flew into my face that tickled me horribly. Then he breathed into the stick once more, and it flew into my nose like lightning and hail. And when I was quite close, he drew a white rib out of his side and beat me with it until I was as good as left there dead."

"See what a braggart you are," said the fox. "You throw your hatchet so far that you can't fetch it back again."

The Wolf and the Fox

The wolf had the fox with him, and whatever the wolf wanted, the fox was obliged to do, because he was the weaker; and he would gladly have been rid of his master.

It happened once, as they were going through the forest, that the wolf said, "Red-fox, get me something to eat, or I'll eat you instead."

Then the fox answered, "I know a farmyard where there are two young lambs. If you like, we'll fetch one of them."

That suited the wolf, and they went there; and the fox stole the little lamb, took it to the wolf and went away. The wolf devoured it, but was not satisfied with one; he wanted the other as well, and went to get it. But he did it so clumsily that the little lamb's mother heard him and began to cry out terribly and to bleat, so that the farmer came running. They found the wolf and beat him so mercilessly that he went back to the fox limping and howling.

"You've led me into a fine thing," said he. "I wanted to fetch the other lamb, and the country folk caught me and beat me to a jelly."

The fox replied, "Why are you such a glutton?"

Next day they went out into the country again, and the greedy wolf said once more, "Red-fox, get me something to eat, or I'll eat you instead."

Then the fox answered, "I know a farmhouse where the woman is baking pancakes tonight. We'll get ourselves some of them."

They went there, and the fox slipped round the house and peeped and sniffed about until he found where the dish was; and then he pulled down six pancakes and carried them to the wolf.

"There's something for you to eat," he said to him, and then went on his way.

The wolf swallowed the pancakes down in an instant and said, "They only make you want more" — and went off there and dragged the whole dish down, so that it smashed to pieces. That made such a noise that the woman came out; and when she saw the wolf she called the people, who came hurrying and beat him as long as their sticks held together, until he got back to the fox in the forest with two lame legs, howling loudly.

"What a shameful way you've led me into," he cried. "The peasants caught me and tanned my hide for me."

But the fox replied, "Why are you such a glutton?"

On the third day, when they were out together and the wolf could only limp along painfully, he said again, "Red-fox, get me something to eat, or I'll eat you instead."

The fox answered, "I know a man who has been killing his pig, and the salted meat is lying in a barrel in the cellar. We'll get that."

Said the wolf, "I'll go when you do, so that you can help me if I can't get away."

"Willingly," said the fox; and he showed him the byways and paths by which they came at last to the cellar.

There was meat in plenty, and the wolf set on it at once and thought, "There's plenty of time before I need stop." The fox liked it too, but he kept looking about him, and often ran back to the hole they had come in by to try whether his body was still thin enough to slip through it.

The wolf said, "Dear fox, tell me why you're running about like that and jumping in and out?"

"I have to see that nobody's coming," replied the crafty fellow. "Don't eat too much!"

Then the wolf said, "I shan't leave until the barrel is empty."

Meanwhile the farmer, who had heard the noise of the fox's jumping, came into the cellar. When the fox saw him he was out of the hole at one bound. The wolf tried to follow him; but he had made himself so fat with eating that he could not get through any more, and stuck fast. Then the farmer came with a cudgel and struck him dead; but the fox bounded off into the forest, glad to be rid of the old glutton.

The Fox and His Cousin

The she-wolf had a cub, and invited the fox to be its godfather. "After all, he's a near relation of ours," said she. "He has a good head on him and plenty of talent; he can teach my little son and help him get on in the world."

The fox, too, seemed perfectly honest about it, and said, "Worthy cousin, I thank you for the honour you're doing me. I'll behave in such a way that you'll be well repaid for it."

He enjoyed himself at the feast and made merry, and afterwards he said, "Dear cousin, it's our duty to take care of the child. It must have good food, so that it grows strong. I know a sheepfold where we could fetch a nice morsel."

The wolf liked the sound of that, and went out with the fox to the farmyard. He pointed out the fold from a distance and said, "You'll be able to creep in there without being seen, and meanwhile I'll look about on the other side and see if I can pick up a chicken."

But he did not go there at all. He sat down at the edge of the forest, stretched out his legs and rested.

The she-wolf crept into the shed. A dog was lying there, and it made such a noise that the farm people came running out, caught cousin wolf, and poured a strong burning wash mixture over her hide. At last she got away and dragged herself outside.

There lay the fox, pretending to be full of complaints, and saying, "Ah, my dear cousin, what a bad time I've had! The peasants set on me and broke every limb I have. If you don't want me to lie here and die, you'll have to carry me away."

The she-wolf could barely walk herself; but she was in such concern about the fox that she took him on her back and slowly carried him — perfectly safe and sound — all the way to her house.

Then the fox called out to her, "Goodbye, dear cousin, and much good may your roasting do you!" — and he laughed heartily at her and bounded off.

The Fox and the Cat

It happened that the cat met the fox in a forest; and as she thought to herself, "He's clever and full of experience, and much respected in the world," she spoke to him in a friendly way. "Good day, dear Mr. Fox. How are you? How is everything with you? How are you getting through these hard times?"

The fox, full of every kind of arrogance, looked the cat over from head to foot, and for a long while did not know whether he would give any answer at all. At last he said, "Oh, you wretched whisker-washer, you piebald fool, you starving mouse-hunter, what can you be thinking of? Do you dare to ask how I'm getting on? What have you learned? How many arts do you understand?"

"I understand only one," replied the cat modestly.

"And what art is that?" asked the fox.

"When the hounds are after me, I can spring up into a tree and save myself."

"Is that all?" said the fox. "I'm master of a hundred arts, and I have a sackful of cunning into the bargain. I'm sorry for you. Come along with me and I'll teach you how people get away from hounds."

Just then a hunter came by with four dogs. The cat sprang nimbly up a tree and sat down at the top of it, where the branches and leaves hid her completely.

"Open your sack, Mr. Fox, open your sack!" the cat called down to him. But the dogs had already seized him and were holding him fast.

"Ah, Mr. Fox," cried the cat, "you and your hundred arts are left in the lurch. If you'd been able to climb like me, you wouldn't have lost your life."

The Pink

There was once a Queen to whom God had given no children. Every morning she went into the garden and prayed to God in heaven to grant her a son or a daughter. Then an angel came to her from heaven and said, "Be at peace. You shall have a son with the power of wishing, so that whatever in the world he wishes for, he shall have."

So she went to the King and told him the joyful news; and when the time came she gave birth to a son, and the King was filled with gladness.

Every morning she went with the child into the garden where the wild animals were kept, and washed herself there in a clear stream. It happened once, when the child was a little older, that he was lying in her arms and she fell asleep. Then the old cook came, who knew that the child had the power of wishing, and stole him away; and he took a hen and cut it in pieces and dropped some of its blood on the Queen's apron and on her dress. Then he carried the child away to a secret place, where a nurse had to feed him; and he ran to the King and accused the Queen of having let the wild beasts take her child from her.

When the King saw the blood on her apron he believed it, and fell into such a rage that he ordered a high tower to be built where neither sun nor moon could be seen, and had his wife put into it and walled up. There she was to stay for seven years without food or drink, and die of hunger. But God sent two angels down from heaven in the shape of white doves, which flew to her twice a day and brought her food until the seven years were over.

The cook, though, thought to himself, "If the child has the power of wishing, and I'm here, he might very easily get me into trouble." So he left the palace and went to the boy, who was already big enough to talk, and said to him, "Wish yourself a beautiful palace, with a garden and everything else that goes with it."

The words were hardly out of the boy's mouth before everything he had wished for was there.

After a while the cook said to him, "It isn't good for you to be so much alone. Wish for a pretty girl to keep you company."

So the King's son wished for one, and she stood before him at once, and she was more beautiful than any painter could have painted her. The two of them played together and loved each other with all their hearts, while the old cook went out hunting like a gentleman.

But it occurred to him that the King's son might one day wish to be with his father, and so bring him into great danger. So he went out and took the girl aside and said, "Tonight, when the boy is asleep, go to his bed and drive this knife into his heart, and bring me his heart and his tongue. And if you don't do it, you'll lose your life."

With that he went away; and when he came back next day she had not done it, and said, "Why should I shed the blood of an innocent boy who has never harmed anybody?"

The cook said once again, "If you don't do it, it will cost you your own life."

When he had gone away she had a little hind brought to her and ordered it to be killed, and took its heart and tongue and laid them on a plate; and when she saw the old man coming she said to the boy, "Lie down in your bed and pull the covers over you."

Then the wicked wretch came in and said, "Where are the boy's heart and tongue?"

The girl held the plate out to him — but the King's son threw off the quilt and said, "You old sinner, why did you want to kill me? Now I'll pronounce your sentence. You shall become a black poodle with a gold collar round your neck, and you shall eat burning coals until the flames come bursting out of your throat."

And when he had spoken these words, the old man was changed into a poodle dog with a gold collar round his neck; and the cooks were ordered to bring up live coals, and he ate them until the flames broke out of his throat.

The King's son stayed there a little while longer, and thought about his mother and wondered whether she was still alive. At length he said to the girl, "I'm going home to my own country. If you'll come with me, I'll take care of you."

"Ah," she answered, "the way is so long; and what should I do in a strange land where nobody knows me?"

As she did not seem quite willing, and as they could not be parted from each other, he wished her changed into a beautiful pink, and took her with him.

Then he went off to his own country, and the poodle had to run after him. He went to the tower where his mother was shut up; and as it was so high, he wished for a ladder that would reach right to the top. Then he climbed up and looked inside and cried, "Beloved mother, my lady Queen, are you still alive, or are you dead?"

She answered, "I have just eaten and am not hungry" — for she thought the angels were there.

Said he, "I'm your own dear son, the one the wild beasts were said to have torn out of your arms. But I'm alive still, and I'll set you free soon."

Then he climbed down again and went to his father, and had himself announced as a huntsman from abroad, and asked whether he could give him a position. The King said yes — if he was skilled and could get game for him, he should come; but that deer had never made their home in any part of the district or the country.

Then the huntsman promised to get him as much game as he could possibly use at the royal table. So he called all the huntsmen together and told them to come out into the forest with him. And he went with them and made them form a great circle, open at one end where he stationed himself, and began to wish. Two hundred deer and more came running into the circle at once, and the huntsmen shot them. Then they were all loaded onto sixty farm carts and driven home to the King; and for once he was able to deck his table with game, after having had none at all for years.

Now the King was overjoyed at this, and gave orders that his whole household should eat with him next day, and made a great feast. When they were all gathered together he said to the huntsman, "Since you're so clever, you shall sit beside me."

He replied, "Lord King, your majesty must excuse me. I'm a poor huntsman."

But the King insisted, and said, "You shall sit beside me" — until he did it.

While he was sitting there he thought of his dearest mother, and wished that one of the King's chief servants would begin to speak of her, and would ask how the Queen was faring in the tower, and whether she was still alive or had died.

Hardly had he formed the wish before the marshal began, and said, "Your majesty, we live joyfully here; but how is the Queen living in the tower? Is she still alive, or is she dead?"

But the King replied, "She let my dear son be torn to pieces by wild beasts. I won't have her named."

Then the huntsman got up and said, "Gracious lord and father, she is alive still, and I am her son; and I was not carried off by wild beasts but by that wretch the old cook, who tore me from her arms while she was asleep and sprinkled her apron with the blood of a chicken."

And with that he took hold of the dog with the golden collar and said, "That's the wretch!" — and had live coals brought, which the dog was made to devour in front of them all, until flames came bursting out of its throat.

At this the huntsman asked the King whether he would like to see the dog in his true shape, and wished him back into the form of the cook, in which he stood there instantly, with his white apron and his knife at his side. When the King saw him he flew into a rage and ordered him to be thrown into the deepest dungeon.

Then the huntsman spoke again and said, "Father, will you see the girl who brought me up so tenderly, and who was afterwards ordered to murder me, and did not do it, though her own life hung on it?"

The King replied, "Yes, I should like to see her."

The son said, "Most gracious father, I'll show her to you first in the form of a beautiful flower." And he put his hand in his pocket and brought out the pink and laid it on the royal table; and it was so beautiful that the King had never seen its equal.

Then the son said, "And now I'll show her to you in her own shape" — and wished her back into a girl; and she stood there looking so beautiful that no painter could have made her more so.

And the King sent two waiting maids and two attendants to the tower to fetch the Queen and bring her to the royal table. But when she was led in she ate nothing, and said, "The gracious and merciful God who has kept me alive in the tower will soon deliver me."

She lived three days more and then died happily; and when she was buried, the two white doves that had brought her food to the tower, and were angels of heaven, followed her body and settled themselves on her grave.

The old King ordered the cook to be torn into four pieces; but grief ate away the King's own heart, and he soon died. His son married the beautiful girl he had brought home as a flower in his pocket; and whether they are still alive or not, God knows.

Clever Gretel

There was once a cook named Gretel, who wore shoes with red rosettes; and when she went out walking in them she turned this way and that, and thought, "You certainly are a pretty girl." And when she came home she drank a draught of wine out of pure gladness of heart; and as wine gives you an appetite, she tasted the best of whatever she was cooking until she had had enough, and said, "A cook has to know what the food is like."

It happened one day that her master said to her, "Gretel, there's a guest coming this evening. Get me two fowls ready, and do them nicely."

"I'll see to it, master," answered Gretel. She killed two fowls, scalded them, plucked them, put them on the spit, and towards evening set them in front of the fire to roast. The fowls began to turn brown and were nearly done, but the guest had still not arrived.

Then Gretel called out to her master, "If the guest doesn't come, I'll have to take the fowls away from the fire; but it'll be a sin and a shame if they're not eaten straight away, while they're at their juiciest."

The master said, "I'll run and fetch the guest myself."

When the master had turned his back, Gretel laid the spit with the fowls on it to one side and thought, "Standing so long by that fire makes you hot and thirsty. Who knows when they'll come? Meanwhile I'll run down to the cellar and have a drink."

She ran down, held a jug under the barrel, said, "God bless it to your use, Gretel" — and took a good drink, and then another hearty draught after it.

Then she went and put the fowls down to the fire again, basted them and turned the spit merrily round. But as the roasting meat smelled so good, Gretel thought, "There might be something wrong with them; they ought to be tasted." She touched one with her finger and said, "Ah, how good fowls are! It's certainly a sin and a shame that they're not being eaten this minute."

She ran to the window to see whether her master was coming with his guest, but she saw nobody; and she went back to the fowls and thought, "One of those wings is burning. I'd better take it off and eat it." So she cut it off and ate it and enjoyed it; and when she had finished she thought, "The other one will have to go down too, or master will notice that something's missing."

When both wings were eaten, she went and looked for her master, and did not see him. It suddenly struck her, "Who knows? Perhaps they aren't coming at all, and have turned in somewhere else." Then she said, "Well, Gretel, enjoy yourself. One fowl has been cut into already; have another drink and finish it off. Once it's eaten you'll have some peace — why should God's good gifts be spoiled?"

So she ran down to the cellar again, took an enormous drink, and ate up the whole of the one chicken in great glee.

When one of the chickens was swallowed down and her master still did not come, Gretel looked at the other one and said, "Where one is, the other ought to be as well; the two of them go together. What's right for one is right for the other. And I think another draught wouldn't do me any harm." So she took another hearty drink, and let the second chicken go and join the first.

She was right in the middle of the best of it when her master came and cried, "Hurry up, Gretel, the guest is coming along right behind me!"

"Yes, sir, I'll serve up at once," answered Gretel.

Meanwhile the master looked to see that the table was properly laid, and took the great knife he was going to carve the chickens with, and sharpened it on the steps.

Just then the guest came and knocked politely and civilly at the front door. Gretel ran and looked to see who was there; and when she saw the guest she put her finger to her lips and said, "Hush! Hush! Get away as fast as you can. If my master catches you it'll be the worse for you. He certainly did invite you to supper, but what he means to do is cut off both your ears. Just listen to him sharpening the knife for it!"

The guest heard the sharpening, and hurried back down the steps as fast as he could.

Gretel was not idle either. She ran screaming to her master and cried, "You've invited a fine guest!"

"Eh? Why, Gretel? What do you mean by that?"

"Yes," said she, "he took the chickens I was just going to serve up right off the dish, and ran away with them."

"That's a nice trick!" said her master, and grieved over the fine chickens. "If he'd only left me one, so that I'd have something to eat."

He called after him to stop, but the guest pretended not to hear. Then he ran after him with the knife still in his hand, calling out, "Just one! Just one!" — meaning that the guest should leave him one chicken and not take both. But the guest could think of nothing except that he was to give up one of his ears, and ran as if there were a fire under him, so as to get them both home safe.

The Old Man and His Grandson

There was once a very old man whose eyes had grown dim and his ears dull of hearing, and whose knees shook; and when he sat at table he could hardly hold his spoon, and spilled the soup on the tablecloth or let it run out of his mouth. His son and his son's wife were disgusted at this, so in the end the old grandfather had to sit in the corner behind the stove, and they gave him his food in an earthenware bowl, and not even enough of it. And he used to look towards the table with his eyes full of tears.

Once his trembling hands could not hold the bowl, and it fell to the ground and broke. The young wife scolded him, but he said nothing and only sighed. Then they bought him a wooden bowl for a few pennies, and he had to eat out of that.

They were all sitting there one day when the little grandson, four years old, began to gather bits of wood together on the floor.

"What are you doing there?" asked his father.

"I'm making a little trough," answered the child, "for father and mother to eat out of when I'm big."

The man and his wife looked at each other for a while, and then began to cry. Then they brought the old grandfather back to the table, and from that time on always let him eat with them, and said nothing either if he did spill a little.

The Water-Nix

A little brother and sister were once playing beside a well, and while they were playing they both fell in. A water-nix lived down below, and she said, "Now I've got you. Now you shall work hard for me!" — and carried them off with her.

She gave the girl dirty tangled flax to spin, and she had to fetch water in a bucket with a hole in it; and the boy had to chop down a tree with a blunt axe; and they got nothing to eat but dumplings as hard as stones.

At last the children grew so out of patience that they waited until one Sunday, when the nix was at church, and ran away. But when church was over the nix saw that the birds had flown, and came after them with great strides.

The children saw her a long way off, and the girl threw a brush behind her, which turned into an immense hill of bristles with thousands and thousands of spikes, and the nix had to scramble over it with great difficulty; but at last she got over.

When the children saw that, the boy threw a comb behind him, which made a great hill of combs with a thousand times a thousand teeth; but the nix managed to keep her footing on them, and at last she crossed that too.

Then the girl threw a looking glass behind her, which turned into a hill of mirrors, and was so slippery that it was impossible for the nix to cross it. Then she thought, "I'll go home quickly and fetch my axe and cut the glass hill in two."

But long before she came back and had chopped her way through the glass, the children had escaped a great distance off, and the water-nix had to take herself back to her well again.

The Death of the Little Hen

Once upon a time the little hen went with the little cock to the nut hill, and they agreed together that whichever of them found the kernel of a nut should share it with the other. Then the hen found a great big nut, but said nothing about it, meaning to eat the kernel herself. The kernel, though, was so big that she could not swallow it, and it stuck in her throat, so that she was afraid she would choke.

Then she cried, "Cock, I beg you, run as fast as you can and fetch me some water, or I shall choke."

The little cock ran as fast as he could to the spring, and said, "Stream, you're to give me some water. The little hen is lying on the nut hill, and she has swallowed a big nut and is choking."

The well answered, "First run to the bride and get her to give you some red silk."

The little cock ran to the bride and said, "Bride, you're to give me some red silk. I'm to give the red silk to the well, and the well is to give me some water, and I'm to take the water to the little hen, who is lying on the nut hill where she has swallowed a great nut kernel and is choking on it."

The bride answered, "First run and bring me my little wreath that's hanging on a willow."

So the little cock ran to the willow and pulled the wreath off the branch and took it to the bride, and the bride gave him some water for it.

Then the little cock took the water to the hen; but when he got there the hen had choked in the meantime, and lay there dead and still.

Then the cock was so grieved that he cried out loud, and every animal came to mourn for the little hen; and six mice built a little carriage to carry her to her grave, and when the carriage was ready they harnessed themselves to it, and the cock drove.

On the way, though, they met the fox, who said, "Where are you going, little cock?"

"I'm going to bury my little hen."

"May I ride with you?"

"Yes, but sit at the back of the carriage; my little horses couldn't drag you at the front."

So the fox sat down at the back, and after him the wolf, the bear, the stag, the lion and all the beasts of the forest did the same.

Then the procession went on, and they came to the stream. "How are we to get across?" said the little cock.

A straw was lying by the stream, and it said, "I'll lay myself across, and you can drive over me." But when the six mice came onto the bridge, the straw slipped and fell into the water, and all six mice fell in and were drowned.

So they were in difficulty again; and a coal came and said, "I'm big enough. I'll lay myself across and you can drive over me." So the coal laid itself across the water too; but unluckily it just touched the water, at which the coal hissed and went out and died.

When a stone saw that, it took pity on the little cock and wanted to help him, and laid itself across the water. Then the cock drew the carriage himself; but when he had got it over and reached the far side with the dead hen, and was about to draw the others across as well, the ones sitting behind, there were too many of them, and the carriage ran backwards, and they all fell into the water together and were drowned.

Then the little cock was left alone with the dead hen, and dug a grave for her and laid her in it, and made a mound over it; and he sat down on the mound and grieved until he died too. And then everybody was dead.

Brother Lustig

There was once a great war, and when it came to an end a great many soldiers were discharged. Brother Lustig — Brother Merry, as his name went — got his discharge too, and with it nothing but a small loaf of army ration bread and four kreuzers in money; and off he went with that.

But St. Peter had put himself in his way in the shape of a poor beggar; and when Brother Lustig came up, he begged alms of him.

Brother Lustig replied, "My dear beggar-man, what am I to give you? I've been a soldier and got my discharge, and I have nothing but this little loaf of ration bread and four kreuzers. When that's gone I shall have to beg the same as you. Still, I'll give you something."

And with that he divided the loaf into four parts and gave the apostle one of them, and a kreuzer as well.

St. Peter thanked him and went on, and threw himself in the soldier's way as a beggar again, but in another shape; and when he came up he asked him for something as before. Brother Lustig said what he had said the first time, and again gave him a quarter of the loaf and one kreuzer.

St. Peter thanked him and went on; and for a third time he stationed himself in the road as a beggar in yet another shape, and spoke to Brother Lustig. Brother Lustig gave him the third quarter of the bread and the third kreuzer too.

St. Peter thanked him and Brother Lustig went on, with only a quarter of the loaf and one kreuzer left. With that he went into an inn, ate the bread and ordered a kreuzer's worth of beer. When he had drunk it he travelled on; and then St. Peter, who had taken the appearance of a discharged soldier, met him and spoke to him.

"Good day, comrade. Can you spare me a bit of bread and a kreuzer for a drink?"

"Where am I to get it?" answered Brother Lustig. "I've been discharged, and I got nothing but a loaf of ration bread and four kreuzers in money. I met three beggars on the road and gave each of them a quarter of my bread and a kreuzer. The last quarter I ate at the inn, and I had a drink with the last kreuzer. Now my pockets are empty, and if you've nothing either, the two of us can go begging together."

"No," answered St. Peter, "we needn't quite do that. I know a little about medicine, and I'll soon earn as much as I need by it."

"Well, then," said Brother Lustig, "I know nothing about that, so I'll have to go begging on my own."

"Just come with me," said St. Peter, "and if I earn anything you shall have half of it."

"All right," said Brother Lustig; and so they went off together.

Then they came to a peasant's house where they could hear loud wailing and crying; so they went in, and there the husband was lying sick to death and very near his end, and his wife was crying and weeping out loud.

"Stop that howling and crying," said St. Peter. "I'll make the man well again." And he took an ointment out of his pocket and healed the sick man in a moment, so that he could get up and was in perfect health.

In their great delight the man and his wife said, "How can we reward you? What shall we give you?"

But St. Peter would take nothing; and the more the country people offered him, the more he refused.

Brother Lustig, though, nudged St. Peter and said, "Take something. Sure enough we've need of it."
