At length the woman brought a lamb and told St. Peter that he really must take it; but he would not.

Then Brother Lustig gave him a poke in the ribs and said, "Do take it, you stupid fool. We're in great want of it."

So St. Peter said at last, "Very well, I'll take the lamb, but I won't carry it. If you must have it, you must carry it."

"That's nothing," said Brother Lustig. "I'll carry it easily enough" — and took it on his shoulder.

Then they set off and came to a wood; but by then Brother Lustig was beginning to find the lamb heavy, and he was hungry, so he said to St. Peter, "Look, that's a good spot. We could cook the lamb there and eat it."

"As you like," answered St. Peter, "but I'll have nothing to do with the cooking. If you want to cook, there's a kettle for you, and in the meantime I'll walk about a little until it's ready. But you mustn't begin eating until I come back. I'll come at the right moment."

"Off you go, then," said Brother Lustig. "I understand cooking. I'll manage it."

So St. Peter went away, and Brother Lustig killed the lamb, lit a fire, threw the meat into the kettle and boiled it. But the lamb was quite done and the apostle Peter had still not come back; so Brother Lustig took it out of the kettle and cut it up, and found the heart.

"They say that's the best part," said he, and tasted it — and in the end he ate the whole of it.

At length St. Peter came back and said, "You may eat the whole lamb yourself. I'll have nothing but the heart. Give me that."

Then Brother Lustig took a knife and fork and pretended to search anxiously about among the lamb's meat without being able to find the heart, and at last said abruptly, "There isn't one here."

"But where can it be?" said the apostle.

"I don't know," replied Brother Lustig. "But look what fools the two of us are, hunting for a lamb's heart, and neither of us remembering that a lamb has no heart!"

"Oh," said St. Peter, "that's something entirely new. Every animal has a heart. Why should a lamb have none?"

"No, take my word for it, brother," said Brother Lustig, "a lamb has no heart. Just think it over seriously and you'll see that it really hasn't."

"Well, all right," said St. Peter. "If there's no heart, then I want none of the lamb. You may eat it on your own."

"What I can't eat now I'll carry away in my knapsack," said Brother Lustig — and he ate half the lamb and put the rest in his knapsack.

They went on further, and then St. Peter made a great stream of water flow right across their path, so that they had to go through it.

Said St. Peter, "You go first."

"No," answered Brother Lustig, "you must go first" — and he thought, "If the water's too deep, I'll stay behind."

Then St. Peter strode through it, and the water came only to his knee. So Brother Lustig started to go through as well; but the water grew deeper and came up to his throat. Then he cried, "Brother, help me!"

St. Peter said, "Then will you confess that you ate the lamb's heart?"

"No," said he, "I haven't eaten it."

Then the water grew deeper still and rose to his mouth. "Help me, brother!" cried the soldier.

St. Peter said, "Then will you confess that you ate the lamb's heart?"

"No," he replied, "I haven't eaten it."

But St. Peter would not let him drown, and made the water sink and helped him through.

Then they travelled on and came to a kingdom where they heard that the King's daughter lay sick to death.

"Hey there, brother!" said the soldier to St. Peter. "Here's a chance for us. If we can heal her we're provided for, for life."

But St. Peter was not half quick enough for him. "Come on, pick up your feet, my dear brother," said he, "so that we get there in time."

But St. Peter walked slower and slower, however hard Brother Lustig tried to drive and push him along; and at last they heard that the princess was dead.

"Now we're done for," said Brother Lustig. "That comes of your sleepy way of walking."

"Just be quiet," answered St. Peter. "I can do more than cure sick people. I can bring dead ones back to life."

"Well, if you can do that," said Brother Lustig, "it's all right. But you ought to earn us at least half the kingdom for it."

Then they went to the royal palace, where everyone was in deep grief; but St. Peter told the King that he would restore his daughter to life. He was taken to her, and said, "Bring me a kettle and some water"; and when that was brought he told everybody to go out, and let nobody stay with him but Brother Lustig.

Then he cut off all the dead girl's limbs and threw them in the water, lit a fire under the kettle and boiled them. And when the flesh had fallen away from the bones, he took out the beautiful white bones and laid them on a table and arranged them together in their natural order. When he had done that he stepped forward and said three times, "In the name of the holy Trinity, dead woman, arise."

And at the third time the princess rose up, living, healthy and beautiful.

Then the King was overjoyed, and said to St. Peter, "Name your reward. Even if it were half my kingdom, I would give it you."

But St. Peter said, "I want nothing for it."

"Oh, you tomfool," thought Brother Lustig to himself, and nudged his comrade in the ribs and said, "Don't be so stupid. If you have no need of anything, I have."

But St. Peter would take nothing; and as the King saw that the other would very much like to have something, he ordered his treasurer to fill Brother Lustig's knapsack with gold.

Then they went on their way; and when they came to a forest St. Peter said to Brother Lustig, "Now we'll divide the gold."

"Yes," he replied, "we will."

So St. Peter divided the gold — into three heaps.

Brother Lustig thought to himself, "What notion has he got in his head now? He's making three shares and there are only two of us."

But St. Peter said, "I've divided it exactly. There's one share for me, one for you, and one for whoever ate the lamb's heart."

"Oh, I ate that!" replied Brother Lustig, and hastily swept up the gold. "You may take my word for it."

"But how can that be true," said St. Peter, "when a lamb has no heart?"

"Eh, what, brother, what can you be thinking of? Lambs have hearts like other animals. Why should they be the only ones with none?"

"Well, so be it," said St. Peter. "Keep the gold to yourself; but I'll stay with you no longer. I'll go my way alone."

"As you like, dear brother," answered Brother Lustig. "Goodbye."

Then St. Peter took a different road; but Brother Lustig thought, "It's a good thing he's taken himself off. He's a strange sort of saint after all."

Now he had money enough, but he did not know how to handle it. He squandered it and gave it away, and after a while he had nothing again.

Then he came to a certain country where he heard that a King's daughter was dead. "Aha," thought he, "this may be a good thing for me. I'll bring her back to life and see that I'm paid properly for it."

So he went to the King and offered to raise the dead girl to life. Now the King had heard that a discharged soldier was travelling about bringing dead people back to life, and thought that Brother Lustig was the man; but as he had no confidence in him, he consulted his councillors first, who said he might as well let him try, since his daughter was dead.

Then Brother Lustig had water brought to him in a kettle, told everybody to go out, cut off the limbs, threw them in the water and lit a fire underneath, just as he had seen St. Peter do. The water began to boil, the flesh fell off; and then he took the bones out and laid them on the table — but he did not know the order they went in, and laid them all wrong and in confusion.

Then he stood in front of them and said, "In the name of the most holy Trinity, dead maiden, I bid you arise" — and he said it three times, but the bones did not stir. So he said it three times more, and that was no good either.

"You confounded girl, get up!" he cried. "Get up, or it'll be the worse for you!"

When he had said that, St. Peter suddenly appeared in his old shape as a discharged soldier. He came in by the window and said, "Godless man, what are you doing? How can the dead girl arise when you've thrown her bones about in such confusion?"

"Dear brother, I've done everything as well as I could," he answered.

"This once I'll help you out of your difficulty; but I tell you one thing, and that is that if ever you undertake anything of the sort again it will be the worse for you — and also that you must neither demand nor accept the smallest thing from the King for this."

With that St. Peter laid the bones in their right order, said to the girl three times, "In the name of the most holy Trinity, dead maiden, arise" — and the King's daughter got up, healthy and beautiful as before.

Then St. Peter went out by the window again; and Brother Lustig was glad that it had all gone off so well, but very much put out at the thought that he was not to take anything for it after all. "I should just like to know," he thought, "what notion that fellow has in his head. What he gives with one hand he takes away with the other. There's no sense in it whatever."

Then the King offered Brother Lustig whatever he wanted, but he did not dare to take anything; all the same, by hints and cunning he managed to get the King to order his knapsack filled with gold for him, and off he went with that.

When he got outside, St. Peter was standing by the door, and said, "Just look at the sort of man you are. Didn't I forbid you to take anything? And there's your knapsack full of gold."

"How can I help that," answered Brother Lustig, "if people will put it in for me?"

"Well, I tell you this: if ever you set about anything of this kind again, you shall suffer for it."

"Eh, brother, no fear of that. Now that I have money, why should I trouble myself with washing bones?"

"Faith," said St. Peter, "the gold will last a long time! But so that you never walk in forbidden paths after this, I'll give your knapsack this property: whatever you wish to have inside it shall be there. Goodbye — you'll never see me again."

"Goodbye," said Brother Lustig, and thought to himself, "I'm very glad you've taken yourself off, you strange fellow. I certainly shan't follow you." But of the magic power that had been given to his knapsack he thought no more.

Brother Lustig travelled about with his money and squandered and wasted it as he had before. When at last he had no more than four kreuzers, he came past an inn and thought, "The money will have to go," and ordered three kreuzers' worth of wine and a kreuzer's worth of bread.

As he was sitting there drinking, the smell of roast goose found its way to his nose. Brother Lustig looked about and peeped around, and saw that the landlord had two geese in the oven. Then he remembered that his comrade had said whatever he wished to have in his knapsack would be there. "Aha," said he, "I must try that with the geese."

So he went out; and when he was outside the door he said, "I wish those two roast geese out of the oven and into my knapsack." And when he had said it, he unbuckled it and looked in, and there they were inside.

"Ah, that's right," said he. "Now I'm a made man." And he went off to a meadow and took out the roast meat.

He was in the middle of his meal when two journeymen came up and looked with hungry eyes at the second goose, which had not been touched yet. Brother Lustig thought to himself, "One is enough for me," and called the two men over and said, "Take the goose and eat it to my health."

They thanked him and went off with it to the inn, ordered themselves a half bottle of wine and a loaf, took out the goose they had been given and began to eat.

The landlady saw them and said to her husband, "Those two are eating a goose. Just go and see whether it isn't one of ours out of the oven."

The landlord ran there, and behold, the oven was empty. "What!" he cried. "You thieving crew, you want to eat goose as cheap as that? Pay for it this minute, or I'll wash you down well with green hazel-sap."

The two said, "We're no thieves. A discharged soldier gave us the goose, out there in the meadow."

"You shan't throw dust in my eyes that way. The soldier was here, but he went out of the door like an honest man; I watched him go myself. You're the thieves, and you shall pay."

But as they could not pay, he took a stick and cudgelled them out of the house.

Brother Lustig went on his way and came to a place where there was a magnificent castle, and not far from it a wretched inn. He went to the inn and asked for a night's lodging, but the landlord turned him away and said, "There's no more room here. The house is full of noble guests."

"It surprises me that they should come to you and not go to that splendid castle," said Brother Lustig.

"Ah, yes," replied the host, "but it's no small matter to sleep a night there. Nobody who has tried it so far has ever come out alive."

"If others have tried it," said Brother Lustig, "I'll try it too."

"Leave it alone," said the host. "It will cost you your neck."

"It won't kill me on the spot," said Brother Lustig. "Just give me the key, and some good food and wine."

So the host gave him the key and food and wine; and with these Brother Lustig went into the castle, enjoyed his supper, and at length, as he was sleepy, lay down on the floor, since there was no bed.

He soon fell asleep, but in the night he was disturbed by a great noise; and when he woke he saw nine ugly devils in the room, who had made a ring and were dancing round him.

Brother Lustig said, "Well, dance as long as you like, but none of you come too close."

But the devils pressed nearer and nearer to him, and all but trod on his face with their hideous feet.

"Stop it, you devils' ghosts," said he; but they behaved worse than ever.

Then Brother Lustig grew angry and cried, "Hold on — I'll soon have it quiet in here!" — and got hold of a chair leg and struck out into the middle of them with it. But nine devils against one soldier were still too many; and when he struck the ones in front of him, the others got him from behind by the hair and pulled it unmercifully.

"You devils' crew," he cried, "this is getting too bad. But wait. Into my knapsack, all nine of you!"

In an instant they were in it; and then he buckled it up and threw it into a corner. After that everything was suddenly quiet, and Brother Lustig lay down again and slept till broad day.

Then the innkeeper came, and the nobleman the castle belonged to, to see how he had fared; and when they saw that he was cheerful and well they were astonished, and asked, "Have the spirits done you no harm, then?"

"The reason they haven't," answered Brother Lustig, "is that I've got the whole nine of them in my knapsack. You may live in your castle quite peacefully again — not one of them will ever haunt it any more."

The nobleman thanked him and made him rich presents, and begged him to stay in his service, and he would provide for him as long as he lived.

"No," replied Brother Lustig, "I'm used to wandering about. I'll travel on."

Then he went away and turned in at a smithy, laid the knapsack with the nine devils in it on the anvil, and asked the smith and his apprentices to strike it. So they hammered away with their great hammers with all their strength, and the devils set up howls that were quite pitiable. When he opened the knapsack afterwards, eight of them were dead; but one, which had been lying in a fold of it, was still alive, and slipped out and went back to hell.

After that Brother Lustig travelled about the world for a long time, and those who know the stories could tell you many a one about him. But at last he grew old and began to think about his end; so he went to a hermit who was known to be a pious man, and said to him, "I'm tired of wandering about, and I want to behave from now on in a way that will get me into the kingdom of Heaven."

The hermit replied, "There are two roads. One is broad and pleasant and leads to hell; the other is narrow and rough and leads to heaven."

"I'd be a fool," thought Brother Lustig, "to take the narrow, rough road."

So he set out and took the broad, pleasant one, and came at length to a great black door, which was the door of Hell. Brother Lustig knocked, and the doorkeeper peeped out to see who was there. But when he saw Brother Lustig he was terrified — for he was the very same ninth devil who had been shut up in the knapsack and had got out of it with a black eye. So he shot the bolt back again as fast as he could, ran to the devil's lieutenant and said, "There's a fellow outside with a knapsack who wants to come in. But as you value your lives, don't let him in, or he'll wish the whole of hell into his knapsack. He gave me a frightful hammering once when I was inside it."

So they called out to Brother Lustig that he was to go away again, because he was not getting in there.

"If they won't have me here," thought he, "I'll see whether I can find a place for myself in heaven; for I must be somewhere."

So he turned about and went on until he came to the door of Heaven, and knocked there. St. Peter was sitting close by as doorkeeper. Brother Lustig recognised him at once and thought, "Here's an old friend. I shall get on better now."

But St. Peter said, "I do believe you want to come into Heaven."

"Let me in, brother. I must get in somewhere. If they'd have taken me into Hell I shouldn't have come here."

"No," said St. Peter, "you shan't come in."

"Then if you won't let me in, take your knapsack back; I'll have nothing at all from you."

"Give it here, then," said St. Peter.

So Brother Lustig passed the knapsack through the bars into Heaven, and St. Peter took it and hung it up beside his seat.

Then Brother Lustig said, "And now I wish myself inside my knapsack" — and in a second he was in it, and in Heaven; and St. Peter had to let him stay there.

Gambling Hansel

Once upon a time there was a man who did nothing but gamble, and for that reason people never called him anything but Gambling Hansel; and as he never left off gambling, he played away his house and everything he had.

Now on the very day before his creditors were to take his house from him, the Lord and St. Peter came and asked him to give them shelter for the night. Gambling Hansel said, "For my part you may stay the night, but I can't give you a bed or anything to eat."

So the Lord said he was just to take them in and they would buy something to eat themselves; and Gambling Hansel made no objection to that.

Then St. Peter gave him three groschen and told him to go to the baker's and fetch some bread. So Gambling Hansel went; but when he reached the house where the other gambling vagabonds gathered, they greeted him with a great shout — although they had won everything he owned — and said, "Hansel, do come in."

"Oh," said he, "do you want to win the three groschen as well?"

At that they would not let him go. So he went in, and played away the three groschen too.

Meanwhile St. Peter and the Lord were waiting; and as he was so long coming, they set out to meet him. But when Gambling Hansel saw them he pretended that the money had fallen down a drain, and kept raking about in it to find it — though our Lord already knew that he had lost it at play.

St. Peter gave him three groschen again; and this time he did not let himself be led astray, but brought them the loaf.

Then our Lord asked whether he had no wine, and he said, "Alas, sir, the casks are all empty."

But the Lord told him to go down to the cellar, because the best wine was still there. For a long time he would not believe it, but at length he said, "Well, I'll go down, but I know there's none there."

When he turned the tap, though — lo and behold, the best of wine ran out. So he brought it up to them, and the two of them spent the night there.

Early next day our Lord told Gambling Hansel that he might ask for three favours. The Lord expected that he would ask to go to Heaven; but Gambling Hansel asked for a pack of cards with which he could win everything, and for dice with which he could win everything, and for a tree on which every kind of fruit would grow, and from which nobody who had climbed up could get down again until he told them to.

The Lord gave him everything he had asked for, and went away with St. Peter.

And now Gambling Hansel set about his gambling in real earnest, and before long he had won half the world.

At this St. Peter said to the Lord, "Lord, this can't go on. He'll win the whole world and you'll lose it. We must send Death to him."

When Death appeared, Gambling Hansel had just sat down at the gaming table, and Death said, "Hansel, come outside a moment."

But Gambling Hansel said, "Just wait a little until the game's done; and in the meantime climb up into that tree out there and gather a little fruit, so that we have something to munch on the way."

So Death climbed up; but when he wanted to come down again he could not, and Gambling Hansel left him up there for seven years, during which time nobody died at all.

So St. Peter said to the Lord, "Lord, this can't go on. People aren't dying any more. We must go ourselves."

And they went themselves, and the Lord commanded Hansel to let Death come down. So Hansel went straight to Death and said to him, "Come down" — and Death took hold of him at once and made an end of him.

They went off together and came to the next world; and then Gambling Hansel made straight for the door of Heaven and knocked at it.

"Who's there?"

"Gambling Hansel."

"Ah, we'll have nothing to do with him. Be off!"

So he went to the door of Purgatory and knocked again.

"Who's there?"

"Gambling Hansel."

"Ah, there's quite enough weeping and wailing in here without him. We don't want to gamble. Just go away again."

Then he went to the door of Hell, and there they let him in. But there was nobody at home except old Lucifer and the crooked devils, who had just been about their evil work in the world. And no sooner was Hansel there than he sat down to gamble again. Lucifer, though, had nothing to lose except his misshapen devils; and Gambling Hansel won them off him, as with those cards of his he could not fail to do.

And now he was off again with his crooked devils; and they went to Hohenfurth and pulled up a hop-pole, and with it they went to Heaven and began to shove the pole against it, and Heaven began to crack.

So St. Peter said again, "Lord, this can't go on. We shall have to let him in, or he'll knock us out of Heaven."

And they let him in. But Gambling Hansel started playing again at once, and there was such a noise and confusion that they could not hear what they were saying to each other.

So St. Peter said once more, "Lord, this can't go on. We must throw him out, or he'll set the whole of Heaven in rebellion."

So they went to him and threw him down, and his soul broke into fragments, and went into the gambling vagabonds who are living to this very day.

Hans in Luck

Hans had served his master for seven years, so he said to him, "Master, my time is up. Now I should be glad to go back home to my mother. Give me my wages."

The master answered, "You've served me faithfully and honestly; as the service was, so shall the reward be" — and gave Hans a lump of gold as big as his head. Hans pulled his handkerchief out of his pocket, wrapped the lump up in it, put it on his shoulder and set off on the road home.

As he was going along, always putting one foot in front of the other, he saw a horseman come trotting by, quick and cheerful, on a lively horse.

"Ah," said Hans out loud, "what a fine thing riding is! There you sit as if you were on a chair, you stumble over no stones, you save your shoes, and you get along without knowing how."

The rider had heard him, and stopped and called out, "Hullo, Hans! Why are you going on foot, then?"

"I have to," he answered. "I've this lump to carry home. It's gold, true enough, but I can't hold my head straight for it and it hurts my shoulder."

"I'll tell you what," said the rider. "We'll swap. I'll give you my horse and you can give me your lump."

"With all my heart," said Hans, "but I can tell you, you'll have to crawl along under it."

The rider got down, took the gold and helped Hans up; then he put the bridle tight into his hands and said, "If you want to go at a really good pace, you must click your tongue and call out, 'Gee up! Gee up!'"

Hans was heartily delighted as he sat on the horse and rode away, so bold and free. After a little while he thought it ought to go faster, and he began to click his tongue and call out, "Gee up! Gee up!" The horse broke into a sharp trot, and before Hans knew where he was he had been thrown off and was lying in a ditch that separated the field from the highway. The horse would have gone off too if it had not been stopped by a countryman who was coming along the road driving a cow in front of him.

Hans got his limbs together and stood up on his feet again; but he was annoyed, and said to the countryman, "It's a poor joke, this riding, especially when you get hold of a mare like that, which kicks and throws you off so that you stand a good chance of breaking your neck. I'll never mount her again. Now, I like your cow. You can walk along quietly behind her, and have your milk and butter and cheese into the bargain, every day without fail. What wouldn't I give to have a cow like that!"

"Well," said the countryman, "if it would give you so much pleasure, I don't mind swapping the cow for the horse."

Hans agreed with the greatest delight; the countryman jumped up on the horse and rode quickly away.

Hans drove his cow quietly along in front of him, and thought over his lucky bargain. "If only I have a bit of bread — and that can hardly fail me — I can eat butter and cheese with it as often as I like; and if I'm thirsty I can milk my cow and drink the milk. Good heart, what more can I want?"

When he came to an inn he made a halt, and in his great contentment ate up everything he had with him — his dinner and his supper and all of it — and had half a glass of beer with his last few farthings. Then he drove his cow on along the road to his mother's village.

As it drew on towards midday the heat grew more oppressive, and Hans found himself on a moor that took about an hour to cross. He felt it very hot, and his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth with thirst. "There's a cure for this," thought Hans. "I'll milk the cow now and refresh myself with the milk."

He tied her to a withered tree; and as he had no pail he put his leather cap underneath. But try as he might, not a drop of milk came. And as he set about it in such a clumsy way, the beast lost patience at last and gave him such a blow on the head with her hind foot that he fell to the ground and for a long time could not think where he was.

By good luck a butcher just then came along the road with a wheelbarrow, with a young pig lying in it. "What sort of trick is this?" he cried, and helped good Hans up.

Hans told him what had happened. The butcher gave him his flask and said, "Have a drink and refresh yourself. That cow will certainly give no milk; she's an old beast. At best she's only fit for the plough, or the butcher."

"Well, well," said Hans, smoothing his hair down on his head, "who would have thought it? Of course it's a fine thing when you can kill a beast like that at home — what a lot of meat you have! But I don't care much for beef; it isn't juicy enough for me. A young pig like that, now, is the thing to have. It tastes quite different — and then there are the sausages!"

"Listen, Hans," said the butcher, "out of pure kindness to you I'll swap, and let you have the pig for the cow."

"Heaven reward you for your goodness!" said Hans, and gave up the cow; and the pig was untied from the barrow and the cord it was tied with was put into his hand.

Hans went on, thinking to himself how everything was going just as he wanted; if he did meet with any annoyance, it was set right immediately.

Presently a lad joined him who was carrying a fine white goose under his arm. They said good morning to each other, and Hans began telling of his good luck and how he had always made such good bargains. The boy told him he was taking the goose to a christening feast. "Just lift her," he added, taking hold of her by the wings. "See how heavy she is — she's been fattened up for the last eight weeks. Whoever gets a bit of her when she's roasted will have to wipe the fat off both sides of his mouth."

"Yes," said Hans, weighing her in one hand, "she's a good weight; but my pig's not a bad one either."

Meanwhile the lad was looking suspiciously from one side to the other, and shaking his head. "Look here," he said at length, "it may not be all right about your pig. In the village I came through, the mayor himself had just had one stolen out of its sty. I'm afraid — I'm afraid that's where you got hold of that one. They've sent people out, and it would be a bad business if they caught you with the pig. At the very least you'd be shut up in the dark hole."

Good Hans was terrified. "Goodness," he said, "help me out of this. You know more about this place than I do — take my pig and let me have your goose."

"I'll be running some risk at that game," answered the lad, "but I won't be the cause of your getting into trouble." So he took the cord in his hand and drove the pig quickly away along a side path.

Good Hans, free of his worry, went off homewards with the goose under his arm. "When I think it over properly," he said to himself, "I've actually gained by the exchange. First there's the good roast meat; then all the fat that will drip out of it, which will give me dripping for my bread for a quarter of a year; and last of all the beautiful white feathers. I'll have my pillow stuffed with them, and then I shall certainly go to sleep without any rocking. How glad my mother will be!"

As he was going through the last village there stood a scissors-grinder with his barrow, and as his wheel whirred he sang:

	"I sharpen scissors and quickly grind,
	my coat blows out in the wind behind."

Hans stood still and watched him; and at last he spoke to him and said, "All's well with you, since you're so merry at your grinding."

"Yes," answered the scissors-grinder, "the trade has a golden foundation. A real grinder is a man who finds gold in his pocket as often as he puts his hand in it. But where did you buy that fine goose?"

"I didn't buy it. I swapped my pig for it."

"And the pig?"

"That I got for a cow."

"And the cow?"

"I took that instead of a horse."

"And the horse?"

"For that I gave a lump of gold as big as my head."

"And the gold?"

"Well, that was my wages for seven years' service."

"You've known how to look after yourself every time," said the grinder. "If you can only get on so far as to hear the money jingle in your pocket whenever you stand up, you'll have made your fortune."

"How shall I manage that?" said Hans.

"You must be a grinder, as I am. Nothing much is needed for it but a grindstone; the rest takes care of itself. I've one here — it's certainly a little worn, but you needn't give me anything for it but your goose. Will you do it?"

"How can you ask?" answered Hans. "I shall be the luckiest fellow on earth. If I have money whenever I put my hand in my pocket, what have I got to worry about ever again?" And he handed over the goose and took the grindstone in exchange.

"Now," said the grinder, picking up an ordinary heavy stone that lay beside him, "here's a good strong stone for you into the bargain. You can hammer away on it and straighten your old nails. Take it with you and look after it carefully."

Hans loaded himself with the stones and went on with a contented heart, his eyes shining with joy. "I must have been born lucky," he cried. "Everything I want happens to me just as if I were a Sunday child."

Meanwhile, as he had been on his legs since daybreak, he began to feel tired. Hunger tormented him too, for in his joy over the bargain that got him the cow he had eaten up his whole store of food at once. At last he could only get along with great difficulty, and had to stop every minute; and the stones weighed him down dreadfully. Then he could not help thinking how nice it would be if he did not have to carry them just now.

He crept like a snail to a well in a field, meaning to rest there and refresh himself with a cool drink of water; and so that he should not damage the stones by sitting down on them, he laid them carefully beside him on the rim of the well. Then he sat down on it, and was going to stoop and drink, when he slipped and knocked against the stones, and both of them fell into the water.

When Hans saw them sinking to the bottom with his own eyes, he jumped for joy; and then knelt down and with tears in his eyes thanked God for having shown him this favour too, and delivered him in such a good way — and without his having anything to reproach himself with — from those heavy stones, which had been the only things troubling him.

"There's no man under the sun as fortunate as I am," he cried out. And with a light heart and free of every burden he ran on until he was home with his mother.

Hans Married

There was once a young peasant named Hans, whose uncle wanted to find him a rich wife. So he sat Hans down behind the stove and had it made very hot. Then he fetched a pot of milk and plenty of white bread, and put a bright new-minted farthing in his hand, and said, "Hans, hold that farthing tight, crumble the white bread into the milk, and stay where you are, and don't stir from that spot till I come back."

"Yes," said Hans, "I'll do all that."

Then the matchmaker put on a pair of old patched trousers, went to a rich farmer's daughter in the next village, and said, "Won't you marry my nephew Hans? You'll get an honest, sensible man who'll suit you well."

The greedy father asked, "How does he stand for means? Has he bread to break?"

"My dear friend," replied the matchmaker, "my young nephew has a snug berth, a nice bit of money in hand, and plenty of bread to break; besides, he has quite as many patches as I have." (And as he said it, he slapped the patches on his trousers — but in that district small pieces of land were called patches too.) "If you'll take the trouble to come home with me, you'll see at once that it's all as I've said."

Then the miser did not want to lose such a good opportunity, and said, "If that's how it is, I have nothing further to say against the marriage."

So the wedding was celebrated on the appointed day; and when the young wife went out of doors to see the bridegroom's property, Hans took off his Sunday coat and put on his patched smock and said, "I might spoil my good coat."

Then they went out together; and wherever a boundary line came into sight, or fields and meadows were divided off from one another, Hans pointed with his finger and then slapped a large or a small patch on his smock and said, "That patch is mine, and that one too, my dearest — just look at it" — meaning by this that his wife should not stand staring at the broad lands, but look at his coat, which was his own.

"And were you at the wedding yourself?"

"Yes, indeed I was there, and in full dress. My headdress was made of snow, and then the sun came out and it melted. My coat was made of cobwebs, and I had to pass some thorns, which tore it off me. My shoes were made of glass, and I knocked against a stone, and they went klink and broke in two."

The Gold-Children

There was once a poor man and a poor woman who had nothing but a little cottage, and who earned their bread by fishing and always lived from hand to mouth.

But one day, as the man was sitting by the water casting his net, he drew out a fish that was made entirely of gold. As he was looking at it, full of astonishment, it began to speak and said, "Listen, fisherman: if you'll throw me back into the water, I'll turn your little hut into a splendid castle."

Then the fisherman answered, "What use is a castle to me if I've nothing to eat?"

The gold fish went on, "That will be taken care of. There will be a cupboard in the castle, and when you open it there will be dishes of the most delicate food, as many of them as you could wish for."

"If that's true," said the man, "then I can certainly do you a favour."

"Yes," said the fish, "but there's one condition: you must not tell a single soul in the world, whoever it may be, where your good luck came from. If you speak so much as one word, it will all be over."

So the man threw the wonderful fish back into the water and went home. But where his hovel had stood there now stood a great castle. He opened his eyes wide, went in, and saw his wife sitting in a splendid room dressed in beautiful clothes, and she was quite delighted, and said, "Husband, how has all this come about? It suits me very well."

"Yes," said the man, "it suits me too; but I'm terribly hungry. Give me something to eat."

Said the wife, "But I've nothing, and I don't know where to find anything in this new house."

"There's no need for you to know," said the man. "I can see a great cupboard over there — just unlock it."

When she opened it, there stood cakes, meat, fruit and wine — a fine prospect indeed.

Then the woman cried joyfully, "What more could you want, my dear?" And they sat down and ate and drank together.

When they had had enough, the woman said, "But husband, where do all these riches come from?"

"Alas," he answered, "don't ask me about that, for I daren't tell you anything. If I tell a single person, all our good fortune will fly away."

"Very good," said she. "If I'm not to know anything, then I don't want to know anything."

But she did not mean it. She gave herself no rest day or night, and she goaded her husband until, out of sheer impatience, he let out that it was all owing to a wonderful golden fish he had caught and given its freedom in return.

And as soon as the secret was out, the splendid castle with its cupboard vanished on the instant; they were back in the old fisherman's hut, and the man had to go back to his old trade and fish.

But fortune would have it that he once more drew out the golden fish. "Listen," said the fish, "if you'll throw me back into the water again, I'll give you the castle a second time, with the cupboard full of roast and boiled meat. Only stand firm — for your life's sake don't tell anybody who you had it from, or you'll lose it all again."

"I'll take good care," answered the fisherman, and threw the fish back into the water.

At home everything was in its old magnificence once more, and the wife was overjoyed at their good fortune. But curiosity left her no peace, so that after a couple of days she began asking again how it had come about and how he had managed to get it. The man kept silent for a while, but at last she made him so angry that he burst out and betrayed the secret. In an instant the castle disappeared and they were back in their old hut.

"Now you've got what you wanted," said he. "And we can go back to gnawing a bare bone."

"Ah," said the woman, "I'd rather have no riches at all than not know where they come from — for then I have no peace."

The man went back to fishing; and after a while he happened to draw out the gold fish for a third time.

"Listen," said the fish, "I can see plainly that I'm fated to fall into your hands. Take me home and cut me into six pieces. Give two of them to your wife to eat, two to your horse, and bury two of them in the ground; and then they'll bring you a blessing."

The fisherman took the fish home with him and did as it had told him. And it came about that from the two pieces buried in the ground two golden lilies sprang up; that the horse had two golden foals; and that the fisherman's wife bore two children who were made entirely of gold.

The children grew up tall and handsome, and the lilies and the horses grew as well. Then they said, "Father, we want to mount our golden horses and travel out into the world."

But he answered sorrowfully, "How shall I bear it, if you go away and I don't know how you're faring?"

Then they said, "The two golden lilies stay here. By them you can see how it is with us. If they're fresh, we're in health; if they wither, we're ill; if they die, then we're dead."

So they rode away and came to an inn where there were a great many people; and when the people saw the gold-children they began to laugh and jeer. When one of the brothers heard the mockery he was ashamed, and would not go out into the world after all, but turned back and went home to his father.

But the other rode on and came to a great forest. As he was about to enter it, the people said, "It isn't safe for you to ride through. The wood is full of robbers who'll treat you badly. You'll come off badly; and when they see that you're all of gold, and your horse too, they'll certainly kill you."

But he would not let himself be frightened, and said, "I must and I will ride through it." So he took bearskins and covered himself and his horse with them, so that the gold could not be seen any more, and rode fearlessly into the forest.

When he had ridden on a little he heard a rustling in the bushes, and heard voices talking together. From one side came cries of, "There's one!" — but from the other, "Let him go, he's an idle fellow, as poor and bare as a church mouse. What should we get out of him?"

So the gold-child rode joyfully through the forest and no harm came to him.

One day he came into a village where he saw a girl so beautiful that he did not believe any more beautiful existed in the world. And as such a mighty love took hold of him, he went up to her and said, "I love you with my whole heart. Will you be my wife?"

He too pleased the girl so much that she agreed, and said, "Yes, I'll be your wife and be true to you my whole life long."

So they were married; and just as they were at the height of their happiness, the bride's father came home; and when he saw that his daughter's wedding was being celebrated he was astonished, and said, "Where is the bridegroom?"

They pointed out the gold-child, who was still wearing his bearskins. Then the father said furiously, "No vagabond shall ever have my daughter!" — and was about to kill him.

Then the bride begged as hard as she could, and said, "He's my husband, and I love him with all my heart" — until at last he let himself be pacified.

All the same the thought never left him; so next morning he got up early, wanting to see whether his daughter's husband was a common ragged beggar. But when he peeped in, he saw a magnificent golden man in the bed, and the cast-off bearskins lying on the floor. Then he went back and thought, "What a good thing I held my anger in. I should have committed a great crime."

But the gold-child dreamed that he rode out to hunt a splendid stag; and when he woke in the morning he said to his wife, "I must go out hunting."

She was uneasy and begged him to stay, and said, "You could easily meet with some great misfortune." But he answered, "I must and I will go."

So he got up and rode out into the forest; and it was not long before a fine stag crossed his path, exactly as in his dream. He took aim and was about to shoot it, when the stag ran off. He chased it over hedges and ditches the whole day without feeling tired; but in the evening the stag vanished from his sight, and when the gold-child looked about him he was standing in front of a little house with a witch in it.

He knocked, and a little old woman came out and asked, "What are you doing so late in the middle of the great forest?"

"Haven't you seen a stag?"

"Yes," she answered, "I know that stag well." And at that a little dog, which had come out of the house with her, barked at the man furiously.

"Will you be quiet, you horrid toad," said he, "or I'll shoot you dead."

Then the witch cried out in a rage, "What? You'd kill my little dog?" — and immediately transformed him, so that he lay there like a stone. And his bride waited for him in vain, and thought, "What I dreaded so much, what lay so heavy on my heart, has come upon him."

But at home the other brother was standing by the golden lilies when one of them suddenly drooped. "Good heavens," said he, "my brother has met with some great misfortune. I must be off and see whether I can rescue him."

Then the father said, "Stay here. If I lose you as well, what shall I do?"

But he answered, "I must and I will go."

Then he mounted his golden horse and rode out and came into the great forest where his brother lay turned to stone. The old witch came out of her house and called to him, meaning to trap him too; but he would not go near her, and said, "I'll shoot you if you don't bring my brother back to life."

Very unwillingly, she touched the stone with her forefinger, and he was restored to his human shape at once. And the two gold-children rejoiced when they saw each other again, and kissed and embraced each other, and rode out of the forest together — the one home to his bride, the other to his father.

The father said, "I knew perfectly well that you had rescued your brother, for the golden lily suddenly stood up and blossomed out again."

And after that they lived happily, and everything went well with them until their deaths.

The Fox and the Geese

The fox once came to a meadow where there was a flock of fine fat geese; and he smiled at them and said, "I've come just in the nick of time. You're all sitting together so beautifully that I can eat you up one after the other."

The geese cackled with terror, sprang up, and began to wail and beg piteously for their lives. But the fox would listen to nothing, and said, "There's no mercy to be had. You must die."

At length one of them took heart and said, "If we poor geese are to give up our strong young lives, do us the one favour that's possible and allow us one last prayer, so that we don't die in our sins. And after that we'll set ourselves in a row, so that you can always pick out the fattest."

"Yes," said the fox, "that's reasonable, and a pious request. Pray away — I'll wait till you've finished."

Then the first began a good long prayer, saying, "Ga! Ga!" over and over; and as she showed no sign of finishing, the second did not wait for her turn but began as well, "Ga! Ga!" The third and the fourth followed her, and soon they were all cackling together.

When they have finished praying, the story shall be carried on further; but at present they are still praying, and have not stopped yet.

The Poor Man and the Rich Man

In the old days, when the Lord himself still walked about this earth among men, it happened once that he was tired and overtaken by darkness before he could reach an inn. Now there stood on the road in front of him two houses facing each other: one large and beautiful, the other small and poor. The large one belonged to a rich man and the small one to a poor man.

Then the Lord thought, "I shan't be any burden to the rich man; I'll spend the night with him."

When the rich man heard somebody knocking at his door, he opened the window and asked the stranger what he wanted. The Lord answered, "I only ask for a night's lodging."

Then the rich man looked the traveller over from head to foot; and as the Lord was wearing common clothes and did not look like somebody with much money in his pocket, he shook his head and said, "No, I can't take you in. My rooms are full of herbs and seeds; and if I were to lodge everybody who knocked at my door, I might soon be out begging myself. Go somewhere else for a lodging." And with that he shut the window and left the Lord standing there.

So the Lord turned his back on the rich man and went across to the small house and knocked. He had hardly done so before the poor man opened his little door and told the traveller to come in. "Spend the night with me," he said. "It's dark already; you can't go any further tonight."

This pleased the Lord, and he went in. The poor man's wife shook hands with him and welcomed him, and said he was to make himself at home and put up with what they had; they had not much to offer him, but what they had they would give him with all their hearts.

Then she put the potatoes on the fire; and while they were boiling she milked the goat, so that they could have a little milk with them. When the cloth was laid, the Lord sat down with the man and his wife, and he enjoyed their coarse food, for there were happy faces at the table.

When they had had supper and it was bedtime, the woman called her husband aside and said, "Listen, dear husband, let's make ourselves up a bed of straw tonight, so that the poor traveller can sleep in our bed and have a good rest. He's been walking the whole day through, and that makes a man weary."

"With all my heart," he answered. "I'll go and offer it to him." And he went to the stranger and invited him, if he had no objection, to sleep in their bed and rest his limbs properly.

The Lord was unwilling to take the two old people's bed from them; but they would not be satisfied until at last he did it, and lay down in their bed, while they lay on some straw on the floor.

Next morning they got up before daybreak and made as good a breakfast as they could for their guest. When the sun shone in through the little window and the Lord had got up, he ate with them again, and then made ready to set out on his journey.

But as he was standing in the doorway he turned round and said, "As you are so kind and good, you may wish three things for yourselves, and I'll grant them."

Then the man said, "What else should I wish for but eternal happiness — and that the two of us, as long as we live, should be healthy and have our daily bread every day? For the third wish, I don't know what to have."

And the Lord said to him, "Will you wish for a new house instead of this old one?"

"Oh, yes," said the man. "If I can have that too, I should like it very much."

And the Lord granted his wish and changed their old house into a new one; and gave them his blessing again, and went on his way.

The sun was high when the rich man got up and leaned out of his window and saw, on the other side of the road, a clean-looking new house with red tiles and bright windows, where the old hut used to be. He was very much astonished, and called his wife and said to her, "Tell me, what can have happened? Last night there was a miserable little hut standing there, and today there's a beautiful new house. Run over and see how that came about."

So his wife went and asked the poor man, and he said to her, "Yesterday evening a traveller came here and asked for a night's lodging; and this morning, when he took his leave of us, he granted us three wishes — eternal happiness, health in this life and our daily bread as well; and besides that, a beautiful new house instead of our old hut."

When the rich man's wife heard this she ran back in haste and told her husband how it had happened. The man said, "I could tear myself to pieces! If only I'd known! That traveller came to our house too and wanted to sleep here, and I sent him away."

"Quick," said his wife, "get on your horse. You can still catch the man up, and then you must ask to have three wishes granted to you."

The rich man took the good advice and galloped off on his horse, and soon caught up with the Lord. He spoke to him softly and pleasantly, and begged him not to take it amiss that he had not let him in straight away; he had been looking for the front-door key, and in the meantime the stranger had gone off. If he came back the same way, he must come and stay with him.

"Yes," said the Lord. "If I ever come back this way, I will."

Then the rich man asked whether he might not wish for three things too, as his neighbour had.

"Yes," said the Lord, he might; but it would not be to his advantage, and he had better not wish for anything.

But the rich man thought he could easily ask for something that would add to his happiness, if only he knew it would be granted. So the Lord said to him, "Ride home, then, and the three wishes you make shall be fulfilled."

The rich man had now got what he wanted, so he rode off home and began to consider what he should wish for. As he was thinking he let the bridle fall, and the horse began to caper about, so that he was constantly interrupted in his thoughts and could not gather them at all. He patted its neck and said, "Gently, Lisa" — but the horse only started new tricks. Then at last he lost his temper and cried out impatiently, "I wish your neck was broken!"

The moment he had said the words the horse dropped to the ground, and there it lay dead and never moved again. And that was his first wish fulfilled.

As he was a miserly man by nature, he did not like to leave the harness lying there; so he cut it off and put it on his back, and now he had to go on foot. "I still have two wishes left," said he, and comforted himself with that.

And now, as he walked slowly through the sand with the sun burning hot at midday, he grew quite hot-tempered and angry. The saddle hurt his back, and he still had no idea what to wish for. "If I were to wish for all the riches and treasures in the world," he said to himself, "I should still think of all kinds of other things later on — I know that beforehand. But I'll manage it so that there's nothing at all left for me to wish for afterwards."

Then he sighed and said, "Ah, if only I were that Bavarian peasant who had three wishes granted him too, and knew perfectly well what to do — and wished first for a great deal of beer, and second for as much beer as he was able to drink, and third for a barrel of beer into the bargain."

Many a time he thought he had hit on it, and then it seemed to him too small after all. And then it came into his mind what an easy life his wife had, staying at home in a cool room and enjoying herself. This really did vex him; and before he knew what he was doing, he said, "I just wish she was sitting there on this saddle and couldn't get off it, instead of my having to drag it along on my back."

And as the last word was spoken the saddle disappeared from his back, and he saw that his second wish had been fulfilled. Then he really did feel hot. He began to run, wanting to be quite alone in his own room at home to think of something really big for his last wish.

But when he got there and opened the parlour door, he saw his wife sitting in the middle of the room on the saddle, crying and complaining and quite unable to get off it.

So he said, "Do bear it, and I'll wish all the riches on earth for you — only stay where you are."

But she called him a fool, and said, "What good will all the riches on earth do me if I have to sit on this saddle? You wished me onto it, so you must help me off."

So, whether he wanted to or not, he was forced to make his third wish that she should be rid of the saddle and able to get off it; and the wish was fulfilled at once.

So he got nothing out of it but vexation and trouble and abuse and the loss of his horse; while the poor people lived happily, quietly and piously until their happy death.

The Singing, Springing Lark

There was once a man who was about to set out on a long journey; and as he was leaving he asked his three daughters what he should bring back for them. The eldest wished for pearls, and the second for diamonds; but the third said, "Dear father, I should like a singing, soaring lark."

The father said, "Yes, if I can get it, you shall have it" — and kissed all three and set out.

Now when the time came for him to be on his way home again, he had bought pearls and diamonds for the two eldest; but he had searched everywhere in vain for a singing, soaring lark for the youngest, and he was very unhappy about it, for she was his favourite child.

Then his road led him through a forest, and in the middle of it stood a splendid castle; and near the castle stood a tree, and right at the top of the tree he saw a singing, soaring lark.

"Aha, you've come just at the right moment," he said, quite delighted, and called to his servant to climb up and catch the little creature. But as he came up to the tree, a lion sprang out from under it, shook himself, and roared until the leaves on the trees trembled.

"Whoever tries to steal my singing, soaring lark," he cried, "I'll devour."

Then the man said, "I didn't know the bird belonged to you. I'll make amends for the wrong I've done and buy myself off with a large sum of money — only spare my life."

The lion said, "Nothing can save you unless you'll promise to give me for my own whatever first meets you when you get home. And if you'll do that, I'll grant you your life, and you shall have the bird for your daughter into the bargain."

But the man hesitated and said, "That might be my youngest daughter. She loves me best and always runs out to meet me when I come home."

The servant, though, was terrified, and said, "Why should it be your daughter who meets you? It could just as easily be a cat or a dog."

So the man let himself be talked round, and took the singing, soaring lark, and promised to give the lion whatever first met him when he got home.

When he reached home and went into his house, the first to meet him was none other than his youngest and dearest daughter, who came running up and kissed and hugged him; and when she saw that he had brought a singing, soaring lark with him she was beside herself with joy.

But her father could not rejoice, and began to weep, and said, "My dearest child, I've bought that little bird dear. To get it, I had to promise you to a savage lion; and when he has you he'll tear you to pieces and devour you." And he told her the whole thing just as it had happened, and begged her not to go, come what might.

But she comforted him and said, "Dearest father, your promise must be kept. I'll go there and soften the lion, so that I come back to you safe."

Next morning she had the road pointed out to her, took her leave, and went fearlessly out into the forest.

The lion, however, was an enchanted prince: by day he was a lion, and all his people were lions with him, but at night they took their natural human shapes again. When she arrived she was kindly received and led into the castle. When night came the lion turned into a handsome man, and their wedding was celebrated with great magnificence. They lived happily together, staying awake at night and sleeping through the day.

One day he came and said, "Tomorrow there's a feast at your father's house, because your eldest sister is to be married. If you'd like to go, my lions shall take you there."

She said, "Yes, I should very much like to see my father again" — and off she went, with the lions for company.

There was great rejoicing when she arrived, for they had all believed that she had been torn to pieces by the lion and had long since stopped living. But she told them what a handsome husband she had and how well off she was, and stayed with them as long as the wedding feast lasted, and then went back to the forest.

When the second daughter was about to be married and she was invited to that wedding too, she said to the lion, "This time I won't go alone. You must come with me."

But the lion said it was too dangerous for him; for if a ray of light from a burning candle fell on him there, he would be changed into a dove and would have to fly about with the doves for seven years.

She said, "Ah, but do come with me. I'll take great care of you and keep you from all light."

So they went off together and took their little child with them as well. She had a room built there, so strong and thick that no ray of light could get through it, and he was to shut himself up in it when the candles were lit for the wedding feast. But the door was made of green wood, which warped and left a little crack that nobody noticed.

The wedding was celebrated with great splendour; but when the procession came back from church with all its candles and torches and passed this room, a ray about the width of a hair fell on the King's son; and the moment it touched him he was transformed. When she came in and looked for him she did not see him, but a white dove was sitting there.

The dove said to her, "For seven years I must fly about the world; but at every seventh step you take, I'll let fall a drop of red blood and a white feather, and those will show you the way; and if you follow the trail you can set me free."

With that the dove flew out at the door, and she followed him; and at every seventh step a red drop of blood and a little white feather fell down and showed her the way.

So she went on and on, further and further into the wide world, never looking about her and never resting; and the seven years were almost up. Then she rejoiced, and thought that they would soon be free — and yet they were far from it.

Once, as they were going on like this, no little feather and no drop of red blood fell; and when she raised her eyes the dove had vanished. And as she thought to herself, "No man can help you in this," she climbed up to the sun and said to him, "You shine into every crevice and over every peak. Haven't you seen a white dove flying?"

"No," said the sun, "I've seen none; but I'll make you a present of this casket. Open it when you're in your greatest need."

Then she thanked the sun and went on until evening came and the moon appeared, and she asked her, "You shine the whole night through, over every field and forest. Haven't you seen a white dove flying?"

"No," said the moon, "I've seen no dove; but here, I'll give you this egg. Break it when you're in great need."

She thanked the moon and went on until the night wind got up and blew on her; and then she said to it, "You blow over every tree and under every leaf. Haven't you seen a white dove flying?"

"No," said the night wind, "I've seen none; but I'll ask the three other winds — perhaps they've seen it."

The east wind and the west wind came, and had seen nothing; but the south wind said, "I've seen the white dove. It has flown to the Red Sea, where it has become a lion again, because the seven years are over; and the lion is there fighting with a dragon — and the dragon is an enchanted princess."

Then the night wind said to her, "I'll give you my advice. Go to the Red Sea; on the right-hand bank there are some tall reeds. Count them, break off the eleventh, and strike the dragon with it; then the lion will be able to overcome it, and the two of them will get their human shapes back. After that, look round and you'll see the griffin that lives by the Red Sea. Swing yourself up onto his back with your beloved, and the bird will carry you home across the sea. And here's a nut for you: when you're above the middle of the sea, let the nut fall. It will shoot up at once, and a tall nut tree will grow out of the water for the griffin to rest on; for if he can't rest, he won't be strong enough to carry you across — and if you forget to throw the nut down, he'll let you fall into the sea."

So she went there and found everything as the night wind had said. She counted the reeds by the sea and cut off the eleventh and struck the dragon with it, whereupon the lion overcame it; and immediately both of them got their human shapes back. But when the princess, who had been the dragon, was released from the enchantment, she took the young man by the arm, seated herself on the griffin, and carried him off with her.

And there stood the poor girl who had wandered so far, deserted all over again. She sat down and cried; but at last she took courage and said, "Still, I'll go as far as the wind blows and as long as the cock crows, until I find him." And she went off along long, long roads, until at last she came to the castle where the two of them were living together.

There she heard that a feast was soon to be held at which they would celebrate their wedding; but she said, "God helps me still" — and opened the casket the sun had given her. Inside lay a dress as brilliant as the sun itself. So she took it out and put it on and went up into the castle, and everybody, even the bride herself, looked at her in astonishment.

The dress pleased the bride so much that she thought it might do for her wedding dress, and asked whether it was for sale.

"Not for money or land," she answered, "but for flesh and blood."

The bride asked her what she meant by that, and she said, "Let me sleep one night in the room where the bridegroom sleeps."

The bride did not want to; but she wanted the dress very much, and at last she consented — but the page was to give the prince a sleeping draught.

So when it was night and the young man was already asleep, she was led into the room. She sat down on the bed and said, "I've followed you for seven years. I've been to the sun and the moon and the four winds asking after you, and I helped you against the dragon. Will you forget me altogether now?"

But the prince slept so soundly that it only seemed to him as if the wind were whistling outside in the fir trees.

So when day broke she was led out again, and had to give up the golden dress. And as that had been no use either, she was sad, and went out into a meadow and sat down and wept.

While she was sitting there she thought of the egg the moon had given her. She opened it, and out came a clucking hen with twelve chicks all of gold, running about and cheeping and creeping back under the old hen's wings; nothing more beautiful was ever seen in the world.

Then she got up and drove them across the meadow in front of her until the bride looked out of the window. The little chicks pleased her so much that she came straight down and asked whether they were for sale.

"Not for money or land, but for flesh and blood. Let me sleep another night in the room where the bridegroom sleeps."

The bride said yes, meaning to cheat her as she had the evening before. But when the prince went to bed he asked the page what the murmuring and rustling in the night had been. At that the page told him everything: that he had been made to give him a sleeping draught because a poor girl had slept secretly in the room, and that he was to give him another one that night.

The prince said, "Pour the draught out beside the bed."

At night she was led in again; and when she began to tell how badly everything had gone with her, he knew his own dear wife at once by her voice, and sprang up and cried, "Now I really am set free! I've been as if in a dream, because that strange princess bewitched me so that I had to forget you; but God has delivered me from the spell in good time."

Then the two of them left the castle secretly in the night, for they were afraid of the princess's father, who was a sorcerer; and they seated themselves on the griffin, which carried them across the Red Sea; and when they were in the middle of it she let the nut fall. At once a tall nut tree grew up, and the bird rested on it, and then carried them home, where they found their child, who had grown tall and beautiful; and from that time on they lived happily until their deaths.

The Goose-Girl

There was once an old Queen whose husband had been dead many years, and she had a beautiful daughter. When the princess grew up she was betrothed to a prince who lived a great way off.

When the time came for her to be married and she had to travel away into that distant kingdom, the old Queen packed up for her a great many costly vessels of silver and gold, and ornaments of gold and silver too, and cups and jewels — in short, everything that belonged to a royal dowry, for she loved her child with all her heart. She sent her waiting maid with her as well, who was to ride beside her and hand her over to the bridegroom; and each of them had a horse for the journey. But the King's daughter's horse was called Falada, and could speak.

So when the hour of parting came, the old mother went into her bedroom, took a little knife and cut her finger with it until it bled; then she held a white handkerchief under it and let three drops of blood fall on it, and gave it to her daughter and said, "Dear child, take good care of this. It will be of service to you on your way."

So they took a sorrowful leave of each other. The princess put the piece of cloth in her bosom, mounted her horse, and set off to her bridegroom.

After she had ridden a while she felt a burning thirst, and said to her waiting maid, "Get down and take my cup, the one you're carrying for me, and fetch me some water from the stream. I should like a drink."

"If you're thirsty," said the waiting maid, "get off your horse yourself and lie down and drink out of the water. I don't choose to be your servant."

So in her great thirst the princess got down, bent over the water in the stream and drank, and was not allowed to drink out of the golden cup. Then she said, "Ah, heaven!" — and the three drops of blood answered:

	"If your mother knew, her heart would break."

But the King's daughter was humble, and said nothing, and got back on her horse.

She rode some miles further; but the day was warm and the sun scorched her, and she was thirsty again; and when they came to a stream she called out to her waiting maid once more, "Get down and give me some water in my golden cup" — for she had long since forgotten the girl's unkind words.

But the waiting maid said, more haughtily still, "If you want to drink, drink as best you can. I don't choose to be your maid."

Then in her great thirst the King's daughter got down, bent over the running stream, wept and said, "Ah, heaven!" — and the drops of blood answered again:

	"If your mother knew, her heart would break."

And as she was drinking and leaning right out over the stream, the handkerchief with the three drops of blood fell out of her bosom and floated away with the water, without her noticing it, so great was her distress. But the waiting maid had seen it, and she rejoiced to think that she now had power over the bride; for now that the princess had lost the drops of blood she had become weak and helpless.

So when she wanted to get back on her horse — the one called Falada — the waiting maid said, "Falada suits me better; my nag will do for you." And the princess had to be content with that.

Then the waiting maid, with a great many hard words, told the princess to change her royal clothes for her own shabby ones; and at last she was made to swear by the clear sky above her that she would not say one word of this to anybody at the royal court. And if she had not sworn that oath, she would have been killed on the spot. But Falada saw it all, and marked it well.

So the waiting maid mounted Falada and the true bride the poor horse, and they travelled on until at last they came to the royal palace. There were great rejoicings over her arrival, and the prince sprang forward to meet her and lifted the waiting maid down from her horse, believing that she was his bride. She was led up the stairs; but the real princess was left standing below.

Then the old King looked out of the window and saw her standing in the courtyard, and saw how dainty and delicate and beautiful she was; and he went at once up to the royal apartment and asked the bride about the girl she had brought with her, who was standing down there in the courtyard, and who she was.

"I picked her up on the way, for company. Give the girl some work to do, so that she isn't standing about idle."

But the old King had no work for her and could think of none, so he said, "I have a little boy who looks after the geese. She can help him."

The boy was called Conrad, and the true bride had to help him look after the geese.

Soon afterwards the false bride said to the young King, "Dearest husband, I beg you to do me a favour."

He answered, "I'll do it most willingly."

"Then send for the knacker and have the head cut off the horse I rode here on. It vexed me on the way."

In truth she was afraid the horse might tell how she had treated the King's daughter. And she managed to get the King to promise that it should be done, and faithful Falada was to die.

This came to the real princess's ears, and she secretly promised the knacker a piece of gold if he would do her a small service. There was a great dark gateway in the town through which she had to pass with the geese every morning and evening; would he be so good as to nail Falada's head up on it, so that she might see him again, more than just once?

The knacker's man promised to do it, and cut off the head and nailed it fast under the dark gateway.

Early in the morning, when she and Conrad drove their flock out under this gateway, she said as she passed:

	"Alas, Falada, hanging there!"

Then the head answered:

	"Alas, young Queen, how ill you fare!
	If this your tender mother knew,
	her heart would surely break in two."

Then they went on out of the town and drove their geese into the country. And when they came to the meadow she sat down and unbound her hair, which was like pure gold; and Conrad saw it and was delighted by its brightness, and wanted to pull out a few hairs. Then she said:

	"Blow, blow, you gentle wind, I say,
	blow Conrad's little hat away,
	and make him chase it here and there
	until I have braided all my hair
	and bound it up again."

And there came such a violent gust of wind that it blew Conrad's hat far away across the country, and he had to run after it. When he came back she had finished combing her hair and was putting it up again, and he could not get a single hair of it. So Conrad was angry and would not speak to her; and they watched the geese until evening, and then went home.

Next day, as they were driving the geese out through the dark gateway, the girl said:

	"Alas, Falada, hanging there!"

And Falada answered:

	"Alas, young Queen, how ill you fare!
	If this your tender mother knew,
	her heart would surely break in two."

And she sat down again in the field and began to comb out her hair, and Conrad ran up and tried to snatch at it; so she said quickly:

	"Blow, blow, you gentle wind, I say,
	blow Conrad's little hat away,
	and make him chase it here and there
	until I have braided all my hair
	and bound it up again."

Then the wind blew and blew his little hat off his head and far away, and Conrad had to run after it; and when he came back her hair had been up a long while, and he could get none of it. And so they looked after their geese till evening came.

But that evening, after they had got home, Conrad went to the old King and said, "I won't look after the geese with that girl any longer."

"Why not?" asked the old King.

"Oh, because she vexes me the whole day long."

Then the old King ordered him to tell what it was that she did to him. And Conrad said, "In the morning, when we go under the dark gateway with the flock, there's a sorry old horse's head on the wall, and she says to it, 'Alas, Falada, hanging there!' — and the head answers, 'Alas, young Queen, how ill you fare! If this your tender mother knew, her heart would surely break in two.'"

And Conrad went on to tell what happened out on the goose pasture, and how he had to chase his hat there.

The old King told him to drive his flock out again next day; and as soon as morning came he stationed himself behind the dark gateway and heard how the girl spoke to Falada's head. And then he went out into the country too and hid himself in a thicket in the meadow. There he soon saw with his own eyes the goose-girl and the goose-boy bringing their flock, and how after a while she sat down and unplaited her hair, which shone with a radiance of its own. And soon she said:

	"Blow, blow, you gentle wind, I say,
	blow Conrad's little hat away,
	and make him chase it here and there
	until I have braided all my hair
	and bound it up again."

Then came a gust of wind and carried off Conrad's hat, so that he had to run a long way after it, while the girl quietly went on combing and plaiting her hair; and the King saw it all.

Then he went away unseen; and when the goose-girl came home in the evening he called her aside and asked why she did all these things.

"I may not tell you that, and I dare not pour out my sorrows to any human being; for I've sworn not to, by the heaven above me. If I hadn't sworn it, I should have lost my life."

He pressed her and gave her no peace, but he could get nothing out of her. So he said, "If you won't tell me anything, then tell your sorrows to that iron stove there" — and went away.

Then she crept into the iron stove and began to weep and lament and empty out her whole heart, and said, "Here I am, deserted by the whole world, and yet I'm a King's daughter; and a false waiting maid has forced me to such a pass that I've had to take off my royal clothes, and she has taken my place with my bridegroom, and I have to do servant's work as a goose-girl. If my mother only knew, her heart would break."

But the old King was standing outside by the stovepipe, listening to what she said, and heard it all. Then he came back in and told her to come out of the stove. And royal clothes were put on her, and it was a marvel how beautiful she was.

The old King called his son and told him that he had got the false bride, who was only a waiting maid, and that the true one was standing there — the girl who had been the goose-girl. The young King rejoiced with all his heart when he saw her beauty and her youth; and a great feast was prepared, to which all the people and all their good friends were invited.

At the head of the table sat the bridegroom, with the King's daughter on one side of him and the waiting maid on the other; but the waiting maid was blinded, and did not recognise the princess in her dazzling clothes.

When they had eaten and drunk and were merry, the old King put a riddle to the waiting maid: what did a person deserve who had behaved in such and such a way to her mistress? And he told the whole story, and asked what sentence such a one deserved.

Then the false bride said, "She deserves no better than to be stripped naked and put in a barrel studded on the inside with pointed nails; and two white horses should be harnessed to it and drag her along through one street after another until she is dead."

"That is you," said the old King, "and you have pronounced your own sentence; and that is what shall be done to you."

And when the sentence had been carried out, the young King married his true bride, and the two of them ruled over their kingdom in peace and happiness.

The Young Giant

Once upon a time a countryman had a son who was no bigger than a thumb, and did not get any bigger, and for several years did not grow so much as a hair's breadth.

Once when the father was going out to plough, the little one said, "Father, I'll come out with you."

"You'd come out with me?" said his father. "Stay here. You'll be no use out there — and besides, you might get lost."

Then Thumbling began to cry; and for the sake of peace his father put him in his pocket and took him along. When he got out into the field he took him out again and set him down in a freshly cut furrow.

While he was sitting there, a great giant came over the hill. "Do you see that big bogeyman?" said his father, wanting to frighten the little fellow into being good. "He's coming to fetch you."

But the giant had hardly taken two steps with his long legs before he was at the furrow. He picked little Thumbling up carefully between two fingers, looked him over, and went off with him without saying a word. His father stood there, but could not utter a sound for terror, and thought nothing else but that his child was lost, and that as long as he lived he would never set eyes on him again.
