The giant, though, carried him home and nursed him; and Thumbling grew tall and strong after the fashion of giants.

When two years had gone by, the old giant took him into the forest to try him out, and said, "Pull yourself up a stick."

By then the boy was already so strong that he tore a young tree out of the earth by the roots. But the giant thought, "We must do better than that" — and took him back and nursed him another two years.

When he tried him then, his strength had grown so much that he could tear an old tree out of the ground. That was still not enough for the giant; he nursed him for two years more, and then when he took him into the forest and said, "Now tear me up a proper stick," the boy tore the strongest oak tree out of the earth so that it split — and it was a mere trifle to him.

"That will do," said the giant. "You're finished now" — and took him back to the field he had brought him from.

His father was there, following the plough. The young giant went up to him and said, "Does my father see what a fine man his son has grown into?"

The farmer was alarmed and said, "No, you're not my son. I don't want you — get away from me!"

"But I truly am your son. Let me do your work; I can plough as well as you — better, in fact."

"No, no, you're not my son, and you can't plough. Go away!"

But as he was afraid of this huge man, he let go of the plough and stepped back and stood at the edge of the field. Then the young man took the plough and just pressed on it with one hand; but his grip was so strong that the plough went deep into the earth.

The farmer could not bear to see that, and called out to him, "If you're set on ploughing, you mustn't press so hard. That makes bad work."

But the young man unharnessed the horses and pulled the plough himself, saying, "Just go home, father, and tell my mother to get ready a large dish of food; and meanwhile I'll go over the field."

So the farmer went home and told his wife to prepare the food, while the young man ploughed the field, which was two acres, entirely on his own; and then he harnessed himself to the harrow and harrowed the whole of the land, using two harrows at once.

When he had finished he went into the forest and pulled up two oak trees and laid them across his shoulders, and hung one harrow on them behind and one in front, and one horse behind and one in front too, and carried the lot to his parents' house as if it were a bundle of straw.

When he came into the yard his mother did not know him, and asked, "Who is that horrible tall man?"

The farmer said, "That's our son."

She said, "No, that can't be our son. We never had a tall one; ours was a little thing." And she called out to him, "Go away — we don't want you!"

The young man said nothing, but led his horses to the stable and gave them oats and hay and everything they needed. When he had done that, he went into the parlour, sat down on the bench and said, "Mother, now I should like something to eat. Will it be ready soon?"

Then she said yes, and brought in two enormous dishes full of food, which would have been enough for her and her husband for a week. But the young man ate the whole of it himself, and asked whether she had nothing more to set in front of him.

"No," she replied, "that's all we have."

"But that was only a taste. I must have more."

She did not dare oppose him, and went and put a huge cauldron of food on the fire; and when it was ready she carried it in.

"At last, a few crumbs," said he, and ate everything there was — and it still was not enough to satisfy his hunger.

Then he said, "Father, I can see plainly that with you I shall never get enough to eat. If you'll get me an iron staff that's strong, one I can't break across my knees, I'll go out into the world."

The farmer was glad, and put his two horses in his cart and fetched from the smith a staff so large and thick that the two horses could only just bring it away. The young man laid it across his knees and — snap! — broke it in two in the middle like a beanstalk, and threw it away.

Then his father harnessed four horses and brought a bar so long and thick that the four horses could only just drag it. His son snapped that across his knees too, threw it away, and said, "Father, this is no use to me. You must harness more horses and bring a stronger staff."

So the father harnessed eight horses and brought one so long and thick that the eight horses could only just carry it. But when his son took it in his hand he broke a bit off the top of it as well, and said, "Father, I can see that you won't be able to get me the sort of staff I want. I'll stay with you no longer."

So he went away and gave out that he was a smith's apprentice. He came to a village where there lived a smith who was a greedy fellow and never did anybody a kindness, but wanted everything for himself. The young man went into the smithy and asked whether he needed a journeyman.

"Yes," said the smith, and looked him over, and thought, "There's a strong fellow who will strike out well and earn his bread." So he asked, "How much wages do you want?"

"I don't want any at all," he replied. "Only, every fortnight, when the other journeymen are paid, I'll give you two blows, and you must bear them."

The miser was heartily satisfied, and thought he would save a lot of money that way.

Next morning the new journeyman was to start work; but when the master brought the glowing bar and the young man struck his first blow, the iron flew apart and the anvil sank so deep into the earth that there was no getting it out again.

Then the miser grew angry and said, "Oh, but I can make no use of you. You strike far too hard. What will you have for the one blow?"

Then he said, "I'll only give you quite a small blow, that's all." And he raised his foot and gave him such a kick that he flew away over four loads of hay. Then he picked out the thickest iron bar in the smithy for himself, took it in his hand for a walking stick, and went on his way.

When he had walked some time he came to a small farm, and asked the bailiff whether he did not need a head servant.

"Yes," said the bailiff, "I can make use of one. You look a strong fellow who can do something. How much a year do you want in wages?"

He answered again that he wanted no wages at all, but that every year he would give him three blows, which he must bear. The bailiff was satisfied with that, for he too was a covetous man.

Next morning all the servants were to go into the wood; the others were already up, but the head servant was still in bed. Then one of them called to him, "Get up, it's time. We're going into the wood and you must come with us."

"Ah," said he, quite roughly and surlily, "you go on, then. I'll be back again before any of you."

So the others went to the bailiff and told him the head man was still lying in bed and would not go into the wood with them. The bailiff said they were to wake him again and tell him to harness the horses. But the head man said as before, "Just go on, I'll be back again before any of you." And then he stayed in bed two hours longer.

At length he got out of the feathers; but first he fetched himself two bushels of peas from the loft and made himself some broth with them, and ate it at his leisure; and when that was done he went and harnessed the horses and drove into the wood.

Not far from the wood there was a ravine he had to pass through; so he first drove the horses on through it, and then stopped them and went round behind the cart and took trees and brushwood and made a great barricade, so that no horse could get through.

As he was going into the wood, the others were just driving out of it with their loaded carts to go home; so he said to them, "Drive on. I shall still get home before you do."

He did not drive far into the wood, but immediately tore up two of the very largest trees of all and threw them on his cart and turned round. When he came to the barricade the others were still standing there, unable to get through.

"Don't you see," said he, "that if you'd stayed with me you'd have got home just as fast, and had another hour's sleep besides?"

Now he wanted to drive on, but his horses could not work their way through; so he unharnessed them and laid them on top of the cart, took the shafts in his own hands and pulled the whole lot through — and did it as easily as if it had been loaded with feathers.

When he was over he said to the others, "There, you see — I've got through quicker than you." And he drove on, and the others had to stay where they were.

In the yard he took one of the trees in his hand and showed it to the bailiff and said, "Isn't that a fine bundle of firewood?"

Then the bailiff said to his wife, "That servant is a good one. Even if he does sleep late, he's still home before the others."

So he served the bailiff for a year; and when the year was up and the other servants were getting their wages, he said it was time for him to take his too.

But the bailiff was afraid of the blows he was to be given, and earnestly begged to be let off them; sooner than that, he said, he would be head servant himself and the young man should be bailiff.

"No," said he. "I won't be a bailiff. I'm head servant and I'll stay head servant; but I'll deliver what we agreed on."

The bailiff was willing to give him anything he asked, but it was no use; the head servant said no to everything. Then the bailiff did not know what to do, and begged for a fortnight's grace, for he wanted to find some way out. The head servant agreed to the delay.

The bailiff called all his clerks together, and they were to think it over and give him their advice. The clerks pondered a long time, but at last they said that nobody's life was safe with the head servant, since he could kill a man as easily as a midge; and that the bailiff ought to make him go down the well and clean it, and when he was down at the bottom they would roll up one of the millstones lying there and drop it on his head, and then he would never come up to daylight again.

The advice pleased the bailiff, and the head servant was perfectly willing to go down the well. But when he was standing at the bottom, and they had rolled the biggest millstone down and thought they had broken his skull, he called up, "Chase those hens away from the well! They're scratching in the sand up there and throwing the grains into my eyes, so that I can't see."

So the bailiff cried, "Shoo, shoo!" and pretended to be frightening the hens away.

When the head servant had finished his work he climbed up and said, "Just look what a beautiful necktie I've got on" — and behold, it was the millstone he was wearing round his neck.

Now the head servant wanted to take his reward; but the bailiff begged for another fortnight's grace. The clerks met again and advised him to send the head servant to the haunted mill to grind corn by night, since from there no man had ever yet come back alive in the morning.

The proposal pleased the bailiff. He called the head servant that very evening and told him to take eight bushels of corn to the mill and grind it that night, because it was wanted.

So the head servant went to the loft and put two bushels in his right pocket and two in his left, and took four in a bag, half on his back and half on his chest, and went off to the haunted mill loaded like that.

The miller told him that he could grind there very well by day, but not by night, because the mill was haunted, and that up to now whoever went into it by night had been found lying dead inside in the morning.

He said, "I'll manage it. Just go off to bed."

Then he went into the mill and poured out the corn. About eleven o'clock he went into the miller's room and sat down on the bench. When he had sat there a while, a door suddenly opened and a great table came in; and wine and roast meats set themselves out on the table, and plenty of other good food besides — but everything came by itself, for there was nobody there to carry it. After that the chairs pushed themselves up, but no people came; until all at once he saw fingers, which handled knives and forks and laid food on the plates, but apart from that he could see nothing.

As he was hungry and saw the food, he sat down at the table too, and ate with those who were eating, and enjoyed it. When he had had enough, and the others had emptied their dishes too, he distinctly heard all the candles being suddenly snuffed out; and as it was now pitch dark, he felt something like a box on the ear.

Then he said, "If anything of that sort comes again, I shall hit back."

And when he got a second box on the ear, he hit back too. And so it went on the whole night through. He took nothing without returning it, but paid everything back with interest, and did not lay about him for nothing. At daybreak it all stopped.

When the miller got up he went to look for him and wondered whether he was still alive. Then the young man said, "I've eaten my fill, and I got a few boxes on the ears — but I gave some back."

The miller rejoiced, and said that the mill was released from its spell now, and wanted to give him a great deal of money as a reward. But he said, "Money I won't have. I have enough of it."

So he took his meal on his back and went home, and told the bailiff that he had done what he had been told to do, and would now have the reward they had agreed on.

When the bailiff heard that, he was seriously alarmed and quite beside himself. He walked up and down the room, and the sweat ran down his forehead in drops. Then he opened the window to get some fresh air; but before he knew what was happening, the head servant had given him such a kick that he flew out through the window into the air, and so far away that nobody ever saw him again.

Then the head servant said to the bailiff's wife, "If he doesn't come back, you must take the other blow."

She cried, "No, no, I can't bear it!" — and opened the other window, because the sweat was running down her forehead in drops. Then he gave her such a kick that she flew out too; and as she was lighter, she went much higher than her husband.

Her husband called, "Do come over to me!" — but she answered, "You come to me. I can't come to you."

And they hovered about up there in the air and could not get to each other; and whether they are still hovering about or not, I don't know. But the young giant picked up his iron bar and went on his way.

The Gnome

There was once a rich King who had three daughters, and they went walking every day in the palace garden. The King was a great lover of fine trees of all kinds; but there was one he was so fond of that if anybody picked an apple from it he wished them a hundred fathoms underground. And when harvest time came the apples on this tree were all as red as blood.

The three daughters went under the tree every day and looked to see whether the wind had blown an apple down; but they never once found one, and the tree was so loaded that it was almost breaking, and the branches hung down to the ground.

Then the King's youngest child had a great longing for an apple, and said to her sisters, "Our father loves us far too much to wish us underground. It's my belief that he'd only do that to strangers." And while she was speaking, the child plucked off a great big apple and ran to her sisters, saying, "Just taste it, my dear little sisters — I've never in my life tasted anything so delicious."

Then the two other sisters ate some of the apple too, whereupon all three sank deep down into the earth, where they could hear no cock crow.

When midday came the King wanted to call them in to dinner, but they were nowhere to be found. He looked for them everywhere in the palace and the garden, but could not find them. Then he was greatly distressed, and proclaimed throughout the land that whoever brought his daughters back should have one of them for a wife.

At this so many young men went about the country searching that there was no counting them, for everybody loved the three children, they were so kind to all and so fair of face.

Three young huntsmen went out too; and when they had travelled about for eight days they came to a great castle with beautiful rooms in it; and in one room a table was laid with delicate dishes on it, still so warm that they were steaming — but in the whole castle there was not a human being to be seen or heard. They waited there half a day, and the food stayed warm and steaming; and at length they were so hungry that they sat down and ate.

And they agreed with each other that they would stay and live in that castle, and that one of them, chosen by lot, should stay in the house while the other two went to look for the King's daughters. They cast lots, and the lot fell on the eldest.

So next day the two younger went out searching and the eldest had to stay at home. At midday a very small little man came and begged for a piece of bread; so the huntsman took the bread he had found there and cut a round off the loaf and was about to give it to him. But as he was handing it over, the little man let it fall, and asked the huntsman to be so good as to give him that piece back. The huntsman was about to do it and stooped down — whereupon the little man took a stick, seized him by the hair and gave him a good beating.

Next day the second stayed at home, and he fared no better. When the other two came back in the evening the eldest said, "Well, how did you get on?"

"Oh, very badly," said he. And then they lamented their misfortune together; but they said nothing about it to the youngest, for they did not like him at all, and always called him Stupid Hans, because he did not really belong to the forest.

On the third day the youngest stayed at home, and again the little man came and begged for a piece of bread. When the young man gave it to him he let it fall as before, and asked him to be so good as to give him that piece back.

Then Hans said to the little man, "What? Can't you pick that piece up yourself? If you won't take that much trouble for your daily bread, you don't deserve to have it."

Then the little man grew very angry and said he was to do it; but the huntsman would not, and took hold of my fine little man and gave him a thorough beating. Then the little man screamed terribly and cried, "Stop, stop, and let me go, and I'll tell you where the King's daughters are."

When Hans heard that he left off beating him; and the little man told him that he was an earth gnome, and that there were more than a thousand like him, and that if Hans would come with him he would show him where the King's daughters were.

Then he showed him a deep well with no water in it. And the gnome said he knew very well that the companions Hans had with him did not mean to deal honourably with him; so if he wanted to deliver the King's children he must do it alone. The other two brothers would be very glad to get the King's daughters back, but they did not want any trouble or danger. So Hans was to take a large basket, and get into it with his short sword and a bell, and be let down. Down below there were three rooms, and in each of them was a princess with a many-headed dragon whose heads she had to comb and dress; and he must cut them off.

And having said all this, the gnome vanished.

When evening came the two brothers arrived and asked how he had got on; and he said, "Well enough so far" — and that he had seen nobody except at midday, when a little man had come and begged for a piece of bread; and that he had given him some, but the little man had let it fall and asked him to pick it up again, and as he did not choose to do that, the fellow had lost his temper; and that he had done what he ought not, and given him a beating — whereupon he had told him where the King's daughters were.

The two were so angry at this that they turned green and yellow.

Next morning they went to the well together and drew lots for who should get into the basket first, and again the lot fell on the eldest, and he had to get in and take the bell with him. Then he said, "If I ring, you must draw me up again at once."

When he had gone down a short way he rang, and they drew him up again immediately. Then the second got into the basket, but he did exactly the same as the first. And then it was the youngest's turn, and he let himself be lowered right to the bottom.

When he had got out of the basket he took his short sword, and went and stood outside the first door and listened, and heard the dragon snoring loudly. He opened the door slowly; and there sat one of the princesses with nine dragons' heads lying in her lap, combing them. Then he took his sword and hacked at them, and the nine heads fell off. The princess sprang up and threw her arms round his neck and hugged and kissed him again and again, and took her bodice, which was made of pure gold, and hung it round his neck.

Then he went to the second princess, who had a dragon with five heads to comb, and delivered her too; and to the youngest, who had a dragon with four heads, he went likewise. And they were all overjoyed, and hugged him and kissed him without stopping.

Then he rang very loudly, so that the men above heard him; and he put the princesses one after the other into the basket and had them all drawn up. But when it came to his own turn he remembered the gnome's words, that his comrades did not mean well by him. So he took a great stone that was lying there and put it in the basket; and when it was about halfway up his false brothers cut the rope, so that the basket with the stone fell to the ground. They thought he was dead, and ran off with the three princesses, making them promise to tell their father that it was they who had rescued them; and then they went to the King, and each of them demanded a princess in marriage.

Meanwhile the youngest huntsman was wandering about the three chambers in great distress, fully expecting to end his days down there, when he saw a flute hanging on the wall. "Why are you hanging there?" said he. "Nobody can be merry here." He looked at the dragons' heads too and said, "You can't help me now either."

He walked backwards and forwards for such a long time that he wore the floor quite smooth. But at last other thoughts came into his mind, and he took the flute down from the wall and played a few notes on it; and suddenly a number of gnomes appeared, and with every note he sounded one more came. Then he played until the room was completely full of them. They all asked what he wanted; so he said he wanted to get above ground, back to the daylight. At that they seized him by every hair on his head, and flew up with him onto the earth again.

When he was above ground he went straight to the King's palace, just as the wedding of one of the princesses was about to be celebrated, and went to the room where the King and his three daughters were. When the princesses saw him they fainted. At this the King was angry and ordered him to be put in prison at once, because he thought he must have done the girls some harm.

When the princesses came to themselves, though, they begged the King to set him free again. The King asked why, and they said they were not allowed to tell that; but their father said they were to tell it to the stove. And he went out and listened at the door and heard everything.

Then he had the two brothers hanged on the gallows, and gave the third his youngest daughter. And on that occasion I wore a pair of glass shoes, and I struck them against a stone, and they went klink and broke.

The King of the Golden Mountain

There was once a merchant who had two children, a boy and a girl; they were both little, and could not walk yet. And two richly laden ships of his sailed out to sea with all his property on board; and just as he was expecting to make a great deal of money by them, news came that they had gone to the bottom. So now, instead of being a rich man, he was a poor one, and had nothing left but one field outside the town.

To drive his misfortune a little out of his mind he went out to this field; and as he was walking up and down in it, a little black man suddenly stood beside him and asked why he was so sad, and what it was he was taking so much to heart.

Then said the merchant, "If you could help me, I'd gladly tell you."

"Who knows?" replied the black dwarf. "Perhaps I can help you."

So the merchant told him that everything he had owned had gone to the bottom of the sea, and that he had nothing left but this field.

"Don't trouble yourself," said the dwarf. "If you'll promise to give me the first thing that rubs against your leg when you get home, and to bring it here to this spot in twelve years' time, you shall have as much money as you like."

The merchant thought, "What can that be but my dog?" — and did not remember his little boy; so he said yes, and gave the black man a written and sealed promise, and went home.

When he reached home, his little boy was so delighted that he held on to a bench and tottered over to him and caught him tight by the legs. The father was horrified, for he remembered his promise and now knew what he had pledged himself to do. But as he still found no money in his chest, he thought the dwarf had only been joking.

A month afterwards he went up to the attic, meaning to collect some old tin and sell it, and saw a great heap of money lying there. Then he was happy again, and made purchases, and became a greater merchant than before, and felt that this world was well governed.

Meanwhile the boy grew tall, and sharp and clever with it. But the nearer the twelfth year came, the more anxious the merchant grew, so that his distress could be read in his face. One day his son asked what was the matter with him, but his father would not say. The boy, though, kept on so long that at last he told him: that without knowing what he was doing he had promised him to a black dwarf, and been given a great deal of money for it. He said too that he had set his hand and seal to it, and that now the twelve years had gone by he would have to give him up.

Then his son said, "Oh, father, don't be uneasy. It will all go well. The black man has no power over me."

The son had himself blessed by the priest; and when the time came, father and son went out to the field together, and the son drew a circle and placed himself inside it with his father.

Then the black dwarf came and said to the old man, "Have you brought what you promised me?"

He was silent; but the son asked, "What do you want here?"

Then said the black dwarf, "I have to speak with your father, not with you."

The son replied, "You cheated and misled my father. Give back the writing."

"No," said the black dwarf, "I won't give up my rights."

They argued together a long while after that; but at last they agreed that the son, since he belonged neither to the enemy of mankind nor to his father any longer, should seat himself in a little boat on water that was flowing away from them, and that the father should push it off with his own foot, and then the son should be left given up to the water.

So he took leave of his father and got into a little boat, and the father had to push it off with his own foot. The boat capsized, so that the keel was uppermost; and the father believed his son was lost, and went home and mourned for him.

But the boat did not sink. It floated quietly away with the boy sitting safely inside it, and it floated on for a long time until at last it came to rest on an unknown shore. Then he landed, and saw a beautiful castle in front of him, and set out towards it.

But when he went in, he found that it was under a spell. He went through every room, and they were all empty until he reached the last, where a snake lay coiled in a ring. The snake, though, was an enchanted girl, who rejoiced to see him, and said, "Have you come, my deliverer? I've been waiting twelve years for you. This kingdom is under a spell and you must set it free."

"How can I do that?" he asked.

"Tonight twelve black men covered with chains will come and ask what you're doing here. Keep silent; give them no answer, and let them do whatever they like with you. They'll torment you, beat you, stab you; let it all pass, only don't speak. At twelve o'clock they must go away again. On the second night twelve others will come, and on the third four-and-twenty, who will cut off your head; but at twelve o'clock their power will be over. And then, if you've endured it all and haven't spoken the slightest word, I shall be released. I'll come to you, and I'll have some of the water of life in a bottle. I'll rub you with it, and then you'll come back to life and be as well as before."

Then he said, "I'll gladly set you free."

And everything happened just as she had said. The black men could not force a single word out of him; and on the third night the snake became a beautiful princess, who came with the water of life and brought him back to life again. So she threw herself into his arms and kissed him, and there was joy and gladness in the whole castle. After this their marriage was celebrated, and he was King of the Golden Mountain.

They lived very happily together, and the Queen bore a fine boy. Eight years had gone by when the King's thoughts turned to his father; his heart was moved, and he wanted to visit him. The Queen, though, would not let him go, and said, "I know beforehand that it will bring me unhappiness." But he gave her no rest until she agreed.

At their parting she gave him a wishing ring and said, "Take this ring and put it on your finger, and then you'll be carried at once wherever you want to be. Only you must promise me not to use it to wish me away from this place and to your father."

He promised her that, put the ring on his finger, and wished himself home, just outside the town where his father lived. Instantly he was there, and made for the town; but when he came to the gate the sentries would not let him in, because his clothes were so strange, and yet so rich and magnificent. So he went to a hill where a shepherd was watching his sheep, and changed clothes with him and put on his old shepherd's coat, and then went into the town without any trouble.

When he came to his father he made himself known to him; but his father did not in the least believe that the shepherd was his son, and said that he certainly had had a son, but that he had died long ago. Still, as he could see he was a poor, needy shepherd, he would give him something to eat.

Then the shepherd said to his parents, "I truly am your son. Don't you know of any mark on my body that you could recognise me by?"

"Yes," said his mother, "our son had a raspberry mark under his right arm."

He pushed his shirt back, and they saw the raspberry mark under his right arm, and doubted no longer that he was their son.

Then he told them that he was King of the Golden Mountain, and that a king's daughter was his wife, and that they had a fine son of seven years old.

Then his father said, "That certainly isn't true. A fine sort of king, who goes about in a ragged shepherd's coat!"

At this the son flew into a temper, and without thinking of his promise turned his ring round and wished both his wife and his child there with him. They were there in a second; but the Queen wept and reproached him and said that he had broken his word and brought misfortune on her.

He said, "I did it thoughtlessly, and not with any bad intention" — and tried to calm her; and she pretended to believe him, but she had mischief in her mind.

Then he led her out of the town into the field and showed her the stream where the little boat had been pushed off; and then he said, "I'm tired. Sit down; I'll sleep a while on your lap." And he laid his head on her lap and fell asleep.

When he was asleep she first drew the ring off his finger; then she drew away the foot that was under him, leaving only the slipper behind her; and she took her child in her arms and wished herself back in her own kingdom.

When he woke, there he lay, quite deserted; his wife and child were gone, and so was the ring from his finger, and only the slipper was still there as a token.

"You can't go home to your parents," he thought. "They'd say you were a wizard. You must be off, and walk on until you come to your own kingdom."

So he went away, and came at length to a hill where three giants were standing, arguing with each other because they did not know how to divide their father's property. When they saw him going by they called to him and said that little men had quick wits, and he was to divide their inheritance for them.

The inheritance consisted of a sword, which had the property that if anybody took it in his hand and said, "All heads off but mine," every head would fall to the ground; secondly, of a cloak that made whoever put it on invisible; and thirdly, of a pair of boots that could carry the wearer wherever he wanted in a moment.

He said, "Give me the three things, so that I can see whether they're still in good order."

They gave him the cloak; and when he had put it on he was invisible and had changed into a fly. Then he took his own form again and said, "The cloak's a good one. Now give me the sword."

They said, "No, we won't give you that. If you were to say, 'All heads off but mine,' all our heads would be off and you alone would be left with yours."

All the same they gave it to him, on condition that he only tried it on a tree. He did that, and the sword cut a tree trunk in two as if it had been a straw.

Then he wanted the boots as well; but they said, "No, we won't give you those. If you had them on your feet and wished yourself at the top of the hill, we should be left down here with nothing."

"Oh, no," said he, "I won't do that." So they gave him the boots too.

And now, when he had got all three things, he thought of nothing but his wife and his child, and said as if to himself, "Oh, if I were only on the Golden Mountain" — and at that same moment he vanished from the giants' sight; and so their inheritance was divided.

When he was near his palace he heard sounds of rejoicing, and fiddles and flutes; and the people told him that his wife was celebrating her wedding with another man. Then he flew into a rage and said, "False woman — she betrayed and deserted me while I was asleep."

So he put on his cloak and went into the palace, unseen by anybody. When he came into the dining hall a great table was spread with delicious food, and the guests were eating and drinking and laughing and joking. She sat on a royal seat in the middle of them in splendid clothes, with a crown on her head.

He placed himself behind her, and nobody saw him. When she put a piece of meat on a plate for herself, he took it away and ate it; and when she poured herself out a glass of wine, he took it away and drank it. She kept helping herself to something and never got anything, for plate and glass disappeared at once.

Then, dismayed and ashamed, she got up and went to her room and wept; but he followed her there.

She said, "Has the devil power over me — or did my deliverer never come?"

Then he struck her in the face and said, "Did your deliverer never come? It's he who has you in his power, traitor. Have I deserved this from you?"

Then he made himself visible and went into the hall and cried, "The wedding is over. The true King has come back."

The kings and princes and councillors who were gathered there jeered at him and mocked him; but he did not trouble to answer them, and said, "Will you go, or not?"

At this they tried to seize him and pressed in on him; but he drew his sword and said, "All heads off but mine" — and all the heads rolled on the ground, and he alone was master, and King of the Golden Mountain once more.

The Raven

There was once a Queen who had a little daughter, still so young that she had to be carried. One day the child was naughty, and her mother could say what she liked but the child would not be quiet. Then she lost patience; and as the ravens were flying about the palace, she opened the window and said, "I wish you were a raven and would fly away — then I should have some peace."

She had hardly spoken the words before the child was changed into a raven, and flew out of her arms and out of the window. It flew into a dark forest and stayed there a long time, and the parents heard nothing of their child.

Then one day a man was making his way through this forest and heard the raven calling, and followed the voice; and when he came nearer, the bird said, "I'm a king's daughter by birth, and I'm under a spell; but you can set me free."

"What am I to do?" he asked.

She said, "Go further into the forest and you'll find a house with an old woman sitting in it, who'll offer you food and drink; but you mustn't take anything, for if you eat or drink anything you'll fall asleep, and then you won't be able to deliver me. In the garden behind the house there's a great heap of tanbark; stand on that and wait for me. For three days I'll come every afternoon at two o'clock in a carriage. On the first day it will have four white horses harnessed to it, then four chestnut horses, and last of all four black ones; but if you're not awake, and are sleeping, I shan't be set free."

The man promised to do everything she asked; but the raven said, "Alas, I know already that you won't deliver me. You'll take something from the woman."

Then the man promised once more that he would certainly touch nothing, either to eat or to drink.

But when he came into the house the old woman came up to him and said, "Poor man, how faint you look. Come and refresh yourself — eat and drink."

"No," said the man, "I won't eat or drink."

But she gave him no peace, and said, "If you won't eat, take one drink out of the glass. One is nothing."

Then he let himself be persuaded, and drank.

Shortly before two o'clock in the afternoon he went out into the garden to the tanbark heap to wait for the raven. As he was standing there his weariness all at once became so great that he could not fight it off, and he lay down for a short while — but he was determined not to go to sleep. Hardly had he lain down, though, before his eyes closed of their own accord, and he fell asleep and slept so soundly that nothing in the world could have roused him.

At two o'clock the raven came driving up with four white horses; but she was already in deep grief and said, "I know he's asleep." And when she came into the garden, there indeed he lay, asleep on the heap of tanbark. She got down from the carriage and went to him and shook him and called him, but he did not wake.

Next day about noon the old woman came again and brought him food and drink, but he would take none of it. But she gave him no rest and kept at him until at last he took one drink out of the glass again.

Towards two o'clock he went into the garden to the tanbark heap to wait for the raven; but all at once he felt such a great weariness that his legs would no longer hold him up. He could not help himself, and had to lie down, and fell into a heavy sleep.

When the raven drove up with four brown horses, she was already full of grief, and said, "I know he's asleep." She went to him, but there he lay sleeping, and there was no waking him.

Next day the old woman asked what this meant. He was neither eating nor drinking anything; did he want to die?

He replied, "I'm not allowed to eat or drink, and I won't do it."

But she set a dish of food and a glass of wine in front of him; and when he smelt it he could not resist, and swallowed a deep draught.

When the time came he went out into the garden to the tanbark heap and waited for the King's daughter; but he was wearier still than the day before, and lay down and slept as soundly as a stone.

At two o'clock the raven came with four black horses, and the coachman and everything else was black. She was already in the deepest grief, and said, "I know he's asleep and can't deliver me." When she came to him, there he lay, fast asleep. She shook him and called him, but she could not wake him.

Then she laid a loaf beside him, and after that a piece of meat, and thirdly a bottle of wine; and he might eat and drink as much of them as he liked, but they would never grow any less. After that she took a gold ring off her finger and put it on his, and her name was engraved on it. And last of all she laid a letter beside him, saying what she had given him and that none of the things would ever grow less; and in it was written too, "I see very well that you'll never be able to deliver me here. But if you're still willing to deliver me, come to the golden castle of Stromberg. It's in your power to do it, of that I'm certain."

And when she had given him all these things she got into her carriage and drove to the golden castle of Stromberg.

When the man woke and saw that he had slept, he was sick at heart, and said, "She's certainly driven past, and I haven't set her free." Then he noticed the things lying beside him, and read the letter that said how it had all happened.

So he got up and went away, meaning to go to the golden castle of Stromberg — but he did not know where it was. After he had wandered about the world for a long time, he came into a dark forest and walked in it for a fortnight and still could not find his way out. Then it was evening again, and he was so tired that he lay down in a thicket and fell asleep.

Next day he went on; and in the evening, as he was about to lie down under some bushes again, he heard such a howling and crying that he could not get to sleep. And at the hour when people light their candles, he saw one glimmering, and got up and went towards it. Then he came to a house that looked very small, for a great giant was standing in front of it.

He thought to himself, "If I go in and the giant sees me, it will very likely cost me my life."

At length he risked it and went in. When the giant saw him he said, "It's a good thing you've come, for it's a long while since I've eaten. I'll have you for my supper straight away."

"I'd rather you left that alone," said the man. "I don't like being eaten. But if you have any wish to eat, I've quite enough here to satisfy you."

"If that's true," said the giant, "you may be easy. I was only going to devour you because I had nothing else."

Then they went and sat down at the table, and the man brought out the bread and wine and meat that would never come to an end.

"This pleases me well," said the giant, and ate to his heart's content.

Then the man said to him, "Can you tell me where the golden castle of Stromberg is?"

The giant said, "I'll look at my map. Every town and village and house is on it." He fetched the map he kept in the room and looked for the castle, but it was not to be found on it.

"Never mind," said he. "I have some still bigger maps in my cupboard upstairs; we'll look in those." But there too it was no use.

The man now wanted to go on, but the giant begged him to wait a few days longer, until his brother, who had gone out to fetch provisions, came home. When the brother came home, they asked him about the golden castle of Stromberg.

He replied, "When I've eaten and had enough, I'll look at my map."

Then he went up to his room with them and they searched his map, but could not find it. Then he brought out still older maps, and they did not rest until they had found the golden castle of Stromberg — but it was many thousand miles away.

"How am I to get there?" asked the man.

The giant said, "I have two hours to spare, and I'll carry you into the neighbourhood of it; but after that I must be at home to nurse the child we have."

So the giant carried the man to about a hundred leagues from the castle, and said, "You can easily walk the rest of the way alone." And he turned back; but the man went on day and night, until at length he came to the golden castle of Stromberg.

It stood on a glass mountain; and the bewitched girl drove round the castle in her carriage and then went inside. He was overjoyed when he saw her and wanted to climb up to her; but every time he started he slipped down the glass again. And when he saw that he could not reach her he was filled with distress, and said to himself, "I'll stay down here and wait for her."

So he built himself a hut and stayed in it a whole year, and saw the King's daughter driving about up above every day, and could never get to her.

Then one day he saw from his hut three robbers who were beating each other, and called out to them, "God be with you!"

They stopped when they heard the cry; but as they could see nobody, they began beating each other again, and dangerously hard at that. So he called out again, "God be with you!" Again they stopped and looked about them; but as they could see nobody, they went on beating each other.

Then he called for the third time, "God be with you" — and thought, "I must see what these three are about" — and went over and asked why they were beating each other so furiously.

One of them said he had found a stick, and that when he struck a door with it, that door would spring open. The next said he had found a cloak, and that whenever he put it on he was invisible. But the third said he had found a horse that a man could ride anywhere on, even up the glass mountain. And now they did not know whether they ought to hold these things in common or divide them up.

Then the man said, "I'll give you something in exchange for these three things. Money I haven't got, but I have other things of more value. Only first I must try yours out, to see whether you've told me the truth."

So they put him on the horse, threw the cloak round him and gave him the stick in his hand; and when he had all these things they could see him no longer. So he gave them a few vigorous blows and cried, "Now then, you vagabonds, you've got what you deserve. Are you satisfied?"

And he rode up the glass mountain. But when he came to the front of the castle at the top, it was shut. So he struck the door with his stick and it sprang open at once. He went in and climbed the stairs until he came to the hall, where the girl was sitting with a golden cup of wine in front of her. But she could not see him, because he had the cloak on.

And when he came up to her, he drew the ring she had given him off his finger and dropped it into the cup, so that it rang.

Then she cried, "That's my ring — so the man who is to set me free must be here."

They searched the whole castle and did not find him; but he had gone out and seated himself on the horse and thrown off the cloak. When they came to the door they saw him and cried aloud in their delight. Then he got down and took the King's daughter in his arms; and she kissed him and said, "Now you have set me free, and tomorrow we'll celebrate our wedding."

The Peasant’s Wise Daughter

There was once a poor peasant who had no land, only a small house and one daughter.

Then the daughter said, "We ought to ask our lord the King for a bit of newly cleared land."

When the King heard of their poverty he made them a present of a piece of land, which she and her father dug over, meaning to sow it with a little corn and grain of that sort. When they had dug nearly the whole field, they found in the earth a mortar made of pure gold.

"Listen," said the father to the girl, "since our lord the King has been so gracious and made us a present of the field, we ought to give him this mortar in return."

But the daughter would not agree to it, and said, "Father, if we have the mortar and not the pestle as well, we shall be made to produce the pestle. You had far better say nothing about it."

He would not listen to her, though, but took the mortar and carried it to the King, and said he had found it in the cleared land, and asked whether he would accept it as a present.

The King took the mortar and asked whether he had found nothing else besides.

"No," answered the countryman.

Then the King said that he must now bring him the pestle. The peasant said they had not found it — but he might as well have been talking to the wind. He was put in prison, and was to stay there until he produced the pestle.

The servants had to bring him bread and water every day, which is what people get in prison; and they heard how the man cried out continually, "Ah, if only I'd listened to my daughter! Alas, alas, if only I'd listened to my daughter!" — and would neither eat nor drink.

So the King ordered the servants to bring the prisoner before him, and asked the peasant why he was always crying, "Ah, if only I'd listened to my daughter!" — and what it was his daughter had said.

"She told me I oughtn't to bring you the mortar, because I'd be made to produce the pestle as well."

"If you have a daughter as wise as that, let her come here."

So she had to appear before the King, who asked whether she really was so wise, and said he would set her a riddle, and if she could guess it he would marry her. She said at once that yes, she would guess it.

Then said the King, "Come to me not clothed and not naked, not riding and not walking, not on the road and not off the road; and if you can do that, I'll marry you."

So she went away and took off everything she had on, and then she was not clothed; and she took a great fishing net and sat down in it and wrapped it right round and round her, so that she was not naked; and she hired a donkey and tied the fisherman's net to its tail, so that it had to drag her along, and that was neither riding nor walking. And the donkey had to drag her along in the wheel ruts, so that she touched the ground only with her big toe, and that was neither being on the road nor off it.

And when she arrived in that fashion, the King said she had guessed the riddle and met all the conditions. Then he ordered her father to be released from prison, took her for his wife, and put all the royal property into her care.

Now when some years had gone by, the King was once drawing up his troops on parade, when it happened that some peasants who had been selling wood stopped with their wagons in front of the palace; some of them had oxen yoked to them and some had horses. There was one peasant who had three horses, and one of them gave birth to a foal, and it ran away and lay down between two oxen that were in front of another wagon.

When the peasants came together they began to argue, and to hit each other and make a disturbance; and the peasant with the oxen wanted to keep the foal, and said one of the oxen had given birth to it, and the other said his horse had had it and it was his.

The quarrel came before the King, and he gave the verdict that the foal should stay where it had been found; and so the peasant with the oxen, who had no right to it, got it.

Then the other went away and wept and lamented over his foal. Now he had heard how gracious his lady the Queen was, because she herself came of poor peasant stock; so he went to her and begged her to see whether she could not help him get his foal back.

Said she, "Yes, I'll tell you what to do, if you'll promise not to give me away. Early tomorrow morning, when the King parades the guard, station yourself in the middle of the road he has to pass along; take a great fishing net and pretend to be fishing. Go on fishing, and empty the net out as if you'd got it full." And then she told him too what he was to say if the King questioned him.

So next day the peasant stood there, fishing on dry ground. When the King passed and saw it, he sent his messenger to ask what the stupid fellow was doing.

He answered, "I'm fishing."

The messenger asked how he could be fishing when there was no water there.

The peasant said, "It's as easy for me to fish on dry land as it is for an ox to have a foal."

The messenger went back and took the answer to the King, who ordered the peasant to be brought to him, and told him this was not his own idea, and he wanted to know whose it was; the peasant must confess it at once.

The peasant, though, would not do it, and kept saying, God forbid, the idea was his own. But they laid him on a heap of straw and beat him and tormented him so long that at last he admitted he had got the idea from the Queen.

When the King reached home again he said to his wife, "Why have you dealt so falsely with me? I won't have you for a wife any longer. Your time is up — go back where you came from, to your peasant's hut."

One favour, though, he granted her: she might take with her the one thing that was dearest and best in her eyes. And so she was dismissed.

She said, "Yes, my dear husband, if that's your command, I'll do it" — and she embraced him and kissed him and said she would take her leave of him. Then she ordered a strong sleeping draught to be brought, to drink a farewell with him. The King took a long draught of it, but she took only a little.

He soon fell into a deep sleep; and when she saw it she called a servant and took a fine white linen cloth and wrapped the King in it, and the servant had to carry him out to a carriage that stood before the door; and she drove away with him to her own little house. She laid him in her own little bed, and he slept a day and a night without waking.

And when he woke he looked round and said, "Good God, where am I?" He called his attendants, but not one of them was there.

At length his wife came to his bedside and said, "My dear lord and King, you told me I might take away with me from the palace whatever was dearest and most precious in my eyes. I have nothing more precious or dear than you, so I've brought you with me."

Tears rose to the King's eyes, and he said, "Dear wife, you shall be mine and I will be yours." And he took her back with him to the royal palace and was married to her again; and at this present time they are very likely still living.

Old Hildebrand

Once upon a time there lived a peasant and his wife; and the parson of the village had taken a fancy to the wife, and had wished for a long time to spend a whole day pleasantly with her. The peasant woman was quite willing too.

So one day he said to her, "Listen, my dear friend, I've thought of a way for the two of us to spend a whole day happily together. I'll tell you what. On Wednesday you must take to your bed and tell your husband you're ill; and if you'll only complain and act the invalid properly, and go on doing it until Sunday, when I have to preach, then I'll say in my sermon that whoever has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick brother — or whoever else it may be — and makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerli hill in Italy, where you can get a peck of laurel leaves for a kreuzer, the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, or whoever else it may be, will be restored to health immediately."

"I'll manage it," said the woman promptly.

So on the Wednesday the peasant woman took to her bed and complained and lamented as they had agreed; and her husband did everything for her that he could think of, but nothing did her any good.

And when Sunday came the woman said, "I feel as ill as if I were going to die this minute; but there's one thing I should like to do before my end — I should like to hear the sermon the parson is going to preach today."

At that the peasant said, "Ah, my child, don't do it. You might make yourself worse if you got up. Look, I'll go to the sermon, and I'll pay very close attention and tell you everything the parson says."

"Well," said the woman, "go then, and pay great attention, and repeat to me everything you hear."

So the peasant went to the sermon; and the parson began to preach, and said that if anyone had at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother or anyone else, and would make a pilgrimage to the Göckerli hill in Italy, where a peck of laurel leaves costs a kreuzer, the sick child, sick husband, sick wife, sick father, sick mother, sick sister or brother, or whoever else it might be, would be restored to health instantly; and that whoever wished to undertake the journey was to come to him after the service was over, and he would give him the sack for the laurel leaves and the kreuzer.

Nobody was more delighted than the peasant; and after the service was over he went straight to the parson, who gave him the bag for the laurel leaves and the kreuzer.

After that he went home, and even at the front door he shouted, "Hurrah, dear wife! It's now almost the same as if you were well! The parson preached today that whoever had at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother or whoever it might be, and would make a pilgrimage to the Göckerli hill in Italy, where a peck of laurel leaves costs a kreuzer, the sick child, sick husband, sick wife, sick father, sick mother, sick sister or brother, or whoever else it was, would be cured immediately. And now I've already got the bag and the kreuzer from the parson, and I'll set off at once, so that you get well the sooner." And with that he went off.

But he was hardly gone before the woman got up, and the parson was there directly.

But we'll leave the two of them for a while and follow the peasant, who walked on quickly without stopping so as to get to the Göckerli hill the sooner. And on the way he met his old friend, who was an egg merchant and was just coming back from market, where he had sold his eggs.

"Bless you," said his friend. "Where are you off to in such a hurry?"

"To all eternity, my friend," said the peasant. "My wife is ill, and today I went to hear the parson's sermon, and he preached that if anybody had in his house a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother or anyone else, and made a pilgrimage to the Göckerli hill in Italy, where a peck of laurel leaves costs a kreuzer, the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister or brother, or whoever else it was, would be cured immediately. And so I've got the bag for the laurel leaves and the kreuzer from the parson, and now I'm starting on my pilgrimage."

"But listen, my friend," said the egg merchant to the peasant, "are you really stupid enough to believe a thing like that? Don't you know what it means? The parson wants to spend a whole day alone with your wife in peace, so he's given you this job to get you out of the way."

"My word," said the peasant, "how I'd like to know whether that's true!"

"Come along, then," said his friend. "I'll tell you what to do. Get into my egg basket and I'll carry you home, and then you can see for yourself."

So that was settled, and his friend put the peasant into his egg basket and carried him home.

When they got to the house — hurrah, but things were going merrily there! The woman had already had nearly everything in the farmyard killed, and had made pancakes; and the parson was there, and had brought his fiddle with him.

His friend knocked at the door, and the woman asked who was there.

"It's me, my dear," said the egg merchant. "Give me shelter for the night. I didn't sell my eggs at the market, so now I have to carry them home again, and they're so heavy that I'll never manage it — it's dark already."

"Well, my friend," said the woman, "you come at a very inconvenient time for me; but as you're here it can't be helped. Come in and take a seat there on the bench by the stove."

So she put the man, and the basket he carried on his back, on the bench by the stove. The parson and the woman, meanwhile, were as merry as could be.

At length the parson said, "Listen, my dear friend, you sing beautifully. Sing something for me."

"Oh," said the woman, "I can't sing now. In my young days I could sing well enough, but that's all over now."

"Come," said the parson again, "do sing some little song."

At that the woman began, and sang:

	"I've sent my husband away from me
	to the Göckerli hill in Italy."

Then the parson sang:

	"I wish it were a year before he came back —
	I'd never ask him for the laurel-leaf sack.
	Hallelujah."

Then the friend in the background began to sing (but I ought to tell you that the peasant was called Hildebrand), so he sang:

	"What are you doing, my Hildebrand dear,
	there on the bench by the stove so near?
	Hallelujah."

And then the peasant sang from inside his basket:

	"All singing I ever shall hate from this day,
	and here in this basket no longer I'll stay.
	Hallelujah."

And he got out of the basket and cudgelled the parson out of the house.

The Three Little Birds

About a thousand years ago or more, there were nothing but small kings in this country; and one of them, who lived on the Keuterberg, was very fond of hunting.

Once, when he was riding out from his castle with his huntsmen, three girls were watching their cows on the mountain; and when they saw the King with all his followers, the eldest girl pointed at him and called to the other two, "If I don't get that one, I'll have none."

Then the second girl answered from the other side of the hill, and pointed at the man on the King's right hand, "Hey there! Hey there! If I don't get him, I'll have nobody." And the third pointed at the one on his left. Now these two were the King's ministers.

The King heard all this; and when he came back from the hunt he had the three girls brought to him and asked them what they had said the day before on the mountain. They would not tell him; so the King asked the eldest whether she would really take him for her husband. Then she said yes, and the two ministers married the two sisters — for all three were fair and beautiful of face, and especially the Queen, who had hair like flax.

But the two sisters had no children; and once when the King had to go away from home, he invited them to come and stay with the Queen to cheer her, for she was about to bear a child. She had a little boy, who brought a bright red star into the world with him.

Then the two sisters said to each other that they would throw the beautiful boy into the water. And when they had thrown him in — I believe it was into the Weser — a little bird flew up into the air, singing:

	"To your death you are sped
	till God's own word be said.
	In the white lily's bloom,
	brave boy, is your tomb."

When the two heard that they were frightened to death, and ran away in great haste. When the King came home they told him that the Queen had given birth to a dog. Then the King said, "What God does is well done."

But a fisherman who lived by the water fished the little boy out again while he was still alive; and as his wife had no children, they brought him up.

When a year had gone by, the King went away again, and the Queen had another little boy, whom the false sisters likewise took and threw into the water. Then a little bird flew up again and sang:

	"To your death you are sped
	till God's own word be said.
	In the white lily's bloom,
	brave boy, is your tomb."

And when the King came back they told him that the Queen had given birth to a dog again; and again he said, "What God does is well done." But the fisherman fished this one out of the water too, and brought him up.

Then the King went off on his travels again, and the Queen had a little girl, whom the false sisters also threw into the water. Then again a little bird flew up on high and sang:

	"To your death you are sped
	till God's own word be said.
	In the white lily's bloom,
	bonny girl, is your tomb."

And when the King came home they told him that the Queen had given birth to a cat. Then the King grew angry and ordered his wife to be thrown into prison, and she was shut up there for many long years.

Meanwhile the children had grown up. The eldest went out one day with some other boys to fish; but the other boys would not have him with them, and said, "Go your own way, foundling."

He was much troubled at this, and asked the old fisherman whether it was true. The fisherman told him that once, when he was fishing, he had drawn him out of the water.

So the boy said he would go out and look for his father. The fisherman begged him to stay; but he would not be held back, and at last the fisherman consented.

Then the boy went on his way and walked for many days, and at last he came to a great stretch of water, beside which an old woman was standing, fishing.

"Good day, mother," said the boy.

"Many thanks," said she.

"You'll fish a long while before you catch anything."

"And you'll search a long while before you find your father. How will you get over the water?" said the woman.

"God knows."

Then the old woman took him up on her back and carried him across; and he searched a long time but could not find his father.

When a year had gone by, the second boy set out to look for his brother. He came to the water, and it went with him exactly as it had with his brother.

And now there was nobody left at home but the daughter, and she mourned for her brothers so much that at last she too begged the fisherman to let her go, for she wanted to search for them. So she came to the great stretch of water too, and said to the old woman, "Good day, mother."

"Many thanks," replied the old woman.

"May God help you with your fishing," said the girl.

When the old woman heard that she became quite friendly, and carried her over the water, and gave her a wand, and said to her, "Go on and on along this road, my daughter; and when you come to a great black dog, you must pass it silently and boldly, without laughing or looking at it. Then you'll come to a great high castle, and you must let the wand fall on the threshold and go straight through the castle and out again on the other side. There you'll see an old fountain with a great tree growing out of it, and a bird hanging on the tree in a cage, which you must take down. Take a glass of water out of the fountain as well, and go back the same way with those two things. Pick the wand up again from the threshold and take it with you; and when you pass the dog again, strike him in the face with it — but be sure you hit him — and then come back here to me."

The girl found everything exactly as the old woman had said; and on the way back she found her two brothers, who had been searching for each other over half the world. They went together to the place where the black dog was lying in the road; she struck it in the face, and it turned into a handsome prince, who went with them to the river.

There the old woman was still standing. She rejoiced greatly to see them again, and carried them all over the water; and then she went away too, for now she was free.

The others went to the old fisherman, and everyone was glad that they had found each other again; and they hung the bird up on the wall.

But the second son could not settle down at home, and took his crossbow and went out hunting. When he was tired he took out his flute and made music. The King was out hunting too, and heard it and went over; and when he met the young man he said, "Who gave you leave to hunt here?"

"Oh, nobody."

"Whose son are you, then?"

"I'm the fisherman's son."

"But he has no children."

"If you won't believe me, come with me."

The King did; and he questioned the fisherman, who told him the whole story; and the little bird on the wall began to sing:

	"The mother sits alone
	there in the prison small.
	O King of royal blood,
	these are your children all.
	The sisters twain so false,
	they wrought the children woe,
	there in the waters deep
	where the fishermen come and go."

Then they were all horror-struck; and the King took the bird, the fisherman and the three children back with him to the castle, and ordered the prison to be opened and brought his wife out again. But she had grown quite ill and weak. Then the daughter gave her some of the water from the fountain to drink, and she became strong and healthy.

But the two false sisters were burnt; and the daughter married the prince.

The Water of Life

There was once a King who fell ill, and nobody believed that he would come out of it alive. He had three sons, who were greatly distressed about it, and went down into the palace garden and wept. There they met an old man who asked them the cause of their grief. They told him that their father was so ill that he would certainly die, for nothing seemed to cure him.

Then the old man said, "I know of one more remedy, and that's the water of life. If he drinks of it he'll be well again — but it's hard to find."

The eldest said, "I'll manage to find it" — and went to the sick King and begged to be allowed to go out in search of the water of life, since that alone could save him.

"No," said the King. "The danger is too great. I'd rather die."

But he begged so long that the King consented. The prince thought in his heart, "If I bring back the water, then I shall be my father's favourite and inherit the kingdom."

So he set out; and when he had ridden a little way, a dwarf stood there in the road who called out to him, "Where are you off to in such a hurry?"

"You silly little shrimp," said the prince very haughtily, "it's nothing to do with you" — and rode on.

But the little dwarf had grown angry, and had wished an evil wish. Soon after this the prince rode into a ravine; and the further he rode, the closer the mountains drew together, until at last the road became so narrow that he could not go a step further. It was impossible either to turn his horse or to get down from the saddle, and he was shut in there as if in prison.

The sick King waited a long while for him, but he did not come.

Then the second son said, "Father, let me go and look for the water" — and thought to himself, "If my brother is dead, then the kingdom will fall to me."

At first the King would not let him go either, but at last he gave way. So the prince set out along the same road his brother had taken, and he too met the dwarf, who stopped him to ask where he was going in such haste.

"You little shrimp," said the prince, "that's nothing to do with you" — and rode on without giving him another look.

But the dwarf put a spell on him, and he too rode into a ravine and could go neither forwards nor backwards. That is how it goes with haughty people.

As the second son stayed away as well, the youngest begged to be allowed to go and fetch the water, and at last the King had to let him go.

When he met the dwarf, and the dwarf asked him where he was going in such haste, he stopped and explained, and said, "I'm looking for the water of life, because my father is sick to death."

"Do you know, then, where it's to be found?"

"No," said the prince.

"As you've behaved yourself properly, and not haughtily like your false brothers, I'll give you the information and tell you how you may get the water of life. It springs from a fountain in the courtyard of an enchanted castle; but you'll never be able to make your way to it unless I give you an iron wand and two small loaves of bread. Strike three times with the wand on the castle's iron door, and it will spring open. Inside lie two lions with gaping jaws; but if you throw a loaf to each of them they'll be quiet. Then hurry and fetch some of the water of life before the clock strikes twelve, or the door will shut again and you'll be shut in."

The prince thanked him, took the wand and the bread, and set out on his way.

When he arrived, everything was as the dwarf had said. The door sprang open at the third stroke of the wand; and when he had quieted the lions with the bread, he went into the castle and came to a large and splendid hall, where some enchanted princes were sitting, and he drew the rings off their fingers. A sword and a loaf of bread were lying there, and he carried them away.

After this he came into a chamber where there was a beautiful girl, who rejoiced when she saw him and kissed him, and told him that he had delivered her and should have the whole of her kingdom; and that if he would come back in a year, their wedding should be celebrated. She told him too where the spring of the water of life was, and that he must hurry and draw some of it before the clock struck twelve.

Then he went on, and at last came into a room where there was a beautiful, freshly made bed; and as he was very weary he felt inclined to rest a little. So he lay down and fell asleep.

When he woke it was striking a quarter to twelve. He sprang up in a fright, ran to the spring, drew some water in a cup that stood beside it, and hurried away. But just as he was passing through the iron door the clock struck twelve, and the door slammed with such violence that it carried away a piece of his heel.

All the same, rejoicing that he had got the water of life, he set off home, and passed the dwarf again. When the dwarf saw the sword and the loaf he said, "With those you've won great wealth. With the sword you can slay whole armies, and the bread will never come to an end."

But the prince would not go home to his father without his brothers, and said, "Dear dwarf, can't you tell me where my two brothers are? They went out before I did in search of the water of life, and they haven't come back."

"They're shut up between two mountains," said the dwarf. "I condemned them to stay there, because they were so haughty."

Then the prince begged until the dwarf released them; but he warned him, and said, "Beware of them, for they have bad hearts."

When his brothers came, he rejoiced, and told them how things had gone with him: that he had found the water of life and brought a cupful away with him, and had rescued a beautiful princess who was willing to wait a year for him, and that then their wedding was to be held and he would come into a great kingdom.

After that they rode on together, and came to a land where war and famine were raging, and the King already thought he must perish, the scarcity was so great. Then the prince went to him and gave him the loaf, with which he fed and satisfied his whole kingdom; and then the prince gave him the sword as well, with which he defeated the armies of his enemies, so that he could now live in rest and peace. The prince then took back his loaf and his sword, and the three brothers rode on.

But after that they came into two more countries where war and famine were raging, and each time the prince gave his loaf and his sword to the King; and so he had now delivered three kingdoms.

After that they went on board a ship and sailed over the sea. During the voyage the two eldest talked apart, and said, "The youngest found the water of life and we didn't, so our father will give him the kingdom — the kingdom that belongs to us — and he'll rob us of all our fortune."

So they began to seek revenge, and plotted together to destroy him. They waited until they found him fast asleep, and then poured the water of life out of his cup and took it for themselves, and poured salt sea water into the cup instead.

So when they arrived home, the youngest took his cup to the sick King so that he might drink out of it and be cured. But he had hardly drunk a very little of the salt sea water before he was worse than before. And as he was lamenting over this, the two eldest brothers came in and accused the youngest of having meant to poison him, and said that they had brought him the true water of life, and handed it to him. He had hardly tasted it before he felt his sickness leaving him, and became as strong and healthy as in the days of his youth.

After that the two of them went to the youngest and mocked him, and said, "You certainly found the water of life, but you had the pain and we have the gain. You should have been sharper and kept your eyes open. We took it from you while you were asleep at sea; and when the year is up, one of us will go and fetch the beautiful princess. But mind you don't say a word of this to our father. He doesn't trust you anyway; and if you say one word you'll lose your life into the bargain — but if you keep quiet, we'll make you a present of it."

The old King was angry with his youngest son, and thought he had plotted against his life. So he called the court together and had sentence pronounced on his son: that he should be secretly shot.

And once, when the prince was riding out to the hunt suspecting no evil, the King's huntsman had to go with him; and when they were quite alone in the forest the huntsman looked so sorrowful that the prince said to him, "Dear huntsman, what's the matter with you?"

The huntsman said, "I can't tell you — and yet I ought to."

Then the prince said, "Say straight out what it is. I'll pardon you."

"Alas," said the huntsman, "I'm to shoot you dead. The King has ordered me to."

Then the prince was appalled, and said, "Dear huntsman, let me live. Here — I'll give you my royal clothes; give me your common ones in their place."

The huntsman said, "I'll do it willingly. Indeed, I could never have shot you."

So they exchanged clothes, and the huntsman went home; but the prince went on deeper into the forest.

After a time three wagonloads of gold and precious stones came to the King for his youngest son, sent by the three Kings who had defeated their enemies with the prince's sword and fed their people with his bread, and who wanted to show their gratitude for it.

Then the old King thought, "Can my son have been innocent?" — and said to his people, "If only he were still alive! How it grieves me that I let him be killed."

"He is still alive," said the huntsman. "I couldn't find it in my heart to carry out your command" — and told the King how it had happened.

Then a stone fell from the King's heart, and he had it proclaimed in every country that his son might come back and be received into favour again.

The princess, meanwhile, had had a road made up to her palace that was all bright and golden, and told her people that whoever came riding straight along it to her would be the right suitor and was to be let in; and whoever rode at the side of it was not the right one and was not to be let in.

As the time was now close at hand, the eldest thought he would hurry and go to the King's daughter and give himself out as her deliverer, and so win her for his bride and the kingdom into the bargain. So he rode off; and when he came in front of the palace and saw the splendid golden road, he thought it would be a sin and a shame to ride over it, and turned aside and rode along the right-hand side of it. But when he came to the door, the servants told him that he was not the right man, and was to go away again.

Soon after this the second prince set out; and when he came to the golden road and his horse had put one foot on it, he thought it would be a sin and a shame to tread a piece of it away, and he turned aside and rode along the left-hand side of it. And when he reached the door, the attendants told him he was not the right one, and he was to go away again.

When at last the year was fully up, the third son also wanted to ride out of the forest to his beloved, and forget his sorrows with her. So he set out, and thought about her so constantly, and wanted so much to be with her, that he never noticed the golden road at all. So his horse went straight up the middle of it; and when he came to the door it was opened, and the princess received him with joy and said he was her deliverer and lord of the kingdom; and their wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing.

When it was over she told him that his father had invited him to come to him, and had forgiven him. So he rode there and told him everything: how his brothers had betrayed him, and how he had kept silent all the same.
