The old King wanted to punish them; but they had put to sea, and never came back as long as they lived.

Doctor Knowall

There was once a poor peasant called Crabb, who drove a load of wood to town with two oxen and sold it to a doctor for two thalers. As the money was being counted out to him it happened that the doctor was sitting at table; and when the peasant saw how daintily he ate and drank, his heart longed for what he saw, and he would gladly have been a doctor too.

So he stood there a while, and at length asked whether he too could not be a doctor.

"Oh, yes," said the doctor, "that's soon managed."

"What must I do?" asked the peasant.

"In the first place, buy yourself an ABC book of the kind that has a cock on the front. Secondly, turn your cart and your two oxen into money and get yourself some clothes and whatever else belongs to medicine. And thirdly, have a sign painted for yourself with the words 'I am Doctor Knowall' on it, and have it nailed up over your front door."

The peasant did everything he had been told to do. And when he had been doctoring people for a while — but not long — a rich and great lord had some money stolen. He was told about Doctor Knowall, who lived in such and such a village and must know what had become of the money. So the lord had the horses put to his carriage and drove out to the village and asked Crabb whether he was Doctor Knowall.

Yes, he said, he was.

Then he was to come with him and bring back the stolen money.

"Oh, yes — but Grete, my wife, must come too."

The lord was willing, and let both of them have a seat in the carriage, and they all drove off together.

When they came to the nobleman's castle the table was laid, and Crabb was told to sit down and eat.

"Yes — but my wife Grete too," said he; and he sat down at the table with her.

And when the first servant came in with a dish of delicate food, the peasant nudged his wife and said, "Grete, that was the first" — meaning that was the servant who brought the first dish. But the servant thought he meant by it, "That is the first thief"; and as he actually was, he was terrified, and said to his comrade outside, "The doctor knows everything. It will go badly with us — he said I was the first."

The second did not want to go in at all, but was made to. So when he went in with his dish, the peasant nudged his wife and said, "Grete, that's the second." This servant was just as alarmed, and got out as fast as he could.

The third fared no better, for the peasant again said, "Grete, that's the third."

The fourth had to carry in a dish that was covered, and the lord told the doctor he was to show his skill and guess what was under the cover. The doctor looked at the dish and had no idea what to say, and cried, "Ah, poor Crabb!"

When the lord heard that, he cried, "There! He knows it — he knows who has the money!"

At this the servants looked terribly uneasy, and made a sign to the doctor that they wanted him to step outside for a moment. So when he went out, all four of them confessed to him that they had stolen the money, and said that they would gladly give it back and give him a heavy sum into the bargain if he would not denounce them, for if he did they would be hanged. And they led him to the place where the money was hidden.

With that the doctor was satisfied, and went back into the hall and sat down at the table and said, "My lord, now I'll search in my book to find where the gold is hidden."

The fifth servant, though, crept into the stove to hear whether the doctor knew still more. The doctor sat still and opened his ABC book and turned the pages backwards and forwards, looking for the cock. And as he could not find it straight away, he said, "I know you're in there, so you'd better show yourself."

Then the fellow in the stove thought the doctor meant him, and sprang out in terror, crying, "That man knows everything!"

Then Doctor Knowall showed the count where the money was, but did not say who had stolen it; and he was given a great deal of money in reward by both sides, and became a famous man.

The Spirit in the Bottle

There was once a poor woodcutter who toiled from early morning till late at night. When at last he had put a little money by, he said to his boy, "You're my only child. I'll spend the money I've earned by the sweat of my brow on your education. If you learn some honest trade, you can support me in my old age, when my limbs have grown stiff and I have to stay at home."

So the boy went to a good school and studied hard, so that his masters praised him, and he stayed there a long time. But when he had worked his way through two classes, and was still not perfect in everything, the little store his father had earned was all spent, and the boy had to go back home to him.

"Ah," said his father sorrowfully, "I can give you no more; and in these hard times I can't earn a farthing beyond what's needed for our daily bread."

"Dear father," answered the son, "don't trouble yourself about it. If it's God's will, it will turn out to my advantage. I shall soon get used to it."

When his father was going into the forest to earn money by helping to pile and stack wood, and to chop it as well, his son said, "I'll come with you and help you."

"No, my son," said his father, "that would be hard for you. You're not used to rough work and you won't be able to stand it; and besides, I've only one axe and no money left to buy another."

"Just go to the neighbour," answered the son. "He'll lend you his axe until I've earned one for myself."

So the father borrowed an axe from the neighbour; and next morning at daybreak they went out into the forest together. The son helped his father and was quite merry and brisk about it.

But when the sun was right over their heads the father said, "We'll rest and have our dinner, and then we'll work all the better."

The son took his bread in his hands and said, "You rest, father. I'm not tired. I'll walk up and down in the forest a little and look for birds' nests."

"Oh, you fool," said his father, "why should you want to go running about? Afterwards you'll be tired and won't be able to lift your arm. Stay here and sit down beside me."

But the son went off into the forest and ate his bread, very cheerful, and peered in among the green branches to see whether he could spot a bird's nest anywhere. So he went up and down, looking; until at last he came to a great dangerous-looking oak, which was certainly many hundreds of years old, and which five men together could not have spanned. He stood still and looked at it and thought, "Many a bird must have built its nest in that."

Then all at once it seemed to him that he heard a voice. He listened, and realised that somebody was calling out in a very smothered voice, "Let me out! Let me out!"

He looked around, but could see nothing; all the same, he had the idea that the voice was coming out of the ground. So he cried, "Where are you?"

The voice answered, "I'm down here among the roots of the oak tree. Let me out! Let me out!"

The student began to loosen the earth under the tree and search among the roots, until at last he found a glass bottle in a little hollow. He lifted it up and held it against the light, and then saw a creature shaped like a frog springing up and down inside it.

"Let me out! Let me out!" it cried again; and the student, meaning no harm, drew the cork out of the bottle.

Immediately a spirit rose out of it and began to grow — and grew so fast that within a very few moments he stood in front of the student, a terrible fellow as big as half the tree he was standing beside.

"Do you know," he cried in an awful voice, "what your wages are for letting me out?"

"No," replied the student fearlessly. "How should I know that?"

"Then I'll tell you," cried the spirit. "I must strangle you for it."

"You should have told me that sooner," said the student, "for then I'd have left you shut up. But my head shall stay where it is for anything you can do — more people than one must be consulted about that."

"More people here, more people there," said the spirit. "You shall have the wages you've earned. Do you think I was shut up in there all that time as a favour? No — it was a punishment. I am the mighty Mercurius. Whoever releases me, him I must strangle."

"Gently," answered the student, "not so fast. First I must know that you really were shut up in that little bottle, and that you're the right spirit. If you can indeed get in again, I'll believe it — and then you may do what you like with me."

The spirit said haughtily, "That's a very trifling feat" — and drew himself together and made himself as small and slender as he had been at first, so that he crept in through the same opening and right down through the neck of the bottle.

He was hardly inside before the student thrust the cork he had drawn back into the bottle, and threw it among the roots of the oak in its old place; and the spirit was tricked.

And now the student was about to go back to his father, when the spirit cried out very piteously, "Ah, do let me out! Ah, do let me out!"

"No," answered the student, "not a second time. Somebody who has once tried to take my life shan't be set free by me, now that I've caught him again."

"If you'll set me free," said the spirit, "I'll give you enough to have plenty all the days of your life."

"No," answered the boy, "you'd cheat me the way you did the first time."

"You're throwing away your own good luck," said the spirit. "I'll do you no harm, but reward you richly."

The student thought, "I'll risk it. Perhaps he'll keep his word — and in any case he shan't get the better of me."

So he took out the cork, and the spirit rose up out of the bottle as he had before, and stretched himself and grew as big as a giant.

"Now you shall have your reward," said he — and handed the student a little rag like a strip of plaster, and said, "If you spread one end of this over a wound it will heal; and if you rub steel or iron with the other end, it will be turned into silver."

"I must just try that," said the student; and he went to a tree and tore off the bark with his axe and rubbed it with one end of the plaster. It closed up at once and was healed.

"Now it's all right," he said to the spirit, "and we can part."

The spirit thanked him for his release, and the boy thanked the spirit for his present, and went back to his father.

"Where have you been running about?" said his father. "Why have you forgotten your work? I said straight away that you'd never get on with anything."

"Don't worry, father, I'll make it up."

"Make it up, indeed," said his father angrily. "There's no art in that."

"You watch, father. I'll chop that tree over there so that it splits."

Then he took his plaster and rubbed the axe with it, and struck a mighty blow; but as the iron had turned into silver, the edge bent over.

"Hey, father, just look what a bad axe you've given me — it's gone quite crooked."

His father was appalled and said, "Ah, what have you done? Now I shall have to pay for that, and I've nothing to pay with; and that's all the good I've got out of your work."

"Don't get angry," said his son. "I'll pay for the axe soon enough."

"Oh, you blockhead," cried his father, "what will you pay for it with? You have nothing but what I give you. These are students' tricks stuck in your head, but you know nothing about woodcutting."

After a while the student said, "Father, I really can't work any more. We'd better take a holiday."

"Eh, what!" he answered. "Do you think I'm going to sit with my hands in my lap like you? I must go on working, but you may take yourself off home."

"Father, this is the first time I've been in this wood; I don't know my way alone. Do come with me."

As his anger had died down by now, the father at last let himself be persuaded and went home with him. Then he said to his son, "Go and sell your damaged axe and see what you can get for it; and I must earn the difference, to pay the neighbour."

The son took the axe and carried it into town to a goldsmith, who tested it and laid it in the scales and said, "It's worth four hundred thalers. I haven't as much as that here."

The son said, "Give me what you have. I'll lend you the rest."

The goldsmith gave him three hundred thalers and stayed a hundred in his debt.

The son then went home and said, "Father, I've got the money. Go and ask the neighbour what he wants for the axe."

"I know that already," answered the old man. "One thaler and six groschen."

"Then give him two thalers and twelve groschen — that's double, and more than enough. Look, I've money in plenty." And he gave his father a hundred thalers and said, "You shall never know want. Live as comfortably as you like."

"Good heavens," said his father, "how did you come by these riches?"

The student then told him how it had all come about, and how, trusting to his luck, he had made such a good stroke. But with the money that was left he went back to school and went on learning; and as he could heal every kind of wound with his plaster, he became the most famous doctor in the whole world.

The Devil’s Sooty Brother

A discharged soldier had nothing to live on and did not know how to get by. So he went out into the forest; and when he had walked a little way he met a little man — who was in fact the Devil.

The little man said to him, "What's the matter with you? You look so very downcast."

Then the soldier said, "I'm hungry, and I've no money."

The Devil said, "If you'll hire yourself out to me and be my serving man, you shall have enough for the rest of your life. You shall serve me for seven years, and after that you'll be free again. But there's one thing I must tell you, and that is that you mustn't wash, or comb or tidy yourself, or cut your hair or your nails, or wipe the water out of your eyes."

The soldier said, "All right, if there's no help for it" — and went off with the little man, who led him straight down into hell.

Then he told him what he had to do. He was to poke the fire under the kettles where the hell-broth was stewing, keep the house clean, sweep all the dirt behind the doors, and see that everything was in order — but if he once peeped into the kettles, it would go badly for him.

The soldier said, "Good, I'll take care."

And then the old Devil went out again on his travels, and the soldier began his new duties: made up the fire and swept the dirt well behind the doors, just as he had been told. When the old Devil came back he looked to see whether it had all been done, seemed satisfied, and went off a second time.

Now the soldier took a good look about him on every side. The kettles were standing all round hell with a mighty fire under them, and inside they were boiling and spitting. He would have given anything to look inside them, if the Devil had not so particularly forbidden it. At last he could restrain himself no longer, and raised the lid of the first kettle a little and peeped in; and there he saw his old corporal shut up inside.

"Aha, old bird," said he, "do I meet you here? You once had me in your power; now I have you." And he quickly let the lid fall, poked the fire and threw on a fresh log.

After that he went to the second kettle and raised its lid a little too, and peeped in; his old ensign was in that one. "Aha, old bird, so I find you here! You once had me in your power; now I have you." He closed the lid again and fetched another log, to make it really hot.

Then he wanted to see who might be sitting in the third kettle — and it turned out to be no less than a general. "Aha, old bird, do I meet you here? Once you had me in your power; now I have you." And he fetched the bellows and made the hell-fire blaze right under him.

So he did his work in hell for seven years, and did not wash or comb or tidy himself, or cut his hair or his nails, or wash the water out of his eyes; and the seven years seemed so short to him that he thought he had only been there half a year.

Now when the time was fully up, the Devil came and said, "Well, Hans, what have you done?"

"I poked the fire under the kettles, and I've swept all the dirt well behind the doors."

"But you peeped into the kettles as well. It's lucky for you that you put fresh logs on them, or your life would have been forfeit. Now that your time is up, will you go home again?"

"Yes," said the soldier, "I should very much like to see what my father is doing at home."

The Devil said, "So that you get the wages you've earned, go and fill your knapsack full of the sweepings and take it home with you. And you must go unwashed and uncombed, with long hair on your head and your chin, and with uncut nails and dim eyes; and when you're asked where you come from, you must say, 'From hell'; and when you're asked who you are, you're to say, 'The Devil's sooty brother, and my own King as well.'"

The soldier held his tongue and did as the Devil told him, but he was not at all satisfied with his wages. And then, as soon as he was up in the forest again, he took his knapsack off his back to empty it — and on opening it he found the sweepings had turned into pure gold.

"I should never have expected that," said he, and was well pleased, and went into the town.

The landlord was standing in front of the inn; and when he saw the soldier coming he was terrified, because Hans looked so horrible — worse than a scarecrow. He called out to him and asked, "Where do you come from?"

"From hell."

"Who are you?"

"The Devil's sooty brother, and my own King as well."

Then the landlord would not let him in; but when Hans showed him the gold he came and unlatched the door himself.

Hans then ordered the best room and full attendance, and ate and drank his fill; but he neither washed nor combed himself, as the Devil had told him, and at last lay down to sleep.

But the knapsack full of gold stayed in front of the landlord's eyes and left him no peace; and in the night he crept in and stole it away.

Next morning, though, when Hans got up and wanted to pay the landlord and travel on, behold — his knapsack was gone. But he soon calmed himself, and thought, "You've had bad luck through no fault of your own" — and went straight back to hell and complained of his misfortune to the old Devil, and begged for his help.

The Devil said, "Sit down. I'll wash you and comb you and tidy you up, and cut your hair and nails and wash your eyes for you." And when he had finished with him, he gave him back the knapsack full of sweepings, and said, "Go and tell the landlord that he must give you back your money, or else I'll come and fetch him, and he shall poke the fire in your place."

Hans went up and said to the landlord, "You stole my money. If you don't give it back, you'll go down to hell in my place, and you'll look as horrible as I did."

Then the landlord gave him the money, and more besides, only begging him to keep it quiet; and Hans was now a rich man.

He set out for home to his father, and bought himself a shabby smock to wear, and strolled about making music, for he had learned to do that while he was with the Devil in hell.

Now there was an old King in that country, before whom he had to play; and the King was so delighted with his playing that he promised him his eldest daughter in marriage. But when she heard that she was to marry a common fellow in a smock, she said, "Rather than that, I'd go into the deepest water."

So the King gave him the youngest, who was quite willing to do it to please her father. And so the Devil's sooty brother got the King's daughter — and when the old King died, the whole kingdom as well.

Bearskin

There was once a young fellow who enlisted as a soldier, conducted himself bravely, and was always the first man forward when it rained bullets. As long as the war lasted all went well; but when peace was made he got his discharge, and the captain said he might go where he liked.

His parents were dead and he had no home any more, so he went to his brothers and begged them to take him in and keep him until war broke out again. But his brothers were hard-hearted, and said, "What can we do with you? You're no use to us. Go and make a living for yourself."

The soldier had nothing left but his gun. He put that on his shoulder and went out into the world. He came to a wide heath with nothing to be seen on it but a ring of trees; and he sat down under them sorrowfully and began to think over his lot.

"I've no money," he thought. "I've learned no trade but fighting; and now that they've made peace they don't want me any longer. So I can see already that I shall have to starve."

All at once he heard a rustling; and when he looked round, a strange man was standing in front of him, wearing a green coat and looking very grand — but with a hideous cloven foot.

"I know already what you need," said the man. "Gold and property you shall have, as much of it as you can get through, do what you will. But first I must know whether you're fearless, so that I don't spend my money for nothing."

"A soldier and fear — how do those two go together?" he answered. "You can put me to the test."

"Very well, then," answered the man. "Look behind you."

The soldier turned round and saw a great bear coming growling towards him. "Oho," cried the soldier, "I'll tickle your nose for you, and you'll soon lose your taste for growling" — and he took aim at the bear and shot it through the muzzle. It fell down and never stirred again.

"I can see quite plainly," said the stranger, "that you're not lacking in courage. But there's another condition you'll have to fulfil."

"If it doesn't endanger my salvation," replied the soldier, who knew very well who was standing beside him. "If it does, I'll have nothing to do with it."

"You'll have to see to that for yourself," answered Greencoat. "For the next seven years you shall neither wash yourself nor comb your beard or your hair, nor cut your nails, nor say one Our Father. I'll give you a coat and a cloak, which you must wear all that time. If you die during these seven years you're mine; if you stay alive, you're free — and rich into the bargain for the rest of your life."

The soldier thought of the desperate straits he was now in; and as he had so often gone out to meet death, he decided to risk it now as well, and agreed to the terms.

The Devil took off his green coat, gave it to the soldier and said, "If you have this coat on your back and put your hand in the pocket, you'll always find it full of money." Then he pulled the skin off the bear and said, "This shall be your cloak and your bed as well, for you shall sleep on it and lie in no other bed; and because of these clothes you shall be called Bearskin."

And with that the Devil vanished.

The soldier put the coat on and felt in the pocket at once, and found that the thing was true. Then he put on the bearskin and went out into the world, and enjoyed himself, keeping back from nothing that did him good and his money harm.

During the first year his appearance was passable; but during the second he began to look like a monster. His hair covered nearly the whole of his face, his beard was like a piece of coarse felt, his fingers had claws, and his face was so caked with dirt that if cress had been sown on it, it would have come up. Everybody who saw him ran away; but as he gave the poor money everywhere to pray that he might not die within the seven years, and as he paid well for everything, he still always found shelter.

In the fourth year he came to an inn where the landlord would not take him in, and would not even let him have a place in the stable, because he was afraid the horses would take fright. But when Bearskin put his hand in his pocket and pulled out a handful of ducats, the landlord let himself be persuaded and gave him a room in an outhouse — though Bearskin had to promise not to let himself be seen, in case the inn got a bad name.

One evening, as Bearskin was sitting alone and wishing from the bottom of his heart that the seven years were over, he heard loud lamenting in a room nearby. He had a compassionate heart, so he opened the door and saw an old man weeping bitterly and wringing his hands.

Bearskin went closer, but the man sprang to his feet and tried to get away from him. At last, when the man realised that Bearskin's voice was a human voice, he let himself be talked round; and by kind words Bearskin got so far that the old man told him the cause of his grief. His property had dwindled away bit by bit, he and his daughters would have to starve, and he was so poor that he could not pay the innkeeper and was to be put in prison.

"If that's your only trouble," said Bearskin, "I have plenty of money." He had the innkeeper fetched, paid him, and put a purse full of gold into the poor old man's pocket besides.

When the old man found himself free of all his troubles, he did not know how to be grateful enough. "Come with me," he said to Bearskin. "My daughters are all marvels of beauty; choose one of them for a wife. When she hears what you've done for me, she won't refuse you. You do look a little strange, it's true, but she'll soon put you to rights again."

That pleased Bearskin well, and he went.

When the eldest saw him she was so terrified by his face that she screamed and ran away. The second stood still and looked him over from head to foot, but then she said, "How can I take a husband who has no human shape left? The shaven bear that came here once and passed itself off as a man pleased me far better — at least it wore a hussar's uniform and white gloves. If it were nothing but ugliness, I could get used to that."

The youngest, though, said, "Dear father, that must be a good man, to have helped you out of your trouble. So if you promised him a bride for doing it, your promise must be kept."

It was a pity that Bearskin's face was covered with dirt and hair; otherwise they might have seen how delighted he was when he heard these words. He took a ring off his finger, broke it in two, and gave her one half and kept the other for himself. But he wrote his name on her half and hers on his, and begged her to keep her piece carefully. And then he took his leave and said, "I still have three years to wander; and if I don't come back then, you're free, for I shall be dead. But pray to God to preserve my life."

The poor betrothed bride dressed herself all in black; and when she thought of her future bridegroom, tears came into her eyes. From her sisters she got nothing but contempt and mockery.

"Take care," said the eldest. "If you give him your hand, he'll dig his claws into it."

"Beware," said the second. "Bears like sweet things, and if he takes a fancy to you he'll eat you up."

"You'll always have to do as he likes," the elder began again, "or he'll growl."

And the second went on, "But it'll be a merry wedding, for bears dance well."

The bride kept silent and would not let them vex her.

Bearskin, meanwhile, travelled about the world from one place to another, did good where he could, and gave generously to the poor so that they would pray for him.

At length, as the last day of the seven years dawned, he went out on the heath once more and sat down under the ring of trees. It was not long before the wind whistled and the Devil stood in front of him, looking at him angrily. Then he threw Bearskin his old coat and asked for his own green one back.

"We haven't got that far yet," answered Bearskin. "First you must make me clean."

Whether the Devil liked it or not, he had to fetch water and wash Bearskin and comb his hair and cut his nails. And after this he looked like a fine soldier, and was much handsomer than he had ever been before.

When the Devil had gone away, Bearskin was quite light-hearted. He went into the town, put on a magnificent velvet coat, seated himself in a carriage drawn by four white horses, and drove to his bride's house. Nobody recognised him; her father took him for a distinguished general, and led him into the room where his daughters were sitting.

He was made to sit between the two eldest; they helped him to wine and gave him the best pieces of meat, and thought they had never seen a handsomer man in all the world. But the bride sat opposite him in her black dress and never raised her eyes or spoke a word.

When at length he asked her father whether he would give him one of his daughters for a wife, the two eldest jumped up and ran into their bedrooms to put on splendid dresses, for each of them imagined that she was the chosen one.

As soon as the stranger was alone with his bride, he brought out his half of the ring and dropped it into a glass of wine, which he passed across the table to her. She took the wine; but when she had drunk it and found the half ring lying at the bottom, her heart began to beat. She fetched the other half, which she wore on a ribbon round her neck, and joined them, and saw that the two pieces fitted exactly.

Then he said, "I'm your betrothed bridegroom, the one you saw as Bearskin. But by God's grace I've got my human shape back and become clean again." He went up to her and embraced her and gave her a kiss.

Meanwhile the two sisters came back in full dress; and when they saw that the handsome man had fallen to the youngest, and heard that he was Bearskin, they ran out full of anger and rage. One of them drowned herself in the well and the other hanged herself on a tree.

In the evening somebody knocked at the door; and when the bridegroom opened it, it was the Devil in his green coat, who said, "You see — now I've got two souls in place of your one."

The Willow-Wren and the Bear

One summertime the bear and the wolf were walking in the forest, and the bear heard a bird singing so beautifully that he said, "Brother wolf, what bird is that, singing so well?"

"That's the King of the birds," said the wolf, "and we must bow down before him." In fact it was only the willow-wren — the little bird the Germans call the Zaunkönig, the hedge-king.

"If that's so," said the bear, "I should very much like to see his royal palace. Come, take me there."

"That isn't done quite as easily as you seem to think," said the wolf. "You must wait until the Queen comes."

Soon afterwards the Queen arrived with some food in her beak, and the lord King came too, and they began to feed their young ones. The bear would have liked to go straight over, but the wolf held him back by the sleeve and said, "No, you must wait until my lord and lady have gone away again."

So they took note of the hole the nest was in, and trotted off.

The bear, though, could get no rest until he had seen the royal palace, and after a short while he went back to it. The King and Queen had just flown out, so he peeped in and saw five or six young ones lying in it.

"Is that the royal palace?" cried the bear. "It's a miserable palace, and you're no king's children — you're disreputable children!"

When the young wrens heard that they were furious, and screamed, "No, we're not! Our parents are honest people! Bear, you'll pay for that!"

The bear and the wolf grew uneasy, and turned back and went into their holes. But the young willow-wrens went on crying and screaming; and when their parents brought food again they said, "We won't so much as touch one fly's leg — no, not if we were dying of hunger — until you've settled whether we're respectable children or not. The bear has been here and insulted us!"

Then the old King said, "Be easy, he shall be punished" — and flew off at once with the Queen to the bear's cave and called in, "Old Growler, why have you insulted my children? You shall suffer for it. We'll punish you with a bloody war."

So war was declared on the bear, and all the four-footed animals were summoned to take part in it — oxen, donkeys, cows, deer and every other animal the earth held. And the willow-wren summoned everything that flew in the air: not only birds large and small, but midges and hornets, bees and flies had to come.

When the time came for the war to begin, the willow-wren sent out spies to find out who was the enemy's commander-in-chief. The gnat, who was the craftiest, flew into the forest where the enemy was gathered, and hid under a leaf of the tree where the watchword was to be given.

There stood the bear; and he called the fox in front of him and said, "Fox, you're the cunningest of all the animals. You shall be general and lead us."

"Good," said the fox, "but what signal shall we agree on?"

Nobody knew, so the fox said, "I have a fine long bushy tail that looks almost like a plume of red feathers. When I hold my tail right up in the air, all is going well and you must charge; but if I let it hang down, run away as fast as you can."

When the gnat had heard that, she flew back and reported everything to the willow-wren, in the greatest detail.

When day broke and the battle was to begin, all the four-footed animals came running up with such a noise that the earth trembled. The willow-wren came flying through the air too with his army, with such a humming and whirring and swarming that everybody was uneasy and afraid; and the two sides advanced against each other.

But the willow-wren sent the hornet down with orders to get under the fox's tail and sting with all his might. When the fox felt the first sting he started so with the pain that he drew one leg up; but he bore it, and still kept his tail high in the air. At the second sting he had to let it drop for a moment. At the third he could hold out no longer, and screamed out and put his tail between his legs.

When the animals saw that, they thought all was lost and began to run, each into his own hole; and the birds had won the battle.

Then the King and Queen flew home to their children and cried, "Children, rejoice! Eat and drink to your hearts' content — we've won the battle!"

But the young wrens said, "We won't eat yet. The bear must come to the nest and beg our pardon and say that we're honourable children, before we'll do that."

So the willow-wren flew to the bear's hole and cried, "Growler, you're to come to the nest and beg my children's pardon, or else every rib in your body shall be broken."

So the bear crept over in the greatest fear and begged their pardon. And now at last the young wrens were satisfied, and sat down together and ate and drank and made merry until quite late into the night.

Sweet Porridge

There was a poor but good little girl who lived alone with her mother, and they had nothing left to eat.

So the child went into the forest, and there an old woman met her who knew all about her trouble, and gave her a little pot which, when she said, "Cook, little pot, cook," would cook good sweet porridge; and when she said, "Stop, little pot," it stopped cooking.

The girl took the pot home to her mother, and now they were free of their poverty and hunger, and ate sweet porridge as often as they liked.

Once, when the girl had gone out, her mother said, "Cook, little pot, cook." And it did cook, and she ate until she had had enough; and then she wanted the pot to stop cooking, but she did not know the word. So it went on cooking, and the porridge rose over the edge, and still it cooked on, until the kitchen and the whole house were full, and then the next house, and then the whole street — just as if it wanted to satisfy the hunger of the whole world. And there was the greatest distress, but nobody knew how to stop it.

At last, when only one single house was left, the child came home and just said, "Stop, little pot" — and it stopped and gave up cooking; and anybody who wanted to get back into the town had to eat his way there.

Wise Folks

One day a peasant took his good hazel stick out of the corner and said to his wife, "Trina, I'm going across country and shan't be back for three days. If the cattle dealer should happen to call in that time and want to buy our three cows, you may strike a bargain at once — but not unless you can get two hundred thalers for them. Nothing less, do you hear?"

"For heaven's sake, just go in peace," answered the woman. "I'll manage that."

"You, indeed," said the man. "You fell on your head once when you were a little child, and it affects you to this day. But let me tell you this: if you do anything foolish, I'll make your back black and blue — and not with paint, I assure you, but with the stick I have in my hand; and the colouring will last a whole year, you may rely on it."

And having said that, the man went on his way.

Next morning the cattle dealer came, and the woman had no need to say many words to him. When he had seen the cows and heard the price, he said, "I'm quite willing to give that. To speak honestly, they're worth it. I'll take the beasts away with me at once."

He unfastened their chains and drove them out of the byre; but just as he was going out of the yard gate the woman caught him by the sleeve and said, "You must give me the two hundred thalers now, or I can't let the cows go."

"True enough," answered the man, "but I've forgotten to buckle on my money belt. Don't be afraid, though — you shall have security that I'll pay. I'll take two cows with me and leave one, and then you'll have a good pledge."

The woman saw the force of this, and let the man go off with the cows, and thought to herself, "How pleased Hans will be when he finds out how cleverly I've managed it!"

The peasant came home on the third day, as he had said he would, and asked at once whether the cows were sold.

"Yes indeed, dear Hans," answered his wife, "and for two hundred thalers, just as you said. They're hardly worth so much, but the man took them without a word of objection."

"Where's the money?" asked the peasant.

"Oh, I haven't got the money," replied the woman. "He'd happened to forget his money belt, but he'll bring it soon, and he left good security behind him."

"What sort of security?" asked the man.

"One of the three cows, which he shan't have until he's paid for the other two. I managed it very cunningly, because I kept the smallest one, which eats the least."

The man was enraged and lifted his stick, and was just about to give her the beating he had promised her. But suddenly he let the stick drop and said, "You're the stupidest goose that ever waddled on God's earth — but I'm sorry for you. I'll go out onto the highways and wait for three days to see whether I can find anybody still stupider than you. If I do, you shall go free; but if I don't find him, you shall have your well-deserved reward without any discount."

He went out onto the great highways, sat down on a stone, and waited to see what would happen.

Then he saw a peasant's wagon coming towards him, with a woman standing bolt upright in the middle of it instead of sitting on the bundle of straw that lay beside her, or walking beside the oxen and leading them. The man thought to himself, "There's certainly one of the sort I'm looking for" — and jumped up and ran backwards and forwards in front of the wagon like somebody not quite right in the head.

"What do you want, my friend?" the woman said to him. "I don't know you. Where do you come from?"

"I've fallen down out of heaven," replied the man, "and I don't know how to get back again. Couldn't you drive me up?"

"No," said the woman, "I don't know the way. But if you come from heaven, you can surely tell me how my husband is; he's been there these three years. You must have seen him."

"Oh yes, I've seen him — but not everybody can do well. He keeps sheep, and the sheep give him a great deal of trouble. They run up the mountains and lose their way in the wilderness, and he has to run after them and drive them together again. His clothes are all torn to pieces too, and will soon fall off his body. There's no tailor there, for Saint Peter won't let any of them in, as you know from the story."

"Who would have thought it?" cried the woman. "I'll tell you what: I'll fetch his Sunday coat, which is still hanging at home in the cupboard. He can wear that and look respectable. You'll be so kind as to take it with you."

"That won't do at all," answered the peasant. "People aren't allowed to take clothes into heaven; they're taken away from you at the gate."

"Then listen," said the woman. "I sold my fine wheat yesterday and got a good lot of money for it. I'll send that to him. If you hide the purse in your pocket, nobody will know that you have it."

"If you can't manage it any other way," said the peasant, "I'll do you that favour."

"Just sit still where you are," said she, "and I'll drive home and fetch the purse. I'll soon be back. I don't sit down on the bundle of straw — I stand up in the wagon, because it makes it lighter for the cattle."

She drove her oxen away, and the peasant thought, "That woman has a perfect gift for folly. If she really brings the money, my wife may count herself lucky, for she'll get no beating."

It was not long before she came back in a great hurry with the money, and put it in his pocket with her own hands. Before she went away she thanked him a thousand times over for his courtesy.

When the woman got home again she found her son, who had come in from the field. She told him about the unlooked-for things that had happened to her, and then added, "I'm truly delighted to have found a chance of sending something to my poor husband. Who would ever have imagined that he could be in want of anything up in heaven?"

The son was full of astonishment. "Mother," said he, "it isn't every day that a man comes down from heaven like that. I'll go out at once and see whether he's still to be found. He must tell me what it's like up there and how the work is done."

He saddled the horse and rode off at full speed. He found the peasant sitting under a willow tree, just about to count the money in the purse.

"Have you seen the man who fell down out of heaven?" the young man called to him.

"Yes," answered the peasant. "He's set off on his way back there, and gone up that hill, since it's rather nearer from there. You could still catch him up if you rode fast."

"Alas," said the young man, "I've been doing tiring work all day, and the ride here has completely worn me out. You know the man — be so kind as to get on my horse and go and persuade him to come here."

"Aha," thought the peasant, "here's another with no wick in his lamp." — "Why shouldn't I do you that favour?" said he; and mounted the horse and rode off at a quick trot.

The young man sat there till nightfall, but the peasant never came back. "The man from heaven must have been in a great hurry and wouldn't turn back," he thought, "and the peasant has no doubt given him the horse to take to my father."

He went home and told his mother what had happened, and that he had sent his father the horse so that he would not have to be always running about.

"You did well," she answered. "Your legs are younger than his, and you can go on foot."

When the peasant got home he put the horse in the stable beside the cow he had as a pledge, and then went to his wife and said, "Trina, as your luck would have it, I've found two who are still sillier fools than you. This time you escape without a beating; I'll store it up for another occasion."

Then he lit his pipe and sat down in his grandfather's chair and said, "It was a good stroke of business, getting a sleek horse and a great purse full of money into the bargain, for two lean cows. If stupidity always brought in as much as that, I'd be quite willing to hold it in honour."

That is what the peasant thought — but no doubt you prefer the simple folk.

Stories about Snakes

First Story

There was once a little child whose mother gave her a small bowl of milk and bread every afternoon, and the child sat down in the yard with it. But when she began to eat, a snake came creeping out of a crack in the wall, dipped its little head in the dish, and ate with her.

The child was pleased by this; and when she was sitting there with her little dish and the snake did not come at once, she called:

	"Snake, snake, come swiftly,
	come here, you tiny thing;
	you shall have your crumbs of bread,
	you shall drink your fill of milk."

Then the snake came in a hurry and enjoyed its food. What is more, it showed its gratitude, for it brought the child all kinds of pretty things out of its hidden treasures: bright stones, pearls and golden playthings.

But the snake only drank the milk and left the breadcrumbs alone. So one day the child took her little spoon and tapped the snake gently on the head with it, and said, "Eat the breadcrumbs as well, little thing."

The mother, who was standing in the kitchen, heard the child talking to somebody; and when she saw that she was hitting a snake with her spoon, she ran out with a log of wood and killed the good little creature.

From that time on a change came over the child. As long as the snake had eaten with her she had grown tall and strong; but now she lost her pretty rosy cheeks and wasted away. It was not long before the owl began to cry in the night, and the robin to gather little twigs and leaves for a funeral wreath; and soon afterwards the child lay on her bier.

Second Story

An orphan child was sitting on the town walls spinning, when she saw a snake coming out of a hole low down in the wall. She quickly spread out beside it one of the blue silk handkerchiefs that snakes are so fond of, and that are the only things they will creep onto.

As soon as the snake saw it, it went back; and then it returned, bringing a small golden crown with it, and laid it on the handkerchief, and went away again. The girl picked up the crown; it glittered, and was of delicate golden filigree work.

It was not long before the snake came back a second time; but when it no longer saw the crown, it crept up to the wall and in its grief beat its little head against it as long as it had the strength, until at last it lay there dead.

If the girl had only left the crown where it was, the snake would certainly have brought still more of its treasures out of the hole.

Third Story

A snake cries, "Huhu, huhu."

A child says, "Come out."

The snake comes out; then the child asks after her little sister: "Haven't you seen little Red-stockings?"

The snake says, "No."

"Neither have I."

"Then I'm like you. Huhu, huhu, huhu."

The Poor Miller’s Boy and the Cat

In a certain mill there lived an old miller who had neither wife nor child, and three apprentices served under him. As they had been with him several years, he said to them one day, "I'm old, and I want to sit in the chimney corner. Go out; and whichever of you brings me home the best horse, to him I'll give the mill, and in return he shall take care of me until my death."

The third of the boys, though, was the drudge, whom the others thought a fool. They grudged him the mill, and afterwards he would not take it.

So the three of them went out together; and when they came to the village the two said to stupid Hans, "You may as well stay here. As long as you live you'll never get a horse."

But Hans went along with them; and when it was night they came to a cave and lay down there to sleep. The two sharp ones waited until Hans had fallen asleep, and then got up and went away, leaving him where he was. And they thought they had done a very clever thing — but it was certain to turn out badly for them.

When the sun rose and Hans woke up, he was lying in a deep cave. He looked round on every side and exclaimed, "Oh, heavens, where am I?"

Then he got up and clambered out of the cave and went into the forest, and thought, "Here I am, all alone and deserted. How am I to get a horse now?"

And while he was walking along full of these thoughts, he met a small tabby cat, which said quite kindly, "Hans, where are you going?"

"Alas, you can't help me."

"I know very well what you want," said the cat. "You want a beautiful horse. Come with me and be my faithful servant for seven years, and then I'll give you one more beautiful than any you've seen in your whole life."

"Well, this is a wonderful cat," thought Hans. "But I'm determined to see whether she's telling the truth."

So she took him with her to her enchanted castle, where there was nobody but cats, who were her servants. They leapt nimbly up and down the stairs and were merry and happy.

In the evening, when they sat down to dinner, three of them had to make music. One played the bassoon, another the fiddle, and the third put a trumpet to his lips and blew his cheeks out as far as he possibly could.

When they had dined, the table was carried away, and the cat said, "Now, Hans, come and dance with me."

"No," said he, "I won't dance with a pussycat. I've never done that yet."

"Then take him to bed," said she to the cats.

So one of them lit him to his bedroom, one pulled his shoes off, one his stockings, and at last one of them blew out the candle. Next morning they came back and helped him out of bed: one put his stockings on for him, one tied his garters, one brought his shoes, one washed him, and one dried his face with her tail.

"That feels very soft," said Hans.

But he had to serve the cat and chop wood every day; and to do it he had an axe of silver, and the wedge and the saw were silver too, and the mallet was copper. So he chopped the wood small, and stayed there in the house and had good food and drink — but he never saw anybody except the tabby cat and her servants.

Once she said to him, "Go and mow my meadow and dry the grass" — and gave him a scythe of silver and a whetstone of gold, but told him to hand them back carefully. So Hans went and did as he was told; and when he had finished the work he carried the scythe and the whetstone and the hay back to the house, and asked whether it was not yet time for her to give him his reward.

"No," said the cat, "you must first do something more for me of the same kind. Here is timber of silver, a carpenter's axe, a square and everything else that's needed, all of silver. With these, build me a small house."

So Hans built the small house, and said that he had now done everything, and still had no horse. All the same, the seven years had gone by for him as if they were six months.

The cat asked whether he would like to see her horses. "Yes," said Hans. Then she opened the door of the small house; and when she had opened it, there stood twelve horses — such horses, so bright and shining, that his heart rejoiced at the sight of them.

And now she gave him food and drink, and said, "Go home. I won't give you your horse to take with you; but in three days' time I'll follow you and bring it."

So Hans set out, and she showed him the way to the mill. But she had never once given him a new coat, and he had had to keep on the dirty old smock he had brought with him, which in seven years had grown too small for him everywhere.

When he reached home, the two other apprentices were back as well, and each of them had certainly brought a horse with him — but one of them was blind and the other lame. They asked Hans where his horse was.

"It will follow me in three days' time."

Then they laughed and said, "Really, stupid Hans, where would you get a horse? It'll be a fine one!"

Hans went into the parlour, but the miller said he should not sit down at the table, since he was so ragged and torn that they would all be ashamed of him if anybody came in. So they gave him a mouthful of food outside; and at night, when they went to bed, the other two would not let him have a bed, and at last he had to creep into the goose house and lie down on a little hard straw.

In the morning, when he woke, the three days had passed; and a coach came with six horses, and they shone so brightly that it was a delight to see them; and a servant brought a seventh as well, which was for the poor miller's boy. And a magnificent princess got down from the coach and went into the mill — and this princess was the little tabby cat whom poor Hans had served for seven years.

She asked the miller where the miller's boy, the drudge, was.

Then the miller said, "We can't have him here in the mill, he's so ragged. He's lying in the goose house."

Then the King's daughter said that they were to bring him at once. So they brought him out, and he had to hold his little smock together to cover himself. The servants unpacked splendid clothes, and washed him and dressed him; and when that was done, no king could have looked handsomer.

Then the lady asked to see the horses the other apprentices had brought home, and one of them was blind and the other lame. So she ordered her servant to bring the seventh horse; and when the miller saw it, he said that such a horse as that had never come into his yard before.

"And that's for the third miller's boy," said she.

"Then he must have the mill," said the miller.

But the King's daughter said that the horse was there, and that he was to keep his mill as well; and she took her faithful Hans and set him in the coach and drove away with him.

They drove first to the little house he had built with the silver tools — and behold, it was a great castle, and everything inside it was of silver and gold. And then she married him, and he was rich, so rich that he had enough for the rest of his life.

After this, let nobody ever say that somebody who seems silly can never become a person of importance.

The Two Travellers

Hill and valley never meet, but the children of men do, good and bad. And so it happened that a shoemaker and a tailor once met on their travels.

The tailor was a handsome little fellow, always merry and full of enjoyment. He saw the shoemaker coming towards him from the other side; and as he could tell by his bag what trade he followed, he sang him a little mocking song:

	"Sew me the seam,
	draw me the thread,
	spread it over with pitch,
	knock the nail on the head."

But the shoemaker could not take a joke. He pulled a face as if he had drunk vinegar, and made a movement as though he were about to take the tailor by the throat. The little fellow, though, began to laugh, and held out his bottle to him and said, "No harm was meant. Take a drink and swallow your anger down."

The shoemaker took a very hearty drink, and the storm on his face began to clear. He gave the bottle back to the tailor and said, "I spoke civilly to you. A man speaks well after plenty of drink, but not after plenty of thirst. Shall we travel together?"

"All right," answered the tailor, "so long as it suits you to go to a big town where there's no shortage of work."

"That's exactly where I want to go," answered the shoemaker. "In a little nest there's nothing to earn, and out in the country people like to go barefoot."

So they travelled on together, always setting one foot in front of the other like a weasel in the snow.

Both of them had time enough, but little to bite on. When they reached a town they went round and paid their respects to the tradesmen; and because the tailor looked so lively and merry, and had such pretty red cheeks, everybody gave him work willingly — and when his luck was good, the masters' daughters gave him a kiss under the porch as well. When he met the shoemaker again, the tailor always had the more in his bundle.

The ill-tempered shoemaker pulled a sour face and thought, "The greater the rascal, the greater the luck." But the tailor began to laugh and sing, and shared everything he got with his comrade. If a couple of pennies jingled in his pockets he ordered good cheer, and thumped the table in his joy till the glasses danced; and it was lightly come, lightly go with him.

When they had travelled some time, they came to a great forest that the road to the capital ran through. There were two footpaths through it, though, one of which was a seven days' journey and the other only two; but neither of the travellers knew which was the short one. They sat down under an oak tree and took counsel together about how they should judge it, and how many days' bread they should take with them.

The shoemaker said, "A man must look before he leaps. I'll take bread for a week with me."

"What!" said the tailor. "Drag bread for seven days on my back like a beast of burden, and not be able to look about me? I shall trust in God and not trouble myself about anything. The money I have in my pocket is as good in summer as in winter; but in hot weather bread goes dry, and mouldy into the bargain. Even my coat doesn't reach as far as it might. Besides, why shouldn't we find the right way? Bread for two days, and that's enough."

So each of them bought his own bread, and then they tried their luck in the forest.

It was as quiet in there as in a church. No wind stirred, no brook murmured, no bird sang, and no sunbeam forced its way through the thick-leaved branches. The shoemaker never said a word; the heavy bread weighed his back down until the sweat streamed down his cross, gloomy face. The tailor, though, was quite merry; he jumped about, whistled on a leaf, or sang a song, and thought to himself, "God in heaven must be pleased to see me so happy."

This lasted two days; but on the third the forest showed no sign of ending, and the tailor had eaten all his bread, so his heart did after all sink a yard deeper. Still he did not lose courage, but relied on God and on his luck. On the third day he lay down in the evening hungry under a tree, and got up next morning hungry still. So the fourth day passed too; and when the shoemaker sat down on a fallen tree and devoured his dinner, the tailor could only look on.

If he begged for a little piece of bread, the other laughed mockingly and said, "You've always been so merry — now you can find out for once what it's like to be sad. The birds that sing too early in the morning are struck by the hawk in the evening." In short, he was pitiless.

But on the fifth morning the poor tailor could no longer stand up, and was hardly able to get out one word for weakness; his cheeks were white and his eyes red.

Then the shoemaker said to him, "I'll give you a bit of bread today; but in return I'll put out your right eye."

The unlucky tailor, who still wanted to save his life, could do it no other way. He wept once more with both eyes, and then held them out; and the shoemaker, who had a heart of stone, put out his right eye with a sharp knife.

The tailor remembered what his mother used to say to him when he had been eating secretly in the pantry: "Eat what you can, and suffer what you must."

When he had eaten his dearly bought bread he got on his legs again, forgot his misery and comforted himself with the thought that he could always see enough with one eye.

But on the sixth day hunger made itself felt again, and gnawed him almost to the heart. In the evening he collapsed by a tree, and on the seventh morning he could not raise himself for faintness, and death was close at hand.

Then the shoemaker said, "I'll show mercy and give you bread once more; but you shan't have it for nothing. I shall put out your other eye for it."

And now the tailor felt how thoughtless his life had been, and prayed to God for forgiveness, and said, "Do what you will; I'll bear what I must. But remember that our Lord God doesn't always look on without doing anything, and that an hour will come when the evil deed you've done to me, and which I never deserved of you, will be paid back. When times were good with me, I shared what I had with you. My trade is of the kind where every stitch has to be exactly like the last. If I no longer have my eyes and can sew no more, I must go begging. At least don't leave me here alone when I'm blind, or I shall die of hunger."

But the shoemaker, who had driven God out of his heart, took the knife and put out his left eye. Then he gave him a bit of bread to eat, held out a stick to him, and led him along behind him.

When the sun went down they came out of the forest, and in the open country in front of them stood the gallows. The shoemaker led the blind tailor over to it, and then left him there alone and went his way.

Weariness, pain and hunger made the wretched man fall asleep, and he slept the whole night through. When day dawned he woke, but did not know where he was lying. Two poor sinners were hanging on the gallows, and a crow sat on each of their heads.

Then one of the hanged men began to speak, and said, "Brother, are you awake?"

"Yes, I'm awake," answered the second.

"Then I'll tell you something," said the first. "The dew that has fallen down over us from the gallows tonight gives anybody who washes himself with it his eyes back. If blind people only knew that, how many would get their sight again who don't believe such a thing is possible!"

When the tailor heard that, he took his handkerchief and pressed it on the grass; and when it was wet with dew, he washed his empty eye sockets with it. Immediately what the man on the gallows had said came true, and a pair of healthy new eyes filled the sockets.

It was not long before the tailor saw the sun rise behind the mountains. On the plain in front of him lay the great royal city with its magnificent gates and its hundred towers, and the golden balls and crosses on the spires began to shine. He could make out every leaf on the trees, and see the birds flying past and the midges dancing in the air. He took a needle out of his pocket; and as he could thread it as well as he ever had, his heart danced with delight.

He threw himself on his knees and thanked God for the mercy he had shown him, and said his morning prayer. And he did not forget to pray as well for the poor sinners hanging there, swinging against each other in the wind like the pendulums of clocks. Then he took his bundle on his back and soon forgot the pain of heart he had suffered, and went on his way singing and whistling.

The first thing he met was a brown foal running loose about the fields. He caught it by the mane and wanted to spring onto it and ride into the town. But the foal begged to be let go.

"I'm still too young," it said. "Even a light tailor like you would break my back in two. Let me go until I've grown strong. A time may come when I can repay you for it."

"Off you go," said the tailor. "I can see you're still a giddy thing." And he gave it a touch of a switch across its back, whereupon it kicked up its hind legs for joy, leapt over hedges and ditches, and galloped away into the open country.

But the little tailor had eaten nothing since the day before. "The sun fills my eyes, to be sure," said he, "but the bread doesn't fill my mouth. The first thing that comes my way and is even half edible will have to suffer for it."

Just then a stork came stepping solemnly over the meadow towards him. "Halt, halt!" cried the tailor, and seized him by the leg. "I don't know whether you're good to eat or not, but my hunger doesn't leave me much choice. I must cut your head off and roast you."

"Don't do that," replied the stork. "I'm a sacred bird that brings people great good, and nobody does me any harm. Leave me my life, and I may do you a good turn some other way."

"Well, be off, Cousin Longlegs," said the tailor. The stork rose up, let its long legs hang down, and flew gently away.

"What's to be the end of this?" the tailor said to himself at last. "My hunger grows greater and greater and my stomach emptier and emptier. Whatever comes my way now is lost."

At that moment he saw a couple of young ducks on a pond come swimming towards him. "You come just at the right moment," said he — and caught hold of one of them and was about to wring its neck.

At this an old duck that was hidden among the reeds began to scream loudly, and swam up to him with her beak open, and begged him urgently to spare her dear children. "Can't you imagine," said she, "how your own mother would grieve if somebody wanted to carry you off and finish you?"

"Be quiet, now," said the good-natured tailor. "You shall keep your children" — and he put his prisoner back in the water.

When he turned round he was standing in front of an old tree that was partly hollow, and saw some wild bees flying in and out of it. "There I shall find the reward of my good deed straight away," said the tailor. "The honey will refresh me."

But the queen bee came out and threatened him, and said, "If you touch my people and destroy my nest, our stings shall pierce your skin like ten thousand red-hot needles. But if you'll leave us in peace and go your way, we'll do you a service for it another time."

The little tailor saw that here too there was nothing to be done. "Three dishes empty and nothing on the fourth is a poor dinner."

So he dragged himself with his starved-out stomach into the town; and as it was just striking twelve, everything was cooked and ready for him at the inn, and he could sit straight down to dinner.

When he had had enough he said, "Now I'll get to work." He went round the town, looked for a master, and soon found a good place. And as he had thoroughly learned his trade, it was not long before he became famous, and everybody wanted his new coat made by the little tailor, whose importance grew daily.

"I can go no further in skill," said he, "and yet things improve every day."

At last the King appointed him court tailor.

But see how things happen in this world! On the very same day his old comrade the shoemaker became court shoemaker. And when the shoemaker caught sight of the tailor and saw that he had two healthy eyes again, his conscience troubled him. "Before he takes his revenge on me," he thought, "I must dig a pit for him." But he who digs a pit for another falls into it himself.

In the evening, when work was over and it had grown dusk, he stole to the King and said, "My lord King, the tailor is an arrogant fellow, and he has boasted that he'll get back the gold crown that was lost in ancient times."

"That would please me very much," said the King; and he had the tailor brought before him next morning and ordered him to get the crown back, or leave the town for ever.

"Oho," thought the tailor, "a rogue gives more than he has got. If the surly King wants me to do what nobody can do, I won't wait till morning — I'll go out of the town this very day."

So he packed his bundle; but once he was outside the gate he could not help being sorry to give up his good fortune and turn his back on the town where everything had gone so well for him.

He came to the pond where he had made the acquaintance of the ducks; and at that very moment the old duck whose young ones he had spared was sitting there on the bank, preening herself with her beak. She recognised him at once, and asked why he was hanging his head so.

"You won't be surprised when you hear what's happened to me," replied the tailor, and told her his story.

"If that's all," said the duck, "we can help you. The crown fell into the water and is lying down there at the bottom; we'll soon bring it up again for you. Meanwhile, just spread your handkerchief out on the bank."

She dived down with her twelve young ones; and in five minutes she was up again, sitting with the crown resting on her wings, while the twelve young ones swam round about with their beaks under it, helping to carry it. They swam to the bank and laid the crown on the handkerchief.

Nobody could imagine how magnificent that crown was; when the sun shone on it, it gleamed like a hundred thousand rubies. The tailor tied his handkerchief together by its four corners and carried it to the King, who was full of joy, and put a gold chain round the tailor's neck.

When the shoemaker saw that one stroke had failed, he contrived a second, and went to the King and said, "My lord King, the tailor has become insolent again. He boasts that he'll make a copy in wax of the whole royal palace, with everything belonging to it, loose or fixed, inside and out."

The King sent for the tailor and ordered him to make a copy in wax of the whole royal palace, with everything belonging to it, movable or immovable, inside and out; and if he did not manage it, or if so much as a single nail in the wall were missing, he should be imprisoned underground for the rest of his life.

The tailor thought, "It gets worse and worse. Nobody can stand this." And he threw his bundle on his back and went out.

When he came to the hollow tree he sat down and hung his head. The bees came flying out, and the queen bee asked him whether he had a stiff neck, since he was holding his head so crookedly.

"Alas, no," answered the tailor. "Something quite different is weighing me down" — and he told her what the King had demanded of him.

The bees began to buzz and hum among themselves, and the queen bee said, "Just go home again; but come back tomorrow at this time and bring a large sheet with you, and then all will be well."

So he turned back; but the bees flew to the royal palace and straight in at the open windows, and crept round into every corner and inspected everything most carefully. Then they hurried back and modelled the palace in wax so quickly that anybody watching would have thought it was growing in front of his eyes.

By the evening it was all ready; and when the tailor came next morning, the whole splendid building was there, and not one nail in the wall or tile on the roof was missing; and it was delicate too, and white as snow, and it smelt as sweet as honey.

The tailor wrapped it carefully in his cloth and took it to the King, who could not admire it enough, and set it up in his largest hall, and in return presented the tailor with a large stone house.

The shoemaker, though, did not give up, but went to the King a third time and said, "My lord King, it has come to the tailor's ears that no water will spring up in the castle courtyard, and he has boasted that it shall rise up in the middle of the courtyard as high as a man and be as clear as crystal."

Then the King had the tailor brought before him and said, "If a stream of water doesn't rise in my courtyard by tomorrow, as you've promised, the executioner shall make you shorter by the head on that very spot."

The poor tailor did not take long to think about it, but hurried out to the gate; and because this time it was a matter of life and death for him, tears rolled down his face.

And as he was going out like that, full of sorrow, the foal he had once given its freedom to, and which had now become a beautiful chestnut horse, came leaping towards him.

"The time has come," it said to the tailor, "when I can repay you for your good deed. I know already what you need, but you shall soon have help. Get on my back — it can carry two such as you."

The tailor's courage came back to him. He jumped up at a single bound, and the horse went at full speed into the town and right up into the castle courtyard. It galloped round it three times as quick as lightning, and the third time it fell violently to the ground.

At that same instant there was a terrific clap of thunder; a lump of earth in the middle of the courtyard flew up into the air like a cannonball, and right over the castle; and directly after it a jet of water rose as high as a man on horseback, and the water was as pure as crystal, and the sunbeams began to dance on it.

When the King saw that, he got up in amazement and went and embraced the tailor in front of everybody.

But his good fortune did not last long. The King had daughters in plenty, one prettier than the next, but he had no son. So the malicious shoemaker took himself to the King for the fourth time, and said, "My lord King, the tailor hasn't given up his arrogance. Now he has boasted that if he liked, he could have a son brought to my lord King through the air."

The King had the tailor summoned, and said, "If you have a son brought to me within nine days, you shall have my eldest daughter for a wife."

"The reward is indeed great," thought the little tailor. "A man would gladly do something for that; but the cherries grow too high for me. If I climb for them, the branch will break under me and I shall fall."

He went home, sat himself down cross-legged on his work table and thought over what was to be done. "It can't be managed," he cried at last. "I'll go away. After all, I can't live in peace here."

He tied up his bundle and hurried away to the gate. When he got to the meadow he caught sight of his old friend the stork, walking up and down like a philosopher. Now and then he stood still, gave a frog his close consideration, and at length swallowed it down.

The stork came over and greeted him. "I see," he began, "that you've got your pack on your back. Why are you leaving the town?"

The tailor told him what the King had demanded of him, and how he could not do it, and lamented his misfortune.

"Don't let your hair go grey over that," said the stork. "I'll help you out of your difficulty. I've been carrying children in swaddling clothes into the town for a long while now, so for once in a way I can fetch a little prince out of the well. Go home and set your mind at rest. Nine days from now, go to the royal palace, and I'll come there."

The little tailor went home; and at the appointed time he was at the castle. It was not long before the stork came flying up and tapped at the window. The tailor opened it, and Cousin Longlegs came carefully in and walked with solemn steps over the smooth marble floor. And he had a baby in his beak, as lovely as an angel, that stretched out its little hands to the Queen. The stork laid it in her lap, and she caressed it and kissed it, and was beside herself with delight.

Before the stork flew away he took his travelling bag off his back and handed it over to the Queen. In it were little paper parcels of coloured sweets, and they were shared out among the little princesses. The eldest, though, got none of them — she got the merry tailor for a husband.

"It seems to me," said he, "just as if I'd won the highest prize of all. My mother was right after all: she always said that whoever trusts in God and has good luck can never fail."

The shoemaker had to make the shoes the little tailor danced in at the wedding feast, and after that he was ordered to leave the town for ever. The road to the forest led him past the gallows. Worn out with anger and rage and the heat of the day, he threw himself down. And when he had closed his eyes and was about to sleep, the two crows flew down from the heads of the hanged men and pecked his eyes out.

In his madness he ran off into the forest, and he must have died there of hunger, for nobody has ever seen him again or heard of him since.

Hans the Hedgehog

There was once a countryman who had money and land in plenty; but rich as he was, one thing was still missing from his happiness: he had no children. Often, when he went into the town with the other farmers, they mocked him and asked why he had no children. At last he grew angry, and when he got home he said, "I will have a child, even if it's a hedgehog."

Then his wife had a child that was a hedgehog in the upper part of its body and a boy in the lower; and when she saw the child she was horrified, and said, "There, you see what ill luck you've brought on us."

Then the man said, "What can be done now? The boy must be christened — but we'll never get a godfather for him."

The woman said, "And we can't call him anything but Hans the Hedgehog."

When he was christened, the parson said, "He can't go into any ordinary bed because of his spikes." So a little straw was put behind the stove, and Hans the Hedgehog was laid on it. His mother could not nurse him, for he would have pricked her with his quills. So he lay there behind the stove for eight years; and his father grew tired of him and thought, "If only he would die!" But he did not die; he went on lying there.

Now it happened that there was a fair in the town, and the farmer was about to go to it, and asked his wife what he should bring her back.

"A little meat and a couple of white rolls that are wanted for the house," said she.

Then he asked the servant girl, and she wanted a pair of slippers and some stockings with clocks embroidered on them. And at last he said, "And what will you have, Hans my Hedgehog?"

"Dear father," he said, "do bring me bagpipes."

So when the father came home again, he gave his wife what he had bought her, meat and white rolls; and then he gave the maid the slippers and the stockings with clocks; and last of all he went behind the stove and gave Hans the Hedgehog his bagpipes.

And when Hans the Hedgehog had the bagpipes, he said, "Dear father, do go to the forge and have the cock shod, and then I'll ride away and never come back again."

At this his father was delighted at the thought of getting rid of him, and had the cock shod for him. And when it was done, Hans the Hedgehog got on it and rode away — but took pigs and donkeys with him, which he meant to keep in the forest.

When they got there he made the cock fly up to the top of a high tree with him, and there he sat for many a long year and watched his donkeys and his pigs until the herd was very large; and his father knew nothing about him. And as he sat in the tree he played his bagpipes, and made music that was very beautiful.

Once a King came travelling by who had lost his way, and heard the music. He was astonished at it, and sent his servant out to look all round and see where this music came from. The servant looked about, but saw nothing except a little animal sitting up aloft in the tree, which looked like a cock with a hedgehog on it, and which was making this music.

Then the King told the servant to ask why he was sitting there, and whether he knew the road that led to his kingdom. So Hans the Hedgehog came down out of the tree, and said he would show the way if the King would write out a bond and promise him whatever first met him in the royal courtyard when he reached home.

Then the King thought, "I can easily do that. Hans the Hedgehog understands nothing, and I can write what I like."

So the King took pen and ink and wrote something; and when he had done it, Hans the Hedgehog showed him the way, and he got safely home.

But his daughter, when she saw him from a distance, was so overjoyed that she ran to meet him and kissed him. Then he remembered Hans the Hedgehog, and told her what had happened: that he had been forced to promise whatever first met him when he got home to a very strange animal that sat on a cock as if it were a horse and made beautiful music — but that instead of writing that he should have what he wanted, he had written that he should not have it.

At this the princess was glad, and said he had done well, for she would never have gone away with the hedgehog.

Hans the Hedgehog, meanwhile, looked after his donkeys and pigs, and was always merry, and sat in the tree and played his bagpipes.

Now it happened that another King came journeying by with his attendants and his runners; and he too had lost his way, and did not know how to get home again, because the forest was so large. He too heard the beautiful music from a distance, and asked his runner what it could be, and told him to go and see.

Then the runner went under the tree and saw the cock sitting at the top of it and Hans the Hedgehog on the cock. The runner asked him what he was doing up there.

"I'm keeping my donkeys and my pigs. But what is it you want?"

The messenger said that they had lost their way and could not get back into their own kingdom, and asked whether he would not show them the way.

Then Hans the Hedgehog came down out of the tree with the cock, and told the old King that he would show him the way if he would give him for his own whatever first met him in front of his royal palace. The King said yes, and wrote out a promise to Hans the Hedgehog that he should have it.
