That done, Hans rode on ahead of him on the cock and pointed out the way, and the King reached his kingdom again safely.

When he got to the courtyard there was great rejoicing. Now he had an only daughter who was very beautiful; she ran to meet him and threw her arms round his neck, delighted to have her old father back again. She asked him where in the world he had been so long.

So he told her how he had lost his way and had very nearly not come back at all; but that as he was travelling through a great forest, a creature half hedgehog and half man, sitting astride a cock in a high tree and making music, had shown him the way and helped him out — but that in return he had promised him whatever first met him in the royal courtyard, and that was herself, which made him unhappy now.

But at this she promised that, for love of her father, she would gladly go with this Hans if he came.

Hans the Hedgehog, meanwhile, took care of his pigs, and the pigs multiplied until there were so many of them that the whole forest was full. So Hans the Hedgehog decided not to live in the forest any longer, and sent word to his father to have every sty in the village emptied, for he was coming with such a great herd that anybody who wanted to could kill.

When his father heard that he was troubled, for he thought Hans the Hedgehog had died long ago. But Hans the Hedgehog seated himself on the cock and drove the pigs into the village before him, and ordered the slaughter to begin. And there was such a killing and a chopping as might have been heard two miles off.

After this Hans the Hedgehog said, "Father, let me have the cock shod once more at the forge, and then I'll ride away and never come back as long as I live."

So his father had the cock shod once more, and was pleased that Hans the Hedgehog would never come back again.

Hans the Hedgehog rode away to the first kingdom. There the King had commanded that anybody who came riding on a cock and carrying bagpipes should be shot at, cut down or stabbed by everyone, so that he should not get into the palace.

So when Hans the Hedgehog came riding up, they all pressed forward against him with their pikes; but he spurred the cock, and it flew up over the gate and in front of the King's window and settled there; and Hans cried that the King must give him what he had promised, or he would take both his life and his daughter's.

Then the King began to speak kindly to his daughter, and to beg her to go away with Hans in order to save her own life and her father's. So she dressed herself in white, and her father gave her a carriage with six horses and magnificent attendants, and gold and property with them. She seated herself in the carriage and put Hans the Hedgehog beside her, with the cock and the bagpipes; and then they took their leave and drove away, and the King thought he would never see her again.

But he was wrong in what he expected. When they were a short way out of the town, Hans the Hedgehog stripped her pretty clothes off her and pierced her with his hedgehog's skin until she bled all over. "That's the reward of your falseness," said he. "Go your way — I won't have you." And with that he chased her home again, and she was disgraced for the rest of her life.

Hans the Hedgehog, though, rode on further on the cock, with his bagpipes, to the lands of the second King, the one he had shown the way to. This King, however, had given orders that if anybody resembling Hans the Hedgehog should come, they were to present arms, give him safe conduct, cry long life to him, and lead him to the royal palace.

But when the King's daughter saw him she was terrified, for he looked altogether too strange. All the same she remembered that she could not change her mind, because she had given her promise to her father. So Hans the Hedgehog was made welcome by her and married to her, and had to go with her to the royal table; and she sat down beside him, and they ate and drank.

When evening came and they wanted to go to sleep, she was afraid of his quills; but he told her she need not be afraid, for no harm would come to her. And he told the old King to appoint four men to keep watch by the door of the room and light a great fire; and said that when he went into the room and was about to get into bed, he would creep out of his hedgehog's skin and leave it lying beside the bed, and the men were to run quickly and pick it up and throw it in the fire, and stay by it until it was burnt up.

When the clock struck eleven he went into the room, stripped off the hedgehog's skin and left it lying by the bed. Then the men came and snatched it up quickly and threw it in the fire; and when the fire had burnt it up, he was released, and lay there in bed in human shape — but he was coal-black, as if he had been burnt. The King sent for his physician, who washed him with precious salves and anointed him; and he became white, and was a handsome young man.

When the King's daughter saw that, she was glad; and next morning they got up joyfully and ate and drank, and then the marriage was properly celebrated, and Hans the Hedgehog received the kingdom from the old King.

When several years had gone by, he went with his wife to his father and said that he was his son. His father, though, declared that he had no son — he had had only one, and it had been born like a hedgehog, with spikes, and had gone out into the world. Then Hans made himself known, and the old father rejoiced and went with him to his kingdom.

	My tale is done,
	and away it has run
	to little August's house.

The Shroud

There was once a mother who had a little boy of seven years old, who was so handsome and so lovable that nobody could look at him without liking him; and she herself worshipped him above everything in the world.

Now it happened that he suddenly fell ill, and God took him to himself; and the mother could not be comforted for it, and wept both day and night.

But soon afterwards, when the child had been buried, it appeared at night in the places where it had sat and played while it was alive; and if the mother wept, it wept too, and when morning came it disappeared.

But as the mother would not stop crying, it came one night in the little white shroud it had been laid in its coffin in, with its wreath of flowers round its head, and stood at the foot of her bed and said, "Oh, mother, do stop crying, or I shall never fall asleep in my coffin; my shroud won't dry, because of all your tears falling on it."

The mother was frightened when she heard that, and wept no more.

The next night the child came again, holding a little light in its hand, and said, "Look, mother, my shroud is nearly dry, and I can rest in my grave."

Then the mother gave her sorrow into God's keeping and bore it quietly and patiently; and the child came no more, but slept in its little bed beneath the earth.

The Jew Among Thorns

[Editor's note: this tale, and two others in this collection — "The Good Bargain" and "The Bright Sun Brings It to Light" — turn on hostile caricatures of Jews. This edition prints all two hundred and ten tales the Grimms gathered, and prints them whole; nothing here has been softened or cut. This note is set once, at the harshest of the three, to say what the edition has done and why. An edition that quietly dropped them would misrepresent both the book and the century that made it.]

There was once a rich man who had a servant who served him diligently and honestly. He was the first out of bed every morning and the last to go to rest at night; and whenever there was a hard job to be done that nobody else cared to take on, he was always the first to set about it. What is more, he never complained, but was contented with everything, and always cheerful.

When a year was up, his master gave him no wages, for he said to himself, "That's the cleverest way; I shall save something, and he won't go away, but will stay quietly in my service."

The servant said nothing, but did his work the second year as he had the first; and when at the end of that he got no wages either, he made the best of it and still stayed on.

When the third year had gone by as well, the master thought it over, put his hand in his pocket, but pulled nothing out. Then at last the servant said, "Master, I've served you honestly for three years. Be so good as to give me what I'm owed, for I want to leave and look about me a little more in the world."

"Yes, my good fellow," answered the old miser, "you've served me industriously, and so you shall be cheerfully rewarded." And he put his hand in his pocket, but counted out only three farthings, saying, "There — a farthing for each year. That's large and liberal pay, such as you'd have got from few masters."

The honest servant, who understood little about money, put his fortune in his pocket and thought, "Ah, now that my purse is full, why should I trouble and plague myself any longer with hard work?"

So on he went, up hill and down dale, singing and jumping to his heart's content.

Now it happened that as he was going past a thicket, a little man stepped out and called to him, "Where away, merry brother? I can see you don't carry many cares."

"Why should I be sad?" answered the servant. "I have plenty. Three years' wages are jingling in my pocket."

"How much is your treasure?" the dwarf asked him.

"How much? Three farthings sterling, all told."

"Look here," said the dwarf, "I'm a poor needy man. Give me your three farthings. I can work no longer, but you're young and can easily earn your bread."

And as the servant had a good heart and felt sorry for the old man, he gave him the three farthings, saying, "Take them in heaven's name; I shall be none the worse for it."

Then the little man said, "As I can see you have a good heart, I grant you three wishes — one for each farthing; and they shall all be fulfilled."

"Aha," said the servant, "you're one of those who can work wonders. Well, then, if that's how it is, I wish, first, for a gun that will hit everything I aim at; secondly, for a fiddle that will make everybody who hears me play it dance; and thirdly, that if I ask a favour of anybody, he won't be able to refuse it."

"All that you shall have," said the dwarf; and he put his hand into the bush — and only think, there lay a fiddle and a gun, all ready, just as if they had been ordered. He gave them to the servant, and then said to him, "Whatever you may ask at any time, no man in the world shall be able to refuse you."

"Heart alive! What more could anybody want?" said the servant to himself, and went merrily on.

Soon afterwards he met a Jew with a long goat's beard, who was standing listening to the song of a bird sitting at the top of a tree. "Good heavens," he was exclaiming, "that such a small creature should have such a fearfully loud voice! If only it were mine! If only somebody would sprinkle salt on its tail!"

"If that's all," said the servant, "the bird shall soon be down here." And taking aim, he pulled the trigger, and down fell the bird into the thorn bushes. "Go on, you rogue," he said to the Jew, "and fetch the bird out for yourself."

"Oh," said the Jew, "leave out the rogue, my master, and I'll do it at once. I'll get the bird out for myself, since you really have hit it." Then he lay down on the ground and began to crawl into the thicket.

When he was well in among the thorns, the good servant's humour so tempted him that he took up his fiddle and began to play. In a moment the Jew's legs began to move and to jump into the air; and the more the servant fiddled, the better the dance went. But the thorns tore his shabby coat off him, combed his beard, and pricked and plucked him all over his body.

"Oh dear," cried the Jew, "what do I want with your fiddling? Leave the fiddle alone, master; I don't want to dance."

But the servant did not listen to him, and thought, "You've fleeced people often enough — now the thorn bushes shall do the same to you." And he began to play again, so that the Jew had to jump higher than ever, and scraps of his coat were left hanging on the thorns.

"Oh, woe is me!" cried the Jew. "I'll give the gentleman whatever he asks, if only he'll leave off fiddling — a purse full of gold."

"If you're so liberal," said the servant, "I'll stop my music. But this I must say to your credit: you dance to it so well that it's quite an art." And having taken the purse, he went his way.

The Jew stood still and watched the servant quietly until he was far off and out of sight, and then he screamed out with all his might, "You miserable musician, you beer-house fiddler! Wait till I catch you alone — I'll hunt you till the soles of your shoes fall off! You ragamuffin! Just put five farthings in your mouth, and then you might be worth three halfpence!" — and went on abusing him as fast as he could speak.

As soon as he had refreshed himself a little this way and got his breath back, he ran into the town to the justice.

"My lord judge," he said, "I've come to make a complaint. See how a rascal has robbed and ill-treated me on the public highway! A stone on the ground might pity me. My clothes all torn, my body pricked and scratched, my little all gone along with my purse — good ducats, every piece better than the last. For God's sake let the man be thrown into prison!"

"Was it a soldier," said the judge, "who cut you about like that with his sabre?"

"Nothing of the sort," said the Jew. "It was no sword he had, but a gun hanging on his back and a fiddle at his neck. The wretch can easily be known."

So the judge sent his people out after the man, and they found the good servant, who had been going along quite slowly; and they found the purse with the money on him too.

As soon as he was brought before the judge he said, "I never touched the Jew or took his money. He gave it to me of his own free will, so that I'd leave off fiddling, because he couldn't bear my music."

"Heaven defend us!" cried the Jew. "His lies are as thick as flies on a wall."

But the judge did not believe his tale either, and said, "This is a poor defence. No Jew would do that." And because he had committed robbery on the public highway, he sentenced the good servant to be hanged.

As he was being led away, the Jew screamed after him again, "You vagabond! You dog of a fiddler! Now you're going to get your well-earned reward!"

The servant walked quietly up the ladder with the hangman; but on the last step he turned round and said to the judge, "Grant me just one request before I die."

"Yes — as long as you don't ask for your life," said the judge.

"I'm not asking for my life," answered the servant. "But as a last favour, let me play once more on my fiddle."

The Jew raised a great cry of "Murder! Murder! For goodness' sake don't allow it! Don't allow it!"

But the judge said, "Why shouldn't I let him have this short pleasure? It's been granted to him and he shall have it." And in any case he could not have refused, because of the gift that had been given to the servant.

Then the Jew cried, "Oh, woe is me! Tie me, tie me fast!"

Meanwhile the good servant took his fiddle from his neck and made ready. As he gave the first scrape, they all began to quiver and shake — the judge, his clerk, the hangman and his men; and the cord fell out of the hand of the one who was going to tie the Jew fast. At the second scrape they all raised their legs, and the hangman let go of the good servant and got himself ready to dance. At the third scrape they all leapt up and began to dance, the judge and the Jew being the best jumpers of them all.

Soon everybody who had gathered in the marketplace out of curiosity was dancing with them, old and young, fat and thin, one with another. The dogs that had run over got up on their hind legs and capered about too; and the longer he played, the higher the dancers sprang, until they knocked their heads together and began to shriek terribly.

At length the judge cried, quite out of breath, "I'll give you your life, if you'll only stop fiddling."

The good servant took pity on him, and took his fiddle and hung it round his neck again, and came down the ladder. Then he went up to the Jew, who was lying on the ground gasping for breath, and said, "You rascal, now confess where you got that money, or I'll take my fiddle and start playing again."

"I stole it, I stole it!" cried he. "But you've honestly earned it."

So the judge had the Jew taken to the gallows and hanged as a thief.

The Skilful Huntsman

There was once a young fellow who had learned the locksmith's trade, and told his father he would now go out into the world and seek his fortune.

"Very well," said his father, "I'm quite content with that" — and gave him some money for the journey.

So he travelled about and looked for work. After a time he decided not to follow the locksmith's trade any more, for he had lost his liking for it; but he took a fancy to hunting.

Then on his wanderings he met a huntsman dressed in green, who asked where he came from and where he was going. The young man said he was a locksmith's apprentice, but that the trade no longer pleased him and he had a liking for huntsmanship; would he teach it to him?

"Oh, yes," said the huntsman, "if you'll come with me."

So the young fellow went with him, bound himself to him for some years, and learned the art of hunting. After that he wanted to try his luck elsewhere; and the huntsman gave him nothing by way of payment but an air gun, which had this property, though: that it hit its mark without fail whenever he shot with it.

Then he set out, and found himself in a very large forest that he could not get to the end of in a day. When evening came he sat himself up in a high tree to be out of reach of the wild beasts. Towards midnight it seemed to him that a tiny little light was glimmering in the distance. So he looked down through the branches towards it, and fixed firmly in his mind where it was. But first of all he took off his hat and threw it down in the direction of the light, so that when he had climbed down he could go to the hat as a marker. Then he got down and went to his hat, put it on again, and went straight on.

The further he went, the bigger the light grew; and when he got close to it he saw that it was an enormous fire, with three giants sitting by it, who had an ox on a spit and were roasting it.

Presently one of them said, "I must just taste whether the meat will soon be fit to eat" — and pulled a piece off, and was about to put it in his mouth when the huntsman shot it out of his hand.

"Well, really," said the giant, "if the wind hasn't blown the bit out of my hand!" — and helped himself to another. But just as he was about to bite into it, the huntsman shot it away from him again.

At this the giant gave the one sitting next to him a box on the ear, and cried angrily, "Why are you snatching my piece away from me?"

"I haven't snatched it away," said the other. "Some sharpshooter must have shot it away from you."

The giant took another piece, but he could not keep it in his hand either, for the huntsman shot it out. Then the giant said, "That must be a good shot, to shoot the bit out of a man's very mouth. Somebody like that would be useful to us." And he called out loudly, "Come here, sharpshooter! Sit down by the fire beside us and eat your fill. We won't hurt you. But if you won't come, and we have to bring you by force, you're a lost man."

At this the young man went up to them and told them he was a skilled huntsman, and that whatever he aimed his gun at, he was sure to hit.

Then they said that if he would come with them he should be well treated; and they told him that outside the forest there was a great lake, and behind it stood a tower, and in the tower was a lovely princess shut up, whom they very much wanted to carry off.

"Yes," said he, "I'll soon get her for you."

Then they added, "But there's something else. There's a tiny little dog that starts barking the moment anybody comes near; and as soon as it barks, everybody in the royal palace wakes up. That's why we can't get in. Can you undertake to shoot it dead?"

"Yes," said he, "that will be a bit of fun for me."

After this he got into a boat and rowed across the lake; and as soon as he landed the little dog came running out and was about to bark, but the huntsman took his air gun and shot it dead.

When the giants saw that they rejoiced, and thought they had the King's daughter safe already; but the huntsman wanted first to see how things stood, and told them they must stay outside until he called them.

Then he went into the castle, and inside all was perfectly quiet and everybody was asleep. When he opened the door of the first room, there was a sword hanging on the wall made of pure silver, with a golden star on it and the King's name; and on a table near it lay a sealed letter, which he broke open, and inside it was written that whoever had the sword could kill everything that opposed him. So he took the sword down from the wall, hung it at his side and went on.

Then he came into the room where the King's daughter lay sleeping; and she was so beautiful that he stood still and held his breath and looked at her. He thought to himself, "How can I hand an innocent girl over to those wild giants, who have evil in their minds?"

He looked further about him; and under the bed stood a pair of slippers, with her father's name and a star on the right one and her own name and a star on the left. She was wearing a great silk neckerchief embroidered with gold, and on the right side was her father's name and on the left her own, all in golden letters.

So the huntsman took a pair of scissors and cut the right corner off it and put it in his knapsack; and then he took the right slipper too, with the King's name on it, and pushed that in. And the girl still lay sleeping; and she was sewn right into her nightdress, and he cut a piece from that as well and pushed it in with the rest — but he did it all without touching her. Then he went out and left her lying asleep and undisturbed.

And when he came back to the gate, the giants were still standing outside waiting for him, expecting that he was bringing the princess. But he called to them to come in, since the girl was already in their power; and said that he could not open the gate to them, but there was a hole they must creep through.

So the first came up; and the huntsman wound the giant's hair round his hand, pulled his head through, and cut it off at one stroke with his sword, and then dragged the rest of him in. He called the second and cut his head off likewise, and then he killed the third as well.

And he was well pleased that he had freed the beautiful girl from her enemies; and he cut out the giants' tongues and put them in his knapsack. Then he thought, "I'll go home to my father and let him see what I've done already, and after that I'll travel about the world. The luck God is pleased to grant me will find me easily enough."

But when the King in the castle woke up, he saw the three giants lying there dead. So he went into his daughter's bedroom and woke her and asked who could have killed the giants.

Then she said, "Dear father, I don't know. I was asleep."

But when she got up and went to put on her slippers, the right one was gone; and when she looked at her neckerchief it was cut, and the right corner was missing; and when she looked at her nightdress a piece was cut out of it.

The King called his whole court together, soldiers and everybody else who was there, and asked who had set his daughter free and killed the giants. Now it happened that he had a captain who was one-eyed and a hideous man, and he said that he had done it. So the old King said that as he had accomplished it, he should marry his daughter.

But the girl said, "Rather than marry him, dear father, I'll go away into the world as far as my legs will carry me."

But the King said that if she would not marry him, she should take off her royal clothes and wear peasant's clothing and go out; and that she should go to a potter and start a trade in earthenware pots.

So she took off her royal clothes and went to a potter and borrowed enough crockery for a stall, and promised him too that if she sold it by the evening she would pay him for it. Then the King said she was to sit down in a corner with it and sell it; and he arranged with some peasants to drive their carts over it, so that everything would be broken into a thousand pieces.

So when the King's daughter had set out her stall in the street, along came the carts and broke everything she had into tiny fragments. She began to weep and said, "Alas, how shall I ever pay for the pots now?"

The King had meant by this to force her into marrying the captain; but instead she went to the potter again and asked whether he would lend to her once more. He said no; she must first pay for the things she had already had.

Then she went to her father and cried and lamented, and said she would go out into the world.

Then he said, "I'll have a little hut built for you out in the forest, and you shall stay in it all your life long and cook for everybody — but you shall take no money for it."

When the hut was ready, a sign was hung on the door with these words on it: "Today given, tomorrow sold."

She stayed there a long time, and word went about the world that there was a girl there who cooked without asking for payment, and that this was set out on a sign outside her door. The huntsman heard it too, and thought to himself, "That would suit you. You're poor, and you have no money."

So he took his air gun and his knapsack — in which all the things he had carried away from the castle as proofs of his honesty were still lying — and went into the forest and found the hut with its sign, "Today given, tomorrow sold." He had put on the sword he had cut off the three giants' heads with, and so he went into the hut and asked to be given something to eat.

He was charmed by the beautiful girl, who was indeed as lovely as a picture. She asked him where he came from and where he was going, and he said, "I'm roaming about the world."

Then she asked him where he had got the sword, since her father's name was on it. He asked her whether she was the King's daughter.

"Yes," she answered.

"With this sword," said he, "I cut off the heads of three giants." And he took their tongues out of his knapsack as proof. Then he showed her the slipper too, and the corner of the neckerchief and the piece of the nightdress.

At this she was overjoyed, and said that he was the man who had delivered her.

So the two of them went to the old King and brought him back to the hut; and she led him into her room and told him that the huntsman was the man who had really freed her from the giants. And when the old King saw all the proofs of it, he could doubt no longer, and said he was very glad to know how it had all happened, and that the huntsman should have her for a wife; at which the girl was glad at heart.

Then she dressed the huntsman up as though he were a foreign lord, and the King ordered a feast to be prepared. When they went to table, the captain sat on the left side of the King's daughter and the huntsman on the right; and the captain thought he was a foreign lord who had come on a visit.

When they had eaten and drunk, the old King said to the captain that he would set him something to guess. "Suppose somebody said that he had killed three giants, and he were asked where the giants' tongues were, and he were made to go and look, and there were none in their heads — how could that happen?"

The captain said, "Then they can't have had any."

"Not so," said the King. "Every animal has a tongue." And then he asked as well what a man would deserve who gave such an answer.

The captain replied, "He ought to be torn to pieces."

Then the King said he had pronounced his own sentence; and the captain was put in prison and then torn into four pieces. But the King's daughter was married to the huntsman.

After this he fetched his father and mother, and they lived with their son in happiness; and after the old King's death he received the kingdom.

The Flail From Heaven

A countryman was once going out to plough with a pair of oxen. When he got to the field, both the animals' horns began to grow, and went on growing; and when he wanted to go home they were so big that the oxen could not get through the gateway for them.

By good luck a butcher came by just then, and he handed them over to him, and made the bargain this way: that he should bring the butcher a measure of turnip seed, and then the butcher was to count him out a Brabant thaler for every seed. Now, I call that well sold.

The peasant went home and carried the measure of turnip seed to him on his back. On the way, though, he lost one seed out of the bag. The butcher paid him fairly, as agreed; and if the peasant had not lost that seed he would have had one thaler more.

Meanwhile, as he went back along the road, the seed had grown into a tree that reached right up to the sky. Then the peasant thought, "Since you have the chance, you must just see what the angels up there are doing, and have them before your eyes for once."

So he climbed up, and saw that the angels up above were threshing oats, and he stood watching them. And while he was watching, he noticed that the tree he was standing on was beginning to sway. He peeped down and saw that somebody was just about to cut it down.

"It would be a bad business if I fell down from here," he thought. And in his need he could think of no better way to save himself than to take the chaff of the oats, which was lying about in heaps, and twist a rope out of it. He also grabbed a hoe and a flail that were lying about in heaven, and let himself down by the rope.

But he came down on earth exactly in the middle of a deep, deep hole. So it was a real piece of luck that he had brought the hoe, for he hoed himself a flight of steps with it and climbed up; and he took the flail with him as a token of his truthfulness, so that nobody could have any doubt about his story.

The Two Kings’ Children

There was once a King who had a little boy about whom it had been foretold that he would be killed by a stag when he was sixteen years old. And when he had reached that age, the huntsmen went hunting with him one day.

In the forest the King's son was separated from the others, and all at once he saw a great stag that he wanted to shoot but could not hit. At length he chased the stag so far that they were right out of the forest; and then suddenly a great tall man was standing there instead of the stag, and said, "It's a good thing I've got you. I've already worn out six pairs of glass skates running after you, and never managed to catch you."

Then he took the King's son with him and dragged him through a great lake to a great palace, and then he had to sit down at table with him and eat something.

When they had eaten together, the King said, "I have three daughters. You must keep watch over the eldest for one night, from nine in the evening till six in the morning; and every time the clock strikes I'll come myself and call. If you give me no answer, tomorrow morning you shall be put to death; but if you always give me an answer, you shall have her for your wife."

When the young people went to the bedroom, there stood a stone image of St. Christopher, and the King's daughter said to it, "My father will come at nine o'clock, and every hour until it strikes three. When he calls, answer him instead of the King's son."

Then the stone image of St. Christopher nodded its head quite quickly, and then more and more slowly, until at last it stood still.

Next morning the King said to him, "You've done the business well; but I can't give my daughter away. Now you must watch a night by my second daughter, and then I'll consider with myself whether you can have my eldest daughter for a wife. But I shall come every hour myself; and when I call you, answer me — and if I call you and you don't reply, your blood shall flow."

Then they both went into the bedroom, and there stood a still larger stone image of St. Christopher, and the King's daughter said to it, "If my father calls, you answer him."

Then the great stone image of St. Christopher again nodded its head quite quickly, and then more and more slowly, until at last it stood still again. And the King's son lay down on the threshold, put his hand under his head and slept.

Next morning the King said to him, "You've done the business really well; but I can't give my daughter away. Now you must watch a night by the youngest princess, and then I'll consider with myself whether you can have my second daughter for a wife. But I shall come every hour myself; and when I call you, answer me — and if I call you and you don't answer, your blood shall flow for me."

So they went to the bedroom together once more, and there was a much greater and much taller image of St. Christopher than either of the first two. The King's daughter said to it, "When my father calls, you answer."

Then the great tall stone image of St. Christopher nodded its head for a good half hour, until at length the head stood still again. And the King's son lay down on the threshold of the door and slept.

Next morning the King said, "You've watched well indeed; but I can't give you my daughter yet. I have a great forest. If you cut it down for me between six o'clock this morning and six tonight, I'll think about it."

Then he gave him a glass axe, a glass wedge and a glass mallet. When he got into the wood he began cutting at once, but the axe broke in two. Then he took the wedge and struck it once with the mallet, and it crumbled as short and as small as sand.

Then he was greatly troubled and believed he would have to die, and sat down and wept.

Now when it was noon the King said, "One of you girls must take him something to eat."

"No," said the two eldest. "We won't take it to him. The one he watched by last can take him something."

So the youngest had to go and take him something to eat. When she got into the forest she asked him how he was getting on.

"Oh," said he, "I'm getting on very badly."

Then she said he was to come and just eat a little.

"No," said he, "I can't do that. I shall have to die anyway, so I'll eat no more."

But she spoke so kindly to him and begged him just to try, that he came and ate something.

When he had eaten, she said, "I'll comb your hair a while, and then you'll feel happier."

So she combed his hair, and he grew drowsy and fell asleep. And then she took her handkerchief and made a knot in it and struck it three times on the earth, and said, "Earth-workers, come out."

In a moment numbers of little earth-men came out, and asked what the King's daughter commanded. Then she said, "In three hours' time the great forest must be cut down, and the whole of the wood laid in heaps."

So the little earth-men went about and gathered all their kindred together to help them with the work. They began at once; and when the three hours were over it was all done, and they came back to the King's daughter and told her so.

Then she took her white handkerchief again and said, "Earth-workers, go home." At which they all disappeared.

When the King's son woke he was delighted, and she said, "Come home when it's struck six o'clock." He did as she told him; and then the King asked, "Have you done away with the forest?"

"Yes," said the King's son.

When they were sitting at table, the King said, "I can't give you my daughter for a wife yet. You must do something more for her sake."

So he asked what it was to be, then.

"I have a great fishpond," said the King. "You must go to it tomorrow morning and clear all the mud out of it until it's as bright as a mirror, and fill it with every kind of fish."

Next morning the King gave him a glass shovel and said, "The fishpond must be done by six o'clock."

So he went off; and when he came to the fishpond he stuck his shovel into the mud and it broke in two; then he stuck his hoe into the mud, and broke that as well. Then he was greatly troubled.

At noon the youngest daughter brought him something to eat, and asked him how he was getting on. So the King's son said that everything was going very badly for him and he would certainly lose his head. "My tools have broken to pieces again."

"Oh," said she, "just come and eat something, and then you'll be in a different frame of mind."

"No," said he, "I can't eat. I'm far too unhappy for that."

But she gave him so many good words that at last he came and ate something. Then she combed his hair again and he fell asleep; and once more she took her handkerchief and tied a knot in it and struck the ground three times with the knot, and said, "Earth-workers, come out."

In a moment a great many little earth-men came and asked what she wanted; and she told them that in three hours' time the fishpond must be entirely cleaned out, and so clear that people could see themselves reflected in it, and every kind of fish must be in it.

The little earth-men went away and called all their kindred to help them, and in two hours it was done. Then they came back to her and said, "We've done as you commanded."

The King's daughter took the handkerchief and struck the ground three times with it once more, and said, "Earth-workers, go home again." Then they all went away.

When the King's son woke, the fishpond was finished. Then the King's daughter went away too, telling him that he was to come to the house at six. When he got to the house the King asked, "Have you got the fishpond done?"

"Yes," said the King's son. That was very good.

When they were sitting at table again the King said, "You've certainly done the fishpond; but I can't give you my daughter yet. You must just do one more thing."

"What's that, then?" asked the King's son.

The King said he had a great mountain with nothing on it but briars, which must all be cut down; and at the top of it the young man must build a great castle, as strong as anybody could imagine, and all the furniture and fittings belonging to a castle must be inside it.

And when he got up next morning, the King gave him a glass axe and a glass gimlet, and he was to have it all done by six o'clock.

As he was cutting down the first briar with the axe it snapped off short, and into pieces so small that they flew all round about; and he could not use the gimlet either. Then he was quite miserable, and waited for his dearest to see whether she would not come and help him in his need.

At midday she came and brought him something to eat. He went to meet her and told her everything, and ate something, and let her comb his hair, and fell asleep.

Then once more she took the knot and struck the earth with it and said, "Earth-workers, come out!" And once again numbers of earth-men came and asked what she wanted.

Then she said, "Within three hours the whole of the briars must be cut down, and a castle must be built on the top of the mountain, as strong as anybody could imagine, and all the furniture that belongs to a castle must be inside it."

They went away and called their kindred to help them; and when the time came it was all ready. Then they came to the King's daughter and told her so; and the King's daughter took her handkerchief and struck the earth three times with it and said, "Earth-workers, go home" — at which they all disappeared.

So when the King's son woke and saw everything done, he was as happy as a bird in the air.

When it had struck six they went home together. Then the King said, "Is the castle ready?"

"Yes," said the King's son.

When they sat down at table the King said, "I can't give my youngest daughter away until the two eldest are married."

Then the King's son and the King's daughter were quite dismayed, and the King's son had no idea what to do. But he went by night to the King's daughter and ran away with her.

When they had got a little distance off, the King's daughter looked round and saw her father behind them. "Oh," said she, "what are we to do? My father is behind us and will take us back with him. I'll change you at once into a briar and myself into a rose, and I'll shelter in the middle of the bush."

When her father reached the place, there stood a briar with one rose on it; and he was about to pick the rose when a thorn came and pricked his finger, so that he had to go home again.

His wife asked why he had not brought their daughter back with him. So he said he had nearly caught up with her, but that all at once he had lost sight of her, and a briar with one rose on it was growing on the spot.

Then the Queen said, "If you'd only picked the rose, the briar would have had to come too."

So he went back again to fetch the rose; but meanwhile the two of them were already far out over the plain, and the King ran after them.

Then the daughter looked round once more and saw her father coming, and said, "Oh, what shall we do now? I'll change you this instant into a church and myself into a priest, and I'll stand up in the pulpit and preach."

When the King got to the place, there stood a church, and in the pulpit was a priest preaching. So he listened to the sermon and then went home again.

Then the Queen asked why he had not brought their daughter with him, and he said, "No — I ran after her a long time; and just as I thought I should soon overtake her, a church was standing there and a priest was in the pulpit preaching."

"You should just have brought the priest," said his wife, "and then the church would soon have come. It's no use sending you. I must go there myself."

When she had walked for a while and could see the two of them in the distance, the King's daughter looked round and saw her mother coming, and said, "Now we're undone, for my mother is coming herself. I'll change you this instant into a fishpond and myself into a fish."

When her mother came to the place, there was a large fishpond, and in the middle of it a fish was leaping about and peeping out of the water, quite merrily. She tried to catch the fish, but she could not. Then she was very angry, and drank up the whole pond in order to catch the fish; but it made her so ill that she had to be sick, and she brought the whole pond up again.

Then she cried, "I can see very well that nothing can be done now" — and said that they might come back to her.

So the King's daughter went back; and the Queen gave her daughter three walnuts and said, "With these you can help yourself when you're in your greatest need."

So the young people went away together once more. And when they had walked a good ten miles, they came to the castle the King's son had come from, and close beside it was a village.

When they reached it, the King's son said, "Stay here, my dearest. I'll just go up to the castle, and then I'll come with a carriage and attendants to fetch you."

When he got to the castle they were all overjoyed to have the King's son back again; and he told them that he had a bride who was in the village now, and they must go with the carriage to fetch her. So they harnessed the horses at once, and a great many attendants took their places outside the carriage.

But as the King's son was about to get in, his mother gave him a kiss — and he forgot everything that had happened, and what he was about to do as well. At this his mother ordered the horses to be taken out of the carriage again, and everybody went back into the house.

But the girl sat in the village and watched and watched, and thought he would come and fetch her; and nobody came. Then the King's daughter took service at the mill belonging to the castle, and had to sit by the pond every afternoon and clean the tubs.

And one day the Queen came down on foot from the castle and went walking by the pond, and saw the well-grown girl sitting there, and said, "What a fine strong girl that is! She pleases me well." Then she and everybody with her looked at the girl, but nobody knew her.

So a long time went by, and the girl served the miller honourably and faithfully.

Meanwhile the Queen had found a wife for her son, who came from a quite distant part of the world. When the bride arrived, they were to be married at once; and a great many people came hurrying together, all of whom wanted to see everything.

Then the girl asked the miller if he would be so good as to give her leave to go too. So the miller said, "Yes, do go."

When she was about to go she opened one of the three walnuts, and a beautiful dress lay inside it. She put it on, and went into the church and stood by the altar.

Presently the bride and bridegroom came and sat down in front of the altar; and just as the priest was about to bless them, the bride glanced half round and saw the girl standing there. Then she stood up again and said she would not be given away until she had as beautiful a dress as that lady's.

So they went back to the house again and sent to ask the lady whether she would sell that dress. No, she would not sell it — but the bride might perhaps earn it. Then the bride asked how she was to do that. And the girl said that if she might sleep one night outside the King's son's door, the bride might have what she wanted. So the bride said yes, she was willing to do that.

But the servants were ordered to give the King's son a sleeping draught; and then the girl lay down on the threshold and lamented all night long. She had had the forest cut down for him; she had had the fishpond cleaned out for him; she had had the castle built for him; she had changed him into a briar, and then into a church, and at last into a fishpond — and yet he had forgotten her so quickly.

The King's son did not hear one word of it; but the servants had woken up and had listened to it, and did not know what it could mean.

Next morning, when they were all up, the bride put on the dress and went off to the church with the bridegroom. Meanwhile the girl opened the second walnut, and a still more beautiful dress was inside it. She put it on, and went and stood by the altar in the church, and everything happened as it had the time before.

And again the girl lay all night on the threshold leading to the King's son's room, and the servant was once more to give him a sleeping draught. The servant, though, went to him and gave him something to keep him awake; and then the King's son went to bed, and the miller's girl lamented as before on the threshold of the door and told of everything she had done.

The King's son heard it all, and was sorely troubled, and everything that was past came back to him. Then he wanted to go to her, but his mother had locked the door.

Next morning, though, he went straight to his beloved and told her everything that had happened to him, and begged her not to be angry with him for having forgotten her.

Then the King's daughter opened the third walnut, and inside it was a still more magnificent dress. She put it on and went with her bridegroom to church; and crowds of children came and gave them flowers and offered them gay ribbons to tie round their feet; and they were blessed by the priest and had a merry wedding.

But the false mother and the bride had to go away.

And the mouth of the person who told all this last is still warm.

The Cunning Little Tailor

There was once a princess who was extremely proud. If a suitor came, she set him some riddle to guess; and if he could not find it out, he was sent contemptuously away. She had it made known, too, that whoever solved her riddle should marry her, whoever he might be.

At length three tailors fell in with each other. The two eldest thought that they had brought off so many clever bits of work successfully that they could not fail to succeed at this as well; the third was a useless little vagabond who did not even know his trade, but thought he must have some luck coming in this venture — for where else was it to come from?

Then the other two said to him, "Just stay at home. You won't get far with your little bit of understanding."

But the little tailor would not let himself be discouraged, and said he had set his mind to work on this for once, and he would manage well enough; and off he went as if the whole world belonged to him.

All three of them announced themselves to the princess, and said she was to set them her riddle, and that the right men had come now, with understandings so fine that they could be threaded through a needle.

Then the princess said, "I have two kinds of hair on my head. What colour are they?"

"If that's all," said the first, "they must be black and white, like the cloth they call pepper and salt."

The princess said, "Wrongly guessed. Let the second answer."

Then the second said, "If they're not black and white, then they're brown and red, like my father's best coat."

"Wrongly guessed," said the princess. "Let the third give the answer, for I can see very well that he knows it for certain."

Then the little tailor stepped boldly forward and said, "The princess has one silver hair and one gold hair on her head, and those are the two different colours."

When the princess heard that she turned pale and nearly fell down with terror, for the little tailor had guessed her riddle, and she had firmly believed that no man on earth could find it out.

When her courage came back she said, "You haven't won me yet by that. There's still something else you must do. Down in the stable is a bear, and you shall spend the night with it; and when I get up in the morning, if you're still alive, you shall marry me."

She expected to be rid of the tailor this way, for the bear had never yet left anybody alive who had fallen into his clutches.

The little tailor did not let himself be frightened off, but was quite delighted, and said, "Boldly ventured is half won."

So when evening came, our little tailor was taken down to the bear. The bear was about to go for the little fellow at once and give him a hearty welcome with his paws.

"Gently, gently," said the little tailor. "I'll soon quiet you down." And quite calmly, as if he had not a care in the world, he took some nuts out of his pocket, cracked them and ate the kernels.

When the bear saw that, he was seized with a longing to have some nuts as well. The tailor felt in his pockets and handed him a handful; but they were not nuts, they were pebbles. The bear put them in his mouth, but could get nothing out of them, bite as he would.

"Eh," he thought, "what a stupid blockhead I am! I can't even crack a nut." And then he said to the tailor, "Here, crack me the nuts."

"There, see what a stupid fellow you are," said the little tailor, "to have such a great mouth and not be able to crack a little nut!" And he took the pebble and nimbly put a nut in his mouth in its place — and crack, it was in two.

"I must try the thing again," said the bear. "When I watch you doing it, I think I ought to be able to do it too."

So the tailor gave him another pebble, and the bear tried and tried to bite into it with all the strength in his body. But nobody will suppose that he managed it.

When that was over, the tailor took a violin out from under his coat and played himself a tune on it. When the bear heard the music he could not help beginning to dance; and when he had danced a while the thing pleased him so much that he said to the little tailor, "Listen — is a fiddle heavy?"

"Light enough for a child. Look: with my left hand I lay my fingers on it, and with my right I stroke it with the bow, and then it goes merrily, hop sa sa vivallalera!"

"So," said the bear. "Fiddling is a thing I should like to understand too, so that I could dance whenever I felt like it. What do you say to that? Will you give me lessons?"

"With all my heart," said the tailor, "if you have a talent for it. But just let me see your claws — they're terribly long. I must cut your nails a little."

So a vice was brought, and the bear put his claws in it, and the little tailor screwed it up tight and said, "Now wait until I come with the scissors" — and he let the bear growl as much as he liked, and lay down in the corner on a bundle of straw and fell asleep.

When the princess heard the bear growling so fiercely in the night, she believed nothing else than that he was growling for joy, and had made an end of the tailor. In the morning she got up carefree and happy; but when she peeped into the stable, there stood the tailor in front of her looking cheerful, and as healthy as a fish in water.

Now she could not say another word against the wedding, because she had given her promise in front of everybody; and the King ordered a carriage to be brought for her to drive to church in with the tailor, and there she was to be married.

When they had got into the carriage, the two other tailors, who had false hearts and envied him his good luck, went into the stable and unscrewed the bear again. The bear ran after the carriage in a great fury. The princess heard him snorting and growling; she was terrified, and cried, "Ah, the bear is behind us and wants to get you!"

The tailor was quick. He stood on his head, stuck his legs out of the window and cried, "Do you see this vice? If you don't be off, you'll be put in it again."

When the bear saw that, he turned round and ran away. The tailor drove quietly on to church; and the princess was married to him at once, and he lived with her as happy as a lark.

Whoever doesn't believe this must pay a thaler.

The Bright Sun Brings It to Light

A tailor's apprentice was travelling about the world looking for work; and at one time he could find none, and his poverty was so great that he had not a farthing to live on.

Presently he met a Jew on the road; and as he thought he would have a great deal of money on him, the tailor thrust God out of his heart, fell on the Jew, and said, "Give me your money, or I'll strike you dead."

Then the Jew said, "Grant me my life; I have no money, only eight farthings."

But the tailor said, "You have money, and it shall be produced" — and used violence and beat him until he was near death. And when the Jew was dying, the last words he said were, "The bright sun will bring it to light." And with that he died.

The tailor's apprentice felt in his pockets and searched for money, but he found nothing except eight farthings, exactly as the Jew had said. Then he picked him up and carried him behind a clump of trees, and went on to look for work.

After he had travelled about a long while he got work in a town, with a master who had a pretty daughter, whom he fell in love with and married; and he lived in good and happy wedlock.

After a long time, when he and his wife had two children, the wife's father and mother died, and the young people kept house alone.

One morning, when the husband was sitting on the table in front of the window, his wife brought him his coffee; and when he had poured it out into the saucer and was just about to drink, the sun shone on it, and the reflection gleamed to and fro on the wall above and made circles on it.

Then the tailor looked up and said, "Yes — it would very much like to bring it to light, and it can't."

His wife said, "Oh, my dear husband, and what's that, then? What do you mean by it?"

He answered, "I mustn't tell you."

But she said, "If you love me, you must tell me" — and used her most affectionate words, and said that nobody should ever know it, and gave him no rest.

Then he told her how, years ago, when he was travelling about looking for work and was quite worn out and penniless, he had killed a Jew; and that in his last agonies the Jew had spoken the words, "The bright sun will bring it to light." And now the sun had wanted to bring it to light, and had gleamed and made circles on the wall, and had not been able to do it.

After this he charged her again, most particularly, never to tell it, or he would lose his life; and she did promise.

But when he had sat down to work again, she went to her closest friend and confided the story to her — but she was never to repeat it to any living soul. And within two days the whole town knew it, and the tailor was brought to trial and condemned.

And so, after all, the bright sun did bring it to light.

The Blue Light

There was once a soldier who had served the King faithfully for many years; but when the war came to an end he could serve no longer, because of the many wounds he had received.

The King said to him, "You may go home. I don't need you any more, and you won't get any more money; for only the man who does me service gets wages from me."

So the soldier did not know how to earn a living, and went away greatly troubled, and walked the whole day, until in the evening he came into a forest.

When darkness came on he saw a light, and went towards it, and came to a house where a witch lived. "Do give me a night's lodging and a little to eat and drink," he said to her, "or I shall starve."

"Oho," she answered, "who gives anything to a runaway soldier? Still, I'll be merciful and take you in — if you'll do what I want."

"What do you want?" said the soldier.

"That you dig all round my garden for me tomorrow."

The soldier agreed, and next day laboured with all his strength, but could not finish it by evening.

"I can see well enough," said the witch, "that you can do no more today. But I'll keep you another night; and in payment you must chop me a load of wood tomorrow, and chop it small."

The soldier spent the whole day doing it; and in the evening the witch proposed that he should stay one more night.

"Tomorrow you shall do me only a very trifling piece of work. Behind my house there's an old dry well, and my light has fallen into it; it burns blue and never goes out, and you shall bring it up again for me."

Next day the old woman took him to the well and let him down in a basket. He found the blue light and signalled to her to draw him up again. She did draw him up; but when he came near the edge she stretched down her hand and tried to take the blue light away from him.

"No," said he, seeing her evil intention. "I won't give you the light until I'm standing with both feet on the ground."

The witch flew into a rage, let him down into the well again and went away.

The poor soldier fell without hurting himself on the damp ground, and the blue light went on burning — but what use was that to him? He saw very well that he could not escape death. He sat there for a while, very sorrowful; and then suddenly he felt in his pocket and found his tobacco pipe, still half full.

"This shall be my last pleasure," he thought — and pulled it out, lit it at the blue light and began to smoke.

When the smoke had circled about the cavern, a little black dwarf suddenly stood in front of him and said, "Lord, what are your commands?"

"What commands should I have to give you?" replied the soldier, quite astonished.

"I must do everything you tell me," said the little man.

"Good," said the soldier. "Then in the first place, help me out of this well."

The little man took him by the hand and led him through an underground passage — but he did not forget to take the blue light with him. On the way the dwarf showed him the treasures the witch had gathered and hidden there, and the soldier took as much gold as he could carry.

When he was up above, he said to the little man, "Now go and tie up the old witch and carry her before the judge."

In a short time she came riding by with frightful cries, as swift as the wind, on a wild tomcat; and it was not long after that before the little man reappeared.

"It's all done," said he. "The witch is hanging on the gallows already. What further commands has my lord?"

"For the moment, none," answered the soldier. "You can go home; only be at hand at once if I call you."

"Nothing more is needed than that you light your pipe at the blue light, and I'll appear before you at once."

And with that he vanished from his sight.

The soldier went back to the town he had come from. He went to the best inn, ordered himself handsome clothes, and then told the landlord to furnish him a room as handsomely as possible. When it was ready and the soldier had taken possession of it, he summoned the little black man and said, "I served the King faithfully, and he dismissed me and left me to go hungry; and now I mean to take my revenge."

"What am I to do?" asked the little man.

"Late at night, when the King's daughter is in bed, bring her here in her sleep. She shall do servant's work for me."

The little man said, "That's an easy thing for me to do, but a very dangerous thing for you; for if it's discovered, it will go badly with you."

When twelve o'clock had struck, the door sprang open and the little man carried the princess in.

"Aha! Are you there?" cried the soldier. "Get to your work at once! Fetch the broom and sweep the room."

When she had done that, he ordered her to come to his chair; and then he stretched out his feet and said, "Pull off my boots for me" — and then he threw them in her face and made her pick them up again and clean them and polish them. And she did everything he told her, without resistance, silently, with her eyes half shut.

When the first cock crowed, the little man carried her back to the royal palace and laid her in her bed.

Next morning, when the princess got up, she went to her father and told him that she had had a very strange dream. "I was carried through the streets as fast as lightning," said she, "and taken into a soldier's room, and I had to wait on him like a servant, and sweep his room and clean his boots and do all kinds of menial work. It was only a dream, and yet I'm just as tired as if I'd really done it all."

"The dream may have been true," said the King. "I'll give you a piece of advice. Fill your pocket full of peas and make a small hole in it; and then if you're carried away again, they'll fall out and leave a trail in the streets."

But unseen by the King, the little man was standing beside him as he said it, and heard everything. And at night, when the sleeping princess was carried through the streets again, some peas certainly did fall out of her pocket — but they made no trail, for the crafty little man had scattered peas in every street in the town just beforehand. And again the princess was made to do servant's work until cockcrow.

Next morning the King sent his people out to look for the trail; but it was all in vain, for in every street poor children were sitting picking up peas and saying, "It must have rained peas last night."

"We must think of something else," said the King. "Keep your shoes on when you go to bed; and before you come back from the place they take you to, hide one of them there. I'll soon manage to find it."

The black dwarf heard this plan; and at night, when the soldier again ordered him to bring the princess, he told him about it, and said that he knew of no way to counter this stratagem, and that if the shoe were found in the soldier's house it would go badly with him.

"Do what I tell you," replied the soldier. And so this third night the princess had to work like a servant again; but before she went away she hid her shoe under the bed.

Next morning the King had the whole town searched for his daughter's shoe. It was found at the soldier's; and the soldier himself, who had gone outside the gate at the dwarf's urging, was soon brought back and thrown into prison. In his flight he had forgotten the most valuable things he had, the blue light and the gold, and had only one ducat in his pocket.

And now, loaded with chains, he was standing at the window of his cell when he happened to see one of his old comrades going by. The soldier tapped on the pane; and when the man came up, he said to him, "Be so kind as to fetch me the little bundle I've left lying at the inn, and I'll give you a ducat for it."

His comrade ran there and brought him what he wanted. And as soon as the soldier was alone again he lit his pipe and summoned the black dwarf.

"Have no fear," said the dwarf to his master. "Go wherever they take you and let them do what they will — only take the blue light with you."

Next day the soldier was tried; and although he had done nothing wicked, the judge condemned him to death. When he was led out to die, he begged one last favour of the King.

"What is it?" asked the King.

"That I may smoke one more pipe on the way."

"You may smoke three," answered the King, "but don't imagine that I'll spare your life."

Then the soldier pulled out his pipe and lit it at the blue light; and as soon as a few wreaths of smoke had risen, the little man was there with a small cudgel in his hand, and said, "What does my lord command?"

"Strike that false judge to the ground, and his constable — and don't spare the King, who has treated me so badly."

Then the little man fell on them like lightning, darting this way and that; and whoever was so much as touched by his cudgel fell to the ground and did not dare stir again.

The King was terrified; he threw himself on the soldier's mercy, and merely to be allowed to live at all, gave him his kingdom for his own, and the princess for a wife.

The Wilful Child

Once upon a time there was a child who was wilful and would not do what her mother wanted. For this reason God took no pleasure in her, and let her fall ill; and no doctor could do her any good, and in a short time she lay on her deathbed.

When she had been lowered into her grave and the earth spread over her, all at once her arm came out again and stretched upwards; and when they had put it back in and spread fresh earth over it, it was all no use, for the arm always came out again.

Then the mother herself had to go to the grave and strike the arm with a rod; and when she had done that, it was drawn in, and then at last the child had rest beneath the ground.

The Three Army-Surgeons

Three army surgeons who thought they knew their art perfectly were travelling about the world, and they came to an inn where they wanted to spend the night. The landlord asked where they came from and where they were going.

"We're roaming about the world practising our art."

"Just show me for once what you can do," said the landlord.

Then the first said he would cut off his hand and put it back on early next morning; the second said he would tear out his heart and put it back next morning; the third said he would cut out his eyes and heal them again next morning.

"If you can do that," said the innkeeper, "you've learned everything there is."

But they had a salve they rubbed themselves with, which joined parts back together, and they always carried the little bottle it was in with them.

So they cut the hand and heart and eyes out of their bodies as they had said they would, and laid them all together on a plate and gave it to the innkeeper. The innkeeper gave it to a servant girl, who was to put it in the cupboard and take good care of it.

But the girl had a lover in secret, who was a soldier. So when the innkeeper and the three army surgeons and everybody else in the house were asleep, the soldier came and wanted something to eat. The girl opened the cupboard and brought him some food; and being in love she forgot to shut the cupboard door again. She sat down at the table beside her lover and they chattered away together.

And while she was sitting there so contentedly, thinking of no ill luck, the cat came creeping in and found the cupboard open, and took the hand and the heart and the eyes of the three army surgeons and ran off with them.

When the soldier had finished eating, and the girl was clearing the things away and going to shut the cupboard, she saw that the plate the innkeeper had given her to look after was empty.

Then she said to her lover in a fright, "Oh, wretched girl that I am, what shall I do? The hand is gone, and the heart and the eyes are gone too. What will become of me in the morning?"

"Be easy," said he. "I'll help you out of your trouble. There's a thief hanging outside on the gallows; I'll cut off his hand. Which hand was it?"

"The right one."

Then the girl gave him a sharp knife, and he went and cut the poor sinner's right hand off and brought it to her. After that he caught the cat and cut its eyes out; and now nothing was missing but the heart.

"Haven't you been killing pigs? Aren't there dead pigs in the cellar?" said he.

"Yes," said the girl.

"That's good," said the soldier — and he went down and fetched a pig's heart.

The girl put them all together on the plate and put it in the cupboard; and when her lover had taken his leave of her after this, she went quietly to bed.

In the morning, when the three army surgeons got up, they told the girl to bring them the plate with the hand and the heart and the eyes on it. So she brought it out of the cupboard; and the first fixed the thief's hand on and smeared it with his salve, and it grew onto his arm directly. The second took the cat's eyes and put them into his own head. The third fixed the pig's heart firmly in the place where his own had been. And the innkeeper stood by and admired their skill, and said that he had never seen such a thing done before, and would sing their praises and recommend them to everybody.

Then they paid their bill and travelled on.

As they went along their way, the one with the pig's heart would not stay with them at all, but wherever there was a corner he ran to it and rooted about in it with his nose, the way pigs do. The others tried to hold him back by the tail of his coat, but it was no use; he tore himself loose and ran wherever the dirt was thickest.

The second behaved very strangely as well. He rubbed his eyes and said to the others, "Comrades, what's the matter? I can't see at all. Will one of you lead me, so that I don't fall?"

So with difficulty they travelled on until the evening, when they reached another inn. They went into the bar together; and there at a table in the corner sat a rich man counting money. The one with the thief's hand walked round about him, made a sudden movement twice with his arm, and at last, when the stranger turned away, snatched at the pile of money and took a handful of it.

One of them saw this and said, "Comrade, what are you doing? You mustn't steal! Shame on you."

"Eh," said he, "but how can I stop myself? My hand twitches, and I'm forced to snatch at things whether I want to or not."

After this they lay down to sleep; and as they lay there it was so dark that nobody could see his own hand. All at once the one with the cat's eyes woke up and roused the others and said, "Brothers, just look up. Do you see the white mice running about there?"

The two sat up but could see nothing. Then he said, "Things aren't right with us. We haven't got our own back again. We must go back to the innkeeper — he's deceived us."

So next morning they went back and told the landlord that they had not got their own back again: that the first had a thief's hand, the second cat's eyes and the third a pig's heart.

The innkeeper said that the girl must be to blame for it, and was going to call her; but when she had seen the three of them coming she had run out by the back door, and had not come back.

Then the three said he must give them a great deal of money, or they would set his house on fire. He gave them what he had and whatever else he could get together, and the three went away with it. It was enough for the rest of their lives — but they would rather have had their own proper organs.

The Seven Swabians

Seven Swabians were once together. The first was Master Schulz, the second Jackli, the third Marli, the fourth Jergli, the fifth Michal, the sixth Hans and the seventh Veitli. All seven of them had made up their minds to travel about the world, seek adventures and perform great deeds.

But so that they could go in safety and with weapons in their hands, they thought it would be sensible to have a single spear made for them, but a very strong and very long one. All seven of them took hold of this spear at once; in front walked the boldest and bravest, and that was Master Schulz; all the others followed in a row, and Veitli was last.

Now it happened one day in the haymaking month of July, when they had walked a long way and still had a long way to go before they reached the village they were to spend the night in, that as they were crossing a meadow in the twilight, a great beetle or hornet flew past them from behind a bush and hummed in a menacing manner.

Master Schulz was so terrified that he nearly dropped the spear, and a cold sweat broke out all over his body. "Listen! Listen!" he cried to his comrades. "Good heavens, I hear a drum!"

Jackli, who was behind him holding the spear, and who caught some kind of smell, said, "Something is certainly going on, for I can taste powder and matches."

At these words Master Schulz took to flight, and in a trice jumped over a hedge; but as he happened to land on the teeth of a rake that had been left lying there after the haymaking, the handle of it flew up and struck his face and gave him a tremendous blow.

"Oh dear! Oh dear!" screamed Master Schulz. "Take me prisoner! I surrender! I surrender!"

The other six all leapt over one on top of another, crying, "If you surrender, I surrender too! If you surrender, I surrender too!"

At length, as there was no enemy there to tie them up and take them away, they saw that they had been mistaken; and so that the story should not get about and they be treated as fools and laughed at, they all swore to each other to hold their peace about it, until one of them should let it out by accident.

Then they travelled on.

The second danger they came through cannot be compared with the first. Some days afterwards their path led them through a fallow field where a hare was sitting asleep in the sun. Her ears were standing straight up and her great glassy eyes were wide open.

They were all alarmed at the sight of this horrible wild beast, and consulted together about what would be the least dangerous thing to do. For if they ran away, they knew the monster would chase them and swallow them whole.

So they said, "We must go through a great and dangerous struggle. Boldly ventured is half won." And all seven grasped the spear, Master Schulz in front and Veitli behind. Master Schulz kept trying to hold the spear back; but Veitli had grown quite brave back there, and wanted to dash forward, and cried:

	"Strike home, in every Swabian's name,
	or else I hope you go home lame."

But Hans knew how to answer that, and said:

	"Thunder and lightning, it's fine to prate,
	but for dragon-hunting you're always late."

Michal cried:

	"There's nothing missing, not even a hair;
	be sure the Devil himself is there."

Then it was Jergli's turn to speak:

	"If it's not him, it's at least his mother,
	or else it's the Devil's own step-brother."

And now Marli had a bright idea, and said to Veitli:

	"Advance there, Veitli, advance, advance,
	and I'll stay behind and hold the lance."

Veitli, though, paid no attention to that; and Jackli said:

	"It's Schulz's place the first to be —
	nobody deserves that honour but he."

Then Master Schulz plucked up his courage and said gravely:

	"Then let us boldly advance to the fight,
	and so we shall show our valour and might."

At this they all set on the dragon together. Master Schulz crossed himself and prayed for God's help; but as none of it did any good, and he was getting nearer and nearer to the enemy, he screamed, "Oho! Oho! Ho! Ho! Ho!" in the greatest anguish.

This woke the hare, which darted swiftly away in great alarm. And when Master Schulz saw her flying from the field of battle like that, he cried out in his joy:

	"Quick, Veitli, quick, look there, look there —
	the monster's nothing but a hare!"

But the Swabian allies went off in search of further adventures, and came to the Moselle, a mossy, quiet, deep river with few bridges over it, which in many places people have to cross by boat.

As the seven Swabians did not know this, they called out to a man who was working on the opposite bank, to ask how people managed to get across. The distance and their way of speaking made the man unable to understand what they wanted, and he said "Wat? Wat?" — which is how people say "What?" in the country round Trier.

Master Schulz thought he was saying, "Wade, wade through the water"; and as he was the first, he set off and went into the Moselle. It was not long before he sank in the mud and the deep waves that drove against him. But his hat was blown to the opposite bank by the wind, and a frog sat down beside it and croaked, "Wat, wat, wat."

The other six on the near bank heard that and said, "Oho, comrades, Master Schulz is calling us. If he can wade across, why can't we?"

So they all jumped into the water together in a great hurry, and were drowned. And so one frog took the lives of all six of them, and not one of the Swabian allies ever reached home again.

The Three Apprentices

There were once three apprentices who had agreed always to stay together on their travels and always to work in the same town. At one time, though, their masters had no more work to give them, so that at last they were in rags and had nothing to live on.

Then one of them said, "What shall we do? We can't stay here any longer. We'll travel on once more; and if we find no work in the town we go to, we'll arrange with the innkeeper there that we're to write and tell him where we're staying, so that we can always have news of one another; and then we'll separate."

That seemed best to the others too. They set out, and on the way they met a richly dressed man who asked who they were.

"We're apprentices looking for work. Up to now we've kept together, but if we can't find anything to do we're going to separate."

"There's no need for that," said the man. "If you'll do what I tell you, you shall want for neither gold nor work; indeed, you shall become great lords and drive about in your carriages."

One of them said, "If our souls and our salvation aren't endangered, we'll certainly do it."

"They won't be," replied the man. "I have no claim on you."

But one of the others had looked at his feet; and when he saw a horse's hoof and a man's foot, he wanted nothing to do with him. The Devil, though, said, "Be easy. I have no designs on you, but on another soul, which is half mine already, and whose measure has only to run full."

As they were safe now, they agreed; and the Devil told them what he wanted. The first was to answer, "All three of us," to every question; the second was to say, "For money"; and the third, "And quite right too!" They were always to say this, one after another; but they were not to say one word more. And if they disobeyed this order, all their money would disappear at once; but as long as they kept to it, their pockets would always be full.

To begin with, he gave them as much as they could carry there and then, and told them to go to such and such an inn when they got to the town.

They went there, and the innkeeper came to meet them and asked whether they wanted anything to eat.

The first replied, "All three of us."

"Yes," said the landlord, "that's what I mean."

The second said, "For money."

"Of course," said the landlord.

The third said, "And quite right too!"

"Certainly it's right," said the landlord.

Good food and drink were brought to them now, and they were well waited on. After dinner came the reckoning, and the innkeeper gave the bill to the one who said, "All three of us"; the second said, "For money"; and the third, "And quite right too!"

"Indeed it's right," said the landlord. "All three pay; and without money I can give nothing."
