But they paid still more than he had asked.

The other guests, who were looking on, said, "These people must be mad."

"Yes, indeed they are," said the landlord. "They're not very wise."

So they stayed some time at the inn and said nothing else but "All three of us," "For money" and "And quite right too!" But they saw and knew everything that went on.

It happened that a great merchant came with a large sum of money, and said, "Landlord, take care of my money for me. There are three crazy apprentices here who might steal it from me."

The landlord did as he was asked. As he was carrying the trunk into his room he felt how heavy it was with gold. So he gave the three apprentices a lodging downstairs, but the merchant went up to a separate room.

When it was midnight, and the landlord thought that everybody was asleep, he came with his wife, and they had an axe, and they struck the rich merchant dead; and after they had murdered him they went back to bed.

When it was day there was a great outcry: the merchant lay dead in bed, bathed in blood. All the guests came running at once; but the landlord said, "The three crazy apprentices have done this" — and the other guests confirmed it and said, "It can have been nobody else."

The innkeeper, though, had them called in and said to them, "Did you kill the merchant?"

"All three of us," said the first.

"For money," said the second.

And the third added, "And quite right too!"

"There now, you hear," said the landlord. "They confess it themselves."

So they were taken to prison and were to be tried. When they saw that things were becoming so serious, they were afraid after all; but at night the Devil came and said, "Bear it just one day longer, and don't throw away your luck. Not a hair of your heads shall be hurt."

Next morning they were led into court, and the judge said, "Are you the murderers?"

"All three of us."

"Why did you kill the merchant?"

"For money."

"You wicked wretches, have you no horror of your sins?"

"And quite right too!"

"They've confessed and they're still defiant," said the judge. "Take them to their deaths at once."

So they were taken out, and the landlord had to go with them into the circle. And when they had been taken hold of by the executioner's men and were just about to be led up to the scaffold where the headsman stood with his naked sword, a coach drawn by four blood-red chestnut horses came up suddenly, driving so fast that sparks flew from the stones; and somebody made signs from the window with a white handkerchief.

Then the headsman said, "It's a pardon coming" — and "Pardon! Pardon!" was called from the carriage as well.

Then the Devil stepped out as a very noble gentleman, beautifully dressed, and said, "You three are innocent. You may speak now — make known what you've seen and heard."

Then the eldest said, "We didn't kill the merchant. The murderer is standing there in the circle" — and he pointed to the innkeeper. "In proof of it, go into his cellar, where many others he has killed are still hanging."

Then the judge sent the executioner's men there, and they found it was as the apprentices had said; and when they had told the judge of it, he had the innkeeper led up, and his head was cut off.

Then the Devil said to the three, "Now I have the soul I wanted; and you are free, and have money for the rest of your lives."

The King’s Son Who Feared Nothing

There was once a King's son who was no longer content to stay at home in his father's house; and as he was afraid of nothing, he thought, "I'll go out into the wide world. Time won't hang heavy on me there, and I shall see wonders enough."

So he took leave of his parents and went out, on and on from morning till night; and whichever way his path led, it was all the same to him.

It happened that he came to a giant's house; and as he was so tired, he sat down by the door and rested. And as he let his eyes wander here and there, he saw the giant's playthings lying in the yard. They were a couple of enormous balls and skittles as tall as a man.

After a while he took a fancy to set the skittles up, and then rolled the balls at them, and shouted and cried out when the skittles fell, and had a merry time of it.

The giant heard the noise and stuck his head out of the window, and saw a man no taller than other men, and yet playing with his skittles.

"Little worm," cried he, "why are you playing with my balls? Who gave you the strength to do it?"

The King's son looked up, saw the giant, and said, "Oh, you blockhead, you really think you're the only one with strong arms. I can do anything I want to do."

The giant came down and watched the bowling with great admiration, and said, "Child of man, if you're of that sort, go and bring me an apple from the tree of life."

"What do you want with it?" said the King's son.

"I don't want the apple for myself," answered the giant, "but I have a betrothed bride who wants it. I've travelled far about the world and can't find the tree."

"I'll soon find it," said the King's son, "and I don't know what could stop me getting the apple down."

The giant said, "You really think it's as easy as that? The garden the tree stands in is surrounded by an iron railing, and in front of the railing lie wild beasts, each one close beside the next, and they keep watch and let nobody in."

"They'll let me in, sure enough," said the King's son.

"Yes; but even if you do get into the garden and see the apple hanging on the tree, it's still not yours. There's a ring hanging in front of it, and anybody who wants to reach the apple and break it off has to put his hand through it — and nobody yet has had the luck to do it."

"That luck will be mine," said the King's son.

Then he took his leave of the giant, and went out over mountain and valley and through plains and forests, until at length he came to the wonderful garden.

The beasts lay round about it, but they had put their heads down and were asleep. What is more, they did not wake when he went up to them; so he stepped over them and climbed the fence and got safely into the garden.

There in the very middle of it stood the tree of life, with the red apples shining on the branches. He climbed up the trunk to the top; and as he was about to reach out for an apple, he saw a ring hanging in front of it. But he pushed his hand through it without any difficulty and picked the apple. The ring closed tightly round his arm, and all at once he felt a prodigious strength flowing through his veins.

When he had come down out of the tree with the apple, he would not climb back over the fence, but took hold of the great gate; and he had no need to shake it more than once before it sprang open with a loud crash. Then he went out; and the lion that had been lying there was awake now, and sprang after him — not in rage or fierceness, but following him humbly as its master.

The King's son took the giant the apple he had promised him, and said, "You see, I've brought it without any difficulty."

The giant was glad that his wish had been granted so soon, and hurried off to his bride and gave her the apple she had wanted. She was a beautiful and clever girl; and as she did not see the ring on his arm, she said, "I shall never believe you brought the apple until I see the ring on your arm."

The giant said, "I've only to go home and fetch it" — and thought it would be easy to take by force from the weak man what he would not give of his own free will.

So he demanded the ring from him; but the King's son refused it.

"Where the apple is, the ring must be too," said the giant. "If you won't give it of your own accord, you must fight me for it."

They wrestled with each other for a long time, but the giant could not get the better of the King's son, who was strengthened by the magic power of the ring. Then the giant thought of a trick, and said, "I've grown hot with fighting, and so have you. Let's bathe in the river and cool ourselves before we begin again."

The King's son, who knew nothing of falsehood, went with him to the water, and pulled the ring off his arm along with his clothes, and sprang into the river. The giant instantly snatched the ring and ran off with it; but the lion, which had seen the theft, chased the giant and tore the ring out of his hand and brought it back to its master.

Then the giant stationed himself behind an oak tree; and while the King's son was busy putting his clothes on again, he took him by surprise and put out both his eyes.

And now the unhappy King's son stood there blind, and did not know how to help himself. Then the giant came back to him and took him by the hand as if he were somebody who meant to guide him, and led him to the top of a high rock. There he left him standing, and thought, "Just two steps more, and he'll fall and kill himself, and I can take the ring off him."

But the faithful lion had not deserted its master. It held him fast by the clothes and drew him gradually back again. And when the giant came to rob the dead man, he saw that his cunning had been for nothing.

"Is there no way at all of destroying a weak child of man like that?" he said to himself angrily. And he took hold of the King's son and led him back to the precipice by another way; but the lion, seeing his evil design, helped its master out of danger here too.

When they had got close to the edge, the giant let the blind man's hand drop and was going to leave him there alone; but the lion pushed the giant so that he was thrown over and fell and was dashed to pieces on the ground.

The faithful animal drew its master back from the precipice again and guided him to a tree with a clear brook running past it. The King's son sat down there, but the lion lay down and splashed the water into his face with its paws.

Hardly had a couple of drops wetted his empty eye sockets before he could see something again; and he noticed a little bird flying past quite close, which struck itself against a tree trunk. At this it went down to the water and bathed in it, and then it soared up and swept between the trees without touching them, as if it had got its sight back.

Then the King's son recognised a sign from God, and stooped down to the water and washed and bathed his face in it. And when he stood up he had his eyes again, brighter and clearer than they had ever been.

The King's son thanked God for his great mercy, and travelled on through the world with his lion. And it happened that he came to a castle that was under a spell. In the gateway stood a girl of beautiful figure and fine face; but she was black from head to foot.

She spoke to him and said, "Ah, if only you could deliver me from the evil spell that has been cast over me!"

"What must I do?" said the King's son.

The girl answered, "You must spend three nights in the great hall of this enchanted castle; but you must let no fear into your heart. When they're doing their worst to torment you, if you bear it without letting a sound escape you, I shall be free. Your life they dare not take."

Then said the King's son, "I have no fear. With God's help I'll try it."

So he went cheerfully into the castle; and when it grew dark he sat down in the great hall and waited. Everything was quiet, though, until midnight, when all at once a great uproar began, and out of every hole and corner came little devils. They behaved as if they did not see him, and settled down in the middle of the room and lit a fire and began to gamble.

When one of them lost, he said, "This isn't right. There's somebody here who doesn't belong to us; it's his fault I'm losing."

"Wait, you fellow behind the stove, I'm coming," said another.

The screeching grew louder and louder, so that nobody could have heard it without terror. But the King's son went on sitting quite quietly and was not afraid. At last, though, the devils jumped up from the floor and fell on him, and there were so many of them that he could not defend himself. They dragged him about the floor, pinched him, pricked him, beat him and tormented him — but not a sound escaped him.

Towards morning they disappeared, and he was so exhausted that he could hardly move his limbs. But when day dawned the girl came to him. She carried in her hand a little bottle with the water of life in it, and she washed him with it; and at once he felt all the pain leave him and new strength flow through his veins.

She said, "You've held out successfully for one night, but two more lie ahead of you."

Then she went away again; and as she went, he noticed that her feet had turned white.

The next night the devils came and began their games afresh. They fell on the King's son and beat him far more severely than the night before, until his body was covered with wounds. But as he bore it all quietly, they had to leave him; and when dawn came the girl came and healed him with the water of life. And as she went away, he saw with joy that she had turned white already to the tips of her fingers.

And now he had only one night more to get through — but it was the worst. The goblins came again. "Are you still there?" they cried. "You shall be tormented till your breath stops."

They pricked him and beat him and threw him about, and pulled him by the arms and legs as if they wanted to tear him to pieces; but he bore it all and never uttered a cry.

At last the devils vanished; but he lay there fainting and did not stir, and could not even raise his eyes to look at the girl who came in and sprinkled him and bathed him with the water of life. But suddenly he was freed from all pain, and felt fresh and healthy, as if he had woken out of sleep; and when he opened his eyes he saw the girl standing beside him, snow-white and as fair as day.

"Get up," said she, "and swing your sword three times over the stairs, and then everything will be delivered."

And when he had done that, the whole castle was released from its enchantment, and the girl was a rich King's daughter.

The servants came and said that the table was already laid in the great hall and dinner was served. So they sat down and ate and drank together; and in the evening the wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing.

Donkey Cabbages

There was once a young huntsman who went into the forest to lie in wait for game. He had a fresh and cheerful heart; and as he was going along, whistling on a leaf, an ugly old woman came up and spoke to him and said, "Good day, dear huntsman. You're merry and contented, to be sure; but I'm suffering from hunger and thirst. Do give me something."

The huntsman felt sorry for the poor old creature, and felt in his pocket and gave her what he could spare. He was about to go on then, but the old woman stopped him and said, "Listen, dear huntsman, to what I'm going to tell you. I'll make you a present in return for your kindness. Go on your way now; and in a little while you'll come to a tree with nine birds sitting in it that have a cloak in their claws and are pulling at it. Take your gun and shoot into the middle of them, and they'll let the cloak drop down to you; but one of the birds will be hit and will fall down dead. Take the cloak away with you: it's a wishing cloak. When you throw it over your shoulders, you only have to wish to be in a certain place and you'll be there in the twinkling of an eye. And take the heart out of the dead bird and swallow it whole, and every morning early, when you get up, you'll find a gold piece under your pillow."

The huntsman thanked the wise woman, and thought to himself, "Those are fine things she's promised me — if only it all comes true."

And sure enough, when he had walked about a hundred paces, he heard such a screaming and twittering in the branches above him that he looked up and saw a crowd of birds tearing at a piece of cloth with their beaks and claws, tugging and fighting as if each one wanted it all to itself.

"Well," said the huntsman, "this is wonderful. It's really come about just as the old woman foretold." And he took the gun off his shoulder, aimed and fired right into the middle of them, so that the feathers flew about. The birds instantly took flight with loud cries, but one dropped down dead, and the cloak fell at the same moment.

Then the huntsman did as the old woman had told him: cut the bird open, found the heart and swallowed it down, and took the cloak home with him.

Next morning when he woke, the promise came back to him, and he wanted to see whether that had come true as well. When he lifted the pillow, the gold piece shone up at him; and next day he found another, and so it went on, every time he got up.

He gathered a heap of gold together; but at last he thought, "What use is all my gold to me if I stay at home? I'll go out and see the world."

So he took his leave of his parents, buckled on his huntsman's pouch and his gun, and went out into the world.

It happened that one day he travelled through a dense forest; and when he came out of it, on the plain in front of him stood a fine castle. An old woman was standing at one of the windows with a wonderfully beautiful girl, looking out.

But the old woman was a witch, and said to the girl, "There's one coming out of the forest who has a wonderful treasure inside him. We must steal it from him, my dear daughter; it suits us better than it does him. He has a bird's heart in him, and because of it a gold piece lies under his pillow every morning."

She told her what she was to do to get it, and what part she had to play; and finally she threatened her, and said with angry eyes, "And if you don't do as I say, it will be the worse for you."

Now when the huntsman came nearer he caught sight of the girl, and said to himself, "I've been travelling about for such a long while, I'll take a rest for once and go into that beautiful castle. I certainly have money enough." But the real reason was that he had caught sight of the pretty girl.

He went into the house and was well received and courteously entertained. Before long he was so much in love with the young witch that he thought of nothing else, and saw everything only as she saw it, and did whatever she wanted.

Then the old woman said, "Now we must have the bird's heart. He'll never miss it."

She prepared a drink; and when it was ready she poured it into a cup and gave it to the girl, who was to hand it to the huntsman. She did so, saying, "Now, my dearest, drink to me."

So he took the cup; and when he had swallowed the draught, he brought up the bird's heart. The girl had to take it away secretly and swallow it herself, for the old woman would have it so.

From then on he found no more gold under his pillow; it lay under the girl's instead, and the old woman fetched it away every morning. But he was so much in love and so befooled that he thought of nothing but spending his time with the girl.

Then the old witch said, "We have the bird's heart, but we must take the wishing cloak away from him too."

The girl answered, "Let's leave him that. He's lost his wealth already."

The old woman was angry and said, "A cloak like that is a wonderful thing and rarely to be found in this world. I must and will have it." She struck the girl several blows, and said that if she did not obey it would go badly for her.

So she did as the old woman told her: stationed herself at the window and looked out over the distant country as if she were very sorrowful.

The huntsman asked, "Why are you standing there so sadly?"

"Ah, my beloved," she answered, "over yonder lies the Garnet Mountain, where the precious stones grow. I long for them so much that when I think of them I feel quite miserable. But who can get them? Only the birds — they fly and can reach them; a man never can."

"Is that all you have to complain of?" said the huntsman. "I'll soon take that burden off your heart."

And with that he drew her under his cloak, wished himself on the Garnet Mountain, and in the twinkling of an eye they were sitting on it together. Precious stones were glittering on every side, so that it was a joy to see them; and together they gathered the finest and costliest of them.

Now the old woman had contrived by her sorcery that the huntsman's eyes should grow heavy. He said to the girl, "Let's sit down and rest a while. I'm so tired I can't stand on my feet any longer."

So they sat down, and he laid his head in her lap and fell asleep. And when he was asleep she unfastened the cloak from his shoulders and wrapped herself in it, picked up the garnets and the stones, and wished herself home again with them.

But when the huntsman had had his sleep out and woke and saw that his sweetheart had betrayed him and left him alone on the wild mountain, he said, "Oh, what treachery there is in the world!" — and sat down there in care and sorrow, not knowing what to do.

But the mountain belonged to some wild and monstrous giants who lived on it and led their lives there; and he had not sat long before he saw three of them coming towards him, so he lay down as if he were sunk in a deep sleep.

Then the giants came up, and the first kicked him with his foot and said, "What sort of an earthworm is this, lying curled up here?"

The second said, "Step on him and kill him."

But the third said, "That would hardly be worth your trouble. Just let him live — he can't stay here; and when he climbs higher, towards the summit of the mountain, the clouds will take hold of him and carry him away."

And so saying they went on by.

But the huntsman had paid attention to their words; and as soon as they were gone he got up and climbed to the summit of the mountain. And when he had sat there a while, a cloud floated towards him and caught him up and carried him away, and travelled about the sky with him for a long time. Then it sank lower and let itself down on a great walled cabbage garden, so that he came softly to the ground among cabbages and vegetables.

Then the huntsman looked around him and said, "If only I had something to eat! I'm so hungry, and my hunger will only get worse as time goes on. But I see neither apples nor pears here, nor any other kind of fruit — nothing anywhere but cabbages."

At length, though, he thought, "At a pinch I can eat some of the leaves. They don't taste particularly good, but they'll refresh me." So he picked himself out a fine head of cabbage and ate it; but hardly had he swallowed a couple of mouthfuls before he felt very strange, and quite different.

Four legs grew on him, and a large head and two thick ears; and he saw with horror that he had been changed into a donkey. All the same, as his hunger grew greater every minute, and as the juicy leaves suited his present nature, he went on eating with great relish.

At last he came to a different kind of cabbage; but as soon as he had swallowed it he felt another change, and took his old human shape again.

Then the huntsman lay down and slept off his weariness. When he woke next morning he broke off one head of the bad cabbages and one of the good ones, and thought to himself, "This shall help me to get back my own and punish treachery."

Then he took the cabbages with him, climbed over the wall and set out to look for his sweetheart's castle. After wandering about for a couple of days he was lucky enough to find it again.

He dyed his face brown, so that his own mother would not have known him, and asked for shelter. "I'm so tired," said he, "that I can go no further."

The witch asked, "Who are you, countryman, and what's your business?"

"I'm a King's messenger, and I was sent out to look for the most delicious salad that grows under the sun. I've even been lucky enough to find it, and I'm carrying it about with me; but the sun's heat is so fierce that the delicate cabbage is threatening to wither, and I don't know whether I can carry it any further."

When the old woman heard about this exquisite salad she was greedy for it, and said, "Dear countryman, do let me just taste this wonderful salad."

"Why not?" answered he. "I've brought two heads with me, and I'll give you one of them." And he opened his pouch and handed her the bad cabbage.

The witch suspected nothing amiss, and her mouth watered so for this new dish that she went into the kitchen and dressed it herself. When it was ready she could not wait until it was set on the table, but took a couple of leaves at once and put them in her mouth. But hardly had she swallowed them before she lost her human shape, and ran out into the courtyard in the form of a donkey.

Presently the servant girl came into the kitchen and saw the salad standing there ready prepared, and was about to carry it up. But on the way, out of habit, she was seized with the wish to taste it, and ate a couple of leaves. Instantly the magic worked, and she became a donkey too and ran out to the old woman; and the dish of salad fell to the floor.

Meanwhile the messenger was sitting beside the beautiful girl; and as nobody came with the salad, and she too was longing for it, she said, "I don't know what has become of the salad."

The huntsman thought, "The salad must have taken effect already" — and said, "I'll go down to the kitchen and ask about it."

As he went down he saw the two donkeys running about the courtyard; but the salad was lying on the floor. "All right," said he, "those two have taken their portion" — and he picked up the remaining leaves and laid them on the dish and carried them up to the girl.

"I bring you the delicate dish myself," said he, "so that you don't have to wait any longer."

Then she ate of it, and like the others she was immediately deprived of her human shape, and ran out into the courtyard in the form of a donkey.

After the huntsman had washed his face, so that the transformed ones could recognise him, he went down into the courtyard and said, "Now you shall have the wages of your treachery." And he tied all three of them together with one rope and drove them along until he came to a mill.

He knocked at the window; the miller put his head out and asked what he wanted.

"I have three unmanageable beasts here," answered he, "that I don't want to keep any longer. Will you take them in and give them food and stable room and treat them as I tell you? And then I'll pay you what you ask."

The miller said, "Why not? But how am I to treat them?"

The huntsman said that he was to give the old donkey — that was the witch — three beatings and one meal a day; the younger one, which was the servant girl, one beating and three meals; and the youngest, which was the girl, no beatings and three meals — for he could not bring himself to have the girl beaten.

After that he went back to the castle and found everything there that he needed.

After a couple of days the miller came and said he must inform him that the old donkey, which had had three beatings and only one meal a day, was dead. "The other two," he went on, "certainly aren't dead, and they're fed three times a day; but they're so sad that they can't last much longer."

The huntsman was moved to pity, put his anger away and told the miller to drive them back to him. And when they came, he gave them some of the good salad, so that they became human again.

The beautiful girl fell on her knees before him and said, "Ah, my beloved, forgive me for the wrong I've done you. My mother drove me to it; it was done against my will, for I love you dearly. Your wishing cloak is hanging in a cupboard; and as for the bird's heart, I'll take a potion to bring it up."

But he thought otherwise, and said, "Keep it. It's all the same, for I'll take you for my true wife."

So the wedding was celebrated, and they lived happily together until their deaths.

The Old Woman in the Wood

A poor servant girl was once travelling through a great forest with the family she was in service with; and when they were in the middle of it, robbers came out of the thicket and murdered everybody they found. All of them died together except the girl, who had jumped out of the carriage in fright and hidden herself behind a tree.

When the robbers had gone away with their plunder, she came out and saw the great disaster. Then she began to weep bitterly and said, "What can a poor girl like me do now? I don't know how to get out of the forest, and no human being lives in it, so I must certainly starve."

She walked about and looked for a road, but could find none. When it was evening she sat down under a tree and gave herself into God's keeping, and resolved to sit and wait there and not go away, come what might.

But when she had sat there a while, a white dove came flying to her with a little golden key in its beak. It put the little key in her hand and said, "Do you see that great tree? There's a little lock in it, and this tiny key opens it, and inside you'll find food enough, and go hungry no more."

So she went to the tree and opened it, and found milk in a little dish and white bread to break into it, so that she could eat her fill.

When she had had enough she said, "This is the hour when the hens at home go to roost. I'm so tired I could go to bed too."

Then the dove flew to her again and brought another golden key in its beak, and said, "Open that tree there, and you'll find a bed."

So she opened it and found a beautiful white bed; and she prayed God to protect her during the night, and lay down and slept.

In the morning the dove came for the third time and again brought a little key, and said, "Open that tree there, and you'll find clothes." And when she opened it she found garments set with gold and jewels, more splendid than any king's daughter's.

So she lived there for some time, and the dove came every day and provided her with everything she needed; and it was a quiet, good life.

Once, though, the dove came and said, "Will you do something for my sake?"

"With all my heart," said the girl.

Then the little dove said, "I'll guide you to a small house. Go in; and inside it an old woman will be sitting by the fire, and she'll say, 'Good day.' But for your life, give her no answer; let her do what she likes, but pass by her on the right side. Further on there's a door; open it, and you'll come into a room where a quantity of rings of all kinds are lying, among them some magnificent ones with shining stones. Leave those where they are, though, and look out a plain one, which must be among them too, and bring it here to me as fast as you can."

The girl went to the little house and came to the door. There sat an old woman, who stared when she saw her, and said, "Good day, my child."

The girl gave her no answer, and opened the door.

"Where are you going?" cried the old woman, and seized her by the gown and tried to hold her fast, saying, "This is my house; nobody can go in there if I choose not to allow it."

But the girl was silent, and got away from her and went straight into the room. Now on the table lay an enormous quantity of rings, which gleamed and glittered before her eyes. She turned them over and looked for the plain one, but could not find it.

While she was searching, she saw the old woman stealing away and trying to make off with a birdcage she had in her hand. So she went after her and took the cage out of her hand; and when she raised it up and looked inside, there was a bird in it with the plain ring in its beak.

So she took the ring and ran home with it quite joyfully, and thought the little white dove would come and get the ring; but it did not.

Then she leaned against a tree and made up her mind to wait for the dove; and as she stood there, it seemed just as if the tree were growing soft and pliant, and letting its branches down. And suddenly the branches twined round her and turned into two arms; and when she looked round, the tree was a handsome man, who embraced her and kissed her heartily and said, "You have delivered me from the power of the old woman, who is a wicked witch. She had changed me into a tree, and every day for two hours I was a white dove; and as long as she had the ring, I could not get my human shape back."

Then his servants and his horses, who had likewise been changed into trees, were freed from the enchantment too, and stood beside him. And he led them away to his kingdom, for he was a King's son; and they married, and lived happily.

The Three Brothers

There was once a man who had three sons and nothing else in the world but the house he lived in. Now each of the sons wanted to have the house after his father's death; but the father loved them all alike and did not know what to do. He did not want to sell the house, because it had belonged to his forefathers, or else he could have divided the money among them.

At last a plan came into his head, and he said to his sons, "Go out into the world and each of you try to learn a trade; and when you all come back, whoever makes the best masterpiece shall have the house."

The sons were well content with this; and the eldest decided to be a blacksmith, the second a barber and the third a fencing master. They fixed a time when they should all come home again, and then each went his own way.

It happened that they all found skilful masters who taught them their trades well. The blacksmith had to shoe the King's horses, and he thought to himself, "The house is mine, without a doubt." The barber shaved only great people, and he too already looked on the house as his own. The fencing master got many a blow, but he only bit his lip and let nothing upset him; "for," he said to himself, "if you're afraid of a blow, you'll never win the house."

When the appointed time had gone by, the three brothers came home to their father; but they did not know how to find the best opportunity for showing their skill, so they sat down and talked it over together.

As they were sitting there, all at once a hare came running across the field. "Aha, just in time!" said the barber. So he took his basin and soap and lathered away until the hare came up; and then he soaped and shaved off the hare's whiskers while it was running at top speed, and did not even cut its skin or injure a hair on its body.

"Well done," said the old man. "Your brothers will have to exert themselves wonderfully, or the house will be yours."

Soon afterwards a nobleman came along in his coach, dashing by at full speed. "Now you shall see what I can do, father," said the blacksmith. And away he ran after the coach, and took all four shoes off the feet of one of the horses while it was galloping, and fitted it with four new shoes without stopping it.

"You're a fine fellow, and as clever as your brother," said his father. "I don't know which of you I ought to give the house to."

Then the third son said, "Father, let me have my turn, if you please." And as it was beginning to rain, he drew his sword and flourished it backwards and forwards above his head so fast that not a drop fell on him. It rained harder and harder, until at last it came down in torrents; but he only flourished his sword faster and faster, and stayed as dry as if he were sitting indoors.

When his father saw this he was amazed, and said, "This is the masterpiece. The house is yours."

His brothers were satisfied with this, as had been agreed beforehand; and as they loved one another very much, all three of them stayed together in the house and followed their trades. And since they had learned them so well and were so clever, they earned a great deal of money.

So they lived together happily until they grew old; and at last, when one of them fell sick and died, the two others grieved over it so sorely that they fell ill as well, and soon died too. And because they had been so clever, and had loved one another so much, all three of them were laid in the same grave.

The Devil and his Grandmother

There was a great war, and the King had many soldiers but gave them small pay — so small that they could not live on it. So three of them agreed among themselves to desert.

One of them said to the others, "If we're caught we shall be hanged on the gallows. How are we to manage it?"

Another said, "Look at that great cornfield. If we hid ourselves in there, nobody could find us; the troops aren't allowed into it, and tomorrow they're to march away."

So they crept into the corn. Only the troops did not march away, but stayed lying all round about it. They stayed in the corn two days and two nights, and were so hungry that they nearly died; but if they had come out, their death would have been certain.

Then they said, "What was the use of deserting, if we have to die miserably here?"

But just then a fiery dragon came flying through the air; and it came down to them and asked why they were hiding there.

They answered, "We're three soldiers who deserted because the pay was so bad; and now we shall have to die of hunger if we stay here, or dangle on the gallows if we go out."

"If you'll serve me for seven years," said the dragon, "I'll carry you through the army so that nobody catches you."

"We've no choice, and are forced to accept," they replied.

Then the dragon took hold of them in his claws and carried them away through the air over the army, and set them down on the earth again a long way off. But the dragon was none other than the Devil.

He gave them a small whip and said, "Whip with it and crack it, and then as much gold will spring up round about as you could wish for. Then you can live like great lords, keep horses and drive about in your carriages. But when the seven years have come to an end, you are my property."

Then he put a book in front of them, which all three of them were made to sign.

"I'll set you a riddle, though," said he. "And if you can guess it, you shall be free and released from my power."

Then the dragon flew away from them; and they went off with their whip, and had gold in plenty, and ordered themselves rich clothes and travelled about the world. Wherever they went they lived in pleasure and magnificence, rode on horseback, drove in carriages, ate and drank — but did nothing wicked.

The time slipped quickly away; and when the seven years were coming to an end, two of them were terribly anxious and alarmed. But the third took the business easily, and said, "Brothers, fear nothing. My head is sharp enough — I shall guess the riddle."

They went out into the open country and sat down, and the two pulled sorrowful faces. Then an old woman came up to them and asked why they were so sad.

"Alas," said they, "what business is that of yours? You can't help us anyway."

"Who knows?" said she. "Tell me your trouble."

So they told her that they had been the Devil's servants for nearly seven years, and that he had provided them with gold as plentifully as if it had been blackberries; but that they had sold themselves to him, and were forfeit to him if at the end of the seven years they could not guess a riddle.

The old woman said, "If you're to be saved, one of you must go into the forest. There he'll come to a fallen rock that looks like a little house; he must go into it, and then he'll get help."

The two gloomy ones thought to themselves, "That still won't save us" — and stayed where they were. But the third, the merry one, got up and walked on into the forest until he found the rock house.

In the little house, though, a very old woman was sitting, who was the Devil's grandmother; and she asked the soldier where he came from and what he wanted there. He told her everything that had happened; and as he pleased her well, she took pity on him and said she would help him.

She lifted up a great stone that lay over a cellar, and said, "Hide yourself down there. You can hear everything that's said up here; only sit still and don't stir. When the dragon comes I'll question him about the riddle — he tells me everything — so listen carefully to his answer."

At twelve o'clock at night the dragon came flying in and asked for his dinner. The grandmother laid the table and served food and drink, so that he was pleased; and they ate and drank together.

In the course of the conversation she asked him what sort of day he had had, and how many souls he had got.

"Nothing went very well today," he answered, "but I've laid hold of three soldiers. I have them safe."

"Indeed — three soldiers? That's something. But they may escape you yet."

The Devil said mockingly, "They're mine. I'll set them a riddle they'll never in this world be able to guess."

"What riddle is that?" she asked.

"I'll tell you. In the great North Sea lies a dead dogfish, and that shall be your roast meat; and the rib of a whale shall be your silver spoon; and a hollow old horse's hoof shall be your wineglass."

When the Devil had gone to bed, the old grandmother raised the stone and let the soldier out. "Did you pay careful attention to it all?"

"Yes," said he. "I know enough, and I'll contrive to save myself."

Then he had to go back another way, out through the window, secretly and at full speed, to his companions. He told them how the Devil had been outwitted by his old grandmother, and how he had learned the answer to the riddle from him.

Then they were all joyful and in good spirits, and took the whip and whipped up so much gold for themselves that it ran all over the ground.

When the seven years were fully up, the Devil came with the book and showed them their signatures and said, "I'll take you with me to hell. There you shall have a meal. If you can guess what kind of roast meat you'll have to eat, you shall be free and released from your bargain, and may keep the whip as well."

Then the first soldier began and said, "In the great North Sea lies a dead dogfish; that, no doubt, is the roast meat."

The Devil was angry, and began to mutter, "Hm! Hm! Hm!" And he asked the second, "But what will your spoon be?"

"The rib of a whale — that's to be our silver spoon."

The Devil pulled a sour face, growled again, "Hm! Hm! Hm!" — and said to the third, "And do you know too what your wineglass is to be?"

"An old horse's hoof is to be our wineglass."

Then the Devil flew away with a loud cry and had no more power over them; but the three kept the whip and whipped up as much money for themselves with it as they wanted, and lived happily to the end of their days.

Ferdinand the Faithful

Once upon a time there lived a man and a woman who had no children as long as they were rich; but when they were poor, they had a little boy. They could find no godfather for him, though; so the man said he would go to another place and see whether he could get one there.

As he went, a poor man met him and asked where he was going. He said he was going to see whether he could find a godfather, since he was poor and nobody would stand godfather for him.

"Oh," said the poor man, "you're poor and I'm poor. I'll be godfather for you; but I'm so badly off that I can give the child nothing. Go home and tell the nurse to come to the church with the child."

When they all got to the church together, the beggar was already there, and he gave the child the name of Ferdinand the Faithful.

As he was going out of the church the beggar said, "Now go home. I can give you nothing, and you likewise ought to give me nothing." But he gave a key to the nurse, and told her that when she got home she was to give it to the father, who was to take care of it until the child was fourteen years old; and then he was to go out onto the heath, where there was a castle that the key would fit, and everything in it should be his.

Now when the child was seven years old and had grown very big, he went out one day to play with some other boys, and each of them boasted that he had got more from his godfather than the rest; but the child could say nothing, and he was upset, and went home and said to his father, "Did I get nothing at all, then, from my godfather?"

"Oh, yes," said his father, "you got a key. If there's a castle standing on the heath, just go there and open it."

So the boy went there; but no castle was to be seen or heard of.

Seven years later, when he was fourteen, he went there again — and there stood the castle. When he had opened it, there was nothing inside but a horse, a white one. Then the boy was so full of joy at having a horse that he mounted it and galloped back to his father.

"Now I have a white horse, and I'm going travelling," said he.

So he set out; and as he was on his way, a pen was lying in the road. At first he thought he would pick it up; but then he thought to himself, "You should leave it lying there. You'll easily find a pen where you're going, if you need one."

And as he was riding away, a voice called after him, "Ferdinand the Faithful, take it with you."

He looked round, but saw nobody. So he went back and picked it up.

When he had ridden a little further he passed a lake, and a fish was lying on the bank gasping and panting for breath. So he said, "Wait, my dear fish, I'll help you into the water" — and took hold of it by the tail and threw it into the lake.

Then the fish put its head out of the water and said, "As you've helped me out of the mud, I'll give you a flute. When you're in any trouble, play on it, and then I'll help you; and if you ever let anything fall into the water, just play and I'll fetch it out for you."

Then he rode away, and a man came up to him who asked him where he was going. "Oh, to the next town."

Then what was his name? "Ferdinand the Faithful."

"Well! Then we have almost the same name. I'm called Ferdinand the Unfaithful."

And the two of them set off to the inn in the next town.

Now unfortunately Ferdinand the Unfaithful knew everything the other had ever thought and everything he was about to do; he knew it by all kinds of wicked arts.

There was, though, an honest girl at the inn, with a bright face and very pretty ways. She fell in love with Ferdinand the Faithful, because he was a handsome man, and she asked him where he was going.

"Oh, I'm just travelling about," said he.

Then she said he ought to stay there, because the King of that country wanted an attendant or an outrider, and he ought to enter his service. He answered that he could not very well go to somebody like that and offer himself.

Then the girl said, "Oh, but I'll soon do that for you."

And she went straight to the King and told him she knew of an excellent servant for him. He was well pleased with that, and had Ferdinand the Faithful brought to him, and wanted to make him his servant. But he would rather be an outrider, for wherever his horse was, there he wanted to be too; so the King made him an outrider.

When Ferdinand the Unfaithful learned that, he said to the girl, "What? You help him and not me?"

"Oh," said the girl, "I'll help you too." She thought, "I must keep friends with that man, for he isn't to be trusted."

So she went to the King and offered him as a servant, and the King was willing.

Now when the King met his lords in the morning, he always lamented and said, "Oh, if only I had my love here with me."

But Ferdinand the Unfaithful was always hostile to Ferdinand the Faithful. So once, when the King was complaining like this, he said, "You have the outrider; send him off to fetch her, and if he doesn't do it, his head must come off."

Then the King sent for Ferdinand the Faithful and told him that in such and such a place there was a girl he loved, and that he was to bring her to him, and if he did not do it he should die.

Ferdinand the Faithful went into the stable to his white horse, and complained and lamented, "Oh, what an unhappy man I am!"

Then somebody behind him cried, "Ferdinand the Faithful, why are you weeping?"

He looked round but saw nobody, and went on lamenting. "Oh, my dear little white horse, now I must leave you; now I must die."

Then somebody cried once more, "Ferdinand the Faithful, why are you weeping?"

And then for the first time he realised that it was his little white horse that was asking.

"Do you speak, my little white horse? Can you do that?" And he went on, "I'm to go to such and such a place and bring back the bride. Can you tell me how I'm to set about it?"

Then the little white horse answered, "Go to the King and say that if he'll give you what you must have, you'll get her for him. If he'll give you a ship full of meat and a ship full of bread, it will succeed. Great giants live on the lake, and if you take no meat with you for them they'll tear you to pieces; and there are the great birds, which would pick the eyes out of your head if you had no bread for them."

So the King made all the butchers in the land slaughter and all the bakers bake, so that the ships could be filled. And when they were full, the little white horse said to Ferdinand the Faithful, "Now mount me and come with me onto the ship; and then when the giants come, say:

	'Peace, peace, my dear little giants,
	I have had you in my thoughts;
	something I have brought for you.'

And when the birds come, you shall say again:

	'Peace, peace, my dear little birds,
	I have had you in my thoughts;
	something I have brought for you.'

Then they'll do nothing to you; and when you come to the castle the giants will help you. Then go up to the castle and take a couple of giants with you. The princess is lying there asleep; but you mustn't wake her — the giants must lift her up and carry her in her bed to the ship."

And now everything happened as the little white horse had said. Ferdinand the Faithful gave the giants and the birds what he had brought with him for them, and that made the giants willing; and they carried the princess in her bed to the King.

And when she came to the King, she said she could not live without her papers, which had been left behind in her castle. Then, at Ferdinand the Unfaithful's prompting, Ferdinand the Faithful was called, and the King told him he must fetch the papers from the castle, or he should die.

So he went into the stable once more and lamented and said, "Oh, my dear little white horse, now I'm to go away again. How am I to do it?"

Then the little white horse said he was simply to load the ships full again. So it all happened as it had happened before, and the giants and the birds were satisfied and made gentle by the meat.

When they came to the castle, the white horse told Ferdinand the Faithful that he must go in, and that the papers were lying on the table in the princess's bedroom. And Ferdinand the Faithful went in and fetched them.

When they were out on the lake he let his pen fall into the water; and the white horse said, "Now I can't help you at all."

But he remembered his flute and began to play on it, and the fish came with the pen in its mouth and gave it to him.

So he took the papers to the castle, where the wedding was celebrated.

The Queen, however, did not love the King, because he had no nose; but she would very much have liked to love Ferdinand the Faithful.

So once, when all the lords of the court were together, the Queen said that she could do feats of magic — that she could cut off anybody's head and put it on again, and that one of them ought to try it. But none of them would be the first; so Ferdinand the Faithful, again at Ferdinand the Unfaithful's prompting, undertook it. And she struck off his head and put it on again for him, and it healed together directly, so that it looked as though he had a red thread round his throat.

Then the King said to her, "My child, where did you learn that?"

"Yes," she said, "I understand the art. Shall I try it on you as well?"

"Oh, yes," said he.

But she cut off his head and did not put it back on; she pretended that she could not get it on, and that it would not stay fixed.

So the King was buried; and she married Ferdinand the Faithful.

He, though, always rode on his white horse; and once, when he was mounted on it, it told him that he was to ride out to the heath he knew and gallop three times round it. And when he had done that, the white horse stood up on its hind legs and was changed into a King's son.

The Iron Stove

In the days when wishing was still of some use, a King's son was bewitched by an old witch and shut up in an iron stove in a forest. There he passed many years, and nobody could deliver him.

Then a King's daughter came into the forest who had lost her way and could not find her father's kingdom again. After she had wandered about for nine days, she came at length to the iron stove. Then a voice came out of it and asked her, "Where do you come from, and where are you going?"

She answered, "I've lost my father's kingdom and can't get home again."

Then the voice inside the iron stove said, "I'll help you get home again, and very quickly too, if you'll promise to do what I ask of you. I'm the son of a far greater King than your father, and I'll marry you."

Then she was afraid, and thought, "Good heavens, what should I do with an iron stove?" But as she badly wanted to get home to her father, she promised to do as he asked.

But he said, "You must come back here and bring a knife with you, and scrape a hole in the iron."

Then he gave her a companion who walked beside her but did not speak, and in two hours he brought her home. There was great joy in the castle when the King's daughter came home, and the old King fell on her neck and kissed her.

She, though, was sorely troubled, and said, "Dear father, what I've been through! I should never have got home again out of that great wild forest if I hadn't come to an iron stove; but I've had to give my word that I'll go back to it and set it free and marry it."

Then the old King was so horrified that he nearly fainted, for she was his only daughter. So they decided that they would send the miller's daughter in her place, who was very beautiful. They took her there and gave her a knife and said she was to scrape at the iron stove.

So she scraped at it for four-and-twenty hours, but could not get the least particle off it. When day dawned, a voice in the stove said, "It seems to me it's day outside."

Then she answered, "It seems so to me too. I fancy I can hear the noise of my father's mill."

"So you're a miller's daughter! Then go your way at once, and let the King's daughter come here."

So she went away at once and told the old King that the man out there would have nothing to do with her; he wanted the King's daughter.

They still had a swineherd's daughter, though, who was even prettier than the miller's daughter; and they decided to give her a piece of gold to go to the iron stove in the King's daughter's place. So she was taken there, and she too had to scrape for four-and-twenty hours. But she made nothing of it.

When day broke, a voice inside the stove cried, "It seems to me it's day outside."

Then she answered, "So it seems to me too. I fancy I can hear my father's horn blowing."

"Then you're a swineherd's daughter! Go away at once, and tell the King's daughter to come; and tell her that everything must be done as promised, and if she doesn't come, everything in the kingdom shall be ruined and destroyed, and not one stone left standing on another."

When the King's daughter heard that, she began to weep; but now there was nothing for it but to keep her promise. So she took her leave of her father, put a knife in her pocket and went out to the iron stove in the forest.

When she got there she began to scrape, and the iron gave way; and when two hours were over she had already scraped a small hole. Then she peeped in and saw a young man so handsome, and so brilliant with gold and precious jewels, that her very soul was delighted. So she went on scraping and made the hole so large that he could get out.

Then he said, "You are mine and I am yours. You are my bride, and you have set me free."

He wanted to take her away with him to his kingdom, but she begged him to let her go to her father just once more; and the King's son allowed it, but she was not to say more than three words to her father, and then she was to come back again.

So she went home; but she said more than three words. And instantly the iron stove disappeared and was carried far away over glass mountains and piercing swords. But the King's son was set free and no longer shut up in it.

After this she said goodbye to her father, took some money with her, though not much, and went back to the great forest and looked for the iron stove; but it was nowhere to be found. For nine days she searched for it, and then her hunger grew so great that she did not know what to do, for she could not live any longer.

When it was evening she sat herself up in a small tree and made up her mind to spend the night there, since she was afraid of wild beasts. As midnight drew near she saw a small light in the distance, and thought, "Ah, there I might be saved."

She climbed down out of the tree and went towards the light; but as she went, she prayed. Then she came to a little old house with a great deal of grass grown up all round it and a small heap of wood lying in front. She thought, "Ah, where have I come to?" — and peeped in at the window; but she saw nothing inside except toads, big and little, and a table well covered with wine and roast meat, with plates and glasses of silver.

Then she took courage and knocked at the door. The fat toad cried:

	"Little green waiting-maid,
	waiting-maid with the limping leg,
	little dog with the limping leg,
	hop this way and that
	and quickly see who's outside."

And a small toad came walking up and opened the door to her. When she came in, they all bade her welcome and made her sit down. They asked, "Where have you come from, and where are you going?"

Then she told them everything that had happened to her: how, because she had broken the order she had been given not to say more than three words, the stove had disappeared, and the King's son with it, and how she meant now to look for him over hill and dale until she found him.

Then the old fat one said:

	"Little green waiting-maid,
	waiting-maid with the limping leg,
	little dog with the limping leg,
	hop this way and that
	and bring me the great box."

Then the little one went and brought the box.

After this they gave her food and drink and took her to a well-made bed, which felt like silk and velvet; and she lay down in it in God's name and slept.

When morning came she got up, and the old toad gave her three needles out of the great box to take with her. She would need them, for she had to cross a high glass mountain and go over three piercing swords and a great lake. If she did all this, she would get her lover back again.

So she gave her three things to take the greatest care of: three large needles, a plough wheel and three nuts.

With these she travelled on. And when she came to the glass mountain, which was so slippery, she stuck the three needles first behind her feet and then in front of them, and so got over it; and when she was over, she hid them in a place she marked carefully.

After this she came to the three piercing swords; and then she seated herself on her plough wheel and rolled over them.

At last she arrived at a great lake; and when she had crossed it, she came to a large and beautiful castle. She went and asked for a place: she was a poor girl, she said, and would like to be taken on. But she knew that the King's son whom she had released from the iron stove in the great forest was in that castle. So she was taken on as a scullery maid at low wages.

But the King's son already had another girl at his side whom he meant to marry, for he thought that she had long been dead.

In the evening, when she had finished washing up, she felt in her pocket and found the three nuts the old toad had given her. She cracked one with her teeth and was going to eat the kernel, when — lo and behold — there was a stately royal gown inside it.

But when the bride heard of this, she came and asked for the dress and wanted to buy it, and said, "That's not a dress for a servant girl."

But she said no, she would not sell it; but if the bride would grant her one thing she should have it, and that was leave to sleep one night in the bridegroom's room. The bride gave her permission, because the dress was so pretty and she had never had one like it.

When evening came she said to her bridegroom, "That silly girl is going to sleep in your room."

"If you're willing, so am I," said he.

But she gave him a glass of wine into which she had poured a sleeping draught. So the bridegroom and the scullery maid went to sleep in the room, and he slept so soundly that she could not wake him.

She wept the whole night and cried, "I set you free when you were in an iron stove in the wild forest; I searched for you, and walked over a glass mountain and three sharp swords and a great lake before I found you — and yet you won't hear me!"

The servants sat by the bedroom door and heard how she wept the whole night through, and in the morning they told their lord about it.

And the next evening, when she had washed up, she opened the second nut, and there was a far more beautiful dress inside it. When the bride saw it, she wanted to buy that as well. But the girl would take no money, and asked that she might sleep once more in the bridegroom's room.

The bride, though, gave him a sleeping draught, and he slept so soundly that he could hear nothing. But the scullery maid wept the whole night long and cried, "I set you free when you were in an iron stove in the wild forest; I searched for you, and walked over a glass mountain and over three sharp swords and a great lake before I found you — and yet you won't hear me!"

The servants sat by the bedroom door and heard her weeping the whole night through, and in the morning told their lord about it.

And on the third evening, when she had washed up, she opened the third nut, and inside it was a still more beautiful dress, stiff with pure gold. When the bride saw it she wanted to have it; but the girl would only give it up on condition that she might sleep in the bridegroom's room for a third time.

The King's son, though, was on his guard, and threw the sleeping draught away. So now, when she began to weep and cry, "Dearest love, I set you free when you were in the iron stove in that terrible wild forest," the King's son leapt up and said, "You are the true one. You are mine and I am yours."

And with that, while it was still night, he got into a carriage with her; and they took away the false bride's clothes so that she could not get up.

When they came to the great lake they sailed across it; and when they reached the three sharp swords they seated themselves on the plough wheel; and when they got to the glass mountain they stuck the three needles into it. And so at length they came to the little old house — but when they went inside it, it was a great castle, and the toads were all disenchanted and were king's children, and full of happiness.

Then the wedding was celebrated, and the King's son and the princess stayed in the castle, which was much larger than either of their fathers' castles. But as the old King grieved at being left alone, they fetched him away and brought him to live with them; and they had two kingdoms, and lived in happy marriage.

	A mouse did run;
	this story's done.

The Lazy Spinner

In a certain village there once lived a man and his wife; and the wife was so idle that she would never work at anything. Whatever her husband gave her to spin she never got done; and what she did spin she did not wind, but let it all lie tangled in a heap.

If the man scolded her, she was always ready with her tongue, and said, "Well, how am I to wind it, when I have no reel? You just go into the forest and get me one."

"If that's all," said the man, "then I'll go into the forest and get some wood to make reels with."

Then the woman was afraid that if he had the wood he would make her a reel out of it, and she would have to wind her yarn off and then start spinning again. She thought about it a little, and then a lucky idea came to her; and she secretly followed the man into the forest. And when he had climbed a tree to choose and cut his wood, she crept into the thicket below, where he could not see her, and cried:

	"He who cuts wood for reels shall die,
	and he who winds shall perish."

The man listened, laid his axe down for a moment, and began to think about what that could mean. "Hallo," he said at last, "what can that have been? My ears must have been singing. I won't alarm myself for nothing."

So he took up the axe again and began to chop; and then there came a cry from below again:

	"He who cuts wood for reels shall die,
	and he who winds shall perish."

He stopped, and felt afraid and alarmed, and pondered over it. But when a few moments had gone by, he took heart again, and a third time he stretched out his hand for the axe and began to cut.

But somebody called out a third time, and said loudly:

	"He who cuts wood for reels shall die,
	and he who winds shall perish."

That was enough for him, and all his inclination had gone; so he climbed hastily down out of the tree and set off home.

The woman ran as fast as she could by side paths so as to get home first. So when he came into the parlour she put on an innocent face, as though nothing had happened, and said, "Well, have you brought a nice piece of wood for reels?"

"No," said he. "I can see very well that winding won't do." And he told her what had happened to him in the forest, and from that time on left her in peace about it.

All the same, after some time the man began to complain again about the disorder in the house. "Wife," said he, "it's really a shame that the spun yarn should lie there all tangled up."

"I'll tell you what," said she. "Since we still haven't come by any reel, you go up into the loft and I'll stand down below and throw the yarn up to you, and you throw it down to me; and so we'll get a skein after all."

"Yes, that will do," said the man.

So they did that; and when it was done he said, "The yarn's in skeins; now it must be boiled."

The woman was distressed again. She did say, "Yes, we'll boil it early tomorrow morning" — but she was secretly contriving another trick.

Early in the morning she got up, lit a fire and put the kettle on; only instead of the yarn she put in a lump of tow, and let it boil. After that she went to the man, who was still lying in bed, and said to him, "I have to go out. You must get up and look after the yarn in the kettle on the fire — but you must be there at once, mind that. For if the cock should happen to crow and you're not attending to the yarn, it will turn into tow."

The man was willing, and took good care not to loiter. He got up as quickly as he could and went into the kitchen. But when he reached the kettle and peeped in, he saw to his horror nothing but a lump of tow.

Then the poor man was as still as a mouse, thinking that he had neglected it and was to blame; and in future he said no more about yarn and spinning.

But you must admit yourself that she was an odious woman.

The Four Skilful Brothers

There was once a poor man who had four sons; and when they were grown up he said to them, "My dear children, you must go out into the world now, for I have nothing to give you. So set out, and go some distance off and learn a trade, and see how you can make your way."

So the four brothers took their sticks, said goodbye to their father, and went out through the town gate together. When they had travelled for some time, they came to a crossroads that branched off in four different directions.

Then the eldest said, "Here we must separate; but four years from today we'll meet each other again at this spot, and in the meantime we'll seek our fortunes."

Then each of them went his own way. The eldest met a man who asked him where he was going and what he meant to do.

"I want to learn a trade," he replied.

Then the other said, "Come with me and be a thief."

"No," he answered. "That's no longer thought a respectable trade, and the end of it is that a man swings on the gallows."

"Oh," said the man, "you needn't be afraid of the gallows. I'll only teach you to get hold of things no other man could ever lay hands on, and nobody will ever catch you at it."

So he let himself be talked into it; and while he was with the man he became an accomplished thief, and so dexterous that nothing was safe from him once he took a fancy to it.

The second brother met a man who put the same question to him: what did he want to learn in the world?

"I don't know yet," he replied.

"Then come with me and be an astronomer. There's nothing better than that, for nothing is hidden from you."

He liked the idea, and became such a skilful astronomer that when he had learned everything and was about to travel on, his master gave him a telescope and said to him, "With this you can see whatever happens either on earth or in heaven, and nothing can stay hidden from you."

A huntsman took the third brother into training, and gave him such excellent instruction in everything to do with huntsmanship that he became an experienced hunter. When he went away his master gave him a gun and said, "It will never fail you. Whatever you aim at, you're certain to hit."

The youngest brother also met a man, who spoke to him and asked what his intentions were. "Wouldn't you like to be a tailor?" said he.

"Not that I know of," said the young man. "Sitting doubled up from morning till night, driving the needle and the pressing iron backwards and forwards, is not to my taste."

"Oh, but you're speaking in ignorance," answered the man. "With me you'd learn a very different kind of tailoring, one that's respectable and proper, and for the most part very honourable."

So he let himself be persuaded and went with the man, and learned his art from the very beginning. When they parted, the man gave the young man a needle and said, "With this you can sew together whatever is given you, whether it's as soft as an egg or as hard as steel; and it will all become one piece of stuff, so that no seam is visible."

When the appointed four years were over, the four brothers arrived at the crossroads at the same time, embraced and kissed each other, and went home together to their father.

"So now," said he, quite delighted, "the wind has blown you back to me again."

They told him everything that had happened to them, and that each of them had learned his own trade.

Now they were sitting just in front of the house under a large tree, and their father said, "I'll put you all to the test and see what you can do." Then he looked up and said to his second son, "Between two branches at the top of this tree there's a chaffinch's nest. Tell me how many eggs are in it."

The astronomer took his glass, looked up and said, "There are five."

Then the father said to the eldest, "Fetch the eggs down without disturbing the bird that's sitting on them."

The skilful thief climbed up and took the five eggs from under the bird, which never noticed what he was doing and stayed quietly sitting where she was; and he brought them down to his father.

The father took them and put one of them on each corner of the table and the fifth in the middle, and said to the huntsman, "With one shot you shall shoot me all five eggs in two, through the middle."

The huntsman took aim and shot the eggs, all five of them, just as his father had asked, and all at one shot. He must certainly have had some of that powder that shoots round corners.

"Now it's your turn," said the father to the fourth son. "You shall sew the eggs together again, and the young birds inside them as well; and you must do it so that they're not harmed by the shot."

The tailor brought his needle and sewed them as his father wanted. When he had done it, the thief had to climb the tree again and carry them back to the nest and put them under the bird without her noticing.

The bird sat her full time; and after a few days the young ones crept out, and they had a red line round their necks where the tailor had sewn them together.

"Well," said the old man to his sons, "I begin to think you're worth more than green clover. You've used your time well and learned something good. I can't say which of you deserves the most praise. That will be proved if you only get an early chance to use your talents."

Not long after this there was a great uproar in the country, for the King's daughter had been carried off by a dragon. The King was full of trouble about it, day and night, and had it proclaimed that whoever brought her back should have her for a wife.

The four brothers said to each other, "This would be a fine opportunity for us to show what we can do." And they decided to go out together and set the King's daughter free.

"I'll soon know where she is," said the astronomer — and looked through his telescope and said, "I can see her already. She's far away from here on a rock in the sea, and the dragon is beside her, watching her."

Then he went to the King and asked for a ship for himself and his brothers, and sailed with them over the sea until they came to the rock. There the King's daughter was sitting, with the dragon lying asleep in her lap.

The huntsman said, "I daren't fire; I should kill the beautiful girl at the same time."

"Then I'll try my art," said the thief; and he crept over and stole her away from under the dragon so quietly and dexterously that the monster never noticed, but went on snoring.

Full of joy, they hurried off with her on board ship and steered out into the open sea. But the dragon, who when he woke found no princess there, came after them, snorting angrily through the air. And just as he was circling above the ship and about to come down on it, the huntsman shouldered his gun and shot him through the heart.

The monster fell down dead; but he was so large and heavy that his fall smashed the whole ship to pieces. Luckily, though, they got hold of a couple of planks and swam about on the wide sea.

Then again they were in great danger; but the tailor was not idle. He took his wonderful needle and with a few stitches sewed the planks together, and they seated themselves on them and collected all the fragments of the vessel. Then he sewed those together so skilfully that in a very short time the ship was seaworthy again and they could go home in safety.

When the King saw his daughter once more there were great rejoicings. He said to the four brothers, "One of you shall have her for a wife; but which of you it's to be, you must settle among yourselves."

Then a warm dispute arose among them, for each of them pressed his own claim.

The astronomer said, "If I hadn't seen the princess, all your arts would have been useless. So she's mine."

The thief said, "What use would your seeing have been if I hadn't got her away from the dragon? So she's mine."

The huntsman said, "You and the princess and all the rest of you would have been torn to pieces by the dragon if my ball hadn't hit him. So she's mine."

The tailor said, "And if I hadn't sewn the ship together again with my art, every one of you would have been miserably drowned. So she's mine."

Then the King delivered this judgement: "Each of you has an equal right; and since all of you can't have the girl, none of you shall have her. But I'll give each of you half a kingdom as a reward."

The brothers were pleased with this decision, and said, "It's better this way than that we should quarrel with one another."

So each of them received half a kingdom, and they lived with their father in the greatest happiness as long as it pleased God.

One-eye, Two-eyes, and Three-eyes

There was once a woman who had three daughters. The eldest was called One-eye, because she had only one eye, in the middle of her forehead; the second Two-eyes, because she had two eyes like other people; and the youngest Three-eyes, because she had three eyes, and her third eye was in the middle of her forehead too.

But because Two-eyes saw just as other human beings did, her sisters and her mother could not endure her. They said to her, "You, with your two eyes, are no better than the common people. You don't belong to us." They pushed her about and threw old clothes at her and gave her nothing to eat but what they left, and did everything they could to make her unhappy.

It happened that Two-eyes had to go out into the fields and mind the goat; and she was still quite hungry, because her sisters had given her so little to eat. So she sat down on a bank and began to weep, and so bitterly that two streams ran down out of her eyes.

And once, when she looked up in her grief, a woman was standing beside her, who said, "Why are you weeping, little Two-eyes?"

Two-eyes answered, "Haven't I reason to weep? I have two eyes like other people, and my sisters and my mother hate me for it and push me from one corner to another, and throw old clothes at me, and give me nothing to eat but the scraps they leave. Today they've given me so little that I'm still quite hungry."

Then the wise woman said, "Wipe away your tears, Two-eyes, and I'll tell you something that will stop you ever going hungry again. Just say to your goat:

	'Bleat, my little goat, bleat,
	cover the table with something to eat' —

and then a clean, well-spread little table will stand in front of you with the most delicious food on it, and you may eat as much of it as you like. And when you've had enough and have no more need of the little table, just say:

	'Bleat, bleat, my little goat, I pray,
	and take the table quite away' —

and then it will vanish from your sight again."

With that the wise woman went away. But Two-eyes thought, "I must try it at once and see whether what she said is true, for I'm far too hungry." And she said:

	"Bleat, my little goat, bleat,
	cover the table with something to eat."

And hardly had she spoken the words before a little table stood there covered with a white cloth, and on it a plate with a knife and fork and a silver spoon; and the most delicious food was there too, warm and steaming as if it had just come out of the kitchen.

Then Two-eyes said the shortest prayer she knew — "Lord God, be with us always, amen" — and helped herself to some food and enjoyed it. And when she had had enough, she said what the wise woman had taught her:

	"Bleat, bleat, my little goat, I pray,
	and take the table quite away."

And immediately the little table and everything on it was gone.

"That's a delightful way of keeping house," thought Two-eyes, and was quite glad and happy.

In the evening, when she went home with her goat, she found a small earthenware dish with some food in it that her sisters had set out for her; but she did not touch it. Next day she went out with her goat again, and left the few bits of broken bread they had handed her lying untouched.

The first and second time she did this her sisters did not notice at all; but as it happened every time, they did notice, and said, "There's something wrong about Two-eyes. She always leaves her food untasted; and she used to eat up everything she was given. She must have found other ways of getting food."

So that they could learn the truth, they decided to send One-eye out with Two-eyes when she drove the goat to pasture, to watch what Two-eyes did there, and whether anybody brought her something to eat and drink.

So when Two-eyes set out next time, One-eye came to her and said, "I'll come with you to the pasture and see that the goat is properly looked after and driven where there's food."

But Two-eyes knew what was in One-eye's mind, and drove the goat into high grass and said, "Come, One-eye, we'll sit down and I'll sing you something."

One-eye sat down; and she was tired from the unaccustomed walk and the heat of the sun. And Two-eyes sang over and over again:

	"One eye, are you waking?
	One eye, are you sleeping?"
