until One-eye shut her one eye and fell asleep. And as soon as Two-eyes saw that One-eye was fast asleep and could find nothing out, she said:

	"Bleat, my little goat, bleat,
	cover the table with something to eat."

And she sat down at her table and ate and drank until she had had enough; and then she said again:

	"Bleat, bleat, my little goat, I pray,
	and take the table quite away."

And in an instant it was all gone.

Then Two-eyes woke One-eye and said, "One-eye, you meant to look after the goat, and you go to sleep doing it; and meanwhile the goat could have run off all over the world. Come, let's go home again."

So they went home; and again Two-eyes left her little dish untouched, and One-eye could not tell her mother why she would not eat it, and said, to excuse herself, "I fell asleep out there."

Next day the mother said to Three-eyes, "This time you shall go and watch whether Two-eyes eats anything when she's out, and whether anybody brings her food and drink; for she must be eating and drinking in secret."

So Three-eyes went to Two-eyes and said, "I'll come with you and see whether the goat is properly looked after and driven where there's food."

But Two-eyes knew what was in Three-eyes' mind, and drove the goat into high grass and said, "We'll sit down and I'll sing you something, Three-eyes."

Three-eyes sat down, and she was tired from the walk and the heat of the sun; and Two-eyes began the same song as before, and sang:

"Three eyes, are you waking?"

But then, instead of singing:

"Three eyes, are you sleeping?"

as she should have done, she thoughtlessly sang:

"Two eyes, are you sleeping?"

and went on singing all the time:

	"Three eyes, are you waking?
	Two eyes, are you sleeping?"

Then two of the eyes Three-eyes had shut and fell asleep; but the third, because it had not been named in the song, did not sleep. Three-eyes shut it, it is true — but only out of cunning, to pretend that it was asleep too; and it blinked, and could see everything perfectly well.

And when Two-eyes thought that Three-eyes was fast asleep, she used her little charm:

	"Bleat, my little goat, bleat,
	cover the table with something to eat."

And she ate and drank as much as her heart desired, and then ordered the table to go away again:

	"Bleat, bleat, my little goat, I pray,
	and take the table quite away."

And Three-eyes had seen everything.

Then Two-eyes came to her and woke her and said, "Have you been asleep, Three-eyes? You're a fine caretaker! Come, we'll go home."

And when they got home Two-eyes again did not eat; and Three-eyes said to her mother, "Now I know why that stuck-up thing there doesn't eat. When she's out, she says to the goat:

	'Bleat, my little goat, bleat,
	cover the table with something to eat' —

and then a little table appears in front of her covered with the best of food, much better than anything we have here. And when she's eaten all she wants, she says:

	'Bleat, bleat, my little goat, I pray,
	and take the table quite away' —

and it all disappears. I watched everything closely. She put two of my eyes to sleep with a certain form of words, but luckily the one in my forehead stayed awake."

Then the envious mother cried, "Do you want to fare better than we do? That wish shall soon pass off." And she fetched a butcher's knife and drove it into the heart of the goat, which fell down dead.

When Two-eyes saw that, she went out full of grief and sat down on the grassy bank at the edge of the field and wept bitter tears.

Suddenly the wise woman was standing beside her once more, and said, "Two-eyes, why are you weeping?"

"Haven't I reason to weep?" she answered. "The goat that covered the table for me every day when I spoke your charm has been killed by my mother, and now I shall have to bear hunger and want again."

The wise woman said, "Two-eyes, I'll give you a piece of good advice. Ask your sisters to give you the innards of the slaughtered goat, and bury them in the ground in front of the house, and your fortune will be made."

Then she vanished; and Two-eyes went home and said to her sisters, "Dear sisters, do give me some part of my goat. I don't ask for anything good — just give me the innards."

Then they laughed and said, "If that's all you want, you can have it."

So Two-eyes took the innards and buried them quietly in the evening in front of the house door, as the wise woman had advised her.

Next morning, when they all woke and came to the house door, there stood a strangely magnificent tree with leaves of silver and fruit of gold hanging among them, so that in all the wide world there was nothing more beautiful or precious. They did not know how the tree could have come there in the night; but Two-eyes saw that it had grown up out of the innards of the goat, for it was standing on the exact spot where she had buried them.

Then the mother said to One-eye, "Climb up, my child, and gather some of the fruit of the tree for us."

One-eye climbed up; but when she was about to take hold of one of the golden apples, the branch escaped out of her hands; and that happened every time, so that she could not pick a single apple, do what she might.

Then the mother said, "Three-eyes, you climb up. You with your three eyes can look about you better than One-eye."

One-eye slid down and Three-eyes climbed up. But Three-eyes was no more skilful, and search as she liked, the golden apples always escaped her.

At length the mother lost patience and climbed up herself; but she could get hold of the fruit no better than One-eye and Three-eyes, for she always clutched empty air.

Then Two-eyes said, "I'll just go up. Perhaps I shall do better."

The sisters cried, "You, indeed — with your two eyes! What can you do?"

But Two-eyes climbed up, and the golden apples did not get out of her way, but came into her hand of their own accord, so that she could pick them one after another; and she brought a whole apronful down with her.

Her mother took them away from her; and instead of treating poor Two-eyes any better for it, she and One-eye and Three-eyes were only envious that Two-eyes alone had been able to get the fruit, and they treated her still more cruelly.

Now it happened once, when they were all standing together by the tree, that a young knight came up.

"Quick, Two-eyes," cried the two sisters, "get under this, and don't disgrace us!" And with all speed they turned an empty barrel that was standing close by the tree over poor Two-eyes, and pushed the golden apples she had been gathering under it as well.

When the knight came nearer, he turned out to be a handsome lord; and he stopped and admired the magnificent gold and silver tree, and said to the two sisters, "Whose is this fine tree? Anybody who would give me one branch of it might ask whatever he wanted in return."

Then One-eye and Three-eyes replied that the tree belonged to them, and that they would give him a branch. They both took great trouble over it, but they could not do it, for the branches and the fruit moved away from them every time.

Then the knight said, "It's very strange that the tree should belong to you and you still can't break a piece off it."

They insisted again that the tree was their property. But while they were saying so, Two-eyes rolled a couple of golden apples out from under the barrel to the knight's feet, for she was annoyed with One-eye and Three-eyes for not telling the truth.

When the knight saw the apples he was astonished, and asked where they came from. One-eye and Three-eyes answered that they had another sister, who was not allowed to show herself, because she had only two eyes, like any common person.

The knight, though, wanted to see her, and cried, "Two-eyes, come out."

Then Two-eyes, quite comforted, came out from under the barrel; and the knight was struck by her great beauty, and said, "You, Two-eyes, can surely break a branch off the tree for me."

"Yes," replied Two-eyes, "I shall certainly be able to, for the tree belongs to me." And she climbed up and with the greatest ease broke off a branch with beautiful silver leaves and golden fruit, and gave it to the knight.

Then the knight said, "Two-eyes, what shall I give you for it?"

"Alas," answered Two-eyes, "I suffer hunger and thirst and grief and want from early morning till late at night. If you would take me with you and free me from all this, I should be happy."

So the knight lifted Two-eyes onto his horse and took her home with him to his father's castle; and there he gave her beautiful clothes and food and drink to her heart's content. And as he loved her so much, he married her, and the wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing.

When Two-eyes had been carried away like this by the handsome knight, her two sisters grudged her her good fortune in downright earnest. "The wonderful tree is still ours, though," they thought, "and even if we can gather no fruit from it, everybody will still stop and look at it, and come to us and admire it. Who knows what good things may be in store for us?"

But next morning the tree had vanished, and all their hopes were at an end. And when Two-eyes looked out of the window of her own little room, there it was standing in front of it, to her great delight; and so it had followed her.

Two-eyes lived a long time in happiness. Once two poor women came to her at her castle and begged for alms. She looked in their faces and recognised her sisters, One-eye and Three-eyes, who had fallen into such poverty that they had to wander about and beg their bread from door to door.

But Two-eyes made them welcome and was kind to them and took care of them; so that both of them repented with all their hearts of the wrong they had done their sister in their youth.

Fair Katrinelje and Pif-Paf-Poltrie

"Good day, Father Hollenthe."

"Many thanks, Pif-paf-poltrie."

"May I have your daughter?"

"Oh, yes — if Mother Malcho, and Brother High-and-Mighty, and Sister Käsetraut, and fair Katrinelje are willing, you can have her."

"Where's Mother Malcho, then?"

"She's in the cowshed, milking the cow."

"Good day, Mother Malcho."

"Many thanks, Pif-paf-poltrie."

"May I have your daughter?"

"Oh, yes — if Father Hollenthe, and Brother High-and-Mighty, and Sister Käsetraut, and fair Katrinelje are willing, you can have her."

"Where's Brother High-and-Mighty, then?"

"He's in the room chopping wood."

"Good day, Brother High-and-Mighty."

"Many thanks, Pif-paf-poltrie."

"May I have your sister?"

"Oh, yes — if Father Hollenthe, and Mother Malcho, and Sister Käsetraut, and fair Katrinelje are willing, you can have her."

"Where's Sister Käsetraut, then?"

"She's in the garden cutting cabbages."

"Good day, Sister Käsetraut."

"Many thanks, Pif-paf-poltrie."

"May I have your sister?"

"Oh, yes — if Father Hollenthe, and Mother Malcho, and Brother High-and-Mighty, and fair Katrinelje are willing, you may have her."

"Where's fair Katrinelje, then?"

"She's in the room counting out her farthings."

"Good day, fair Katrinelje."

"Many thanks, Pif-paf-poltrie."

"Will you be my bride?"

"Oh, yes — if Father Hollenthe, and Mother Malcho, and Brother High-and-Mighty, and Sister Käsetraut are willing, I'm ready."

"Fair Katrinelje, how much dowry have you?"

"Fourteen farthings in ready money, three and a half groschen owing to me, half a pound of dried apples, a handful of fried bread and a handful of spices.

	And many other things are mine —
	haven't I a dowry fine?

"Pif-paf-poltrie, what's your trade? Are you a tailor?"

"Something better."

"A shoemaker?"

"Something better."

"A farmer?"

"Something better."

"A joiner?"

"Something better."

"A smith?"

"Something better."

"A miller?"

"Something better."

"Perhaps a broom-maker?"

"Yes, that's what I am. Isn't that a fine trade?"

The Fox and the Horse

A peasant had a faithful horse that had grown old and could do no more work; so his master would give him nothing more to eat, and said, "I can certainly make no more use of you; but still, I mean you well. If you prove yourself still strong enough to bring me a lion, I'll keep you. But for now, take yourself off out of my stable." And with that he chased him out into the open country.

The horse was sad, and went to the forest to look for a little shelter there from the weather. Then the fox met him and said, "Why are you hanging your head like that, and going about all alone?"

"Alas," replied the horse, "greed and loyalty don't live together in one house. My master has forgotten the services I've done him all these years; and because I can no longer plough well, he'll give me no more food and has driven me out."

"Without giving you a chance?" asked the fox.

"The chance was a bad one. He said that if I were still strong enough to bring him a lion he'd keep me; but he knows perfectly well that I can't do that."

The fox said, "I'll help you. Just lie down and stretch yourself out as though you were dead, and don't stir."

The horse did as the fox asked; and the fox went to the lion, who had his den not far off, and said, "There's a dead horse lying out there. Just come with me — you can have a rich meal."

The lion went with him; and when they were both standing beside the horse, the fox said, "After all, it isn't very comfortable for you here. I'll tell you what — I'll tie it to you by the tail, and then you can drag it into your cave and devour it in peace."

This advice pleased the lion. He lay down; and so that the fox could tie the horse fast to him, he kept quite still.

But the fox tied the lion's legs together with the horse's tail, and twisted and fastened it all so well and so strongly that no strength could break it. And when he had finished his work he tapped the horse on the shoulder and said, "Pull, white horse, pull."

Then up sprang the horse at once and dragged the lion away with him. The lion began to roar so that all the birds in the forest flew up in terror; but the horse let him roar, and drew him and dragged him over the country to his master's door.

When the master saw the lion he was of a better mind, and said to the horse, "You shall stay with me and fare well." And he gave him plenty to eat until he died.

The Shoes That Were Danced to Pieces

There was once a King who had twelve daughters, each one more beautiful than the last. They all slept together in one room, with their beds standing side by side; and every night, when they were in them, the King locked the door and bolted it. But in the morning, when he unlocked the door, he saw that their shoes were worn out with dancing, and nobody could find out how it came about.

So the King had it proclaimed that whoever could discover where they danced at night should choose one of them for a wife and be King after his death — but that whoever came forward and had not discovered it within three days and nights should forfeit his life.

It was not long before a King's son presented himself and offered to undertake the business. He was well received, and in the evening was taken into a room next to the princesses' bedroom. His bed was set up there, and he was to watch where they went and danced; and so that they could do nothing in secret or go off somewhere else, the door of their room was left open.

But the prince's eyelids grew heavy as lead and he fell asleep; and when he woke in the morning, all twelve of them had been to the dance, for their shoes were standing there with holes in the soles. On the second and third nights it happened just the same; and then his head was struck off without mercy.

Many others came after this and undertook the business, but all of them forfeited their lives.

Now it happened that a poor soldier who had a wound and could serve no longer found himself on the road to the town where the King lived. There he met an old woman, who asked him where he was going.

"I hardly know myself," he answered — and added as a joke, "I had half a mind to discover where the princesses dance their shoes into holes, and so become King."

"That's not so difficult," said the old woman. "You mustn't drink the wine that will be brought to you at night, and you must pretend to be fast asleep." And with that she gave him a little cloak and said, "If you put that on, you'll be invisible, and then you can steal after the twelve of them."

When the soldier had been given this good advice, he went into the business in earnest, took heart, went to the King and announced himself as a suitor. He was as well received as the others, and royal clothes were put on him.

That evening at bedtime he was taken into the antechamber; and as he was about to go to bed, the eldest princess came and brought him a cup of wine. But he had tied a sponge under his chin and let the wine run down into it, without drinking a drop.

Then he lay down; and when he had lain a while he began to snore, as though in the deepest sleep. The twelve princesses heard that and laughed, and the eldest said, "He might as well have saved his life too."

And with that they got up and opened wardrobes and chests and cupboards and brought out pretty dresses, and dressed themselves in front of their mirrors and sprang about, delighted at the prospect of the dance.

Only the youngest said, "I don't know how it is. You're all very happy, but I feel very strange. Some misfortune is certainly going to come to us."

"You're a goose, always frightened," said the eldest. "Have you forgotten how many kings' sons have already come here for nothing? I hardly needed to give the soldier a sleeping draught; the clown wouldn't have woken anyway."

When they were all ready they looked carefully at the soldier; but he had shut his eyes and did not move or stir, so they felt themselves quite safe.

The eldest then went to her bed and tapped it. It sank into the earth at once; and one after another they went down through the opening, the eldest going first. The soldier, who had watched everything, waited no longer, put on his little cloak and went down last, with the youngest.

Halfway down the stairs he trod a little on her dress. She was terrified at that and cried out, "What's that? Who's pulling my dress?"

"Don't be so silly," said the eldest. "You've caught it on a nail."

Then they went all the way down; and when they were at the bottom they were standing in a wonderfully pretty avenue of trees, all of whose leaves were of silver and shone and glistened.

The soldier thought, "I must carry away some token with me" — and broke off a twig from one of them, at which the tree cracked with a loud report.

The youngest cried out again. "Something's wrong! Did you hear that crack?"

But the eldest said, "That's a gun fired for joy, because we've got rid of our prince so quickly."

After that they came into an avenue where all the leaves were of gold, and at last into a third where they were of bright diamonds. He broke a twig off in each, and each time it made such a crack that the youngest started back in terror; but the eldest still insisted that they were salutes.

They went on and came to a great lake, on which stood twelve little boats, and in every boat sat a handsome prince, all of them waiting for the twelve. Each took one of them with him; but the soldier seated himself beside the youngest.

Then her prince said, "I can't think why the boat is so much heavier today. I shall have to row with all my strength if I'm to get it across."

"What would cause that," said the youngest, "except the warm weather? I feel very warm too."

On the other side of the lake stood a splendid, brightly lit castle, from which came the joyful music of trumpets and kettledrums. They rowed over there and went in; and each prince danced with the girl he loved. But the soldier danced along with them unseen; and when one of them had a cup of wine in her hand, he drank it up, so that the cup was empty when she raised it to her mouth. The youngest was alarmed at this, but the eldest always made her be quiet.

They danced there till three o'clock in the morning, when all their shoes were danced into holes and they had to leave off. The princes rowed them back across the lake, and this time the soldier seated himself beside the eldest. On the shore they took their leave of their princes and promised to come back the following night.

When they reached the stairs the soldier ran on ahead and lay down in his bed; and when the twelve came up slowly and wearily, he was already snoring so loudly that they could all hear him, and they said, "As far as he's concerned, we're safe."

They took off their beautiful dresses and put them away, and set their worn-out shoes under the bed, and lay down.

Next morning the soldier decided to say nothing, but to watch the wonderful goings-on again; and he went with them again. Then everything happened just as it had the first time, and each time they danced until their shoes were worn to pieces. But the third time he took a cup away with him as a token.

When the hour came for him to give his answer, he took the three twigs and the cup and went to the King; but the twelve stood behind the door and listened for what he was going to say.

When the King put the question, "Where have my twelve daughters danced their shoes to pieces in the night?" he answered, "In an underground castle, with twelve princes" — and told how it had all come about, and brought out the tokens.

The King then summoned his daughters and asked whether the soldier had told the truth; and when they saw that they were betrayed and that lying would be no use, they had to confess it all.

At this the King asked him which of them he would have for a wife. He answered, "I'm no longer young, so give me the eldest."

Then the wedding was celebrated on that very day, and the kingdom was promised him after the King's death. But the princes were kept under their spell for as many days as they had danced nights with the twelve.

The Six Servants

In former times there lived an old Queen who was a sorceress, and her daughter was the most beautiful girl under the sun. The old woman, though, had no thought in her head but how to lure men to their destruction; and when a suitor appeared, she said that whoever wanted her daughter must first perform a task, or die.

Many had been dazzled by the daughter's beauty and had actually risked it; but they could never accomplish what the old woman set them to do, and then no mercy was shown: they had to kneel down and their heads were struck off.

A certain King's son who had also heard of the girl's beauty said to his father, "Let me go there. I want to ask for her in marriage."

"Never," answered the King. "If you went, you'd be going to your death."

At this his son lay down and was sick to death; and he lay there seven years, and no physician could heal him. When his father saw that all hope was gone, he said to him with a heavy heart, "Go there and try your luck; I know no other way of curing you."

When his son heard that, he rose from his bed and was well again, and set out joyfully on his way.

And it happened that as he was riding across a heath, he saw from a distance something like a great heap of hay lying on the ground; and when he came nearer he could see that it was the belly of a man who had laid himself down there — but the belly looked like a small mountain.

When the fat man saw the traveller he stood up and said, "If you're in need of anybody, take me into your service."

The prince answered, "What can I do with such a great big man?"

"Oh," said the Stout One, "this is nothing. When I stretch myself out properly, I'm three thousand times fatter."

"If that's the case," said the prince, "I can make use of you. Come with me."

So the Stout One followed the prince; and after a while they found another man lying on the ground with his ear laid to the turf.

"What are you doing there?" asked the King's son.

"I'm listening," replied the man.

"What are you listening to so attentively?"

"I'm listening to what's going on in the world at this moment, for nothing escapes my ears. I can even hear the grass growing."

"Tell me," said the prince, "what you hear at the court of the old Queen who has the beautiful daughter."

Then he answered, "I hear the whizzing of the sword that's striking off a suitor's head."

The King's son said, "I can make use of you. Come with me."

They went on, and then saw a pair of feet lying there, and part of a pair of legs, but could not see the rest of the body. When they had walked on a great distance they came to the body, and at last to the head as well.

"Why," said the prince, "what a tall rascal you are!"

"Oh," replied the Tall One, "that's nothing at all yet. When I really stretch out my limbs, I'm three thousand times as tall, and taller than the highest mountain on earth. I'll gladly enter your service, if you'll take me."

"Come with me," said the prince. "I can make use of you."

They went on and found a man sitting by the road who had bound up his eyes. The prince said to him, "Have you weak eyes, that you can't look at the light?"

"No," replied the man. "But I mustn't take the bandage off, for whatever I look at with my eyes splits to pieces, my gaze is so powerful. If you can use that, I'll gladly serve you."

"Come with me," replied the King's son. "I can make use of you."

They journeyed on and found a man lying in the hot sunshine, trembling and shivering all over his body, so that not a limb of him was still.

"How can you be shivering when the sun's shining so warm?" said the King's son.

"Alas," replied the man, "I'm of quite a different nature. The hotter it is, the colder I am, and the frost cuts through all my bones; and the colder it is, the hotter I am. In the middle of ice I can't endure the heat, nor in the middle of fire the cold."

"You're a strange fellow," said the prince, "but if you'll enter my service, follow me."

They travelled on and saw a man standing there who stretched out a long neck and looked about him and could see over all the mountains.

"What are you looking at so eagerly?" said the King's son.

The man replied, "I have such sharp eyes that I can see into every forest and field and hill and valley all over the world."

The prince said, "Come with me if you will, for I'm still in want of somebody like you."

And now the King's son and his six servants came to the town where the old Queen lived. He did not tell her who he was, but said, "If you'll give me your beautiful daughter, I'll perform any task you set me."

The sorceress was delighted to get such a handsome young man as this into her net, and said, "I'll set you three tasks; and if you can perform them all, you shall be my daughter's husband and master."

"What's the first to be?"

"You shall fetch me my ring, which I dropped into the Red Sea."

So the King's son went home to his servants and said, "The first task is not easy. A ring has to be got out of the Red Sea. Come, find some way of doing it."

Then the man with the sharp sight said, "I'll see where it's lying" — and looked down into the water and said, "It's caught there, on a pointed stone."

The Tall One carried them there and said, "I'd soon get it out, if I could only see it."

"Oh, is that all?" cried the Stout One — and lay down and put his mouth to the water, at which all the waves fell into it as if it were a whirlpool; and he drank the whole sea up until it was as dry as a meadow. The Tall One stooped down a little and brought out the ring with his hand.

Then the King's son rejoiced to have the ring, and took it to the old Queen. She was astonished, and said, "Yes, that's the right ring. You've safely performed the first task; but now comes the second. Do you see the meadow in front of my palace? Three hundred fat oxen are grazing there, and you must eat them — skin, hair, bones, horns and all. And down below in my cellar lie three hundred casks of wine, and you must drink those up as well. And if one hair of the oxen or one little drop of the wine is left, your life will be forfeit to me."

"May I invite no guests to this meal?" asked the prince. "No dinner is good without some company."

The old woman laughed maliciously and replied, "You may invite one, for the sake of the company — but no more."

The King's son went to his servants and said to the Stout One, "You shall be my guest today, and eat your fill."

At this the Stout One stretched himself out and ate the three hundred oxen without leaving a single hair; and then he asked whether he was to have nothing but his breakfast. He drank the wine straight out of the casks without feeling any need of a glass, and licked the last drop off his fingernails.

When the meal was over, the prince went to the old woman and told her that the second task was performed too. She wondered at this and said, "Nobody has ever done so much before; but one task still remains." And she thought to herself, "You shan't escape me, and you shan't keep your head on your shoulders."

"Tonight," said she, "I'll bring my daughter to you in your room, and you shall put your arms round her; but when the two of you are sitting there together, beware of falling asleep. When twelve o'clock strikes I'll come; and if she's no longer in your arms then, you are lost."

The prince thought, "The task is easy. I shall certainly keep my eyes open." All the same he called his servants and told them what the old woman had said, and remarked, "Who knows what treachery lies behind this? Foresight is a good thing. Keep watch, and take care that the girl doesn't go out of my room again."

When night fell, the old woman came with her daughter and put her into the prince's arms; and then the Tall One wound himself round the two of them in a circle, and the Stout One placed himself at the door, so that no living creature could come in.

There the two of them sat, and the girl never spoke a word; but the moon shone on her face through the window, and the prince could see her wonderful beauty. He did nothing but gaze at her, and was filled with love and happiness, and his eyes never grew weary.

This lasted until eleven o'clock, when the old woman cast such a spell over all of them that they fell asleep; and at that same moment the girl was carried away.

Then they all slept soundly until a quarter to twelve, when the magic lost its power and they all woke again.

"Oh, misery and misfortune!" cried the prince. "Now I'm lost."

The faithful servants began to lament too; but the Listener said, "Be quiet, I want to listen." Then he listened for an instant and said, "She's on a rock three hundred leagues from here, bewailing her fate. You alone, Tall One, can help her; if you stand up, you'll be there in a couple of steps."

"Yes," answered the Tall One, "but the one with the sharp eyes must come with me, so that we can destroy the rock."

Then the Tall One took the one with the bandaged eyes on his back, and in the twinkling of an eye they were on the enchanted rock. The Tall One immediately took the bandage off the other's eyes; and he had only to look round, and the rock shivered into a thousand pieces.

Then the Tall One took the girl in his arms and carried her back in a second, and fetched his companion just as fast; and before it struck twelve they were all sitting as they had sat before, quite merry and happy.

When twelve struck, the old sorceress came stealing in with a malicious face that seemed to say, "Now he's mine!" — for she believed that her daughter was on the rock three hundred leagues away. But when she saw her in the prince's arms she was alarmed, and said, "Here's one who knows more than I do."

She dared not raise any objection, and had to give him her daughter. But she whispered in the girl's ear, "It's a disgrace for you to have to obey common people, and not to be allowed to choose a husband to your own liking."

At this the girl's proud heart filled with anger, and she plotted revenge.

Next morning she had three hundred great bundles of wood gathered together, and told the prince that although the three tasks were performed, she still would not be his wife until somebody was willing to sit in the middle of the wood and bear the fire. She thought that none of his servants would let himself be burnt for him, and that out of love for her he would climb onto it himself, and then she would be free.

But the servants said, "Every one of us has done something except the Frosty One; he must get to work." And they set him in the middle of the pile and set fire to it.

Then the fire began to burn, and burned for three days until all the wood was consumed; and when the flames had burned out, the Frosty One was standing among the ashes, trembling like an aspen leaf, and saying, "I never felt such a frost in the whole course of my life. If it had lasted much longer, I should have been numb."

As no other excuse was to be found, the beautiful girl now had to take the unknown young man as her husband.

But when they drove away to church, the old woman said, "I can't endure the disgrace" — and sent her warriors after them with orders to cut down everybody who opposed them and bring her daughter back.

But the Listener had sharpened his ears and heard the old woman's secret orders. "What shall we do?" he said to the Stout One.

But the Stout One knew what to do, and spat out behind the carriage, once or twice, some of the sea water he had drunk; and a great sea rose up, in which the warriors were caught and drowned.

When the sorceress saw that, she sent her armoured knights. But the Listener heard the rattling of their armour, and undid the bandage from one of Sharp-eyes' eyes; and he looked rather fixedly at the enemy troops for a while, at which they all sprang to pieces like glass.

Then the young man and the girl went on their way undisturbed; and when the two of them had been blessed in church, the six servants took their leave and said to their master, "Your wishes are satisfied now; you need us no longer. We'll go our way and seek our fortunes."

Half a league from the palace of the prince's father there was a village, and near it a swineherd was minding his herd. And when they came there, the prince said to his wife, "Do you know who I really am? I'm no prince, but a herder of swine; and the man over there with that herd is my father. We two shall have to set to work as well and help him."

Then he took her into the inn, and told the innkeepers secretly to take away her royal clothes during the night. So when she woke in the morning she had nothing to put on; and the innkeeper's wife gave her an old gown and a pair of worsted stockings, and at the same time seemed to think it a great present, and said, "If it weren't for your husband's sake, I should have given you nothing at all."

Then the princess believed that he really was a swineherd, and minded the herd with him, and thought to herself, "I've deserved this for my haughtiness and pride."

This lasted a week, and then she could bear it no longer, for she had sores on her feet.

And now a couple of people came who asked her whether she knew who her husband was.

"Yes," she answered, "he's a swineherd, and he's just gone out with cords and ropes to try to drive a little bargain."

But they said, "Just come with us, and we'll take you to him." And they brought her up to the palace; and when she came into the hall, there stood her husband in kingly clothes. But she did not recognise him until he took her in his arms and kissed her and said, "I suffered much for you, and now you too have had to suffer for me."

And then the wedding was celebrated; and the man who has told you all this wishes that he had been there too.

The White Bride and the Black One

A woman was going about the open land with her daughter and her stepdaughter, cutting fodder, when the Lord came walking towards them in the shape of a poor man, and asked, "Which is the way into the village?"

"If you want to know," said the mother, "find it for yourself." And the daughter added, "If you're afraid you won't find it, take a guide with you."

But the stepdaughter said, "Poor man, I'll take you there. Come with me."

Then God was angry with the mother and the daughter, and turned his back on them, and wished that they should become as black as night and as ugly as sin.

To the poor stepdaughter, though, God was gracious, and went with her; and when they were near the village he spoke a blessing over her and said, "Choose three things for yourself, and I'll grant them to you."

Then the girl said, "I should like to be as beautiful and bright as the sun." And instantly she was white and bright as day.

"And then I should like to have a purse of money that never grows empty."

The Lord gave her that as well; but he said, "Don't forget what is best of all."

She said, "For my third wish, I ask that after my death I may live in the eternal kingdom of Heaven."

That too was granted her; and then the Lord left her.

When the stepmother came home with her daughter and they saw that they were both as black as coal and ugly, but that the stepdaughter was white and beautiful, the wickedness in their hearts grew greater still, and they thought of nothing but how they could do her some injury.

The stepdaughter, though, had a brother called Reginer, whom she loved dearly, and she told him everything that had happened.

Once Reginer said to her, "Dear sister, I want to paint your likeness, so that I can see you before my eyes all the time; for my love for you is so great that I should like always to be looking at you."

Then she answered, "But I beg you, let nobody see the picture."

So he painted his sister and hung the picture up in his room. He lived in the King's palace, though, for he was the King's coachman. Every day he went and stood in front of the picture and thanked God for the happiness of having such a dear sister.

Now it happened that the King he served had just lost his wife, who had been so beautiful that nobody could be found to compare with her; and on this account the King was in deep grief.

But the attendants about the court noticed that the coachman stood in front of this beautiful picture every day, and they were jealous of him, and told the King.

Then the King ordered the picture to be brought to him; and when he saw that it was like his lost wife in every way, only still more beautiful, he fell mortally in love with it. He had the coachman brought before him and asked whom the portrait showed. The coachman said it was his sister.

So the King decided to take nobody but her for his wife, and gave him a carriage and horses and splendid clothes of cloth of gold, and sent him off to fetch his chosen bride.

When Reginer came on this errand his sister was glad; but the black girl was jealous of her good fortune and grew angry beyond all measure, and said to her mother, "What use are all your arts to us now, if you can't get me a piece of luck like that?"

"Be quiet," said the old woman. "I'll soon turn it your way."

And by her arts of witchcraft she so troubled the coachman's eyes that he was half blind, and stopped the white girl's ears so that she was half deaf.

Then they got into the carriage: first the bride in her noble royal clothes, then the stepmother with her daughter; and Reginer sat on the box to drive.

When they had been on the road some time, the coachman called out:

	"Cover yourself well, my sister dear,
	so that the rain may not wet you,
	so that the wind may not load you with dust,
	so that you may be fair and beautiful
	when you come before the King."

The bride asked, "What is my dear brother saying?"

"Ah," said the old woman, "he says you ought to take off your golden dress and give it to your sister."

So she took it off and put it on the black girl, who gave her a shabby grey gown in exchange for it.

They drove on; and a short time afterwards the brother called out again:

	"Cover yourself well, my sister dear,
	so that the rain may not wet you,
	so that the wind may not load you with dust,
	so that you may be fair and beautiful
	when you come before the King."

The bride asked, "What is my dear brother saying?"

"Ah," said the old woman, "he says you ought to take off your golden hood and give it to your sister."

So she took off the hood and put it on her sister, and sat there with her own head uncovered.

And they drove on further. After a while the brother called out once more:

	"Cover yourself well, my sister dear,
	so that the rain may not wet you,
	so that the wind may not load you with dust,
	so that you may be fair and beautiful
	when you come before the King."

The bride asked, "What is my dear brother saying?"

"Ah," said the old woman, "he says you must look out of the carriage."

But they were just then on a bridge crossing deep water. When the bride stood up and leaned forward out of the carriage, the two of them pushed her out, and she fell into the middle of the water.

At the same moment that she sank, a snow-white duck rose out of the mirror-smooth water and swam away down the river.

The brother had noticed nothing of it, and drove the carriage on until they reached the court. Then he brought the black girl to the King as his sister, and believed that she really was, because his eyes were dim and he saw the golden clothes glittering.

When the King saw the boundless ugliness of his intended bride he was very angry, and ordered the coachman to be thrown into a pit full of adders and nests of snakes. But the old witch knew so well how to flatter the King and deceive his eyes by her arts that he kept her and her daughter until she seemed quite bearable to him, and he actually married her.

One evening, when the black bride was sitting on the King's knee, a white duck came swimming up the gutter to the kitchen, and said to the kitchen boy, "Boy, light a fire, so that I can warm my feathers."

The kitchen boy did it, and lit a fire on the hearth. Then the duck came and sat down by it, and shook herself and smoothed her feathers straight with her bill.

And while she was sitting there enjoying herself, she asked, "What is my brother Reginer doing?"

The kitchen boy replied, "He's shut up in the pit with the adders and the snakes."

Then she asked, "What is the black witch doing in the house?"

The boy answered, "She's loved by the King, and happy."

"May God have mercy on him," said the duck, and swam out again by the sink.

The next night she came again and asked the same questions, and the third night too. Then the kitchen boy could bear it no longer, and went to the King and told him everything.

But the King wanted to see it for himself, and went there the next evening; and when the duck put her head in through the sink, he took his sword and cut through her neck — and suddenly she changed into a most beautiful girl, exactly like the picture her brother had painted of her.

The King was full of joy; and as she stood there quite wet, he had splendid clothes brought and had her dressed in them. Then she told him how she had been betrayed by cunning and falsehood and at last thrown down into the water; and her first request was that her brother should be brought up out of the pit of snakes.

And when the King had granted this request, he went into the room where the old witch was and asked, "What does she deserve who does such and such a thing?" — and told what had happened.

Then she was so blinded that she saw nothing at all, and said, "She deserves to be stripped naked and put into a barrel full of nails, and a horse harnessed to the barrel and sent off with it all over the world."

All of which was done to her, and to her black daughter. But the King married the white and beautiful bride, and rewarded her faithful brother and made him a rich and distinguished man.

Iron John

There was once a King who had a great forest near his palace, full of all kinds of wild animals. One day he sent a huntsman out to shoot him a roe, but he did not come back.

"Perhaps some accident has happened to him," said the King; and next day he sent out two more huntsmen to search for him — but they stayed away too.

Then on the third day he sent for all his huntsmen and said, "Scour the whole forest through, and don't give up until you've found all three."

But of these too, none came home again; and of the pack of hounds they had taken with them, not one was ever seen again.

From that time on nobody would venture into the forest any more, and it lay there in deep stillness and solitude, and nothing was seen of it except sometimes an eagle or a hawk flying over.

This lasted for many years; and then a huntsman from abroad presented himself to the King, looking for a position, and offered to go into the dangerous forest. But the King would not give his consent, and said, "It isn't safe in there. I'm afraid it would go no better with you than with the others, and you'd never come out again."

The huntsman replied, "My lord, I'll venture it at my own risk. I know nothing of fear."

So the huntsman took himself off to the forest with his dog. It was not long before the dog fell in with some game on the way and wanted to chase it; but the dog had hardly run two steps before it stood in front of a deep pool and could go no further, and a naked arm stretched itself out of the water and seized it and dragged it under.

When the huntsman saw that, he went back and fetched three men to come with buckets and bale the water out. And when they could see to the bottom, there lay a wild man whose body was brown like rusty iron, and whose hair hung down over his face to his knees. They bound him with cords and led him away to the castle.

There was great astonishment at the wild man; and the King had him put in an iron cage in his courtyard, and forbade anybody to open the door on pain of death, and the Queen herself was to keep the key. And from that time on everybody could go into the forest in safety again.

The King had a son of eight years old, who was playing in the courtyard one day; and while he was playing, his golden ball fell into the cage. The boy ran over and said, "Give me my ball back."

"Not until you've opened the door for me," answered the man.

"No," said the boy, "I won't do that. The King has forbidden it" — and ran away.

Next day he went again and asked for his ball; the wild man said, "Open my door" — but the boy would not.

On the third day the King had ridden out hunting, and the boy went once more and said, "I couldn't open the door even if I wanted to, for I haven't the key."

Then the wild man said, "It lies under your mother's pillow; you can get it there."

The boy, who wanted his ball back, threw all caution to the winds and fetched the key. The door opened with difficulty, and the boy pinched his fingers. When it was open, the wild man stepped out, gave him the golden ball and hurried away.

The boy had grown frightened; he called and cried after him, "Oh, wild man, don't go away, or I shall be beaten!"

The wild man turned back, picked him up, set him on his shoulder and went off into the forest with hasty steps.

When the King came home he noticed the empty cage, and asked the Queen how that had happened. She knew nothing about it, and looked for the key, but it was gone. She called the boy, but nobody answered. The King sent people out to look for him in the fields, but they did not find him. Then he could easily guess what had happened, and there was great grief in the royal court.

When the wild man had reached the dark forest again, he took the boy down off his shoulder and said to him, "You'll never see your father and mother again; but I'll keep you with me, for you set me free and I feel pity for you. If you do everything I tell you, you shall fare well. Of treasure and gold I have enough, and more than anybody in the world."

He made the boy a bed of moss to sleep on; and next morning the man took him to a well and said, "Look — the gold well is as bright and clear as crystal. You shall sit beside it and take care that nothing falls into it, or it will be spoiled. I'll come every evening to see whether you've obeyed my order."

The boy sat down at the edge of the well, and often saw a golden fish or a golden snake show itself in it, and took care that nothing fell in. But as he was sitting there, his finger hurt him so violently that without meaning to he put it in the water. He drew it out again quickly, but saw that it was entirely gilded; and however hard he tried to wash the gold off, it was no use.

In the evening Iron John came back, looked at the boy and said, "What has happened to the well?"

"Nothing, nothing," he answered, and held his finger behind his back so that the man should not see it.

But he said, "You've dipped your finger in the water. This time it may pass; but take care you don't let anything go in again."

By daybreak the boy was already sitting by the well and watching it. His finger hurt him again and he passed it over his head, and then unluckily a hair fell down into the well. He took it out quickly, but it was already quite gilded.

Iron John came and knew already what had happened. "You've let a hair fall into the well," said he. "I'll let you watch by it once more; but if it happens a third time, then the well is spoiled and you can stay with me no longer."

On the third day the boy sat by the well and did not stir his finger, however much it hurt him. But the time hung heavy on him, and he looked at the reflection of his face on the surface of the water. And as he bent down more and more, trying to look straight into his own eyes, his long hair fell down from his shoulders into the water. He straightened up quickly, but all the hair on his head was already golden and shone like the sun.

You can imagine how terrified the poor boy was. He took his handkerchief and tied it round his head, so that the man should not see it. But when he came he knew everything already, and said, "Take the handkerchief off."

Then the golden hair streamed out; and the boy might excuse himself as he liked, it was no use.

"You haven't stood the test, and you can stay here no longer. Go out into the world; there you'll learn what poverty is. But as you haven't a bad heart, and as I mean you well, there's one thing I'll grant you: if you ever fall into any difficulty, come to the forest and call 'Iron John,' and then I'll come and help you. My power is great, greater than you think, and I have gold and silver in abundance."

So the King's son left the forest, and walked by beaten and unbeaten paths, always onwards, until at length he reached a great city. There he looked for work, but could find none, and he had learned nothing that could help him. At length he went to the palace and asked whether they would take him in. The people about the court did not at all know what use they could make of him; but they liked him, and told him to stay. At length the cook took him into his service and said he might carry wood and water and rake the cinders together.

Once, when it happened that nobody else was at hand, the cook ordered him to carry the food to the royal table; but as he did not want to let his golden hair be seen, he kept his little cap on. Such a thing as that had never come under the King's notice before, and he said, "When you come to the royal table you must take your hat off."

He answered, "Ah, my lord, I can't; I have a bad sore place on my head."

Then the King had the cook called before him and scolded him, and asked how he could take such a boy as that into his service, and said he was to turn him off at once. The cook, though, had pity on him, and exchanged him for the gardener's boy.

And now the boy had to plant and water the garden, hoe and dig, and bear the wind and bad weather. Once in summer, when he was working alone in the garden, the day was so warm that he took his little cap off to let the air cool him. And as the sun shone on his hair, it glittered and flashed so that the rays fell into the King's daughter's bedroom, and up she sprang to see what it could be.

Then she saw the boy, and called out to him, "Boy, bring me a wreath of flowers."

He put his cap on in all haste, and gathered wild field flowers and bound them together. As he was going up the stairs with them, the gardener met him and said, "How can you take the King's daughter a garland of such common flowers? Go quickly and get another, and pick out the prettiest and rarest."

"Oh, no," replied the boy, "the wild ones have more scent, and will please her better."

When he came into the room, the King's daughter said, "Take your cap off. It isn't proper to keep it on in my presence."

He said again, "I mustn't; I have a sore head."

She, though, caught at his cap and pulled it off, and then his golden hair rolled down on his shoulders, and it was splendid to see. He wanted to run out, but she held him by the arm and gave him a handful of ducats. He went off with them, but he cared nothing for the gold pieces. He took them to the gardener and said, "I make a present of them to your children; they can play with them."

The following day the King's daughter called to him again to bring her a wreath of field flowers; and when he came in with it she instantly snatched at his cap and tried to take it off him, but he held it fast with both hands. She gave him a handful of ducats again, but he would not keep them, and gave them to the gardener as playthings for his children.

On the third day it went just the same: she could not get his cap off him, and he would not have her money.

Not long afterwards the country was overrun by war. The King gathered his people together and did not know whether he could put up any resistance to the enemy, who was superior in strength and had a mighty army.

Then the gardener's boy said, "I'm grown up, and I'll go to the war too; only give me a horse."

The others laughed and said, "Look for one yourself when we've gone; we'll leave one behind in the stable for you."

When they had ridden out, he went into the stable and got the horse out. It was lame in one foot and went hobbling along, hobblety-jig, hobblety-jig; all the same he mounted it and rode away to the dark forest.

When he came to the edge of it, he called "Iron John" three times, so loudly that it echoed through the trees. At this the wild man appeared immediately and said, "What do you want?"

"I want a strong horse, for I'm going to the war."

"That you shall have, and more than you ask for."

Then the wild man went back into the forest; and it was not long before a stable boy came out of it leading a horse that snorted through its nostrils and could hardly be held in; and behind them followed a great troop of soldiers all equipped in iron, and their swords flashed in the sun.

The young man handed his three-legged horse over to the stable boy, mounted the other and rode at the head of the soldiers.

When he got near the battlefield, a great part of the King's men had already fallen, and it needed very little to make the rest give way. Then the young man galloped up with his iron soldiers, broke like a hurricane over the enemy and beat down everybody who stood against him. They began to run, but the young man pursued them and never stopped until there was not a single man left.

Instead of going back to the King, though, he led his troop by side roads back to the forest and called out Iron John.

"What do you want?" asked the wild man.

"Take back your horse and your troops, and give me my three-legged horse again."

Everything he asked was done, and soon he was riding on his three-legged horse.

When the King returned to his palace, his daughter went to meet him and wished him joy of his victory.

"I'm not the one who carried off the victory," said he, "but a strange knight who came to my help with his soldiers."

His daughter wanted to hear who the strange knight was; but the King did not know, and said, "He followed the enemy, and I never saw him again."

She asked the gardener where his boy was; but he smiled and said, "He's just come home on his three-legged horse, and the others have been mocking him and crying, 'Here comes our hobblety-jig back again!' And they asked him too, 'Under what hedge have you been lying asleep all this time?' But he said, 'I did the best of anybody, and it would have gone badly without me.' And then they laughed at him all the more."

The King said to his daughter, "I'll proclaim a great feast that shall last three days, and you shall throw a golden apple. Perhaps the stranger will come to it."

When the feast was announced, the young man went out to the forest and called Iron John.

"What do you want?" he asked.

"That I may catch the King's daughter's golden apple."

"It's as safe as if you had it already," said Iron John. "You shall have a suit of red armour for the occasion too, and ride a spirited chestnut horse."

When the day came, the young man galloped to the place and took his stand among the knights, and nobody recognised him. The King's daughter came forward and threw a golden apple to the knights; but none of them caught it but he — only, as soon as he had it, he galloped away.

On the second day Iron John equipped him as a white knight and gave him a white horse. Again he was the only one to catch the apple, and he did not linger an instant, but galloped off with it.

The King grew angry and said, "That isn't allowed. He must come before me and tell me his name." And he gave orders that if the knight who caught the apple should go away again, they were to pursue him; and if he would not come back willingly, they were to cut him down and stab him.

On the third day he received from Iron John a suit of black armour and a black horse, and again he caught the apple. But as he was riding off with it the King's attendants pursued him, and one of them got so near that he wounded the young man's leg with the point of his sword. The young man escaped from them all the same; but his horse leapt so violently that the helmet fell off his head and they could see that he had golden hair. They rode back and reported this to the King.

The following day the King's daughter asked the gardener about his boy.

"He's at work in the garden. The queer creature has been at the festival too, and only came home yesterday evening; and he has shown my children three golden apples that he won."

The King had him summoned into his presence; and he came, and again had his little cap on his head. But the King's daughter went up to him and took it off, and then his golden hair fell down over his shoulders, and he was so handsome that they were all amazed.

"Are you the knight who came to the festival every day, always in different colours, and who caught the three golden apples?" asked the King.

"Yes," answered he, "and here the apples are" — and he took them out of his pocket and gave them back to the King. "If you want further proof, you can see the wound your people gave me when they chased me. But I'm also the knight who helped you to your victory over your enemies."

"If you can perform such deeds as that, you're no gardener's boy. Tell me, who is your father?"

"My father is a mighty King, and I have gold in plenty, as much as I need."

"I can see plainly," said the King, "that I owe you thanks. Is there anything I can do to please you?"

"Yes," answered he, "there certainly is. Give me your daughter for a wife."

The girl laughed and said, "He doesn't stand much on ceremony; but I could see already by his golden hair that he was no gardener's boy" — and then she went and kissed him.

His father and mother came to the wedding and were in great delight, for they had given up all hope of ever seeing their dear son again. And as they were sitting at the wedding feast, the music suddenly stopped, the doors opened, and a stately King came in with a great retinue. He went up to the young man and embraced him and said, "I am Iron John, and I was a wild man by enchantment; but you set me free. All the treasures I possess shall be yours."

The Three Black Princesses

East India was besieged by an enemy who would not withdraw until he had been given six hundred dollars. Then the townspeople had it proclaimed by beat of drum that whoever could provide the money should be burgomaster.

Now there was a poor fisherman who fished on the lake with his son, and the enemy came and took his son prisoner and gave the father six hundred dollars for him. So the father went and gave the money to the great men of the town, and the enemy went away, and the fisherman became burgomaster. Then it was proclaimed that whoever did not say "Mr. Burgomaster" should be put to death on the gallows.

The son got away from the enemy again, and came to a great forest on a high mountain. The mountain opened, and he went into a great enchanted castle where the chairs and tables and benches were all hung with black.

Then three young princesses came who were dressed entirely in black, and whose faces were black too, except for a little white; and they told him he was not to be afraid, they would not hurt him, and that he could deliver them.

He said he would gladly do that, if only he knew how. At this they told him that for a whole year he must not speak to them and must not look at them either; and that whatever he wanted to have, he was just to ask for, and if they were allowed to give him an answer they would.

When he had been there a long while he said he should like to go to his father, and they told him he might go. He was to take this purse of money with him and put on this coat, and in a week he must be back there again.

Then he was caught up, and was instantly in East India. He could no longer find his father in the fisherman's hut, and asked the people where the poor fisherman might be; and they told him he must not say that, or he would come to the gallows.

Then he went to his father and said, "Fisherman, how did you get here?"

Then his father said, "You mustn't say that. If the great men of the town knew, you'd come to the gallows."

But he would not stop, and he was brought to the gallows. When he was there he said, "Oh, my masters, just give me leave to go to the old fisherman's hut."

Then he put on his old smock and came back to the great men and said, "Don't you see now? Am I not the poor fisherman's son? Didn't I earn bread for my father and mother in these clothes?"

At this his father knew him again, and begged his pardon and took him home with him. And then he told them everything that had happened to him: how he had come to a forest on a high mountain, and the mountain had opened, and he had gone into an enchanted castle where everything was black, and three young princesses had come to him who were black except for a little white on their faces. And they had told him not to be afraid, and that he could deliver them.

Then his mother said that might very well not be a good thing to do, and that he ought to take a holy-water vessel with him and drop some boiling water on their faces.

He went back again, and he was in great fear; and he dropped the water on their faces as they were sleeping, and they all turned half white.

Then all three princesses sprang up and said, "You accursed dog, our blood shall cry out for vengeance on you! Now there's no man born into the world, nor ever will be born, who can set us free. We still have three brothers who are bound with seven chains — they shall tear you to pieces."

Then there was a loud shrieking all over the castle, and he sprang out of the window and broke his leg; and the castle sank into the earth again, and the mountain closed up again, and nobody ever knew where the castle had stood.

Knoist and his Three Sons

Between Werrel and Soest there lived a man whose name was Knoist, and he had three sons. One was blind, another lame, and the third stark naked.

Once they went out into a field, and there they saw a hare. The blind one shot it, the lame one caught it, and the naked one put it in his pocket.

Then they came to a mighty big lake, on which there were three boats: one sailed, one sank, and the third had no bottom to it. All three of them got into the one with no bottom.

Then they came to a mighty big forest, and in it there was a mighty big tree; and in the tree was a mighty big chapel; and in the chapel was a sexton made of beechwood and a boxwood parson, who dealt out holy water with cudgels.

	How truly happy is that one
	who from the holy water can run.

The Maid of Brakel

A girl from Brakel once went to St. Anne's Chapel at the foot of the Hinnenberg; and as she wanted a husband and thought there was nobody else in the chapel, she sang:

	"Oh, holy Saint Anne,
	help me soon to a man.
	You know him right well,
	by Suttmer gate does he dwell,
	his hair it is golden —
	you know him right well."

The clerk, though, was standing behind the altar and heard it; so he cried out in a very gruff voice, "You shan't have him! You shan't have him!"

The girl thought that it was the child Mary, who stood beside her mother Anne, who had called that out to her; and she was angry, and cried, "Fiddle-de-dee, you conceited thing, hold your tongue and let your mother speak!"

Domestic Servants

"Where are you going?"

"To Walpe."

"I to Walpe, you to Walpe — so, so, together we'll go."

"Have you a man? What's your man's name?"

"Tame."

"My man Tame, your man Tame; I to Walpe, you to Walpe — so, so, together we'll go."

"Have you a child? How is the child styled?"

"Wild."

"My child Wild, your child Wild; my man Tame, your man Tame; I to Walpe, you to Walpe — so, so, together we'll go."

"Have you a cradle? What do you call your cradle?"

"Hippodadle."

"My cradle Hippodadle, my child Wild, your child Wild, my man Tame, your man Tame; I to Walpe, you to Walpe — so, so, together we'll go."

"And have you a drudge? What's the name of your drudge?"

"From-your-work-don't-budge."

"My drudge From-your-work-don't-budge, my cradle Hippodadle, my child Wild, your child Wild, my man Tame, your man Tame; I to Walpe, you to Walpe — so, so, together we'll go."

The Lambkin and the Little Fish

There were once a little brother and a little sister who loved each other with all their hearts. Their own mother was dead, though, and they had a stepmother who was not kind to them, and secretly did everything she could to hurt them.

It happened that the two of them were playing with some other children in a meadow in front of the house; and there was a pond in the meadow that came right up to one side of the house. The children ran about it and chased each other and played at counting out:

	"Eneke Beneke, let me live,
	and I to you my bird will give.
	The little bird, it straw shall seek,
	the straw I'll give the cow to eat.
	The pretty cow shall give me milk,
	the milk I'll to the baker take.
	The baker he shall bake a cake,
	the cake I'll give unto the cat.
	The cat shall catch some mice for that,
	the mice I'll hang up in the smoke —
	and then you'll see the snow."

They stood in a circle while they played this; and whoever the word "snow" fell on had to run away, and all the others ran after him and caught him.

And as they were running about so merrily, the stepmother watched them from the window and grew angry. And as she understood the arts of witchcraft, she bewitched them both, and changed the little brother into a fish and the little sister into a lamb.

Then the fish swam here and there about the pond and was very sad, and the lamb walked up and down the meadow and was miserable, and could not eat or touch a single blade of grass.

A long time passed like this, and then strangers came to the castle as visitors. The false stepmother thought, "This is a good opportunity" — and called the cook and said to him, "Go and fetch the lamb from the meadow and kill it; we have nothing else for the visitors."

So the cook went and got the lamb and took it into the kitchen and tied its feet; and it bore all this patiently.

And when he had drawn out his knife and was whetting it on the doorstep to kill the lamb, he noticed a little fish swimming backwards and forwards in the water in front of the kitchen sink, and looking up at him. This, though, was the brother; for when the fish saw the cook take the lamb away, it followed them and swam along the pond to the house.

Then the lamb called down to it:

	"Ah, brother, in the pond so deep,
	how sad is my poor heart!
	Even now the cook he whets his knife
	to take away my tender life."

The little fish answered:

	"Ah, little sister, up on high,
	how sad is my poor heart
	while in this pond I lie."

When the cook heard that the lamb could speak and was saying such sad words to the fish down below, he was terrified, and thought this could be no ordinary lamb, but must have been bewitched by the wicked woman in the house.

So he said, "Be easy, I won't kill you" — and took another sheep and prepared it for the guests, and took the lamb to a good peasant woman, and told her everything he had seen and heard.

But the peasant woman was the very one who had been foster-mother to the little sister, and she guessed at once who the lamb was, and went with it to a wise woman. Then the wise woman spoke a blessing over the lamb and the little fish, by which they got their human shapes back again; and after this she took them both to a little hut in a great forest, where they lived alone, but were contented and happy.

Simeli Mountain

There were once two brothers, one rich and the other poor. The rich one, though, gave the poor one nothing; and he made a scanty living by trading in corn, and often did so badly that he had no bread for his wife and children.

Once, as he was wheeling a barrow through the forest, he saw a great bare, naked-looking mountain at one side of him; and as he had never seen it before, he stood still and stared at it in amazement.

And while he was standing there he saw twelve great wild men coming towards him; and as he thought they were robbers, he pushed his barrow into the thicket and climbed up a tree and waited to see what would happen.

The twelve men, though, went up to the mountain and cried, "Semsi Mountain, Semsi Mountain, open" — and immediately the barren mountain opened down the middle, and the twelve went into it, and as soon as they were inside it shut.

After a short time, though, it opened again, and the men came out carrying heavy sacks on their shoulders; and when they were all in the daylight again they said, "Semsi Mountain, Semsi Mountain, shut yourself." Then the mountain closed up, and there was no entrance to it to be seen any more; and the twelve went away.

When they were quite out of sight, the poor man got down from the tree and was curious to know what really was hidden away in the mountain. So he went up to it and said, "Semsi Mountain, Semsi Mountain, open" — and the mountain opened for him too.

Then he went inside; and the whole mountain was a cavern full of silver and gold, and at the back lay great piles of pearls and sparkling jewels, heaped up like corn. The poor man hardly knew what to do, or whether he might take any of these treasures for himself or not; but at last he filled his pockets with gold, though he left the pearls and precious stones where they were.

When he came out again he said too, "Semsi Mountain, Semsi Mountain, shut yourself" — and the mountain closed itself up, and he went home with his barrow.

And now he had no more cause for worry, but could buy bread for his wife and children with his gold, and wine into the bargain. He lived joyfully and honestly, gave help to the poor, and did good to everybody.

When the money came to an end, though, he went to his brother and borrowed a bushel measure, and fetched himself some more — but did not touch any of the more valuable things. And when he wanted to fetch something for the third time, he borrowed his brother's measure again.

The rich man, though, had long been envious of his brother's possessions and of the handsome way of life he had set up, and could not understand where the riches came from, or what his brother wanted with the measure. So he thought of a cunning trick, and covered the bottom of the measure with pitch; and when he got the measure back, a piece of money was sticking to it.

He went straight to his brother and asked him, "What have you been measuring in the bushel measure?"

"Corn and barley," said the other.

Then he showed him the piece of money, and threatened that if he did not tell the truth he would accuse him before a court of justice. So the poor man told him everything, just as it had happened.

But the rich man ordered his carriage to be got ready, and drove off, determined to use the opportunity better than his brother had and to bring back quite different treasures.

When he came to the mountain he cried, "Semsi Mountain, Semsi Mountain, open." The mountain opened and he went inside. There lay all the treasures in front of him, and for a long time he did not know what to snatch at first. At length he loaded himself with as many precious stones as he could carry.

He wanted to carry his burden outside; but as his heart and soul were entirely full of the treasures, he had forgotten the name of the mountain, and cried, "Simeli Mountain, Simeli Mountain, open."

But that was not the right name, and the mountain never stirred, but stayed shut. Then he grew alarmed; but the longer he thought about it, the more confused his thoughts became, and his treasures were of no use to him at all.

In the evening the mountain opened and the twelve robbers came in; and when they saw him they laughed and cried out, "Bird, have we caught you at last? Did you think we'd never noticed that you'd been in here twice? We couldn't catch you then; this third time you shan't get out again."

Then he cried, "It wasn't me, it was my brother" — but beg for his life and say what he might, they cut his head off.

Going A-Travelling

There was once a poor woman who had a son who very much wanted to travel; but his mother said, "How can you travel? We have no money at all for you to take with you."

Then her son said, "I'll manage very well for myself. I'll always say, 'Not much, not much, not much.'"

So he walked a long time and always said, "Not much, not much, not much."

Then he passed a company of fishermen and said, "God speed you! Not much, not much, not much."

"What do you say, you lout — 'not much'?"

And when the net was drawn in they had not caught much fish. So one of them set on the young man with a stick and said, "Have you never seen me threshing?"

"What ought I to say, then?" asked the young man.

"You must say, 'Get it full, get it full.'"

After this he walked a long time again and said, "Get it full, get it full" — until he came to the gallows, where they had a poor sinner they were about to hang.

Then he said, "Good morning; get it full, get it full."

"What do you say, you rogue — 'get it full'? Do you want to make out that there are still more wicked people in the world? Isn't this enough?"

And he got some more blows on his back.

"What am I to say, then?" said he.

"You must say, 'May God have pity on the poor soul.'"

Again the young man walked on a long while and said, "May God have pity on the poor soul!" Then he came to a pit where a knacker was standing, cutting up a horse.

The young man said, "Good morning; God have pity on the poor soul!"

"What do you say, you ill-tempered rogue?" — and the knacker gave him such a box on the ear that he could not see out of his eyes.

"What am I to say, then?"

"You must say, 'There lies the carrion in the pit.'"

So he walked on and always said, "There lies the carrion in the pit, there lies the carrion in the pit." And he came to a cart full of people, so he said, "Good morning; there lies the carrion in the pit!"

Then the cart pushed him into a hole, and the driver took his whip and cracked it over the young man until he had to crawl back to his mother; and as long as he lived he never went out travelling again.

The Donkey

Once upon a time there lived a King and a Queen who were rich and had everything they wanted, but no children. The Queen lamented over this day and night, and said, "I'm like a field where nothing grows."

At last God granted her her wish; but when the child came into the world it did not look like a human child, but was a little donkey.

When the mother saw that, her lamenting and crying began in real earnest. She said she would far rather have had no child at all than have a donkey, and that they were to throw it into the water for the fish to devour.

But the King said, "No. Since God has sent him, he shall be my son and heir, and after my death he shall sit on the royal throne and wear the kingly crown."

So the donkey was brought up and grew bigger, and his ears grew up beautifully high and straight. He was of a merry disposition, though; he jumped about and played, and took a particular pleasure in music, so that he went to a famous musician and said, "Teach me your art, so that I can play the lute as well as you do."

"Ah, dear little master," answered the musician, "that would come very hard to you. Your fingers are certainly not made for it, and are far too big. I'm afraid the strings wouldn't last."

But no excuses were any use. The donkey was determined to play the lute; he was persevering and hard-working, and at last learned to do it as well as the master himself.

The young lordling went out walking one day full of thought, and came to a well; he looked into it, and in the mirror-clear water he saw his donkey's shape. He was so distressed about it that he went out into the wide world, and took only one faithful companion with him.

They travelled up and down, and at last came into a kingdom where an old King reigned who had an only daughter, and she was wonderfully beautiful.

The donkey said, "We'll stay here" — and knocked at the gate and cried, "A guest is outside; open, so that he can come in."

But as the gate was not opened, he sat down and took his lute and played it in the most delightful manner with his two forefeet. Then the doorkeeper opened his eyes wonderfully wide, and ran to the King and said, "Outside by the gate sits a young donkey that plays the lute as well as an experienced master."

"Then let the musician come to me," said the King.

But when a donkey came in, everybody began to laugh at the lute player. And now the donkey was asked to sit down and eat with the servants. But he was unwilling, and said, "I'm no common stable ass, I'm a noble one."

Then they said, "If that's what you are, sit yourself down with the men of war."

"No," said he, "I'll sit by the King."

The King smiled and said good-humouredly, "Yes, it shall be as you wish, little ass. Come here to me." Then he asked, "Little ass, how does my daughter please you?"

The donkey turned his head towards her, looked at her, nodded and said, "I like her beyond measure. I've never yet seen anybody as beautiful as she is."

"Well then, you shall sit next to her too," said the King.

"That's exactly what I want," said the donkey — and placed himself at her side, and ate and drank, and knew how to behave himself daintily and cleanly.

When the noble beast had stayed a long while at the King's court, he thought, "What good does all this do me? I shall have to go home again in the end" — and let his head hang sadly, and went to the King and asked for his leave to go.

But the King had grown fond of him and said, "Little ass, what's the matter with you? You look as sour as a jug of vinegar. I'll give you whatever you want. Do you want gold?"

"No," said the donkey, and shook his head.

"Do you want jewels and rich clothes?"

"No."

"Do you want half my kingdom?"

"Indeed, no."
