Then the King said, "If only I knew what would make you content. Will you have my pretty daughter for a wife?"

"Ah, yes," said the ass, "I should indeed like her." And all at once he grew quite merry and full of happiness, for that was exactly what he had been wishing for.

So a great and splendid wedding was held. And in the evening, when the bride and bridegroom were led into their bedroom, the King wanted to know whether the ass would behave well, and ordered a servant to hide himself there.

When the two of them were inside, the bridegroom bolted the door and looked round; and as he believed they were quite alone, he suddenly threw off his ass's skin and stood there in the shape of a handsome royal youth.

"Now," said he, "you see who I am; and you see too that I'm not unworthy of you."

Then the bride was glad, and kissed him and loved him dearly.

When morning came he jumped up and put his animal's skin on again, and nobody could have guessed what sort of shape was hidden beneath it.

Soon the old King came. "Ah," cried he, "is the little ass merry? But surely you're sad," he said to his daughter, "that you haven't got a proper man for a husband?"

"Oh, no, dear father. I love him as much as if he were the handsomest man in the world, and I'll keep him as long as I live."

The King was surprised; but the servant who had hidden himself came and told him everything.

The King said, "That can't be true."

"Then watch yourself the next night and you'll see it with your own eyes. And listen, my lord King: if you were to take his skin away and throw it in the fire, he'd be forced to show himself in his true shape."

"Your advice is good," said the King. And at night, when they were asleep, he stole in; and when he got to the bed he saw by the light of the moon a noble-looking young man lying there, with the skin stretched out on the floor. So he took it away and had a great fire lit outside and threw the skin into it, and stayed by it himself until it was all burnt to ashes.

But as he was anxious to see how the robbed man would behave, he stayed awake the whole night and watched.

When the young man had slept his sleep out, he got up at the first light of morning and wanted to put the ass's skin on; but it was not to be found. At this he was alarmed, and full of grief and anxiety said, "Now I shall have to find some way of escaping."

But when he went out, there stood the King, who said, "My son, where away in such haste? What have you in mind? Stay here — you're such a handsome man, you shan't go away from me. I'll give you half my kingdom now, and after my death you shall have the whole of it."

"Then I hope that what begins so well may end well; and I'll stay with you," said the young man.

And the old man gave him half the kingdom; and in a year's time, when he died, the young man had the whole of it. And after his own father's death he had another kingdom as well, and lived in all magnificence.

The Ungrateful Son

A man and his wife were once sitting by the door of their house with a roast chicken set in front of them, and were about to eat it together.

Then the man saw that his aged father was coming, and hastily took the chicken and hid it, for he would not let him have any of it. The old man came, took a drink, and went away.

Now the son wanted to put the roast chicken back on the table; but when he picked it up, it had turned into a great toad, which jumped into his face and sat there and never went away again. And if anybody tried to take it off, it looked venomously at him as if it would jump in his face too, so that nobody dared touch it.

And the ungrateful son was forced to feed the toad every day, or else it fed itself on his face; and so he went about the world without ever knowing rest.

The Turnip

There were once two brothers who both served as soldiers; one of them was rich and the other poor. Then the poor one, to escape from his poverty, took off his soldier's coat and turned farmer. He dug and hoed his bit of land and sowed it with turnip seed.

The seed came up, and one turnip grew there that became large and strong, and visibly grew bigger and bigger and seemed as if it would never stop growing, so that it might have been called the princess of turnips; for such a one was never seen before and never will be seen again.

At length it was so enormous that by itself it filled a whole cart, and two oxen were needed to draw it; and the farmer had not the least idea what he was to do with the turnip, or whether it would be a fortune to him or a misfortune.

At last he thought, "If you sell it, what will you get for it that's worth anything? And if you eat it yourself, the small turnips would do you just as much good. It would be better to take it to the King and make him a present of it."

So he put it on a cart and harnessed two oxen and took it to the palace and presented it to the King.

"What strange thing is this?" said the King. "Many wonderful things have come before my eyes, but never such a monster as this. What seed can it have sprung from? Or are you a luck-child, and came upon it by chance?"

"Ah, no," said the farmer, "I'm no luck-child. I'm a poor soldier who, because he could no longer support himself, hung his soldier's coat on a nail and took to farming. I have a brother who is rich and well known to you, my lord King; but I, because I have nothing, am forgotten by everybody."

Then the King felt pity for him, and said, "You shall be raised out of your poverty, and shall have such gifts from me that you'll be your rich brother's equal." And he bestowed on him a great deal of gold, and lands and meadows and herds, and made him immensely rich, so that his brother's wealth could not be compared with it.

When the rich brother heard what the poor one had got for himself with one single turnip, he envied him, and thought in every way he could how he too might get hold of a similar piece of luck. He would set about it in a much cleverer way, though; and he took gold and horses and carried them to the King, quite certain that the King would give him a far larger present in return. If his brother had got so much for one turnip, what would he not carry away in return for such beautiful things as these?

The King accepted his present, and said that he had nothing to give him in return that was more rare and excellent than the great turnip. So the rich man had to put his brother's turnip on a cart and have it taken home.

Once there, he did not know whom to vent his rage and anger on, until bad thoughts came to him and he resolved to kill his brother. He hired murderers, who were to lie in ambush; and then he went to his brother and said, "Dear brother, I know of a hidden treasure. We'll dig it up together and divide it between us."

The other agreed to this and went with him without suspicion. But while they were on their way, the murderers fell on him and bound him and would have hanged him from a tree.

But just as they were doing it, loud singing and the sound of a horse's hoofs were heard in the distance. At this their hearts were filled with terror, and they pushed their prisoner head first into a sack and hung it on a branch and took to flight.

He, though, worked away up there until he had made a hole in the sack he could put his head through. The man who was coming along was none other than a travelling student, a young fellow who was riding on his way through the wood, joyfully singing his song.

When the one up aloft saw that somebody was passing below him, he cried, "Good day! You've come at a lucky time."

The student looked round on every side, but did not know where the voice came from. At last he said, "Who's calling me?"

Then an answer came from the top of the tree. "Raise your eyes; here I sit aloft in the Sack of Wisdom. In a short time I've learned great things; compared with this, all schools are a joke. In a very short while I shall have learned everything, and shall come down wiser than all other men. I understand the stars and the signs of the Zodiac and the tracks of the winds, the sand of the sea, the healing of illness and the virtues of all herbs and birds and stones. If you were once inside it, you'd feel what noble things come out of the Sack of Knowledge."

When the student heard all this he was astonished, and said, "Blessed be the hour in which I found you! May I not get into the sack for a while too?"

The one above replied, as if unwillingly, "For a short time I'll let you get into it, if you reward me and give me good words. But you must wait an hour longer, for there's one thing left that I must learn before I do it."

When the student had waited a while he grew impatient and begged to be let in at once; his thirst for knowledge was so very great. So the one above pretended to give way at last, and said, "So that I can come out of the house of knowledge, you must let it down by the rope, and then you shall get in."

So the student let the sack down and untied it and set him free, and then cried, "Now draw me up at once" — and was about to get into the sack.

"Stop!" said the other. "That won't do." And he took him by the head and put him upside down into the sack and fastened it, and drew the disciple of wisdom up the tree by the rope. Then he swung him about in the air and said, "How goes it with you, my dear fellow? Look — you can feel the wisdom coming already, and you're gaining valuable experience. Keep perfectly quiet until you grow wiser."

And with that he mounted the student's horse and rode away — but in an hour's time he sent somebody to let the student out again.

The Old Man Made Young Again

In the days when our Lord still walked this earth, he and St. Peter stopped one evening at a smith's and were given free lodging. Then it happened that a poor beggar, hard pressed by age and infirmity, came to this house and begged alms of the smith.

St. Peter had pity on him and said, "Lord and master, if it please you, cure his troubles so that he can earn his own bread."

The Lord said kindly, "Smith, lend me your forge and put some coals on for me, and then I'll make this ailing old man young again."

The smith was quite willing, and St. Peter blew the bellows; and when the coal fire sparked up large and high, our Lord took the little old man and pushed him into the forge in the middle of the red-hot fire, so that he glowed like a rose bush and praised God in a loud voice.

After that the Lord went to the quenching tub and put the glowing little man into it, so that the water closed over him; and when he had carefully cooled him he gave him his blessing — and behold, the little man sprang nimbly out, looking fresh and straight and healthy, and as if he were only twenty.

The smith, who had watched everything closely and attentively, invited them all to supper. But he had an old, half-blind, crooked mother-in-law, who went to the young man and asked him very earnestly whether the fire had burned him much. He answered that he had never felt more comfortable, and that he had sat in the red heat as if he were sitting in cool dew.

The young man's words echoed in the old woman's ears all night long; and early next morning, when the Lord had gone on his way again and been heartily thanked by the smith, the smith thought that he might make his old mother-in-law young again in the same way, since he had watched everything so carefully and it lay within his own trade.

So he called to ask her whether she too would like to go bounding about like a girl of eighteen.

She said, "With all my heart, since the young man came out of it so well."

So the smith made a great fire and thrust the old woman into it; and she writhed about this way and that and uttered terrible cries of murder.

"Sit still! Why are you screaming and jumping about like that?" cried he. And as he spoke he blew the bellows again, until all her rags were burnt.

The old woman cried without stopping, and the smith thought to himself, "I haven't quite got the right art" — and took her out and threw her into the cooling tub. Then she screamed so loudly that the smith's wife upstairs and her daughter-in-law heard her, and both of them came running downstairs and saw the old woman lying in a heap in the quenching tub, howling and screaming, with her face wrinkled and shrivelled and all out of shape.

At this the two of them, who were both with child, were so terrified that that very night two boys were born who were not made like men but like apes; and they ran off into the woods, and from them sprang the race of apes.

The Lord’s Animals and the Devil’s

The Lord God had created all the animals, and had chosen the wolf to be his dog; but he had forgotten the goat.

Then the Devil made ready and began to create as well, and created goats with fine long tails. Now when they went out to pasture they generally got caught in the hedges by their tails, and then the Devil had to go and disentangle them, with a great deal of trouble. This enraged him at last, and he went and bit off the tail of every goat, as may be seen to this day by the stump.

Then he let them go out to pasture alone; but it came about that the Lord God saw how at one time they gnawed away at a fruit tree, at another damaged the noble vines, or destroyed other tender plants. This distressed him, so that in his goodness and mercy he summoned his wolves, who soon tore to pieces the goats that went there.

When the Devil saw this he went before the Lord and said, "Your creatures have destroyed mine."

The Lord answered, "Why did you create things that do harm?"

The Devil said, "I was forced to it. Since my thoughts run on evil, what I create can have no other nature; and you must pay me heavy damages."

"I'll pay you as soon as the oak leaves fall. Come then, and your money will be counted out ready."

When the oak leaves had fallen the Devil came and demanded what was due to him. But the Lord said, "In the church of Constantinople stands a tall oak tree that still has all its leaves."

With raging and cursing the Devil went off, and went to look for the oak; and he wandered in the wilderness for six months before he found it — and when he came back, all the other oaks had covered themselves with green leaves again in the meantime.

So he had to forfeit his compensation; and in his rage he put out the eyes of all the remaining goats and put his own in instead.

That is why all goats have devil's eyes and their tails bitten off, and why he likes to take on their shape.

The Beam

There was once an enchanter who was standing in the middle of a great crowd of people performing his wonders. He had a cock brought in, which lifted a heavy beam and carried it as if it were as light as a feather.

But a girl was there who had just found a four-leaved clover, and had become so wise by it that no deception could stand up against her; and she saw that the beam was nothing but a straw. So she cried out, "You people, don't you see that what the cock is carrying is a straw and no beam?"

Immediately the enchantment vanished, and the people saw what it was, and drove the magician away in shame and disgrace. But he, full of inward anger, said, "I'll soon have my revenge."

After some time the girl's wedding day came, and she was dressed up and went in a great procession over the fields to the place where the church was. All at once she came to a stream that was very much swollen, and there was no bridge and no plank to cross by. So the bride nimbly took her clothes up and meant to wade through it.

And just as she was standing in the water like this, a man — and it was the enchanter — cried mockingly close beside her, "Aha! Where are your eyes, that you take that for water?"

Then her eyes were opened, and she saw that she was standing with her clothes lifted up in the middle of a field that was blue with the flowers of blue flax. And all the people saw it too, and chased her away with jeers and laughter.

The Old Beggar-Woman

There was once an old woman — but you've surely seen an old woman go begging before now? This woman begged too, and when she was given anything she said, "May God reward you."

The beggar-woman came to a door, and there by the fire a friendly rogue of a boy was standing warming himself. The boy said kindly to the poor old woman, as she stood shivering there by the door, "Come in, old mother, and warm yourself."

She came in, but stood too close to the fire, so that her old rags began to burn, and she did not notice it. The boy stood and saw it — but he ought to have put the flames out. Isn't it true that he ought to have put them out? And if he had no water, then he should have wept all the water in his body out of his eyes, and that would have made two pretty streams to put them out with.

The Three Sluggards

A certain King had three sons who were all equally dear to him, and he did not know which of them to appoint as his successor after his death.

When the time came that he was about to die, he called them to his bedside and said, "Dear children, I've been thinking of something that I'll now tell you. Whichever of you is the laziest shall have the kingdom."

The eldest said, "Then, father, the kingdom is mine; for I'm so idle that if I lie down to rest and a drop falls in my eye, I won't open it, so that I can go on sleeping."

The second said, "Father, the kingdom belongs to me; for I'm so idle that when I'm sitting by the fire warming myself, I'd sooner let my heel burn off than draw my leg back."

The third said, "Father, the kingdom is mine; for I'm so idle that if I were going to be hanged and had the rope round my neck already, and somebody put a sharp knife into my hand to cut the rope with, I'd sooner let myself be hanged than raise my hand to the rope."

When their father heard that he said, "You've carried it furthest, and you shall be King."

The Twelve Idle Servants

Twelve servants who had done nothing all day would not exert themselves at night either, but laid themselves down on the grass and boasted about their idleness.

The first said, "What's your laziness to me? I have my own to think about. The care of my body is my chief work: I eat not a little and drink still more. When I've had four meals I fast a short while until I feel hungry again, and that suits me best. Getting up early isn't for me; when it's getting on towards midday I'm already looking out a resting place for myself. If the master calls, I behave exactly as if I hadn't heard him; and if he calls a second time, I wait a while before I get up, and go to him very slowly. Life is bearable that way."

The second said, "I have a horse to look after, but I leave the bit in his mouth; and if I don't feel like it, I give him no food and say he's had it already. But I lay myself down in the oat chest and sleep for four hours. After that I stretch out one foot and move it a couple of times over the horse's body, and then he's combed and cleaned. Who's going to make a great business of that? All the same, service is too toilsome for me."

The third said, "Why plague yourself with work? Nothing comes of it. I laid myself down in the sun and fell asleep. It began to rain a little — but why should I get up? I let it rain on, in God's name. At last a splashing shower came, so heavy that it pulled the hair out of my head and washed it away, and I got a hole in my skull. I put a plaster on it, and then it was all right. I've had several injuries of that kind already."

The fourth said, "If I'm to undertake a piece of work, I first loiter about for an hour to save up my strength. After that I begin quite slowly, and ask whether there's nobody about who could help me. Then I let him do the chief part of the work, and really only look on — but even that's still too much for me."

The fifth said, "What does that matter? Just think — I'm supposed to take the manure out of the horse's stable and load the cart with it. I let it go on slowly; and if I've got anything on the fork, I only half raise it, and then I rest for a good quarter of an hour before I throw it in. It's enough and to spare if I take out one cartload in the day. I've no fancy for killing myself with work."

The sixth said, "Shame on you. I'm afraid of no work — but I lie down for three weeks at a time and never once take my clothes off. What's the use of buckling your shoes on? For all I care they can fall off my feet, it doesn't matter. If I'm going up some steps, I drag one foot slowly after the other onto the first step, and then I count the rest of them so that I know where I have to rest."

The seventh said, "That won't do for me; my master keeps an eye on my work — only he's not at home all day. But I neglect nothing; I run as fast as it's possible to run when you're crawling. If I'm to get on at all, four sturdy men have to push me with all their might. I came where six men were lying asleep on a bed side by side. I lay down beside them and slept too. There was no waking me again, and when they wanted me home they had to carry me."

The eighth said, "I can see plainly that I'm the only active fellow here. If a stone lies in front of me, I don't give myself the trouble of raising my legs and stepping over it. I lay myself down on the ground; and if I'm wet and covered with mud and dirt, I stay lying there until the sun has dried me again. At the very most I only turn myself over so that it can shine on me."

The ninth said, "That's the right way. Today the bread was in front of me, but I was too idle to take it, and nearly died of hunger. There was a jug standing by it too, but it was so big and heavy that I didn't care to lift it, and preferred to bear the thirst. Just turning myself over was too much for me; I stayed lying like a log the whole day."

The tenth said, "Laziness has brought misfortune on me — a broken leg and a swollen calf. Three of us were lying in the road and I had my legs stretched out. Somebody came along with a cart, and the wheels went over me. I could have drawn my legs back, of course, but I didn't hear the cart coming, because the midges were humming about my ears and creeping in at my nose and out again at my mouth. Who can take the trouble to drive the vermin away?"

The eleventh said, "I gave up my place yesterday. I'd no fancy for carrying the heavy books to my master any longer, or fetching them away again. There was no end to it all day long. But to tell the truth, he gave me my notice and wouldn't keep me any longer, because his clothes, which I'd left lying in the dust, were all moth-eaten. And I'm very glad of it."

The twelfth said, "Today I had to drive the cart out into the country, and I made myself a bed of straw on it and had a good sleep. The reins slipped out of my hand; and when I woke, the horse had nearly torn itself loose, the harness was gone, the strap that fastens the horse to the shafts was gone, and so were the collar and the bridle and bit. Somebody had come by and carried it all off. On top of that the cart had got into a bog and stuck fast. I left it standing and stretched myself out on the straw again. At last the master came himself and pushed the cart out; and if he hadn't come, I shouldn't be lying here but there, and sleeping in perfect peace."

The Shepherd Boy

There was once a shepherd boy whose fame spread far and wide because of the wise answers he gave to every question. The King of the country heard of it too, but did not believe it, and sent for the boy.

Then he said to him, "If you can give me an answer to three questions I'll ask you, I'll look on you as my own child, and you shall live with me in my royal palace."

The boy said, "What are the three questions?"

The King said, "The first is: how many drops of water are there in the ocean?"

The shepherd boy answered, "My lord King, if you'll have all the rivers on earth dammed up so that not a single drop runs from them into the sea until I've counted it, I'll tell you how many drops there are in the sea."

The King said, "The next question is: how many stars are there in the sky?"

The shepherd boy said, "Give me a great sheet of white paper." And then he made so many fine points on it with a pen that they could hardly be seen, and it was all but impossible to count them; anybody who looked at them would have lost his sight. Then he said, "There are as many stars in the sky as there are points on this paper. Just count them." But nobody was able to do it.

The King said, "The third question is: how many seconds of time are there in eternity?"

Then the shepherd boy said, "In Lower Pomerania is the Diamond Mountain, which is two and a half miles high, two and a half miles wide and two and a half miles deep. Every hundred years a little bird comes and sharpens its beak on it; and when the whole mountain has been worn away by this, then the first second of eternity will be over."

The King said, "You've answered the three questions like a wise man, and from now on you shall live with me in my royal palace, and I'll regard you as my own child."

The Star-Money

There was once a little girl whose father and mother were dead, and she was so poor that she no longer had any little room to live in or bed to sleep in, and at last had nothing at all but the clothes she was wearing and a little bit of bread in her hand that some charitable soul had given her. She was good and pious, though.

And as she was forsaken like this by the whole world, she went out into the open country, trusting in the good God.

Then a poor man met her, who said, "Ah, give me something to eat — I'm so hungry!" She held out the whole of her piece of bread to him and said, "May God bless it to your use" — and went on.

Then came a child who moaned and said, "My head is so cold; give me something to cover it with." So she took off her hood and gave it to him.

And when she had walked a little further she met another child who had no jacket and was frozen with cold; so she gave the child her own. And a little further on one begged for a frock, and she gave that away as well.

At length she came into a forest, and it had already grown dark; and there came yet another child and asked for a little shirt. And the good little girl thought to herself, "It's a dark night and nobody can see you; you can easily give your little shirt away" — and took it off and gave that away too.

And as she stood there, without one single thing left, suddenly some stars fell down out of heaven; and they were nothing else but hard, smooth pieces of money. And although she had just given her little shirt away, she had a new one on, of the very finest linen. So she gathered the money together into it, and was rich all the days of her life.

The Stolen Farthings

A father was sitting at dinner one day with his wife and his children, and a good friend who had come on a visit was with them.

And as they were sitting there, and it was striking twelve o'clock, the visitor saw the door open and a very pale child dressed in snow-white clothes come in. It did not look round, and it did not speak, but went straight into the next room. Soon afterwards it came back and went out at the door again in the same quiet way.

On the second and the third day it came in exactly the same way.

At last the visitor asked the father whom the beautiful child belonged to that went into the next room every day at noon.

"I've never seen it," said he — nor did he know whom it could belong to.

Next day, when it came again, the visitor pointed it out to the father; but he did not see it, and the mother and the children saw nothing either.

At this the visitor got up and went to the door of the room and opened it a little way and looked in. And then he saw the child sitting on the floor, digging and searching busily among the cracks between the floorboards; but when it saw the visitor it disappeared.

He told them now what he had seen, and described the child exactly; and the mother recognised it and said, "Ah, it's my dear child who died a month ago."

They took up the boards and found two farthings that the child had once been given by its mother to give to a poor man. But it had thought, "You can buy yourself a biscuit with that" — and had kept the farthings and hidden them in the gaps between the boards. And so it had had no rest in its grave, and had come every day at noon to search for these farthings.

The parents gave the money at once to a poor man, and after that the child was never seen again.

Brides On Their Trial

There was once a young shepherd who very much wanted to marry, and who knew three sisters who were all equally pretty, so that it was hard for him to make a choice and he could not decide which of them to prefer.

So he asked his mother for advice, and she said, "Invite all three, and set some cheese in front of them, and watch how they eat it."

The young man did so. The first, though, swallowed the cheese with the rind on. The second cut the rind off the cheese in a hurry — but she cut it so fast that she left a lot of good cheese on it and threw that away too. The third peeled the rind off carefully, and cut away neither too much nor too little.

The shepherd told his mother all this, and she said, "Take the third for your wife." And he did, and lived contentedly and happily with her.

Odds And Ends

There was once a girl who was pretty, but idle and careless. When she had to spin she got so out of temper that if there was a little knot in the flax she pulled out a whole heap of it at once and strewed it about on the ground beside her.

Now she had a servant who was hard-working, and who gathered up the bits of flax that were thrown away, and cleaned them and spun them fine and had a beautiful gown made out of them for herself.

A young man had courted the lazy girl, and the wedding was to take place. On the eve of the wedding the hard-working one was dancing merrily about in her pretty dress, and the bride said:

"Ah, how that girl does jump about, dressed in my odds and ends."

The bridegroom heard that, and asked the bride what she meant by it. Then she told him that the girl was wearing a dress made out of the flax she had thrown away.

When the bridegroom heard that, and saw how idle she was and how hard-working the poor girl was, he gave her up and went to the other and chose her for his wife.

The Sparrow And His Four Children

A sparrow had four young ones in a swallow's nest. When they were fledged, some naughty boys pulled the nest down; but luckily all the birds got safely away in the high wind.

Then the old bird was grieved that his sons had all gone out into the world without his having first warned them of every kind of danger and given them good instruction in how to deal with each.

In the autumn a great many sparrows gathered together in a wheatfield, and there the old bird met his four children again, and full of joy took them home with him.

"Ah, my dear sons, what pain I've been in about you all through the summer, because you got away in the wind without my teaching. Listen to my words, obey your father, and be well on your guard. Little birds have great dangers to meet."

And then he asked the eldest where he had spent the summer and how he had supported himself.

"I stayed in the gardens and looked for caterpillars and small worms, until the cherries got ripe."

"Ah, my son," said the father, "titbits are not bad, but there's great risk about them. On that account take great care of yourself from now on — and particularly when people are going about the gardens carrying long green poles that are hollow inside and have a little hole at the top."

"Yes, father; but what if a little green leaf is stuck over the hole with wax?" said the son.

"Where have you seen that?"

"In a merchant's garden," said the youngster.

"Oh, my son, merchant folk are quick folk," said the father. "If you've been among the children of the world, you've learned worldly shiftiness enough. Only see that you use it well, and don't be too confident."

After this he asked the next, "Where have you passed your time?"

"At court," said the son.

"Sparrows and silly little birds are of no use in that place. There you find plenty of gold, velvet, silk, armour, harness, sparrowhawks, screech owls and hen harriers. Keep to the horses' stable, where they winnow oats or thresh; and then fortune may give you your daily grain of corn in peace."

"Yes, father," said the son, "but when the stable boys make traps and set their gins and snares in the straw, many a bird is caught fast."

"Where have you seen that?" said the old bird.

"At court, among the stable boys."

"Oh, my son, court boys are bad boys. If you've been to court and among the lords and left no feathers there, you've learned a fair amount and will know very well how to go about the world; but look around you and above you, for the wolves devour the wisest dogs."

The father examined the third as well. "Where did you seek your safety?"

"I've broken up tubs and ropes on the cart roads and highways, and sometimes came upon a grain of corn or barley."

"That's dainty fare indeed," said the father, "but take care what you're about and look carefully around you — especially when you see anybody stooping down and about to pick up a stone; there isn't much time to linger then."

"That's true," said the son, "but what if somebody has a bit of rock or ore ready beforehand in his shirt or his pocket?"

"Where have you seen that?"

"Among the mountain men, dear father. When they go out they generally take little bits of ore with them."

"Mountain folk are working folk, and clever folk. If you've been among mountain lads you've seen and learned something; but when you go there, beware, for many a sparrow has come to a bad end through a mountain boy."

At length the father came to the youngest son. "You, my dear chirping nestling, were always the silliest and weakest. Stay with me. The world has many rough, wicked birds in it, with crooked beaks and long claws, that lie in wait for poor little birds and swallow them. Keep with your own kind, and pick up little spiders and caterpillars from the trees or the house, and then you'll live long in peace."

"My dear father, whoever feeds himself without harming other people fares well; and no sparrowhawk or eagle or kite will hurt him, if he faithfully commits himself and his lawful food to God, evening and morning — God, who is the Creator and Preserver of all forest and village birds, who hears the cry and prayer of the young ravens too; for no sparrow or wren ever falls to the ground except by his will."

"Where did you learn this?"

The son answered, "When the great blast of wind tore me away from you I came to a church; and there through the summer I've picked up the flies and spiders from the windows, and heard this preached. The Father of all sparrows fed me all the summer through, and kept me from all mischance and from savage birds."

"In truth, my dear son, if you take refuge in the churches and help to clear away the spiders and the buzzing flies, and cry out to God like the young ravens and commend yourself to the eternal Creator, all will be well with you — and that even if the whole world were full of wild, malicious birds.

	He who to God commits his ways,
	in silence suffers, waits and prays,
	preserves his faith and conscience pure —
	he is of God's protection sure."

The Story of Schlauraffen Land

In the time of Schlauraffen I went there, and saw Rome and the Lateran hanging by a small silken thread, and a man without feet who outran a swift horse, and a keen sharp sword that cut through a bridge.

There I saw a young donkey with a silver nose that chased two swift hares, and a lime tree that was very large, on which hot cakes were growing.

There I saw a lean old goat that carried about a hundred cartloads of fat on his body, and sixty loads of salt.

Have I not told enough lies?

There I saw a plough ploughing without horse or cow; and a child of one year old threw four millstones from Regensburg to Trier, and from Trier to Strasbourg; and a hawk swam over the Rhine, which he had a perfect right to do.

There I heard some fishes start making such a commotion with each other that it echoed as far as heaven; and sweet honey flowed like water from a deep valley at the top of a high mountain; and these were strange things.

There were two crows mowing a meadow, and I saw two gnats building a bridge, and two doves tore a wolf to pieces; two children gave birth to two kids, and two frogs threshed corn together.

There I saw two mice consecrating a bishop, and two cats scratching out a bear's tongue. Then a snail came running up and killed two furious lions.

There stood a barber shaving a woman's beard off; and two suckling children told their mother to hold her tongue.

There I saw two greyhounds bringing a mill out of the water; and a sorry old horse stood beside it and said it was right. And four horses were standing in the yard threshing corn with all their might, and two goats were heating the stove, and a red cow shot the bread into the oven.

Then a cock crowed, "Cock-a-doodle-doo!" The story is all told — cock-a-doodle-doo!

The Ditmarsch Tale of Wonders

I'll tell you something. I saw two roast fowls flying; they flew quickly, and had their breasts turned to heaven and their backs to hell; and an anvil and a millstone swam across the Rhine prettily, slowly and gently; and a frog sat on the ice at Whitsuntide and ate a ploughshare.

Three fellows who wanted to catch a hare went on crutches and stilts; one of them was deaf, the second blind, the third could not speak, and the fourth could not stir a step. Do you want to know how it was done? First the blind man saw the hare running across the field, the one who could not speak called to the lame one, and the lame one seized it by the neck.

There were certain men who wanted to sail on dry land, and they set their sails in the wind and sailed away over great fields. Then they sailed over a high mountain, and there they were miserably drowned.

A crab was chasing a hare that was running away at full speed; and high up on the roof lay a cow that had climbed up there. In that country the flies are as big as the goats are here.

Open the window, so that the lies can fly out.

A Riddling Tale

Three women were changed into flowers that grew in a field; but one of them was allowed to be in her own home at night.

Then once, when day was drawing near and she had to go back to her companions in the field and become a flower again, she said to her husband, "If you'll come this afternoon and pick me, I shall be set free and stay with you from then on." And he did so.

Now the question is: how did her husband know her, when the flowers were exactly alike, without any difference between them?

Answer: as she had been at her home during the night and not in the field, no dew fell on her as it did on the others; and by this her husband knew her.

Snow-White and Rose-Red

There was once a poor widow who lived in a lonely cottage. In front of the cottage was a garden with two rose trees in it, one of which bore white roses and the other red. She had two children who were like the two rose trees, and one was called Snow-White and the other Rose-Red. They were as good and happy, as busy and cheerful, as any two children in the world ever were — only Snow-White was more quiet and gentle than Rose-Red.

Rose-Red liked better to run about the meadows and fields looking for flowers and catching butterflies; but Snow-White sat at home with her mother and helped her with the housework, or read to her when there was nothing to do.

The two children were so fond of each other that they always held each other by the hand when they went out together; and when Snow-White said, "We won't leave each other," Rose-Red answered, "Never, as long as we live" — and their mother would add, "What one of you has, she must share with the other."

They often ran about the forest alone and gathered red berries, and no animals did them any harm, but came close to them trustfully. The little hare would eat a cabbage leaf out of their hands, the roe deer grazed at their side, the stag leapt merrily past them, and the birds sat still on the boughs and sang whatever they knew.

No mishap ever came to them. If they had stayed too late in the forest and night came on, they lay down next to each other on the moss and slept until morning came; and their mother knew this and felt no distress about them.

Once, when they had spent the night in the wood and the dawn had woken them, they saw a beautiful child in a shining white dress sitting near their bed. He got up and looked at them quite kindly, but said nothing, and went away into the forest. And when they looked round they found that they had been sleeping quite close to a precipice, and would certainly have fallen into it in the darkness if they had gone only a few steps further. And their mother told them that it must have been the angel who watches over good children.

Snow-White and Rose-Red kept their mother's little cottage so neat that it was a pleasure to look inside it. In the summer Rose-Red took care of the house, and every morning laid a wreath of flowers by her mother's bed before she woke, with a rose from each tree in it. In the winter Snow-White lit the fire and hung the kettle on the hook over it. The kettle was of copper and shone like gold, it was polished so brightly.

In the evening, when the snowflakes fell, the mother said, "Go, Snow-White, and bolt the door" — and then they sat round the hearth, and their mother took her spectacles and read aloud out of a large book, and the two girls listened as they sat and spun. And close beside them a lamb lay on the floor, and behind them a white dove sat on a perch with its head hidden under its wing.

One evening, as they were sitting comfortably together like this, somebody knocked at the door as if he wanted to be let in.

Their mother said, "Quick, Rose-Red, open the door; it must be a traveller looking for shelter."

Rose-Red went and pushed back the bolt, thinking that it was a poor man; but it was not. It was a bear, that stretched his broad black head in at the door.

Rose-Red screamed and sprang back, the lamb bleated, the dove fluttered, and Snow-White hid behind her mother's bed. But the bear began to speak, and said, "Don't be afraid, I'll do you no harm. I'm half frozen, and only want to warm myself a little beside you."

"Poor bear," said the mother, "lie down by the fire; only take care you don't burn your coat." Then she called, "Snow-White, Rose-Red, come out; the bear will do you no harm, he means well."

So they both came out; and by and by the lamb and the dove came nearer too, and were not afraid of him.

The bear said, "Here, children, knock the snow out of my coat a little." So they brought the broom and swept the bear's hide clean; and he stretched himself out by the fire and growled contentedly and comfortably.

It was not long before they grew quite at home with him and played tricks on their clumsy guest. They tugged his hair with their hands, put their feet on his back and rolled him about, or took a hazel switch and beat him; and when he growled, they laughed. But the bear took it all in good part; only when they were too rough he called out, "Leave me alive, children:

	Snowy-White, Rosy-Red,
	will you beat your lover dead?"

When it was bedtime, and the others went to bed, the mother said to the bear, "You can lie there by the hearth, and then you'll be safe from the cold and the bad weather." And as soon as day dawned the two children let him out, and he trotted away across the snow into the forest.

From then on the bear came every evening at the same time, laid himself down by the hearth and let the children amuse themselves with him as much as they liked; and they got so used to him that the doors were never fastened until their black friend had arrived.

When spring had come and everything outside was green, the bear said one morning to Snow-White, "Now I must go away, and I can't come back the whole summer."

"Where are you going, then, dear bear?" asked Snow-White.

"I must go into the forest and guard my treasures from the wicked dwarfs. In the winter, when the earth is frozen hard, they have to stay down below and can't work their way through; but now, when the sun has thawed and warmed the earth, they break through it and come out to pry and steal. And whatever once gets into their hands and into their caves doesn't easily see daylight again."

Snow-White was quite sorry that he was going away; and as she unbolted the door for him and the bear was hurrying out, he caught against the bolt and a piece of his hairy coat was torn off; and it seemed to Snow-White as if she had seen gold shining through it, though she was not sure about it. The bear ran away quickly and was soon out of sight behind the trees.

A short time afterwards their mother sent the children into the forest to get firewood. There they found a big tree lying felled on the ground, and close by the trunk something was jumping backwards and forwards in the grass, though they could not make out what it was.

When they came nearer they saw a dwarf with an old withered face and a snow-white beard a yard long. The end of the beard was caught in a crack in the tree, and the little fellow was jumping backwards and forwards like a dog tied to a rope, and did not know what to do.

He glared at the girls with his fiery red eyes and cried, "Why are you standing there? Can't you come over and help me?"

"What are you doing there, little man?" asked Rose-Red.

"You stupid, prying goose!" answered the dwarf. "I was going to split the tree to get a little wood for cooking. The little bit of food that one of us needs gets burnt up at once with thick logs; we don't swallow so much as you coarse, greedy folk. I'd just driven the wedge safely in and everything was going as I wanted; but the wretched wood was too smooth and suddenly sprang apart, and the tree closed so quickly that I couldn't pull out my beautiful white beard. So now it's held fast and I can't get away — and the silly, sleek, milk-faced things laugh! Ugh, how odious you are!"

The children tried very hard, but they could not pull the beard out; it was caught too fast.

"I'll run and fetch somebody," said Rose-Red.

"You senseless goose!" snarled the dwarf. "Why should you fetch somebody? There are two of you already, and that's two too many for me. Can't you think of something better?"

"Don't be impatient," said Snow-White, "I'll help you" — and she pulled her scissors out of her pocket and cut off the end of the beard.

As soon as the dwarf felt himself free, he took hold of a bag that lay among the roots of the tree, which was full of gold, and lifted it up, grumbling to himself, "Uncouth people, to cut off a piece of my fine beard. Bad luck to you!" And then he swung the bag onto his back and went off without so much as looking at the children once.

Some time after that, Snow-White and Rose-Red went to catch a dish of fish. As they came near the brook they saw something like a large grasshopper hopping towards the water, as if it were going to leap in. They ran to it and found it was the dwarf.

"Where are you going?" said Rose-Red. "You surely don't want to go into the water?"

"I'm not such a fool!" cried the dwarf. "Don't you see that the accursed fish wants to pull me in?"

The little man had been sitting there fishing, and unluckily the wind had twisted his beard round the fishing line. Just then a big fish bit, and the feeble creature had not the strength to pull it out; the fish had the upper hand and was dragging the dwarf towards it. He held on to all the reeds and rushes, but it was of little use; he had to follow the movements of the fish, and was in real danger of being dragged into the water.

The girls came just in time. They held him fast and tried to free his beard from the line, but all in vain: beard and line were tangled fast together. Nothing was left but to bring out the scissors and cut the beard, by which a small part of it was lost.

When the dwarf saw that, he screamed out, "Is that civil, you toadstool, to disfigure a man's face? Wasn't it enough to clip off the end of my beard? Now you've cut off the best part of it. I can't let myself be seen by my own people. I wish you'd been made to run the soles off your shoes!"

Then he took out a sack of pearls that was lying in the rushes, and without another word he dragged it away and disappeared behind a stone.

It happened that soon afterwards their mother sent the two children into the town to buy needles and thread and laces and ribbons. The road led them across a heath where huge pieces of rock lay strewn here and there.

Now they noticed a large bird hovering in the air, flying slowly round and round above them; it sank lower and lower, and at last settled near a rock not far off. Directly afterwards they heard a loud, piteous cry. They ran up and saw with horror that the eagle had seized their old acquaintance the dwarf and was about to carry him off.

The children, full of pity, at once took tight hold of the little man and pulled against the eagle so long that at last it let its prey go. As soon as the dwarf had recovered from his first fright he cried in his shrill voice, "Couldn't you have done it more carefully? You dragged at my brown coat so that it's all torn and full of holes, you helpless, clumsy creatures!"

Then he took up a sack full of precious stones and slipped away again under the rock into his hole. The girls, who by this time were used to his ingratitude, went on their way and did their business in the town.

As they crossed the heath again on their way home, they came upon the dwarf by surprise. He had tipped his bag of precious stones out on a clean patch of ground, and had not thought that anybody would come that way so late. The evening sun shone on the brilliant stones; they glittered and sparkled in all colours so beautifully that the children stood still and looked at them.

"Why are you standing there gaping?" cried the dwarf, and his ash-grey face turned copper-red with rage.

He was going on with his bad words when a loud growling was heard, and a black bear came trotting towards them out of the forest. The dwarf sprang up in a fright, but he could not get to his cave, for the bear was already close by.

Then in the dread of his heart he cried, "Dear Mr. Bear, spare me, and I'll give you all my treasures! Look — the beautiful jewels lying there! Grant me my life; what do you want with a slender little fellow like me? You wouldn't feel me between your teeth. Come, take these two wicked girls; they're tender morsels for you, fat as young quails. For mercy's sake, eat them!"

The bear took no notice of his words, but gave the wicked creature a single blow with his paw, and he never moved again.

The girls had run away; but the bear called after them, "Snow-White and Rose-Red, don't be afraid. Wait — I'll come with you."

Then they knew his voice and waited; and when he came up to them, his bearskin suddenly fell off, and he stood there a handsome man, clothed all in gold.

"I'm a King's son," he said, "and I was bewitched by that wicked dwarf, who had stolen my treasures. I've had to run about the forest as a savage bear until I was freed by his death. Now he's had his well-deserved punishment."

Snow-White was married to him, and Rose-Red to his brother; and they divided between them the great treasure the dwarf had gathered together in his cave. Their old mother lived peacefully and happily with her children for many years. She took the two rose trees with her, and they stood in front of her window and bore the most beautiful roses every year, white and red.

The Wise Servant

How fortunate the master is, and how well everything goes in his house, when he has a wise servant who listens to his orders and does not obey them, but prefers to follow his own wisdom.

A clever John of this kind was once sent out by his master to look for a lost cow. He stayed away a long time, and his master thought, "Faithful John spares no pains over his work."

But as he did not come back at all, his master began to fear that some misfortune had happened to him, and set out himself to look for him. He had to search a long time, but at last he caught sight of the boy running up and down a large field.

"Now, dear John," said his master when he had got up to him, "have you found the cow I sent you to look for?"

"No, master," he answered, "I haven't found the cow — but then I haven't looked for it."

"Then what have you been looking for, John?"

"Something better; and luckily I've found it."

"What's that, John?"

"Three blackbirds," answered the boy.

"And where are they?" asked his master.

"I can see one of them, I can hear the second, and I'm running after the third," answered the wise boy.

Take an example from this: don't trouble yourselves about your masters or their orders, but do whatever comes into your head and pleases you, and then you'll be acting just as wisely as prudent John.

The Glass Coffin

Let nobody ever say that a poor tailor can't do great things and win high honours. All that's needed is that he should go to the right smithy — and, what matters most, that he should have good luck.

A civil, capable tailor's apprentice once went out travelling and came into a great forest; and as he did not know the way, he lost himself. Night fell, and nothing was left for him to do but look for a bed in that painful solitude. He could certainly have found a good bed on the soft moss, but his fear of wild animals gave him no rest there, and at last he had to make up his mind to spend the night in a tree. He picked out a high oak, climbed to the top of it, and thanked God that he had his pressing iron with him, for otherwise the wind blowing over the top of the tree would have carried him away.

After he had spent some hours in the darkness — not without fear and trembling — he saw the glimmer of a light a very short way off; and as he thought there might be a human dwelling there, where he would be better off than on the branches of a tree, he climbed carefully down and went towards the light.

It led him to a small hut woven together out of reeds and rushes. He knocked boldly; the door opened, and by the light that came out he saw a little hoary old man wearing a coat made of scraps of coloured stuff sewn together.

"Who are you, and what do you want?" the man asked in a grumbling voice.

"I'm a poor tailor," he answered, "whom night has caught out here in the wilderness; and I beg you earnestly to take me into your hut until morning."

"Go your way," replied the old man in a surly voice. "I'll have nothing to do with vagabonds. Find yourself a shelter somewhere else."

And after these words he was about to slip back into his hut; but the tailor held him so tightly by the corner of his coat and pleaded so piteously that the old man, who was not as ill-natured as he wanted to appear, was softened at last, and took him into the hut, where he gave him something to eat and then pointed out a very good bed in a corner.

The weary tailor needed no rocking, but slept sweetly till morning; and even then he would not have thought of getting up if he had not been roused by a great noise. A violent sound of screaming and roaring forced its way through the thin walls of the hut. The tailor, full of unaccustomed courage, jumped up, put his clothes on in haste and hurried out.

Then close by the hut he saw a great black bull and a beautiful stag just preparing for a violent struggle. They rushed at each other with such extreme rage that the ground shook with their trampling and the air rang with their cries. For a long time it was uncertain which of the two would win; but at length the stag drove his horns into his opponent's body, whereupon the bull fell to the earth with a terrific roar and was thoroughly finished off by a few strokes from the stag.

The tailor, who had watched the fight in astonishment, was still standing there motionless when the stag came bounding up to him at full speed; and before he could get away, it caught him up on its great horns. He had not much time to collect his thoughts, for it went at a swift race over stock and stone, mountain and valley, wood and meadow. He held on with both hands to the tops of the horns and gave himself up to his fate. It seemed to him just as if he were flying.

At length the stag stopped in front of a wall of rock and gently let the tailor down. The tailor, more dead than alive, needed a good while longer than that to come to himself.

When he had recovered a little, the stag, which had stayed standing beside him, pushed its horns with such force against a door in the rock that it sprang open. Flames of fire shot out, and after them came a great cloud of smoke that hid the stag from his sight.

The tailor did not know what to do or where to turn to get out of this wilderness and back among human beings again. But while he was standing there undecided, a voice sounded out of the rock and cried to him, "Come in without fear; no harm shall come to you."

He hesitated; but driven by some mysterious force he obeyed the voice and went through the iron door into a large, spacious hall, whose ceiling and walls and floor were made of shining polished squared stones, and on every one of them were carved letters he did not know. He looked at everything full of wonder, and was on the point of going out again, when he heard the voice once more, saying to him, "Step on the stone that lies in the middle of the hall, and great good fortune awaits you."

His courage had already grown so great that he obeyed the order. The stone began to give way under his feet and sank slowly down into the depths. When it was firm again and the tailor looked round, he found himself in a hall like the first one in size. Here, though, there was more to look at and to admire.

Hollow places were cut in the walls, and in them stood vases of transparent glass filled with coloured spirit or with a bluish vapour. On the floor of the hall two great glass chests stood facing each other, and these at once roused his curiosity.

When he went to one of them he saw inside it a handsome building like a castle, surrounded by farm buildings, stables and barns and a quantity of other good things. Everything was small, but made with exceeding care and delicacy, and seemed to have been cut out by a skilful hand with the greatest exactness.

He might not have taken his eyes off this rarity for some while, if the voice had not made itself heard once more. It told him to turn round and look at the glass chest standing opposite.

How his wonder grew when he saw in it a girl of the greatest beauty! She lay there as if asleep, and was wrapped in her long fair hair as in a precious mantle. Her eyes were tightly shut; but the brightness of her complexion, and a ribbon that her breathing stirred to and fro, left no doubt that she was alive.

The tailor was gazing at this beauty with a beating heart, when she suddenly opened her eyes and started up at the sight of him in joyful terror.

"Just heaven!" cried she. "My deliverance is at hand! Quick, quick, help me out of my prison — if you push back the bolt of this glass coffin I shall be free."

The tailor obeyed without delay, and she at once raised the glass lid and came out and hurried into the corner of the hall, where she covered herself with a large cloak. Then she seated herself on a stone and told the young man to come to her; and after she had planted a friendly kiss on his lips, she said, "My long-desired deliverer, kind heaven has guided you to me and put an end to my sorrows. On the very day they end, your happiness shall begin. You are the husband heaven has chosen for me, and you shall pass your life in unbroken joy, loved by me and richer than you can spend in every earthly possession. Sit down and listen to the story of my life.

"I am the daughter of a rich count. My parents died when I was still very young, and in their last will they commended me to my elder brother, who brought me up. We loved each other so tenderly, and were so alike in our way of thinking and in our tastes, that we both took the resolution never to marry, but to stay together to the end of our lives.

"There was no lack of company in our house; neighbours and friends visited us often, and we showed the greatest hospitality to everybody. So it came about one evening that a stranger came riding to our castle and, on the excuse that he could not get on to the next place, begged for shelter for the night. We granted his request with ready courtesy, and during supper he entertained us in the most agreeable way with conversation and stories mixed together. My brother liked the stranger so much that he begged him to spend a couple of days with us, to which, after some hesitation, he agreed.

"We did not get up from the table until late in the night; the stranger was shown to his room, and I hurried away, as I was tired, to lay my limbs in my soft bed.

"I had hardly slept a short while when the sound of faint and delightful music woke me. As I could not imagine where it came from, I wanted to call my waiting maid, who slept in the next room; but to my astonishment I found that my speech had been taken away from me by some unknown force. I felt as if a mountain were weighing down my chest, and I was unable to make the slightest sound.

"Meanwhile, by the light of my night lamp, I saw the stranger come into my room through two doors that were firmly bolted. He came up to me and said that by the magic arts at his command he had made this lovely music sound in order to wake me, and that he had now forced his way through all the fastenings with the intention of offering me his hand and heart.

"My revulsion at his magic arts was so great, though, that I gave him no answer. He stood there for a time without moving, apparently expecting a favourable decision; but as I went on keeping silent, he angrily declared that he would take his revenge and find means to punish my pride, and left the room.

"I passed the night in the greatest disquiet, and only fell asleep towards morning. When I woke I hurried to my brother, but did not find him in his room; and the servants told me that he had ridden out with the stranger to the hunt at daybreak.

"I suspected at once that nothing good was afoot. I dressed quickly, ordered my horse to be saddled, and rode off at full gallop to the forest with only one servant. The servant fell with his horse and could not follow me, for the horse had broken its leg. I went on my way without stopping; and in a few minutes I saw the stranger coming towards me with a beautiful stag, which he was leading on a cord.

"I asked him where he had left my brother, and how he had come by this stag, out of whose great eyes I saw tears flowing. Instead of answering me, he began to laugh loudly. I flew into a great rage at this, pulled out a pistol and fired it at the monster; but the ball rebounded from his chest and went into my horse's head. I fell to the ground, and the stranger muttered some words that took away my consciousness.

"When I came to my senses again, I found myself in this underground cave in a glass coffin. The magician appeared once more and said that he had changed my brother into a stag; that my castle and everything belonging to it, shrunk in size by his arts, he had shut up in the other glass chest; and that my people, all of whom he had turned into smoke, he had confined in glass bottles. He told me that if I would now comply with his wish, it was an easy thing for him to put everything back as it had been, since he had only to open the vessels and everything would return to its natural form.

"I answered him as little as I had the first time. He vanished and left me in my prison, where a deep sleep came over me. Among the visions that passed before my eyes, the most comforting was one in which a young man came and set me free; and when I opened my eyes today I saw you, and saw my dream fulfilled.

"Help me to accomplish the other things that happened in those visions. The first is that we lift the glass chest with my castle in it onto that broad stone."

As soon as the stone was loaded it began to rise up with the girl and the young man, and went up through the opening in the ceiling into the upper hall, from where they could easily reach the open air.

Here the girl opened the lid; and it was marvellous to see how the castle and the houses and the farm buildings inside it stretched themselves out and grew to their natural size with the greatest rapidity.

After this the girl and the tailor went back to the cave underground and had the vessels full of smoke carried up by the stone. The girl had hardly opened the bottles when the blue smoke rushed out and changed itself into living men, in whom she recognised her servants and her people.

Her joy was greater still when her brother, who had killed the magician in the shape of the bull, came out of the forest towards them in his human form; and on that very day the girl, keeping her promise, gave her hand at the altar to the lucky tailor.

Lazy Harry

Harry was lazy; and although he had nothing else to do but drive his goat out to pasture every day, he still groaned when he went home after his day's work was done.

"It's a heavy burden, indeed," said he, "and a wearisome business, driving a goat into the field like this year after year, right into late autumn. If a man could only lie down and sleep! But no — you have to keep your eyes open in case it damages the young trees, or squeezes through the hedge into a garden, or runs away altogether. How is a man to get any rest, or any peace in his life?"

He sat down and collected his thoughts and considered how he might get this burden off his shoulders. For a long time all his thinking was no use; but suddenly it was as though scales fell from his eyes.

"I know what I'll do," he cried. "I'll marry fat Trina, who has a goat as well, and she can take mine out with hers, and then I'll have no more need to trouble myself."

So Harry got up and set his weary legs in motion and went right across the street — for it was no further than that — to where fat Trina's parents lived, and asked for their hard-working and virtuous daughter in marriage. The parents did not think it over long. "Birds of a feather flock together," they thought, and gave their consent.

So fat Trina became Harry's wife, and took both the goats out. Harry had a good time of it, and had no work to rest from but his own idleness. He only went out with her now and then, and said, "I only do it so that I can enjoy the rest more afterwards; otherwise a man loses all feeling for it."

But fat Trina was no less idle. "Dear Harry," said she one day, "why should we make our lives so toilsome when there's no need for it, and ruin the best days of our youth? Wouldn't it be better to give the two goats — which disturb us every morning in our sweetest sleep with their bleating — to our neighbour, and he'll give us a beehive for them? We'll put the beehive in a sunny place behind the house and trouble ourselves about it no more. Bees don't need to be looked after, or driven out into the field; they fly out and find their own way home again, and collect honey without giving the least trouble."

"You've spoken like a sensible woman," replied Harry. "We'll carry out your proposal without delay. And besides all that, honey tastes better and nourishes a man better than goat's milk, and it keeps longer too."

The neighbour willingly gave a beehive for the two goats. The bees flew in and out from early morning till late evening without ever tiring, and filled the hive with the most beautiful honey, so that in the autumn Harry was able to take a whole pitcherful out of it.

They put the jug on a board fixed to the wall of their bedroom; and as they were afraid it might be stolen from them, or that the mice might find it, Trina brought in a stout hazel stick and put it beside her bed, so that she could reach it with her hand without needlessly getting up, and drive the uninvited guests away.

Lazy Harry did not like to leave his bed before noon. "He who rises early," said he, "wastes his substance."

One morning, when he was still lying among the feathers in broad daylight, resting after his long sleep, he said to his wife, "Women are fond of sweet things, and you're always tasting the honey in secret. It would be better for us to trade it for a goose with a young gosling, before you eat the whole of it."

"But," answered Trina, "not before we have a child to look after them! Am I to worry myself with the little geese and spend all my strength on them for nothing?"

"Do you think," said Harry, "that the youngster will look after geese? Children don't obey any more nowadays; they do as they please, because they think themselves cleverer than their parents — just like that lad who was sent to look for the cow and chased three blackbirds."

"Oh," replied Trina, "this one will fare badly if he doesn't do as I say. I'll take a stick and belabour his skin for him with more blows than I can count. Look, Harry," cried she in her zeal, and seized the stick she used for driving the mice away, "this is the way I'll fall on him!"

She reached her arm out to strike — and unluckily hit the honey pitcher above the bed. The pitcher struck against the wall and fell down in pieces, and the fine honey streamed down onto the floor.

"There lie the goose and the young gosling," said Harry, "and they want no looking after. But it's lucky the pitcher didn't fall on my head. We have every reason to be satisfied with our lot."

And then, as he saw that there was still some honey in one of the pieces, he reached out his hand for it and said quite cheerfully, "The remains, wife, we'll still eat with a relish; and then we'll rest a little after the fright we've had. What does it matter if we get up a little later? The day is always long enough."

"Yes," answered Trina, "we shall always get to the end of it at the proper time. Do you know that the snail was once invited to a wedding and set out to go, but arrived at the christening? In front of the house it fell over the fence, and said, 'Hurrying does no good.'"

The Griffin

There was once a King — but where he reigned and what he was called, I don't know. He had no son, but an only daughter who had always been ill, and no doctor had been able to cure her.

Then it was foretold to the King that his daughter would eat herself well with an apple. So he had it proclaimed throughout his whole kingdom that whoever brought his daughter an apple she could eat herself well with should have her for a wife, and be King.

This came to the ears of a peasant who had three sons; and he said to the eldest, "Go out into the garden and take a basketful of those beautiful apples with the red cheeks and carry them to the court. Perhaps the King's daughter will be able to eat herself well with them, and then you'll marry her and be King."

The lad did so, and set out. When he had gone a short way he met a little iron man, who asked him what he had there in the basket. Uele — for that was his name — replied, "Frogs' legs."

At this the little man said, "Well, so it shall be, and so it shall stay" — and went away.

At length Uele arrived at the palace and announced that he had brought apples that would cure the King's daughter if she ate them. This delighted the King hugely, and he had Uele brought before him. But alas — when he opened the basket, instead of apples he had frogs' legs in it, still kicking about. At this the King grew angry and had him driven out of the house.

When he got home he told his father how it had gone with him. So the father sent the next son, who was called Seame; but it all went with him just as it had with Uele. He too met the little iron man, who asked what he had there in the basket. Seame said, "Hogs' bristles" — and the iron man said, "Well, so it shall be, and so it shall stay."

When Seame got to the King's palace and said he had brought apples the King's daughter could eat herself well with, they did not want to let him in, and said that one fellow had been there already and had treated them as if they were fools. Seame, though, insisted that he certainly did have the apples, and that they ought to let him in. At length they believed him and took him to the King. But when he uncovered the basket, all he had was hogs' bristles.

This enraged the King most terribly, and he had Seame whipped out of the house.

When he got home he told them everything that had happened to him. And then the youngest boy, whose name was Hans but who was always called Stupid Hans, came and asked his father whether he might go with some apples.

"Oh," said his father, "you'd be just the right fellow for a thing like that. If the clever ones can't manage it, what can you do?"

The boy, though, did not believe him, and said, "Indeed, father, I want to go."

"Just get away, you stupid fellow; you must wait till you're wiser," said his father to that, and turned his back.

But Hans pulled at the back of his smock and said, "Indeed, father, I want to go."

"Well then, as far as I'm concerned you may go — but you'll soon be home again," replied the old man in a spiteful voice.

The boy, though, was tremendously delighted and jumped for joy.

"Well, act like a fool! You grow more stupid every day," said his father again.

But Hans did not care about that, and would not let it spoil his pleasure. And as it was night by then, he thought he might as well wait until the next day, for he could not get to court that day. All night long he could not sleep in his bed; and if he did doze for a moment, he dreamed of beautiful girls, of palaces, of gold and silver and all kinds of things of that sort.

Early in the morning he set out on his way; and directly afterwards the little shabby-looking man in his iron clothes came up to him and asked what he was carrying in the basket. Hans answered that he was carrying apples for the King's daughter to eat herself well with.

"Then," said the little man, "so they shall be, and so they shall stay."

But at the court not one of them would let Hans in, for they said two had already been there who had told them they were bringing apples, and one of them had had frogs' legs and the other hogs' bristles. Hans, though, insisted stoutly that he most certainly had no frogs' legs, but some of the most beautiful apples in the whole kingdom. And as he spoke so pleasantly, the doorkeeper thought he could not be telling a lie, and asked him to come in.

And he was right; for when Hans uncovered his basket in the King's presence, golden-yellow apples came tumbling out. The King was delighted, and had some of them taken to his daughter, and then waited in anxious expectation until news should be brought him of the effect they had.

But before much time had gone by, news was brought him — and who do you think it was that came? It was his daughter herself. As soon as she had eaten some of those apples she was cured, and sprang out of her bed.

The joy the King felt cannot be described. But now he did not want to give his daughter in marriage to Hans, and said he must first make him a boat that would go faster on dry land than on water.

Hans agreed to the condition and went home and told them how it had gone with him. Then his father sent Uele into the forest to make a boat of that kind. He worked hard, and whistled all the time.

At midday, when the sun was at its highest, the little iron man came and asked what he was making. Uele answered, "Wooden bowls for the kitchen."

The iron man said, "So it shall be, and so it shall stay."

By evening Uele thought he had made the boat; but when he tried to get into it, he had nothing but wooden bowls.

Next day Seame went into the forest, but it all went with him just as it had with Uele.

On the third day Stupid Hans went. He worked away most industriously, so that the whole forest rang with his heavy strokes; and all the while he sang and whistled right merrily.

At midday, when it was hottest, the little man came again and asked what he was making.

"A boat that will go faster on dry land than on water," replied Hans; "and when I've finished it, I'm to have the King's daughter for my wife."

"Well," said the little man, "such a one it shall be, and such it shall stay."

In the evening, when the sun had turned to gold, Hans finished his boat and everything that was needed for it. He got into it and rowed to the palace. The boat went as swiftly as the wind.

The King saw it from a long way off; but he still would not give his daughter to Hans, and said he must first take a hundred hares out to pasture from early morning until late evening — and if one of them got away, he should not have his daughter.

Hans was content with this, and next day went out to pasture with his flock and took great care that none of them ran away.

Before many hours had passed a servant girl came from the palace and told Hans that he must give her a hare instantly, because some visitors had arrived unexpectedly. But Hans knew very well what that meant, and said he would not give her one; the King could set some hare soup in front of his guests the next day.

The maid, though, would not accept his refusal, and at last she began to get angry with him. Then Hans said that if the King's daughter came herself, he would give her a hare.

The maid reported this at the palace, and the daughter did come herself. Meanwhile, though, the little man came to Hans again and asked what he was doing there. He said he had to watch a hundred hares and see that none of them ran away, and then he could marry the King's daughter and be King.

"Good," said the little man. "Here's a whistle for you; and if one of them runs away, just blow it and it will come back again."

When the King's daughter came, Hans put a hare into her apron; but when she had gone about a hundred steps with it he whistled, and the hare jumped out of the apron and was back with the flock again before she could turn round.

When evening came the hare-herd whistled once more and looked to see whether they were all there, and then drove them to the palace.

The King wondered how Hans had been able to graze a hundred hares without losing any of them. All the same he still would not give him his daughter, and said he must now bring him a feather from the Griffin's tail.

Hans set out at once and walked straight on. In the evening he came to a castle, and there he asked for a night's lodging, for in those days there were no inns. The lord of the castle promised it with much pleasure, and asked where he was going.

Hans answered, "To the Griffin."

"Oh — to the Griffin! They tell me he knows everything. I've lost the key of an iron money chest; perhaps you'd be so good as to ask him where it is."

"Yes, indeed," said Hans, "I'll do that."

Early next morning he went on; and on his way he came to another castle, where he stayed the night again. When the people who lived there learned that he was going to the Griffin, they said they had a daughter in the house who was ill, and that they had already tried every means to cure her but none had done her any good; would he be so kind as to ask the Griffin what would make their daughter well again?

Hans said he would gladly do that, and went on.

Then he came to a lake; and instead of a ferry boat there was a tall, tall man there who had to carry everybody across. The man asked Hans where he was journeying.

"To the Griffin," said Hans.
