"Then when you get to him," said the man, "just ask him why I'm forced to carry everybody over the lake."

"Yes, indeed, I'll certainly do that," said Hans.

Then the man took him up on his shoulders and carried him across.

At length Hans arrived at the Griffin's house; but only the wife was at home, and not the Griffin himself. The woman asked him what he wanted, and he told her everything: that he had to get a feather out of the Griffin's tail; that there was a castle where they had lost the key of their money chest, and he was to ask the Griffin where it was; that in another castle the daughter was ill, and he was to find out what would cure her; and that not far from there was a lake with a man beside it who was forced to carry people across, and he was very anxious to learn why the man had to do it.

Then the woman said, "But look here, my good friend, no Christian can talk to the Griffin; he devours them all. But if you like, you can lie down under his bed; and in the night, when he's fast asleep, you can reach out and pull a feather out of his tail. And as for the things you want to know, I'll ask about them myself."

Hans was quite satisfied with this and got under the bed.

In the evening the Griffin came home; and as soon as he came into the room he said, "Wife, I smell a Christian."

"Yes," said the woman, "one was here today, but he went away again." And at that the Griffin said no more.

In the middle of the night, when the Griffin was snoring loudly, Hans reached out and plucked a feather from his tail. The Griffin woke up instantly and said, "Wife, I smell a Christian, and it seems to me that somebody was pulling at my tail."

His wife said, "You've certainly been dreaming. And I told you before that a Christian was here today, but that he went away again. He told me all kinds of things — that in one castle they'd lost the key of their money chest and could find it nowhere."

"Oh, the fools!" said the Griffin. "The key is in the woodshed, under a log of wood behind the door."

"And then he said that in another castle the daughter was ill, and they knew no remedy to cure her."

"Oh, the fools!" said the Griffin. "Under the cellar steps a toad has made its nest out of her hair; and if she got her hair back, she'd be well."

"And then he also said that there was a place with a lake, and a man beside it who was forced to carry everybody across."

"Oh, the fool!" said the Griffin. "If he only set one man down in the middle, he'd never have to carry another across."

Early next morning the Griffin got up and went out. Then Hans came out from under the bed; and he had a beautiful feather, and had heard what the Griffin had said about the key and the daughter and the ferryman. The Griffin's wife repeated it all over to him once more so that he should not forget it, and then he went home again.

First he came to the man by the lake, who asked him what the Griffin had said; but Hans replied that he must carry him across first, and then he would tell him. So the man carried him across; and when he was over, Hans told him that all he had to do was set one person down in the middle of the lake, and then he would never have to carry anybody over again.

The man was hugely delighted, and told Hans that out of gratitude he would take him across once more and back again. But Hans said no, he would save him the trouble; he was quite satisfied already — and went on his way.

Then he came to the castle where the daughter was ill. He took her on his shoulders, for she could not walk, and carried her down the cellar steps and pulled out the toad's nest from under the lowest step and put it into her hand; and she sprang off his shoulder and up the steps ahead of him, and was quite cured. Then her father and mother were overjoyed beyond measure, and they gave Hans gifts of gold and silver, and whatever else he wished for they gave him.

And when he got to the other castle he went straight into the woodshed and found the key under the log of wood behind the door, and took it to the lord of the castle. He too was not a little pleased, and gave Hans as a reward a great deal of the gold that was in the chest, and all kinds of things besides — cows and sheep and goats.

When Hans arrived before the King with all these things — with the money and the gold and the silver, and the cows and sheep and goats — the King asked him how he had come by them. Then Hans told him that the Griffin gave everybody whatever he wanted.

So the King thought he could make use of such things himself, and set out on his way to the Griffin. But when he got to the lake, it happened that he was the very first to arrive there after Hans; and the man set him down in the middle of it and went away, and the King was drowned.

But Hans married the daughter and became King.

Strong Hans

There were once a man and a woman who had an only child, and lived quite alone in a lonely valley.

It happened that the mother went into the wood one day to gather fir branches, and took little Hans with her, who was just two years old. As it was springtime, and the child took pleasure in the many-coloured flowers, she went further and further on with him into the forest.

Suddenly two robbers sprang out of the thicket, seized the mother and child, and carried them far away into the black forest, where nobody ever came from one year's end to another. The poor woman begged the robbers urgently to set her and her child free; but their hearts were made of stone, and they would not listen to her prayers and entreaties, but drove her on further by force.

After they had worked their way through bushes and briars for about two miles, they came to a rock with a door in it, at which the robbers knocked, and it opened at once. They had to go through a long dark passage, and at last came into a great cavern lit by a fire burning on the hearth. On the wall hung swords and sabres and other deadly weapons, which gleamed in the light; and in the middle stood a black table at which four more robbers were sitting gambling, with the captain at the head of it.

As soon as he saw the woman he came and spoke to her, and told her to set her mind at rest and have no fear; they would do nothing to hurt her, but she must look after the housekeeping, and if she kept everything in order she would not fare badly with them. And with that they gave her something to eat, and showed her a bed where she could sleep with her child.

The woman stayed many years with the robbers, and Hans grew tall and strong. His mother told him stories, and taught him to read out of an old book of tales about knights that she found in the cave.

When Hans was nine years old he made himself a strong club out of a fir branch and hid it behind the bed, and then went to his mother and said, "Dear mother, please tell me who my father is. I must and will know."

His mother was silent and would not tell him, so that he should not grow homesick; besides, she knew that the godless robbers would not let him go away. But it all but broke her heart that Hans should not go to his father.

In the night, when the robbers came home from their robbing expedition, Hans brought out his club, stood in front of the captain and said, "I want to know now who my father is; and if you don't tell me at once, I'll strike you down."

Then the captain laughed, and gave Hans such a box on the ear that he rolled under the table. Hans got up again, held his tongue, and thought, "I'll wait another year and then try again; perhaps I'll do better then."

When the year was up he brought out his club again, rubbed the dust off it, looked it over well and said, "It's a stout, strong club."

At night the robbers came home and drank one jug of wine after another, and their heads began to grow heavy. Then Hans brought out his club, placed himself in front of the captain and asked him who his father was.

But the captain again gave him such a vigorous box on the ear that Hans rolled under the table. It was not long, though, before he was up again; and he beat the captain and the robbers so with his club that they could no longer move either their arms or their legs. His mother stood in a corner full of admiration for his bravery and his strength.

When Hans had finished his work he went to his mother and said, "Now I've shown that I'm in earnest; but now I must know as well who my father is."

"Dear Hans," answered his mother, "come, we'll go and look for him until we find him."

She took the key of the entrance door from the captain, and Hans fetched a great meal sack and packed into it gold and silver and whatever else he could find that was beautiful, until it was full, and then he took it on his back.

They left the cave — and how Hans opened his eyes when he came out of the darkness into daylight and saw the green forest and the flowers and the birds and the morning sun in the sky! He stood there and marvelled at everything just as if he had no sense at all.

His mother looked for the way home; and when they had walked for a couple of hours they got safely into their lonely valley and to their little house. His father was sitting in the doorway. He wept for joy when he recognised his wife and heard that Hans was his son, for he had long thought them both dead. But Hans, although he was not twelve years old yet, was a head taller than his father.

They went into the little room together; but Hans had hardly put his sack down on the bench by the stove before the whole house began to crack. The bench broke down, and then the floor, and the heavy sack fell through into the cellar.

"God save us!" cried his father. "What's that? Now you've broken our little house to pieces!"

"Don't get any grey hairs over that, dear father," answered Hans. "There's more in that sack than is needed for a new house."

His father and Hans set about building a new house at once, and buying cattle and land and setting up a farm. Hans ploughed the fields; and when he walked behind the plough and pushed it into the ground, the oxen had hardly any need to pull.

The next spring Hans said, "Keep all the money, and have a walking stick made for me that weighs a hundredweight, so that I can go travelling."

When the stick he had asked for was ready, he left his father's house and went out, and came to a deep, dark forest. There he heard something crunching and cracking; he looked round and saw a fir tree that was twisted round like a rope from the bottom to the top; and when he looked upwards he saw a great fellow who had hold of the tree and was twisting it like a willow wand.

"Hey!" cried Hans. "What are you doing up there?"

The fellow replied, "I got some faggots together yesterday, and I'm twisting a rope for them."

"That's what I like," thought Hans; "he has some strength in him." And he called to him, "Leave that alone and come with me."

The fellow came down, and he was a whole head taller than Hans — and Hans was not small.

"Your name is Fir-Twister from now on," said Hans to him.

And with that they went on further, and heard something knocking and hammering with such force that the ground shook at every stroke. Shortly afterwards they came to a mighty rock, in front of which a giant was standing and striking great pieces off it with his fist.

When Hans asked what he was doing, he answered, "At night, when I want to sleep, bears and wolves and vermin of that kind come and sniff and snuffle about me and won't let me rest. So I want to build myself a house and lay myself inside it, so that I can have some peace."

"Oh, indeed," thought Hans, "I can make use of this one too" — and said to him, "Leave your house-building alone and come with me. You shall be called Rock-Splitter."

The man agreed; and all three of them roamed through the forest, and wherever they went the wild beasts were terrified and ran away from them.

In the evening they came to an old deserted castle, and went up into it and lay down in the hall to sleep.

Next morning Hans went into the garden. It had run quite wild and was full of thorns and bushes. And as he was walking about in it, a wild boar rushed at him; but he gave it such a blow with his club that it fell down on the spot. He took it on his shoulders and carried it in, and they put it on a spit and roasted it and enjoyed themselves.

Then they arranged that each day two of them should go out hunting in turn and one should stay at home and cook nine pounds of meat for each of them.

Fir-Twister stayed at home first, and Hans and Rock-Splitter went out hunting. And when Fir-Twister was busy cooking, a little shrivelled-up old man came to him in the castle and asked for some meat.

"Be off, you sly hypocrite," he answered. "You need no meat."

But how astonished Fir-Twister was when the insignificant little dwarf sprang at him and belaboured him so with his fists that he could not defend himself, but fell on the ground and gasped for breath. The dwarf did not go away until he had thoroughly vented his anger on him.

When the other two came home from hunting, Fir-Twister said nothing to them about the old man or the blows he had taken, and thought, "When they stay at home, they can try their luck with the little scrubbing-brush" — and the mere thought of it gave him pleasure already.

Next day Rock-Splitter stayed at home, and he fared just as Fir-Twister had; he was badly beaten by the dwarf because he would not give him any meat. When the others came home in the evening, Fir-Twister could easily see what he had suffered; but both of them kept quiet, and thought, "Hans must taste some of that soup too."

Hans, who had to stay at home the next day, did his work in the kitchen as it had to be done; and as he was standing skimming the pan, the dwarf came and demanded a piece of meat without any ceremony.

Then Hans thought, "He's a poor wretch; I'll give him some of my own share, so that the others don't go short" — and handed him a piece.

When the dwarf had devoured it he asked for more meat, and good-natured Hans gave it to him, and told him it was a handsome piece and he must be content with it. But the dwarf begged for it a third time.

"You're shameless," said Hans, and gave him none.

Then the malicious dwarf tried to spring on him and treat him as he had treated Fir-Twister and Rock-Splitter; but he had come to the wrong man. Hans, without exerting himself much, gave him a couple of blows that sent him jumping down the castle steps.

Hans was going to run after him, but fell right over him, he was so tall. When he got up again the dwarf had a start on him. Hans hurried after him as far as the forest, and saw him slip into a hole in the rock. Then Hans went home — but he had marked the spot.

When the other two came back they were surprised that Hans was so well. He told them what had happened, and then they no longer concealed how it had gone with them.

Hans laughed and said, "It served you right. Why were you so greedy with your meat? It's a disgrace that two big men like you should have let yourselves be beaten by a dwarf."

At that they took a basket and a rope, and all three went to the hole in the rock the dwarf had slipped into, and let Hans and his club down in the basket.

When Hans reached the bottom he found a door; and when he opened it, a girl was sitting there who was as lovely as a picture — no, so beautiful that no words can express it. And beside her sat the dwarf, grinning at Hans like an ape. But she was bound with chains, and looked at him so mournfully that Hans felt great pity for her, and thought to himself, "You must deliver her out of the power of that wicked dwarf" — and gave him such a blow with his club that he fell down dead.

Immediately the chains fell away from the girl, and Hans was enraptured with her beauty. She told him she was a King's daughter whom a savage count had stolen away from her home and imprisoned there among the rocks, because she would have nothing to do with him. The count had set the dwarf there as a watchman, and he had made her suffer misery and vexation enough.

And now Hans put the girl in the basket and had her drawn up. The basket came down again; but Hans did not trust his two companions, and thought, "They've already shown themselves false and told me nothing about the dwarf. Who knows what they may be planning against me?"

So he put his club in the basket — and it was lucky he did; for when the basket was halfway up they let it fall again, and if Hans had really been sitting in it he would have been killed.

But now he did not know how he was to work his way out of the depths; and turn it over and over in his mind as he might, he could think of nothing. "It's a sad thing," said he to himself, "that I have to waste away down here."

And as he was walking backwards and forwards, he came once more to the little chamber where the girl had been sitting, and saw that the dwarf had a ring on his finger that shone and sparkled. So he drew it off and put it on; and when he turned it round on his finger, he suddenly heard something rustling over his head. He looked up and saw spirits of the air hovering above him, who told him he was their master and asked what he desired.

Hans was struck dumb at first; but afterwards he said that they were to carry him up again. They obeyed instantly, and it was just as if he had flown up himself.

When he was above ground, though, he could see nobody. Fir-Twister and Rock-Splitter had hurried away and taken the beautiful girl with them. But Hans turned the ring, and the spirits of the air came and told him that the two of them were at sea.

Hans ran and ran without stopping until he came to the shore; and there, far, far out on the water, he could make out a little boat with his faithless comrades sitting in it. And in fierce anger, without thinking what he was doing, he leapt into the water club in hand and began to swim; but the club, which weighed a hundredweight, dragged him deep down until he was all but drowned.

Then, in the very nick of time, he turned his ring; and immediately the spirits of the air came and carried him as swift as lightning into the boat. He swung his club and gave his wicked comrades the reward they deserved, and threw them into the water; and then he sailed home with the beautiful girl, who had been in the greatest alarm and whom he had now delivered for the second time, to her father and mother, and married her; and everybody rejoiced exceedingly.

The Peasant in Heaven

Once upon a time a poor, pious peasant died and arrived before the gate of heaven. At the same time a very rich, rich lord came there who also wanted to get into heaven.

Then Saint Peter came with the key and opened the door and let the great man in — but apparently did not see the peasant, and shut the door again.

And now the peasant outside heard how the great man was received in heaven with every kind of rejoicing, and how they were making music and singing inside. At length everything grew quiet again, and Saint Peter came and opened the gate of heaven and let the peasant in.

The peasant expected that they would make music and sing when he went in too; but everything stayed quite quiet. He was received with great affection, it's true, and the angels came to meet him — but nobody sang.

So the peasant asked Saint Peter how it was that they did not sing for him as they had done when the rich man went in, and said that it seemed to him that up there in heaven things were done with just as much partiality as on earth.

Then Saint Peter said, "By no means. You are just as dear to us as anybody else, and you'll enjoy every heavenly delight the rich man enjoys. But poor fellows like you come to heaven every day, and a rich man like that doesn't come more than once in a hundred years."

Lean Lisa

Lean Lisa was of a very different way of thinking from lazy Harry and fat Trina, who never let anything disturb their peace. She scoured everything with ashes from morning till evening, and loaded her husband, Long Laurence, with so much work that he had heavier weights to carry than a donkey with three sacks. It was all no use, though: they had nothing and came to nothing.

One night, as she lay in bed and could hardly move a limb for weariness, she still would not let her thoughts go to sleep. She dug her elbows into her husband's side and said, "Listen, Lenz, to what I've been thinking. If I were to find one florin, and another was given to me, I'd borrow another to add to them, and you'd give me another too; and then, as soon as I had the four florins together, I'd buy a young cow."

This pleased her husband well enough. "It's true," said he, "that I don't know where I'm to get the florin you want as a gift from me; but if you can get the money together and buy a cow with it, you'll do well to carry out your plan. I'll be glad," he added, "if the cow has a calf, and then I'll often get a drink of milk to refresh me."

"The milk isn't for you," said his wife. "We must let the calf suck, so that it grows big and fat and we can sell it well."

"Certainly," replied her husband, "but all the same we'll take a little milk; that will do no harm."

"Who taught you how to manage cows?" said his wife. "Whether it does harm or not, I won't allow it; and even if you stood on your head for it, you shouldn't have a drop of the milk. Do you think, because there's no satisfying you, Long Laurence, that you're to eat up what I earn with so much difficulty?"

"Wife," said the man, "be quiet, or I'll give you a blow on the mouth."

"What!" cried she. "You threaten me, you glutton, you rascal, you lazy Harry!"

She was just taking hold of his hair, but Long Laurence got up, seized both of Lean Lisa's withered arms in one hand and pressed her head down into the pillow with the other, and let her scold, and held her there until she fell asleep out of sheer weariness.

Whether she went on quarrelling when she woke next morning, or whether she went out to look for the florin she wanted to find, that I do not know.

The Hut in the Forest

A poor woodcutter lived with his wife and three daughters in a little hut on the edge of a lonely forest.

One morning, as he was about to go off to his work, he said to his wife, "Let my dinner be brought out to me in the forest by my eldest daughter, or I shall never get my work done. And so that she doesn't lose her way," he added, "I'll take a bag of millet with me and scatter the seeds along the path."

So when the sun was just above the middle of the forest, the girl set out on her way with a bowl of soup. But the field sparrows and wood sparrows, the larks and finches, the blackbirds and siskins had picked up the millet long before, and the girl could not find the trail.

Then, trusting to chance, she went on and on, until the sun sank and night began to fall. The trees rustled in the darkness, the owls hooted, and she began to be afraid.

Then in the distance she saw a light glimmering between the trees. "There must be people living there who can take me in for the night," she thought — and went towards the light.

It was not long before she came to a house with all its windows lit up. She knocked, and a rough voice from inside cried, "Come in."

The girl stepped into the dark entry and knocked at the door of the room.

"Just come in," cried the voice; and when she opened the door, an old grey-haired man was sitting at the table with his face propped in both hands, and his white beard fell down over the table almost to the ground. By the stove lay three animals: a hen, a cock and a brindled cow.

The girl told the old man her story and begged for shelter for the night. The man said:

	"Pretty little hen,
	pretty little cock,
	and pretty brindled cow,
	what do you say to that?"

"Duks," answered the animals — and that must have meant, "We're willing," for the old man said, "Here you shall have shelter and food. Go to the fire and cook us our supper."

The girl found plenty of everything in the kitchen and cooked a good supper, but she gave no thought to the animals. She carried the full dishes to the table, sat down beside the grey-haired man, and ate and satisfied her hunger.

When she had had enough she said, "But now I'm tired. Where is there a bed I can lie down and sleep in?"

The animals replied:

	"You have eaten with him,
	you have drunk with him,
	you have had no thought for us —
	so find out for yourself where you can pass the night."

Then the old man said, "Just go upstairs, and you'll find a room with two beds. Shake them up and put white linen on them, and then I'll come and lie down to sleep too."

The girl went up; and when she had shaken the beds and put clean sheets on them, she lay down in one of them without waiting any longer for the old man.

After some time, though, the grey-haired man came up and took his candle and looked at the girl and shook his head. And when he saw that she had fallen into a sound sleep, he opened a trapdoor and let her down into the cellar.

Late that night the woodcutter came home and reproached his wife for leaving him to go hungry all day.

"It isn't my fault," she replied. "The girl went out with your dinner and must have lost herself; but she's sure to come back tomorrow."

The woodcutter, though, got up before dawn to go into the forest, and asked that the second daughter should take him his dinner that day. "I'll take a bag of lentils," said he. "The seeds are larger than millet; the girl will see them better and can't lose her way."

So at dinner time the girl took out the food — but the lentils had disappeared. The birds of the forest had picked them up as they had the day before, and had left none.

The girl wandered about the forest until nightfall, and then she too came to the old man's house, and was told to come in, and begged for food and a bed. The man with the white beard asked the animals again:

	"Pretty little hen,
	pretty little cock,
	and pretty brindled cow,
	what do you say to that?"

The animals answered "Duks" again, and everything happened just as it had the day before. The girl cooked a good meal and ate and drank with the old man, and did not concern herself about the animals; and when she asked about her bed they answered:

	"You have eaten with him,
	you have drunk with him,
	you have had no thought for us —
	so find out for yourself where you can pass the night."

When she was asleep the old man came and looked at her and shook his head, and let her down into the cellar.

On the third morning the woodcutter said to his wife, "Send our youngest child out with my dinner today. She's always been good and obedient, and she'll stay on the right path and not run about after every wild bumblebee the way her sisters did."

The mother did not want to do it, and said, "Am I to lose my dearest child as well?"

"Have no fear," he replied. "The girl won't go astray; she's too careful and sensible. Besides, I'll take some peas with me and scatter them about. They're bigger still than lentils, and they'll show her the way."

But when the girl went out with her basket on her arm, the wood pigeons had already got all the peas in their crops, and she did not know which way to turn. She was full of sorrow, and never stopped thinking how hungry her father would be, and how her good mother would grieve, if she did not get home.

At length, when it grew dark, she saw the light and came to the house in the forest. She begged very prettily to be allowed to spend the night there, and the man with the white beard once more asked his animals:

	"Pretty little hen,
	pretty little cock,
	and beautiful brindled cow,
	what do you say to that?"

"Duks," said they.

Then the girl went over to the stove where the animals were lying, and petted the cock and the hen and stroked their smooth feathers with her hand, and caressed the brindled cow between her horns. And when, following the old man's orders, she had made ready some good soup and the bowl was set on the table, she said, "Am I to eat as much as I want, and the good animals to have nothing? Outside there's food in plenty; I'll see to them first."

So she went and brought some barley and put it to soak for the cock and the hen, and a whole armful of sweet-smelling hay for the cow. "I hope you'll like it, dear animals," said she, "and you shall have a refreshing drink too, in case you're thirsty."

Then she fetched in a bucketful of water; and the cock and the hen jumped up onto the edge of it and dipped their beaks in and then held up their heads the way birds do when they drink, and the brindled cow took a hearty draught as well.

When the animals had been fed, the girl sat down at the table beside the old man and ate what he had left. It was not long before the cock and the hen began to tuck their heads under their wings, and the cow's eyes began to blink too.

Then the girl said, "Oughtn't we to go to bed?"

	"Pretty little hen,
	pretty little cock,
	and pretty brindled cow,
	what do you say to that?"

The animals answered "Duks":

	"You have eaten with us,
	you have drunk with us,
	you have had a kind thought for all of us —
	we wish you good night."

So the girl went upstairs and shook up the feather beds and laid clean sheets on them; and when she had done it the old man came and lay down on one of the beds, and his white beard reached down to his feet. The girl lay down on the other, said her prayers, and fell asleep.

She slept quietly till midnight, and then there was such a noise in the house that she woke. There was a sound of cracking and splitting in every corner, and the doors sprang open and banged against the walls. The beams groaned as if they were being torn out of their joints; it seemed as if the staircase were falling down; and at length there was a crash as if the whole roof had fallen in. But as everything grew quiet again and the girl was not hurt, she stayed quietly lying where she was and fell asleep again.

But when she woke in the morning in the brilliance of the sunshine — what did her eyes behold? She was lying in a vast hall, and everything around her shone with royal splendour. On the walls golden flowers grew up a ground of green silk; the bed was of ivory and the canopy of red velvet; and on a chair close by was a pair of shoes embroidered with pearls.

The girl believed that she was dreaming; but three richly dressed attendants came in and asked what orders she wished to give.

"If you'll go," she replied, "I'll get up at once and make some soup ready for the old man, and then I'll feed the pretty little hen and the cock and the beautiful brindled cow."

She thought the old man was up already, and looked round at his bed; but he was not lying in it — a stranger was. And while she was looking at him, and realising that he was young and handsome, he woke and sat up in bed and said, "I'm a King's son, and I was bewitched by a wicked witch and made to live in this forest as an old grey-haired man. Nobody was allowed to be with me but my three attendants, in the shapes of a cock, a hen and a brindled cow. The spell was not to be broken until a girl came to us whose heart was so good that she showed herself full of love not only to human beings but to animals — and that you have done. And by you, at midnight, we were set free, and the old hut in the forest was changed back into my royal palace."

And when they had got up, the King's son ordered the three attendants to set out and fetch the girl's father and mother to the wedding feast.

"But where are my two sisters?" asked the girl.

"I've locked them in the cellar; and tomorrow they shall be taken into the forest and live as servants to a charcoal burner, until they've grown kinder and don't leave poor animals to go hungry."

Sharing Joy and Sorrow

There was once a tailor who was a quarrelsome fellow; and his wife, who was good and hard-working and pious, could never please him. Whatever she did, he was not satisfied, but grumbled and scolded and knocked her about and beat her.

As the authorities heard of it at last, they had him summoned and put in prison to improve him. He was kept for a while on bread and water and then set free again. He was made to promise, though, that he would not beat his wife any more, but would live with her in peace and share joy and sorrow with her, as married people should.

All went well for a time; but then he fell into his old ways and was surly and quarrelsome. And because he dared not beat her, he would seize her by the hair and tear it out. His wife got away from him and ran out into the yard; but he ran after her with his yardstick and his scissors, and chased her about, and threw the yardstick and the scissors at her, and whatever else came to hand. When he hit her he laughed, and when he missed her he stormed and swore.

This went on so long that the neighbours came to the wife's help. The tailor was summoned before the magistrates again and reminded of his promise.

"Dear gentlemen," said he, "I've kept my word. I haven't beaten her, but have shared joy and sorrow with her."

"How can that be," said the judge, "when she keeps bringing such heavy complaints against you?"

"I haven't beaten her. Just because she looked so strange, I wanted to comb her hair with my hand; but she got away from me and left me quite spitefully. So I hurried after her, and to bring her back to her duty I threw at her — as a well-meant reminder — whatever came readily to hand. And I've shared joy and sorrow with her too: for whenever I hit her I was full of joy and she of sorrow, and if I missed her, then she was joyful and I was sorry."

The judges were not satisfied with this answer, but gave him the reward he deserved.

The Willow-Wren

In the old days every sound still had its meaning and its application. When the smith's hammer rang out, it cried, "Strike away! Strike away!" When the carpenter's plane grated, it said, "Here goes! Here goes!" If the mill wheel began to clack, it said, "Help, Lord God! Help, Lord God!" And if the miller was a cheat and happened to leave the mill, it spoke proper High German, and first asked slowly, "Who is there? Who is there?" and then answered quickly, "The miller! The miller!" and at last, quite in a hurry, "He steals bravely! He steals bravely! Three pecks in a bushel."

In those days the birds had their own language too, which everybody understood; now it only sounds like chirping and screeching and whistling, and to some people like music without words.

It came into the birds' minds, though, that they would be without a ruler no longer, and would choose one of themselves to be their King. Only one among them, the green plover, was against it. He had lived free and would die free; and flying anxiously here and there he cried, "Where shall I go? Where shall I go?" He withdrew into a lonely, unfrequented marsh, and showed himself among his fellows no more.

The birds now wanted to discuss the matter; and on a fine May morning they all gathered together from the woods and fields: eagles and chaffinches, owls and crows, larks and sparrows — how can I name them all? Even the cuckoo came, and the hoopoe, his clerk, who is so called because he is always heard a few days before him; and a very small bird that had no name yet mingled with the crowd.

The hen, who by some accident had heard nothing of the whole business, was astonished at the great gathering. "What, what, what's going to be done?" she cackled. But the cock calmed his beloved hen and said, "Only rich folk showing off" — and told her what they were about.

It was decided, though, that whichever of them could fly the highest should be King. A tree frog sitting among the bushes cried a warning when he heard that — "No, no, no! No!" — because he thought many tears would be shed over it; but the crow said, "Caw, caw," and that it would all pass off peaceably.

It was now settled that they should begin the ascent at once, on that fine morning, so that nobody could say afterwards, "I could easily have flown much higher, but evening came on and I could do no more."

So at a given signal the whole company rose up into the air. The dust rose from the ground, and there was tremendous fluttering and whirring and beating of wings, and it looked as if a black cloud were rising up.

The little birds were soon left behind, though. They could go no further, and fell back to the ground. The larger birds held out longer; but none could match the eagle, who mounted so high that he could have picked the eyes out of the sun. And when he saw that the others could not get up to him, he thought, "Why should you fly still higher? You are the King" — and began to let himself down again.

The birds below at once called to him, "You must be our King; nobody has flown as high as you."

"Except me," screamed the little fellow without a name, who had crept into the eagle's breast feathers. And as he was not at all tired, he rose up and mounted so high that he reached heaven itself. And when he had gone as far as that, he folded his wings together and called down in a clear, penetrating voice, "I am King! I am King!"

"You, our King?" cried the birds angrily. "You've managed it by trickery and cunning!"

So they set another condition. He should be King who could get furthest down into the ground.

How the goose did flap about with her broad breast when she was on land again! How quickly the cock scratched a hole! The duck came off worst of all, for she leapt into a ditch and sprained her legs, and waddled away to a nearby pond crying, "Cheating! Cheating!"

The little bird without a name, though, sought out a mouse hole and slipped down into it, and cried out of it in his small voice, "I am King! I am King!"

"You, our King?" cried the birds, angrier still. "Do you think your cunning will win?"

They decided to keep him prisoner in the hole and starve him out. The owl was posted as sentry in front of it, and was not to let the rascal out if she valued her life.

When evening came all the birds were feeling very tired after exerting their wings so much, and went to bed with their wives and children. The owl alone stayed standing by the mouse hole, gazing steadily into it with her great eyes.

Meanwhile she too had grown tired, and thought to herself, "You could certainly shut one eye; you'll still be watching with the other, and the little wretch shan't come out of his hole." So she shut one eye, and with the other looked straight at the mouse hole.

The little fellow put his head out and peeped, and meant to slip away; but the owl came forward immediately, and he drew his head back again. Then the owl opened the one eye again and shut the other, meaning to shut them in turn all through the night.

But when she next shut the one eye, she forgot to open the other; and as soon as both her eyes were shut, she fell asleep. The little fellow soon noticed that, and slipped away.

From that day on, the owl has never dared show herself by daylight; for if she does, the other birds chase her and pluck her feathers out. She only flies out at night; but she hates and hunts mice, because they make such ugly holes.

The little bird, too, is very unwilling to let himself be seen, because he's afraid it will cost him his life if he's caught. He steals about in the hedges; and when he's quite safe he sometimes cries, "I am King!" — and for this reason the other birds call him in mockery the King of the Hedges, the Zaunkönig.

But nobody was as happy as the lark at not having to obey the little King. As soon as the sun appears she rises high in the air and cries, "Ah, how beautiful that is! Beautiful that is! Beautiful, beautiful! Ah, how beautiful that is!"

The Sole

The fishes had been discontented for a long time because no order was kept in their kingdom. None of them would turn aside for the others, but they all swam to the right or the left as the fancy took them, or darted between those who wanted to stay together, or got in their way; and a strong one would give a weak one a blow with its tail that drove it away, or else swallowed it without any more ado.

"How delightful it would be," said they, "if we had a king who enforced law and justice among us." And they met together to choose as their ruler the one who could cut through the water fastest and give help to the weak.

They lined up in rank and file by the shore, and the pike gave the signal with his tail, at which they all started. The pike darted away like an arrow, and with him the herring, the gudgeon, the perch, the carp and all the rest of them. Even the sole swam with them, and hoped to reach the winning place.

All at once the cry was heard, "The herring is first!"

"Who's first?" screamed the flat, envious sole angrily, who had been left far behind. "Who's first?"

"The herring! The herring!" was the answer.

"The naked herring?" cried the jealous creature. "The naked herring?"

Since that time the sole's mouth has been on one side, as a punishment.

The Bittern and the Hoopoe

"Where do you like best to graze your flocks?" said a man to an old cowherd.

"Here, sir, where the grass is neither too rich nor too poor; otherwise it's no use."

"Why not?" asked the man.

"Do you hear that melancholy cry from the meadow over there?" answered the herdsman. "That's the bittern; he was once a herdsman, and so was the hoopoe. I'll tell you the story.

"The bittern pastured his cattle on rich green meadows where flowers grew in abundance, and so his cows became wild and unmanageable. The hoopoe drove his cattle up onto high barren hills where the wind plays with the sand, and his cows grew thin and got no strength.

"When it was evening and the herdsmen wanted to drive their cows home, the bittern could not get his together again; they were too high-spirited and ran away from him. He called, 'Come, cows, come' — but it was no use; they took no notice of his calling.

"The hoopoe, though, could not even get his cows up on their legs, they had grown so faint and weak. 'Up, up, up!' he screamed — but it was in vain; they stayed lying on the sand.

"That's what happens when a man has no moderation. And to this day, though they have no herds now to watch, the bittern cries, 'Come, cows, come' — and the hoopoe, 'Up, up, up.'"

The Owl

Two or three hundred years ago, when people were far from being as crafty and cunning as they are nowadays, an extraordinary thing happened in a little town.

By some mischance one of the great owls, the kind called horned owls, had come from the neighbouring woods into a townsman's barn during the night; and when day broke it did not dare venture out of its hiding place again, for fear of the other birds, which raised a terrible outcry whenever it appeared.

In the morning, when the manservant went into the barn to fetch some straw, he was so mightily alarmed at the sight of the owl sitting there in a corner that he ran away and announced to his master that a monster was sitting in the barn rolling its eyes about in its head — the like of which he had never set eyes on in his life, and which could devour a man without the slightest difficulty.

"I know you already," said his master. "You've courage enough to chase a blackbird about the fields; but when you see a dead hen lying, you have to fetch a stick before you go near it. I must go and see for myself what sort of monster it is."

And he went quite boldly into the granary and looked around him. But when he saw the strange grim creature with his own eyes, he was no less terrified than his servant had been. With two bounds he sprang out, ran to his neighbours, and begged them imploringly to lend him help against an unknown and dangerous beast, or the whole town might be in danger if it broke loose out of the barn where it was shut up.

A great noise and clamour arose in all the streets. The townsmen came armed with spears, hayforks, scythes and axes, as if they were going out against an enemy; and finally the senators appeared with the burgomaster at their head. When they had drawn up in the marketplace they marched to the barn and surrounded it on all sides.

Then one of the most courageous of them stepped forward and went in with his spear lowered — but came running out immediately afterwards with a shriek, as pale as death, and could not utter a single word. Two others ventured in, but they fared no better.

At last one man stepped forward — a great strong man who was famous for his warlike deeds — and said, "You won't drive the monster away by merely looking at him. We must be in earnest here; but I see you've all turned into women, and not one of you dares face the animal."

He ordered them to give him some armour, had a sword and spear brought and armed himself. Everybody praised his courage, though many feared for his life.

The two barn doors were opened, and they saw the owl, which had meanwhile perched herself in the middle of a great crossbeam. He had a ladder brought; and when he raised it and made ready to climb up, they all cried out to him to bear himself bravely, and commended him to St. George, who slew the dragon.

When he had just got to the top, and the owl saw that he had designs on her — and was bewildered too by the crowd and the shouting, and did not know how to escape — she rolled her eyes, ruffled her feathers, flapped her wings, snapped her beak, and cried "Tu-whit, tu-whoo" in a harsh voice.

"Strike home! Strike home!" screamed the crowd outside to the valiant hero.

"Anybody standing where I'm standing," answered he, "wouldn't cry 'Strike home!'"

He did indeed plant his foot one rung higher on the ladder — but then he began to tremble, and went back down again half fainting.

And now there was nobody left who dared put himself in such danger. "The monster," said they, "has poisoned and mortally wounded the very strongest man among us, just by snapping at him and breathing on him. Are we to risk our lives too?"

They took counsel about what they ought to do to keep the whole town from being destroyed. For a long time nothing seemed any use; but at length the burgomaster found a way out.

"My opinion," said he, "is that we ought to pay for this barn out of the common purse, and for whatever corn or straw or hay it contains, and so make good the owner's loss — and then burn the whole building down, and the terrible beast with it. That way nobody will have to endanger his life. This is no time to be thinking of expense, and stinginess would be out of place."

Everybody agreed with him. So they set fire to the barn at all four corners, and the owl was miserably burnt with it.

Let anybody who won't believe it go there and ask for himself.

The Moon

In days gone by there was a land where the nights were always dark and the sky spread over it like a black cloth; for there the moon never rose, and no star shone in the darkness. At the creation of the world the light at night had been enough.

Three young fellows once went out of this country on a travelling expedition, and came into another kingdom where, in the evening when the sun had disappeared behind the mountains, a shining globe was set on an oak tree, which shed a soft light far and wide. By its help everything could be seen and made out quite well, even though it was not as brilliant as the sun.

The travellers stopped and asked a countryman who was driving past with his cart what kind of a light that was.

"That's the moon," answered he. "Our mayor bought it for three thalers and fastened it to the oak tree. He has to pour oil into it every day and keep it clean, so that it always burns brightly. He gets a thaler a week from us for doing it."

When the countryman had driven off, one of them said, "We could make some use of this lamp. We've an oak tree at home just as big as this, and we could hang it on that. What a pleasure it would be not to have to feel our way about in the dark at night!"

"I'll tell you what we'll do," said the second. "We'll fetch a cart and horses and carry the moon away. The people here can buy themselves another."

"I'm a good climber," said the third. "I'll bring it down."

The fourth brought a cart and horses, and the third climbed the tree and bored a hole in the moon and passed a rope through it and let it down. When the shining ball was lying in the cart they covered it over with a cloth, so that nobody should notice the theft.

They carried it safely into their own country and set it up on a high oak. Old and young rejoiced when the new lamp let its light shine over the whole land, and bedrooms and sitting rooms were filled with it. The dwarfs came out of their caves in the rocks, and the tiny elves in their little red coats danced in rings on the meadows.

The four took care that the moon was kept supplied with oil, and cleaned the wick, and received their weekly thaler. But they grew to be old men; and when one of them fell ill and saw that he was about to die, he directed that one quarter of the moon should be laid in the grave with him as his property.

When he died, the mayor climbed the tree and cut off a quarter with the hedge shears, and it was put in his coffin. The moon's light grew less, but not yet visibly.

When the second died, the second quarter was buried with him, and the light grew dimmer. It grew weaker still after the death of the third, who likewise took his share away with him; and when the fourth was carried to his grave, the old state of darkness began again, and whenever people went out at night without their lanterns they knocked their heads together.

But when the pieces of the moon had joined themselves together again in the world below, where darkness had always reigned, it came about that the dead grew restless and woke from their sleep. They were astonished to find that they could see again; the moonlight was quite enough for them, for their eyes had grown so weak that they could not have borne the brilliance of the sun.

They got up and were merry, and fell back into their old ways of living. Some of them went to the play and to dance, others hurried to the taverns, where they called for wine and got drunk and brawled and quarrelled, and at last took up cudgels and belaboured one another. The noise grew greater and greater, and at last reached even to heaven.

Saint Peter, who guards the gate of heaven, thought the lower world had broken out in revolt, and gathered together the heavenly troops that are to drive back the Evil One when he and his companions storm the abode of the blessed. But as they did not come, he got on his horse and rode out through the gate of heaven and down into the world below. There he brought the dead to order and told them to lie down in their graves again, and took the moon away with him and hung it up in heaven.

The Duration of Life

When God had created the world and was about to fix the length of each creature's life, the donkey came and asked, "Lord, how long shall I live?"

"Thirty years," replied God. "Does that content you?"

"Ah, Lord," answered the donkey, "that's a long time. Think of my painful existence! To carry heavy burdens from morning till night, to drag sacks of corn to the mill so that others can eat bread, to be cheered and refreshed with nothing but blows and kicks. Relieve me of a part of this long time."

Then God had pity on him and relieved him of eighteen years. The donkey went away comforted, and the dog appeared.

"How long would you like to live?" said God to him. "Thirty years is too many for the donkey, but you'll be satisfied with it."

"Lord," answered the dog, "is that your will? Consider how much running I shall have to do; my feet will never hold out so long. And when I've once lost my voice for barking and my teeth for biting, what will be left for me to do but run from one corner to another and growl?"

God saw that he was right, and released him from twelve years of life.

Then came the monkey. "You'll certainly be willing to live thirty years?" said the Lord to him. "You've no need to work as the donkey and the dog do, and you'll always enjoy yourself."

"Ah, Lord," he answered, "it may look as if that were so, but it's quite different. When it rains porridge, I have no spoon. I'm always expected to play merry pranks and pull faces that make people laugh; and if they give me an apple and I bite into it — why, it's sour. How often sadness hides itself behind mirth! I shall never be able to hold out for thirty years."

God was gracious and took off ten.

At last man appeared, joyful, healthy and vigorous, and begged God to appoint his time for him.

"Thirty years you shall live," said the Lord. "Is that enough for you?"

"What a short time!" cried man. "When I've built my house and my own fire burns on my own hearth; when I've planted trees that blossom and bear fruit, and am just meaning to enjoy my life — then I'm to die! O Lord, lengthen my time."

"I'll add the donkey's eighteen years to it," said God.

"That's not enough," replied the man.

"You shall have the dog's twelve years as well."

"Still too little."

"Well then," said God, "I'll give you the monkey's ten years too; but more you shall not have."

The man went away, but was not satisfied.

So man lives seventy years. The first thirty are his human years, and they're soon gone; then he's healthy and merry, works with pleasure and is glad of his life. Then follow the donkey's eighteen years, when one burden after another is laid on him, and he has to carry the corn that feeds others, and blows and kicks are the reward of his faithful service. Then come the dog's twelve years, when he lies in the corner and growls and has no teeth left to bite with. And when this time is over, the monkey's ten years make the end. Then a man is weak in the head and foolish, does silly things, and becomes the joke of the children.

Death’s Messengers

In ancient times a giant was once travelling along a great highway, when suddenly an unknown man sprang up in front of him and said, "Halt! Not one step further."

"What!" cried the giant. "A creature I could crush between my fingers wants to block my way? Who are you, that you dare to speak so boldly?"

"I am Death," answered the other. "Nobody resists me, and you too must obey my commands."

But the giant refused, and began to wrestle with Death. It was a long, violent battle; but at last the giant got the upper hand and struck Death down with his fist, so that he dropped beside a stone. The giant went his way, and Death lay there beaten, and so weak that he could not get up again.

"What's to be done now," said he, "if I stay lying here in a corner? Nobody will die in the world, and it will get so full of people that they won't have room to stand next to each other."

Meanwhile a young man came along the road, strong and healthy, singing a song and glancing about him on every side. When he saw the half-fainting figure he went to him with compassion, raised him up, poured a strengthening draught out of his flask for him, and waited until he came round.

"Do you know," said the stranger as he was getting up, "who I am, and whom you've helped back onto his legs?"

"No," answered the young man, "I don't know you."

"I am Death," said he. "I spare nobody, and I can make no exception for you; but so that you can see that I'm grateful, I promise you that I won't fall on you unexpectedly, but will send my messengers to you before I come and take you away."

"Well," said the young man, "it's something gained that I shall know when you're coming, and be safe from you at least until then."

Then he went on his way, and was light-hearted and enjoyed himself and lived without a thought.

But youth and health did not last long. Soon came sicknesses and sorrows, which tormented him by day and took away his rest at night.

"Die I shan't," said he to himself, "for Death will send his messengers before that; but I do wish these wretched days of sickness were over."

As soon as he felt well again he began to live merrily once more.

Then one day somebody tapped him on the shoulder. He looked round, and Death was standing behind him, and said, "Follow me. The hour of your departure from this world has come."

"What!" replied the man. "Will you break your word? Didn't you promise me that you'd send your messengers to me before you came yourself? I've seen none."

"Silence!" answered Death. "Have I not sent you one messenger after another? Didn't fever come and strike you and shake you and cast you down? Hasn't dizziness bewildered your head? Hasn't gout twitched you in every limb? Didn't your ears ring? Didn't toothache bite into your cheeks? Wasn't it dark before your eyes? And besides all that, hasn't my own brother Sleep reminded you of me every night? Didn't you lie at night as if you were already dead?"

The man could make no answer. He yielded to his fate and went away with Death.

Master Pfriem (Master Cobbler’s Awl)

Master Pfriem was a short, thin but lively man who never rested a moment. His face, of which his turned-up nose was the only prominent feature, was marked with smallpox and pale as death; his hair was grey and shaggy, and his eyes were small, but they glanced about perpetually on every side. He saw everything, criticised everything, knew everything best, and was always in the right.

When he went into the streets he moved his arms about as though he were rowing; and once he knocked the pail of a girl who was carrying water so high in the air that he was drenched all over by it himself. "Stupid thing," cried he to her, while he shook himself, "couldn't you see that I was coming up behind you?"

By trade he was a shoemaker; and when he worked he pulled his thread out with such force that he drove his fist into anybody who did not keep far enough away. No apprentice stayed more than a month with him, for he always found some fault with even the very best work. At one time it was that the stitches were not even, at another that one shoe was too long, or one heel higher than the other, or the leather not cut large enough. "Wait," said he to his apprentice, "I'll soon show you how we make skins soft" — and fetched a strap and gave him a couple of strokes across the back.

He called them all sluggards. He himself did not turn out much work, though, for he never sat still for a quarter of an hour.

If his wife got up very early in the morning and lit the fire, he jumped out of bed and ran barefoot into the kitchen, crying, "Are you going to burn my house down? That's a fire you could roast an ox by. Does wood cost nothing?"

If the servants were standing by their washtubs laughing and telling each other everything they knew, he scolded them and said, "There stand the geese, cackling and forgetting their work to gossip. And why fresh soap? Disgraceful extravagance, and shameful idleness into the bargain! They want to save their hands, and not rub the things properly." And out he would run and knock over a pail full of soap and water, so that the whole kitchen was flooded.

Somebody was building a new house, so he hurried to the window to watch. "There, they're using that red sandstone again that never dries!" cried he. "Nobody will ever be healthy in that house. And just look how badly the fellows are laying the stones! Besides, the mortar is good for nothing; it ought to have gravel in it, not sand. I shall live to see that house come down on the people inside it."

He sat down and put a couple of stitches in, and then jumped up again and unfastened his leather apron and cried, "I'll just go out and appeal to those men's consciences."

He came upon the carpenters. "What's this?" cried he. "You're not working to the line! Do you expect the beams to be straight? One thing wrong will put everything wrong." He snatched an axe out of a carpenter's hand and was going to show him how he ought to cut; but as a cart loaded with clay came by, he threw the axe away and hurried over to the peasant walking beside it.

"You're not in your right mind," said he. "Who harnesses young horses to a heavily loaded cart? The poor beasts will die on the spot."

The peasant gave him no answer, and Pfriem ran back into his workshop in a rage.

When he was settling to his work again, his apprentice handed him a shoe.

"Well, what's this now?" he screamed. "Haven't I told you you shouldn't cut shoes so broad? Who would buy a shoe like this, which is hardly anything but a sole? I insist that my orders are followed exactly."

"Master," answered the apprentice, "you may well be quite right that the shoe is a bad one; but it's the very one that you cut out yourself, and set to work on yourself. When you jumped up a while ago you knocked it off the table, and I've only just picked it up. But an angel from heaven would never make you believe it."

One night Master Pfriem dreamed that he was dead and on his way to heaven. When he got there he knocked loudly at the door. "I'm surprised," said he to himself, "that they have no knocker on the door; a man knocks his knuckles sore."

The apostle Peter opened the door and wanted to see who was demanding admission so noisily. "Ah, it's you, Master Pfriem," said he. "Well, I'll let you in; but I warn you that you must give up that habit of yours and find fault with nothing you see in heaven, or you may fare badly."

"You might have spared your warning," answered Pfriem. "I know already what's proper; and here, God be thanked, everything is perfect, and there's nothing to blame as there is on earth."

So he went in and walked up and down the wide spaces of heaven. He looked around him to the left and to the right, but now and then he shook his head or muttered something to himself.

Then he saw two angels carrying away a beam. It was the beam that a man had had in his own eye while he was looking for the splinter in somebody else's. They were not carrying the beam lengthways, though, but at an angle. "Did anybody ever see such a piece of stupidity?" thought Master Pfriem — but he said nothing and seemed satisfied with it. "It comes to the same thing after all, whichever way they carry the beam, straight or crooked, so long as they get along with it; and truly I don't see them knocking against anything."

Soon after this he saw two angels drawing water out of a well into a bucket; but at the same time he noticed that the bucket was full of holes and that the water was running out of it on every side. They were watering the earth with rain.

"Hang it!" he exclaimed — but luckily caught himself, and thought, "Perhaps it's only a pastime. If it's an amusement, then it seems they can do useless things of this kind even here in heaven, where people, as I've already noticed, do nothing but idle about."

He went further and saw a cart that had stuck fast in a deep hole. "It's no wonder," said he to the man standing beside it. "Who would load a cart so unreasonably? What have you got there?"

"Good wishes," replied the man. "I couldn't go along the right way with it; but still I've pushed it safely up here, and they won't leave me stuck here."

And in fact an angel did come and harness two horses to it. "That's quite right," thought Pfriem, "but two horses won't get that cart out; it must have at least four."

Another angel came and brought two more horses; she did not harness them in front of it, though, but behind.

That was too much for Master Pfriem. "Clumsy creature," he burst out, "what are you doing there? Has anybody, since the world began, ever seen a cart drawn like that? But you, in your conceited arrogance, think you know everything best."

He was going to say more, but one of the inhabitants of heaven seized him by the throat and pushed him out with irresistible strength. Under the gateway Master Pfriem turned his head round to take one more look at the cart, and saw that it was being lifted into the air by four winged horses.

At this moment Master Pfriem woke. "Things are certainly arranged differently in heaven from on earth," said he to himself, "and that excuses a good deal. But who can watch horses harnessed both behind and in front with any patience? To be sure they had wings — but who was to know that? Besides, it's great folly to fix a pair of wings on a horse that has four legs to run with already. But I must get up, or they'll do nothing but make mistakes for me in my house. It's a lucky thing for me, though, that I'm not really dead."

The Goose-Girl at the Well

There was once a very old woman who lived with her flock of geese in a waste place among the mountains, where she had a little house. The waste was surrounded by a large forest, and every morning the old woman took her crutch and hobbled into it.

Once there, though, the old dame was quite active — more so than anybody would have thought, considering her age. She gathered grass for her geese, picked all the wild fruit she could reach, and carried everything home on her back. Anybody would have thought that the heavy load must weigh her to the ground, but she always brought it safely home.

If anyone met her, she greeted him quite courteously. "Good day, dear neighbour, it's a fine day. Ah, you wonder that I should drag grass about; but everybody has to take his burden on his back."

All the same, people did not like to meet her if they could help it, and would take a roundabout way by choice. And when a father passed her with his boys, he whispered to them, "Beware of that old woman. She has claws under her gloves; she's a witch."

One morning a handsome young man was going through the forest. The sun shone bright, the birds sang, a cool breeze crept through the leaves, and he was full of joy and gladness. He had met nobody yet, when he suddenly caught sight of the old witch kneeling on the ground cutting grass with a sickle. She had already stuffed a whole load into her cloth, and near it stood two baskets filled with wild apples and pears.

"But, good little mother," said he, "how can you carry all that away?"

"I have to carry it, dear sir," answered she. "Rich folk's children have no need to do such things; but among peasant folk the saying goes, 'Don't look behind you — you'll only see how crooked your back is.'"

"Will you help me?" she said, as he stayed standing beside her. "You still have a straight back and young legs; it would be nothing to you. Besides, my house isn't so very far from here — it stands over there on the heath behind the hill. How soon you'd be up there!"

The young man took pity on the old woman. "My father is certainly no peasant," replied he, "but a rich count; still, so that you can see that it isn't only peasants who can carry things, I'll take your bundle."

"If you'll try it," said she, "I shall be very glad. You'll certainly have to walk for an hour — but what will that matter to you? Only you must carry the apples and pears as well."

It began to seem a little serious to the young man when he heard about the hour's walk; but the old woman would not let him off, and packed the bundle on his back and hung the two baskets on his arm.

"See, it's quite light," said she.

"No, it isn't light," answered the count, and pulled a rueful face. "Truly, the bundle weighs as heavily as if it were full of cobblestones, and the apples and pears are as heavy as lead. I can hardly breathe."

He had a mind to put everything down again, but the old woman would not allow it. "Just look," said she mockingly, "the young gentleman won't carry what I, an old woman, have dragged along so often. You're ready enough with fine words; but when it comes to earnest, you want to take to your heels. Why are you standing there loitering?" she went on. "Step out. Nobody's going to take that bundle off you again."

As long as he walked on level ground it was still bearable; but when they came to the hill and had to climb, and the stones rolled away under his feet as if they were alive, it was beyond his strength. The drops of sweat stood on his forehead and ran down his back, hot and cold.

"Dame," said he, "I can go no further. I want to rest a little."

"Not here," answered the old woman. "When we've reached our journey's end you can rest; but now you must go on. Who knows what good it may do you?"

"Old woman, you're becoming shameless," said the count, and tried to throw off the bundle. But he laboured in vain; it stuck as fast to his back as if it had grown there. He turned and twisted, but could not get rid of it.

The old woman laughed at this, and sprang about on her crutch quite delighted. "Don't get angry, dear sir," said she. "You're going as red in the face as a turkey-cock. Carry your bundle patiently; I'll give you a good present when we get home."

What could he do? He had to submit to his fate and crawl along patiently behind the old woman. She seemed to grow more and more nimble, and his burden heavier and heavier. All at once she made a spring, jumped up onto the bundle and seated herself on top of it; and however withered she might be, she was heavier than the stoutest country lass.

The young man's knees trembled; and when he did not go on, the old woman hit him about the legs with a switch and with stinging nettles. Groaning all the way, he climbed the mountain, and at length reached the old woman's house just as he was about to drop.

When the geese saw the old woman they flapped their wings and stretched out their necks and ran to meet her, cackling all the while. Behind the flock walked an old girl, stick in hand, strong and big, but as ugly as night.

"Good mother," said she to the old woman, "has anything happened to you? You've stayed away so long."

"Not at all, my dear daughter," answered she. "Nothing bad has happened to me. On the contrary, I met this kind gentleman, who has carried my burden for me. Only think — he even took me on his back when I was tired. The way hasn't seemed long to us either; we've been merry, and cracking jokes with each other the whole time."

At last the old woman slid down and took the bundle off the young man's back and the baskets off his arm, and looked at him quite kindly and said, "Now sit down on the bench in front of the door and rest. You've fairly earned your wages, and they shan't be wanting."

Then she said to the goose-girl, "Go into the house, my dear daughter. It isn't fitting for you to be alone with a young gentleman; one mustn't pour oil on the fire — he might fall in love with you."

The count did not know whether to laugh or cry. "A sweetheart like that," thought he, "couldn't touch my heart, even if she were thirty years younger."

Meanwhile the old woman stroked and fondled her geese as if they were children, and then went into the house with her daughter.

The young man lay down on the bench under a wild apple tree. The air was warm and mild; on all sides stretched a green meadow set with cowslips and wild thyme and a thousand other flowers; through the middle of it rippled a clear brook with the sun sparkling on it, and the white geese walked to and fro or paddled in the water.

"It's quite delightful here," said he, "but I'm so tired that I can't keep my eyes open. I'll sleep a little. If only a gust of wind doesn't come and blow my legs off my body — they're as rotten as tinder."

When he had slept a while, the old woman came and shook him till he woke. "Sit up," said she. "You can't stay here. I've certainly treated you hard, but it hasn't cost you your life. Of money and land you have no need; here's something else for you."

And with that she thrust a little book into his hand, which was cut out of a single emerald. "Take great care of it," said she. "It will bring you good fortune."

The count sprang up; and as he felt himself quite fresh and with his strength back, he thanked the old woman for her present and set off without so much as one backward look at her beautiful daughter. When he was already some way off he could still hear the noisy cry of the geese in the distance.

The count had to wander in the wilderness for three days before he could find his way out. He then reached a large town; and as nobody knew him, he was taken into the royal palace, where the King and Queen were sitting on their thrones.

The count fell on one knee and drew the emerald book out of his pocket and laid it at the Queen's feet. She told him to rise and hand her the little book. But she had hardly opened it and looked inside before she fell to the ground as if dead.

The count was seized by the King's servants and was being led off to prison, when the Queen opened her eyes and ordered them to release him; and everybody was to go out, as she wished to speak with him in private.

When the Queen was alone she began to weep bitterly, and said, "What use to me are the splendours and honours I'm surrounded by? Every morning I wake in pain and sorrow. I had three daughters, the youngest of whom was so beautiful that the whole world looked on her as a wonder. She was as white as snow, as rosy as apple blossom, and her hair as radiant as sunbeams. When she cried, it was not tears that fell from her eyes but pearls and jewels.

"When she was fifteen years old, the King summoned all three sisters to come before his throne. You should have seen how all the people stared when the youngest came in — it was just as if the sun were rising.

"Then the King said, 'My daughters, I don't know when my last day may come. I'll decide today what each of you shall receive at my death. You all love me; but whichever of you loves me best shall fare best.'

"Each of them said she loved him best.

"'Can't you tell me,' said the King, 'how much you love me? Then I shall see what you mean.'

"The eldest said, 'I love my father as dearly as the sweetest sugar.'

"The second said, 'I love my father as dearly as my prettiest dress.'

"But the youngest was silent. So her father said, 'And you, my dearest child, how much do you love me?'

"'I don't know, and I can compare my love with nothing.'

"But her father insisted that she should name something. So at last she said, 'The best food doesn't please me without salt; and so I love my father like salt.'

"When the King heard that he flew into a passion, and said, 'If you love me like salt, then your love shall be repaid you with salt.'

"Then he divided the kingdom between the two elder ones; but he had a sack of salt bound on the youngest one's back, and two servants had to lead her out into the wild forest.

"We all begged and prayed for her," said the Queen, "but the King's anger was not to be softened. How she cried when she had to leave us! The whole road was strewn with the pearls that flowed from her eyes.

"The King soon afterwards repented of his great severity and had the whole forest searched for the poor child, but nobody could find her. When I think that the wild beasts have devoured her, I don't know how to contain myself for sorrow; and many a time I comfort myself with the hope that she's still alive, and may have hidden herself in a cave, or found shelter with compassionate people.

"But imagine — when I opened your little emerald book, a pearl lay inside it, of exactly the same kind as those that used to fall from my daughter's eyes; and then you can imagine too how the sight of it stirred my heart. You must tell me how you came by that pearl."

The count told her that he had been given it by the old woman in the forest, who had seemed very strange to him and must be a witch; but that he had neither seen nor heard anything of the Queen's child.

The King and the Queen resolved to seek out the old woman. They thought that where the pearl had been, they would get news of their daughter.

The old woman was sitting in that lonely place at her spinning wheel, spinning. It was already dusk, and a log burning on the hearth gave a scanty light. All at once there was a noise outside: the geese were coming home from the pasture, uttering their hoarse cries. Soon afterwards the daughter came in too.

But the old woman hardly thanked her, and only shook her head a little. The daughter sat down beside her and took up her spinning wheel and twisted the threads as nimbly as a young girl. So the two of them sat for two hours and never exchanged a word.

At last something rustled at the window, and two fiery eyes peered in. It was an old night owl, which cried "Uhu!" three times. The old woman looked up just a little, and then she said, "Now, my little daughter, it's time for you to go out and do your work."

She got up and went out — and where did she go? Over the meadows, on and on into the valley. At last she came to a well with three old oak trees standing beside it. Meanwhile the moon had risen large and round over the mountain, and it was so light that you could have found a needle.

She took off a skin that covered her face, then bent down to the well and began to wash herself. When she had finished, she dipped the skin in the water too, and then laid it on the meadow to bleach in the moonlight and dry again.

But how the girl was changed! Such a change was never seen. When the grey mask fell away, her golden hair broke out like sunbeams and spread about her whole figure like a mantle. Her eyes shone out as brightly as the stars in heaven, and her cheeks bloomed a soft red like apple blossom.

But the fair girl was sad. She sat down and wept bitterly. One tear after another forced itself out of her eyes and rolled down through her long hair to the ground. There she sat, and would have gone on sitting a long time, if there had not been a rustling and cracking in the boughs of a nearby tree.

She sprang up like a deer that has been caught by the hunter's shot. Just then the moon was hidden by a dark cloud, and in an instant the girl had put on the old skin and vanished, like a light blown out by the wind.

She ran home again, trembling like an aspen leaf. The old woman was standing on the threshold, and the girl was about to tell her what had happened; but the old woman laughed kindly and said, "I know it all already."

She led her into the room and lit a new log. But she did not sit down to her spinning again; she fetched a broom and began to sweep and scour. "Everything must be clean and sweet," she said to the girl.

"But, mother," said the girl, "why do you begin work at such a late hour? What are you expecting?"

"Do you know what time it is, then?" asked the old woman.

"Not midnight yet," answered the girl, "but past eleven o'clock already."

"Don't you remember," the old woman went on, "that it's three years today since you came to me? Your time is up; we can stay together no longer."

The girl was terrified, and said, "Alas, dear mother, will you cast me off? Where shall I go? I have no friends and no home to go to. I've always done as you told me, and you've always been satisfied with me. Don't send me away."

The old woman would not tell the girl what lay ahead of her. "My stay here is over," she said to her, "but when I go, house and parlour must be clean; so don't hinder me in my work. Have no fear for yourself. You shall find a roof to shelter you, and the wages I'll give you will content you too."

"But tell me what's about to happen," the girl went on entreating.

"I tell you again, don't hinder me in my work. Don't say another word. Go to your room, take the skin off your face, and put on the silk gown you were wearing when you came to me; and then wait in your room until I call you."

But I must tell once more of the King and Queen, who had set out with the count to seek the old woman in the wilderness.

The count had strayed away from them in the wood by night, and had to walk on alone. Next day it seemed to him that he was on the right track. He kept going on until darkness came, and then he climbed a tree, meaning to spend the night there, for he was afraid of losing his way.
