When the moon lit up the countryside he saw a figure coming down the mountain. She had no stick in her hand, but he could see all the same that it was the goose-girl he had seen before at the old woman's house.

"Oho," cried he, "there she comes; and if I once get hold of one of the witches, the other shan't escape me."

But how astonished he was when she went to the well and took off the skin and washed herself, and her golden hair fell down all about her, and she was more beautiful than anybody he had ever seen in the whole world. He hardly dared to breathe, but stretched his head as far forward through the leaves as he dared, and stared at her.

Either he leaned over too far, or whatever the cause may have been, the bough suddenly cracked — and that very moment the girl slipped into the skin and sprang away like a deer, and as the moon was suddenly covered, she disappeared from his sight.

Hardly had she gone before the count climbed down from the tree and hurried after her with quick steps. He had not been going long before he saw two figures coming over the meadow in the twilight. It was the King and Queen, who had seen the light shining in the old woman's little house from a distance and were making for it.

The count told them the wonderful things he had seen at the well, and they did not doubt that it had been their lost daughter. They walked on full of joy, and soon came to the little house. The geese were sitting all round it with their heads tucked under their wings, asleep, and not one of them stirred.

The King and Queen looked in at the window. The old woman was sitting there quite quietly spinning, nodding her head and never looking round. The room was perfectly clean, as if the little mist men, who carry no dust on their feet, lived there. But they did not see their daughter.

They gazed at all this for a long time; and at last they took heart and knocked softly at the window. The old woman seemed to have been expecting them; she got up and called out quite kindly, "Come in — I know you already."

When they had come into the room, the old woman said, "You could have spared yourselves the long walk, if three years ago you hadn't unjustly driven away your child, who is so good and lovable. No harm has come to her; for three years she has had to mind the geese, and with them she has learned no evil, but has kept her purity of heart. You, though, have been punished enough by the misery you've lived in."

Then she went to the room and called, "Come out, my little daughter."

At this the door opened, and the princess stepped out in her silk clothes, with her golden hair and her shining eyes, and it was as if an angel from heaven had come in.

She went up to her father and mother and fell on their necks and kissed them; there was no help for it, they all had to weep for joy. The young count stood near them; and when she caught sight of him she turned as red in the face as a moss rose, and she herself did not know why.

The King said, "My dear child, I've given away my kingdom. What shall I give you?"

"She needs nothing," said the old woman. "I give her the tears she has wept on your account; they are precious pearls, finer than any that are found in the sea, and worth more than your whole kingdom. And I give her my little house as payment for her services."

When the old woman had said that, she disappeared from their sight. The walls rattled a little; and when the King and Queen looked round, the little house had turned into a splendid palace, and a royal table had been spread, and servants were running here and there.

The story goes on further still; but my grandmother, who told it to me, had partly lost her memory and had forgotten the rest. I shall always believe that the beautiful princess married the count, and that they stayed together in the palace and lived there in all happiness as long as God willed it.

Whether the snow-white geese that were kept near the little hut were truly young girls (let nobody take offence) whom the old woman had taken under her protection, and whether they now got their human shapes back and stayed as handmaids to the young Queen, I don't exactly know — but I suspect it.

This much is certain: that the old woman was no witch, as people thought, but a wise woman who meant well. Very likely it was she who at the princess's birth gave her the gift of weeping pearls instead of tears. That doesn't happen nowadays, or else the poor would soon become rich.

Eve’s Various Children

When Adam and Eve were driven out of Paradise, they had to build themselves a house on unfruitful ground and eat their bread in the sweat of their brows. Adam dug the land and Eve spun.

Every year Eve brought a child into the world; but the children were unlike each other, some pretty and some ugly. After a considerable time had gone by, God sent an angel to them to announce that he was coming to inspect their household.

Eve, delighted that the Lord should be so gracious, cleaned her house thoroughly, decked it with flowers and strewed reeds on the floor. Then she brought in her children — but only the beautiful ones. She washed and bathed them, combed their hair, put clean clothes on them, and told them to conduct themselves properly and modestly in the Lord's presence. They were to bow to him civilly, hold out their hands, and answer his questions modestly and sensibly.

The ugly children, though, were not to let themselves be seen. One hid under the hay, another under the roof, a third in the straw, the fourth in the stove, the fifth in the cellar, the sixth under a tub, the seventh under the wine cask, the eighth under an old fur cloak, the ninth and tenth under the cloth she always made their clothes out of, and the eleventh and twelfth under the leather she cut their shoes from.

She had hardly got ready before there was a knock at the door. Adam looked through a chink and saw that it was the Lord. Adam opened the door respectfully, and the Heavenly Father came in.

There, in a row, stood the pretty children, and they bowed to him and held out their hands and knelt down. And the Lord began to bless them. He laid his hands on the first and said, "You shall be a powerful king"; and to the second, "You a prince"; to the third, "You a count"; to the fourth, "You a knight"; to the fifth, "You a nobleman"; to the sixth, "You a citizen"; to the seventh, "You a merchant"; to the eighth, "You a scholar." And he bestowed on them all his richest blessings besides.

When Eve saw that the Lord was so mild and gracious, she thought, "I'll bring my ill-favoured children here too; it may be that he'll give them his blessing as well." So she ran and brought them out of the hay and the straw and the stove and wherever else she had hidden them; and along came the whole coarse, dirty, shabby, sooty band.

The Lord smiled and looked at them all and said, "I'll bless these too." He laid his hands on the first and said to him, "You shall be a peasant"; to the second, "You a fisherman"; to the third, "You a smith"; to the fourth, "You a tanner"; to the fifth, "You a weaver"; to the sixth, "You a shoemaker"; to the seventh, "You a tailor"; to the eighth, "You a potter"; to the ninth, "You a carter"; to the tenth, "You a sailor"; to the eleventh, "You an errand boy"; and to the twelfth, "You a kitchen boy, all the days of your life."

When Eve had heard all this she said, "Lord, how unequally you divide your gifts! They are all of them my children after all, whom I brought into the world; your favours ought to be given to all of them alike."

But God answered, "Eve, you don't understand. It's right and necessary that the whole world should be supplied out of your children. If they were all princes and lords, who would grow the corn and thresh it and grind it and bake it? Who would be blacksmiths, weavers, carpenters, masons, labourers, tailors and seamstresses? Each shall have his own place, so that one supports another, and all are fed like the limbs of one body."

Then Eve answered, "Ah, Lord, forgive me; I spoke to you too quickly. Do your divine will with my children."

The Nix of the Mill-Pond

There was once a miller who lived with his wife in great contentment. They had money and land, and their prosperity grew year by year, more and more.

But bad luck comes like a thief in the night. As their wealth had increased, so it decreased again, year by year; and at last the miller could hardly call the mill he lived in his own. He was in great distress; and when he lay down after his day's work he found no rest, but tossed about in his bed full of care.

One morning he got up before daybreak and went out into the open air, thinking that perhaps his heart might grow lighter there. As he was stepping over the mill dam the first sunbeam was just breaking out, and he heard a rippling sound in the pond. He turned round and saw a beautiful woman rising slowly out of the water. Her long hair, which she was holding off her shoulders with her soft hands, fell down on both sides and covered her white body.

He soon saw that she was the nix of the mill-pond; and in his fright he did not know whether to run away or stay where he was. But the nix let her sweet voice be heard, and called him by his name and asked why he was so sad.

The miller was struck dumb at first; but when he heard her speak so kindly he took heart, and told her how he had once lived in wealth and happiness, but was now so poor that he did not know what to do.

"Be easy," answered the nix. "I'll make you richer and happier than you've ever been before — only you must promise to give me the young thing that has just been born in your house."

"What can that be," thought the miller, "but a puppy or a kitten?" — and he promised her what she wanted.

The nix went down into the water again, and he hurried back to his mill, comforted and in good spirits. He had not reached it yet when the maidservant came out of the house and called to him to rejoice, for his wife had given birth to a little boy.

The miller stood as if struck by lightning. He saw very well that the cunning nix had known about it and had cheated him. Hanging his head, he went up to his wife's bedside; and when she said, "Why don't you rejoice over the fine boy?" he told her what had happened to him and what he had promised the nix.

"What use are riches and prosperity to me," he added, "if I'm to lose my child? But what can I do?"

Even the relations, who had come to wish them joy, did not know what to say.

Meanwhile prosperity came back to the miller's house. Everything he undertook succeeded; it was as if presses and coffers filled themselves of their own accord, and as if money multiplied in the cupboards overnight. It was not long before his wealth was greater than it had ever been.

But he could not rejoice in it untroubled, for the bargain he had made with the nix tormented his soul. Whenever he passed the mill-pond, he was afraid she might rise up and remind him of his debt. He never let the boy himself go near the water. "Beware," he said to him. "If you so much as touch the water, a hand will rise up and seize you and drag you down."

But as year after year went by and the nix did not show herself again, the miller began to feel easy. The boy grew up into a young man and was apprenticed to a huntsman. When he had learned everything and had become an excellent huntsman, the lord of the village took him into his service.

In the village lived a beautiful and true-hearted girl who pleased the huntsman; and when his master saw it, he gave him a little house. The two were married, and lived peacefully and happily and loved each other with all their hearts.

One day the huntsman was chasing a roe; and when the animal turned aside out of the forest into the open country, he pursued it and at last shot it. He did not notice that he was now near the dangerous mill-pond; and after he had dressed the deer he went to the water to wash his bloodstained hands.

But hardly had he dipped them in before the nix rose up, wound her dripping arms round him with a smile, and drew him swiftly down under the waves, which closed over him.

When it was evening and the huntsman did not come home, his wife grew alarmed. She went out to look for him; and as he had often told her that he had to be on his guard against the nix's snares and dared not go near the mill-pond, she suspected already what had happened. She hurried to the water; and when she found his hunting pouch lying on the shore, she could have no more doubt about the misfortune.

Lamenting in her sorrow and wringing her hands, she called her beloved by name, but in vain. She hurried across to the other side of the pond and called him again; she reviled the nix with harsh words, but no answer came. The surface of the water stayed calm; only the crescent moon stared steadily back at her.

The poor woman did not leave the pond. She paced round and round it with hasty steps, never resting a moment, sometimes in silence, sometimes uttering a loud cry, sometimes softly sobbing. At last her strength gave out; she sank down to the ground and fell into a heavy sleep.

Presently a dream took hold of her. She was anxiously climbing up between great masses of rock; thorns and briars caught her feet, the rain beat in her face, and the wind tossed her long hair about. When she reached the summit, quite a different sight met her: the sky was blue, the air soft, the ground sloped gently downwards, and on a green meadow gay with flowers of every colour stood a pretty cottage. She went up to it and opened the door; and there sat an old woman with white hair, who beckoned to her kindly.

At that very moment the poor woman woke. Day had already dawned, and she resolved at once to act on her dream. She laboriously climbed the mountain, and everything was exactly as she had seen it in the night. The old woman received her kindly and pointed out a chair for her to sit on.

"You must have met with some misfortune," she said, "since you've sought out my lonely cottage."

In tears, the woman told her what had happened.

"Be comforted," said the old woman. "I'll help you. Here is a golden comb for you. Wait until the full moon has risen, then go to the mill-pond, sit down on the shore and comb your long black hair with this comb. When you've done, lay it down on the bank, and you'll see what happens."

The woman went home, but the time until the full moon came passed slowly. At last the shining disc appeared in the sky; and then she went out to the mill-pond and sat down and combed her long black hair with the golden comb, and when she had finished she laid it down at the water's edge.

It was not long before there was a movement in the depths; a wave rose and rolled to the shore and carried the comb away with it. In no more time than the comb needed to sink to the bottom, the surface of the water parted, and the huntsman's head rose up. He did not speak, but looked at his wife with sorrowful eyes. At the same instant a second wave came rushing up and covered the man's head. It was all gone; the mill-pond lay as peaceful as before, and nothing but the face of the full moon shone on it.

Full of sorrow, the woman went back; but again the dream showed her the old woman's cottage. Next morning she set out again and told her troubles to the wise woman.

The old woman gave her a golden flute and said, "Wait until the full moon comes again, then take this flute; play a beautiful air on it, and when you've finished, lay it on the sand. Then you'll see what happens."

The wife did as the old woman told her. No sooner was the flute lying on the sand than there was a stirring in the depths, and a wave rushed up and carried the flute away with it. Immediately afterwards the water parted, and not only her husband's head but half his body rose up. He stretched his arms out longingly towards her — but a second wave came up and covered him and drew him down again.

"Alas, what good does it do me," said the unhappy woman, "to see my beloved only to lose him again?"

Despair filled her heart afresh; but the dream led her a third time to the old woman's house. She set out, and the wise woman gave her a golden spinning wheel and comforted her and said, "It isn't all fulfilled yet. Wait until the time of the full moon, then take the spinning wheel and sit down on the shore and spin the spool full; and when you've done that, set the spinning wheel down near the water, and you'll see what happens."

The woman obeyed everything she said exactly. As soon as the full moon showed itself she carried the golden spinning wheel to the shore and spun industriously until the flax came to an end and the spool was quite filled with thread. No sooner was the wheel standing on the shore than there was a more violent movement than before in the depths of the pond, and a mighty wave rushed up and carried the wheel away with it.

Immediately the head and then the whole body of her husband rose into the air on a spout of water. He sprang quickly to the shore, caught his wife by the hand and fled with her.

But they had gone only a very little way when the whole pond rose with a frightful roar and streamed out over the open country. The fugitives already saw death before their eyes, when the woman in her terror called on the old woman for help; and in an instant they were transformed, she into a toad and he into a frog.

The flood that had overtaken them could not destroy them; but it tore them apart and carried them far away. When the water had drained off and they both touched dry land again, they got their human shapes back — but neither knew where the other was. They found themselves among strangers who had never heard of their native country. High mountains and deep valleys lay between them.

To keep themselves alive, they both had to mind sheep. For many long years they drove their flocks through field and forest and were full of sorrow and longing.

When spring had broken out over the earth once more, they both went out one day with their flocks; and as chance would have it, they came near each other. They met in a valley, but did not recognise each other; yet they were glad not to be so lonely any more. From then on they drove their flocks to the same place every day. They did not speak much, but they felt comforted.

One evening, when the full moon was shining in the sky and the sheep were already at rest, the shepherd pulled the flute out of his pocket and played a beautiful but sorrowful air on it. When he had finished, he saw that the shepherdess was weeping bitterly.

"Why are you weeping?" he asked.

"Alas," answered she, "the full moon shone like this when I played this air on the flute for the last time, and the head of my beloved rose out of the water."

He looked at her, and it seemed as if a veil fell from his eyes, and he recognised his dear wife; and when she looked at him, and the moon shone on his face, she knew him too. They embraced and kissed each other — and nobody need ask whether they were happy.

The Little Folks’ Presents

A tailor and a goldsmith were travelling together; and one evening, when the sun had sunk behind the mountains, they heard the sound of distant music, which grew more and more distinct. It sounded strange, but so pleasant that they forgot all their weariness and stepped out quickly.

The moon had already risen when they reached a hill, where they saw a crowd of little men and women who had taken each other by the hands and were whirling round in a dance with the greatest pleasure and delight. They sang to it most charmingly, and that was the music the travellers had heard.

In the middle of them sat an old man who was rather taller than the rest. He wore a many-coloured coat, and his iron-grey beard hung down over his chest. The two of them stood still, full of astonishment, and watched the dance.

The old man made a sign that they should come in, and the little folks willingly opened their circle. The goldsmith, who had a hump and, like all hunchbacks, was brave enough, stepped in. The tailor felt a little afraid at first and held back; but when he saw how merrily it was all going, he plucked up his courage and followed.

The circle closed again at once, and the little folks went on singing and dancing with the wildest leaps. But the old man took a large knife that hung at his belt and whetted it; and when it was sharp enough he looked round at the strangers.

They were terrified; but they had not much time for reflection, for the old man seized the goldsmith and with the greatest speed shaved the hair of his head clean off, and then the same thing happened to the tailor.

But their fear left them when, after he had finished his work, the old man clapped them both on the shoulder in a friendly way, as much as to say that they had done well to let it all be done to them willingly and without any struggle. He pointed with his finger to a heap of coals lying at one side, and made signs to the travellers that they should fill their pockets with them.

Both of them obeyed, although they did not know what use the coals could be to them, and then they went on their way to find a shelter for the night. When they had got down into the valley, the clock of the nearby monastery struck twelve, and the singing stopped. In a moment everything had vanished, and the hill lay lonely in the moonlight.

The two travellers found an inn and covered themselves up on their straw beds with their coats; but in their weariness they forgot to take the coals out of them first. A heavy weight on their limbs woke them earlier than usual. They felt in their pockets, and could not believe their eyes when they saw that the pockets were not filled with coals but with pure gold. And happily, too, the hair of their heads and beards had come back as thick as ever.

They had now become rich men; but the goldsmith, who in keeping with his greedy nature had filled his pockets better, was twice as rich as the tailor. And a greedy man, even if he has much, still wants more; so the goldsmith proposed to the tailor that they should stay another day and go out again in the evening, to bring back still greater treasures from the old man on the hill.

The tailor refused, and said, "I have enough and I'm content. Now I'll be a master and marry my dear one" — for so he called his sweetheart — "and I'm a happy man." But he stayed another day to please him.

In the evening the goldsmith hung a couple of bags over his shoulders so as to be able to stow away a great deal, and took the road to the hill. He found the little folks at their singing and dancing as on the night before, and the old man shaved him clean again and made signs to him to take some coal away with him. He was not slow about stuffing as much into his bags as would go, and went back quite delighted and covered himself over with his coat.

"Even if the gold does weigh heavily," said he, "I'll gladly bear it" — and at last he fell asleep with the sweet expectation of waking in the morning an enormously rich man.

When he opened his eyes he got up in haste to look in his pockets; but how amazed he was when he drew nothing out of them but black coals, however often he put his hands in.

"The gold I got the night before is still there for me," thought he — and went and fetched it out; but how appalled he was to see that it too had turned back into coal.

He struck his forehead with his dusty black hand, and then he felt that his whole head was bald and smooth, and so was the place where his beard should have been. But his misfortunes were not over yet: he now noticed for the first time that, besides the hump on his back, a second one just as large had grown in front on his chest.

Then he recognised the punishment for his greed, and began to weep aloud.

The good tailor, who was woken by this, comforted the unhappy fellow as well as he could, and said, "You've been my comrade in my travelling days; you shall stay with me and share in my wealth."

He kept his word — but the poor goldsmith had to carry his two humps as long as he lived, and to cover his bald head with a cap.

The Giant and the Tailor

A certain tailor, who was great at boasting but poor at doing, took it into his head to go abroad for a while and look about the world. As soon as he could manage it he left his workshop and wandered on his way, over hill and dale, sometimes this way and sometimes that, but always on and on.

Once, while he was out, he saw in the blue distance a steep hill, and behind it a tower reaching to the clouds, which rose up out of a wild dark forest.

"Thunder and lightning," cried the tailor, "what's that?" And as curiosity strongly goaded him, he went boldly towards it.

But what made the tailor open his eyes and his mouth, when he came near, was to see that the tower had legs, and leapt over the steep hill in a single bound, and was now standing in front of him as an all-powerful giant.

"What do you want here, you tiny fly's leg?" cried the giant, in a voice like thunder on every side.

The tailor whimpered, "I only want to look about and see whether I can earn myself a bit of bread in this forest."

"If that's what you're after," said the giant, "you can have a place with me."

"If it must be, why not? What wages shall I get?"

"You shall hear what wages you'll get. Every year three hundred and sixty-five days — and when it's leap year, one more into the bargain. Does that suit you?"

"All right," replied the tailor, and thought to himself, "A man must cut his coat according to his cloth. I'll try to get away as fast as I can."

At this the giant said to him, "Go, little ragamuffin, and fetch me a jug of water."

"Hadn't I better bring the well itself at once, and the spring too?" asked the boaster, and went off with the pitcher to the water.

"What — the well and the spring too?" growled the giant into his beard; for he was rather clownish and stupid, and began to be afraid. "That rascal is no fool; he has a wizard inside him. Be on your guard, old Hans; this is no serving man for you."

When the tailor had brought the water, the giant told him to go into the forest and cut a couple of blocks of wood and bring them back.

"Why not the whole forest at once, with one stroke? The whole forest, young and old, with everything in it, both rough and smooth?" asked the little tailor, and went off to cut the wood.

"What — the whole forest, young and old, with everything in it, both rough and smooth? And the well and its spring too?" growled the credulous giant into his beard, and was more terrified still. "That rascal can do a great deal more than bake apples; he has a wizard inside him. Be on your guard, old Hans; this is no serving man for you."

When the tailor had brought the wood, the giant ordered him to shoot two or three wild boars for supper.

"Why not a thousand at one shot, and bring them all here?" asked the boastful tailor.

"What!" cried the timid giant in great terror. "Let well alone for tonight, and lie down and rest."

The giant was so terribly alarmed that he could not close an eye all night long for thinking of the best way to get rid of this accursed sorcerer of a servant. Time brings counsel.

Next morning the giant and the tailor went to a marsh with a number of willow trees standing round it. Then the giant said, "Listen, tailor, sit yourself down on one of these willow branches. I'd like more than anything to see whether you're heavy enough to bend it down."

In a moment the tailor was sitting on it, holding his breath and making himself so heavy that the bough bent down. But when he had to draw breath, it flung him — for unluckily he had not put his pressing iron in his pocket — so high into the air that he was never seen again; and this to the giant's great delight.

If the tailor has not fallen down again, he must still be hovering about up there in the air.

The Nail

A merchant had done good business at the fair; he had sold his wares and lined his money bags with gold and silver. Then he wanted to travel home and be in his own house before nightfall. So he packed his trunk of money on his horse and rode away.

At noon he rested in a town; and when he wanted to go on, the stable boy brought out his horse and said, "There's a nail missing, sir, from the shoe on its left hind foot."

"Let it be missing," answered the merchant. "The shoe will certainly stay on for the six miles I still have to go. I'm in a hurry."

In the afternoon, when he dismounted once more and had his horse fed, the stable boy came into the room to him and said, "Sir, there's a shoe missing from your horse's left hind foot. Shall I take him to the blacksmith?"

"Let it still be missing," answered the man. "The horse can hold out well enough for the couple of miles that are left. I'm in haste."

He rode off; but before long the horse began to limp. It had not limped long before it began to stumble, and it had not stumbled long before it fell down and broke its leg. The merchant had to leave the horse where it lay, and unbuckle the trunk and take it on his back and go home on foot. And he did not get there until quite late at night.

"And that unlucky nail," said he to himself, "has caused the whole disaster."

Hurry slowly.

The Poor Boy in the Grave

There was once a poor shepherd boy whose father and mother were dead, and he was placed by the authorities in the house of a rich man, who was to feed him and bring him up.

But the man and his wife had bad hearts, and were greedy and anxious about their riches, and vexed whenever anybody put a morsel of their bread in his mouth. The poor young fellow might do what he liked, he got little to eat — only so many the more blows.

One day he had to watch a hen and her chicks; but she ran through a hedge with them, and a hawk darted down instantly and carried her off through the air. The boy shouted "Thief! Thief! Rascal!" with all the strength in his body — but what good did that do? The hawk did not bring its prey back.

The man heard the noise and ran to the spot; and as soon as he saw that his hen was gone, he flew into a rage and gave the boy such a beating that he could not stir for two days.

Then he had to look after the chicks without the hen; but now his difficulty was greater, for one ran here and another there. He thought he was doing a very clever thing when he tied them all together with a string, because then the hawk would not be able to steal any of them away from him. But he was very much mistaken.

After two days, worn out with running about and with hunger, he fell asleep. The bird of prey came and seized one of the chicks; and as the others were tied fast to it, it carried them all off together, perched itself on a tree and devoured them.

The farmer was just coming home; and when he saw the disaster he grew angry and beat the boy so unmercifully that he had to lie in bed for several days.

When he was on his legs again the farmer said to him, "You're too stupid for me; I can't make a herdsman of you. You must go as errand boy."

Then he sent him to the judge, to whom he was to carry a basketful of grapes, and gave him a letter as well.

On the way, hunger and thirst tormented the unhappy boy so violently that he ate two of the bunches of grapes. He took the basket to the judge; but when the judge had read the letter and counted the bunches he said, "Two clusters are missing."

The boy confessed quite honestly that, driven by hunger and thirst, he had eaten the two that were missing.

The judge wrote a letter to the farmer and asked for the same number of grapes again. These too the boy had to carry to him, with a letter. And as he was again so extremely hungry and thirsty, he could not help himself, and again ate two bunches. But first he took the letter out of the basket and put it under a stone and sat down on top of it, so that the letter could not see him and betray him.

The judge, though, again made him explain about the missing bunches.

"Ah," said the boy, "how did you find out? The letter couldn't have known about it, because I put it under a stone before I did it."

The judge could not help laughing at the boy's simplicity, and sent the man a letter warning him to look after the poor boy better and not let him go short of food and drink, and also to teach him what was right and what was wrong.

"I'll soon show you the difference," said the hard man. "If you want to eat, you must work; and if you do anything wrong, you'll be taught quite well enough by blows."

The next day he set him a hard task. He was to chop up two bundles of straw for the horses' food; and then the man threatened him. "In five hours," said he, "I'll be back; and if the straw isn't cut into chaff by then, I'll beat you until you can't move a limb."

The farmer went off with his wife and the manservant and the girl to the yearly fair, and left nothing behind for the boy but a small bit of bread.

The boy sat down on the bench and began to work with all his might. As he grew warm over it he took his little coat off and threw it down on the straw. In his terror that he would not get done in time, he kept on cutting without stopping; and in his haste, without noticing it, he chopped up his little coat along with the straw.

He realised the disaster too late; there was no repairing it. "Ah," cried he, "now it's all over with me. That wicked man didn't threaten me for nothing; if he comes back and sees what I've done, he'll kill me. Rather than that, I'll take my own life."

The boy had once heard the farmer's wife say, "I've got a pot of poison under my bed." She had only said it to keep greedy people away, though, for there was honey in it.

The boy crept under the bed and brought out the pot and ate everything in it. "I don't know," said he. "People say death is bitter, but it tastes very sweet to me. It's no wonder the farmer's wife has so often longed for death."

He sat himself down in a little chair and made ready to die. But instead of growing weaker, he felt strengthened by the nourishing food.

"It can't have been poison," thought he. "But the farmer once said there was a small bottle of fly poison in the box where he keeps his clothes. That, no doubt, will be the true poison, and will bring death to me."

It was no fly poison, though, but Hungarian wine. The boy got the bottle out and emptied it.

"This death tastes sweet too," said he. But shortly afterwards, when the wine began to rise into his head and stupefy him, he thought his end was drawing near. "I feel that I must die," said he. "I'll go away to the churchyard and find a grave."

He staggered out, reached the churchyard and laid himself down in a newly dug grave. He lost his senses more and more. Nearby was an inn where a wedding was being held; and when he heard the music he thought he was already in Paradise, until at length he lost all consciousness.

The poor boy never woke again; the heat of the strong wine and the cold night dew took his life from him, and he stayed in the grave he had laid himself down in.

When the farmer heard the news of the boy's death he was terrified and afraid of being brought to justice; indeed, his distress took such a powerful hold on him that he fell fainting to the ground. His wife, who was standing at the hearth with a pan of hot fat, ran to help him. But the flames leapt against the pan, and the whole house caught fire; and in a few hours it lay in ashes. And the rest of the years they had to live they passed in poverty and misery, tormented by the pangs of conscience.

The True Sweethearts

There was once a girl who was young and beautiful; but she had lost her mother when she was quite a child, and her stepmother did everything she could to make the girl's life wretched.

Whenever this woman gave her anything to do, she worked at it tirelessly and did everything that lay in her power. Still she could not touch the wicked woman's heart by it; she was never satisfied, it was never enough. The harder the girl worked, the more work was put on her; and all the woman thought about was how to weigh her down with still heavier burdens and make her life still more miserable.

One day she said to her, "Here are twelve pounds of feathers that you must strip; and if they aren't done by this evening, you can expect a good beating. Do you imagine you're going to idle the whole day away?"

The poor girl sat down to the work; but the tears ran down her cheeks as she did it, for she saw plainly enough that it was quite impossible to finish the work in one day. Whenever she had a little heap of feathers lying in front of her, and she sighed or clapped her hands together in her anguish, they flew away, and she had to pick them up again and start her work afresh.

Then she put her elbows on the table and laid her face in her two hands and cried, "Is there nobody, then, on God's earth to have pity on me?"

Then she heard a low voice, which said, "Be comforted, my child; I've come to help you."

The girl looked up, and an old woman was beside her. She took the girl kindly by the hand and said, "Just tell me what's troubling you."

As she spoke so kindly, the girl told her about her miserable life, and how one burden after another was laid on her, and how she could never get to the end of the work she was given. "If I haven't done these feathers by this evening, my stepmother will beat me. She's threatened she will, and I know she keeps her word."

Her tears began to flow again; but the good old woman said, "Don't be afraid, my child. Rest a while, and I'll see to your work in the meantime."

The girl lay down on her bed and soon fell asleep. The old woman sat down at the table with the feathers — and how they flew off the quills, which she scarcely touched with her withered hands! The twelve pounds were soon finished; and when the girl woke, great snow-white heaps were lying there piled up, and everything in the room was neatly cleared away; but the old woman had vanished.

The girl thanked God and sat still until evening came, when her stepmother came in and marvelled to see the work finished.

"Just look, you clumsy creature," said she, "what can be done when people work hard. And why couldn't you have set about something else? There you sit with your hands folded."

When she went out she said, "The creature is worth more than her salt. I must give her some work that's harder still."

Next morning she called the girl and said, "Here's a spoon for you. With that you must empty out the great pond beside the garden for me; and if it isn't done by night, you know what will happen."

The girl took the spoon and saw that it was full of holes; but even if it had not been, she could never have emptied the pond with it. She set to work at once, kneeling down beside the water, into which her tears were falling, and began to empty it.

But the good old woman appeared again; and when she learned the cause of her grief she said, "Be of good cheer, my child. Go into the thicket and lie down and sleep; I'll soon do your work."

As soon as the old woman was alone, she barely touched the pond, and a vapour rose up high out of the water and mingled with the clouds. Little by little the pond was emptied; and when the girl woke before sunset and came there, she saw nothing but the fish struggling in the mud.

She went to her stepmother and showed her that the work was done. "It ought to have been done long before this," said she, and went white with anger; but she was already planning something new.

On the third morning she said to the girl, "You must build me a castle on the plain over there, and it must be ready by evening."

The girl was dismayed and said, "How can I finish such a great work?"

"I'll put up with no arguing," screamed her stepmother. "If you can empty a pond with a spoon full of holes, you can build a castle too. I'll take possession of it this very day; and if anything is missing — even the most trifling thing in the kitchen or the cellar — you know what lies in store for you."

She drove the girl out; and when she came into the valley, the rocks lay there piled one above another, and all her strength would not have let her move even the smallest of them. She sat down and wept, and still she hoped the old woman would help her.

The old woman was not long in coming. She comforted her and said, "Lie down there in the shade and sleep, and I'll soon build the castle for you. If it would give you pleasure, you can live in it yourself."

When the girl had gone away, the old woman touched the grey rocks. They began to rise, and moved together at once as if giants had built the walls; and on these the building rose up, and it seemed as if countless hands were working invisibly and setting one stone on another. There was a dull heavy noise from the ground; pillars rose of their own accord and set themselves in order beside each other. The tiles laid themselves in order on the roof; and when midday came, the great weathervane was already turning itself on the top of the tower, like a golden figure of the Virgin with fluttering garments.

The inside of the castle was being finished as evening drew on. How the old woman managed it I don't know; but the walls of the rooms were hung with silk and velvet, embroidered chairs stood there and richly ornamented armchairs by marble tables; crystal chandeliers hung down from the ceilings and were mirrored in the smooth floor; green parrots sat in gilt cages, and strange birds too that sang most beautifully; and there was as much magnificence on every side as if a king were going to live there.

The sun was just setting when the girl woke and the brightness of a thousand lights flashed in her face. She hurried to the castle and went in by the open door. The steps were spread with red cloth and the golden banister set about with flowering trees. When she saw the splendour of the rooms she stood as if turned to stone.

Who knows how long she might have stood there, if she had not remembered her stepmother? "Alas," she said to herself, "if only she could be satisfied at last, and would give up making my life a misery."

The girl went and told her that the castle was ready. "I'll move into it at once," said she, and rose from her seat.

When they came into the castle she had to hold her hand in front of her eyes, the brilliance of everything was so dazzling. "You see," said she to the girl, "how easy it's been for you to do this. I ought to have given you something harder."

She went through all the rooms and examined every corner to see whether anything was missing or wrong; but she could find nothing.

"Now we'll go down below," said she, looking at the girl with malicious eyes. "The kitchen and the cellar still have to be looked at; and if you've forgotten anything, you shan't escape your punishment."

But the fire was burning on the hearth and the meat cooking in the pans, the tongs and shovel were leaning against the wall, and the shining brass utensils were all set out in sight. Nothing was missing, not even a coal box and a water pail.

"Which is the way to the cellar?" she cried. "If that isn't well filled, it will go badly with you."

She raised the trapdoor herself and went down; but she had hardly taken two steps before the heavy trapdoor, which was only laid back, fell down. The girl heard a scream and lifted the door very quickly to go to her help; but she had fallen, and the girl found her lying lifeless at the bottom.

And now the magnificent castle belonged to the girl alone. At first she did not know how to reconcile herself to her good fortune. Beautiful dresses hung in the wardrobes, the chests were filled with gold and silver, or with pearls and jewels; and she never felt a wish that she could not satisfy.

And soon the fame of the girl's beauty and riches went over all the world. Suitors presented themselves daily, but none of them pleased her. At length the King's son came, and he knew how to touch her heart, and she betrothed herself to him.

In the garden of the castle was a lime tree, and they were sitting under it together one day when he said to her, "I'll go home and get my father's consent to our marriage. I beg you to wait for me here under this lime tree; I'll be back with you in a few hours."

The girl kissed him on his left cheek and said, "Stay true to me, and never let anybody else kiss you on this cheek. I'll wait here under the lime tree until you come back."

The girl stayed under the lime tree until sunset, but he did not come back. She sat there three days from morning till evening, waiting for him, but in vain.

As he was still not there on the fourth day, she said, "Some accident must have happened to him. I'll go out and look for him, and won't come back until I've found him."

She packed up three of her most beautiful dresses — one embroidered with bright stars, the second with silver moons, the third with golden suns — tied a handful of jewels up in her handkerchief, and set out.

She asked everywhere for her betrothed, but nobody had seen him; nobody knew anything about him. Far and wide she wandered through the world, but she did not find him. At last she hired herself out to a farmer as a cowherd, and buried her dresses and jewels under a stone.

And now she lived as a herdswoman, minding her herd, and was very sad and full of longing for her beloved. She had a little calf that she taught to know her and fed out of her own hand; and when she said:

	"Little calf, little calf, kneel by my side,
	and do not forget your shepherd maid,
	as the prince forgot his betrothed bride
	who waited for him in the lime tree's shade" —

the little calf knelt down, and she stroked it.

And when she had lived alone and full of grief for a couple of years, word went round the whole country that the King's daughter was about to celebrate her marriage. The road to the town passed through the village where the girl was living; and it happened that once, when she was driving her herd out, her bridegroom travelled past. He sat proudly on his horse and never looked round; but when she saw him she recognised her beloved, and it was just as if a sharp knife had pierced her heart.

"Alas," said she, "I believed he was true to me; but he has forgotten me."

Next day he came along the road again. When he was near her she said to the little calf:

	"Little calf, little calf, kneel by my side,
	and do not forget your shepherd maid,
	as the prince forgot his betrothed bride
	who waited for him in the lime tree's shade."

When he caught the sound of her voice he looked down and reined in his horse. He looked into the herdswoman's face, and then put his hands in front of his eyes as if he were trying to remember something; but he soon rode on and was out of sight.

"Alas," said she, "he doesn't know me any more" — and her grief was greater than ever.

Soon after this a great festival, three days long, was to be held at the King's court, and the whole country was invited to it.

"Now I'll try my last chance," thought the girl. And when evening came she went to the stone she had buried her treasures under. She took out the dress with the golden suns and put it on and adorned herself with the jewels. She let down her hair, which she had kept hidden under a handkerchief, and it fell about her in long curls; and so she went into the town, and in the darkness nobody noticed her.

When she came into the brightly lit hall everybody drew back in amazement, but nobody knew who she was. The King's son went to meet her, but he did not recognise her. He led her out to dance, and was so enchanted with her beauty that he thought no more of his other bride. When the feast was over she vanished into the crowd, and hurried back before daybreak to the village, where she put her herdswoman's clothes on again.

Next evening she took out the dress with the silver moons and put a half-moon of precious stones in her hair. When she appeared at the festival every eye turned on her; but the King's son hurried to meet her, and, filled with love for her, danced with her alone and no longer so much as glanced at anybody else. Before she went away she was made to promise to come to the festival again on the last evening.

When she appeared for the third time she wore the star dress, which sparkled at every step she took, and her hair ribbon and her girdle were starred with jewels. The prince had already been waiting for her a long while, and forced his way through to her.

"Only tell me who you are," said he. "I feel just as if I'd known you a long time already."

"Don't you know what I did when you left me?"

Then she stepped up to him and kissed him on his left cheek; and in a moment it was as if scales fell from his eyes, and he recognised his true bride.

"Come," said he to her, "I'll stay here no longer" — and gave her his hand and led her down to the carriage. The horses hurried away towards the magic castle as if the wind had been harnessed to the carriage. The lit windows were already shining in the distance. When they drove past the lime tree, countless glow-worms were swarming about it; it shook its branches and sent out their fragrance. On the steps flowers were blooming, and the room echoed with the song of strange birds; and in the hall the whole court was assembled, and the priest was waiting to marry the bridegroom to his true bride.

The Hare and the Hedgehog

This story, my dear young folks, seems to be false, but it really is true; for my grandfather, whom I had it from, always used to say complacently when he told it, "It must be true, my son, or else nobody could tell it to you." The story goes like this.

One Sunday morning about harvest time, just as the buckwheat was in bloom, the sun was shining brightly in heaven, the east wind was blowing warm over the stubble fields, the larks were singing in the air, the bees buzzing among the buckwheat, and the people were all going to church in their Sunday clothes; and every creature was happy, and the hedgehog was happy too.

The hedgehog was standing by his door with his arms folded, enjoying the morning breeze and slowly trilling a little song to himself, which was neither better nor worse than the songs hedgehogs are in the habit of singing on a blessed Sunday morning.

And while he was singing half aloud to himself like this, it suddenly occurred to him that, while his wife was washing and drying the children, he might very well take a walk into the field and see how his turnips were getting on. The turnips were in fact right beside his house, and he and his family were used to eating them, which was why he looked on them as his own.

No sooner said than done. The hedgehog shut the house door behind him and took the path to the field. He had not gone very far from home, and was just turning round the sloe bush that stands out there at the edge of the field to go up into the turnip field, when he noticed the hare, who had come out on business of the same kind — namely, to visit his cabbages.

When the hedgehog caught sight of the hare he wished him a friendly good morning. But the hare, who was a distinguished gentleman in his own way, and frightfully haughty, did not return the hedgehog's greeting, but said to him — putting on a very contemptuous manner at the same time — "How do you come to be running about in the field so early in the morning?"

"I'm taking a walk," said the hedgehog.

"A walk!" said the hare with a smile. "It seems to me you might use your legs for a better purpose."

This answer made the hedgehog furiously angry, for he can bear anything but an attack on his legs, just because they are crooked by nature. So the hedgehog said to the hare, "You seem to imagine that you can do more with your legs than I can with mine."

"That's just what I do think," said the hare.

"That can be put to the test," said the hedgehog. "I'll wager that if we run a race, I'll outstrip you."

"That's ridiculous — you, with your short legs!" said the hare. "But for my part I'm willing, if you have such a monstrous fancy for it. What shall we wager?"

"A gold sovereign and a bottle of brandy," said the hedgehog.

"Done," said the hare. "Shake hands on it, and then we may as well start at once."

"No," said the hedgehog, "there's no such great hurry. I'm still fasting; I'll go home first and have a little breakfast. In half an hour I'll be back here."

At this the hedgehog went off, for the hare was quite satisfied with the arrangement.

On his way the hedgehog thought to himself, "The hare relies on his long legs, but I'll contrive to get the better of him. He may be a great man, but he's a very silly fellow, and he shall pay for what he's said."

So when the hedgehog reached home he said to his wife, "Wife, get dressed quickly; you must come out to the field with me."

"What's going on, then?" said his wife.

"I've made a wager with the hare for a gold sovereign and a bottle of brandy. I'm to run a race with him, and you must be there."

"Good heavens, husband," his wife cried now, "are you not right in your mind? Have you completely lost your wits? What can make you want to run a race with the hare?"

"Hold your tongue, woman," said the hedgehog. "That's my affair. Don't start arguing about matters for men. Off with you, get dressed and come with me."

What could the hedgehog's wife do? She had to obey him, whether she liked it or not.

So when they had set out together, the hedgehog said to his wife, "Now pay attention to what I'm going to say. Look — I'll make the long field our racecourse. The hare shall run in one furrow and I in another, and we'll start running from the top. All you have to do is take your place down here in the furrow; and when the hare arrives at the end of the furrow on the other side of you, you must call out to him, 'I'm here already!'"

Then they reached the field, and the hedgehog showed his wife her place, and then walked up the field. When he reached the top, the hare was there already.

"Shall we start?" said the hare.

"Certainly," said the hedgehog.

"Then both at once." And so saying, each placed himself in his own furrow. The hare counted, "Once, twice, thrice — and away!" and went off down the field like a whirlwind.

The hedgehog, though, only ran about three paces, and then he crouched down in the furrow and stayed quietly where he was.

So when the hare arrived at full speed at the lower end of the field, the hedgehog's wife met him with the cry, "I'm here already!"

The hare was shocked and wondered not a little; he thought it was nothing other than the hedgehog himself calling to him, for the hedgehog's wife looked just like her husband. But the hare thought to himself, "That wasn't done fairly" — and cried, "It must be run again; let's have it again." And once more he went off like the wind in a storm, so that he seemed to fly.

But the hedgehog's wife stayed quietly in her place. So when the hare reached the top of the field, the hedgehog himself cried out to him, "I'm here already!"

The hare, quite beside himself with anger, cried, "It must be run again; we must have it again."

"All right," answered the hedgehog. "For my part, we'll run as often as you choose."

So the hare ran seventy-three times more, and the hedgehog always held out against him; and every time the hare reached either the top or the bottom, either the hedgehog or his wife said, "I'm here already."

At the seventy-fourth time, though, the hare could no longer reach the end. In the middle of the field he fell to the ground, blood streamed out of his mouth, and he lay dead on the spot.

But the hedgehog took the sovereign he had won and the bottle of brandy, called his wife out of the furrow, and the two of them went home together in great delight; and if they aren't dead, they're living there still.

That is how it came about that the hedgehog made the hare run races with him on the Buxtehude heath until he died; and since that time no hare has ever had any fancy for running races with a Buxtehude hedgehog.

The moral of this story, though, is, first, that nobody, however great he may be, should let himself make fun of anybody beneath him, even if it's only a hedgehog. And second, it teaches that when a man marries, he should take a wife of his own kind, who looks just as he looks himself. So whoever is a hedgehog, let him see to it that his wife is a hedgehog too, and so on.

The Spindle, The Shuttle, and the Needle

There was once a girl whose father and mother died while she was still a little child. All alone, in a small house at the end of the village, lived her godmother, who supported herself by spinning and weaving and sewing. The old woman took the forlorn child in to live with her, kept her to her work, and brought her up in everything that is good.

When the girl was fifteen years old the old woman fell ill, called the child to her bedside and said, "Dear daughter, I feel my end drawing near. I leave you the little house, which will protect you from wind and weather, and my spindle and shuttle and needle, which you can earn your bread with."

Then she laid her hands on the girl's head and blessed her and said, "Only keep the love of God in your heart, and all will go well with you."

With that she closed her eyes; and when she was laid in the earth, the girl followed the coffin weeping bitterly, and paid her the last mark of respect.

And now the girl lived quite alone in the little house, and was hard-working, and spun and wove and sewed; and the good old woman's blessing was on everything she did. It seemed as if the flax in the room increased of its own accord; and whenever she wove a piece of cloth or carpet or made a shirt, she at once found a buyer who paid her amply for it, so that she wanted for nothing and even had something to share with others.

About this time the King's son was travelling about the country looking for a bride. He was not to choose a poor one, and he did not want a rich one. So he said, "She shall be my wife who is the poorest and at the same time the richest."

When he came to the village where the girl lived he asked, as he did wherever he went, who was the richest and also the poorest girl in the place. They named the richest first; and the poorest, they said, was the girl who lived in the small house right at the end of the village.

The rich girl was sitting in all her splendour in front of her door; and when the prince came up to her she got up and went to meet him and made him a low curtsey. He looked at her, said nothing, and rode on.

When he came to the poor girl's house she was not standing at the door but sitting in her little room. He stopped his horse and saw through the window, on which the bright sun was shining, the girl sitting at her spinning wheel, busily spinning. She looked up; and when she saw that the prince was looking in she blushed all over her face, let her eyes fall, and went on spinning. I don't know whether the thread was quite even just at that moment; but she went on spinning until the King's son had ridden away again.

Then she went to the window and opened it and said, "It's so warm in this room" — but she still looked after him as long as she could make out the white feathers in his hat.

Then she sat down to work again in her own room and went on with her spinning; and a saying the old woman had often repeated when she was sitting at her work came into her mind, and she sang the words to herself:

	"Spindle, my spindle, haste, haste you away,
	and here to my house bring the wooer, I pray."

And what do you think happened? The spindle sprang out of her hand in an instant and out of the door; and when, in her astonishment, she got up and looked after it, she saw it dancing merrily out into the open country, drawing a shining golden thread behind it. Before long it had vanished entirely from her sight.

As she now had no spindle, the girl took the weaver's shuttle in her hand and sat down at her loom and began to weave.

The spindle, meanwhile, danced on and on; and just as the thread came to an end it reached the prince.

"What's this I see?" he cried. "The spindle must want to show me the way." And he turned his horse about and rode back alongside the golden thread.

The girl, though, was sitting at her work, singing:

	"Shuttle, my shuttle, weave well this day,
	and guide the wooer to me, I pray."

Immediately the shuttle sprang out of her hand and out of the door. In front of the threshold, though, it began to weave a carpet more beautiful than the eyes of man had ever seen. Lilies and roses bloomed on both sides of it; and on a golden ground in the middle green branches climbed up, with hares and rabbits bounding beneath them, and stags and deer stretching their heads in between; and brightly coloured birds sat in the branches above — they lacked nothing but the gift of song. The shuttle leapt this way and that, and everything seemed to grow of its own accord.

As the shuttle had run away, the girl sat down to sew. She held the needle in her hand and sang:

	"Needle, my needle, sharp-pointed and fine,
	prepare for a wooer this house of mine."

Then the needle leapt out of her fingers and flew about the room everywhere, as quick as lightning. It was just as if invisible spirits were at work: they covered tables and benches with green cloth in an instant, and the chairs with velvet, and hung silk curtains at the windows.

Hardly had the needle put in the last stitch before the girl saw through the window the white feathers of the prince, whom the spindle had brought there by the golden thread. He dismounted, stepped over the carpet into the house; and when he came into the room, there stood the girl in her poor clothes, but shining out from them like a rose surrounded by leaves.

"You are the poorest, and also the richest," said he to her. "Come with me; you shall be my bride."

She did not speak, but she gave him her hand. Then he gave her a kiss and led her out and lifted her onto his horse, and took her to the royal castle, where the wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing. And the spindle and the shuttle and the needle were kept in the treasure chamber and held in great honour.

The Peasant and the Devil

There was once a far-sighted, crafty peasant whose tricks were much talked about. The best story, though, is how he once got hold of the Devil and made a fool of him.

The peasant had been working in his field one day; and as twilight had set in he was making ready for the journey home, when he saw a heap of burning coals in the middle of his field. And when he went up to it, full of astonishment, a little black devil was sitting on the live coals.

"You're sitting on a treasure, I do believe," said the peasant.

"Yes, truly," replied the Devil, "on a treasure that holds more gold and silver than you've ever seen in your life."

"The treasure is in my field and belongs to me," said the peasant.

"It's yours," answered the Devil, "if for two years you'll give me half of everything your field produces. I have money enough, but I've a longing for the fruits of the earth."

The peasant agreed to the bargain. "But so that no dispute can arise about the division," said he, "everything above the ground shall belong to you, and what's under the earth to me."

The Devil was quite satisfied with that — but the cunning peasant had sown turnips.

Now when harvest time came, the Devil appeared and wanted to take away his crop; but he found nothing but the yellow withered leaves, while the peasant, full of delight, was digging up his turnips.

"You've had the best of it for once," said the Devil, "but next time that won't do. What grows above ground shall be yours, and what's under it, mine."

"I'm willing," replied the peasant. But when the time came to sow, he did not sow turnips again, but wheat. The grain ripened, and the peasant went into the field and cut the full stalks down to the ground. When the Devil came he found nothing but the stubble, and went off in a fury down into a cleft in the rocks.

"That's the way to cheat the Devil," said the peasant — and went and fetched the treasure away.

The Crumbs on the Table

A countryman said to his little puppies one day, "Come into the parlour and enjoy yourselves, and pick up the breadcrumbs on the table. Your mistress has gone out to pay some visits."

Then the little dogs said, "No, no, we won't go. If the mistress finds out, she'll beat us."

The countryman said, "She'll know nothing about it. Do come; after all, she never gives you anything good."

Then the little dogs said again, "No, no, we must let it alone; we mustn't go."

But the countryman gave them no peace until at last they went, and got up on the table and ate up the breadcrumbs with all their might.

But at that very moment the mistress came in, and seized the stick in great haste and beat them and treated them very hard indeed.

And when they were outside the house, the little dogs said to the countryman, "D'you, d'you, d'you, d'you, d'you see?"

Then the countryman laughed and said, "Didn't, didn't, didn't you expect it?"

So they just had to run away.

The Sea-Hare

There was once a princess who had a room high up under the battlements of her castle, with twelve windows in it that looked out in every possible direction; and when she climbed up to it and looked around her, she could survey her whole kingdom.

When she looked out of the first, her sight was keener than any other human being's; from the second she could see better still; from the third more distinctly still; and so it went on, up to the twelfth, from which she saw everything above the earth and under it, and nothing at all could be kept secret from her.

And as she was haughty, and would be subject to nobody but wanted to keep the rule for herself alone, she had it proclaimed that nobody should ever be her husband who could not hide himself from her so well that it would be quite impossible for her to find him. But whoever tried it and was discovered by her was to have his head struck off and stuck on a post.

Ninety-seven posts with the heads of dead men on them were already standing in front of the castle, and nobody had come forward for a long time. The princess was delighted, and thought to herself, "Now I shall be free as long as I live."

Then three brothers appeared before her and announced that they wished to try their luck.

The eldest thought he would be quite safe if he crept into a lime pit; but she saw him from the first window and made him come out, and had his head cut off.

The second crept into the cellar of the palace, but she saw him too from the first window, and his fate was sealed. His head was set on the ninety-ninth post.

Then the youngest came to her and begged her to give him a day to think about it, and also to be so gracious as to overlook it if she happened to discover him twice; but if he failed the third time, he would consider his life over.

As he was so handsome and begged so earnestly, she said, "Yes, I'll grant you that — but you won't succeed."

Next day he thought for a long time how he should hide himself, but all in vain. So he took his gun and went out hunting. He saw a raven, took good aim at him and was just about to fire, when the bird cried, "Don't shoot; I'll make it worth your while not to."

He put his gun down and went on, and came to a lake, where he surprised a large fish that had come up from the depths below to the surface of the water. When he had aimed at it, the fish cried, "Don't shoot, and I'll make it worth your while."

He let it dive down again, and went on, and met a fox that was lame. He fired and missed it, and the fox cried, "You'd do much better to come here and draw the thorn out of my foot for me."

He did it; but then he wanted to kill the fox and skin it, and the fox said, "Stop, and I'll make it worth your while."

The young man let him go; and then, as it was evening, he went home.

Next day he was to hide himself; but however much he racked his brains over it, he did not know where. He went into the forest to the raven and said, "I let you live; so now tell me where I'm to hide myself, so that the King's daughter won't see me."

The raven hung his head and thought it over for a long time. At length he croaked, "I have it."

He fetched an egg out of his nest and cut it into two parts and shut the young man inside it, and then made it whole again and sat down on it.

When the King's daughter went to the first window she could not find him, nor from the others either, and she began to grow uneasy; but from the eleventh she saw him. She ordered the raven to be shot and the egg to be brought and broken, and the young man was forced to come out.

She said, "For once you're excused; but if you don't do better than this, you're lost."

Next day he went to the lake and called the fish to him and said, "I let you live; now tell me where to hide myself, so that the King's daughter won't see me."

The fish thought for a while, and at last cried, "I have it! I'll shut you up in my stomach." He swallowed him and went down to the bottom of the lake.

The King's daughter looked out through her windows, and even from the eleventh she did not see him, and was alarmed; but at length from the twelfth she saw him. She ordered the fish to be caught and killed, and then the young man appeared. Anybody can imagine what state of mind he was in.

She said, "Twice you're forgiven; but be sure your head will be set on the hundredth post."

On the last day he went out into the country with a heavy heart and met the fox. "You know how to find all kinds of hiding places," said he. "I let you live; now advise me where to hide myself, so that the King's daughter doesn't discover me."

"That's a hard task," answered the fox, looking very thoughtful. At length he cried, "I have it!" — and went with him to a spring and dipped himself in it, and came out as a stallholder in the market, a dealer in animals. The young man had to dip himself in the water too, and was changed into a small sea-hare.

The dealer went into the town and showed the pretty little animal, and a great many people gathered to see it. At length the King's daughter came too; and as she liked it very much, she bought it and gave the dealer a good deal of money for it. Before he handed it over to her, he said to it, "When the King's daughter goes to the window, creep quickly under the braids of her hair."

And now the time came for her to look for him. She went to one window after another in turn, from the first to the eleventh, and did not see him. And when she did not see him from the twelfth either, she was full of anxiety and anger, and slammed it shut with such violence that the glass in every window shivered into a thousand pieces and the whole castle shook.

She went back and felt the sea-hare under the braids of her hair. Then she seized it and threw it on the ground, exclaiming, "Away with you! Get out of my sight!"

It ran to the dealer, and the two of them hurried to the spring and plunged into it and got their true shapes back.

The young man thanked the fox and said, "The raven and the fish are idiots compared with you. You know the right tune to play, there's no denying it."

The young man went straight to the palace. The princess was already expecting him, and reconciled herself to her fate. The wedding was celebrated, and now he was king and lord of the whole kingdom.

He never told her where he had hidden himself the third time, or who had helped him; so she believed that he had done it all by his own skill, and she had great respect for him, for she thought to herself, "He can do more than I can."

The Master-Thief

One day an old man and his wife were sitting in front of a miserable house, resting a while from their work. Suddenly a splendid carriage with four black horses came driving up, and a richly dressed man got down out of it.

The peasant stood up and went to the great man and asked what he wanted, and how he could be of use to him.

The stranger held out his hand to the old man and said, "I want nothing but to enjoy a country dish for once. Cook me some potatoes the way you always have them, and then I'll sit down at your table and eat them with pleasure."

The peasant smiled and said, "You're a count, or a prince, or perhaps even a duke; noble gentlemen often have fancies like that. But you shall have your wish."

His wife went into the kitchen and began to wash and scrub the potatoes and make them into balls, the way country folk eat them.

While she was busy with this work, the peasant said to the stranger, "Come into my garden with me for a while; I still have something to do there." He had dug some holes in the garden and now wanted to plant some trees in them.

"Have you no children," asked the stranger, "who could help you with your work?"

"No," answered the peasant. "I had a son, it's true, but it's long since he went out into the world. He was a ne'er-do-well — sharp and knowing, but he'd learn nothing and was full of bad tricks. At last he ran away from me, and since then I've heard nothing of him."

The old man took a young tree and put it in a hole and drove a post in beside it; and when he had shovelled some earth in and trampled it firmly down, he tied the stem of the tree to the post with a rope of straw, above, below and in the middle.

"But tell me," said the stranger, "why don't you tie that crooked, knotted tree lying over there in the corner, bent down almost to the ground, to a post as well, so that it grows straight like these?"

The old man smiled and said, "Sir, you speak according to your knowledge; it's easy to see that you know nothing about gardening. That tree there is old and misshapen; nobody can make it straight now. Trees must be trained while they're young."

"That's how it was with your son," said the stranger. "If you'd trained him while he was still young, he wouldn't have run away; now he too must have grown hard and misshapen."

"It's a long time indeed since he went away," replied the old man. "He must have changed."

"Would you know him again if he came to you?" asked the stranger.

"Hardly by his face," replied the peasant, "but he has a mark about him — a birthmark on his shoulder that looks like a bean."

When he had said that, the stranger pulled off his coat and bared his shoulder and showed the peasant the bean.

"Good God!" cried the old man. "You really are my son!" And love for his child stirred in his heart. "But," he added, "how can you be my son, when you've become a great lord and live in wealth and luxury? How have you managed that?"

"Ah, father," answered his son, "the young tree was tied to no post and has grown crooked; now it's too old, and it will never be straight again. How did I get all this? I've become a thief. But don't be alarmed — I'm a master-thief. For me there are neither locks nor bolts; whatever I want is mine. Don't imagine that I steal like a common thief; I only take a little of the surplus of the rich. Poor people are safe from me — I'd rather give to them than take anything from them. And it's the same with anything I can have without trouble and cunning and skill: I never touch it."

"Alas, my son," said his father, "it still doesn't please me. A thief is a thief; I tell you it will end badly."

He took him to his mother; and when she heard that this was her son she wept for joy — but when he told her that he had become a master-thief, two streams flowed down her face. At length she said, "Even if he's become a thief, he's still my son, and my eyes have seen him once more."

They sat down at the table, and once again he ate with his parents the poor food he had not eaten for so long.

His father said, "If our lord the count, up there in the castle, learns who you are and what trade you follow, he won't take you in his arms and cradle you the way he did when he held you at the font — he'll have you swing from a rope."

"Be easy, father, he'll do me no harm, for I understand my trade. I'll go to him myself this very day."

When evening drew near, the master-thief got into his carriage and drove to the castle. The count received him civilly, taking him for a distinguished man. But when the stranger made himself known, the count went pale and was quite silent for some time.

At length he said, "You're my godson, and on that account mercy shall take the place of justice, and I'll deal leniently with you. Since you pride yourself on being a master-thief, I'll put your art to the test; but if you don't stand the test, you must marry the ropemaker's daughter, and the croaking of the raven shall be your music on the occasion."

"My lord count," answered the master-thief, "think of three things, as difficult as you like; and if I don't perform your tasks, do with me what you will."

The count thought for a few minutes, and then said, "Well then: first, you shall steal the horse I keep for my own riding out of the stable. Second, you shall steal the sheet from under my wife and me while we're asleep, without our noticing it, and my wife's wedding ring as well. And third and last, you shall steal the parson and the clerk out of the church. Mark what I'm saying, for your life depends on it."

The master-thief went to the nearest town, where he bought the clothes of an old peasant woman and put them on. Then he stained his face brown and painted wrinkles on it too, so that nobody could have recognised him. Then he filled a small cask with old Hungarian wine, into which he mixed a powerful sleeping draught. He put the cask in a basket and took it on his back, and walked with slow and tottering steps to the count's castle.

It was already dark when he arrived. He sat down on a stone in the courtyard and began to cough like an asthmatic old woman, and to rub his hands as if he were cold.

In front of the stable door some soldiers were lying round a fire. One of them noticed the woman and called out to her, "Come nearer, old mother, and warm yourself beside us. After all, you've no bed for the night, and must take one where you can find it."

The old woman tottered up to them, begged them to lift the basket off her back, and sat down beside them at the fire.

"What have you got in your little cask, old lady?" one of them asked.

"A good mouthful of wine," she answered. "I live by trade; for money and fair words I'm quite ready to let you have a glass."

"Let's have it here, then," said the soldier; and when he had tasted one glass he said, "When wine is good, I like another glass" — and had another poured out for himself; and the rest followed his example.

"Hey, comrades," cried one of them to the men in the stable, "here's an old body with wine as old as herself. Take a draught; it'll warm your stomachs far better than our fire."

The old woman carried her cask into the stable. One of the soldiers had seated himself on the saddled riding horse, another held its bridle in his hand, a third had hold of its tail. She poured out as much as they wanted, until the cask ran dry.

It was not long before the bridle fell out of the first one's hand, and he dropped down and began to snore. The second let go of the tail and lay down and snored still louder. The one sitting in the saddle did stay sitting, but bent his head almost down to the horse's neck, and slept and blew with his mouth like the bellows of a forge. The soldiers outside had been asleep a long while already, and lay motionless on the ground as if dead.

When the master-thief saw that he had succeeded, he put a rope in the first one's hand instead of the bridle, and gave the one who had been holding the tail a wisp of straw. But what was he to do with the one sitting on the horse's back? He did not want to throw him down, for he might have woken and cried out.
