He had a good idea. He unbuckled the girths of the saddle, tied a couple of ropes that were hanging from a ring on the wall fast to the saddle, and hauled the sleeping rider up into the air on it; then he twisted the rope round the posts and made it fast.

He soon unfastened the horse from its chain; but if he had ridden over the stone pavement of the yard they would have heard the noise in the castle. So he wrapped the horse's hoofs in old rags and led him carefully out, and leapt on him and galloped off.

When day broke, the master galloped up to the castle on the stolen horse. The count had just got up and was looking out of the window.

"Good morning, my lord count," he called to him. "Here's the horse, which I've got safely out of the stable. And just look how beautifully your soldiers are lying there asleep; and if you'll only go into the stable, you'll see how comfortable your watchmen have made themselves."

The count could not help laughing. Then he said, "For once you've succeeded; but things won't go so well the second time. And I warn you that if you come before me as a thief, I'll handle you as I would a thief."

When the countess went to bed that night she closed her hand tightly over her wedding ring; and the count said, "All the doors are locked and bolted. I'll stay awake and wait for the thief; and if he gets in by the window I'll shoot him."

The master-thief, though, went in the dark to the gallows, cut down a poor sinner who was hanging there, and carried him on his back to the castle. Then he set a ladder up to the bedroom, put the dead body on his shoulders and began to climb.

When he had got so high that the dead man's head showed at the window, the count, who was watching from his bed, fired a pistol at him; and immediately the master let the poor sinner drop and hid himself in a corner.

The night was light enough with the moon for the master to see distinctly how the count climbed out of the window onto the ladder and came down, and carried the dead body into the garden and began to dig a hole to lay it in.

"Now," thought the thief, "the moment has come." He stole nimbly out of his corner and climbed up the ladder straight into the countess's bedroom.

"Dear wife," he began, in the count's voice, "the thief is dead; but after all he's my godson, and has been more of a scapegrace than a villain. I won't put him to open shame; besides, I'm sorry for his parents. I'll bury him myself before daybreak in the garden, so that the thing isn't known. So give me the sheet — I'll wrap the body in it and bury him the way a dog buries things, by scratching."

The countess gave him the sheet.

"I'll tell you what," the thief went on, "I have a fit of generosity on me. Give me the ring too — the unhappy man risked his life for it, so he may as well take it with him into his grave."

She would not gainsay the count; and although she did it unwillingly, she drew the ring off her finger and gave it to him.

The thief made off with both these things, and got home safely before the count in the garden had finished his work of burying.

What a long face the count pulled when the master came next morning and brought him the sheet and the ring!

"Are you a wizard?" said he. "Who fetched you out of the grave I laid you in myself, and brought you back to life?"

"You didn't bury me," said the thief, "but the poor sinner from the gallows" — and he told him exactly how it had all happened; and the count had to admit to him that he was a clever, crafty thief.

"But you haven't reached the end yet," he added. "You still have the third task to perform; and if you don't succeed at that, all the rest is no use."

The master smiled and gave no answer.

When night had fallen he went to the village church with a long sack on his back, a bundle under his arm and a lantern in his hand. In the sack he had some crabs, and in the bundle short wax candles. He sat down in the churchyard, took out a crab and stuck a wax candle on its back. Then he lit the little light and put the crab on the ground and let it creep about. He took a second out of the sack and treated it the same way, and so on until the last one was out of the sack.

After this he put on a long black garment that looked like a monk's habit, and stuck a grey beard on his chin. When at last he was quite unrecognisable, he took the sack the crabs had been in, went into the church and climbed up into the pulpit.

The clock in the tower was just striking twelve; and when the last stroke had sounded, he cried out in a loud, piercing voice, "Hearken, sinful men! The end of all things has come! The last day is at hand! Hearken! Hearken! Whoever wants to go to heaven with me must creep into this sack. I am Peter, who opens and shuts the gate of heaven. Behold how the dead out there in the churchyard are wandering about gathering up their bones. Come, come, and creep into the sack; the world is about to be destroyed!"

The cry echoed through the whole village. The parson and the clerk, who lived nearest the church, heard it first; and when they saw the lights moving about the churchyard, they realised that something unusual was going on, and went into the church.

They listened to the sermon for a while, and then the clerk nudged the parson and said, "It wouldn't be amiss if we used this opportunity together, and found an easy way of getting to heaven before the last day dawns."

"To tell the truth," answered the parson, "that's what I've been thinking myself. So if you're willing, we'll set out on our way."

"Yes," answered the clerk, "but you, as pastor, have precedence. I'll follow."

So the parson went first and climbed up into the pulpit, where the master opened his sack. The parson crept in first and then the clerk.

The master immediately tied the sack up tightly, seized it by the middle and dragged it down the pulpit steps; and whenever the heads of the two fools bumped against the steps he cried, "We're going over the mountains."

Then he drew them through the village the same way; and when they were passing through puddles he cried, "Now we're going through the wet clouds." And when at last he was dragging them up the castle steps, he cried, "Now we're on the steps of heaven, and we'll soon be in the outer court."

When he had got to the top he pushed the sack into the dovecote; and when the pigeons fluttered about he said, "Hear how glad the angels are, and how they're flapping their wings." Then he bolted the door on them and went away.

Next morning he went to the count and told him that he had performed the third task as well, and had carried the parson and the clerk out of the church.

"Where have you left them?" asked the lord.

"They're lying upstairs in a sack in the dovecote, and imagine they're in heaven."

The count went up himself and satisfied himself that the master had told the truth. When he had delivered the parson and the clerk from their captivity, he said, "You're an arch-thief and you've won your wager. For once you escape with a whole skin; but see that you leave my land, for if you ever set foot on it again you may count on your elevation to the gallows."

The arch-thief took leave of his parents, went out once more into the wide world, and nobody has ever heard of him since.

The Drummer

A young drummer went out quite alone into the country one evening, and came to a lake, on the shore of which he saw three pieces of white linen lying. "What fine linen," said he, and put one piece in his pocket.

He went home, thought no more about what he had found, and went to bed. But just as he was falling asleep, it seemed to him that somebody was saying his name. He listened, and made out a soft voice calling to him, "Drummer, drummer, wake up!"

As it was a dark night he could see nobody; but it seemed to him that a figure was hovering about his bed.

"What do you want?" he asked.

"Give me back my dress," answered the voice, "that you took away from me last evening by the lake."

"You shall have it back," said the drummer, "if you'll tell me who you are."

"Ah," replied the voice, "I'm the daughter of a mighty King; but I've fallen into a witch's power and am shut up on the glass mountain. Every day I have to bathe in the lake with my two sisters; but I can't fly back again without my dress. My sisters have gone away, but I've been left behind. I beg you to give me my dress back."

"Be easy, poor child," said the drummer. "I'll gladly give it back to you." He took it out of his pocket and held it out to her in the dark. She snatched it in haste and wanted to go off with it.

"Stop a moment — perhaps I can help you."

"You can only help me by climbing the glass mountain and freeing me from the witch's power. But you can't get to the glass mountain; and indeed, if you were right beside it, you couldn't climb it."

"When I want to do a thing, I always can do it," said the drummer. "I'm sorry for you, and I'm not afraid of anything. But I don't know the road that leads to the glass mountain."

"The road goes through the great forest where the man-eaters live," she answered; "and more than that I dare not tell you."

And then he heard her wings quiver as she flew away.

At daybreak the drummer got up, buckled on his drum, and went fearlessly straight into the forest. After he had walked a while without seeing any giants, he thought to himself, "I must wake the sluggards up" — and hung his drum in front of him and beat such a reveille that the birds flew out of the trees with loud cries.

It was not long before a giant who had been lying asleep among the grass got up, and he was as tall as a fir tree.

"Wretch," cried he, "what are you drumming here for, and waking me out of my best sleep?"

"I'm drumming," he replied, "because I want to show the way to the many thousands who are following me."

"What do they want in my forest?" demanded the giant.

"They want to make an end of you, and clear the forest of a monster like you."

"Oho," said the giant, "I'll trample the lot of you to death like so many ants."

"Do you think you can do anything against us?" said the drummer. "If you stoop to take hold of one, he'll jump away and hide himself; but when you're lying down asleep, they'll come out of every thicket and creep up on you. Every one of them has a steel hammer in his belt, and with those they'll beat your skull in."

The giant grew angry, and thought, "If I meddle with this crafty crew it might turn out badly for me. I can strangle wolves and bears, but I can't protect myself from these earthworms."

"Listen, little fellow," said he, "go back again, and I'll promise you that in future I'll leave you and your comrades in peace; and if there's anything else you want, tell me, for I'm quite willing to do something to please you."

"You have long legs," said the drummer, "and can run faster than I can. Carry me to the glass mountain, and I'll give my followers the signal to go back, and they'll leave you in peace this time."

"Come here, worm," said the giant. "Sit yourself on my shoulder and I'll carry you where you want to be."

The giant lifted him up, and the drummer began to beat his drum up there to his heart's delight. The giant thought, "That's the signal for the others to turn back."

After a while a second giant was standing in the road, who took the drummer from the first and stuck him in his buttonhole. The drummer took hold of the button, which was as large as a dish, and held on by it and looked merrily about him.

Then they came to a third giant, who took him out of the buttonhole and set him on the brim of his hat. Then the drummer walked backwards and forwards up there and looked out over the trees; and when he saw a mountain in the blue distance he thought, "That must be the glass mountain" — and so it was.

The giant only took two steps more, and they reached the foot of the mountain, where the giant put him down. The drummer demanded to be put on the summit of the glass mountain; but the giant shook his head, growled something into his beard, and went back into the forest.

And now the poor drummer was standing in front of the mountain, which was as high as if three mountains had been piled one on another, and at the same time as smooth as a looking glass; and he did not know how to get up it. He began to climb, but it was useless, for he always slipped back down again. "If a man were a bird now," thought he; but what was the use of wishing? No wings grew for him.

While he was standing there, not knowing what to do, he saw two men not far off who were struggling fiercely together. He went over to them and saw that they were arguing about a saddle that lay on the ground in front of them, which both of them wanted.

"What fools you are," said he, "to quarrel about a saddle when you have no horse for it."

"The saddle is worth fighting about," answered one of the men. "Whoever sits on it and wishes himself in any place, even if it's the very end of the earth, gets there the instant he's spoken the wish. The saddle belongs to both of us. It's my turn to ride on it, but this other man won't let me."

"I'll soon settle the quarrel," said the drummer; and he went a short distance off and stuck a white rod in the ground. Then he came back and said, "Now run to the goal, and whoever gets there first shall ride first."

Both of them set off at a trot; but hardly had they gone a couple of steps before the drummer swung himself onto the saddle, wished himself on the glass mountain — and before anybody could turn round, he was there.

On top of the mountain was a plain; and on it stood an old stone house, with a great fishpond in front of it and a dark forest behind. He saw neither people nor animals; everything was quiet, and only the wind rustled among the trees, and the clouds moved past quite close above his head.

He went to the door and knocked. When he had knocked for the third time, an old woman with a brown face and red eyes opened the door. She had spectacles on her long nose and looked at him sharply, and then asked what he wanted.

"To come in, and food, and a bed for the night," replied the drummer.

"That you shall have," said the old woman, "if you'll perform three services in return."

"Why not?" he answered. "I'm not afraid of any kind of work, however hard it may be."

The old woman let him in and gave him some food and a good bed for the night.

Next morning, when he had had his sleep out, she took a thimble off her wrinkled finger and held it out to the drummer and said, "Get to work now, and empty out that pond with this thimble. But you must have it done before night; and you must have sorted out all the fish in the water and laid them side by side according to their kind and size."

"That's strange work," said the drummer; but he went to the pond and began to empty it. He baled all morning; but what can anybody do to a great lake with a thimble, even if he baled for a thousand years?

At noon he thought, "It's all useless; whether I work or not, it will come to the same thing." So he gave up and sat down.

Then a girl came out of the house who set a little basket of food in front of him and said, "What ails you, that you sit here so sadly?"

He looked at her and saw that she was wonderfully beautiful. "Ah," said he, "I can't finish the first piece of work; how will it be with the others? I came out to look for a King's daughter who is said to live here, but I haven't found her, and I'll go on further."

"Stay here," said the girl. "I'll help you out of your difficulty. You're tired; lay your head in my lap and sleep. When you wake again, your work will be done."

The drummer did not need to be told that twice. As soon as his eyes were shut she turned a wishing ring and said, "Rise, water. Fishes, come out."

Instantly the water rose up on high like a white mist and moved away with the other clouds, and the fish sprang out onto the shore and laid themselves side by side, each according to his size and kind.

When the drummer woke he saw with amazement that it was all done. But the girl said, "One of the fish isn't lying with its own kind, but quite alone. When the old woman comes tonight and sees that everything she demanded has been done, she'll ask you, 'What is this fish lying alone for?' Then throw the fish in her face and say, 'This one is for you, old witch.'"

In the evening the witch came; and when she had asked this question, he threw the fish in her face. She behaved as though she had not noticed it and said nothing, but looked at him with malicious eyes.

Next morning she said, "Yesterday was too easy for you; I must give you harder work. Today you must chop down the whole of the forest, split the wood into logs and pile them up; and everything must be finished by the evening."

She gave him an axe, a mallet and two wedges. But the axe was made of lead, and the mallet and the wedges of tin. When he began to cut, the edge of the axe turned back, and the mallet and wedges were beaten out of shape. He did not know how to manage; but at midday the girl came once more with his dinner and comforted him.

"Lay your head in my lap," said she, "and sleep; when you wake, your work will be done."

She turned her wishing ring, and in an instant the whole forest fell down with a crash, the wood split, and it arranged itself in heaps; and it seemed just as if unseen giants were doing the work.

When he woke, the girl said, "You see that the wood is piled up and arranged; only one bough is left. But when the old woman comes this evening and asks you about that bough, hit her with it and say, 'That's for you, witch.'"

The old woman came. "There, you see how easy the work was," said she. "But who have you left that bough lying there for?"

"For you, witch," he replied, and hit her with it. But she pretended not to feel it, and laughed scornfully and said, "Early tomorrow morning you shall arrange all the wood in one heap, set fire to it and burn it."

He got up at daybreak and began to gather the wood; but how can one man get a whole forest together? The work made no progress.

The girl, though, did not desert him in his need. She brought him his food at noon; and when he had eaten he laid his head in her lap and went to sleep. When he woke, the whole pile of wood was burning in one enormous flame that stretched its tongues out into the sky.

"Listen to me," said the girl. "When the witch comes, she'll give you all kinds of orders. Do whatever she asks without fear, and then she won't be able to get the better of you; but if you're afraid, the fire will take hold of you and consume you. And at the end, when you've done everything, seize her with both hands and throw her into the middle of the fire."

The girl went away, and the old woman came sneaking up to him. "Oh, I'm cold," said she, "but that's a fire that burns; it warms my old bones for me and does me good. But there's a log lying there that won't burn — bring it out for me. When you've done that you're free and can go where you like. Come — go in with a good will."

The drummer did not stop to think; he sprang into the middle of the flames, but they did not hurt him and could not even singe a hair of his head. He carried the log out and laid it down.

But hardly had the wood touched the earth before it was transformed, and the beautiful girl who had helped him in his need stood before him; and by the shining silk and gold clothes she wore, he knew very well that she was the King's daughter.

But the old woman laughed venomously and said, "You think you have her safe, but you haven't got her yet."

And just as she was about to fall on the girl and take her away, the young man seized the old woman with both hands and lifted her up high and threw her into the jaws of the fire, which closed over her as if it were delighted to have an old witch to burn.

Then the King's daughter looked at the drummer; and when she saw that he was a handsome young man, and remembered how he had risked his life to deliver her, she gave him her hand and said, "You've ventured everything for my sake; and I too will do everything for yours. Promise to be true to me, and you shall be my husband. We shan't want for riches; we'll have enough with what the witch has gathered together here."

She led him into the house, where there were chests and coffers crammed with the old woman's treasures. The girl left the gold and silver where it was and took only the precious stones.

She would not stay any longer on the glass mountain, so the drummer said to her, "Sit beside me on my saddle, and then we'll fly down like birds."

"I don't like the old saddle," said she. "I need only turn my wishing ring and we shall be at home."

"Very well, then," answered the drummer. "Then wish us in front of the town gate."

In the twinkling of an eye they were there; but the drummer said, "I'll just go to my parents and tell them the news. Wait for me out here; I'll soon be back."

"Ah," said the King's daughter, "I beg you to be careful. When you arrive, don't kiss your parents on the right cheek, or you'll forget everything, and I shall be left out here alone and deserted."

"How could I forget you?" said he — and promised to come back very soon, and gave her his hand on it.

When he went into his father's house he had changed so much that nobody knew who he was; for the three days he had spent on the glass mountain had been three years. Then he made himself known, and his parents fell on his neck with joy; and his heart was so moved that he forgot what the girl had said, and kissed them on both cheeks. And when he had given them the kiss on the right cheek, every thought of the King's daughter vanished from him.

He emptied out his pockets and laid handfuls of the largest jewels on the table. His parents had not the least idea what to do with such riches. Then his father built a magnificent castle, all surrounded by gardens and woods and meadows, as if a prince were going to live in it. And when it was ready his mother said, "I've found a girl for you, and the wedding shall be in three days." And her son was content to do as his parents wished.

The poor King's daughter had stood a long while outside the town waiting for the young man to come back. When evening came she said, "He must have kissed his parents on the right cheek, and has forgotten me."

Her heart was full of sorrow. She wished herself into a lonely little hut in a forest, and would not go back to her father's court. Every evening she went into the town and passed the young man's house; he often saw her, but he no longer knew her.

At length she heard people saying, "The wedding will be tomorrow." Then she said, "I'll try whether I can win his heart back."

On the first day of the wedding celebrations she turned her wishing ring and said, "A dress as bright as the sun." Instantly the dress lay in front of her, and it was as bright as if it had been woven out of real sunbeams.

When all the guests had gathered, she came into the hall. Everybody was amazed at the beautiful dress, and the bride most of all; and as pretty dresses were what she took most delight in, she went to the stranger and asked whether she would sell it to her.

"Not for money," she answered. "But if I may spend the first night outside the door of the room where your betrothed sleeps, I'll give it up to you."

The bride could not overcome her desire, and consented; but she mixed a sleeping draught with the wine her betrothed drank that night, which made him fall into a deep sleep.

When everything had grown quiet, the King's daughter crouched down by the bedroom door, opened it just a little, and called:

	"Drummer, drummer, I pray you hear!
	Have you forgotten you held me dear?
	That on the glass mountain we sat hour by hour?
	That I rescued your life from the witch's power?
	Did you not plight your troth to me?
	Drummer, drummer, hearken to me!"

But it was all in vain; the drummer did not wake; and when morning dawned the King's daughter had to go back again as she had come.

On the second evening she turned her wishing ring and said, "A dress as silvery as the moon." When she appeared at the feast in the dress, which was as soft as moonbeams, it roused the bride's desire again; and the King's daughter gave it to her for permission to spend the second night outside the bedroom door too.

Then in the stillness of the night she called:

	"Drummer, drummer, I pray you hear!
	Have you forgotten you held me dear?
	That on the glass mountain we sat hour by hour?
	That I rescued your life from the witch's power?
	Did you not plight your troth to me?
	Drummer, drummer, hearken to me!"

But the drummer, stupefied by the sleeping draught, could not be roused. Sadly, next morning, she went back to her hut in the forest.

But the people in the house had heard the stranger girl's lament and told the bridegroom about it. They told him too that it was impossible for him to have heard any of it, because the girl he was going to marry had poured a sleeping draught into his wine.

On the third evening the King's daughter turned her wishing ring and said, "A dress glittering like the stars." When she showed herself in it at the feast, the bride was quite beside herself at the splendour of the dress, which far surpassed the others, and said, "I must and will have it."

The girl gave it as she had given the others — for permission to spend the night outside the bridegroom's door.

The bridegroom, though, did not drink the wine that was handed to him before he went to bed, but poured it out behind the bed. And when everything was quiet he heard a sweet voice calling to him:

	"Drummer, drummer, I pray you hear!
	Have you forgotten you held me dear?
	That on the glass mountain we sat hour by hour?
	That I rescued your life from the witch's power?
	Did you not plight your troth to me?
	Drummer, drummer, hearken to me!"

Suddenly his memory came back to him. "Ah," cried he, "how could I have acted so unfaithfully? But the kiss I gave my parents on the right cheek in the joy of my heart — that's to blame for it all; that's what stupefied me."

He sprang up and took the King's daughter by the hand and led her to his parents' bed. "This is my true bride," said he. "If I marry the other, I'll be doing a great wrong."

His parents, when they heard how it had all happened, gave their consent. Then the lights in the hall were lit again, drums and trumpets were brought, friends and relations were invited to come, and the real wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing. The first bride was given the beautiful dresses as compensation, and declared herself satisfied.

The Ear of Corn

In former times, when God himself still walked the earth, the soil was much more fruitful than it is now; then the ears of corn bore not fifty or sixty grains but four or five hundred. In those days the corn grew from the bottom to the very top of the stalk, and the ear was as long as the stalk was.

But men are so made that when they are too well off they no longer value the blessings that come from God, but grow indifferent and careless.

One day a woman was passing a cornfield when her little child, who was running beside her, fell into a puddle and dirtied her frock. At this the mother tore up a handful of the beautiful ears of corn and cleaned the frock with them.

When the Lord, who came by just then, saw it, he was angry, and said, "From now on the stalks of corn shall bear no more ears. Men are no longer worthy of heavenly gifts."

The bystanders who heard this were terrified, and fell on their knees and prayed that he would still leave something on the stalks, even if the people did not deserve it — for the sake of the innocent birds, which would otherwise have to starve.

The Lord, who foresaw their suffering, had pity on them and granted the request. And so the ears were left as they grow now.

The Grave-Mound

A rich farmer was standing in his yard one day, looking over his fields and gardens. The corn was growing up vigorously and the fruit trees were heavily laden. Last year's grain still lay in such immense heaps on the floors that the rafters could hardly bear it. Then he went into the stable, where there were well-fed oxen and fat cows and horses shining like looking glass. And at length he went back into his sitting room and cast a glance at the iron chest his money lay in.

While he was standing there surveying his riches, all at once there came a loud knock close by him. The knock was not at the door of his room but at the door of his heart. It opened, and he heard a voice that said to him, "Have you done good to your family with it? Have you thought about the needs of the poor? Have you shared your bread with the hungry? Have you been contented with what you have, or have you always wanted more?"

His heart was not slow in answering. "I have been hard and pitiless, and have never shown any kindness even to my own family. If a beggar came, I turned my eyes away from him. I haven't troubled myself about God, but have thought only of increasing my wealth. If everything the sky covers had been mine, I still shouldn't have had enough."

When he heard this answer he was greatly alarmed; his knees began to tremble and he had to sit down.

Then there was another knock — but this knock was at the door of his room. It was his neighbour, a poor man with a number of children whom he could no longer feed enough.

"I know," the poor man had thought, "that my neighbour is rich; but he's as hard as he is rich. I don't believe he'll help me — but my children are crying for bread, so I'll risk it."

He said to the rich man, "You don't readily give away anything of yours; but I stand here like a man who feels the water rising over his head. My children are starving. Lend me four measures of corn."

The rich man looked at him a long while; and then the first sunbeam of mercy began to melt away a drop of the ice of greed. "I won't lend you four measures," he answered, "but I'll make you a present of eight — only you must fulfil one condition."

"What am I to do?" said the poor man.

"When I'm dead, you shall keep watch for three nights by my grave."

The peasant was uneasy in his mind at this request; but in the need he was in he would have agreed to anything. So he accepted, and carried the corn home with him.

It seemed as if the rich man had foreseen what was going to happen; for when three days had gone by he suddenly dropped down dead. Nobody knew exactly how it came about, but nobody grieved for him.

When he was buried, the poor man remembered his promise. He would gladly have been released from it; but he thought, "After all, he acted kindly towards me. I've fed my hungry children with his corn; and even if that weren't so, where I've once given my promise I must keep it."

At nightfall he went into the churchyard and sat down on the grave mound. Everything was quiet; only the moon showed above the grave, and now and then an owl flew past and uttered her melancholy cry. When the sun rose, the poor man took himself safely home; and in the same way the second night passed quietly by.

On the evening of the third day he felt a strange uneasiness; it seemed to him that something was going to happen. When he went out he saw a man by the churchyard wall whom he had never seen before. He was no longer young, had scars on his face, and his eyes looked about him sharply and eagerly. He was covered all over with an old cloak, and nothing could be seen of him but his great riding boots.

"What are you looking for here?" the peasant asked. "Aren't you afraid of a lonely churchyard?"

"I'm looking for nothing," he answered, "and I'm afraid of nothing. I'm like the youngster who went out to learn how to shiver and got nothing for his labour — except that he got a King's daughter for a wife, and great wealth with her; only I've stayed poor. I'm nothing but a discharged soldier, and I mean to spend the night here, because I have no other shelter."

"If you're without fear," said the peasant, "stay with me and help me watch over that grave there."

"Keeping watch is a soldier's business," he replied. "Whatever we meet with here, whether it's good or bad, we'll share it between us."

The peasant agreed to that, and they sat down on the grave together.

All was quiet until midnight, when suddenly a shrill whistling was heard in the air, and the two watchers saw the Evil One standing bodily before them.

"Be off, you ragamuffins!" cried he to them. "The man lying in that grave belongs to me; I've come to take him, and if you don't go away I'll wring your necks."

"Sir with the red feather," said the soldier, "you're not my captain; I've no need to obey you, and I haven't yet learned how to be afraid. Go away — we shall stay sitting here."

The Devil thought to himself, "Money is the best thing to get hold of these two vagabonds with." So he began to play a softer tune, and asked quite kindly whether they would not accept a bag of money and go home with it.

"That's worth listening to," answered the soldier, "but one bag of gold won't do for us. If you'll give as much as will go into one of my boots, we'll quit the field for you and go away."

"I haven't as much as that on me," said the Devil, "but I'll fetch it. In the next town lives a money-changer who's a good friend of mine and will readily advance it to me."

When the Devil had vanished, the soldier took his left boot off and said, "We'll soon pull the charcoal-burner's nose for him. Just give me your knife, comrade." He cut the sole off the boot and set it in the long grass near the grave, on the edge of a half-overgrown hole. "That will do," said he. "Now the chimney-sweep may come."

They both sat down and waited; and it was not long before the Devil came back with a small bag of gold in his hand.

"Just pour it in," said the soldier, raising the boot up a little. "But that won't be enough."

The Black One shook out everything in the bag; the gold fell through, and the boot stayed empty.

"Stupid Devil," cried the soldier, "it won't do! Didn't I say so at once? Go back and bring more."

The Devil shook his head, went, and in an hour's time came back with a much larger bag under his arm.

"Now pour it in," cried the soldier, "but I doubt the boot will be full."

The gold clinked as it fell, but the boot stayed empty. The Devil looked into it himself with his burning eyes and satisfied himself that it was true.

"You have shamefully big calves to your legs," cried he, and pulled a sour face.

"Did you think," replied the soldier, "that I had a cloven hoof like yours? Since when have you got so stingy? See that you get more gold together, or our bargain comes to nothing."

The Wicked One went off again. This time he stayed away longer; and when at length he appeared he was panting under the weight of a sack on his shoulders. He emptied it into the boot, which was just as far from being full as before.

He grew furious and was just about to tear the boot out of the soldier's hands, when at that moment the first ray of the rising sun broke out from the sky, and the Evil Spirit fled away with loud shrieks. The poor soul was saved.

The peasant wanted to divide the gold; but the soldier said, "Give what falls to my share to the poor. I'll come with you to your cottage, and together we'll live in rest and peace on what's left, as long as God is pleased to allow it."

Old Rinkrank

There was once a King who had a daughter; and he had a glass mountain made, and said that whoever could cross to the other side of it without falling should have his daughter for a wife.

Now there was a man who loved the King's daughter, and he asked the King whether he might have her.

"Yes," said the King. "If you can cross the mountain without falling, you shall have her."

And the princess said she would go over it with him and would hold him if he was about to fall. So they set out together to go over it; but when they were halfway up the princess slipped and fell, and the glass mountain opened and shut her up inside it, and her betrothed could not see where she had gone, for the mountain closed immediately.

Then he wept and lamented bitterly, and the King was miserable too, and had the mountain broken open where she had been lost, thinking he would be able to get her out again; but they could not find the place she had fallen into.

Meanwhile the King's daughter had fallen a long way down into the earth, into a great cave. An old fellow with a very long grey beard came to meet her, and told her that if she would be his servant and do everything he told her, she might live; and if not, he would kill her.

So she did everything he told her. In the mornings he took his ladder out of his pocket and set it up against the mountain and climbed to the top by it, and then he drew the ladder up after him. The princess had to cook his dinner and make his bed and do all his work; and when he came home again he always brought a heap of gold and silver with him.

When she had lived with him many years and had grown quite old, he called her Mother Mansrot, and she had to call him Old Rinkrank.

Then once, when he was out and she had made his bed and washed his dishes, she shut all the doors and windows fast — all but one little window that the light shone in at, which she left open.

When Old Rinkrank came home he knocked at his door and cried, "Mother Mansrot, open the door for me."

"No," said she, "Old Rinkrank, I won't open the door for you."

Then he said:

	"Here stand I, poor Rinkrank,
	on my seventeen long shanks,
	on my weary, worn-out foot —
	wash my dishes, Mother Mansrot."

"I've washed your dishes already," said she.

Then again he said:

	"Here stand I, poor Rinkrank,
	on my seventeen long shanks,
	on my weary, worn-out foot —
	make me my bed, Mother Mansrot."

"I've made your bed already," said she.

Then again he said:

	"Here stand I, poor Rinkrank,
	on my seventeen long shanks,
	on my weary, worn-out foot —
	open the door, Mother Mansrot."

Then he ran all round his house and saw that the little window was open, and thought, "I'll look in and see what she can be up to, and why she won't open the door for me."

He tried to peep in, but could not get his head through because of his long beard. So he put his beard through the open window first; but just as he had got it through, Mother Mansrot came by and pulled the window down with a cord she had tied to it, and his beard was shut fast in it.

Then he began to cry most piteously, for it hurt him very much, and to beg her to let him go again. But she said not until he gave her the ladder he climbed the mountain with. Then, whether he wanted to or not, he had to tell her where the ladder was.

And she fastened a very long ribbon to the window, and then set up the ladder and climbed the mountain; and when she was at the top of it she opened the window.

She went to her father and told him everything that had happened to her. The King rejoiced greatly; and her betrothed was still there, and they went and dug up the mountain and found Old Rinkrank inside it with all his gold and silver. Then the King had Old Rinkrank put to death, and took all his gold and silver; and the princess married her betrothed, and lived right happily in great magnificence and joy.

The Crystal Ball

There was once an enchantress who had three sons who loved each other like brothers; but the old woman did not trust them, and thought they wanted to steal her power from her.

So she changed the eldest into an eagle, which had to live in the rocky mountains, and was often seen sweeping in great circles in the sky. The second she changed into a whale, which lived in the deep sea, and all that was seen of it was that it sometimes spouted a great jet of water up into the air. Each of them wore his human shape only for two hours a day.

The third son, who was afraid she might change him into a raging wild beast — a bear, perhaps, or a wolf — went away secretly. He had heard that a King's daughter who was under a spell was imprisoned in the Castle of the Golden Sun, and was waiting for deliverance. But those who tried to free her risked their lives; three-and-twenty young men had already died a miserable death, and now only one more might make the attempt, after which no others must come.

And as his heart was without fear, he seized on the idea of seeking out the Castle of the Golden Sun. He had already travelled about a long time without being able to find it, when he came by chance into a great forest and did not know the way out of it.

All at once he saw two giants in the distance, who signalled to him with their hands; and when he came up to them they said, "We're quarrelling about a cap and which of us it's to belong to; and as we're equally strong, neither of us can get the better of the other. Small men are cleverer than we are, so we'll leave the decision to you."

"How can you argue about an old cap?" said the young man.

"You don't know what properties it has. It's a wishing cap; whoever puts it on can wish himself away wherever he likes, and in an instant he's there."

"Give me the cap," said the young man. "I'll go a short distance off, and when I call you, you must run a race, and the cap shall belong to whichever of you gets to me first."

He put it on and went away — and thought of the King's daughter, and forgot the giants, and walked on and on. At length he sighed from the very bottom of his heart and cried, "Ah, if only I were at the Castle of the Golden Sun!" And hardly had the words passed his lips before he was standing on a high mountain in front of the castle gate.

He went in and walked through all the rooms, until in the last one he found the King's daughter. But how shocked he was when he saw her! She had an ash-grey face full of wrinkles, dim eyes and red hair.

"Are you the King's daughter, whose beauty the whole world praises?" cried he.

"Ah," she answered, "this isn't my true shape. Human eyes can only see me in this state of ugliness; but so that you may know what I'm like, look in this mirror — it doesn't let itself be misled; it will show you my image as it truly is."

She put the mirror into his hand, and he saw in it the likeness of the most beautiful girl on earth — and saw too how the tears were rolling down her cheeks with grief.

Then he said, "How can you be set free? I fear no danger."

She said, "Whoever gets the crystal ball and holds it in front of the enchanter will destroy his power with it, and I shall get my true shape back again. Ah," she added, "so many have already gone to their deaths for this, and you are so young; it grieves me that you should meet with such great danger."

"Nothing can keep me from doing it," said he. "But tell me what I must do."

"You shall know everything," said the King's daughter. "When you go down the mountain the castle stands on, a wild bull will be standing below by a spring, and you must fight it. And if you have the luck to kill it, a fiery bird will spring out of it, which carries a burning egg in its body, and in the egg the crystal ball lies like a yolk. The bird won't let the egg fall, though, unless it's forced to; and if it falls to the ground it will flame up and burn everything near it, and melt even ice itself, and the crystal ball with it — and then all your trouble will have been for nothing."

The young man went down to the spring, where the bull snorted and bellowed at him. After a long struggle he plunged his sword into the animal's body, and it fell down.

Instantly a fiery bird rose out of it and was about to fly away; but the young man's brother, the eagle, who was passing between the clouds, swooped down and chased it away to the sea and struck it with his beak until, in its extremity, it let the egg fall.

The egg did not fall into the sea, though, but onto a fisherman's hut standing on the shore; and the hut at once began to smoke and was about to break out in flames. Then waves as high as a house rose in the sea and streamed over the hut and put out the fire. The other brother, the whale, had come swimming to them and had driven the water up on high.

When the fire was out, the young man looked for the egg and happily found it. It had not melted yet; but the shell was broken by being so suddenly cooled with the water, and he could take out the crystal ball unhurt.

When the young man went to the enchanter and held it in front of him, the enchanter said, "My power is destroyed, and from this time on you are King of the Castle of the Golden Sun. And with this you can give your brothers their human shapes back too."

Then the young man hurried to the King's daughter; and when he came into the room she was standing there in the full splendour of her beauty, and joyfully they exchanged rings with each other.

Maid Maleen

There was once a King who had a son who asked for the hand of the daughter of a mighty King. She was called Maid Maleen, and was very beautiful. But as her father wanted to give her to another, the prince was refused; and as the two of them loved each other with all their hearts, they would not give each other up, and Maid Maleen said to her father, "I can and will take no other man for my husband."

Then the King flew into a passion and ordered a dark tower to be built into which no ray of sunlight or moonlight could enter. When it was finished, he said, "In there you shall be shut up for seven years, and then I'll come and see whether your stubborn spirit is broken."

Food and drink for the seven years were carried into the tower, and then she and her waiting-woman were led into it and walled up, and so cut off from the sky and from the earth. There they sat in the darkness and did not know when day or night began. The King's son often went round and round the tower and called their names, but no sound from outside pierced the thick walls. What else could they do but lament and complain?

Meanwhile the time passed; and by the dwindling of the food and drink they knew that the seven years were coming to an end. They thought the moment of their deliverance had come; but no stroke of a hammer was heard, no stone fell out of the wall, and it seemed to Maid Maleen that her father had forgotten her.

As they had food for only a short while longer, and saw a miserable death waiting for them, Maid Maleen said, "We must try our last chance, and see whether we can break through the wall."

She took the bread knife and picked and bored at the mortar round a stone; and when she was tired the waiting-maid took her turn. With great labour they succeeded in getting out one stone, and then a second and a third; and when three days were over, the first ray of light fell into their darkness, and at last the opening was so large that they could look out.

The sky was blue and a fresh breeze played on their faces — but how melancholy everything looked all around! Her father's castle lay in ruins; the town and the villages were burned down, as far as they could see; the fields far and wide were laid waste, and there was not a human being in sight.

When the opening in the wall was large enough for them to slip through, the waiting-maid sprang down first, and then Maid Maleen followed. But where were they to go? The enemy had ravaged the whole kingdom, driven the King out and killed all the people.

They wandered off to look for another country; but nowhere did they find shelter, or a human being to give them a mouthful of bread, and their need was so great that they had to satisfy their hunger with nettles.

When at last, after long journeying, they came into another country, they tried to get work everywhere; but wherever they knocked they were turned away, and nobody would take pity on them. At last they reached a large city and went to the royal palace. There too they were told to go away; but at last the cook said they might stay in the kitchen and be scullions.

Now the son of the King in whose kingdom they were was the very man who had been betrothed to Maid Maleen. His father had chosen another bride for him, whose face was as ugly as her heart was wicked. The wedding was fixed and the bride had already arrived; but because of her great ugliness she shut herself in her room and let nobody see her, and Maid Maleen had to bring her her meals from the kitchen.

When the day came for the bride and the bridegroom to go to church, she was ashamed of her ugliness and afraid that if she showed herself in the streets the people would mock and laugh at her.

So she said to Maid Maleen, "A great piece of luck has come your way. I've sprained my foot and can't walk through the streets properly. You shall put on my wedding clothes and take my place — a greater honour than that you couldn't have."

Maid Maleen, though, refused, and said, "I want no honour that isn't suitable for me."

It was in vain, too, that the bride offered her gold. At last she said angrily, "If you don't obey me, it will cost you your life. I have only to say the word and your head will be lying at your feet."

Then she was forced to obey, and put on the bride's magnificent clothes and all her jewels.

When she came into the royal hall, everybody was amazed at her great beauty, and the King said to his son, "This is the bride I've chosen for you, and whom you must lead to church."

The bridegroom was astonished, and thought, "She's like my Maid Maleen, and I'd believe it was she herself — but she's been shut up in the tower a long while now, or is dead." He took her by the hand and led her to church.

On the way there was a nettle plant, and she said:

	"Oh, nettle plant,
	little nettle plant,
	what are you doing here alone?
	I have known the time
	when I ate you unboiled,
	when I ate you unroasted."

"What are you saying?" asked the King's son.

"Nothing," she replied. "I was only thinking of Maid Maleen."

He was surprised that she knew about her, but said nothing.

When they came to the footbridge into the churchyard, she said:

	"Footbridge, do not break —
	I am not the true bride."

"What are you saying there?" asked the King's son.

"Nothing," she replied. "I was only thinking of Maid Maleen."

"Do you know Maid Maleen?"

"No," she answered, "how should I know her? I've only heard of her."

When they came to the church door, she said once more:

	"Church door, do not break —
	I am not the true bride."

"What are you saying there?" asked he.

"Ah," she answered, "I was only thinking of Maid Maleen."

Then he took out a precious chain and put it round her neck and fastened the clasp. And with that they went into the church, and the priest joined their hands together before the altar and married them.

He led her home; but she did not speak a single word the whole way. When they got back to the royal palace she hurried into the bride's room, took off the magnificent clothes and the jewels, dressed herself in her grey gown and kept nothing but the jewel at her neck that she had been given by the bridegroom.

When night came and the bride was to be led into the prince's room, she let her veil fall over her face so that he should not notice the deception. As soon as everybody had gone away, he said to her, "What did you say to the nettle plant growing by the wayside?"

"Which nettle plant?" said she. "I don't talk to nettle plants."

"If you didn't do it, then you're not the true bride," said he.

So she thought a moment, and said:

	"I must go out unto my maid,
	who keeps my thoughts for me."

She went out and looked for Maid Maleen. "Girl, what did you say to the nettle?"

"I said nothing but this:

	Oh, nettle plant,
	little nettle plant,
	what are you doing here alone?
	I have known the time
	when I ate you unboiled,
	when I ate you unroasted."

The bride ran back into the room and said, "I know now what I said to the nettle" — and repeated the words she had just heard.

"But what did you say to the footbridge when we went over it?" asked the King's son.

"To the footbridge?" she answered. "I don't talk to footbridges."

"Then you're not the true bride."

She said again:

	"I must go out unto my maid,
	who keeps my thoughts for me" —

and ran out and found Maid Maleen. "Girl, what did you say to the footbridge?"

"I said nothing but this:

	Footbridge, do not break —
	I am not the true bride."

"That costs you your life!" cried the bride — but she hurried into the room and said, "I know now what I said to the footbridge" — and repeated the words.

"But what did you say to the church door?"

"To the church door?" she replied. "I don't talk to church doors."

"Then you're not the true bride."

She went out and found Maid Maleen and said, "Girl, what did you say to the church door?"

"I said nothing but this:

	Church door, do not break —
	I am not the true bride."

"That will break your neck for you!" cried the bride, and flew into a terrible passion; but she hurried back into the room and said, "I know now what I said to the church door" — and repeated the words.

"But where is the jewel I gave you at the church door?"

"What jewel?" she answered. "You didn't give me any jewel."

"I put it round your neck myself, and I fastened it myself. If you don't know that, you're not the true bride."

He drew the veil away from her face; and when he saw her immeasurable ugliness he sprang back in terror and said, "How did you come here? Who are you?"

"I'm your betrothed bride; but because I was afraid the people would mock me if they saw me out of doors, I ordered the scullery maid to dress herself in my clothes and go to church instead of me."

"Where is the girl?" said he. "I want to see her. Go and bring her here."

She went out and told the servants that the scullery maid was an impostor, and that they must take her out into the courtyard and strike off her head. The servants seized Maid Maleen and were going to drag her out; but she screamed so loudly for help that the King's son heard her voice and hurried out of his room and ordered them to set the girl free at once.

Lights were brought, and then he saw at her neck the gold chain he had given her at the church door. "You are the true bride," said he, "who went with me to the church. Come with me now to my room."

When they were alone together he said, "On the way to church you named Maid Maleen, who was my betrothed bride. If I could believe it possible, I'd think she was standing in front of me — you're like her in every way."

She answered, "I am Maid Maleen, who for your sake was shut up seven years in the darkness, who suffered hunger and thirst and has lived so long in want and poverty. But today the sun is shining on me once more. I was married to you in the church, and I am your lawful wife."

Then they kissed each other and were happy all the days of their lives. And the false bride was rewarded for what she had done by having her head cut off.

The tower Maid Maleen had been imprisoned in stood for a long time afterwards; and when the children went past it they sang:

	"Kling, klang, gloria,
	who sits within this tower?
	A King's daughter, she sits within;
	a sight of her I cannot win.
	The wall it will not break,
	the stone cannot be pierced.
	Little Hans, with your coat so gay,
	follow me, follow me, fast as you may."

The Boots of Buffalo-Leather

A soldier who is afraid of nothing troubles himself about nothing. One of this kind had been given his discharge; and as he had learned no trade and could earn nothing, he travelled about and begged alms from kind people. He had an old waterproof on his back, and a pair of riding boots of buffalo leather that were still left to him.

One day he was walking he did not know where, straight out into open country, and at length came to a forest. He did not know where he was, but saw a man sitting on the trunk of a felled tree who was well dressed and wore a green shooting coat. The soldier shook hands with him, sat down on the grass beside him and stretched out his legs.

"I see you've got good boots on, and well polished," said he to the huntsman; "but if you had to travel about the way I do, they wouldn't last long. Look at mine — they're buffalo leather, and they've been worn a long time, but in them I can go through thick and thin."

After a while the soldier got up and said, "I can't stay any longer; hunger drives me on. But, Brother Bright-Boots, where does this road lead to?"

"I don't know that myself," answered the huntsman. "I've lost my way in the forest."

"Then you're in the same plight as I am," said the soldier. "Birds of a feather flock together; let's stay together and look for our way."

The huntsman smiled a little, and they walked on further and further, until night fell.

"We're not getting out of this forest," said the soldier, "but over there in the distance I can see a light shining, which will help us to something to eat."

They found a stone house and knocked at the door, and an old woman opened it.

"We're looking for lodging for the night," said the soldier, "and some lining for our stomachs, for mine is as empty as an old knapsack."

"You can't stay here," answered the old woman. "This is a robbers' house, and you'd do wisely to get away before they come home, or you're lost."

"It won't be as bad as that," answered the soldier. "I haven't had a mouthful for two days, and whether I'm murdered here or die of hunger in the forest is all the same to me. I'm going in."

The huntsman would not follow, but the soldier drew him in with him by the sleeve. "Come, my dear brother, we shan't come to our end as quickly as that."

The old woman took pity on them and said, "Creep in here behind the stove, and if they leave anything I'll give it to you on the sly when they're asleep."

Hardly were they in the corner before twelve robbers came bursting in, sat down at the table, which was already laid, and vehemently demanded food. The old woman brought in some great dishes of roast meat, and the robbers thoroughly enjoyed it.

When the smell of the food reached the soldier's nostrils he said to the huntsman, "I can't hold out any longer. I'm going to sit down at the table and eat with them."

"You'll bring us to destruction," said the huntsman, and held him back by the arm. But the soldier began to cough loudly.

When the robbers heard that, they threw down their knives and forks and leapt up and found the two of them behind the stove.

"Aha, gentlemen, so you're in the corner?" cried they. "What are you doing here? Have you been sent as spies? Wait a while, and you'll learn how to fly on a dry bough."

"But do be civil," said the soldier. "I'm hungry. Give me something to eat, and then you can do what you like with me."

The robbers were astonished, and the captain said, "I see you have no fear. Well, you shall have some food; but after that you must die."

"We'll see," said the soldier — and sat down at the table and began to cut away valiantly at the roast meat. "Brother Bright-Boots, come and eat," he called to the huntsman. "You must be as hungry as I am, and you can't have better roast meat at home." But the huntsman would not eat.

The robbers looked at the soldier in astonishment and said, "The rascal stands on no ceremony."

After a while he said, "I've had enough food; now get me something good to drink."

The captain was in the mood to humour him in this too, and called to the old woman, "Bring a bottle out of the cellar, and mind it's the best."

The soldier drew the cork out with a loud pop, and then went with the bottle to the huntsman and said, "Pay attention, brother, and you'll see something that will surprise you. I'm going to drink the health of the whole clan."

Then he brandished the bottle over the robbers' heads and cried, "Long life to you all — but with your mouths open and your right hands lifted up." And then he drank a hearty draught.

Hardly were the words said before they all sat motionless as if they had been made of stone, with their mouths open and their right hands stretched up in the air.

The huntsman said to the soldier, "I see you know tricks of another kind. But come now, let's go home."

"Oho, my dear brother, that would be marching away far too soon. We've beaten the enemy, and we must take the booty first. Those men are sitting fast and opening their mouths in astonishment, but they won't be allowed to move until I let them. Come, eat and drink."

The old woman had to bring another bottle of the best wine, and the soldier would not stir until he had eaten enough to last three days.

At last, when day came, he said, "Now it's time to strike our tents; and so that our march may be a short one, the old woman shall show us the nearest way to the town."

When they had got there, he went to his old comrades and said, "Out in the forest I've found a nest full of gallows birds; come with me and we'll take it." The soldier led them; and he said to the huntsman, "You must come back with me too, to see how they shake when we seize them by the feet."

He placed the men round the robbers, and then took the bottle and drank a mouthful and brandished it over them and cried, "Live again!" Instantly they all got the power of movement back — but were thrown down and bound hand and foot with cords.

Then the soldier ordered them to be thrown into a cart as if they had been so many sacks, and said, "Now drive them straight to prison."

The huntsman, though, took one of the men aside and gave him another errand besides.

"Brother Bright-Boots," said the soldier, "we've safely routed the enemy and been well fed; now we'll walk quietly along behind them, like stragglers."

When they got near the town, the soldier saw a crowd of people pouring out through the town gate, raising loud cries of joy and waving green boughs in the air. Then he saw that the whole bodyguard was coming up.

"What can this mean?" said he to the huntsman.

"Don't you know," he replied, "that the King has been absent from his kingdom a long time, and that today he's coming back, and everybody is going out to meet him?"

"But where's the King?" said the soldier. "I don't see him."

"Here he is," answered the huntsman. "I am the King, and I sent word of my arrival." Then he opened his hunting coat and his royal clothes could be seen.

The soldier was alarmed and fell on his knees and begged him to forgive him for having, in his ignorance, treated him as an equal and spoken to him by such a name.

But the King shook hands with him and said, "You're a brave soldier and you've saved my life. You shall never be in want again; I'll take care of you. And if you ever want to eat a piece of roast meat as good as the one in the robbers' house, come to the royal kitchen. But if you want to drink a health, you must ask my permission first."

The Golden Key

In the winter, when deep snow lay on the ground, a poor boy had to go out on a sledge to fetch wood. When he had gathered it together and packed it, he was so frozen with cold that he did not want to go home at once, but to light a fire and warm himself a little.

So he scraped the snow away; and as he was clearing the ground like this, he found a tiny golden key. Then he thought that where the key was, the lock must be too; and he dug in the ground and found an iron chest.

"If only the key fits it!" thought he. "No doubt there are precious things in that little box."

He looked, but there was no keyhole. At last he found one, but so small that it was hardly visible. He tried the key, and it fitted exactly. Then he turned it once round — and now we must wait until he has quite unlocked it and opened the lid, and then we shall learn what wonderful things were lying in that box.

St. Joseph in the Forest

There was once a mother who had three daughters. The eldest was rude and wicked, the second much better, though she had her faults; but the youngest was a pious, good child. Their mother, though, was so strange that it was the eldest daughter she loved most, and she could not bear the youngest.

For this reason she often sent the poor girl out into the great forest, to be rid of her, thinking she would lose herself and never come back. But the guardian angel that every good child has did not desert her, and always brought her back onto the right path again.

Once, though, the guardian angel behaved as if he were not there, and the child could not find her way out of the forest again. She walked on and on until evening came, and then she saw a tiny light burning in the distance. She ran up to it at once and came to a little hut.

She knocked; the door opened, and she came to a second door and knocked again. An old man with a snow-white beard, who looked venerable, opened it for her — and he was none other than St. Joseph.

He said quite kindly, "Come in, dear child, and sit yourself on my little chair by the fire and warm yourself. I'll fetch you clear water if you're thirsty; but here in the forest I have nothing for you to eat but a couple of little roots, which you must scrape and boil first."

St. Joseph gave her the roots. The girl scraped them clean, and then brought out a piece of pancake and the bread her mother had given her to take with her, and mixed it all together in a pan and cooked herself a thick soup.

When it was ready, St. Joseph said, "I'm so hungry; give me some of your food."

The child was quite willing, and gave him more than she kept for herself; but God's blessing was with her, so that she had enough.

When they had eaten, St. Joseph said, "Now we'll go to bed. I have only one bed, though; lie down in it. I'll lie on the ground, on the straw."

"No," answered she, "stay in your own bed; the straw is soft enough for me."

But St. Joseph took the child in his arms and carried her to the little bed; and there she said her prayers and fell asleep.

Next morning when she woke she wanted to say good morning to St. Joseph, but she did not see him. So she got up and looked for him, but could not find him anywhere. And at last she noticed behind the door a bag of money, so heavy that she could only just carry it; and on it was written that it was for the child who had slept there that night.

So she took the bag and bounded away with it and got safely home to her mother; and as she gave her mother all the money, her mother could not help being satisfied with her.

The next day the second child took a fancy to go into the forest too. Her mother gave her a much larger piece of pancake and bread. It went with her just as it had with the first child. In the evening she came to St. Joseph's little hut, and he gave her roots for a thick soup.

When it was ready he said to her too, "I'm so hungry; give me some of your food."

Then the child said, "You may have your share."

Afterwards, when St. Joseph offered her his bed and wanted to lie on the straw, she replied, "No, lie down in the bed; there's plenty of room for both of us." St. Joseph took her in his arms and put her in the bed, and laid himself down on the straw.

In the morning, when the child woke and looked for St. Joseph, he had vanished; but behind the door she found a little sack of money about as long as a hand, and on it was written that it was for the child who had slept there the night before. So she took the little bag and ran home with it and took it to her mother — but she secretly kept two pieces for herself.

By this time the eldest daughter had grown curious, and the next morning she insisted on going out into the forest too. Her mother gave her pancakes to take — as many as she wanted — and bread and cheese as well.

In the evening she found St. Joseph in his little hut, just as the other two had. When the soup was ready and St. Joseph said, "I'm so hungry; give me some of your food," the girl answered, "Wait until I've had enough; then if there's anything left you shall have it."

She ate nearly all of it, though, and St. Joseph had to scrape the dish.

Afterwards the good old man offered her his bed and wanted to lie on the straw. She took it without any objection, lay down in the little bed, and left the hard straw to the white-haired man.

Next morning when she woke, St. Joseph was nowhere to be found; but she did not trouble herself about that. She looked behind the door for a money bag. She thought something was lying on the ground; but as she could not quite make out what it was, she stooped down and examined it closely — and it stayed hanging to her nose; and when she straightened up she saw to her horror that it was a second nose, hanging fast to her own.

Then she began to scream and howl; but that did no good. She had to see it always in front of her, for it stuck out so far. So she ran out and screamed without stopping, until she met St. Joseph; and she fell at his feet and begged until, out of pity, he took the nose off her again, and even gave her two farthings.

When she got home her mother was standing in front of the door, and asked, "What were you given?"

Then she lied and said, "A great bag of money — but I lost it on the way."

"Lost it!" cried her mother. "Oh, but we'll soon find it again" — and took her by the hand and wanted to go and look for it with her.

At first she began to cry and did not want to go; but at last she went. On the way, though, so many lizards and snakes came at the two of them that they did not know how to save themselves. At last they stung the wicked child to death; and they stung the mother in the foot, because she had not brought her up better.

The Twelve Apostles

Three hundred years before the birth of the Lord Christ, there lived a mother who had twelve sons, but was so poor and needy that she no longer knew how she was to keep them alive at all. She prayed to God daily that he would grant that all her sons might be on the earth together with the Redeemer who was promised.

When her need grew still greater, she sent them out one after another into the world to look for bread for her.

The eldest was called Peter; and he went out and had already walked a long way, a whole day's journey, when he came into a great forest. He looked for a way out but could find none, and went further and further astray; and at the same time he felt such great hunger that he could hardly stand. At length he grew so weak that he had to lie down, and he believed death was at hand.

Suddenly there stood beside him a small boy who shone with brightness, and was as beautiful and kind as an angel. The child clapped his little hands together until Peter had to look up and saw him.

Then the child said, "Why are you sitting there in such trouble?"

"Alas," answered Peter, "I'm going about the world looking for bread, so that I may yet see the dear Saviour who is promised. That's my greatest desire."

The child said, "Come with me, and your wish shall be fulfilled."

He took poor Peter by the hand and led him between some cliffs to a great cavern. When they went in, everything was shining with gold and silver and crystal; and in the middle of it twelve cradles were standing side by side.

Then the little angel said, "Lie down in the first and sleep a while; I'll rock you."

Peter did so, and the angel sang to him and rocked him until he was asleep. And when he was asleep the second brother came too, guided there by his guardian angel, and was rocked to sleep like the first; and so came the others one after another, until all twelve lay there sleeping in the golden cradles.

They slept, though, for three hundred years, until the night when the Saviour of the world was born. Then they woke, and were with him on earth, and were called the twelve apostles.

The Rose

There was once a poor woman who had two children. The youngest had to go into the forest every day to fetch wood.

Once, when she had gone a long way to look for it, a little child who was quite strong came and helped her industriously to pick up the wood and carry it home — and then, before a moment had passed, the strange child disappeared.

The child told her mother about this, but at first she would not believe it. At length she brought a rose home, and told her mother that the beautiful child had given her this rose, and had told her that when it was in full bloom he would come back. Her mother put the rose in water.

One morning her child could not get out of bed. Her mother went to the bed and found her dead — but she lay looking very happy. And on that same morning the rose was in full bloom.

Poverty and Humility Lead to Heaven

There was once a King's son who went out into the world, and he was full of thought and sad. He looked at the sky, which was so beautifully pure and blue, and then he sighed and said, "How well everything must be with a man up there in heaven."

Then he saw a poor grey-haired man coming along the road towards him; and he spoke to him and asked, "How can I get to heaven?"

The man answered, "By poverty and humility. Put on my ragged clothes, wander about the world for seven years and get to know what misery is. Take no money; but if you're hungry, ask compassionate hearts for a bit of bread. That way you'll reach heaven."

So the King's son took off his magnificent coat and wore the beggar's clothes in its place, and went out into the wide world and suffered great misery. He took nothing but a little food, and said nothing, but prayed to the Lord to take him into his heaven.

When the seven years were over he came back to his father's palace, but nobody recognised him. He said to the servants, "Go and tell my parents that I've come back." But the servants did not believe it, and laughed and left him standing there.

Then he said, "Go and tell my brothers, so that they'll come down; I should so much like to see them again." The servants would not do that either; but at last one of them went and told the King's children — and they did not believe it, and did not trouble themselves about it.

Then he wrote a letter to his mother describing all his misery — but he did not say that he was her son. So the Queen, out of pity, had a place under the stairs assigned to him, and food taken to him every day by two servants.

But one of them was ill-natured and said, "Why should the beggar have the good food?" — and kept it for himself, or gave it to the dogs, and took the weak, wasted beggar nothing but water. The other, though, was honest, and took the beggar what was sent to him. It was little, but he could live on it for a while; and all the time he was quite patient, though he grew steadily weaker.

But as his illness grew worse he asked to receive the last sacrament. And when the host was raised down below, all the bells in the town and the country round began to ring.

After mass the priest went to the poor man under the stairs — and there he lay dead. In one hand he had a rose, in the other a lily, and beside him lay a paper with his history written in it.

When he was buried, a rose grew on one side of his grave and a lily on the other.

God’s Food

There were once two sisters, one of whom had no children and was rich, and the other had five and was a widow, and was so poor that she no longer had enough food to feed herself and her children.

In her need she went to her sister and said, "My children and I are suffering the greatest hunger. You're rich; give me a mouthful of bread."

The very rich sister was as hard as a stone, and said, "I have nothing in the house myself" — and drove the poor creature away with harsh words.

Some time later the rich sister's husband came home and was just going to cut himself a piece of bread; but when he made the first cut into the loaf, red blood flowed out.

When his wife saw that she was terrified and told him what had happened. He hurried away to help the widow and her children; but when he came into her room he found her praying. She had her two youngest children in her arms, and the three eldest were lying dead.

He offered her food, but she answered, "For earthly food we have no more desire. God has already satisfied the hunger of three of us, and he will hear our prayers too."

Hardly had she spoken these words before the two little ones drew their last breath; whereupon her heart broke and she sank down dead.

The Three Green Twigs

There was once a hermit who lived in a forest at the foot of a mountain, and passed his time in prayer and good works; and every evening he carried two pails of water up the mountain, to the glory of God. Many an animal drank of it, and many a plant was refreshed by it; for up on the heights a strong wind blew continually, which dried the air and the ground, and the wild birds that dread mankind wheel about there and search with their sharp eyes for a drink.

And because the hermit was so pious, an angel of God, visible to his eyes, went up with him and counted his steps; and when the work was finished, brought him his food, just as the prophet of old was fed by the raven at God's command.

When in his piety the hermit had already reached a great age, it happened that he once saw from a distance a poor sinner being taken to the gallows. He said carelessly to himself, "There — that one is getting what he deserves."

In the evening, when he was carrying the water up the mountain, the angel who usually went with him did not appear, and brought him no food either. Then he was terrified, and searched his heart and tried to think how he could have sinned, that God should be so angry; but he could not find it out. So he neither ate nor drank, but threw himself down on the ground and prayed day and night.

And as he was weeping bitterly in the forest one day, he heard a little bird singing beautifully and delightfully; and then he was more troubled still, and said, "How joyfully you sing! The Lord isn't angry with you. Ah, if only you could tell me how I've offended him, so that I could do penance, and then my heart would be glad again too."

Then the bird began to speak and said, "You have done an injustice, in that you condemned a poor sinner who was being led to the gallows; and for that the Lord is angry with you. He alone sits in judgement. But if you'll do penance and repent your sins, he'll forgive you."

Then the angel stood beside him with a dry branch in his hand and said, "You shall carry this dry branch until three green twigs sprout out of it; and at night, when you sleep, you shall lay it under your head. You shall beg your bread from door to door, and not stay more than one night in the same house. That is the penance the Lord lays on you."

Then the hermit took the piece of wood and went back into the world, which he had not seen for so long. He ate and drank nothing but what he was given at the doors; but many of his requests were not listened to, and many doors stayed shut to him, so that he often did not get a crumb of bread.

Once, when he had gone from door to door from morning till night and nobody had given him anything and nobody would shelter him for the night, he went out into a forest and at last found a cave that somebody had made, with an old woman sitting in it.

Then he said, "Good woman, keep me in your house for this one night."

But she said, "No, I daren't, even if I wanted to. I have three sons who are wicked and wild; if they come home from their robbing and find you, they'd kill us both."

The hermit said, "Let me stay; they'll do no harm to you or to me." And the woman was compassionate and let herself be persuaded.

So the man lay down under the stairs and put the piece of wood under his head. When the old woman saw him do that she asked the reason for it; and he told her that he carried the piece of wood about with him for a penance and used it at night for a pillow, and that he had offended the Lord because, when he saw a poor sinner on the way to the gallows, he had said that he was getting what he deserved.
